[Page 215]

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate, and from the two of them spread forth many men and women.﴾

The address "O mankind" (*ya ayyuha al-nas*) comes so that it includes the whole community of the call, those who hear the Qur'an on that day and those who will come later in time. The pronoun of address in His words "who created you" (*khalaqakum*) refers to the people addressed by the Qur'an. That is, it is not restricted to the believers, since the non-believers at that time were the disbelieving Arabs. They were the first to receive the call of Islam before all of humanity, because the address came in their language, and they were the ones commanded to convey it to the rest of the nations. The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote his letters to the Romans, the Persians and Egypt in Arabic so that they could be translated for them into their own languages. Since what follows this call includes what people are commanded to do, both believers and disbelievers, all people are addressed. God calls them to remember that their origin is one, saying: ﴿Fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾. This is a call in which the connection between the unity of the human species and the unity of belief becomes evident. The purpose of "fear" (*taqwa*) in "fear your Lord" is to guard against His wrath and to observe His rights, and that is the right of His unity, acknowledging Him with the attributes of perfection, and declaring Him exempt from partners in existence, actions and attributes.

In this connection there is an excellent opening (*bara'at istihlal*) suited to the main aims contained in the surah, so it stands as a preface (*dibaja*).

He used "your Lord" (*rabbakum*) rather than the proper name, because the meaning of "Lord" (*rabb*) contains what moves the servants to be eager in believing in His oneness. The *rabb* is the owner who nurtures his property, that is, who manages its affairs. The use of the word "Lord" with the possessive also serves to indicate that they are owed the fear of Him that is due, and indicates that there is a bond between the Lord and those addressed whose neglect would be folly and error. As for the fear in His words ﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾, the main purpose of it is the fear of the believer in being careless about the rights of kin and of orphans, both women and men. Then the relative pronoun "who created you" (*alladhi khalaqakum*) is used to hint at the reason for the construction of the statement, because He who created humankind deserves to be feared.

The joining of "created you" with the clause ﴿from a single soul﴾ is an incorporation (*idmaj*) that calls attention to the wonder of this creation and its worthiness of reflection. In the verse there is also an allusion (*talwih*) to the polytheists, that they have more right to follow the call of Islam, since people are the sons of one father. This religion calls all people to follow it and does not single out any nation or lineage, so it is worthy of being the religion of all humanity, unlike the other laws, which explicitly declare that they are restricted to specific nations. In the verse there is also an indirect hint (*ta'rid*) to the polytheists that the people most entitled to follow him is Muhammad (ﷺ), because he is of their kin. In the verse there is also a preparation for the rulings in this surah that are based on lineage and kinship.

"The single soul" (*al-nafs al-wahida*) is Adam. "Its mate" (*al-zawj*) is Eve, since Eve was brought forth from Adam from his rib, as the apparent meaning of His words "from it" indicates.

The "min" (*min*) in "from it" is partitive (*tab'idiyya*). The meaning of partition is that Eve was created from a part of Adam. It has been said: from the remainder of the clay from which Adam was created. And it has been said: a piece was separated from his rib, and this is the apparent meaning of the hadith reported in the two Sahihs (*al-Sahihayn*).

As for the one who said that the meaning is "and created its mate from its kind," he has brought nothing of substance, because that is not specific to the human species, since the female of every species is of its own species.

His words "and created from it its mate" are joined to "created you from a single soul," so it is a second relative clause (*sila thaniya*). His words "and spread forth from the two of them" are a third relative clause, because the One who creates this wondrous creation deserves to be feared, and because the meanings of these clauses contain an increased confirmation of the connection of people with one another, since all come from one origin. Although their creation came about only from a pair, each origin among their origins traces back to an origin above it.

From the mention of these clauses there results a detailed explanation of how God created people from a single soul. The discourse in this arrangement comes in fulfilment of the requirement of the situation which calls for the use of the relative pronoun, and the requirement of the situation which calls for detailing the state of this wondrous creation. If this style were changed, and the detailed form were given without prior summary, so that it said "the One who created you from a single soul and spread forth from it many men and women," the indication of the wondrous state would be lost. It is reported in a hadith: "Eve was created from a rib of Adam." Therefore the particle "min" in His words "and created from it" is for the starting point (*li'l-ibtida'*), meaning that He brought forth the creation of Eve from the rib of Adam. "Zawj" here is meant to refer to the first female from whom humankind multiplied, who is Eve. She was called "zawj" because a man is alone, and when he takes a woman as a wife, the two become a pair (*zawj*) in a house, so each of them is a pair for the other in this respect. Although the original usage of the word *zawj* is to apply to the two together, the application of *zawj* to each of the man and the woman who contract marriage is a loose usage that has become a customary literal meaning. For this reason the word applies equally to the man and the woman, since it is among descriptive nouns that are invariable in form (*jamid*), so one does not say *zawja* for a woman, and it is not heard in eloquent speech. For this reason some lexicographers counted it as a solecism (*lahn*). Al-Asma'i used to deny it most strongly. It was said to him: Dhu al-Rumma says:

"Is it a wife in the city, or a dispute? I see you staying in Basra this year because of her."

He said: Dhu al-Rumma indeed used to eat salted food and herbs in the shops of the grocers, meaning that he was a muwallad (a later, non-classical Arabic speaker).

And al-Farazdaq said:

"Whoever seeks to corrupt my wife
is like one who approaches a lion of the thicket to steal from it."

This usage became widespread in the speech of the jurists, who intended by it to distinguish between the man and the woman when mentioning rulings, and this is a good distinction. It occurred earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell you and your spouse in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqara: 35], in Surat al-Baqara.

His words "and created from it its mate" comprised the lesson of this wondrous creation whose origin is one, yet which emerges with varied forms and characteristics. There is also the favour upon males in the creation of women for them, and the favour upon women in the creation of men for them. Then He favoured the species with the blessing of offspring in His words ﴿and spread forth from the two of them many men and women﴾, together with what there is in that of a lesson from this wondrous formation.

"Al-bath" (*al-bath*) means spreading out and scattering things in great numbers. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the day when people will be like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'a: 4].

He described "men" (*rijal*), which is plural, with "kathir" (*kathir*), which is singular, because "kathir" applies equally to the singular and the plural. This was mentioned earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a prophet has fought, with whom were many devoted men (*ribbiyyun kathir*)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146], in Surat Al 'Imran. He dispensed with describing the women with "kathir" because the description of the men with it indicates them, together with what the verb "spread forth" (*bath*) implies of multiplicity.

﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Surely God is ever watching over you.﴾

This is the beginning of the legislation that is the purpose of the surah. The verb "fear" (*ittaqu*) is repeated because this fear is what the Muslims specifically are commanded to observe, since among them there remains a remnant of the customs of the Jahiliyya which they are not aware of, namely, neglect of the rights of kin and orphans.

He brought the proper name God here, without a pronoun referring to "your Lord," in order to instil awe into the hearts of the listeners, because the context is one of legislation, to which the choice of awe is suited, unlike the context of His words "fear your Lord," which is a context of encouragement. The meaning of "tasa'alun bihi" (*tasa'alun bihi*) is that some of you ask others by Him in oaths, so asking by Him indicates the utmost of greatness, so how could you not fear Him?

The majority of readers read *tasa'alun* with a doubled sin, through assimilation of the second *ta'* which is the *ta'* of reciprocity (*ta' al-tafa'ul*) into the sin, because of the closeness of their articulation points and the unity of their quality, which is whispering (*hams*). Hamza, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *tasa'alun* with a single sin, on the basis that the *ta'* of the reflexive form (*ta' al-iftial*) was deleted for lightness.

The majority read "wal-arham" (*wal-arham*) in the accusative, coordinated with the name of God. Hamza read it in the genitive, coordinated with the pronoun in the genitive. According to the majority reading, "al-arham" is commanded to be feared in the verbal-noun sense, that is, the guarding of them, and this is by omission of a modifier, meaning the guarding of their rights, so it is from the use of a homonym in both its meanings. On this reading, the verse is the beginning of legislation, and it is among what His words, exalted is He, ﴿and created from it its mate﴾ point to. On Hamza's reading, it is an exaltation of the status of the wombs, that is, those by which some of you ask others, and this is the saying of the Arabs: "I adjure you by God and by the womb (*al-rahim*)." As is reported in the Sahih: that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he recited to 'Utba ibn Rabi'a the surah of Fussilat until he reached ﴿But if they turn away, say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13], 'Utba was seized with fear and said: "I adjure you by God and by the womb." This is the apparent sense of this report, although the majority of grammarians rejected it, considering it grave to coordinate a noun with a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition. Al-Mubarrad even said: "If an imam recited with this reading, I would take off my sandal and leave the prayer." This is from narrowness of outlook and conceit that Arabic is confined to what he knows. Ibn Malik was indeed correct in permitting coordination with the genitive pronoun without repeating the preposition. Thus the verse is an allusion to the customs of the Jahiliyya, since they ask one another by the womb and the ties of kinship, then neglect its rights and do not keep its ties, and they wrong the orphans among their brothers and paternal cousins, so their deeds contradicted their words. Also, they harmed the Prophet (ﷺ) and wronged him, though he is of their kin and the most entitled of people to their ties, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawba: 128], and He said: ﴿God certainly conferred a favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from among themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164], and He said: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. On Hamza's reading, the meaning of the verse is a completion of the meaning of the verse before it.

﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not consume their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin.﴾

The connection of this command to what precedes it is that it is one of the branches of fear of God concerning the rights of kinship, because those who dispose of orphans' property are, in most cases, their own relatives. Or it is one of the branches of fear of God, by whom they ask one another, "and [by] the kinship ties," so they gave the kinship ties a share of what made them swear by them as they swear by God. Something of this nature deserves that its ties and bonds be observed, yet they did not heed that. This is among what His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And He spread from the two of them many men and women﴾ [4:1] alludes to.

[Page 219]

Ita' (giving; the act of giving) in its literal sense is physically pushing and handing over. It is also applied to specifying a thing for something and making it a right of that thing, like the use of "giving" in His saying, ﴿Indeed We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ [108:1], and in the hadith: "A man whom God has given wealth and empowered him to spend it in the right way, and a man whom God has given wisdom, and he judges by it."

Yatama is the plural of yatim and also the plural of yatima. When yatima is pluralized, the form is fa'a'il, its original form being يتائم (yatā'im). A metathesis occurred in it, so they said يتامئ (yatāmi'), then they lightened the hamza so it became an alif, and the mim was vocalized with a fatha. When yatim is pluralized, it is either a plural of a plural, being first pluralized as يتمى (yatmā), as they said أسير (asīr) and أسرى (asrā), then pluralized as يتامى (yatāmā), like أسارى (asārā) with a fatha on the hamza; or it is the plural of fa'il on the pattern fa'a'il, because it became a noun, like أفيل (afīl) and أفائل (afā'il), and then the metathesis mentioned above was applied to it. The Arabs have indeed used the plural of yatima as يتائم (yatā'im), and the plural of fa'il as fa'a'il, in the verse of Bishr al-Najdi:

"Are these the ruins of beauty in al-Biraq of the orphans?
Peace upon your ancient ruins."

The derivation of yatim is from solitude, and from it comes the phrase "the unique pearl" (al-durra al-yatima), meaning the one that stands alone in its beauty. Its verb is of the pattern ḍaraba and is intransitive. The Arabs applied it to one whose father has died while he was young, as if he remained alone, with no one to defend him. The Arabs did not count the death of the mother in applying the description of yatim, since a child does not lack a guardian (kāfila), but he is deprived, by the death of his father, of one who defends him and provides for him. It has become clear from what they took into account in the derivation that one who reaches the status of men does not deserve to be called yatim, since he has already reached the point of defending himself. This is the application of the term yatim by the Shari'a, and the original is the absence of transfer (of meaning).

It has been said: in the language, it is one whose father has died, even if he is an adult, or one who was young and grew up. I do not think this usage is correct. The word yatama here is intended to include males and females, and the masculine pronoun predominated in His saying "their property."

The apparent meaning of the verse is a command to hand over property to the orphan. In the ruling of the Shari'a, it is not permitted to hand property to him as long as the name of yatim applies to him, since yatim is specific to one who has not reached maturity, and he is then not fit to manage his property. Therefore, the verse must be interpreted either by interpreting the word ītā' or by interpreting yatim. So we may interpret "give" (ātū) not in the sense of "hand over." This is supported by what is reported from Jabir ibn Zayd, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning those who did not give inheritance to the young in the presence of the adults in the pre-Islamic era." Then "give" (ātū) would mean "specify for them their rights," and this command and what is mentioned after it would be establishments of rulings, not an emphasis of some of them on others or a restriction of some of them by others.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "What is meant by giving them their property is that the guardians, the executors, and the wicked rulers and their judges should not covet it, and should withhold their snatching hands from it, until the orphans come of age and receive it intact." This is an interpretation of giving by one of its necessary consequences, which is the preservation on which giving depends, as a kināya (metonymy) by mentioning the necessary consequence while meaning what it necessarily entails; or it is a majāz (figurative usage) by its outcome, since preservation ends in giving. On this basis, it is the meaning of His saying, ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾. On both of these interpretations, what is meant here is a command to preserve the rights of orphans from being wasted, not to hand the property over to them. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, since it will come in His saying ﴿And test the orphans﴾ [4:6], and so on.

We may also interpret yatama as referring to those who have passed the limit of orphanhood, and "giving" would remain in the sense of handing over. The expression of them as "orphans" would then be to indicate the obligation to hand their property to them immediately upon their exit from the status of yatim. Or it may remain as it is, and this application would be restricted by His later saying: ﴿Until, when they reach marriageable age, if you perceive in them maturity, then hand over to them their property﴾ [4:6].

Some people said: yatim is applied to the young and the old, because it is derived from the meaning of solitude, i.e., his being alone away from his father. It is not hidden that this view is a rigid adherence to the assumption that solitude is literal, whereas the word was only set for figurative solitude, which is the absence of the father, treated as if the child were left alone, though he is not truly alone, for he has a mother and a people.

It was said: this verse was revealed concerning a man of the Ghatafan who had a nephew in his care. When the boy reached maturity, he demanded his property, but his uncle refused him. So this verse was revealed, and he returned the property to his nephew. On this view, this is what is meant by His saying, ﴿And do not consume their property﴾.

His saying, ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾, means: do not take the bad and give the good. The discussion of the transitivity of the verb tabaddala and its counterparts has passed at His saying, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqara, ﴿He said: Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ [2:61]. According to what was established there, it is necessary that the bad be what is taken and the good be what is left.

The bad (al-khabīth) and the good (al-ṭayyib) are intended here in their moral sense, not their physical sense, and both are metaphors. The bad is the blameworthy or the forbidden, and the good is its opposite, which is the lawful. This was mentioned at His saying, ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on earth, lawful and good﴾ [2:168] in al-Baqara. The meaning is: do not earn forbidden property and leave lawful property. That is, if you were concerned with producing and multiplying your property through work and trade, you would have from it what suffices you without the forbidden. So what is prohibited here is the opposite of what was commanded earlier, as an emphasis of the command. But the prohibition makes clear the abomination of failing to comply with the command. This view indicates that the substitution is figurative, and the bad and the good are likewise. The verse should not be taken to mean anything other than this meaning and this usage. What al-Suddi reported contradicts this meaning, and it is not acceptable.

His saying, ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾, is a third prohibition against taking the property of orphans and adding it to the property of their guardians. Thus the verse consists of one command and two prohibitions: they were commanded not to withhold from the orphans their inheritances; then they were forbidden to acquire what is unlawful; then they were forbidden to seize their property or part of it. The last prohibition and command are emphases of the first command.

The word "consume" (akl) is a metaphor for benefiting in a way that prevents others from benefiting, which is complete ownership, because consuming is the strongest form of appropriating a thing, since it secures it within the body, and there is no hope of its return. The verb ta'kulū (consume) is construed as implying "add" (taḍummū), therefore it is followed by "to" (ilā), meaning: do not consume their property by adding it to your property.

The clause "to your property" is not the focus of the prohibition. Rather, the prohibition falls on consuming their property absolutely, whether or not the consumer has property to which he adds his orphan's property. But since most guardians have their own property, and they intend by consuming the orphans' property to increase their own wealth, the verse mentions this restriction out of regard for what is most common. It is also included in the prohibition because of the reproach it contains against them, since they consume the rights of others while they are wealthy. Moreover, the addition is not a restriction, but rather stands in the place of two prohibitions. For this reason it was narrated that after this verse the Muslims avoided mixing with the property of orphans, so the verse of al-Baqara was revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [2:220]. They understood that adding the property of the orphan to the property of the guardian is forbidden, while knowing that this is not covered by the prohibition on consuming, but by the prohibition on adding. In the understanding of the Arabs, these are two prohibitions. It is not a prohibition on the rich consuming orphans' property, such that the prohibition on the poor would be established by analogy and not by the implicit meaning of agreement (mafhūm al-muwāfaqa), since the lesser is not suitable to be an implicit meaning of agreement.

Al-ḥūb, with a ḍamma on the ḥā', is the dialect of the Ḥijāz, and with a fatḥa is the dialect of Tamīm. It was said: it is Abyssinian. Its meaning is sin. The clause is a justification for the prohibition, because of the position of inna in it. That is, God has forbidden you to consume their property because it is a great sin. Since inna in such a position is merely for emphasis to restrict the justification, he emphasized the predicate with the additional kāna.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry what seems good to you of women, two or three or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one, or what your right hands possess. That is more suitable, that you may not deviate.﴾

The inclusion of the word "orphans" (al-yatama) in this verse indicates its connection to the preceding verse. However, the command to marry women and their number as the answer to the condition of fearing injustice toward orphans is something whose wisdom was hidden from many of the scholars of the early generations of the Ummah, since no clear connection (i.e., necessary relation) appears between the condition and its answer. Know that in the verse there is a wonderful conciseness (ijaz): the word "orphans" is used in the condition and is paired with the word "women" in the answer, so the listener understands that "orphans" here is the plural of "yatima" (orphan girl), which is a category of orphans in His earlier saying ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisa': 2]. Know that between not acting justly toward orphan girls and the command to marry women there is an unavoidable connection, otherwise the condition would be pointless. Its explanation is what is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: that 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr asked 'A'isha about this verse, and she said: "O son of my sister, this is the orphan girl who is under the guardianship of her guardian, who shares with him his property, and he is attracted to her wealth and beauty, so her guardian wishes to marry her without acting justly regarding her dowry, so he does not give her what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them and bring them to the highest of their customary dowries; and they were commanded to marry other women who are good for them." Then the people asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a ruling after this verse, and Allah revealed ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan girls to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, and whom you desire to marry﴾ [al-Nisa': 127].

The words of Allah the Exalted ﴿and whom you desire to marry﴾ [al-Nisa': 127] mean the desire of one of you to turn away from his orphan girl when she is lacking in wealth and beauty. So they were forbidden to marry those orphan girls whose wealth and beauty attracted them, unless with justice, because of their aversion to them when they were lacking in wealth and beauty. 'A'isha did not attribute this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but the context of her speech indicates that it is from a tawqif (revealed prescription),

Page 223

and for this reason al-Bukhari included it in the chapter on the tafsir of Surat al-Nisa' among the raised (marfu') hadiths, considering that she only said that from directly witnessing the situation of the revelation and the understanding of the Muslims which the Messenger (peace be upon him) approved. Especially since she said: "Then the people asked the Messenger of Allah for a ruling." Accordingly, the conciseness of the wording of the verse is based on what the people understood from what they knew of their circumstances, and it combines with the ruling of preserving the rights of orphans in their inherited property the preservation of their rights in the property that orphan girls deserve from the dowries of their equals, and an admonition to men: since they did not make the ties of kinship an intercessor for women whom they had no desire for, so that they would turn away from marrying them, likewise they should not make kinship a cause for wronging them in their dowries. Her saying "Then the people asked the Messenger of Allah" means they asked him seeking clarification of this verse, or they asked him about the ruling on marrying orphans, and they had not been guided to deriving it from this verse, so the saying of Allah ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women﴾ [al-Nisa': 127] was revealed, and the reference in His saying ﴿and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan girls﴾ [al-Nisa': 127] is to what is recited of this first verse; that is, this questioning occurred at the time of the revelation of this surah, and her statement here is the best explanation of this verse.

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and Qatada said: The Arabs were scrupulous about the property of orphans but were not scrupulous about justice among women, so they would marry ten or more, and this verse was revealed concerning that. According to this view, the connection between the condition and the answer is in what branches from the answer, namely His saying ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one﴾; so the structure of the verse is woven in this manner so that the limit of four is included within it. Ikrima said: It was revealed concerning Quraysh; a man would marry ten or more, and when his wealth could not sustain their expenses, he would take the property of his orphan and marry from it. According to this aspect the connection is clear, because marrying more than one can sustain becomes a means (dhari'a) to consuming the property of orphans, so the verse is evidence for the legitimacy of blocking means (sadd al-dhara'i') when they predominate. Mujahid said: The verse is a warning against fornication (zina), because they were scrupulous about consuming the property of orphans but were not scrupulous about fornication, so it was said to them: if you fear regarding the property of orphans, then fear fornication, for the conduct of one who is devout is to shun all sins, especially those whose harm is greater. According to this aspect the connection between the condition and its answer is weak, and the verb of the condition is past in both form and meaning. Other views have been stated, which are weaker than what we have mentioned.

The meaning of "what is good (ma tāba)" is what is pleasing, as evidenced by His saying "for you," and it is understood from it that it is among what is permitted to you, since the discourse is in the context of legislation.

As for what "ma tāba" refers to, namely the women, the expected form would have been "man" (the relative pronoun for persons), but "ma" (which is predominantly used for non-rational beings) is used because it is treated as a descriptive, namely "good," without specifying an individual essence. Had he said "man," it would have immediately suggested the intention of specific good women known among them. Similarly is the case of "ma" in interrogation, as the author of al-Kashshaf and the author of al-Miftah said: when you say "What did you marry?" you mean what her attributes are, whether a virgin or a non-virgin, for example; and when you say "Whom did you marry?" you mean identifying her name and lineage.

This verse is not the one that establishes the legitimacy of marriage, because the command in it is conditional upon the state of fearing injustice toward orphans. Apparently the command in it is for guidance, and marriage was legislated by affirmation of the original permissibility that people had before Islam, together with the nullification of what the religion does not accept, such as exceeding four, marrying those one hates, the forbidden relations through nursing, and the command that it not be devoid of a dowry, and similar matters.

His saying ﴿two or three or four﴾ describes the state of "those who are good (tāba)," and it is not permissible for them to be states of "women," because "women" is intended as the whole genus, since "min" is either partitive or explanatory, and both require the explanation to remain general so that it can accommodate partition and its like. The meaning: Allah has made things easy for you, so for you there is an alternative to marrying those orphans, despite the harm to them in the dowry. In this there is an incorporation (idmaj) of another legal ruling within the ruling on justice for orphans up to His saying ﴿That is more suitable, that you may not deviate﴾.

The forms mathna, thulath, and ruba' (pattern maf'al and fu'al) in number names from one to four, and it has been said up to six, and it has been said up to ten, and this is the most correct, and it is the position of the Kufans; al-Ma'arri authenticated it in his commentary on the Diwan of al-Mutanabbi at the words of Abu al-Tayyib:

"Single or six, among the units of our night, which is tied to the calling."

All of them indicate the meaning of repeating a number for the purpose of distribution, as in His saying ﴿wings, two or three or four﴾ [Fatir: 1], meaning for one group two wings, for another three, and for another four. The distribution here is in terms of the differing capacities and means of those addressed: among them is a group who can marry two, so their wives are two and two, and so on, like your saying to a group: divide this money two by two, three by three, and four by four, according to the eldest among you in age. This is indicated by His later saying ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one﴾. The apparent view is that the prohibition of exceeding four is derived from other than this verse, because mere limitation is not sufficient for proof, but it is supported by it; and that this verse confirmed what was established of limiting to four wives, as indicated by the authentic hadith: that Ghaylan ibn Salama embraced Islam while having ten wives, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Keep four and separate from the rest." Perhaps the verse was introduced with mention of the number established before its revelation, as a preparation for the commencement of justice among wives, for His saying ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one﴾ is explicit in requiring justice in descending through the levels of number, reducing the responsible person to one wife. Therefore, his fear at each level of number is what brings him down to the one below it. Among the strange things is what Ibn al-'Arabi related in al-Ahkam from a group of ignorant people, whom he did not specify, who imagined that this verse permits men to marry nine women, imagining that "mathna wa thulath wa ruba'" is synonymous with "two, three, and four," and that the waw is for collection, so the total came to nine, which is the number the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered among his wives. This is a shameful ignorance of the knowledge of Arabic speech. In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi this view is attributed to the Rafida and to some of the people of the literal (zahir) school, without specifying them; but it is not the view of Dawud al-Zahiri or his followers. Ibn al-Faras in Ahkam al-Qur'an attributed it to a group whose disagreement is not considered; al-Fakhr said: they are a heedless people; and al-Jassas did not mention it, being an opponent of the principle. Ibn al-Faras attributed to a group the view that there is no restriction on the number of wives, and they took the limitation in the verse to mean: up to the number that was. These two groups held that the Prophet (ﷺ) died leaving nine wives, but this is a weak argument, for that was a specific privilege for him, as consensus indicates. Seeking decisive proofs in deriving rulings from the Qur'an is a search that places the mujtahids in a position of bewilderment in their deduction, for the foundation of Arabic speech rests on the basis of discernment, and its method is the method of the indicative allusion.

Page 226

The apparent address to people includes both free and slave, so a slave may marry four wives according to the correct view, and this is the view of Malik; it is attributed to Abu al-Darda', al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Salim, Rabi'a ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman, and Mujahid, and Dawud al-Zahiri adopted it. It was said: a slave may not marry more than two, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, and it is attributed to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Ibn Sirin, and al-Hasan; but this is not consistent with halving for slaves, because this follows from the disposition of nature, which does not differ between free men and slaves. Whoever claims the consensus of the Companions that one may not marry more than two has spoken rashly.

His saying ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one﴾, meaning one for each one who fears not being just. He did not say "fa-uhad" or "fa-mawhad" because the pattern maf'al and fu'al only come after a plural, and no plural occurred here. The majority read "fa-wahida" with the accusative (naṣb), where wāḥida is the object of an implied verb, meaning "then marry one." Abu Ja'far read it with the nominative (raf'), as a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "sufficiency" (kifaya).

The fear of not being just means the absence of justice among wives, that is, lack of equality, and this covers maintenance, clothing, cheerfulness, companionship, and avoiding harm in everything that falls under the responsible person's ability and capacity, apart from inclination of the heart.

God has prescribed plurality of wives for the one who is able and just, for many benefits. Among them: that it is a means of increasing the number of the community through the growth of births within it. Among them: that it helps in providing for women, who are more numerous than men in every community, because females are more numerous than males among births; and because men are exposed to causes of death in wars and hardships that do not befall women; and because women generally live longer than men, by the nature God has created them with. Among them: that the Shariah has prohibited fornication and has been strict in its prohibition, because of the corruption it leads to in morals, lineages and the order of families; so it was fitting to grant people latitude in plurality of wives for the man who is inclined to plurality and disposed to it. Among them: the intent to keep away from divorce except in case of necessity.

Page 227

There was no limit on wives in earlier religious laws or in the pre-Islamic era. It is not established that 'Isa (peace be upon him) brought any limitation on marriage, although some of our scholars, such as al-Qarafi, imagined that this was so; I do not think it is correct. It was Islam that brought the limitation. As for the basis of limitation, its wisdom is evident: since not everyone is able to be just, and if plurality of wives is not founded on the rule of justice among them, the order of the family is disturbed, strife arises within it, wives rebel against their husbands, and children disobey their fathers by harming them through their wives and their children. Therefore it is necessary that the permission of plurality, for a benefit, be regulated and not turned back upon the original principle by nullification.

As for restricting plurality to four, many scholars have tried to explain it but have not reached a satisfying conclusion. I reckon that its wisdom relates to the ratio of women to men in most circumstances. Taking into account the average in plurality, not every man marries four. Let us suppose the average reveals two women for every man, which indicates that women are double the men. This is pointed to by what is reported in the Sahih: that "women will increase at the end of time, until fifty women will have one guardian (qayyim)."

As for His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾: if it is joined to His saying "then one," then He has given the choice between it and one, with respect to plurality, meaning: one wife, or a number of what your right hands possess. This is because slave women are not subject to the same condition of justice as wives, but good treatment and avoiding harm are required. If you join it to His saying ﴿marry what is good for you﴾, it becomes a choice between marriage and concubinage according to people's circumstances; justice toward concubines taken for concubinage is then a requirement by analogy with wives, and likewise the number is according to capacity. However, in concubinage it is not forbidden to exceed four, since the conditions mentioned between the clauses refer to what came before them. The consensus has prevented analogizing slave women to free women regarding the final limit of number. This interpretation is more fitting to the wisdom of legislation and more in harmony with the meaning of His saying ﴿That is nearer to not being unjust﴾.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿That is nearer to not being unjust﴾ refers to the preceding ruling, namely His saying ﴿then marry what is good for you﴾ up to His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, in respect of what it contains of distribution according to justice. The demonstrative is singular in view of what is mentioned, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

"Adna" means "aqrab" (nearer), and this nearness is figurative, meaning more entitled and more helpful toward ﴿not being unjust﴾ (an taʿūlū). "Ta'ūlū" is the imperfect of "ʿāla ʿawlan," a verb with a waw as its middle radical, meaning "to deviate and incline" (jāra wa māla). It is well known in the speech of the Arabs, and Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of the early scholars interpreted it thus. It is said: "al-mizan ʿāla ʿawlan" when the scale tilts, and "fulan ʿāla fī ḥukmihi" meaning he was unjust in his judgment. It is evident that a person's reduction to the number about which one does not fear failing to be just is nearer to avoiding injustice. Thus His saying ﴿That is nearer to not being unjust﴾ carries the meaning of His saying ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just﴾, adding further emphasis to the aversion to injustice.

It may also be that the demonstrative refers to the ruling implied by His saying ﴿then one, or what your right hands possess﴾, meaning: that is safer from injustice, because plurality exposes the responsible person to injustice even if he exerts his utmost effort toward justice, since the self has desires and heedlessnesses. In this reading, His saying ﴿That is nearer to not being unjust﴾ is not an emphasis of the content of ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just﴾, but an encouragement to limit oneself to one wife or to plurality through ownership of the right hand, since it blocks the means to injustice. In this reading, justice is not a condition for ownership of the right hand, and this is what the majority of the jurists of the cities set aside regarding ownership of the right hand.

It has also been said: the meaning of "an taʿūlū" is "that your dependants not increase," derived from the expression "ʿāla al-rajulu ahlahu yaʿūluhum," meaning he supported them. That is, the negation of the increase of dependants is used as a kinayah (indirect expression), because "ʿawl" implies the existence of dependants, and describing a man as one who "supports" implies many dependants, since it is a report of something no one is free of; one would not report it about someone unless one saw him exceed the customary limit. Just as you say "so-and-so eats" and "so-and-so sleeps," meaning he eats a lot and sleeps a lot. It is not valid to intend that this is a literal meaning of "ʿāla," because one does not say "ʿāla" to mean that his dependants increased; rather one says "aʿāla." This interpretation is transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam, was held by al-Shafi'i, and was adopted by Ibn al-A'rabi among the linguists. But it is a distant interpretation and a hidden kinayah, which only suits the reading in which the demonstrative "that" refers to what His saying ﴿then one, or what your right hands possess﴾ contains, and the verse would then encourage limiting oneself to one wife for one who cannot bear the expense of wide provision, because limiting oneself to one wife

Page 229

reduces expenditure and reduces offspring, thereby preserving his wealth and warding off need. However, this reading does not suit His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, because the multiplying of concubines leads to an increase of dependants in maintaining them and their offspring. For this reason, a group of scholars rejected this reading against al-Shafi'i, some excessively and some moderately.

Abu Bakr al-Jassas severely rejected it in his Ahkam, to the point of claiming it was a linguistic error, arising from confusing "ʿāla yaʿīlu" with "ʿāla yaʿūlu." Ibn al-'Arabi moderately refuted this view in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an. The author of al-Kashshaf defended al-Shafi'i, and raised the objection that this interpretation does not match His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, since multiplying concubines is like multiplying free wives, so there is no escape from dependants on this interpretation. It was answered with a reply that involves some strain.

The ruling of this verse is among what His saying refers to: ﴿And He spread from them many men and women﴾ [al-Nisa': 1].

**Page 230 (text begins)**

Two groups were weak in the pre-Islamic period: orphans and women. And two rights whose holders were cheated were the property of orphans and the property of women. For this reason the Qur'an guarded both with the utmost care. It began with the injunction concerning the right to an orphan's property and followed it with the injunction concerning the woman's right to property that would inevitably come to her. The placement of the ruling on marriage between the two injunctions is the most fitting arrangement, preparing the way for this passage to be linked.

His words ﴿Give the women their bridal gifts graciously﴾ are conjoined with His words ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisa': 2]. The discussion of the meaning of "giving" here is the same. What further connects it to the preceding discussion is that what came before it dealt with the obligation of justice toward orphan girls, and so this formed a natural transition. The addressee of the command in such cases is everyone who has a share in acting upon it. It is thus an address to the whole community, in the sense that it includes everyone who has a hand in this matter: husbands, guardians, and then the rulers, to whom recourse is made in striking the hands of those who wrong people in their rights. The primary intended addressees of the address are the husbands,

**Page 231**

so that they do not use the women's shyness, weakness and desire for their approval as a pretext to diminish their rights to their dowries, or make the women's need to marry, in order to secure a provider for them, a means of dropping the mahr (bridal gift) in the marriage contract. This is what is possible concerning the consumption of their dowries. Otherwise, women have guardians who demand from the husbands that the dowries be fixed. But reaching the rulers involves hardships and burdens which the rightful owner may find tiresome, so that he abandons his claim, especially women who are married. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jurayj held that the address is to the husbands. According to this view, the verse established the payment of dowries and made it a legal requirement, so the mahr became a pillar of the marriage contract in Islam. This has been affirmed in several verses, such as His words ﴿So give them their wages as an obligation﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], and others.

The mahr is a well-known sign distinguishing marriage from illicit companionship. However, in the pre-Islamic period, the husband would give property to the woman's guardian, and they called it ḥulwān (a gift to the guardian), with a ḥā' that is vowelled with a ḍamma, while the woman received nothing. God abolished this practice in Islam by making the property belong to the woman, through His words ﴿And give the women their bridal gifts﴾.

Others said the address is to the guardians. This was related from Abu Ṣāliḥ, who said: "Because it was the custom of some Arabs for a woman's guardian to consume her mahr, and God removed this practice with Islam." And from al-Ḥaḍramī: the verse addressed those who engaged in *shighār* (exchange marriage), who would marry one woman in exchange for another. Perhaps this view was derived from implicit indication (*dalālat al-ishāra*) rather than the explicit wording. All of this is something the general meaning of "women" and the general meaning of "bridal gifts" can accommodate.

*Ṣadaqāt* is the plural of *ṣadaqa* (with a ḍamma on the dāl), and *ṣadaqa* means a woman's mahr. It is derived from *ṣidq* (truthfulness), because it is a gift preceded by a promise, which the giver fulfils.

*Niḥla* (with a kasra on the nūn) means a gift without intent of return. It is also said *nuḥl* (with a ḍamma and then a sukūn).

*Niḥla* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of *ṣadaqātihinna*. The occurrence of a singular circumstantial state with a plural referent is valid, because what is meant by this singular noun is the category which is suitable for all its individuals. It is also permissible that *niḥla* be in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) of *ātū*, specifying the type of giving, that is, giving as an honour.

The bridal gifts were called *niḥla* to distance them from types of exchange, and to bring them closer to the concept of a gift. The mahr is not, on careful analysis, a compensation for the woman's benefits, since marriage is a contract between a man and a woman aimed at companionship, establishing a great bond, and the exchange of rights between the spouses. These are too precious to have a financial counter-value. If a counter-value were attached to them, it would be considerable and renewed with the renewal of the benefits and the extension of their durations, as is the nature of all exchanges. Instead, God made it an obligatory gift from the husbands, as an honour to their wives. God made it obligatory because it is established that it is what distinguishes marriage from companionship and fornication. The origin of marriage among humans was the exclusive attachment of a man to a woman who would belong only to him, and this exclusivity was obtained by force. Later, people substituted for force the payment of prices to the guardians of women, by selling their daughters and clients. Then legislation advanced, the marriage contract was perfected, and the woman became the spouse, the partner of the man in his affairs. The bridal gifts remained as signs of that ancient exclusivity, distinguishing the marriage contract from the other kinds of relations that are blameworthy both legally and socially. Relations outside the form of marriage were free of paying property to the guardians, since they arose from love or lust on the part of the man towards the woman, in privacy and secrecy from her family. Among these is temporary fornication (*zinā al-muwaqqat*), and among them is *mukhādana* (a sustained secret liaison), which is continuous fornication. The Qur'an alluded to it in His words ﴿chaste, not fornicators nor taking secret lovers﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. Below these is *bighā'*, which is fornication with slave-women for fixed fees, and this is what God forbade in His words ﴿And do not compel your slave-girls into prostitution, if they desire chastity, in order to seek the fleeting goods of this life﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. There are other kinds of relationships, such as *ḍimād*, in which a married woman takes a male lover in a year of drought to spend on her in addition to her husband's maintenance. For this reason God called the mahr *niḥla*. Thus He distanced from its meaning those who interpreted it by its necessary implication, making it a metaphor for the husbands' or guardians' contentment in giving the bridal gifts. Those who interpreted it as a gift from God to women, which He prescribed for them, and those who interpreted it as the law which is *yuntaḥal* (i.e. followed).

His words ﴿But if they willingly give you some of it of their own accord﴾ etc.: that is, if their souls are content to give you something of it, that is, of what was mentioned. He used the singular pronoun in *minhu* ("of it") by interpreting it as referring to what was mentioned, following the demonstrative. As Ru'ba said:

*In it are lines of black and white, as if in the skin is the spotting of leprosy.*

Abu 'Ubayda said to him: "Either say *ka'annahā* ("as if it") if you mean the lines, or *ka'annahumā* ("as if they both") if you mean the black and the white." He replied: "I meant *ka'anna dhālik* ("as if that"), woe to you!" That is, he made the pronoun agree as the demonstrative is made to agree. This was discussed earlier under His words ﴿neither old nor young, but between that﴾ [al-Baqara: 68] in Surat al-Baqara. The discussion of a similar pronoun will come under His words ﴿and the like thereof with it, to ransom themselves thereby﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 36] in Surat al-'Uqud.

The phrase *nafsan* is in the singular, although it is a specifier (*tamyīz*) of the attribution of *ṭibna* to the plural pronoun of the women, because the specifier is an indefinite generic noun, in which the singular and plural are equal. The good quality (*ṭīb*) was attributed first to the persons of the women, and then the specifier was introduced to show the strength of this goodness, according to what is established in the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-ma'ānī*): the difference between *ishta'al al-ra'su shaybā* ("the head flamed with white hair") and *ishta'ala shaybu ra'sī* ("the white hair of my head flamed"). This is to show that it is a contentment of the soul, unmixed with any pressure or compulsion.

The literal meaning of the verb *ṭāba* is the object's being suitable to the soul. Its original sense is of a pleasant fragrance, because of the goodness of what is smelled. The pleasant wind is one that suits the traveller at sea, as in His words ﴿and they sailed with them by a good wind﴾ [Yunus: 22]. From this also comes what the soul accepts, as previously mentioned in His words ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqara: 168]. Then it was borrowed for what thrives among its kind, as in His words ﴿and do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ [al-Nisa': 2]. From this comes the verb in ﴿they are content to give you of it, of their own souls﴾ here, meaning they are pleased to give it without hardship or oppression. So it is a metaphor (*istiʿāra*).

His words *fa-kulūhu* use "eating" here to mean the benefit that leaves no possibility of return to the owner of the thing benefited, that is, the sense of complete ownership. Originally, in their speech, eating is borrowed for seizing another's property in a way that cannot be reversed, because eating is the strongest kind of benefit that prevents the thing from returning to its rightful owner. But here it is used for benefit, for the sake of *mushākala* (mutual correspondence) with His earlier words ﴿and do not consume their property with your property﴾ [al-Nisa': 2]. This is the embellishment (*muḥassin*) of the metaphor.

*Hanīʾan marīʾan* are two circumstantial states from the pronoun in the accusative. They are two adjectives of the similar-pattern form from *hanā* and *hani'a* (with the nūn vowelled both with a fatḥa and a kasra), meaning "went down smoothly and without any bitter aftertaste." *Marī'* comes from *marā'a al-ṭa'ām* (with the rā' vowelled three ways), meaning the same as *hani'a*, so it is an emphasis resembling an echo. It was said: *hanī'* is what the eater finds pleasant, and *marī'* is what has a praiseworthy outcome. These two descriptions may be a continuation of the metaphor in *kulūhu* in the sense of *khudhūhu* (take it) as taking ownership, and they may be used to express the absence of liability for the husbands in taking what their wives have given them with contentment, that is, lawful and permitted, or lawful with no debt involved.

**Page 233**

His words *ʿan shay'in minhu* use the partitive particle, pointing out that the normal state is that the contract should not be devoid of a mahr, so one should not waive it entirely. However, the jurists, when they interpreted the apparent sense of the verse as partial, made the gift of the entire mahr like the gift of all of it, following the basic principle of gifts, since once she has taken possession of it her ownership is established. The Mālikī scholars did not regard this as suspect, because the basis of marriage is generosity. Otherwise, they said in matters of sale that what leaves the hand and then returns to it is considered as if it had never left. Here, according to us, the matter applies to women who have authority over themselves, not to those under restriction (*maḥjūrāt*), specifying the verse by other evidences for restriction, since young girls are by consensus not included here. Thus the specification was applied to the verse. Most jurists said: it applies to both previously married women and virgins, relying on the generality. But this is weak in the matter of interpreting the proofs by one another.

The jurists differed about a woman's retraction of a gift of part of her mahr. The majority said: she has no right of retraction. Sharīḥ and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwān said: she has the right of retraction, because if her soul had been content she would not have retracted. They related that 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to his judges: "Women give out of desire or fear, so whichever woman gives, and then wants to retract, that is for her." This applies when the time between the gift and the retraction is short, and when the husband's treatment after the gift has produced something contrary to what the good companionship prior to the gift would indicate.

The ruling of this verse is among what His words indicated: ﴿And He spread from them both many men and women﴾ [al-Nisa': 1].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 5:

﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made for you a means of support, but provide for them from it, clothe them, and speak to them in a kind manner.﴾

This is conjoined (*'ataf*) to His saying ﴿And give the women their dowries﴾ [an-Nisa 4:4], to remove the presumption that every property must be given to its owner because the command to give property to its owners has come twice: in His saying ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [an-Nisa 4:2] and ﴿And give the women their dowries﴾ [an-Nisa 4:4]. Or it is conjoined to His saying ﴿And give the orphans﴾ [an-Nisa 4:2], and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraq*).

[Page 234]

The purpose is to state the condition under which the foolish person is prevented from his property, and the condition under which his property is given to him. It might be said that, on this reading, the apparent arrangement would have been to mention first the ruling forbidding the handing over of the orphans' property, since it precedes in occurrence. Thus, to explain why the ruling of handing over was placed first, we say: it placed the ruling of handing over first, because people are more eager for its opposite. Had it begun with the prohibition on handing property to the foolish, the wrongdoers would have taken it as an argument for themselves, and would have pretended that they withhold the orphans' property only out of fear that foolishness will persist in them, as many guardians and unrighteous managers do today, who set themselves up to oppose the evidence of the attainment of maturity (*rushd*), merely out of contention and to weary the wards (*mahajir*) in pursuing their rights.

The address in ﴿do not give the foolish﴾ is like the address in ﴿give the orphans﴾ and ﴿give the women﴾: it is addressed to people in general, those addressed by ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾ [an-Nisa 4:1], so that each person who is fit for this ruling may take his share in carrying it out.

The word *al-sufaha'* (the foolish) may refer to orphans, because childhood is the most prevalent state of foolishness. It then corresponds to ﴿And give the orphans﴾ [an-Nisa 4:2], to show the difference between giving in the sense of safeguarding and giving in the sense of enabling. The shift from describing them as "orphans" to describing them here as "the foolish" serves to state the cause of the prohibition. It may also refer to anyone who is established as foolish, whether through childhood or through disorder in his conduct. In that case the verse touches incidentally on restricting the foolish adult, by way of association with the context. This is the more apparent reading, because it has broader meaning and wider legislative scope. The meanings of foolishness were explained earlier at His saying ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

By "property" is meant the property of the wards that belongs to them. Do you not see His saying ﴿and provide for them from it﴾? The property is ascribed to the pronoun of those addressed by "O mankind", as a subtle indication that the wealth circulating among people is the right of its owners, who have exclusive possession of it in outward appearance; but upon reflection, the rights of the entire community become apparent in it, because its existence benefits the whole nation. What is in the hands of some of its members of wealth returns to everyone for good, since its owners spend from it, hire, buy, and give in charity, and then it is inherited from them when they die, so that the wealth passes from one hand to another. Thus the helpless, the worker, the merchant, the poor, and the one who has just enough all benefit. When wealth decreases in people's hands, they come close to one another in need and poverty, and fall into hardship and misery, and they become in need of another tribe or nation. That is one of the causes of the loss of their dignity, the seizure of their lands, and the turning of their resources to serve others. For this wisdom, Allah, exalted is He, attributed the property to all those addressed, so that they have the right to establish the rulings that protect property and public wealth.

[Page 235]

This is an indication which I do not think any wise economist has preceded the Qur'an in stating. Some have strayed far in making the ascription refer to the slightest connection, because the property is in the hands of the guardians, and they have made the address specific to the guardians alone. Others made the ascription refer to those addressed because the property is of the same kind as their property, even though it is not really their property; this is the view al-Zamakhshari inclined to. Others made the ascription refer to the fact that the foolish are of the same kind as those addressed, so that their property is as if it were their property; this is the view Fakhr al-Din inclined to. Ibn al-'Arabi came close when he said: "because property is shared among creatures, passing from hand to hand and moving from one ownership to another." And with what I have explained, his statement has its significance. Others went even further and made the ascription literal, meaning: O owners of property, do not give your property to those who waste it among your children and wives. This is the most distant of the readings, and I suspect that what led to this interpretation is only bewilderment as to how to reconcile the fact that those prevented from property are foolish with the ascription of that property to the pronoun of those addressed. I have described it as distant only because its proponent made it the intended meaning of the verse. Had he presented it as a permissible reading that the wording of the verse can bear, it would have had a sound basis, in light of what was established in the ninth introduction.

The property is qualified by a description that makes its ascription to those addressed clearer, namely His saying ﴿which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾. The description uses a relative clause, both as a hint to the reason for the prohibition and as a clarification of the meaning of the ascription. The word *qiyaman* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) on the pattern *fi'al*, with the meaning of *fi'al* (*fi'am*), like *'iwadh* meaning *'iyadh* (protection). It derives from the root with waw, and its regular form would be *qiwam*, but it was irregularly altered to *qiyam* with a ya', as *jiyad* is irregular for the plural of *jawad*, and *tiyal* in the dialect of Dabba for the plural of *tawil*. They intended to convert the waw into an alif after a kasra, as they did in *qiyam* and similar words. However, that conversion is regular in the pattern *fi'al*, and irregular in other patterns, because *fi'al* is very common in verbal nouns while *fi'al* is rare among them, and *qiyam* is outside the usual pattern. This is how Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it: *qiyaman*, on the pattern *fi'al*. The majority read *qiyaman* as *qiyaman*, and *al-qiyam* is that by which livelihood is sustained; it is also from the waw root. On both readings, describing property by it is a description using a verbal noun for emphasis, like the saying of al-Khansa':

*So it is only advance and retreat.*

The meaning is that property is a great means of establishing the affairs of people. It has been said that *qiyaman* is the plural of *qimah* (value), meaning that which Allah made as values (*athman*) for things; but this does not carry the sublime meaning mentioned above.

The meaning of His saying ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them﴾ comes as a precaution, meaning: do not give them the property as a grant of unrestricted disposal, but give them only as much as meets their needs for sustenance and clothing. For this reason our jurists said: the ward is given his maintenance and clothing when it is secure to do so, in accordance with his condition and his property. He turned from governing *arzuquhum* and *uksuhum* with *min* to governing them with *fi*, which indicates figurative containment, following the usage in such cases, where there is no intent of partitive meaning that would suggest diminishing the thing itself. Rather, what is meant is that within the totality of the thing there is that by which the act is accomplished: sometimes from its substance, sometimes from its price, sometimes from its offspring, and that this is repeated and continuous. Consider this in the words of Sabrah ibn 'Amr al-Fa qa'si:

*We favor our equals with them and humiliate [others] with them, and we drink their price and gamble.*

He means the camels that were brought to them as blood-money (*diyah*) for one of their dead, i.e., we drink with their price and gamble. Whether we drank with all of it or part of it, or we recover some of it through gambling. This is a remarkable meaning in usage, which none of the exegetes here had anticipated. Most of them neglected to point out the reason for the shift to *fi*. The author of the Kashshaf came close to grasping it, when he said: "that is, make them a place for their provision by trading in them and profiting from them, so that their maintenance comes from the profit and not from the principal of the property." His saying "and not from the principal of the property" is an added qualification, for if it were as he said, it would imply a prohibition on spending from the principal of the property. He said ﴿and speak to them in a kind manner﴾ so that giving them maintenance and clothing may be free from harm, for the nature of one who takes property out of his hand is to find the one who asks for it burdensome; and this applies equally to gifts from the giver's own property and gifts from the recipient's property. Also, because the foolish person's standing is open to reproach for his lack of judgment, the guardian may become anxious at dealing with the orphan and say to him what he dislikes, although the lack of intelligence is a defect in creation, so he should not be insulted for it. And because the foolish person often rejects the refusal of what he seeks from among his many desires, he may come to show it, or utter hurtful words to his guardian. For all this, Allah commanded the guardians not to begin with bad speech toward their wards, nor to answer them with what is hurtful. Rather, they should admonish their wards, teach them the paths of right guidance as far as they are able, and remind them that the property is theirs, and that preserving it is preserving their own interests, for in that there is much good, namely the preservation of dignity between guardians and those under them, and the hope that those under their charge will benefit from such admonitions in correcting their conditions, so that they will not be as the poet said:

*When the foolish one is forbidden, he rushes toward it, and opposes, and the foolish one turns to opposition.*

The phrase "kind speech" includes every speech that has an appropriate place in its context, and excludes every objectionable speech that neither reason nor good character would accept as fitting. Thus what is kind may sometimes be what the foolish person dislikes, when it contains the good of his own self.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 4, verse 6 (part 1 of 3)**

﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property, and do not consume it extravagantly or hastily, fearing that they will grow up.﴾

It is permissible for the clause "wabtalū" (وابْتَلُوا, "and test") to be conjoined (ma'ṭūfa) to the clause "wa lā tu'tu al-sufahā'a amwālakum" (﴿and do not give the foolish your property﴾), because it is placed in relation to it as the limit (ghāya, "endpoint") of the prohibition. If the intended meaning of "al-sufahā'" (السُّفَهاءَ, "the foolish") there is specifically the orphans, then it is appropriate to ask: why did the speech shift from the pronoun to the apparent noun, and from the apparent noun equivalent to the first to a different and more specific term, "al-yatāmā" (الْيَتامى, "the orphans")? The answer is that moving away from the pronoun serves to increase clarity and to emphasise the ruling. Also, moving away from repeating the word "al-sufahā'" signals that, during the time of testing, their full mental maturity is hoped for and their foolishness is expected to disappear, so that there would not appear to be a kind of contradiction between describing them as foolish and perceiving sound judgment in them.

If, however, the intended meaning of "al-sufahā'" there is more general than the orphans, which is the more apparent reading, then it is appropriate to ask: what is the reason for restricting the ruling of testing and of perceiving sound judgment to the orphans and not to the foolish in general? The answer is that such information (ikhbār, here meaning the command to test) is given only at the time when a change of condition is expected, namely the period of adolescence approaching maturity (murāhaqat al-bulūgh), when the perfection of intellect is hoped for and the movement from a state of weakness to a state of sound judgment is anticipated. As for one whose foolishness continues into old age, no time is known that is a likely point for the change of his condition and for his testing.

It is also permissible for the clause "wabtalū" to be conjoined to the clause "wa ātū al-yatāmā amwālahum" (﴿and give the orphans their property﴾), in order to explain the manner of giving and its preliminaries. On this reading, the use of the apparent noun "al-yatāmā" in the phrase instead of a pronoun is because of the distance between the referent and the pronoun, had he expressed it with a pronoun.

"Al-ibtilā'" (الِابْتِلاءُ) means testing (ikhtibār). "Ḥattā" (حَتّى) here is a particle of beginning (ibtidā'iyya), and it conveys the notion of a limit (ghāya), because its primary function (waḍ') is to express a limit; its being an inceptive particle or a preposition is a usage determined by what follows it, as was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿until when you lost heart﴾ in Surah Āl 'Imrān. "Idhā" (إذا) is an adverb of time that carries the sense of a conditional. Most grammarians hold that "ḥattā" when it precedes "idhā" is inceptive, not a preposition.

The meaning is: test the orphans up to the time when, if they reach marriageable age, then hand over to them their property. Beyond that point, testing ends. Since it is known that testing is for the purpose of handing over the property, it is established that the implied meaning of the limit (mafhūm al-ghāya) is intended in the form of its necessary consequence and its result, which is the handing over of the property. This will be stated explicitly in the answer to the second condition.

The testing here is, by the consensus of the scholars, the examination of the orphan's handling of property. The Mālikīs said: some property is given to the orphan that he is able to manage without causing him ruin, and his conduct in running the household expenses is examined for a full month. If the orphan is a girl, she is entrusted with what is entrusted to the mistress of the household: managing affairs, distinguishing the good from the bad, and similar matters, according to the customs of the times and of the households. Some scholars added testing in religion; this was said by al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and al-Shāfi'ī. But it should be that this is not a condition, since the purpose of the Sharia here is the preservation of property, and this ruling is not one of the effects of the universal objective of preserving religion.

"Bulūgh al-nikāh" (بُلُوغُ النِّكاحِ, "reaching marriage") is an elliptical construction (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning "the time of reaching marriage", i.e. the time of marrying. It is a metaphor (kināya) for leaving the state of childhood, for both males and females. Puberty has well-known signs, but the verse expressed it as reaching marriage, based on the Arab custom of early marriage for girls upon puberty and of a man seeking marriage upon reaching maturity. The readiness for marriage varies with the differences of lands in heat and cold, and with the differing temperaments of people within the same land in strength and weakness, and in the sanguine and bilious temperaments. For this reason the Qur'an referred it to the time of reaching the appropriate age for marriage. Generally, girls reach puberty earlier than boys. If the girl is late beyond her expected time, the majority of scholars said that one relies on an age beyond which puberty is normally not delayed. Mālik, in the narration of Ibn al-Qāsim from him, said that it is eighteen years for males and females. The same was narrated from Abū Ḥanīfa for males, and he said for a girl it is seventeen years. A narrator other than Ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Mālik that it is seventeen years. The well-known view from Abū Ḥanīfa is nineteen years for males and seventeen years for girls. The majority said fifteen years. This was said by al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar, Isḥāq, al-Shāfi'ī, Aḥmad, al-Awzā'ī, Ibn al-Mājishūn, and with this view said Aṣbagh and Ibn Wahb from the companions of Mālik. Al-Abharī from the Mālikīs chose it. They relied on the ḥadīth of Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) presented him on the day of Badr when he was fourteen years old, and he did not permit him; and he presented him on the day of Uḥud when he was fifteen, and he permitted him.

There is no proof in this, because it does not follow that the puberty of 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar is the standard for the puberty of Muslims in general. It happened that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him and he had the features of men, so he permitted him. The mention of the age in Ibn 'Umar's words does not indicate a fixed rule for permission. Ibn al-'Arabī in Aḥkām al-Qur'ān overlooked this, so I am surprised at these imams for not fixing the age of puberty at fifteen years; and his surprise at them is even greater than theirs at him, because the case of Ibn 'Umar is a particular case (qaḍiyyat 'ayn), and disagreement of scholars in particular cases is well known. The Shāfi'īs relied on what is narrated: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "When a child completes fifteen years, his deeds are recorded for and against him, and the ḥudūd (prescribed punishments) are applied to him." This is a weak ḥadīth and it should not be relied upon as evidence.

The time of testing must necessarily come after discernment (tamyīz), and before puberty. This was said by Ibn al-Mawwāz from Mālik. Perhaps its reasoning is that testing before puberty involves exposing the property to waste, since the orphan's intellect is not yet complete. The Baghdadi Mālikīs said: testing is before puberty.

The completion of the strength of natural growth is expressed by "balaghū al-nikāḥ" (بَلَغُوا النِّكاحَ, "they reach marriage"). Puberty is attributed to their persons, because that time calls a man to marry and calls the guardians of a girl to marry her off. It is the customary puberty after which nothing is later. So it is not objected that people sometimes marry off their daughters, and sometimes their sons, before the age of puberty, because that is a hastening by guardians for temporary purposes, and it is not the puberty of the sons or daughters.

His saying, ﴿then if you perceive in them sound judgment﴾ (فَإنْ آنَسْتُمْ مِنهم رُشْدًا), is a second condition that qualifies the first condition, which is derived from "idhā balaghū" (إذا بَلَغُوا, "when they reach"). This second condition and its answer together form the answer to "idhā," and for this reason it is connected by the particle "fa" (فَ), so that the answer is explicit, and "idhā" is explicit as the condition. Indeed, the answer to "idhā" is independent of the connection by "fa" unless the intention is to make the conditional nature explicit.

The verse came in this structure to show that the end of guardianship comes at puberty in principle, but on the condition that sound judgment is recognised in the ward. All of this cuts off the excuses of guardians who wish to keep the wards' property in their hands for a period, in order to enjoy it more.

From the meaning of combining the two conditions here, since there is no apparent or implied conjunction in the expression, supported by context, it follows that together they are the cause for handing over the property to the ward. Thus the occurrence of one of them alone is not sufficient, nor is consideration given to what happens from either of them individually. This is the general rule for every conditional clause built upon another conditional clause. Their only indication is the necessity that both matters occur in one and the same conditioned matter. On this view the Mālikīs, and Imām al-Ḥaramayn, went. Some scholars claimed that the order of the two conditions indicates that the second one mentioned is the first in occurrence. This was attributed by al-Zajjājī in Kitāb al-Adhkār to Tha'lab, and it was chosen by Ibn Mālik. Among the Shāfi'īs, al-Baghawī and al-Ghazālī in al-Wasīṭ held it. Other scholars claimed that the order of the two conditions in occurrence follows their order in wording. This was attributed by the Shāfi'īs to al-Qaffāl, al-Qāḍī al-Ḥusayn, al-Ghazālī in al-Wajīz, and Imām al-Rāzī in al-Nihāya. They built on this several branch rulings concerning the conditioning of one condition upon another in oaths, and the conditioning of divorce and manumission. Imām al-Ḥaramayn said: there is no meaning in considering the order, and this is the truth, because the intention is that both occur regardless of precedence or subsequence. No effect of the disagreement appears in statements of fact or in the establishment of rulings, as here. It may appear only in the formulation of conditional oaths and oaths of divorce and manumission. I have already shown that the Mālikīs do not regard it as having any effect, and that is the correct view.

Know that this applies when there is evidence that the intention is to make the two conditions a condition of the answer. That is when the clause is free of conjunction by "wa" (و), even if only implied. For this reason it is necessary to take the clause of the second condition with its answer as the answer to the first condition, whether it is connected by "fa" as in this verse or not connected, as in His saying, ﴿My counsel will not benefit you, if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray﴾ (Hūd: 34).
