But when the two conditions are considered in order, each of them has its own independent answer, as in His saying, ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives...﴾ (al-Aḥzāb: 50), up to His saying, ﴿and a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾ (al-Aḥzāb: 50). Here His saying "if she gives herself" is a condition for the lawfulness of a believing woman to him, and His saying "if the Prophet wishes" is a condition for the contracting of the marriage, lest it be imagined that a woman's giving herself to the Prophet automatically binds him to marry her. So the implied answer to the second is: if he wishes, then it is permitted to him. They are not two conditions for the lawfulness, because the lawfulness of the woman has no cause in this case except that she gave herself.

In both situations of a condition that comes upon another condition, one makes the answer of one of them an omitted answer indicated by what is mentioned, or makes the answer of one of them an answer for the other. This is a matter of disagreement between the majority and al-Akhfash, since that is not a case of multiple conditions. It is only found in expressions such as your saying, "If you enter the house of Abū Sufyān, and if you enter the Sacred Mosque, then you are safe," and in expressions such as "If you pray, if you fast, you will be rewarded," in any construction where no necessary connection between the two conditions appears, so that one of them does not become a condition of the other.

This is the verification of this question, which I have extended at length. Taqī al-Dīn al-Subkī devoted a treatise to it. It is a question that the judge Ibn Khallikān asked Shaykh Ibn al-Ḥājib about, as he indicated in his biography in Kitāb al-Wafayāt. Al-Damāmīnī did not elaborate it in the marginal commentary on Mughnī al-Labīb.

The phrase "īnās al-rushd" (إيناسُ الرُّشْدِ, "perceiving sound judgment") here means knowing it. The root meaning of "īnās" is seeing a human being (al-insī, i.e. the human), then it was applied to the first thing that comes to mind from knowledge, whether in things seen, as in His saying, ﴿he perceived a fire from the side of the mount﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ: 29), or in things heard, as in the verse of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza about a wild cow:

*She perceived a sound, and the hunters frightened her, in the afternoon, when evening had drawn near.*

It seems that the choice of "ānastum" (آنَسْتُمْ) here rather than "'alimtum" (عَلِمْتُمْ, "you knew") indicates that as soon as the first knowledge of their sound judgment is obtained, their property is to be handed over to them without delay or procrastination.

"Rushd" (الرُّشْدُ) is pronounced with a damma on the rā' and a sukūn on the shīn, and it may be pronounced with a fatḥa on the rā', in which case the shīn takes a fatḥa too. The two are synonyms. It means the orderly functioning of the intellect and the proper ordering of actions that result from it. Here it is intended to mean the preservation of property and good management of it, as was explained earlier at "wabtalū al-yatāmā."

The addressees in the verse are the guardians. So the requirement of the verse is that the guardians are the ones who undertake this. The jurists made it a ruling, and said: the guardian takes charge of handing over the property of his ward when he perceives sound judgment in him. He is the one who establishes the ward's sound judgment by handing over his property to him.

Al-Lakhmi said: The one whom the father and the judge have appointed, his statement that the ward has become mature in judgment (rushd) is not accepted except after investigation, because of the corruption of people today and their lack of safety from colluding with wards so that they declare them mature and thus they permit them (to take their property) before that time.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The correct view regarding the guardians of our time is that one should not dispense with bringing them before the ruler (sultan) and establishing the maturity of judgment before him, because of what is known of the guardians' collusion so that the guardian declares his ward mature, and the ward releases the guardian from liability, owing to the ward's foolishness and his lack of discernment at that time. However, this has not become established practice, but the notaries (al-muwaththiqun) have considered it good to call witnesses to the establishment of the maturity of judgment of the ward placed under guardianship by his father, as a precaution. As for the guardian appointed by the judge, the opinions of the jurists differ concerning him, and the more sound view is that he may not declare his ward mature except after this has been established before the judge, and this is the practice that has been followed.

In my view, the address in such a passage is to the whole community, and its execution is undertaken by whoever is responsible for that domain among the rulers, like the manner of Qur'anic addresses directed at unspecified groups. There is no doubt that the one responsible for executing the affairs of wards and guardians is the judge, and the objective is achieved without hardship.

The verse clearly indicates that testing and assessing (al-ibtila' wal-istinas) precede puberty, up to the point of reaching the age (of marriage) — the limit that signals the end (of the period of testing). This is the known position of the school, although there is an opinion that no property is to be handed over to the ward for testing purposes except after puberty.

The verse is also explicit that the two conditions, puberty and rushd, must occur together; property is not to be handed over to the ward unless both are present. The general body of Muslim scholars agreed on this. Whoever is not rashid after reaching puberty remains under restriction (hajr). Only Abu Hanifa differed. He said: one waits seven years after puberty, and if rushd is not perceived in him, he is released from restriction. This contradicts the implication of the condition in His words, Exalted is He, "And if you perceive in them rushd," because Abu Hanifa does not accept the argument from the implication (mafhum) of a condition. It also contradicts analogy, since restriction exists only for the sake of foolishness and poor disposal of affairs; what effect would puberty have were it not that it is the presumed locus of rushd? And if rushd is not present together with puberty, what effect do seven years have on the completion of his rushd?

The verse also indicates, by way of analogy, that whoever becomes foolish while mature, or whose intellect is impaired due to an illness affecting his thinking, or due to senility from extreme old age, is to be placed under restriction, since the reason for restriction is established. Abu Hanifa also differed in this, saying: there is no restriction on a mature adult.

The ruling of the verse applies to males and females alike by way of predominance: an orphan girl who attains maturity with rushd has her property handed over to her.

The indefiniteness in His words "rushdan" is indefiniteness of type (tankir al-nau'iyya), meaning the intention is the type of the reality, because intellectual qualities are unified and have no individuals; their individuals are only notional, according to the multiplicity of their loci or the multiplicity of their objects. Thus the rushd of Zayd is other than the rushd of 'Amr, and rushd regarding property is other than rushd in governing the community and in calling to the truth. God, Exalted is He, said: "And the affair of Pharaoh was not rashid" (Hud: 97), and said of the people of Shu'ayb: "Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rashid" (Hud: 87). The reality of rushd is the orderliness of thought and the issuing of actions in accordance with it in an orderly manner. The listeners know that what is intended here is rushd in financial disposal, so the intention of the type is close to the intention of the genus; for this reason, the definite with the article of genus is equivalent to the indefinite. It is among the wonders that al-Jassas imagined that in the indefiniteness of "rushdan" there is evidence for Abu Hanifa regarding the non-requirement of good disposal and the sufficiency of puberty alone, on the claim that God stipulated some rushd, which is satisfied by reason, since reason is a form of rushd in general, and He did not stipulate all rushd. This is a weakness in Arabic usage: how can generality be possible in purely intellectual qualities, given that they have no individuals?

The property is here attributed to the pronoun of the orphans, because their ownership of it has become strongly established once they have become rashid, so that their disposal of it is no longer feared to waste what belongs to the relatives and to the rights of the whole community in property.

His words "and do not consume it extravagantly" (wa la ta'kulu-ha israfan) are coordinated with "and test the orphans" by virtue of what is connected to it in the speech, namely His words "And if you perceive in them rushd" etc. It is a confirmation of the prohibition against consuming the property of orphans, which was mentioned earlier in His words "And do not consume their property into your own," and an exposure of a stratagem they used to employ before the orphans reached their maturity (ashuddahum): that the guardians would hasten to consume the orphans' property before they prepared themselves to demand it from them and call them to account, so they would consume it by extravagance in spending. This was because most of their property at the time of revelation consisted of tangible things: livestock, dates, grain, and wool, which were not of a kind that is hidden or stored, nor of a kind in which transfer of ownership is difficult, like real estate. So consuming them meant using them up in the benefits of the guardians and their households. When the guardian found his ward's property, he would greedily consume it by lavishness in his expenditure, his clothing, his mounts, and honoring his companions, in ways he would not have spent his own wealth. This is the meaning expressed by "extravagance," for israf is excess in spending and indulgence in matters of pleasure.

"Israfan" is in the accusative either as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) or as a substitute for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). In either case, the purpose is not to restrict the prohibition of consumption to that, but rather to depict the ugliness of the manner of consumption.

"Al-bidar" is the verbal noun of badarahu, from the form mufa'ala of al-badr, which is haste toward a thing: badarahu meaning "hastened him," and baadarahu meaning "outpaced him." The mufa'ala here is intended to depict the condition of the guardians in their extravagance in consuming the property of their wards as they approach puberty, and the guardians' anticipation of the imminence of its time, by the state of two people who race each other to a goal, each one hastening towards it: the ward hastens to puberty to take his property, and the guardian hastens to consume it so that the orphan will find nothing to take from him, and so he goes to claim against him, and brings proofs, until he is unable to establish his rights. Thus His words "lest they grow up" (an yakbaru) stand in the position of the object of the verbal noun of the mufa'ala. "Yakbaru" with a fatha on the ba' is the imperfect of kabira, like 'alima, when he increases in age; whereas kabura with a damma on the ba' is when it becomes great in measure, and one says kabura 'alayhi al-amr with a damma on the ba', meaning it was hard upon him.

* * *

"And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat in accordance with what is reasonable."

This is coordinated with "and do not consume it extravagantly," etc. The thing established by it is His words "and do not consume their property into your own," so that the prohibition against consuming their property is confirmed. It is a specification of the general prohibition against consuming orphans' property in the two preceding verses, granting a concession for one kind of consumption: that a poor guardian may eat from his ward's property in accordance with what is reasonable. This returns to spending some of the orphan's property on his welfare, because if the guardian is not given what is reasonable for his poverty, his management for his sustenance distracts him from managing his ward's property.

The expression "al-ma'ruf" (what is reasonable) refers to what suits the guardian's condition and his orphan's according to times and places. The hadith of Abu Dawud points to this: "A man came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said, 'I am poor and have nothing.' He said, 'Eat from the property of your orphan, without extravagance, without squandering, and without accumulating wealth.'" In Sahih Muslim, from 'A'isha: the verse was revealed concerning the guardian of an orphan who, if he is in need, may eat from it in proportion to his labour, in accordance with what is reasonable. For this reason the Malikis said: the guardian takes an amount equal to the wage of his equivalent. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, and Mujahid said: God permitted only borrowing. 'Umar said: "I have placed myself with regard to God's property in the position of the guardian with regard to the orphan's property: if I am rich, I abstain; if I am in need, I eat in accordance with what is reasonable; and when I am well off, I repay." 'Ata' and Ibrahim said: there is no repayment obligation on the guardian if he becomes well off. Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, and Ibn 'Abbas, in one narration, said: its meaning is that he may drink the milk, eat from the dates, anoint the mangy camels from his herd, and mend the watering trough. It was said: that is only in cases of necessity, like eating carrion and pork; this is narrated from 'Ikrima, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Sha'bi, and it is the weakest of the opinions, because God attached the ruling to poverty, not to necessity, and attached it to the orphan's property; and necessity is not specific to the appropriation of the orphan's property but applies to all property. Abu Hanifa and his two companions said: he may take only when he travels on the orphan's business, taking his sustenance during the journey. They differed about whether the guardian appointed by the ruler is like the guardian appointed by the father. The majority said: they are equal, and this is the truth; and there is no specification in the verse.

Then they differed about whether the wealthy guardian takes the wage of his equivalent for his work, based on the disagreement over whether the command in His words "then let him abstain" is for obligation or recommendation. Whoever holds it to be obligation says: the wealthy guardian eats nothing at all. This is the view of everyone who prevents him from benefiting beyond the minimal and small amount, and they are the majority whose names have already been mentioned. It was said: the command is for recommendation, so if he wishes to take the wage of his equivalent, it is permissible for him if he has work and service; but if his work is merely checking on the orphan and overseeing him, then he has no wage.

All of this is based on the premise that the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). Some scholars said: it is abrogated by His words, Exalted is He, "Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly..." (4:10), and His words "And do not consume your property among yourselves in falsehood" (2:188). This was the view of Abu Yusuf, and it is the opinion of Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam.

Among the scholars there are those who took the verse in the way of interpretation (ta'wil). Rabi'a ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman said: the meaning is "whoever is wealthy," i.e., among the orphans, and "whoever is poor," likewise; and it is an explanation of how to spend on the orphans: the wealthy is given his sufficiency, and the poor is given in accordance with what is reasonable. This is far-fetched, for the verb istaʻaffa indicates moderation and abstaining from asking.

Al-Nakha'i said, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: whoever among the guardians is wealthy, let him abstain with his own wealth and not expand with his ward's property; and whoever is poor, let him economize on himself so that he does not extend his hand to his orphan's property. Al-Nahhas and al-Kiya al-Tabari in Ahkam al-Qur'an approved this.

* * *

"And when you hand over to them their property, then call witnesses against them; and God is sufficient as Reckoner."

This is a consequence of His words "then hand over to them their property": the command to call witnesses at the time of handing over, so that what the guardians deliver to their wards is made clear, so that it is possible to have recourse against them one day for what is discovered of what remained with the guardians. In it there is also a discharge for the guardians from the wards' claims afterwards. Sufficient for you as a legislation of this is its cutting off disputes.

The command here admits of both obligation and recommendation, and a group of scholars whose names are not specified held each view: if one considers the caution it contains regarding the right of the guardian, then calling witnesses is recommended.

Because it is his right, he may choose not to exercise it. Yet if one considers what calling witnesses achieves of the Shari'ah's objective of removing mutual strife (*tahaarruj*) and ending disputes, then calling witnesses would be obligatory, as in the earlier verse, ﴿When you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. The Shari'ah is concerned with documenting rights, because this is more upright for the order of transactions.

Whatever the case, the guardian (*wasi*) is not believed in his claim of having paid, except with evidence, according to Malik. Ibn al-Faras said: "Were it not that he is liable if the ward denies it, there would be no benefit in the command to document." Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) transmitted from al-Shafi'i agreement with Malik's view. However, al-Fakhr argued that the apparent meaning of the command is obligation, and this is a weak argument, because whether the command is for obligation or for recommendation has no bearing on the establishment of the ruling of liability. Liability is one of the effects of the declaratory address (*khitab al-wad'*, the address establishing legal causes and conditions), and its cause is the absence of witnessing. Obligation and recommendation, however, derive from the address of obligation (*khitab al-taklif*, the address imposing duties), and their consequences are punishment and reward.

Abu Hanifa said: he is believed on his oath, because he regarded him as trustworthy. It was also said: because he saw the command as recommendation. You have known that the interpretation of the command to call witnesses does not affect the ruling of liability.

He concluded with His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾ as a conclusion to all these rulings, because they are admonitions and exhortations, so He entrusted the matter in them to Allah's watchfulness. *Al-Hasib* means the one who calls to account. The *ba'* in *bi-Llahi* is extra, for emphasis.

**[Qur'an 4:7]** ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and the relatives leave, whether it is little or much, an obligatory share.﴾

This is a new independent statement (isti'naf ibtida'i, a fresh sentence that does not grammatically depend on what precedes it). It serves as a conclusion to the ruling on giving orphans their property, and as an introduction to the laws of inheritance (mawarith) found in His saying: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾ [4:11].

The connection between this verse and the preceding ones is that they had become accustomed to favouring the strong and the powerful with property and depriving the weak, keeping them dependent on their powerful kin so that they would remain under their authority. Guardians (al-awliya') would withhold the property of their wards (mahajir), and the eldest of a family would deprive his brothers of inheritance together with himself. Those weak ones would endure the deprivation, and would persuade the family to live in the shade of their relatives, because if they contested it, they would be driven away and deprived, and so they became a burden on people.

The people most affected by this were women, for they found themselves weak, feared the shame of loss (ar al-ay'ah), and guarded against the deviation of husbands, so they took the pleasure of their guardians as a reserve for themselves against the misfortunes of time. When Allah commanded them to give orphans their property, He followed it by commanding them to give men and women a share of what the parents and relatives leave.

Thus, giving the orphan his property is a means of ensuring that his share of what his parents and relatives leave reaches him, and the granting of inheritance to the relatives is an affirmation of their share of what the parents and relatives leave. Women were mentioned there as a preparation for the legislation of inheritance. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿And when the division takes place, relatives and orphans and the needy are present﴾ [4:8], for that suits inheritance, and does not suit the giving of orphans' property.

Undoubtedly, among the most important rulings of Islam is inheritance. The Arabs in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) used to bequeath their property by will to the chiefs of the tribes and to those who were attached to them by lineage, for good reputation, and to those bound to them by alliance (hilf), or by pride and affection. If they did not make a will, or left some of their property without a will, it would go to the sons of the deceased who were male. If he had no male sons, it is related that they would give it to a group of agnatic relatives ('asabah) from among brothers and paternal cousins, and his daughters would receive nothing. As for wives, they were inherited (mawruthat), not heirs (warithat).

In the Jahiliyyah they did not inherit through descent except when the children were male. Women had no inheritance, because they used to say: "Only he who thrusts with the spear and strikes with the sword inherits our property." If there were no male sons, the nearest of the 'asabah inherited: the father, then the brother, then the paternal uncle, and so on. They also inherited through adoption (tabanni), which is when a man takes another's son as his own son, so that between the adopter and the adopted all the rulings of fatherhood are established.

They also inherited through alliance (hilf), which is when two men desire mutual friendship (khullah) between them, so they contract to make their blood one and to inherit from each other. When Islam came, no change occurred in Mecca in the rulings of inheritance among the Muslims, because it was impossible to implement anything that contradicted the rulings of its inhabitants. Then, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated and most of the relatives of the emigrants (muhajirun) remained as polytheists in Mecca, inheritance became through emigration: the emigrant inherits from the emigrant; and through alliance, and through contract, and through the brotherhood which the Messenger (ﷺ), upon him be prayers and peace, established between the emigrants and the helpers (ansar). In this regard Allah revealed His saying: ﴿And for each We have made heirs (mawali) of what the parents and relatives leave﴾ [4:33], the verse in this same surah.

Allah legislated the obligation of the bequest (wasiyyah) to parents and near relatives through the verse in Surat al-Baqarah. Then the Muslims multiplied, and their fathers and sons joined them as believers, so Allah legislated inheritance by kinship and gave women portions in it. Thus He completed the word and perfected the blessing, and indicated that the wisdom of inheritance is the transfer of property to relatives by birth and what is below it.

His saying ﴿And for women there is a share of what the parents and relatives leave﴾ was the first granting of the right of inheritance to women among the Arabs.

Because this verse is like an introduction, it came with a summary of the right and the share in inheritance, and its detail followed it, for the purpose of preparing souls. The wisdom of this summarisation is the wisdom of revealing rulings that were to be abrogated (naskh) by heavier ones, so that souls might settle into them gradually.

Al-Wahidi, in Asbab al-Nuzul (Occasions of Revelation), and al-Tabari reported from 'Ikrimah, and one of them adds to the other, with the essence being: "Aws ibn Thabit al-Ansari died and left a wife called Umm Kuhhah. She came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'My husband was killed with you at Uhud, and these are his two daughters, and their paternal uncle has taken their property. What do you think, O Messenger of Allah? By Allah, they will never be married unless they have property.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah will decide concerning that.' Then Surat al-Nisa' was revealed, containing: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾ [4:11]." Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Call the woman and her companion to me,' and he said to their paternal uncle: 'Give them two-thirds, and give their mother one-eighth, and what remains is yours.'" It is also narrated that the two sons of his paternal uncle were Suwayd and 'Urfutah, and it is narrated that they were Qatadah and 'Urfujah. It is also narrated that "when the Prophet (ﷺ) summoned the uncle, or the two sons of the uncle, they said, or said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, we do not give to one who does not ride a horse, nor carry a burden, nor strike an enemy.' He said: 'Go away, or go away, until I see what Allah will bring about concerning them.' Then the verse ﴿For men there is a share﴾ was revealed." It is also narrated that "when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) sent to the guardian of the two daughters and said: 'Do not take away anything from their father's property, for Allah has made a share for them.'"

The word nasib (share) was discussed previously at His saying ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a share of the Scripture?﴾ [3:23] in Surat Al 'Imran.

His saying ﴿whether it is little or much﴾ is an explanation of "what they leave" (ma taraka), for the purpose of generalising what the parents and relatives leave, and an explicit statement that the right is attached to every part of the property, so that none of them may monopolise anything. A man in the Jahiliyyah used to give his sons from his property according to his inclination, as Nizar ibn Sa'd ibn 'Adnan bequeathed to his sons Mudar, Rabi'ah, Iyad and Anmar: he gave to Mudar all the red property (al-hamra'), gave to Rabi'ah the horse, gave to Iyad the servant, and gave to Anmar the donkey. He entrusted the distribution of the rest of his property among these four categories to al-Af'a al-Jurhumi in Najran, and they went to him, and he divided it among them. He is the one who gave rise to the proverb: "The staff is from the stick-tree" (inna al-'asa min al-'usayyah).

His saying "an obligatory share" (nasiban mafrudan) is a circumstantial clause (hal) related to "share" (nasib) in His saying "For men there is a share" and "for women there is a share." Where nasib is intended as a genus, the circumstantial clause related to it comes in the singular and is not made plural. So He did not say "two obligatory shares" in view of the mentioned shares being two, nor did He say "obligatory shares" in view of the mentioned share being distributed between men and women. Rather, the genus was observed, so the circumstantial clause came singular, and "obligatory" (mafrudan) is an adjective. The meaning of its being obligatory (mafrud) is that it is fixed in amount for each category of men and women, as He said in the following verse: ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾ [4:11]. This is the clearest evidence that the purpose of this verse is the legislation of inheritance.

[Page 248] [Page 249] [Page 250]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 8:

﴿And when the relatives, the orphans, and the needy are present at the division, provide them from it and speak to them words of kindness.﴾

This is a sentence conjoined to the sentence ﴿For men there is a share﴾ [al-Nisa': 7] and what follows it. It is a command to give a gift from the inherited wealth: the heirs are commanded to set aside a portion for those of their kindred who attend the division and who are not among those who have a right in the inheritance, those who by custom attend the gatherings where kin are settled.

His saying ﴿For men there is a share﴾ [al-Nisa': 7] and His saying ﴿and for women there is a share﴾ [al-Nisa': 7] imply something divided, so the definiteness in His saying ﴿the division﴾ is the definiteness of prior mention (ta'rif al-'ahd al-dhikri).

Page 251

The command in His saying ﴿provide them from it﴾ is understood by the majority of scholars (jumhur ahl al-'ilm) as recommendation (nadb) from the outset, since among obligatory charities there is nothing other than zakat, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Bedouin, when he asked him, "Is there anything else incumbent upon me?": "No, unless you volunteer." This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa, and the jurists of the cities (fuqaha' al-amsar), and they took the addressees of His saying ﴿provide them﴾ to be the heirs who are the owners of their own affairs. According to them the verse is muhkam (not abrogated). A group of scholars, however, took the command in His saying ﴿provide them﴾ to indicate obligation. Thus it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Zuhri, 'Ata', al-Hasan, and al-Sha'bi that this is a binding right upon the heirs who own their own affairs, and they are the ones addressed by His saying ﴿provide them﴾.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and Abu Salih that this was an obligation before the revelation of the verses of inheritance, and then it was abrogated by the verses of inheritance. The outcome of this view returns to agreement with the view of the majority of scholars.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Zayd ibn Aslam, that the command is directed at the owner of the property concerning the bequest, which was prescribed before the legislation of inheritance: it is obligatory upon him to place in his bequest a portion for those who attend his bequest from among the kindred, the orphans, and the needy, other than those to whom he bequeathed. This was abrogated along with the abrogation of the obligation of bequest. This view requires interpreting His saying ﴿the division﴾ as the determination of the amount due to each beneficiary.

It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the verse concerns inheritance itself, and that its intended purpose is His saying ﴿and speak to them words of kindness﴾. He said: His saying ﴿provide them from it﴾ is the inheritance itself.

His saying ﴿and speak to them words of kindness﴾ means: speak to non-heirs by telling them that God has apportioned the inheritances.

You have learned that the position of the verse is as a preface to the detailed explanation of the obligatory shares, and that what the majority of scholars have taken is the correct interpretation of the verse. The confusion in the transmission from Ibn 'Abbas concerning its interpretation is enough to weaken their other interpretations.

Page 252

The command that they say to them "words of kindness" means good speech, which is the opposite of the reprehensible (munkar), as a consolation to some of them for what they were deprived of from the property of the deceased, as they used to do in the Jahiliyya.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 9:

﴿And let those fear who, were they to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them fear God and let them speak words of rectitude.﴾

This is an admonition for everyone who was commanded, forbidden, warned or encouraged in the preceding verses concerning the property of orphans and the property of the weak among women and children. The admonition begins with a command to fear God, that is, to fear His punishment. It then follows with stirring the compassion of parents for their offspring, by having them place themselves in the position of those who were inherited from, whose property others have transgressed against, and by having them place their own offspring in the position of the descendants whose rights others have consumed. This admonition is built upon an analogy with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself." The stirring of compassion is further increased by the reminder that those wronged are weak creatures, through His saying ﴿weak﴾. Then it returns to the purpose from which it had digressed, which is the preservation of the property of orphans, by threatening with the punishment of the Hereafter the one who consumes it, after the threat of an evil state in this world. Thus there is understood from the speech an allusive threat that the share of their own children will be like what they have done to the children of others. The more apparent view is that the object of ﴿yakhsha﴾ [At-Tawbah: 18] has been omitted, so that the mind of the listener may go in estimating it in every possible direction, and so each listener considers, according to what is most important to him, what he fears might befall his offspring.

The phrase ﴿if they were to leave behind﴾ up to ﴿would be anxious for them﴾ is the relative clause (ṣilat al-mawṣūl) of the relative pronoun, and the clause ﴿would be anxious for them﴾ is the response (jawāb) of ﴿law﴾ (if/were).

The relative pronoun is used because, since the relative clause describes a hypothetical attribute, identifying people by it is apt, since the aim is to identify those whose condition is this. That is sufficient for identifying those addressed by the fear, since every listener knows the content of this relative clause, supposing it to be realized in him, for it is something everyone can imagine.

The reason for choosing ﴿law﴾ here from among the conditional particles is that it is the particle suitable for supposing a condition without addressing whether it is possible. Thus with it there holds a condition that is impossible to occur, one that is remote, and one that is possible. Those who have reached despair of childbearing, whether they have grown-up children or none at all, fall under the supposition of this condition, because if they had young children they would be anxious for them. As for those who have young children, their case is more apparent.

The verb ﴿tarakū﴾ is a past-tense verb used metaphorically to express being close to the occurrence of the event, by the relation of the beginning (of the act), as in His saying ﴿And those of you who die and leave behind wives, a bequest for their wives﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 240], and His saying ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 201], and the saying of the poet:

To a king for whose loss the mountains nearly departed, departing as the firm rocks depart from stone.

That is, the firm rocks came close to departing, since fear occurs only at the approach of death, not after death. So the meaning is: were they to come close to leaving behind weak offspring, they would be anxious for them from the evil guardians.

The one addressed by the command is whoever is fit for it among the categories mentioned earlier: among the guardians, and among the men who deprive women of their inheritance and deprive the young of their brothers or the children of their brothers and the children of their paternal uncles of the inheritance of their fathers. All of these are included in the command to fear and the warning by admonition. This address does not relate to the pronoun in His saying ﴿and provide for them from it﴾ [An-Nisa': 8], because that sentence came as a digression, and because its content has no connection with this warning.

In the verse there is that which moves all people to become angry for the sake of right against wrong, to take the hand of the evil guardians, and to guard the property of orphans and deliver the rights of the weak to them, for if they neglect that, there is the likelihood that the same will befall their own children and property, and that the strong among them will consume the weak. For the habit of evil makes people forget its ugliness and instills in souls a keenness for its practice. The explanation of ﴿dhurriyyah﴾ (offspring) has already been given at His saying ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 34] in Surat Ali 'Imran.

As for His saying ﴿So let them fear God and let them speak words of rectitude﴾, the command to piety is made a consequence of the command to fear, though they are two closely related commands, because the first command, when it is supported by proof, is regarded as already accomplished, so it is correct to make the second a consequence of it. The meaning is: so let them fear God regarding the property of people, and let them speak to them in a good manner.

[p. 253]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 10:

[Page 254]
﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly – they are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will [soon] burn in a Blaze.﴾

This is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'taridha) that serves to reiterate the warning against consuming the property of orphans. It was brought about by the occasion of discussing the division of the property of the deceased, because the heirs very often include orphans, given that men marry many times over the course of their lives; thus it is rare for a deceased person to leave no young heirs. This indicates the great concern of the Lawgiver (al-Shari') with this matter, so the discourse returned to it on this occasion.

His saying "unjustly" (zulman) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "they consume," restricting the meaning so as to exclude the consumption that is permitted, such as in His saying ﴿And whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is reasonable﴾ [al-Nisa': 6]. It is thus like His saying ﴿O you who believe, do not consume one another's property unjustly (bil-batil)﴾ [al-Nisa': 29].

Then it is permissible that "fire" in His saying ﴿they are only consuming fire into their bellies﴾ is intended to mean the Fire of Hell, as is most common in the Qur'an. In that case, the verb "they consume" governing "fire" is to be understood as "they consume that which leads them to the Fire." The word "fire" is then used figuratively by way of metonymy (majaz mursal), through the relation of the cause-and-effect ( 'alaqa al-awwal aw al-sababiyya), meaning: that which leads them to the torment of Hell. The meaning is that when they consume the property of orphans, they have consumed that which leads them to Hell.

On this basis, the conjunction of the clause ﴿and they will burn in a Blaze﴾ is a conjunction of equivalence (ataf murádif) to the meaning of the clause ﴿they consume fire in their bellies﴾.

It is also permissible that the name "fire" is used metaphorically for "pain," meaning the causes of pain, in which case it is a threat of worldly punishment; or that it is used metaphorically for "destruction," since the nature of fire is to consume whatever it touches. The meaning is: they only take property which is the cause of calamities that befall them in their persons and their wealth, like fire when it draws near to someone, causing him pain and destroying his goods. In this case it is a threat of calamities in this world, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Allah deprives usury of blessing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276]. The conjunction of the clause ﴿and they will burn in a Blaze﴾ then follows the apparent sense of conjunction, which requires a difference between the two conjoined elements: the first clause is a threat of punishment in this world, and the second clause is a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter.

[Page 255]
The mention of "in their bellies" under both meanings is merely an imaginative depiction (takhyil) and a supporting elaboration (tarshih) for the metaphor of "they consume" in the sense of "they take" and "they seize control."

The sin (sin) in "sa-yaslawna" is the particle of futurity (harf tanfis), i.e., of the future (istiqbal). That is, it enters upon the imperfect verb and makes it purely future, whether the future is near or distant. It is synonymous with "sawfa." It is said that "sawfa" has a wider scope of time. In the context of a promise, both indicate the certainty of the promise, and likewise of a threat.

"Yaslawna" is the imperfect of "saliya" (like "radiya"), when one endures the heat of fire intensely, as here. It is said: "saliya bil-nar." The omission of the preposition with the verb "saliya" and the noun following it being put in the accusative by the removal of the governing particle is common. The poet Humayd ibn Thawr said:

"You do not warm yourself at the fire except at a fragrant brazier, with aloeswood and its sticks, which have been broken up."

This is the regular usage found in the Qur'an.

The Jumhur (majority) read "wa-sa-yaslawna" with a fatha on the ya' (taḥtiyya), as the imperfect of "saliya." Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with a damma on the ya', as the imperfect of "aslahu" (to cause to burn), in the passive voice.

"Sa'ir" means the kindled fire, i.e., the blazing one. It is a form (fa'il) in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), built on the pattern of the bare form, and it derives from the doubled-root (mudá'af) class, just as "sami'" is built from "asma'" and "hakim" from "ahkam."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, the like of the share of two females. And if there are only daughters, two or more, for them is two-thirds of what he leaves; and if there is only one, for her is half.﴾

The verse ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ stands in the position of explanation and detail for His saying ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave﴾ [al-Nisa': 7]. This purpose, for which His saying "for men is a share" etc. serves as an introduction, is why the clause ﴿instructs you﴾ is separated (from what precedes), because both positions require separation.

Among the concern for these rulings is that their legislation is introduced with His saying ﴿instructs﴾, because a wasiyyah (bequest, injunction) is the command to do what benefits the one commanded, and it expresses the concern of the one commanding because of the great good in it. For this reason, what a person entrusts concerning his children, his property and his person after death is called a wasiyyah.

Many reports have been transmitted concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse. In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "I fell ill, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr visited me in Banu Salamah. They found me unconscious, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked for water, performed ablution, then sprinkled some of it on me, and I regained consciousness. I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, how should I deal with my property?' Then ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ was revealed."

Al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah related, on the authority of Jabir, who said: "The wife of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' came to the Messenger of Allah and said, 'Sa'd has died and left two daughters and his brother. His brother took hold of what Sa'd left.' And women are married on account of their property. He did not answer her at that session. Then she came to him again and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, the two daughters of Sa'd.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Call his brother to me.' He came, and he said, 'Give his two daughters two-thirds, his wife one-eighth, and you have what remains.' And the verse of inheritance was revealed."

In these verses Allah has explained the shares of the heirs, and has tied all inheritance to close kinship, whether it is natural, which is lineage (nasab), or near to the natural, which is the bond of marriage (ʿiṣmat al-zawjiyyah), because the male's desire for the female is natural, and her being this specific woman is attained through familiarity, which arises from natural inclination. He specified the sharers of the shares but did not specify the destination of the property after the sharers have been given their shares, and that is because He left it according to what was customary among them before Islam, namely that the nearest of the 'asabah (agnatic residuaries) take possession of the deceased's property. This purpose is explained by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give the shares to their owners, and what remains goes to the nearest male relative."

Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He, after this: ﴿If he has no child and his parents inherit from him, then to his mother is a third﴾? He did not specify the father's share, because in that state the father has returned to his established condition, which is taking the remainder of the property, so there was need to mention the mother's share.

Allah began with the inheritance of the sons, because they are the closest of people.

The word awlad is the plural of walad on the pattern fa'al, like asad and wathan, and there is a dialect form wild with a kasrah on the waw and sukun on the lam, as though it is then a fi'l in the sense of maf'ul, like dhibh and silkh. Walad is a term for a son, whether male or female, and it is applied to the singular and to the plural of children; what occurs in the Qur'an is in the sense of the singular, and its plural is awlad.

Here "fi" (in) is for metaphorical containment: the bequest is treated as though it is contained within the matter of the children, because of the strength of its connection to them, like the connection of the contained to the container. Its genitive is elided, and the mudaf ilayhi (the noun it is attached to) takes its place, since it is evident that the persons of the children cannot serve as a container for a bequest. So it is necessary to estimate an elided mudaf by way of the implication required by the context (dalalat al-iqtida'), and its estimate is: "concerning the inheritance of your children." The context indicates the estimated word, in the manner of ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. He thus made the bequest contained in this matter because of the strength of its connection to it and its encompassing of it.

The clause ﴿for the male, the like of the share of two females﴾ explains the clause ﴿instructs you﴾, because its content is the meaning of the content of the bequest. It is thus like the explanation in His saying, ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120]. The placing of the predicate before the subject in this clause serves to alert from the outset that the male now has a partner in inheritance, namely the female, because they had no prior knowledge of this, since the males used to take the entire inherited property and females had no share, as was mentioned just before in the explanation of His saying ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave﴾ [al-Nisa': 7].

In His saying ﴿for the male, the like of the share of two females﴾, He made the share of the two females the measure by which the male's share is determined. No share had previously been specified for two females so that it could be used as a measure, so it is known that the intended meaning is that the male's share among children is double the female's share. This meaning could have been expressed by saying "for the female, half the share of a male," or "for the two females, the like of a male's share," since the only aim is to state the doubling. But this expression was chosen for a subtle reason: to indicate that the female's share has, in the view of the Law, become more important than the male's share, since she was neglected among the people of ignorance; so Islam proclaims her share at the very first thing that strikes the ears. It is known that the division of property is by reckoning the number of sons and daughters.

His saying ﴿And if they are women, two or more﴾ etc.: the referent of the pronoun is the word awlad, which is the plural of walad. It is not feminine in its wording or in its meaning, since it is applicable to both male and female; but when its referent here is women specifically, the pronoun was returned to it in the feminine.

The meaning of ﴿two or more﴾ is more than two. Among the meanings of fawq is increase in number, and the origin of this is metaphorical, then it became so common that it became like a literal meaning. The verse is explicit that two-thirds are given only to three daughters or more, because the division of shares does not move from one quantity to a greater one except when the one entitled to the first quantity has ended.

The description with ﴿two or more﴾ implies by inference that two daughters do not receive two-thirds. Then He added ﴿And if there is only one, for her is half﴾, so the inheritance of two daughters standing alone was not stated explicitly in the verse, and the majority of scholars attached it to the case of three, because they are more than one. The best explanation of this is what the judge Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: if a daughter takes one-third together with her brother when he stands alone, then it is more fitting that she takes one-third together with her sister, meaning that each of the two daughters is paired with her other sister, so her share with a female sister cannot be less than her share with a male brother, since the male is more entitled to the full portion of his share. The verifying scholars after him adopted this, and it may have been attributed to some of those who adopted it. Others gave a rationale and explanation: that Allah made the two sisters, when standing alone, entitled to two-thirds, so two daughters should not be less than them. Ibn 'Abbas said: for two daughters is half, like one daughter; and it seems he did not see the inheritance of the two as anything more than sharing in the half as the meaning of the verse, and if that were intended, He would not have said ﴿two or more﴾.

Some have considered the word fawq to be superfluous, and compared it with His saying ﴿strike above the necks﴾ [al-Anfal: 12].

But there is a great difference between fawq used with numerals and fawq meaning the place of an action. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: People have agreed in the cities and the ages that two daughters receive two-thirds, meaning that this consensus rests upon a sunnah they knew. Al-Qurtubi rejected the claim of consensus, on the ground that Ibn 'Abbas is authentically reported to have given two daughters a half. I say: perhaps the consensus was formed after Ibn 'Abbas gave two daughters a half, since the breaking of consensus by the dissent of one person whose view is disputed is not decisive. As for the hadith of the wife of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' mentioned above, it is not suitable for deciding this dispute, because in its transmission there is disagreement as to whether he left two daughters or three.

His saying ﴿fa-lahunna﴾ (for them): the pronoun was returned to nisa', and what is meant is what applies to two women as well, by giving the plural precedence over the dual, relying on the context.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa-in kanat wahidatan﴾ with the accusative of wahidatan, taking it as the predicate of kanat, and the subject of kanat is a pronoun referring to what is indicated by His saying ﴿concerning your children﴾, from the singular of walad, meaning: if the child is one daughter. Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read it with the nominative, taking kana as complete (taamma), and the estimate is: "if one daughter is found," according to what is indicated by His saying ﴿if they are women﴾.

The form awladikum is a form of generality, because awlad is a plural definite by annexation, and a plural definite by annexation is among the forms of generality. This generality is specified by four things:

First: the Prophet (ﷺ) is excluded from it according to the Ahl al-Sunnah, because of what Abu Bakr narrated from him that he said: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab agreed with him, as did all the Companions and the Mothers of the Believers. It is authentically reported that 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, agreed with it in the assembly of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and those Companions present, as in the two Sahihs.

Second: difference of religion, Islam and other than Islam. The Muslims have agreed that a Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, nor a disbeliever from a Muslim.

Third: the intentional killer does not inherit from the one he killed in anything.

Fourth: the one who kills by mistake does not inherit anything from the blood-money.

* * *

﴿And for his parents, to each of them is a sixth of what he leaves, if he has a child; but if he has no child and his parents inherit from him, then to his mother is a third; and if he has siblings, then to his mother is a sixth.﴾

The singular pronoun refers to the deceased understood from His saying ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾, since it has been established that the discourse concerns the division of the deceased's property. The discourse came by way of general statement and detail, to serve as a heading, which is why He did not say "for each of his parents a sixth," and it is like His earlier saying ﴿concerning your children, for the male, the like of the share of two females﴾.

His saying ﴿and his parents inherit from him﴾ He added in order to indicate restriction, that is: no one other than them, so that it is known from His saying ﴿then to his mother is a third﴾ that the father has two-thirds. If there is with the mother a sharer of a fixed share who is not excluded, he takes his fixed share along with her, and she takes hers. They differed concerning a wife with two parents, and a husband with two parents: Ibn 'Abbas said: the husband or wife receives their fixed share, and the mother receives a third of what remains, and what remains goes to the father, by analogy with the rule of plurality of sharers. Zayd ibn Thabit said: one of the spouses receives their fixed share, and the mother receives a third of what remains, and what remains goes to the father, lest the mother take more than the father in the case of a husband with two parents. Majority of scholars followed the view of Zayd. In the Sunan of Ibn Abi Shaybah it is reported that Ibn 'Abbas sent to Zayd: "Where do you find in the Book of Allah a third of what remains?" Zayd replied: "You are a man who speaks by his opinion, and I speak by my opinion."

It is known that the father takes two-thirds with the mother, and his mention was left out because the basis of the fara'id is that what remains without a fixed share returns to the principal residuary (asl al-'isabah) among the Arabs.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿fa-li-ummihi﴾ with a damma on the hamzah of ummihi, and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasrah on the hamzah, following the kasrah of the lam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 11 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying, ﴿But if he has brothers, then for his mother is a sixth﴾, meaning: if there are brothers alongside the two parents. This is explicit that brothers exclude the mother (hajb), moving her from a third to a sixth. The term mentioned in the verse is in the plural form, so it indicates that only a group of brothers, three or more, male or mixed, moves her to a sixth. There has been disagreement regarding fewer than a group, and whether the brothers are female. The majority (al-Jumhur) said that two brothers exclude the mother, and so do two sisters. Ibn 'Abbas differed from them, taking the apparent meaning of the verse. As for a single brother or a single sister, they do not exclude the mother, and God knows best the ruling in that. They differed concerning the sixth from which the brothers exclude the mother: does the brothers take it, or does the father take it? Ibn 'Abbas - may Allah be pleased with him - said the first, and it is more apparent. The majority said the second, on the basis that the excluder may himself be excluded. In any case, God has given the brothers a share alongside the presence of both parents in a specific situation. Had there been brothers with the mother and no father, the mother would have had a sixth and the brothers the remainder of the estate by consensus, and perhaps this supports Ibn 'Abbas.

* * *

﴿after bequest he makes or debt﴾.
The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal); it is a stable adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqarr), and it is a restriction returning to the preceding sentences: that is, you divide the property according to those shares, each receiving his share in the state of being after a bequest or a debt.

The phrase ﴿after a bequest he makes or debt﴾ [al-Nisa’: 12] came after mentioning two categories of the obligatory shares: the shares of the children, and the shares of the parents, because these two categories are like a single category, since their cause is the direct line of lineage. The purpose here is to draw attention to the importance of the bequest and its precedence. The debt was mentioned after it to complete what must be given priority over inheritance, with the listeners knowing that debt also precedes bequest, because it is a prior right over the deceased's property, since the debtor owns from his property only what exceeds his creditor's debt. So the placement of "or debt" is that of a caveat, and for this concern God repeated this restriction four times in these verses.

He described the bequest by the clause ﴿he makes﴾ lest it be assumed that what is meant is the bequest that was obligatory before the legislation of the shares, which is the one in His saying ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is the bequest for parents and relatives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. The majority read ﴿yuwṣī bihā﴾ in both places in this verse with a kasra on the ṣād (yūṣī), and the pronoun refers to something known from the context, namely the deceased, just as the pronoun in "what he left" refers to him. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim also read it in both places with a fatha on the ṣād (yūṣā), making the verb passive, indicating the agent: yūṣā bihā, meaning a testator makes it.

* * *

﴿Your fathers and your sons, you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit. An obligation from Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

He concluded these shares concerning the children and parents, which are the roots of the shares, with His saying ﴿Your fathers and your sons﴾ and so on. Either they are the subject, placed first for emphasis, so that the statement settles in the listener's mind, as he gives full attention upon hearing the subject mentioned; or you make them two predicates of an elided subject, according to the ellipsis recognized by the scholars of rhetoric (ʿilm al-maʿani) through standard usage, which occurs when a topic is mentioned and then the predicate about it is to be collected, as in the words of the poet:

A youth not hidden of wealth from his friend, nor one who displays complaint when the sandal slips.

After his saying:

I will thank 'Amr if my death draws near, favors he did not bestow with reproach, however great they were.

That is: those mentioned, your fathers and your sons, there is no doubt about that. Then He said ﴿you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾. This is either a new sentence (mubtada') or a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning that they are not equal in benefiting you; they differ in a way that follows the variation of natural affection among people, and follows dutifulness and the degree of variation in needs. Many a man is never in need of his parents or his children benefiting him, while many needs may arise in both states, or may not arise. They vary in this respect, which was the criterion the people of the Jahiliyyah relied upon in dividing their property. They relied on unreliable and unfixed circumstances, and therefore God said ﴿you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾. The law of Islam attached the shares to what does not admit variation, namely fatherhood and sonship, and so it fixed the share for them in view of their connection, which necessitates that they have the greater right to the property of the children or the parents.

The concluding statement ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ is of clear relevance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 12:

﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, then for you is a fourth of what they leave, after any bequest they make or debt. And for them is a fourth of what you leave, if you have no child. But if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt.﴾

Page 263

This is the prescribed share of inheritance whose cause is the marital bond (al-'ismah), and Allah has given it its right, which had been neglected in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance), when they did not let spouses inherit from each other. As for the husband, he did not inherit from his wife, because if she had no children by him, then upon her death he had become like a stranger to her kin of fathers, brothers and paternal uncles. And if she had children, her children were more entitled to her inheritance if they were adults; but if they were minors, her relatives would take their property and dispose of it. As for the woman, she did not inherit from her husband; rather she was counted as an inheritable possession of his, over which his heirs had control, as will come in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ [al-Nisa': 19]. Thus Allah in this verse honoured the bond of marriage, which He described as a solemn covenant in His saying: ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾ [al-Nisa': 21].

The plural in "azwajukum" and in His saying ﴿what you leave﴾ is like the plural in "the children" and "the parents": it is meant to indicate the multiplicity of individual heirs from among the community. Here the community has agreed that when a man has several wives, they share the quarter or the eighth without any increase for them, because the multiplicity of wives is in the hand of the owner of the property, so their multiplicity would be a means of causing harm to the other heirs. This is unlike the multiplicity of daughters and sisters, for in that case the owner of the property has no choice. The meaning is: for each one of you is half of what each of his wives leaves; and likewise His saying ﴿then for you is a fourth of what they leave﴾.

And His saying ﴿and for them is a fourth of what you leave﴾ means: for all of them together is a fourth of what their husband leaves. Likewise His saying ﴿then for them is an eighth of what you leave﴾, and this is an elegant economy which the conciseness of the speech indicates.

The prescription for spouses is followed by mention of ﴿after any bequest they make or debt﴾, lest someone suppose that they are prevented from making bequests or incurring debts, as was the situation in the time of Jahiliyyah. As for mentioning this clause right after the mention of women's inheritance from their men, it follows the method used throughout these verses, namely that each category of the shares is followed by a notice that it is not deserved except after the execution of the bequest and the settlement of the debt.

* * *

﴿And if a man leaves an inheritance as kalalah, or a woman, and he has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that, they are partners in a third, after any bequest he makes or debt.﴾

Page 264

After having explained the inheritance of those with children or parents, and detailed its circumstances to the extent of the inheritance of spouses, he now moves to the inheritance of one who has neither child nor parent, namely the one who is inherited as kalalah; and for this reason it is set against the inheritance of the two parents.

Al-kalalah is a noun derived from al-kalal, which means weariness and exhaustion. Al-A'sha said:

So I swore I would not grieve for her from kalalah, nor from a close one, until I meet Muhammad.

It is a verbal noun (ism masdar) which is neither dualized nor pluralized.

The Arabs described by kalalah the kinship other than direct kinship, as if they regarded its connection to the lineage of a near relative as remote, so they applied kalalah to it by way of metaphor, and they cited in support the saying of one whom they did not name:

For the father of a man is more protective of him, and the client of kalalah is not angered.

Then they applied it to the inheritance of the distant relative. I think that this is a term of the Qur'an, since I have not seen it in the speech of the Arabs except after the revelation of the verse. Al-Farazdaq said:

You inherited the lance of glory, not from kalalah, from the two sons of Manaf, 'Abd Shams and Hashim.

And from this comes their saying: he inherited glory, not from kalalah. The Companions counted the meaning of kalalah here among the difficult points of the Qur'an, to the extent that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Three things, that the Messenger of Allah would have explained them to me, are dearer to me than the world: the kalalah, usury, and the caliphate." Abu Bakr said: "I will say about it my opinion; if it is correct, it is from Allah, and if it is wrong, it is from me and from Satan, and Allah is free of it: kalalah is what remains apart from the child and the parent." This is the saying of 'Umar, 'Ali, and Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Zuhri, Qatadah and al-Sha'bi held it, and it is the view of the majority; consensus has been reported upon it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that kalalah is one who has no child, even if he has a parent; and this is attributed to Abu Bakr and 'Umar as well, though they later retracted it. It may be supported by the apparent meaning of the verse at the end of the surah: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning kalalah: if a man dies leaving no child﴾ [al-Nisa': 176]. The context of the verse favours what the majority held, because its mention after the inheritance of children and parents indicates that it is a condition different from the two conditions.

Page 265

The phrase ﴿kalalah﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿yurath﴾, which refers to the heir, meaning: a relative who is not a direct relative, because kalalah may be applied as a description to both kinds of relative.

His saying ﴿or a woman﴾ is conjoined to ﴿a man﴾, which is the subject (ism) of kana, so the conjoined word shares with the word it is conjoined to the predicate of kana, since a subject cannot exist without a predicate in the case of its deficiency.

His saying ﴿and he has a brother or a sister﴾: according to the majority's view on the meaning of kalalah, it is necessary that what is meant by them is the brother and sister from the mother alone, because if the deceased has neither child nor parent, and we say he has a brother or a sister, and we assign to each of them a sixth, we know by a ruling resembling the implication of necessity (dalalat al-iqtida') that they are the brother and sister from the mother, for since their share is at most a third, there remain two-thirds. If the brother and sister were full siblings or consanguine siblings, it would imply that they took the smaller part of the property and the rest was left to others; and would another be closer than them? Thus it is determined that the brother and sister meant are those from the mother alone, so that the two-thirds go to the full brothers, or the paternal uncles, or the sons of paternal uncles. By this Allah established a share for the maternal siblings, nullifying what the people of Jahiliyyah had done of disregarding the maternal side altogether, since it was the side of women; and there was no need to draw attention to the fate of the rest of the property, because of what we have already explained a little earlier, that Allah the Exalted left the matter of the residuary heirs to what is customary among those to whom the Qur'an was revealed.

On the view of Ibn 'Abbas in explaining kalalah, it is not necessary that the brother and sister meant are those from the mother; for a share of two-thirds may be assigned to full brothers to a stronger residuary, namely the father, in some cases of kalalah. Nonetheless, Ibn 'Abbas agreed with the majority that the brother and sister meant are those from the mother, and the reason for this in his view was that Allah stated kalalah without qualification, while there may be no father in it; so if the brother and sister meant were full or consanguine siblings, we would give them the third in the absence of the father, and most of the property would remain for someone lower than the brothers in residuary status. This, as I see it, is what led the rest of the Companions and jurists to interpret the brother and sister as those from the mother. Allah the Exalted mentioned kalalah at the end of the surah in another form, which we shall address.

* * *

Page 266

﴿not causing harm; a bequest from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾

﴿not causing harm﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun in ﴿yusa﴾ (is bequeathed), the last one; and since the verb ﴿yusa﴾ is repeated, it is a circumstantial qualifier from the pronouns of its counterparts.

As for ﴿muḍārr﴾, the most apparent view is that it is an active participle, with the first doubled ra' read with a kasra, meaning: not causing harm to his heirs by multiplying bequests. It is a prohibition against intending harm to the heirs through one's bequest. The harm, from the standpoint of the Shari'ah, is defined as the testator exceeding a third of his property in his bequest; the Prophet ﷺ defined it by his saying to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "A third, and a third is much." Among it is also what results from the testator's intention, in his bequest, to harm the heir without seeking nearness to Allah by his bequest; and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿not causing harm﴾. Since the intention of the testator and his purpose of causing harm cannot be known, it is left to his religion and the fear of his Lord; but if something clearly shows his intention to cause harm, then the bequest is to be considered void, because the saying ﴿not causing harm﴾ is a prohibition against harm, and a prohibition implies the corruption of what is prohibited.

This qualifier must necessarily apply to the absolute statements in the three preceding verses, from His saying ﴿after any bequest﴾ etc., because these absolute statements share the same ruling and cause. The absolute among them is therefore understood in light of the restricted, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence.

The jurists have derived from this verse the ruling on the case of a giver who intends, through his gift, to harm his heir, whether in a bequest or in other gifts; and the matter is assumed in the case of bequest specifically. Ibn 'Atiyyah reported from the school of Malik and Ibn al-Qasim that intending harm within the third does not invalidate the bequest, because the third is a right which Allah granted to him, so he has freedom of disposal over it. Ibn 'Arafah disputed this in his commentary, arguing that what is in the second Wasaya of the Mudawwanah clearly states that intending harm necessitates rejecting the bequest. Ibn 'Arafah's argument is firm. The well-known view of Ibn al-Qasim is that the bequest is rejected when intent to harm is manifest. However, Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam does not see harm as having effect. In Ibn Najji's commentary on the Tahdhib of the Mudawwanah, it is stated that intending harm through a bequest of less than a third does not nullify the bequest according to the sound view, and this is the fatwa.

His saying ﴿wasiyyatan﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) which came as a substitute for its verb, and the implied meaning is:

Page 267

Allah enjoins you concerning that as a bequest from Him. It is thus a conclusion to the rulings, matching how they began with His saying ﴿Allah enjoins you﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]; and this is the reversal of the last to match the first (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr).

His saying ﴿and Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil). The mention of the attributes of knowledge and forbearance here is appropriate because the preceding rulings abolish many of the rulings of the Jahiliyyah, which had established their inheritances on a basis arising from ignorance and harshness. Depriving the daughter and the maternal brother of inheritance is ignorance of the fact that the kinship through the mother is equivalent to the kinship through the father; this and similar things are ignorance, and their depriving young children of inheritance is harshness on their part.

The verses in this surah have explained inheritance and its shares among the people of the roots of lineage, its branches and its extended kin, and the bond of marriage; and they have been silent about what lies beyond that, namely the agnatic residuaries, the dhawu al-arham (distant kin), the clients by manumission, and the clients by alliance. The Exalted's saying ﴿and the kinsmen are closer to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 75] in Surat al-Anfal, and His saying ﴿and the kinsmen are closer to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6] in Surat al-Ahzab, have alluded to this, and from it many jurists derived the inheritance of dhawu al-arham. His saying shortly to come, ﴿And for each We have appointed heirs to what the parents and the nearest kin leave, and those with whom your oaths have bound you, give them their share﴾ [al-Nisa': 33], has alluded to what may be derived from it in general concerning inheritance by clientship, as we shall explain. The Prophet ﷺ explained the inheritance of the agnatic residuaries by what the people of the Sahih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Give the fixed shares to their people, and what remains is for the nearest male." And what the five (compilers) other than al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayrah: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I am closer to the believers than their own selves. Whoever dies and leaves property, his property is for the clients of the agnatic residuaries; and whoever leaves debts or dependants, I am his guardian." We shall elaborate on this in its appropriate places.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 13–14:**

﴿Those are the limits of Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him into a Fire, abiding therein forever, and for him is a humiliating punishment.﴾

Page 268

The reference is to the meanings and sentences mentioned earlier.

*Hudud* (limits) is the plural of *hadd*, which is the boundary of a place that distinguishes it from another place in such a way that it prevents crossing it. The word *hudud* is used here figuratively, in the sense of the actions whose violation is not permitted, by way of *tamthil* (figurative illustration).

The meaning of ﴿whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ is that he follows His limits, as indicated by His saying in contrast to it, ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾.

His saying ﴿abiding therein﴾ uses *khulud* (abiding forever) in the sense of a long duration. Alternatively, what is intended by disobedience to Allah and His Messenger is the most complete disobedience, which is rejecting faith, because the people at that time had already entered into faith and rejected disbelief, so they were eager to act upon the commandments of Islam. Only one whose faith is not firm opposes that, except one who repents.

Perhaps His saying ﴿and for him is a humiliating punishment﴾ is a *taqsim* (division), because disobedience has types: among it is what necessitates eternal abiding, and among it is what necessitates the humiliating punishment. The indication of this is that the conjunction *'atf* (coordination) of ﴿and for him is a humiliating punishment﴾ upon the abiding in the Fire would not be needed if it were not intended as a division; otherwise it would have to be treated as an added emphasis. Or you may say that the focus of the conjunction is describing it as *muhin* (humiliating), because the Arabs are proud, unwilling to bear oppression, and high-spirited, so they may dread humiliation more than they dread the punishment of the Fire. Among the proverbs transmitted in their tales is: "The Fire, but not shame." And in the book *al-Adab* (Kitab al-Adab), in the second half of one of its verses: "The free man endures for fear of shame what he endures for fear of the Fire."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read *nudkhiluhu* (We will admit him) in both places here with *nun al-'azama* (the royal "we"). The majority read it with *ya' al-ghayba* (the third-person "ya"), and the pronoun refers back to the Name of Majesty (Allah).
