The pronoun in *so confine them* is specific to those in authority, because the confinement mentioned is imprisonment, and it is a ruling that only judges undertake, and they are the ones who examine the acceptance of testimony. So this is a general wording that intends a specific meaning.

This verse is the basis for the requirement of four witnesses for testimony regarding zinā, and this was established by the verse of Sūrat al-Nūr.

What is required in the testimony that necessitates confinement in houses is the same as what is required in testimony for zinā for the implementation of the hadd (prescribed punishment), with no difference.

*[Page 270]*

The intended meaning of "houses" is the houses that those in authority designate for this purpose. It is not intended that they be confined in their own houses; rather they leave their houses for other houses, unless the house of the imprisoned woman is converted into a place of confinement under the supervision and guard of the judge. This meaning is indicated by God's saying in the verse of Sūrat al-Ṭalāq concerning the waiting period: ﴿Do not turn them out of their houses, nor should they leave, unless they commit a clear immorality﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1].

The meaning of ﴿takes them in death﴾ is "demands them." It is said: "So-and-so fulfilled his right from so-and-so," meaning he took his due in full. The Arabs imagine life as divided into parts. Days, time and death extract it from its owner in installments until death takes it entirely. Ṭarafa said:

*I see life as a treasure diminishing every night, and the days do not diminish it, yet life is exhausted.*

Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī said:

*When a day and a night demand a man, a thing that never tires of demanding demands him.*

Therefore they say: "So-and-so died" in the passive voice, meaning his life was fulfilled. God made death the one who demands people's lives, according to their usage in expression, and although death is the effect of a person's last breath, the word tawaffā in this verse is used in its original, literal linguistic meaning.

The meaning of ﴿or God makes for them a way﴾ is another ruling. The word sabīl is used metaphorically for a clear matter, meaning a fitting punishment, likening it to the paved main road. In this there is an indication that their confinement in houses is a temporary restraint which will be followed by a conclusive ruling for what people find in their souls of anger against them for what they have done.

His saying ﴿those women who commit grave immorality﴾ includes all women who commit grave immorality, whether they are married or otherwise.

As for His saying ﴿and the two men who commit it﴾, it requires two categories of males, since it is the dual of alladhī, which is the relative pronoun for the masculine. It is contrasted with the relative pronoun for women in His saying ﴿those women who commit grave immorality﴾. There is no doubt that by alladhāni is meant two categories of men: the married category and the unmarried category among them. Ibn 'Abbās in the narration of Mujāhid interpreted it this way, and this is the correct interpretation of the verse, by which a clear meaning is established that is neither overlapping nor repeated. The indication of the two categories of male fornicators is to guard against seeking an excuse for the unmarried. It is possible that the phrase refers to two different categories, namely men and women, in the manner of the figure of speech of predominance (taghlīb) which is common in such usage. This is the interpretation of al-Suddī and Qatāda. According to the first view, the verse has made for women a single punishment for zinā, namely the punishment of confinement in houses, and for men a punishment for zinā, namely harm, whether they are married to wives or unmarried, who are the bachelors. According to the second view, it has made for women two punishments: a punishment specific to them, namely confinement, and a punishment applied to them like the punishment of men, namely harm, so confinement is for them together with the punishment of harm. On both views, it is understood that the married and the unmarried of the two categories are equal in both punishments. As for the men, this is by the implication of the dual of the relative pronoun, meaning two categories. As for the women, it is by the implication of the generality of the form *your women*.

The accusative pronoun in His saying *they commit it* (yaʾtiyānihā) refers to the grave immorality mentioned, which is zinā. There is no need to consider the words of anyone who imagines otherwise. Harm (adhā) is pain that is not severe in action, such as a non-severe beating, and pain by speech, such as insult and reproach. So it is more general than flogging, and the verse mentioned it in general terms, so it is left to the judgment of the ruler.

The imams of Islam have differed regarding how these two punishments are derived from this verse. Ibn 'Abbās and Mujāhid said: ﴿those women who commit grave immorality﴾ is general for women alone, so it includes every woman in all circumstances, whether virgin or previously married. His saying *the two* (alladhāni) is a dual meaning two kinds of men, namely the married and the virgin. So this implies that the ruling of confinement in houses is specific to all female fornicators, and the ruling of harm is specific to all male fornicators. Thus generalization is derived in both cases, but its derivation in the first case is from the form of generality, and in the second case from the restriction of the two categories. It would have been sufficient to say: "those women who commit it, and those men who commit it," but this style was chosen so that generality would be achieved by two means, together with explicit mention of the inclusion of both categories.

The word *allātī* (those women) was made to be general so that generality would be derived from the form of the plural alone.

*[Page 271]*

The word *alladhāni* (the two) was made to refer to the two categories because its singular, alladhī, is suitable for indicating the category, since the category is expressed by the masculine, like the individual and similar things. Along with all of this, there is a wonderful variety of expression, so that this verse as a whole is supreme in inimitability. According to this view, the intended meaning of "women" is the meaning opposed to men, and this is the meaning that the verse should be understood to carry.

Harm is intended here as something other than confinement, because confinement has already been specified for women, and other than flogging, because flogging had not yet been legislated. So it was said: harm is harsh speech, insult and reproach. Ibn 'Abbās said: it is attacking with the tongue and the hand and striking with sandals, based on his interpretation that the verse was legislated as a punishment for zinā before the punishment of flogging. The scholars agreed that this ruling was abrogated by the flogging mentioned in Sūrat al-Nūr, and by what was established in the Sunna concerning stoning of the married. Limiting this ruling by the end-point of His saying ﴿or God makes for them a way﴾ is not a conclusive indicator of abrogation of this ruling, as Ibn al-'Arabī imagined, because the end-point was made indefinite. The Muslims await the arrival of another ruling after this, and they have no need to be informed of it.

Know that the way of abrogation in punishments for crimes for which there was no punishment before Islam is that they are abrogated by something heavier. So confinement and harm were legislated for fornicators in this surah, and flogging was legislated by the verse of Sūrat al-Nūr. Flogging is more severe than confinement and than harm. In flogging, women and men are treated equally, since there is no justification for distinguishing between them, for both have violated a legal ruling following either a psychological desire or obedience to another.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 15–16 (part 2 of 2):

Then, the specified flogging was prescribed by the verse of Surat al-Nur, either in absolute terms or as a general ruling, depending on the disagreement over the sense of the definite article in His words: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer﴾ (24:2). If the practice was in fact carried out in this manner against adulterers and adulteresses, whether married or unmarried, then it was abrogated (naskh) by stoning in the case of the married among them. Stoning is established by continuous practice (al-'amal al-mutawatir). If flogging was only applied to the unmarried, then it was restricted or specified (qayyada aw khussisa) to those other than the married, since their ruling was made stoning. The scholars agree that the ruling for married men and women is stoning. A muhsan (married person) is one who has married through a valid, lawful contract and who has consummated the marriage after that contract in a valid manner.

The ruling of stoning existed before Islam in the Law of the Torah for a woman who commits adultery while she is married. Malik has related in the Muwatta', and all the men of the Sahih have related, the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar: "The Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mentioned to him that a man and a woman had committed adultery. The Messenger of God said: 'What do you find in the Torah concerning stoning?' They said: 'We expose them and they are flogged.' 'Abd Allah ibn Salam said: 'You have lied; in it is stoning.' They brought the Torah and unrolled it, and one of them placed his hand over the verse of stoning, reading what came before it and what came after it. 'Abd Allah ibn Salam said to him: 'Lift your hand.' He lifted his hand, and there was the verse of stoning. They said: 'He has spoken the truth, O Muhammad; in it is the verse of stoning.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered them both, and they were stoned."

The ruling on adultery is also mentioned in the Book of Deuteronomy (22), where it says: "If a man is found lying with a woman who is married to a husband, both of them shall die. And if a man finds a virgin who is not betrothed, and lies with her, and they are found, the man who lay with her shall give to the father of the young woman fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife; he may not divorce her all his days."

Stoning was established in Islam by what 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit related, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take from me, take from me. God has made a way for them: the unmarried with the unmarried, a hundred lashes and exile for a year; and the married with the married, a hundred lashes and stoning." Its implication is the combining of stoning and flogging, and I think this is nothing but a misunderstanding by the narrator from 'Ubadah, or a confusion on his part. I believe that for this reason the scholars did not act upon it, so flogging and stoning are not combined.

Ibn al-'Arabi attributed to Ahmad ibn Hanbal the combining of stoning and flogging, but this contradicts what is known of his school. It is also related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he combined flogging and stoning, but this is not authentic.

Then, three hadiths have been established regarding the Prophet's (ﷺ) action in judging by stoning. The first is the case of Ma'iz ibn Malik al-Aslami, who "came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and confessed to adultery. He turned away from him three times. Then he sent to his family and said: 'Is there madness in him?' They said: 'No.' And: 'Is he a virgin or married?' They said: 'Rather, he is married.' So he ordered him, and he was stoned."

The second is the case of the woman of al-Ghamid, that "she came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and confessed to adultery while she was pregnant. He told her to go until she gave birth, then until she nursed him. When she had completed his nursing, she came, and he ordered her, and she was stoned."

The third is the hadith of Abu Hurayra and Khalid al-Juhani, that "two men disputed before the Messenger of God (ﷺ). One of them said: 'O Messenger of God, judge between us by the Book of God.' The other, who was the more learned of the two, said: 'Yes, O Messenger of God, judge between us by the Book of God, and permit me to speak.' He said: 'Speak.' He said: 'My son was a laborer for this man, and he committed adultery with his wife. They informed me that upon my son is stoning, so I ransomed him with a hundred sheep and a slave-girl of mine. Then I asked the people of knowledge, and they informed me that upon my son is a hundred lashes and exile for a year, and that stoning is only upon his wife.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will judge between you by the Book of God. As for your sheep and your slave-girl, they are returned to you.' He flogged his son a hundred times and exiled him for a year. 'And go out, O Unays'—he is Unays ibn al-Dahhak, and it is said Ibn Murthid al-Aslami—'to the wife of this man, and if she confesses, then stone her.' She confessed, and he stoned her."

Malik said: "al-'asif" means the hired laborer.

These hadiths are mursal (with a missing link in the chain); two of them are in the Muwatta', and they are musnad (with a complete chain) in other works. Thus, by them and by practice, the ruling of stoning for the married is established. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It is a widely transmitted report (khabar mutawatir) that abrogated the Qur'an." He means that it is widely transmitted among the Companions, and because of its wide transmission they agreed upon acting by it. As for what reached us, and reached Ibn al-'Arabi and those before him, it consists of solitary reports (akhbar ahad) which do not reach the level of tawatur. So the truth is that the evidence for stoning the married is what has been transmitted to us of the consensus (ijma') of the Companions. We will address this in Surat al-Nur. For this reason, al-Shafi'i held stoning, even though he does not hold that the Qur'an is abrogated by the Sunnah.

Those who hold that the ruling of stoning abrogates the ruling of confinement in houses say that the evidence for abrogation is the hadith "God has made a way for them," and in it: "the unmarried with the unmarried, a hundred lashes and exile for a year," so it includes flogging. This view is attributed to al-Shafi'i and a group. Al-Jassas objected to al-Shafi'i that it necessarily follows that the Qur'an was abrogated by the Sunnah, and the Sunnah was abrogated by the Qur'an, and he does not hold either of these two positions. Al-Khattabi answered that the verse of women is qualified by a limit (mughayyah), so the hadith explained the limit, and the verse of al-Nur was revealed after that, and the hadith specified it before its revelation. I say: according to this, the verse of al-Nur was revealed as an affirmation of part of the ruling that is in the hadith of stoning. Moreover, his statement that the verse of women is qualified by a limit is of no use, because when the ambiguous limit's clarification nullifies the ruling of the limited, then considering it is considering abrogation. Is not all abrogation nothing but an announcement that the intended ruling of God has reached its limit, which is not mentioned in the wording? Mentioning it in some rulings while it remains ambiguous does not clothe the revelation in anything other than the mark of abrogation.

Some have said: the punishment was legislated, then abrogated by confinement in houses, though in recitation it came later. This is an opinion not worth considering. There is no way out of this difficulty except by making the consensus of the Companions on abandoning confinement in houses, and on replacing it with the prescribed penalty (hadd) in the time of Prophethood, which returns to abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah that is mutawatir. This also dispels what al-Jassas objected to al-Shafi'i, because contradicting a consensus with a text implies that the basis of the consensus abrogates the text.

It is necessary that the ruling of stoning for the married was legislated after flogging, because the hadiths narrated about it include exile together with flogging, and exile after stoning is not conceivable; it is an addition that must be, which the Qur'an did not mention. For this reason, Abu Hanifa denied exile, because it is an addition to the text, and so it is abrogation in his view. Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam: "The opinion of the best of the sons of Isma'il agreed that whoever commits an offense in the Sacred Precinct is exiled from it, and this continued in the Jahiliyya, so whoever committed an offense was exiled from his land until Islam came and confirmed it for adultery specifically." I say: among the Arabs there was also al-khal', which is that a man is cast out (yukhla'a) from his tribe, and they bear witness to this at the season of pilgrimage. If he commits a crime, his people are not held responsible for it, and if he is wronged, his people do not seek blood-money or anything like it. Imru' al-Qays said:

"The wolf howls about him like one disowned and impoverished."

They agreed that a woman is not exiled, because her exile is a loss. Abu Hanifa denied exile, because it is the transfer of harm from one place to another, and he replaced it with imprisonment. It is not known among the people of knowledge to combine stoning with beating, and it is not thought that the law of Islam would be so. It is related that 'Ali flogged Shurahah al-Hamdaniyyah and stoned her after the flogging, and he said: "I flogged her by the Book of God, and I stoned her by the Sunnah of the Messenger of God."

The predicate of the two relative clauses is connected by the fa' in His words (fa-istashhidu) and His words (fa-adhuhuma), because the relative pronoun takes on the meaning of a condition, drawing attention to the fact that the relative clause is the cause of the ruling indicated by its predicate. Thus the predicate of the relative clause becomes like the apodosis of a conditional. It appears to me that this is the case when the predicate is a sentence unsuitable for direct attachment to conditional particles, such that if it were a response (jaza') it would require being joined with fa'. This is what we found from inductive study of their speech. This construction only occurs in relative clauses that indicate the manner in which the predicate is built, because they are what gives the sense of causation to the predicate that follows them. You may also take the entry of the fa' as a sign that the fa' substitutes for (amma).

It is clear that the act of women committing indecency is what caused their confinement in houses. Although the structure of the speech was built so that ﴿call four witnesses against them﴾ is the predicate, it is a nominal predicate; otherwise the real predicate is "then confine them," but it was brought as a response to a condition which is consequent upon "if they testify." The fa' of "fa-istashhidu" is the fa' resembling the fa' of the response, and the fa' of "fa-in shahidu" is a consequential fa', while the fa' of "fa-amsikuhunna" is a responsive fa'. Were it not for the intent to emphasize preparing the testimony before ruling on confinement in houses, it would have been said: "And those of your women who commit indecency, then confine them in the houses if four of you testify against them."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Repentance with Allah is only for those who do wrong out of ignorance and then repent soon after. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿Repentance is not for those who keep doing evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I repent now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment.﴾

This is a digression (istitrad) brought about by His saying: ﴿And if they repent and reform, leave them alone﴾ [An-Nisa: 16]. Repentance (tawba) has already been discussed thoroughly in His saying in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief, their repentance will never be accepted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 90].

The particle (innama) indicates exclusivity (hasr).

The particle (ʿala) here is for figurative elevation, in the sense of obligation and certainty, as in your saying: "ʿAlayya laka kadha" (it is incumbent upon me to give you such-and-such). It thus conveys the certainty of the obligation. The meaning is: repentance is due from Allah, and this is a metaphor for emphasizing the promise of its acceptance, to the extent that it is treated as though it were a right owed by Allah. Nothing is obligatory upon Allah except that the obligation of His promise arises from His bounty. Ibn 'Atiyya said: His informing us, exalted is He, about things that He made binding upon Himself implies that those things are obligatory by revelation (sam'), though not obligatory in the sense of a legal duty.

[p. 278]

The exclusivity applies to the predicate, which is (lilladhina ya'malun), and two qualifiers are mentioned for it: (bi-jahala) and (min qarib). The word jahala is used both for bad conduct and for proceeding to an act without deliberation; it is the opposite of forbearance (hilm). For this reason, jahala is also used for injustice. ʿAmr ibn Kulthum said:

"Let no one act with ignorance toward us, lest we act with ignorance beyond the ignorance of the ignorant."

And He, exalted is He, said, recounting Yusuf: ﴿And unless You turn their plotting away from me, I will incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. The intended meaning here is wronging oneself. This qualifier is mentioned here merely to depict the wrongdoing as ugly. The (ba') is for accompaniment (mulabasa), since an evil deed is never anything other than this. The intended meaning of jahala is not what is called ignorance (jahl) in the sense of lacking knowledge of what one did, because that is not called jahala. Rather, it is one of the senses of the word jahl. Had someone committed an act of disobedience while not knowing that it was disobedience, he would not be sinful, and he is only obligated to learn that and avoid it.

His saying ﴿min qarib﴾: (min) here indicates the starting point (ibtida'), and (qarib) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning: from a near time, close to the time of the evil deed.

Some interpreters explained the meaning of (min qarib) as meaning that what is near is the time before the approach of death, and they took His saying after it, ﴿until, when death approaches one of them﴾, as clarifying the intended meaning of "near."

The exegetes of the early generations and those after them differed about applying the implication (mafhum) of the two qualifiers, "out of ignorance" and "soon after," to the extent that it was said that the ruling of the verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 48]. The majority hold that the qualifier "out of ignorance" is a descriptive clause revealing the nature of the evil deed, because the intended evil deed is one committed together with faith. ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Qatada, who said: The Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) gathered and held that every act by which Allah is disobeyed is ignorance (jahala), whether done deliberately or otherwise.

[p. 279]

What appears to be the case is that these are two qualifiers mentioned to draw attention to the fact that the believer's conduct should be such that his deeds proceed in consideration of the implication of the two qualifiers, and that their implications are not conditions for the acceptance of repentance. Also, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Repentance is not for those who do evil deeds﴾ up to ﴿while they are disbelievers﴾ is a counterpart (qasim) to the content of His saying ﴿Repentance with Allah is only﴾, etc., and there is no intermediate category between these two divisions.

The scholars of kalam (theology) differed over whether the acceptance of repentance is definitive (qat'i) or speculative (zanni), because their positions on this follow from their positions on the question of the obligation upon God, exalted is He, of what is best (al-salah wa al-aslah) and the obligation of justice. As for the Mu'tazila, they said: Sincere repentance is accepted with certainty by rational proof (dalil al-'aql). I suppose they intended by this that the penitent has already reformed his condition and desired to join the people of goodness. So if Allah did not accept this from him, He would be leaving him in misguidance and punishment, and He is exalted above that according to their principles. If this is what they meant, it would be sophistry (sofastah), because the matter here concerns pardon for a punishment that the penitent deserved before his repentance, not what he will do after repentance.

As for the scholars of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna), they split into two groups. A group held that the acceptance of repentance is certain by scriptural proofs (adilla sam'iyya). Although these are apparent texts (zawahir), their great number produced certainty, just as the mass-transmitted report (mutawatir) produces certainty, even though each report from individual transmitters only produces speculation. Thus, their collective agreement is what produced certainty. There is room for doubt in comparing this to tawatur. This is the view of al-Ash'ari, al-Ghazali, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya, and his son Abu Bakr ibn 'Atiyya. Another group held that acceptance is speculative, not certain. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, Imam al-Haramayn, al-Mazari, al-Taftazani, Sharaf al-Din al-Fihri, and Ibn al-Furs in Ahkam al-Qur'an, based on the premise that a multitude of apparent texts does not produce certainty. This is what it is fitting to adopt, on reflection. However, the acceptance of repentance is not one of the principles of the religion (usul al-din), so why should we seek a definitive proof for establishing it?

What I think is that when they mentioned acceptance, they mentioned it in a general way, so their disagreement was a disagreement about a state (halah). Acceptance is used to mean Allah's pleasure with the penitent and his inclusion among the God-fearing righteous. This seems to be what the Mu'tazila had in mind when they said that its acceptance is rationally certain. Whether it is certain is clearly open to question. This is supported by the fact that they said repentance is not valid unless it comes after abandoning all other sins, so that the meaning of its righteousness is realized.

[p. 280]

Acceptance is also used to mean what Allah promised of forgiveness of past sins before repentance. I think they do not disagree that this is established by revelation and not by reason, since reason does not require pardoning past sins upon ceasing to commit similar ones in the future. This is what is disputed as to whether it is certain or speculative.

Acceptance is also used to mean the acceptance of repentance insofar as it is in itself an act commanded to every sinner, i.e., in the sense that it is the abandonment of persistence (israr) in the sins that he was persisting in. Abandoning persistence is commanded because it is a sin of the heart, so the heart must be purified of it. From this aspect, the penitent is considered to be fulfilling a legal command. Thus, acceptance in this sense is certain, because it amounts to sufficiency (ijza'). We are certain that whoever performs an act commanded by Allah, with its legal conditions, has performed an accepted act, in the sense that the effects of the prohibition against it are removed. But in the sense of reward for that, it is speculative. Perhaps this is the meaning al-Ghazali had in mind when he said in the Book of Repentance: If you understand the meaning of acceptance, you will not doubt that every valid repentance is accepted, since the heart was created sound originally, as every child is born upon the fitra (natural disposition). Soundness is lost only through a darkness that covers it from the dust of sins, and the light of remorse wipes that darkness from the heart as water and soap wipe filth from a garment. Whoever imagines that repentance is valid but not accepted is like someone who imagines that the sun rises while darkness does not disappear, or that a garment is washed while its dirt does not come out. Yes, the penitent may say with his tongue, "I repent," yet not abandon the sin. That is like the launderer who says with his tongue, "I washed the garment," when he has not washed it; that does not clean the garment. This is a persuasive approximation. But there is clear room for doubt in his words, because we are only investigating whether removing an established punishment is achieved by the recency of repentance.

The reference in the predicate in His saying ﴿So those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness﴾ is to draw attention to bringing them to mind in light of the previously mentioned attributes, which reach the utmost degree of fear of Allah, exalted is He, and hastening to seek His good pleasure, so that it may be known that they are deserving of the meaning of the predicate that comes after the reference. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [Al-Baqara: 5]. The meaning is: These are the ones whom Allah has made deserving of the acceptance of repentance from them. This is an emphasis of His saying ﴿Repentance with Allah is only﴾, to the end.

His saying ﴿Repentance is not for﴾, etc., is a warning that acceptance is denied for a type of repentance, namely that which occurs when one despairs of life, because the purpose of resolve is the effects that follow from it, and the rectification of one's state in this world through legal uprightness. When despair of life sets in, the benefit of repentance is gone.

His saying ﴿nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾: the coordination of "the disbelievers" with "the sinners" in the condition for accepting repentance from them is because the faith of the disbeliever is a repentance from his disbelief, and faith is the most noble kind of repentance. So He clarified that if the disbeliever dies, his repentance from disbelief is not accepted.

Regarding the interpretation of this, scholars have two opinions. The first is to take it at face value: nothing prevents the disbeliever from the acceptance of his repentance from disbelief through faith except death itself. They interpreted the meaning of ﴿Repentance is not for him﴾ as meaning that what is intended is his remorse on the Day of Resurrection if he dies a disbeliever. From this it is derived that if he believes before he dies, his faith is accepted, which is the apparent meaning. It is established in the Sahih that when Abu Talib was on his deathbed, the Prophet (ﷺ) came in while Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya were with him. He said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah." Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah said: "Do you turn away from the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib?" The last thing Abu Talib said was that he was upon the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib. The Prophet said: "I will certainly ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from doing so." Then it was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Hellfire﴾ [At-Tawba: 113]. This is indicated by the coordination of ﴿nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ with the difference between His saying ﴿until, when death approaches one of them﴾, the verse, and His saying ﴿nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾. Accordingly, the reason why the repentance of the disbeliever differs from the repentance of the believing sinner is that faith is an act of the heart and a verbal utterance of the tongue, and it has occurred from the penitent disbeliever while he is alive. He thereby entered the community of the Muslims, their strength was increased by him, and the fame of Islam spread among the people of disbelief through his faith.

The second: the disbeliever and the disobedient believer are equal in the non-acceptance of repentance from what they are upon, when death approaches them. They interpreted His saying ﴿who die while they are disbelievers﴾ to mean that they are about to die, following the style of His saying: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾ [An-Nisa: 9], i.e., if they were about to leave behind offspring. The reason for this interpretation is the structure of the sentence, since (la) (nor) is coordinating with an object of the predicate that negates the acceptance of repentance, so the meaning becomes: Repentance is not for those who die while they are disbelievers, [who] then repent, and repentance cannot be conceived after death. So the interpretation of "die" as "are about to die" is required, as in His saying: ﴿And those of you who die and leave behind wives, [let them make] a bequest for their wives﴾ [Al-Baqara: 240]. They argued with His saying, exalted is He, concerning Pharaoh: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed, and I am among the Muslims"﴾ [Yunus: 90] ﴿"Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters"﴾ [Yunus: 91], which indicates that Allah did not accept his faith at that moment. This argument may be answered by saying that Allah's way with those upon whom punishment descends is that faith does not benefit them after the punishment has come down, except the people of Yunus. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed and whose faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and gave them enjoyment for a time﴾ [Yunus: 98]. Drowning is a punishment with which Allah punished Pharaoh and his army.

Ibn al-Furs said in Ahkam al-Qur'an (the Rulings of the Qur'an): "When a servant's repentance is valid, if it is from disbelief, we are certain of its acceptance; and if it is from other sins, then among the scholars there are those who are certain of its acceptance, and among them are those who are not certain but hold it as a probability (zann)." End of quotation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Repentance with Allah is only for those who do wrong out of ignorance and then repent soon after. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿Repentance is not for those who keep doing evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I repent now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment.﴾

This is a digression (istitrad) brought about by His saying: ﴿And if they repent and reform, leave them alone﴾ [An-Nisa: 16]. Repentance (tawba) has already been discussed thoroughly in His saying in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief, their repentance will never be accepted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 90].

The particle (innama) indicates exclusivity (hasr).

The particle (ʿala) here is for figurative elevation, in the sense of obligation and certainty, as in your saying: "ʿAlayya laka kadha" (it is incumbent upon me to give you such-and-such). It thus conveys the certainty of the obligation. The meaning is: repentance is due from Allah, and this is a metaphor for emphasizing the promise of its acceptance, to the extent that it is treated as though it were a right owed by Allah. Nothing is obligatory upon Allah except that the obligation of His promise arises from His bounty. Ibn 'Atiyya said: His informing us, exalted is He, about things that He made binding upon Himself implies that those things are obligatory by revelation (sam'), though not obligatory in the sense of a legal duty.

[p. 278]

The exclusivity applies to the predicate, which is (lilladhina ya'malun), and two qualifiers are mentioned for it: (bi-jahala) and (min qarib). The word jahala is used both for bad conduct and for proceeding to an act without deliberation; it is the opposite of forbearance (hilm). For this reason, jahala is also used for injustice. ʿAmr ibn Kulthum said:

"Let no one act with ignorance toward us, lest we act with ignorance beyond the ignorance of the ignorant."

And He, exalted is He, said, recounting Yusuf: ﴿And unless You turn their plotting away from me, I will incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. The intended meaning here is wronging oneself. This qualifier is mentioned here merely to depict the wrongdoing as ugly. The (ba') is for accompaniment (mulabasa), since an evil deed is never anything other than this. The intended meaning of jahala is not what is called ignorance (jahl) in the sense of lacking knowledge of what one did, because that is not called jahala. Rather, it is one of the senses of the word jahl. Had someone committed an act of disobedience while not knowing that it was disobedience, he would not be sinful, and he is only obligated to learn that and avoid it.

His saying ﴿min qarib﴾: (min) here indicates the starting point (ibtida'), and (qarib) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning: from a near time, close to the time of the evil deed.

Some interpreters explained the meaning of (min qarib) as meaning that what is near is the time before the approach of death, and they took His saying after it, ﴿until, when death approaches one of them﴾, as clarifying the intended meaning of "near."

The exegetes of the early generations and those after them differed about applying the implication (mafhum) of the two qualifiers, "out of ignorance" and "soon after," to the extent that it was said that the ruling of the verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 48]. The majority hold that the qualifier "out of ignorance" is a descriptive clause revealing the nature of the evil deed, because the intended evil deed is one committed together with faith. ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Qatada, who said: The Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) gathered and held that every act by which Allah is disobeyed is ignorance (jahala), whether done deliberately or otherwise.

[p. 279]

What appears to be the case is that these are two qualifiers mentioned to draw attention to the fact that the believer's conduct should be such that his deeds proceed in consideration of the implication of the two qualifiers, and that their implications are not conditions for the acceptance of repentance. Also, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Repentance is not for those who do evil deeds﴾ up to ﴿while they are disbelievers﴾ is a counterpart (qasim) to the content of His saying ﴿Repentance with Allah is only﴾, etc., and there is no intermediate category between these two divisions.

The scholars of kalam (theology) differed over whether the acceptance of repentance is definitive (qat'i) or speculative (zanni), because their positions on this follow from their positions on the question of the obligation upon God, exalted is He, of what is best (al-salah wa al-aslah) and the obligation of justice. As for the Mu'tazila, they said: Sincere repentance is accepted with certainty by rational proof (dalil al-'aql). I suppose they intended by this that the penitent has already reformed his condition and desired to join the people of goodness. So if Allah did not accept this from him, He would be leaving him in misguidance and punishment, and He is exalted above that according to their principles. If this is what they meant, it would be sophistry (sofastah), because the matter here concerns pardon for a punishment that the penitent deserved before his repentance, not what he will do after repentance.

As for the scholars of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna), they split into two groups. A group held that the acceptance of repentance is certain by scriptural proofs (adilla sam'iyya). Although these are apparent texts (zawahir), their great number produced certainty, just as the mass-transmitted report (mutawatir) produces certainty, even though each report from individual transmitters only produces speculation. Thus, their collective agreement is what produced certainty. There is room for doubt in comparing this to tawatur. This is the view of al-Ash'ari, al-Ghazali, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya, and his son Abu Bakr ibn 'Atiyya. Another group held that acceptance is speculative, not certain. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, Imam al-Haramayn, al-Mazari, al-Taftazani, Sharaf al-Din al-Fihri, and Ibn al-Furs in Ahkam al-Qur'an, based on the premise that a multitude of apparent texts does not produce certainty. This is what it is fitting to adopt, on reflection. However, the acceptance of repentance is not one of the principles of the religion (usul al-din), so why should we seek a definitive proof for establishing it?

What I think is that when they mentioned acceptance, they mentioned it in a general way, so their disagreement was a disagreement about a state (halah). Acceptance is used to mean Allah's pleasure with the penitent and his inclusion among the God-fearing righteous. This seems to be what the Mu'tazila had in mind when they said that its acceptance is rationally certain. Whether it is certain is clearly open to question. This is supported by the fact that they said repentance is not valid unless it comes after abandoning all other sins, so that the meaning of its righteousness is realized.

[p. 280]

Acceptance is also used to mean what Allah promised of forgiveness of past sins before repentance. I think they do not disagree that this is established by revelation and not by reason, since reason does not require pardoning past sins upon ceasing to commit similar ones in the future. This is what is disputed as to whether it is certain or speculative.

Acceptance is also used to mean the acceptance of repentance insofar as it is in itself an act commanded to every sinner, i.e., in the sense that it is the abandonment of persistence (israr) in the sins that he was persisting in. Abandoning persistence is commanded because it is a sin of the heart, so the heart must be purified of it. From this aspect, the penitent is considered to be fulfilling a legal command. Thus, acceptance in this sense is certain, because it amounts to sufficiency (ijza'). We are certain that whoever performs an act commanded by Allah, with its legal conditions, has performed an accepted act, in the sense that the effects of the prohibition against it are removed. But in the sense of reward for that, it is speculative. Perhaps this is the meaning al-Ghazali had in mind when he said in the Book of Repentance: If you understand the meaning of acceptance, you will not doubt that every valid repentance is accepted, since the heart was created sound originally, as every child is born upon the fitra (natural disposition). Soundness is lost only through a darkness that covers it from the dust of sins, and the light of remorse wipes that darkness from the heart as water and soap wipe filth from a garment. Whoever imagines that repentance is valid but not accepted is like someone who imagines that the sun rises while darkness does not disappear, or that a garment is washed while its dirt does not come out. Yes, the penitent may say with his tongue, "I repent," yet not abandon the sin. That is like the launderer who says with his tongue, "I washed the garment," when he has not washed it; that does not clean the garment. This is a persuasive approximation. But there is clear room for doubt in his words, because we are only investigating whether removing an established punishment is achieved by the recency of repentance.

The reference in the predicate in His saying ﴿So those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness﴾ is to draw attention to bringing them to mind in light of the previously mentioned attributes, which reach the utmost degree of fear of Allah, exalted is He, and hastening to seek His good pleasure, so that it may be known that they are deserving of the meaning of the predicate that comes after the reference. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [Al-Baqara: 5]. The meaning is: These are the ones whom Allah has made deserving of the acceptance of repentance from them. This is an emphasis of His saying ﴿Repentance with Allah is only﴾, to the end.

His saying ﴿Repentance is not for﴾, etc., is a warning that acceptance is denied for a type of repentance, namely that which occurs when one despairs of life, because the purpose of resolve is the effects that follow from it, and the rectification of one's state in this world through legal uprightness. When despair of life sets in, the benefit of repentance is gone.

His saying ﴿nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾: the coordination of "the disbelievers" with "the sinners" in the condition for accepting repentance from them is because the faith of the disbeliever is a repentance from his disbelief, and faith is the most noble kind of repentance. So He clarified that if the disbeliever dies, his repentance from disbelief is not accepted.

Regarding the interpretation of this, scholars have two opinions. The first is to take it at face value: nothing prevents the disbeliever from the acceptance of his repentance from disbelief through faith except death itself. They interpreted the meaning of ﴿Repentance is not for him﴾ as meaning that what is intended is his remorse on the Day of Resurrection if he dies a disbeliever. From this it is derived that if he believes before he dies, his faith is accepted, which is the apparent meaning. It is established in the Sahih that when Abu Talib was on his deathbed, the Prophet (ﷺ) came in while Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya were with him. He said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah." Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah said: "Do you turn away from the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib?" The last thing Abu Talib said was that he was upon the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib. The Prophet said: "I will certainly ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from doing so." Then it was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Hellfire﴾ [At-Tawba: 113]. This is indicated by the coordination of ﴿nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ with the difference between His saying ﴿until, when death approaches one of them﴾, the verse, and His saying ﴿nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾. Accordingly, the reason why the repentance of the disbeliever differs from the repentance of the believing sinner is that faith is an act of the heart and a verbal utterance of the tongue, and it has occurred from the penitent disbeliever while he is alive. He thereby entered the community of the Muslims, their strength was increased by him, and the fame of Islam spread among the people of disbelief through his faith.

The second: the disbeliever and the disobedient believer are equal in the non-acceptance of repentance from what they are upon, when death approaches them. They interpreted His saying ﴿who die while they are disbelievers﴾ to mean that they are about to die, following the style of His saying: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾ [An-Nisa: 9], i.e., if they were about to leave behind offspring. The reason for this interpretation is the structure of the sentence, since (la) (nor) is coordinating with an object of the predicate that negates the acceptance of repentance, so the meaning becomes: Repentance is not for those who die while they are disbelievers, [who] then repent, and repentance cannot be conceived after death. So the interpretation of "die" as "are about to die" is required, as in His saying: ﴿And those of you who die and leave behind wives, [let them make] a bequest for their wives﴾ [Al-Baqara: 240]. They argued with His saying, exalted is He, concerning Pharaoh: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed, and I am among the Muslims"﴾ [Yunus: 90] ﴿"Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters"﴾ [Yunus: 91], which indicates that Allah did not accept his faith at that moment. This argument may be answered by saying that Allah's way with those upon whom punishment descends is that faith does not benefit them after the punishment has come down, except the people of Yunus. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed and whose faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and gave them enjoyment for a time﴾ [Yunus: 98]. Drowning is a punishment with which Allah punished Pharaoh and his army.

Ibn al-Furs said in Ahkam al-Qur'an (the Rulings of the Qur'an): "When a servant's repentance is valid, if it is from disbelief, we are certain of its acceptance; and if it is from other sins, then among the scholars there are those who are certain of its acceptance, and among them are those who are not certain but hold it as a probability (zann)." End of quotation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 19 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion.﴾

This is a resumption (*istinaf*) of legislation concerning the rulings on women, which the context of the surah was set to explain. Its verses continue to clarify these rulings, through foundation (*ta'sis*), digression (*istitrad*), beginning, and return. This ruling follows from the nullification of the practice of the people of the Jahiliyyah, who treated a dead man's wife as an inheritance from him. It opens with the words "O you who have believed" to draw attention to what they are being addressed with.

The believers are addressed so that the address encompasses the entire community, and each of them takes his share of it. Thus, one who desires to take exclusive possession of a dead man's wife knows what applies to him, and so does the guardian (*wali*), and so do the rulers of affairs.

The phrase "it is not lawful" (*la yahillu*) is a clear prohibition, because *hill* in the language of the Arabs and the language of the Shari'ah means permissibility, so negating it is synonymous with the meaning of prohibition.

The literal meaning of *irth* (inheritance) is the transfer of property to one person after another. It is used most often for the transfer of wealth. Inheritance is also used figuratively for the complete vesting of ownership in one person after it had been shared, or in a situation where sharing is claimed. From this is the expression: "He inherits the earth and whoever is upon it." It is a verb that takes one object: it takes the inherited property as its object, so you say: "I inherited the wealth of so-and-so." It may also take the deceased person himself as its object, as in: "So-and-so inherited his father." God says: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir who will inherit from me﴾. This is the usual usage when it takes as its object something that is not wealth.

The verb in the phrase ﴿that you inherit women﴾ takes "women" as its object in its first (literal) usage, by treating women as if they were inherited property, in order to convey the abhorrence of the condition in which they were in the Jahiliyyah. Al-Bukhari reported, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When a man died, his guardians had more right to his wife: if some of them wished, they married her; if they wished, they gave her in marriage; and if they wished, they did not give her in marriage. They had more right to her than her own family." So this verse was revealed.

It is also reported from Mujahid, al-Suddi, and al-Zuhri: "The eldest son had more right to his father's wife if she was not his mother. If there were no sons, the guardian of the deceased, if he was quick, would cast his garment over the wife of the deceased, and he had more right to her. If she was quicker and went to her family, she had more right to herself." Among the most famous cases of this in the Jahiliyyah was that when Umayyah ibn 'Abd Shams died, leaving a wife who had children by him: al-'Is, Abu al-'Is, al-'As, and Abu al-'As, and he also had children by another woman, among them Abu 'Amr ibn Umayyah. Abu 'Amr then married his father's wife, and she bore him Musafir and Abu Mu'ayt. Thus al-A'yas were uncles to Musafir, Abu Mu'ayt, and their brothers from the mother.

It has also been said: the verse was revealed when Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat died, and his son wished to marry his wife Kabshah bint Ma'n al-Ansariyyah, so this verse was revealed. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This practice was binding among the Ansar, while among Quraysh it was permissible by mutual consent."

According to this interpretation, His saying "by compulsion" (*karhan*) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to "women," meaning: unwilling, not content, until they are content to be wives of whomever they are content with, while observing the conditions of marriage. The address in this case is to the heirs of the deceased.

This compulsion was repeated through their customs, to which they conspired, such that if a woman attempted to deviate from them, it would become a disgrace for her, and she would find no one to support her. According to this, "women" means the wives, that is, the wives of the dead.

It is also possible that the verb *tarithu* (you inherit) is used in its literal sense and transitive to the inherited object, so that it conveys the prohibition of conditions that existed in the Jahiliyyah. Among them: the guardians would prevent women who had wealth from marrying, out of fear that if they married they would bear children, and their husbands and children would inherit from them, while the agnatic guardian would have no share of their wealth, though they desired to marry. Among them also: husbands used to dislike their wives and refused to divorce them, desiring that they die in their custody so they could inherit from them. This is compulsion on them to remain in a state of aversion, since a woman would not be content with this by choice. According to this, "women" is the plural of *imra'ah* (woman).

Al-Jumhur read *karhan* with a fatha on the kaf, while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with a damma on the kaf. Both are dialects.

* * *

﴿And do not hinder them in order to take away part of what you have given them.﴾

The prohibition of *'adl* (hindering/confining) is conjoined to the prohibition of inheriting women by compulsion, because of the correspondence in compulsion, in that its object is the mistreatment of women, and in that hindering is for the sake of taking wealth from them.

*Al-'adl* is the guardian's preventing a woman from marrying. This was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿So do not hinder them from marrying their husbands﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

Even if the prohibition in His saying "It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion" is the meaning most directly understood from *tarithu*, namely taking a woman's property by force, then the conjunction "and do not hinder them" is either a specific conjoined to a general (*khass 'ala 'amm*), if what is meant is specifically the husbands preventing their wives from divorce while they are averse, desiring the woman to remain with him until she dies so that he inherits her wealth; or it is a conjunction of something distinct (*'atf mubayin*), if what is meant is the prohibition of preventing her from divorce until he compels her to ransom herself from him with part of what he gave her. In either case, applying *'adl* to this withholding is figurative, by way of resemblance, since she is like one who has no husband and is unable to marry.

If the prohibition in His saying "It is not lawful for you to inherit women" is the figurative meaning of *tarithu*, namely that women are made an inheritance, which is what the people of the Jahiliyyah did in dealing with the wives of their relatives, and this is the more apparent view, then the conjunction "and do not hinder them" is the conjunction of another ruling from the conditions of treatment, namely the prohibition against a guardian hindering a woman from marrying so that she remains with him, and when she dies he inherits her. According to this possibility, the plural pronoun in His saying "in order to take away part of what you have given them" must refer to those among the believers from whom such conduct is expected, namely the husbands specifically. It is not rare for a pronoun suitable for the plural to be used while part of that plural is meant, by means of a context. Like His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [An-Nisa': 29], meaning: let none of you kill his brother, since it is known that no one kills himself. Likewise: ﴿then greet one another﴾, meaning: the one who enters greets the one who is seated. So the meaning is: let some of you take away part of what some of you gave them, as when a guardian wishes to take part of his mawla's wealth, which she inherited from her mother, or her relative, or her husband, in the course of his inheritance. Thus there is a distribution in the pronoun. Applying *'adl* to this meaning is literal. The "taking away" (*idhhab*) in His saying "in order to take away part of what you have given them" is figurative for seizing, like His saying: ﴿God took away their light﴾, meaning: He removed it.

* * *

﴿Except if they commit a manifest immorality.﴾

Their committing a manifest immorality is not part of what precedes the exception, neither of the hindering nor of taking away part of the dowry. It is possible that the exception is connected (*istithna' muttasil*), an exception from the general states of the act that occurs as the reason for the prohibition, namely the intention to take away part of what they have given, because the generality of individuals entails the generality of states. That is: except in the state of committing a manifest immorality, in which case your taking away part of what you have given them is permissible. It is also possible that it is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*) with the sense of an adversative correction (*istidrak*): "But if they commit manifest immorality, it becomes lawful for you to take away part of what you have given them." It has been said: this was the ruling for a wife who committed immorality, and it was abrogated by the *hadd* punishment. This is the view of 'Ata'.

Here, according to the majority of scholars, *fahishah* means adultery. That is, if a man establishes his wife's adultery, he may hinder her, and if she then asks for divorce, he may refuse to divorce her until she ransoms herself from him with part of her dowry, because she caused disruption in the state of the household and compelled him to seek another wife. This is left to his religion and the trustworthiness of his faith. If he deviates from this, it is for the judges to bring him back to what is right. The ransom was not made with the entire dowry, lest the duration of the marital bond be devoid of any corresponding compensation. This is what is derived from the words of al-Hasan, Abu Qilabah, Ibn Sirin, and 'Ata'. However, 'Ata' said: this ruling was abrogated by the *hadd* punishment for adultery and by *li'an*, so harm and ransoming were prohibited.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and Qatadah said: *fahishah* here means hatred and disobedience (*nushuz*). So if she is disobedient, he may take from her. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The apparent view of Malik, permitting the taking of *khul'* from a disobedient wife, corresponds to this, except that I do not know of any explicit text concerning *fahishah* in this verse."

Al-Jumhur read *mubayyinah* with a kasra on the ya', an active participle of *bayyana*, intransitive, meaning *tabayyana* (became clear), as in the proverb: "The dawn has become clear to one with two eyes." Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf read it with a fatha on the ya', a passive participle of *bayyana*, transitive, meaning: he made it clear and manifest, such that he had witnesses testify to it against them.

* * *

﴿And live with them honourably. Then if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike something in which God has placed much good.﴾

Having prohibited compelling women and harming them, He followed it with a command to good companionship with them. This is an interjection (*i'tiradh*) that carries the sense of a concluding clause (*tadhyil*) for the preceding prohibition, because good companionship comprehends the negation of harm and compulsion, and adds to it the meanings of excellent fellowship.

*Mu'asharah* is a reciprocal form from *'ishrah*, which is close association. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "I think the word derives from *a'shar al-jazur* (the shares of a slaughtered camel), since it involves division and mixing." That is, the root derives from a fixed noun, namely the number ten. But I think it is derived from *'ashirah*, meaning family, so that *'ashara-hu* means he made him one of his clan, just as one says *akhahu* when he made him a brother. As for *'ashirah* itself, the origin of its derivation is not known. It has been said that it is from *'ashara*, the name of the number. But this is open to question.

*Al-ma'ruf* is the opposite of *al-munkar*. The disliked matter was called *munkar* because souls are not at ease with it; it is as if it were unknown and strange to them, since the usual case is that the unknown is disliked. Then the name *munkar* was applied to the disliked, and its opposite was applied to the beloved, because souls are familiar with it. Here *al-ma'ruf* is what the Shari'ah has defined and custom has described.

The branching (*tafri'*) in His saying "Then if you dislike them" is based on the necessary implication of the command in His saying "And live with them," which is the prohibition of bad companionship. That is: if the cause of bad companionship exists, namely aversion. The clause "perhaps you dislike something" stands in place of the answer of the condition and is its reason, so the answer is understood from it. Its implied sense is: "then be patient, and do not hasten to divorce," because His saying "perhaps you dislike something and God places in it much good" indicates the possibility that a disliked wife may be a source of great goods, and so it requires that one not hasten to separation.

*'Asa* here is for approximation (in a figurative sense) or hope. "That you dislike" fills the place of its two complements. "Places" is conjoined to "dislike," and the basis of the approximation and hope is the combined conjoined and conjoining clause, as indicated by the context.

This is a great wisdom, for souls may dislike what in its outcome is good. Some of it can be grasped by reaching the knowledge of its good through deep reflection, and some of it God knows to contain good but which has not appeared to people. Sahl ibn Hunayf, upon his return from Siffin, said: "Suspect your opinion. We have seen ourselves on the day of Abu Jandal, and if we could have turned back the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), we would have turned it back, and God and His Messenger know best." God has also said, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Perhaps you dislike something while it is good for you, and perhaps you love something while it is bad for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 216].

The purpose of this is guidance toward deep contemplation and the penetration of reason into the outcomes of things, and not being deceived by apparent flashes, nor by the inclination of desires toward what in actions is agreeable, until one tests it with the probe of reason, so that one verifies the soundness of apparent goodness against the hidden evil of the inner reality.

He here limited himself to mentioning the possibility of disliking something in which there is much good, without its counterpart, as in the verse of al-Baqarah: ﴿Perhaps you love a thing while it is bad for you﴾. This is because the context in Surat al-Baqarah is one of explaining the reality with both its sides, since the addressees there disliked fighting and loved peace. Their situation required explaining that fighting may be the good thing because of the lasting security that follows it and the breaking of the enemy's strength, and that peace may be an evil because of the contempt the enemies feel for them, their greed for them, and the loss of their honour that leads to their enslavement. As for the context of this surah, it is to explain the ruling for one who has had an incident with his wife that he dislikes, and who wants to separate from her, while having no inclination toward anyone else. So his situation required explaining that much of what is disliked contains goodness. It does not suit that he be told that some beloved matters contain evils, because that would open the door for them to find excuses through the aspect toward which their desires incline. He attributed the placing of good in the disliked thing here to Allah with His saying: ﴿and Allah places in it much good﴾. This implies that it is an incidental placing in a particular disliked thing. In Surat al-Baqarah He said: ﴿and it is good for you﴾, because that verse explains what accompanies some realities of hidden aspects within the reality itself, so that the hope of good from fighting is constant in all circumstances and is not achieved through an incidental placing. Unlike this verse, the patience with a harmful or disliked wife, when it is for the sake of obeying Allah's command to treat them well, makes the placing of good in that a reward from Allah for obedience.

[Page 288]

[Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 4, verses 20–21]

﴿And if you desire to exchange one spouse for another, and you have given one of them a great amount, do not take from it anything. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ ﴿And how would you take it when you have gone in unto one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾

Without doubt, aversion is followed by the desire to replace what is disliked with its opposite. For this reason, he joined the conditional clause to the one before it by way of *istitrad* (digression) and to complete the rulings (*istifa' al-ahkam*).

The meaning of *al-istibdal* (exchange) is the divorce of the former wife and the marriage of another woman.

*Al-istibdal* means *al-tabdil* (substitution). Its discussion has already been covered at His words, exalted is He: ﴿Will you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. That is: if the only cause for separation is the desire to exchange one spouse for another, then he compels the one he wishes to leave, until she seeks khul' (divorce by compensation) from him, so that he may obtain property to give as a dowry to the one he desires. He forbade them from taking anything of what they had given their wives as dowry or otherwise.

Page 289

*Al-qintar* here is an exaggeration of the amount of property given as a dowry, meaning a great quantity, an abundance that is not customary. This exaggeration indicates that giving a qintar is permissible in the Sharia, because God does not use as an example what He does not approve in His law, such as what is forbidden. For this reason, when 'Umar ibn al-Khattab gave a sermon and forbade excess in dowries, a woman of Quraysh said to him after the verse was revealed: "O Commander of the Faithful, is the Book of God more deserving of being followed, or your statement?" He said: "Rather, the Book of God. What is that?" She said: "You just forbade the people from exceeding in the dowries of women, and God says in His Book: ﴿and you have given one of them a qintar, do not take from it anything﴾." 'Umar said: "Every person is more knowledgeable than 'Umar." In another narration he said: "A woman was correct and a commander erred, and God is the One sought for help." Then he returned to the pulpit and said: "I had forbidden you to exceed in the dowries of women, so let every man do with his property what he wishes." The apparent meaning of this narration is that 'Umar retracted from restricting what is permissible, because he saw that it contradicts permissibility according to the requirement of *dalalat al-isharah* (indication by allusion). He had previously thought that exceeding in dowries had a cause that requires prohibition, so it is possible that he forgot the verse, on the basis that a *mujtahid* (qualified jurist exercising independent reasoning) is not obliged to search for what opposes the evidence of his reasoning. Or he may have understood it as intended for exaggeration, and so considered that it does not indicate permissibility, and then retracted that. Or he may have considered for himself the right to restrict some of what is permissible for the sake of public interest, then departed from that because it contradicts the permission of the Sharia regarding its performance, or something similar.

The pronoun in (*ihdahunna*) refers to the women. This is the woman whose divorce is intended.

The discussion of the *qintar* has already been covered in the explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿and the heaped-up qanatir of gold and silver﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran.

The interrogative in (*a-ta'khudhunahu*) is one of denunciation (*inkari*).

*Al-buhtan* is a verbal noun like *al-shukran* and *al-ghufran*; it is the verbal noun of *bahatahu*, as *manaʿahu*, when one accuses him of what he did not do. The word *al-buht* was discussed at His words, exalted is He: ﴿so the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

(*Buhtanan*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the subject in (*ta'khudhunahu*), by interpreting it as an active participle, meaning "slandering." This taking was called slander because it was among their customs that when they disliked a woman and wished to divorce her, they accused her of bad conduct and fabricated against her what was not in her, so that she would fear bad reputation and offer the husband property as ransom for him to divorce her. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi related this. Thus taking property from a woman at divorce became a sign (*mazzinah*) that she had committed what displeases the husband, which may deter those who desire marriage from proposing to her. For this reason, when God permitted husbands to take property when their wives commit a grave immorality, taking property from them without that cause came to suggest that he took it in a place where taking was permitted. This is the most evident of the explanations for calling the taking slander.

As for it being a manifest sin, it is placed here as a circumstantial state after the denunciation. The nature of such a state is that its attribution to its owner should be known, so that the denunciation applies to it. It is possible that its being a manifest sin had become known to the addressees from His words: ﴿so do not take from it anything﴾, or from the verse of al-Baqarah: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them, unless the two fear that they will not keep within the limits of God﴾, or from what was established among them that the ruling of the Sharia regarding property is that it is not permitted except with genuine consent.

His words (*wa-kayfa ta'khudhunahu*) are an interrogative of wonder after the denunciation, meaning: it is not of good manners that you covet taking a compensation for separation after intimate companionship and a firm covenant. *Al-ifdá'* means arrival, derived from *al-fada'* (open space), because in arrival one crosses the open space between those who are connected. *Al-mithaq al-ghalidh* is the bond of marriage with the intention of sincere intention and lasting affection. The meaning is that you were in a state of love and friendship, so it is in meaning like a covenant of good treatment.

*Al-ghalidh* is an adjective in the form *mushabbahah* from *ghaluḍa* (with the vowel u on the lam), meaning to be hard. Literally, *al-ghilzah* is the hardness of substances, and then it was metaphorically extended to the difficulty and severity of meanings in their various kinds. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near you, and let them find harshness in you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. It has become clear that the criterion of the prohibition is taking property when seeking to replace a wife with another. Therefore this ruling is not abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) by the verse of al-Baqarah, contrary to Jabir ibn Zayd, since there is no nullification of what this verse indicates.
