[Page 291]

It is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause "It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion" (4:19). The connection is that among the circumstances of inheriting women by compulsion was that a dead man's son would have a claim on his father's wife if she was not the son's mother. So this case was forbidden with a specific and emphatic prohibition, and from it the discussion moves on to enumerating the prohibited women.

"Whom your fathers married" (*wa-ma nakaha*): *ma* is used here in the sense of *alladhi* (those whom), and the intended meaning is the category. Hence the use of *ma* in place of *man* is appropriate, because *man* is more common for a relative pronoun referring to known persons. Moreover, the specification "of women" (*min al-nisa'*) made *ma* and *man* equivalent, so *ma* was preferred for its lightness. The specification also determines that *ma* is a relative pronoun. The wording was chosen over "Do not marry the wives of your fathers" so that the word *nakaha* would indicate that the father's contract with a woman is sufficient to make marrying her forbidden to his son. The mention of "of women" specifies that *ma* is a relative pronoun.

The prohibition relates to the future, and the imperfect verb with a prohibition signifies bringing the act into being in the future. This meaning indicates a prohibition of continuing in marriage with such women if the marriage took place before the prohibition was revealed. *Nikah* is in its literal sense, in the legal terminology, a contract between a man and a woman for companionship and enjoyment in the lawful sense. It was previously established that it is literally used in this sense and not for sexual intercourse, in the commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: "And if he divorces her, then she is not lawful to him after that until she marries a husband other than him" (2:230) in Surat al-Baqarah. Therefore it is forbidden for a man to marry a woman whom his father contracted in a valid marriage contract, even if the father did not consummate it.

As for using *nikah* for intercourse by means of a contract, some scholars have construed the word *nikah* that way and claimed that the words of Allah, the Exalted, "then she is not lawful to him after that until she marries a husband other than him" (2:230), use *nikah* to mean intercourse, because a mere contract does not make her lawful to her former husband who divorced her three times. That is, there is no need to rely on the Sunnah to clarify what is meant by "marries" (*tankiha*). I have already refuted this in Surat al-Baqarah at the words of Allah, the Exalted: "then she is not lawful to him after that until she marries a husband other than him."

As for unlawful intercourse through fornication (*zina*), the claim that it is among the meanings of *nikah* in the Arabic language is a feeble assertion.

The jurists have differed concerning a man who commits fornication with a woman: does she become forbidden to his son or to his father? The view of Malik in the *Muwatta'* and al-Shafi'i is that fornication does not establish the prohibition of marriage (*la yanshuru al-hurma*). This is what Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd relates in *al-Risala*, and it is narrated from Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also the view of al-Zuhri, Rabi'a, and al-Layth. Abu Hanifa and Ibn al-Majishun, one of Malik's companions, said: fornication does establish the prohibition. Ibn al-Majishun said: Malik died holding this view. It is also the view of al-Awza'i and al-Thawri. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: it is disliked (*makruh*). The word "he leaves her" (*yufarriquha*) occurs in the *Mudawwana*, and most scholars understood it as obligatory, while some interpreted it as reprehensible. This question was the subject of a debate between al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, which al-Jassas mentioned in his *Ahkam* and al-Fakhr (al-Razi) in *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, and it is lengthy.

"What has already passed" (*wa-ma salafa*) refers to what preceded the revelation of this verse. That is, "except a marriage that has already passed," so it is established that this marriage has become forbidden. Therefore the exception in His words "except what has already passed" must be understood as a figurative exception (*mu'awwal*), since how can what has already passed be excepted from a prohibition of doing it, when it has already occurred? So the exception must refer to what the prohibition entails of sin, meaning: there is no sin upon you for what has already passed. Then the consideration moves to whether such marriages are to be left in place, so that the two spouses who married before the revelation of the verse are not separated. This view was held only by some exegetes, as al-Fakhr reported, and I have not found a report establishing a specific case in which the Prophet (ﷺ) separated a man from his father's wife from a marriage that preceded the revelation, nor the identity of the one who held this view. Perhaps people hastened to separate from their fathers' wives when this verse was revealed.

Many people married their fathers' wives before Islam, among them 'Umar ibn Umayya ibn 'Abd Shams, who succeeded to the wife of his father Umayya, as mentioned earlier. Among them is Safwan ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, who married the wife of his father, Fakhita bint al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Asad. Among them is Manzur ibn Rayyan ibn Sayyar, who married the wife of his father, Mulkiyya bint Kharija. Among them is Hisn ibn Abi Qays, who married, after Abu Qays, his wife. It is not reported that any of these embraced Islam and was then allowed to remain in marriage with his father's wife.

They also permitted that the exception be understood as relating to a necessary consequence of the prohibition, which is punishment: that is, no punishment for what has already passed. In my view, such a thing is evident to people, so it does not need an exception, and when would anyone suppose that he would be held accountable for actions committed in the Jahiliyya, before the coming of the religion and the revelation of the prohibition?

[Page 292]

It is also said that this is an emphasis of a thing by means of something resembling its opposite: that is, "if you are going to do it, then marry what has already passed of the wives of the fathers, the perished ones." It seems to allow them some of it, so the hearer finds what he was permitted to be impossible, and the prohibition is thereby reinforced, like the words of al-Nabigha:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

And like their saying: "until the two evening-travelers return" and "until the crow turns gray." But this is a remote interpretation in verses of legislation.

The apparent meaning is that His words "except what has already passed" were intended to establish the validity of what had passed of such marriages in the time of Jahiliyya, which cannot now be corrected because both spouses are dead, in view of the fact that it entails the establishment of lineages, dower rights, and inheritances. It also clarifies the legitimacy of the lineages of those born from that marriage, and that the Muslims were called upon to desist from it voluntarily. The majority of exegetes interpreted His words, the Exalted, "except what has already passed" in ways that return to figurative usage in the meaning of the exception or in the meaning of "what [men] married" (*ma nakaha*). What led them to this was that the marriage with a father's wife was not affirmed by Islam after the revelation of the verse, because He said: "Indeed, it was an immorality and hatred and an evil way" (4:22). That is, such a thing is not allowed to continue, because it is corrupt in itself.

*Al-maqt* (hatred) is a name by which the Arabs designated the marriage of a man with his father's wife, and they said: "the marriage of hatred," that is, of loathing. They called the doer of that the *dayzan*, and they called the son born of that marriage *maqit* (hated one).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your mothers who have nursed you, your milk-sisters, your wives' mothers, your stepdaughters under your guardianship born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage—but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame upon you—and the wives of your sons who descend from your loins, and that you take two sisters in marriage simultaneously, except what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This is a transition to the mention of the prohibited women, occasioned by the mention of the prohibition of marrying what the fathers had married, and the style of prohibition in it changed. For (lā taf'al, "do not do") is a prohibition against the present-tense verb, which indicates the time of the present, so it implies being engaged in the forbidden act or the possibility of being engaged in it. Unlike (ḥurrimat, "were forbidden"), which indicates that its prohibition is an established matter. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to forbid what Islam forbids, except the wife of the father and the joining of two sisters. Therefore, for this reason too, we find that the ruling on joining two sisters is expressed with the present-tense verb form, so it says: "and that you join two sisters in marriage."

The attachment of prohibition to the names of essences is taken to mean the prohibition of what is generally intended from that essence. Thus, "Forbidden to you is carrion," etc., means: its eating is forbidden; and "Allah has forbidden wine" means its drinking. And in "Forbidden to you are your mothers" it means their marriage.

"Ummahat" is the plural of "ummah" or "ummahah," and the Arabs caused "ummahah" and "ummah" to die out while keeping its plural, just as they kept "umm" and caused its plural to die out, so "al-ummat" was not heard from them. "Ummah" occurs rarely in the verse of a poet recited by Ibn Kaysan:

"You accepted her from a mother of yours whose veil was long contested in the markets."

"Ummahah" occurs rarely in a verse attributed to Qusayy ibn Kilab:

"At their calling out, 'Hāl, my mother!' ... Khindif is my mother, and Ilyas my father."

In the plural, "ummahat" is abundant, and "ummat" occurs rarely in the verse of Jarir:

"Surely the son of Ukhayṭil was born to an evil mother, a bearer of shame, who is adorned with the 'ummat'."

It is said that "ummat" is specific to what does not reason. The poet al-Ra'i said:

"The swift camels of Mundhir and Muhariq were their 'ummat' and their stallions were their mares of breeding."

It is possible that the original of "umm" was "umma" or "ummaha," and deletion occurred in it, then they restored it in the plural.

It is a curious coincidence that the names of family members did not follow a regular pattern like "ab," which was of two letters, and "akh," "ibn," and "bint," and I suppose that this is due to its being from the ancient language that humankind spoke before the language was refined, and then the language developed upon them while remaining as they are. The intended meaning of "the mothers" and what is joined to them is the lower ones and those above them, and these are the prohibited ones by lineage. God Most High has affirmed the prohibition of those He mentioned, and they were already prohibited among the Arabs in their jahiliyyah, as confirmation of that prohibition and its strengthening, since that was already established among people previously. They said: the mother was never lawful for her son since the time of Adam, peace be upon him. The twin sister was forbidden while the non-twin sister was lawful. Then God forbade sisters absolutely from the time of Noah, peace be upon him. Then the daughters of a brother were forbidden, and their prohibition is found in the law of Moses, peace be upon him. The daughters of a sister remained lawful in the law of Moses, and their prohibition was established among the Arabs in their jahiliyyah, as related by Ibn 'Atiyyah in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas: that the prohibited ones mentioned here were prohibited in the jahiliyyah, except the wife of the father and the joining of two sisters. Similarly, al-Qurtubi transmitted from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, companion of Abu Hanifa, with the addition of a note on the exception in the words "except what has already passed" concerning these two only. I suppose all of this is a preparation for interpreting the exception in the words "except what has already passed" as meaning: except what passed from you in the jahiliyyah, so there is no sin upon you for it, as will come. But how can that be consistent, when the prohibition of stepdaughters and milk-sisters is mentioned among them, and I do not think they were prohibited in the jahiliyyah?

Know that the law of Islam has emphasized the clarification of close kinship, so it planted in souls a dignity that is kept free of the impurities of using it for play and lewdness, since marriage, although a suitable aim in view of its end, does not separate from the first thought that moves toward it, which is the thought of play and pleasure.

So the dignity of parenthood, as root and branch, prevents attempting play with the mother or the daughter, and for this reason the laws agreed on forbidding it. Then this extended to brothers' daughters and sisters' daughters. How does dignity spread to the branch of the sisters and not hold for the root? Similarly, the dignity of fathers extended to the sisters of fathers, who are the paternal aunts, and the dignity of mothers extended to their sisters, who are the maternal aunts. Thus the source of prohibiting these prohibited ones is the rule of manliness, following the universal principle of preserving honor, from the category of the necessary appropriate (al-munasib al-darurī), and this is among the earliest manifestations of human advancement. The "al-" in His saying "and daughters of the brother and daughters of the sister" is a substitute for the genitive, meaning: the daughters of your brother and the daughters of your sister.

His saying: "and your mothers who have nursed you" calls the wet-nurses "mothers," in accordance with the language of the Arabs, though they are not mothers in reality; rather they are placed in the position of mothers because children grew by their milk, and because of the love that is in the nature of children for their nursing women, like the love for their birth-mothers, and to increase the affirmation of this extension which the Arabs considered. Then this was attached by His saying: "who have nursed you," to prevent the supposition that the meaning is mothers in general, for had there been no intention to refer to nursing women, this description would have had no benefit.

The description of nursing, its duration, and its number have been left general here, leaving people to their customary understanding. The core of the matter in this is: the prohibition is connected to nursing only because of a meaning in it, namely that it is the nourishment which the child has no other nourishment than, by which he lives. Thus it has an effect on the continuation of the child's life similar to the effect of the mother on the very origin of her child's life. So nursing is not considered a cause of prohibition of the nursing woman upon her nursling except what fulfills this meaning by the child's nourishment being achieved, and that is what occurs during the period in which the child has not yet become independent of it. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "Nursing is only that which results from hunger."

The period of need for nursing has been limited to two years by His saying, Exalted is He: "And mothers nurse their children for two complete years" [al-Baqarah: 233], which has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah. No account is taken of nursing that occurs after the child has passed two years of age. On this view were 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, and Abu Yusuf. Abu Hanifa said: the period is two years and six months. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam related from Malik: two years and a few small days. Ibn al-Qasim related from him: two years and two months. al-Walid ibn Muslim related from him: two months and three. The soundest is the first view; and no account is taken of nursing beyond that

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 2 of 2):

Because His saying "those who are in your guardianship" (*allati fi juhurikum*) is a descriptive qualifier, and the original purpose of such a qualifier is restriction, as was intended in His saying "and your mothers who have nursed you" (*wa ummahatukumu allati arda'nakum*). The apparent meaning of this is that if the stepdaughter were far from his care, she would not be forbidden to him. This apparent reading is attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. Ibn 'Atiyya narrated it, but Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tahawi denied the soundness of its chain of transmission from 'Ali, and Ibn al-'Arabi said that it is a false report. Ibn Hazm, in *al-Muhalla*, affirmed with certainty the attribution of this view to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The Zahiriyya (the literalist school) held this view, and it seems that they considered that the cause of its prohibition is compounded of two things: that she is a stepdaughter (*rabiba*), and the intimacy (*al-waqar*) that arises between her and her stepfather when she is in his custody (*hajir*). As for the majority of scholars, they treated this descriptive qualifier as a clarification of the actual situation, given in the form of what is usual (*kharijan makhraj al-ghalib*), and they held that the stepdaughter is forbidden to the husband of her mother even if she was not in his custody. What seems to have led them to this is consideration of the cause of the prohibition of those forbidden through marriage affinity (*sihr*), which is the cause indicated by the words of al-Fakhr (al-Razi) mentioned earlier. In my view, the more apparent reading is that the qualifier here comes in the form of an explanation of cause: that is, "because they are in your guardianship," and this is a causal indication based on a probable cause (*ta'lil bi-al-mazinna*), so it does not require that the cause apply uniformly in all cases where the ruling applies.

As for His saying "from your women with whom you have consummated (the marriage)" (*min nisaikumu allati dakhaltum bihinna*): the phrase "from your women" (*min nisaikum*) was mentioned so that the clause "with whom you have consummated" could be built upon it. This is a condition for the prohibition of stepdaughters, such that a stepdaughter is not forbidden unless the marriage has been consummated with her mother, and the mere contract with her mother does not make her forbidden. This condition appears here but does not follow His saying "and the mothers of your women" (*wa ummahatu nisaikum*). Rather, the ruling there is stated without restriction. The majority said regarding that: "the mothers of your women" means the mothers of your wives. So the mother of a wife becomes forbidden merely by a man's contract with her daughter, because the contract makes the daughter his wife, and consummation is not required. They did not apply the unrestricted (*mutlaq*, the general or unqualified wording) to the restricted (*muqayyad*, the qualified wording) that comes after it, nor did they make the qualifier refer back to the coordinated items (*al-mutaʻatifat*), because the qualifier was attached to a specific noun whose connection is determined with one of the coordinated items, namely His saying "from your women" (*min nisaikum*), which is connected to His saying "and your stepdaughters" (*wa rabaibukum*). It cannot be connected to "the mothers of your women."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Jabir, and Ibn al-Zubayr said: the mother of a woman is not forbidden to her daughter's husband until he has consummated the marriage with his wife (the daughter). This is by applying the unrestricted to the restricted, and it is the more sound view in terms of its interpretation. The majority were unable to justify their position with a clear cause, nor could they support it with a transmitted report. The cause of the prohibition of a woman upon her daughter's husband equals the cause of the prohibition of a man's stepdaughter upon him. It appears that God mentioned the mothers of women before He mentioned the stepdaughters. Had He intended to make consummation with the mothers a condition for their prohibition upon their daughters' husbands, He would have mentioned it at the beginning of the statement, before mentioning it together with the stepdaughters.

There is a report from Zayd ibn Thabit that he said: if a man divorces the mother before consummation, he may marry her daughter; and if the mother dies, the daughter becomes forbidden to him. It seems that he considered divorce a departure from the contract, while death is an overpowering matter, so it is as if he had intended to consummate the marriage. This view has no merit.

As for His saying "and the wives of your sons" (*wa halaʼilu abna'ikum*): *halaʼil* is the plural of *halila*, which is on the pattern *fa'ila* in the sense of *fa'ila* (the active participle), and it means "wife," because she lawfully lies with him (*tahillu maʻahu*). Al-Zajjaj said: it is *fa'ila* in the sense of *maf'ula* (the passive participle), meaning "made lawful" (*muhallala*), since her family permitted her to him. So it would be from the pattern *fa'il* used for the passive from the quadriliteral form, as in the expression *hakim* (wise). The shift from saying "and the wives of your sons" (*wa ma nakaha abna'ukum* or *wa nisa'u abna'ikum*) to His saying "and the wives of your sons" (*wa halaʼilu abna'ikum*) is a variation (*tafannun*) intended to avoid repeating one of the two previous expressions. Otherwise there is no difference in usage among the three terms.

The husband has also been called *khalil* (intimate friend), and that term may bear both meanings in the same way. The prohibition of a son's wife is clear in its cause, like the prohibition of a father's wife.

As for His saying "who are of your own loins" (*alladhina min aslabikum*): this is an emphasis on the meaning of "sons" (*abna'*), to remove the possibility of metaphor, since the Arabs used to call an adopted child "son" and give him the rights of a son. Islam then abolished this, and God said: "Call them by their fathers' names" (33:5). After that no one was called by the name of his adoptive father, except al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, and this was considered a special privilege. God confirmed this by legislation in practice, by permitting His Messenger ﷺ to marry Zaynab bint Jahsh, after Zayd ibn Haritha, whom he had adopted and who used to be called Zayd ibn Muhammad, had divorced her. The son of a son and the son of a daughter, however far down the line, are "sons of the loins," because the grandfather has an unavoidable relation of begetting (*wilada*) with them.

As for His saying "and that you combine two sisters" (*wa an tajma'u bayna al-ukhtayni*): this is a prohibition on combining two sisters. Its wisdom is to remove jealousy from the one whom the Law wishes to keep complete affection between the two. It is known that the intended meaning of "combining" them applies to matters that involve jealousy, which is primarily marriage. It is extended to combining them in concubinage through ownership by right hand (*tasarri bi-milk al-yamin*), since the cause is the same. Therefore, His saying "And lawful for you is what is beyond these, that you seek with your wealth" (4:24) and His saying "except what your right hands possess" (4:24) are specified to exclude what has been mentioned.

It is reported from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan that he was asked about combining two sisters in concubinage, and he said: "One verse has made both of them lawful," meaning His saying "And He has made lawful for you what is beyond that" (4:24), "and one verse has made both of them unlawful," meaning this verse. That is, the matter is suspended. The same was reported from 'Ali and from a group of the Companions, that combining them in concubinage is forbidden, and this is the view of Malik. Malik said: if a man takes one of two sisters as a concubine and then wishes to take the other as a concubine, he must wait until he makes the first forbidden to himself by means of what makes a concubine forbidden, such as sale, manumission by contract (*kitaba*), or emancipation (*'itq*). And he is not subject to the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) if he combined them. The Zahiriyya said: combining two sisters in concubinage is permitted, because the verse addresses the rulings of marriage, while combining two sisters merely in ownership involves no prohibition.

As for His saying "except what has already passed" (*illa ma qad salaf*): it is like its counterpart mentioned earlier, and the explanation of it is the same as the explanation there. However, al-Qurtubi said here: it may carry an additional meaning, namely the permissibility of what has already passed, and that if the combining occurred in the pre-Islamic period (*jahiliyya*), the marriage is valid; and if the combining occurred in Islam, one is given the choice between the two sisters without applying the contracts of the unbelievers according to the requirements of Islam. He did not attribute this view to any of the jurists.

As for His saying "Indeed God is ever Forgiving and Merciful" (4:23): it suits that the meaning of "except what has already passed" be an affirmation of what they had contracted of such things in the time of ignorance. So forgiveness is for overlooking their continuing in it, and mercy is to explain the reason for that overlooking.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 24 (part 1 of 2):

Page 5
﴿And [also forbidden to you are] the married women, except those whom your right hands possess — the Decree of Allah upon you.﴾
This is coordinated with ﴿and that you combine [two sisters]﴾ [al-Nisa: 23], and the implied sense is: "And there are forbidden to you the married women among women, etc." This category of prohibited persons is due to an external cause, similar to the prohibition on combining two sisters.
Al-muhsanat, with a fatha on the ṣād, is from aḥṣanahā al-rajul: when a man guards her and keeps her to himself apart from others. It is said: imra'a muhsina, with a kasra on the ṣād, meaning a woman who has protected herself from anyone other than her husband. The word (al-muhsanat) in this verse has not been recited except with a fatha.
It is said: aḥsana al-rajul, so he is muhsin with a kasra on the ṣād and no other form; one does not say muhsan. For this reason no one recited muhsinina ghayra musafihin with a fatha on the ṣād. The word (muhsanat) has been recited with both fatha and kasra. And His saying ﴿fa-idha uḥsinna﴾ [al-Nisa: 25] has been recited with a damma on the hamza and kasra on the ṣād, and with a fatha on the hamza and fatha on the ṣād. The meaning intended here is the first meaning, namely: "And there are forbidden to you women who are married, as long as they remain under the bond of their husbands." The aim is the prohibition of two or more men sharing a single woman in marriage. This is an abolition of a type of marriage that existed in the Jahiliyya called al-Ḍimād, and of another type whose mention came in the ḥadīth of 'Ā'isha: that men, fewer than ten, would share a woman; when she conceived and gave birth, she would send to them, and none of them could refuse. She would say to them: "You know what happened between you, and I have given birth; so this is your son, O so-and-so," naming whomever she loved, and the child would be attributed to him. Another type is called nikāh al-istibḍā‘: the husband says to his wife, when she is pure from her menses: "Send to so-and-so and seek his seed." Her husband then withdraws from her and does not touch her until her pregnancy becomes clear from that man whose seed she sought. When her pregnancy is evident, her husband lies with her. ʿĀʾisha said: "They only did this out of desire for a noble child." I think this used to happen by mutual consent between the two men, and the purpose is not limited to the nobility of the child, for it may be for the giving of wealth or companionship. Thus the verse indicates the prohibition of every contract for marrying a woman who is already married, that is, the prohibition of a woman having more than one husband. The verse also conveys the generality of their prohibition even if their husbands were polytheists; for this reason the exception was necessary with His saying: ﴿except those whom your right hands possess﴾, that is, except those whom you have taken captive in war, because the "right hand" in the speech of the Arabs is a metaphor for the hand when it grips the sword.
Allah has made captivity a cause for dissolving marriage, in confirmation of the customary practice of nations in wars, and as a deterrent, so that they would not oppose Islam; for if captivity were removed from them, they would rush to fight the Muslims, since there is nothing an Arab fears more in war than the captivity of his women, and then his own captivity, as al-Nabigha said:
Fearing that our leadership might be seized, and our women not be taken until they die free.
The Muslims agreed that the captivity of a woman without her husband dissolves the marriage and makes her lawful to whoever falls to him in the division at the distribution of spoils. They differed concerning the woman captured together with her husband: the majority hold that her captivity dissolves her marriage. This is an overlooking of the wisdom for which the enslavement by capture was legislated. The relative clause hints at this, with His saying: ﴿what your right hands possess﴾; otherwise He would have said: "except those whose husbands you have abandoned."
Some scholars said: the entry of a female slave who is married into a new ownership, different from the ownership of the one who married her to that husband, permits her new owner to annul the marital bond between her and her husband, like one who is sold, given, or inherited; so the transfer of ownership is, in their view, a divorce. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id, and al-Hasan al-Basri. It is an anomalous view, for her second owner bought her knowing that she was married. It seems that what led them to this was correcting the meaning of the exception, and keeping the past tense in its literal sense in His saying (malakat), that is, "those whom they had owned before." The answer to this is that what is meant by (malakat) is ownership that is renewed after she was free and married. The verb is thus used in the sense of renewal.
It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was perplexed about the interpretation of this verse and said: "If I knew anyone who knows its interpretation, I would ride camels' livers to him," and perhaps he meant one who knows its interpretation from the Prophet (ﷺ).
Page 7
Some Muslims in the early period imagined that if a man married his slave-woman to a husband, it was not forbidden for the master to have intercourse with her while she was still married. I have seen it reported from Malik that a man from Thaqif did this in the time of 'Umar, and that 'Umar asked him about his slave-woman whom he had married off, and whether he had intercourse with her. He denied it, and 'Umar said to him: "If you had confessed, I would have made you an example."
His saying: ﴿the Decree of Allah upon you﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl), and it is an exhortation to the obligation of standing by the Book of Allah. So (ʿalaykum) is a substitute for (ilzamū, "adhere"), and it is treated as having the meaning of a verb-noun (ism al-fiʿl). This is common with adverbs and prepositional phrases placed in the position of verb-nouns by context, as in their saying: ilayka, dūnaka, and ʿalayka. (Kitāb Allāh) has its object placed before it according to the Kufans, or it is made to be in the accusative by an elided (ʿalaykum) that is indicated by what follows it, as an emphasis on it, following Sibawayh's interpretation of the verse of the rajaz poet:
O drawer of water, take my bucket, [be] yours, for I see people praising you.
It is also possible that "kitāb" is a verbal noun standing in the place of its verb, meaning: "Allah has prescribed that as a decree," with (ʿalaykum) related to it.
* * *
﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that, that you seek [them] with your wealth, [as] chaste, not unlawful sexual intercourse.﴾
This is coordinated with His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa: 23] and what follows it, and by this the three sentences harmonize in being informative in form while intended as injunctive, and in being verbal and in the past tense.
The Jumhur recited ﴿wa-uḥilla lakum﴾ with the active voice, and the hidden pronoun refers to the Name of Majesty in His saying: ﴿Decree of Allah upon you﴾.
The attribution of permitting to Allah the Exalted is made to show favour, and for this reason it departs from the manner of attributing prohibition to the passive voice in His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa: 23], because prohibition is a burden, so the context is not one of favour.
Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far recited (wa-uḥilla) with a damma on the hamza and kasra on the ḥa', in the passive voice, following the pattern of ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa: 23].
Page 8
Here (al-waraʾ) has the sense of (ghayr, "other than") and (dūn, "beside"), as in al-Nabigha's saying:
And there is no path for a man beyond God.
This is a metaphor, since (waraʾ) is the direction of the back of that to which it is added. The speech is an image representing the state of those addressed by the state of a traveller who leaves behind what is behind him and passes beyond it.
The meaning: "He has permitted to you all except those prohibited persons." This was revealed before the prohibitions set by the Sunnah, such as "A woman shall not be married on her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt," and such as "What is prohibited by blood kinship is prohibited by fosterage."
His saying: ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ may be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for (mā), with regard to the relative pronoun being the object of (aḥalla), and the implied sense is: "that you seek them with your wealth," for lawful women are not made permissible except after a contract and the giving of dowries. So the contract is the meaning of (tabtaghū), and the giving of the dower is the meaning of (bi-amwālikum), and the connective pronoun is elided: its implied form is "that you seek it." The inclusion here is like the inclusion in al-Nabigha's saying:
Lest ʿAmr's horses be led toward us, between barefoot and shod.
It is also possible to make (an tabtaghū) an object of an elided lām of causation, meaning: "He made them lawful so that you would seek them with your wealth," and the intended meaning is the very same as established in the first view.
(Muḥṣinīn) is a circumstantial accusative from the subject of (tabtaghū), meaning: "guarding yourselves from fornication," and what is intended is "married in the known manner." And ﴿not unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ is a second circumstantial accusative. The (musāfiḥ) is the fornicator, since fornication is called (sifāḥ), derived from (safḥ), which is that water is poured out without restraint; one says: "safaḥa al-mā'" (the water poured). This is because each of the man and the woman gives to the other what he or she desires without restriction or the consent of a guardian; so they derived it from the meaning of giving without restriction to a known matter, for the giver is called sassāḥ. When a man wanted from a woman the lewd act he would say to her: "Sāfiḥīnī" (pour yourself out for me), so the meaning of sifāḥ returned to mutual exchange and free rein. It is also said: because it is without a contract, so it is as if it were poured out pouring, that is, a flow that nothing restrains. Other etymologies are not sound, because the word is not restricted to fornication.

Page 9
﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them, give them their wages as an obligation. And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree after the obligation. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾
This is a branching (tafri') from ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾, and it is a verbal branching to explain the woman's right to the dower, and that it is in exchange for enjoyment, as an emphasis on what preceded it in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And give the women their dowries graciously﴾ [al-Nisa: 4], whether according to the majority, who make the dower a pillar of marriage, or according to Abu Hanifa, who makes it merely a right the wife may demand. Accordingly, the apparent reading is that (mā) be taken as a conditional noun referring to enjoyment, to show that marriage cannot be free of dower, for it is what distinguishes it from fornication. For this reason the predicate is joined with (fa-) in His saying: ﴿then give them their wages as an obligation﴾, because it is treated as the answer to the condition.
Al-istimtā‘ is benefiting, and the sīn and tā' in it are for intensification. Allah called marriage "enjoyment" because it is a worldly benefit, and all the benefits of this world are "matā' (provision)." He, Exalted, said: ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but provision﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26].
The pronoun governed by the bi- refers to (mā). And (min) is partitive, meaning: "If you have enjoyed any of them, then give them [their dowers]; so there is no lawful enjoyment of them without a dower."
Or (mā) refers to women, and the pronoun governed by bi- refers to the enjoyment derived from (istamta‘tum), and (min) is explanatory, meaning: "Whichever woman you have enjoyed, give her [her dower]."
It is also possible to make (mā) a relative pronoun, and the entry of the fā' into its predicate is because it is treated as a conditional; the word (mā) is used here rather than (man) because the intended sense is the category of women, not the aim toward one specific woman, and also because (mā) is often used for rational beings, but not vice versa. "Fariḍatan" is a circumstantial accusative from (ujūrihinna), meaning: "obligatory," that is, "determined among you." The purpose of this is to cut off disputes in the greatest transaction, which is intended for binding commitment and good repute.
As for the marriage of tafwīḍ, which is a contract concluded with silence about the dower, it is permissible according to all jurists; its permissibility rests on the fact that they do not delegate except while knowing the customary amount for women of their standing; and (farīḍa) here carries the meaning of an estimated amount. For this reason He said: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree after the obligation﴾, that is, for what you add for them, or what they remit to you willingly. This is the clear meaning of the verse, with no doubt about it.

A group, including Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Ibn Jubayr, held that it was revealed concerning mut'a marriage, because of His saying: ﴿for what you have enjoyed of them﴾. Mut'a marriage is that in which the spouses agree that the bond between them is limited by a period of time or a condition; when that term ends, the bond is dissolved. It was indeed permitted in Islam without doubt, and a prohibition of it was issued on the day of Khaybar, or on the day of Hunayn according to the more correct view. Those who said it was prohibited on the day of Khaybar said: then it was permitted during the conquest campaign, then it was forbidden on the third day after the conquest. It is also said it was forbidden at the Farewell Pilgrimage; Abu Dawud said: this is the most sound. What we have concluded is that the reports about it are greatly confused.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 24 (part 2 of 2):

The scholars differed about the final ruling on it (mut'ah, temporary marriage). The majority held that the matter settled on its prohibition. Some of them said it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of inheritance, because in it is ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ [al-Nisa': 12] and ﴿And for them is a quarter of what you leave﴾ [al-Nisa': 12], so it gave the spouses a share of the inheritance, and there was no inheritance in mut'ah. It was also said that it was abrogated by what Muslim related from Sabrah al-Juhani, that he saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leaning his back against the Ka'bah on the third day of the Conquest, saying: "O people, I had permitted you to enjoy these women, but Allah has prohibited it until the Day of Resurrection." Sabrah's being alone in reporting this on that day is a flaw in his narration, although it is established that people did enjoy (mut'ah). From 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Imran ibn Husayn, Ibn 'Abbas, and a group of the Successors (tabi'un) and Companions (sahabah), it is reported that they said it was permissible. It was said that it is permissible absolutely, and this is the view of the Imamiyya (the Twelver Shi'a), and it was said that it is permissible only in a state of necessity, according to the followers of Ibn 'Abbas from the people of Makkah and Yemen.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Had 'Umar not forbidden mut'ah, none would have committed fornication except a wretched person." And from 'Imran ibn Husayn, in the Sahih, that he said: "The verse of mut'ah was revealed in the Book of Allah, and no verse came after it abrogating it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us with it." Then a man said according to his own opinion whatever he wished, meaning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, when he forbade it during a period of his caliphate, after people had acted upon it for most of his caliphate. Ibn 'Abbas used to issue fatwas permitting it, and when Sa'id ibn Jubayr said to him: "Do you know what you have done with your fatwa? Caravans have carried it, until a sayer said:
صفحة ١١
I said to the caravan when our stay grew long: "O companion, do you want the fatwa of Ibn 'Abbas?"
A fair-skinned one, soft of extremities, tender, *** who will be your lodging until the people return.
He withdrew from issuing the fatwa and said: "I only permitted it as Allah permitted carrion and blood," meaning in cases of necessity. The scholars differed about whether 'Ali persisted in permitting it and about whether he retracted. What our scholars hold is that he retracted his permission. As for 'Imran ibn Husayn, he persisted in permitting it, and so did Ibn 'Abbas according to the sound view. Malik said: a mut'ah marriage is annulled (yufsakh) both before and after consummation, and its annulment is without divorce, although it was said that it requires divorce. There is no hadd (prescribed punishment) for it according to the sound position within the school. The most preponderant of the opinions is that it is a concession (rukhsah) for the traveler and the like, in circumstances of necessity. The reason it contradicts the purpose of marriage is the time limit it contains. There is room for consideration in this matter.

What is drawn from the various reports is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted mut'ah twice and forbade it twice. What is understood from this is that this was not repeated abrogation, but rather the permissibility of it was tied to the state of necessity, and so the narrators confused the grounds of the concession with abrogation. It is established that people practiced mut'ah in the time of Abu Bakr and 'Umar, and then 'Umar forbade it at the end of his caliphate. What we have concluded regarding the ruling on mut'ah marriage is that it is permissible in a situation of necessity that calls for a limited period of marital restraint, such as estrangement during travel or in military campaign when the man does not have his wife with him. It requires what marriage requires of dowry, witnesses, and a guardian (wali) where that is required. The woman is separated from him when the term ends, there is no inheritance between the man and the woman in it if either of them dies during the period of enjoyment, and her waiting period ('iddah) is one menstrual cycle, and the children are attributed to their father who enjoyed her. Al-Nahhas deviated, claiming that the child is not attributed to his father in a mut'ah marriage. We hold that this verse is far from being revealed about mut'ah marriage, and its context does not allow that. However, it is suitable to include mut'ah within the general scope of ﴿what you enjoy﴾, and so the question of the legitimacy of mut'ah marriage is referred to what you have just heard.
