﴿And whoever among you cannot afford the means to marry free believing women, let them marry from what your right hands possess of your believing young women. And Allah knows best your faith; you are of one another. So marry them with the permission of their people, and give them their bridal payments justly, as chaste women, not fornicators, nor those who take secret lovers. And when they are married, if they commit immorality, they shall receive half the punishment for free women. That is for whoever among you fears hardship, but to be patient is better for you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The phrase ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford﴾ is joined (ʿuṭifa) to the phrase ﴿And lawful to you is what lies beyond these﴾ [al-Nisa: 24]. This restricts its generality to other than slave women, and qualifies its unrestricted scope by the ability to afford the *ṭawl* (means).

*Ṭawl*, with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ and a sukūn on the wāw, means capacity. It is the verbal noun of *ṭāla* in its figurative sense of "to be able." This is because *ṭawl* implies the capacity to reach something. Hence they say *tatāwala li-kadhā*, meaning he stretched out to take it. Then they said *tatāwala*, meaning he strained to attain the capacity, and "where are the Pleiades from the hand of one who stretches?" They gave the literal *ṭāla* a verbal noun with a ḍamma on the ṭāʾ, and gave the figurative *ṭāla* a verbal noun with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ. This is among the cases in which the Arabs distinguished between two homonymous meanings.

*Al-muḥṣanāt* is read with a fatḥa on the ṣād by the majority, and with a kasra on the ṣād by al-Kisāʾī, according to the difference between the two meanings of *aḥṣanna*, as mentioned above. That is, those who have guarded themselves, or whom their guardians have guarded. The meaning is chaste women. *Al-muḥṣanāt* here is a descriptive term that came out in the typical manner, since a Muslim intends to marry only a chaste woman. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The adulterous woman none marries except an adulterer or a polytheist﴾ [al-Nur: 3], that is, according to the character of Islam. It has been said that *iḥṣān* is applied to freedom, and that *al-muḥṣanāt* means free women. But there is no need for this, and the language does not support it.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that *ṭawl* here is the capacity to give a bridal payment (mahr) to a free woman whom one needs to marry, whether first, second, third, or fourth. This is because Allah mentioned the inability to afford *ṭawl* in contrast to His saying:
[Page 13]
﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ [al-Nisa: 24], and His saying: ﴿so give them their payments as an obligation﴾ [al-Nisa: 24]. For this reason, this is the most correct interpretation of *ṭawl*. It is the view of Malik, and it was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and Jabir ibn Zayd.

Abu Hanifa held that whoever has one wife already has *ṭawl*, and so it is not permissible for him to marry slave women, because he is seeking desire, since he already has a woman who keeps him chaste from fornication. Something close to this occurred for Malik in the book of Muhammad ibn al-Mawwaz, and it is the view of Ibn Habib. Al-Lakhmi and al-Tabari found it good. But this is a restriction that does not fit the ease of Islam. Moreover, the need for a second wife may not be for desire, but for a need that one woman cannot meet. Therefore, the matter returns to the seeking of marriage and the existence of capacity.

Rabiʿa, al-Nakhaʿi, Qatada, ʿAta', and al-Thawri said: *ṭawl* is patience and endurance in marrying free women.

It occurred for Malik in the book of Muhammad that one who finds the mahr of a free woman but cannot afford her maintenance (nafaqa) may not marry a slave woman. This is not because maintenance is part of *ṭawl*, but because the existence of the mahr is *ṭawl*, and maintenance is unavoidable in both cases. Ashhab said: it is permissible for such a person to marry a slave woman, because the maintenance of a slave woman falls on her people if the husband does not take her into his household. It is evident that the disagreement concerns a particular situation.

The phrase *an yankiḥa* is the object of *ṭawlan*, with the preposition *li-* or *ʿalā* omitted, since this verbal noun does not take its object directly.

The meaning of ﴿to marry free women﴾ is to marry free women, whether virgins or previously married. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿so from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾.

The application of *al-muḥṣanāt* to women whom men marry is a figurative usage by the relation of what will become (ʿalāqat al-māʾāl), that is, those who will become chaste by that marriage if they were virgins, like His saying: ﴿One of them said: "I see myself pressing wine"﴾ [Yusuf: 36], meaning grapes that will become wine. Or by the relation of what was (ʿalāqat mā kāna), if they were previously married, like His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisa: 2]. This is clear, and it dispenses with interpreting *al-muḥṣanāt* as meaning free women. That interpretation is not supported by the language, neither literally nor figuratively, and the exegetes have been lax in saying so.

*Al-muḥṣanāt* has been described here as ﴿believing﴾, following the typical case. Most scholars of Islam hold that this description came out for the typical case. What probably led them to this is that the capacity to marry free women of the People of the Book is also *ṭawl*, since permission to marry them was not conditioned on inability to marry free Muslim women. But marrying Muslim slave women was conditioned on inability to marry free Muslim women. It therefore follows, by the principle of equality, that it is conditioned on inability to marry women of the People of the Book as well. The reason is that marrying a slave woman exposes the children to slavery, unlike marrying a woman of the People of the Book. Thus, the restriction of the concept of ﴿believing﴾ together with ﴿chaste﴾ is established by other evidences, and so they disregarded the description here and applied it in His saying: ﴿from your believing young women﴾.

Some Shafiʿis deviated and considered the concession of marrying a Muslim slave woman conditioned on inability to marry a free Muslim woman, even when one is able to marry a woman of the People of the Book. It seems that the purpose of mentioning the description ﴿believing﴾ here is that the Lawgiver did not give weight in legislation to mentioning what is not typical and not regarded by Him. Thus ﴿believing﴾ here functions like a title, as in the saying: "A believer is not stung from the same hole twice."

*Fatayat* is the plural of *fatat*, which originally means a young person, like *fata*. Here it means slave woman. It was applied to her as *jariya* was, and the slave man as *ghulam*. This is a figurative usage by the relation of necessity, because the male and female slave are treated as children in service and in little regard.

The description ﴿believing﴾ placed right after ﴿young women﴾ is meant as a restriction according to all the early scholars and the majority of jurists, because the basic principle is that a description has an implied meaning (mafhum), and there is no evidence that would nullify it. Therefore, marrying a woman of the People of the Book who is a slave is not permitted according to them. The wisdom in this is that the combination of slavery and disbelief distances the woman from the esteem that a Muslim accords her, so mutual harmony becomes less. Unlike the case when only one of the two descriptions applies. The effect of this appears in the children, who would be slaves while witnessing the conditions of a different religion, and so the gap widens between them and their father.

Abu Hanifa said: the position of the description ﴿believing﴾ here is like its position with His saying: ﴿chaste believing women﴾. Therefore he did not condition, for marrying a slave woman, that she be a believer. Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: I do not know of this view held by any of the early scholars except ʿAmr ibn Shurahbil, who was an early Successor (tabiʿi) and who narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ali ibn Abi Talib. Also, because Abu Hanifa does not hold to acting upon the implied meaning.

The meaning of ﴿what your right hands possess﴾ was mentioned earlier [al-Nisa: 24].

The idafa (genitive construction) in His saying ﴿your right hands﴾ and His saying ﴿from your young women﴾ is for bringing closer, and for removing what remained in the souls of the Arabs of despising slaves and slave women, and of being too proud to marry them or to marry them off. Likewise, the description ﴿believing﴾, although we consider it a restriction, does not lack, along with that, the benefit of bringing closer, since equality in marriage (kafaʾa) according to Malik relies first on religion.

[Page 15]

His saying ﴿And Allah knows best your faith﴾ is a parenthetical clause (iʿtiraḍ) that gathers several meanings. Among them: it is a command, and it is a qualification of the command in His saying: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford *ṭawl*﴾, and so on. Desire and haste may prevent people from fulfilling Allah's conditions, so He referred them to their faith, which their Lord knows. Among those meanings: He commanded marrying slave women when one is unable to marry free women. In the Jahiliyya they did not accept marrying a slave woman and making her a wife, but they satisfied their desires with them through prostitution. So Allah willed to honor believing slave women, as a reward for their faith, and to indicate that the unity of faith brought free people closer to slaves. When He had legislated all of this, He concluded it with His saying ﴿And Allah knows best your faith﴾, meaning its strength. Since faith is what raised the believers in rank before Allah, the faith of slave women became a persuasion to free men to abandon their aversion to marrying them. Also, because there may be a slave woman whose faith is better than the faith of a free man. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the most honorable of you before Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. Al-Zamakhshari, author of *al-Kashshaf*, and Ibn ʿAtiyya have pointed to this last point.

His saying ﴿you are of one another﴾ is a second concluding clause (tadhyil), by which He emphasized the second meaning intended by His saying ﴿And Allah knows best your faith﴾. After He brought the slave women close to them from the side of religious unity, He brought them close from the side of human unity, namely that free people and slaves are all from the children of Adam. Therefore *min* here is for connection (ittiṣaliyya).

Having made the command to marry slave women a consequence, He explained how this is done, saying: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾. He made the permission a condition, lest it become secret and fornication, and because marrying them without it is a transgression upon the rights of the slave women's people.

*Ahl* here means the masters and owners. This usage is common for the masters of slaves in Islamic speech. I suppose it is among the terms of the Qur'an, out of gentleness toward slaves, just as a slave was forbidden to say to his master "my lord (sayyidi)," but rather "my patron (mawlaya)." In the hadith of Barira, her people refused except that the patronage (walaʾ) should belong to them.

The verse is evidence for the guardianship (wilaya) of the master over his slave woman, and that if a slave woman marries without the master's permission, the marriage is annulled, even if her master permits it afterward. There is disagreement concerning the male slave. Al-Shaʿbi, al-Awzaʿi, and Dawud said he is like the slave woman. Malik, Abu Hanifa, and a group of the Successors said: if his master permits it, it is valid. The verse is cited as a weak argument for requiring the basic guardianship of the woman. The Hanafis argued with it to the opposite effect, since God called that *idhn* (permission) and did not call it a contract (ʿaqd). This is a weak argument, because *idhn* is also applied to the contract, especially after the particle of causation *bāʾ* was attached to it, which relates to ﴿marry them﴾.

[Page 16]

Concerning the bridal payments and what is reasonable (*maʿrūf*), what was said shortly before applies. However, His saying ﴿and give them﴾ and the attribution of ﴿payments﴾ to them is evidence that the slave woman has greater right to her mahr than her master. For this reason Malik said in the book of Mortgages (*Kitab al-Rahun*) of the *Mudawwana*: her master must equip her with her mahr. In the second book of Marriage (*Kitab al-Nikah al-Thani*) of the same work it occurred: her master has the right to take her mahr. It was said: this is a disagreement in Malik's view. It was also said: his statement in the Book of Marriage is about when she has not been prepared (*lam tubawwa'*), or when he has equipped her from his own before that. The meaning of *tubawwa'* is when he has made her residence with her husband in the house of her master.

His saying ﴿muḥṣanāt﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the slave women, and *iḥṣān* is a valid marriage. So it is a presumptive circumstance (ḥāl muqaddara), meaning in order that they become chaste.

His saying ﴿not fornicators﴾ is a description of the circumstance. Likewise ﴿nor those who take secret lovers﴾. The purpose of these is to express the abhorrence of what slave women used to commit in the Jahiliyya with their masters' permission, to earn money through prostitution and the like. People at that time were close to the Jahiliyya era.

*Al-musafihat* are women who commit fornication with an unspecified person. *Muttakhidhat al-akhdan* are women who take secret male friends; one of them takes a lover to whom she is exclusively devoted and does not associate with anyone else. Although this resembles marriage in terms of not having multiple partners, it differs from it in terms of concealment, unknown paternity, and removing the veil of honor. Therefore He joined it with His saying ﴿not fornicators﴾, blocking all avenues to fornication. The discussion of the types of relationships that the people of the Jahiliyya practiced was given at the beginning of this surah.

Al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the ṣād, and the majority read it with a fatḥa on the ṣād.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 25 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿So when they become chaste (uhsinna)﴾, meaning: when their husbands have made them chaste, i.e., when they have married. The verse thus implies that marriage is a condition for enforcing the penalty for fornication upon slave women, and that the penalty is the specified flogging, because it is the one in which halving by number is possible. Know that if we follow what we have verified earlier regarding the meaning of the previous verse, it becomes certain that this verse was revealed after the legislation of the flogging penalty for the adulterous woman and the adulterer by the verse in Surat al-Nur. It would then be specifying the general wording regarding the adulterous woman as applying to other than the slave woman, and the placement of this verse in this position is among what was appended to this surah to complete the rulings related to slave women, as occurs in many similar cases, as was mentioned in the eighth introduction among the introductions of this tafsir.

This verse has perplexed the interpreters, because it implies that a slave woman is not to be flogged for fornication unless she is married. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar interpreted it by saying that ihsan here means Islam, and they held that a slave woman is flogged for fornication whether she is married or unmarried, and the Four Imams went to this view. I do not think that the evidence of the Four Imams is taking ihsan here to mean Islam; rather it is what is established in the two Sahihs, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "was asked about a slave woman who commits fornication and is not made chaste, so he made the penalty obligatory upon her." Ibn Shihab said: a married slave woman is subject to the penalty by the Qur'an, and an unmarried slave woman is subject to the penalty by the Sunnah. And this statement is excellent. The Qadi Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: taking ihsan in the verse to mean Islam is far-fetched, because the mention of their faith ("iman") has already preceded in His saying: ﴿from your believing slave girls﴾, and this is an over-refinement, though Ibn 'Atiyyah rejected it.

The verse has indicated that the penalty for a slave woman is flogging, and it does not mention stoning. If stoning was legislated before its revelation, the verse indicates that a slave woman is not to be stoned, which is the view of the majority; Abu Thawr hesitated on this matter. If stoning was legislated after that, the verse does not indicate the negation of stoning for a slave woman; yet the intent of halving in her penalty indicates that she is not to be subjected to the penalty of a free woman, so stoning is excluded, because it does not admit of division, and this is what Abu Thawr overlooked. It has been related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he was asked about the penalty for a slave woman, and he said: "The slave woman has cast the covering of her head from behind the house," i.e., she has cast her veil within the house of her people, meaning she goes out to every place her family sends her to, and cannot refrain from that, so she comes to a place where she cannot refrain from immorality. They said: he held that there is no penalty upon her if she commits fornication so long as she is not married, and it seems he thought that if she is married, her husband has restrained her. This statement, although it is not the well-known one from him, we have mentioned because in it there is a lesson for one who is discerning in the ways of the Shari'ah regarding the intensification of punishment in proportion to the strength of the betrayal and the weakness of the excuse.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (uhsinna) with a dammah on the hamzah and a kasrah on the sad, in the passive voice, and it has the meaning of muhsanat with a fathah on the sad. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim and Khalaf read it with a fathah on the hamzah and a fathah on the sad, and this has the meaning of muhsinat with a kasrah on the sad.

And His saying: ﴿That is for whoever of you fears hardship (al-'anat)﴾ is a reference to the ruling that is suitable to be restricted by fear of hardship, and that ruling is marrying slave women.

Al-'anat means hardship. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have put you in hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. It is meant here as the hardship of celibacy, which becomes a means to fornication; therefore some said: al-'anat is meant as fornication.

And His saying: ﴿And that you be patient is better for you﴾ means: if you are able to be patient with the hardship until it becomes easy for him to marry a free woman, that is better, so that he does not put his children into the humiliation of the detested servitude, which the Lawgiver disliked except out of necessity, and so that he does not put himself into the degradation of others dealing with his wife.

And His saying: (﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾) means: if you fear hardship and are not patient with it, and you marry slave women, then this confirms the meaning of permissibility, indicating that the permission for this is for the sake of lifting hardship, because Allah is Merciful to His servants and Forgiving. So forgiveness here means overlooking what the aim of the Shari'ah requires to be prohibited, and there is no sin here at all for forgiveness to apply to.

This is a tadhyil (a closing affirmation) whose purpose is to reassure the believers and to win their souls over to carrying out the rulings laid down from the beginning of the surah up to this point. These are numerous rulings, commands and prohibitions that require them to cast off customs they had grown accustomed to and to turn away from desires they had considered permissible. This is what His saying after this indicates: ﴿And those who follow their desires wish that you would deviate with a great deviation﴾ [al-Nisa: 27], meaning, that they should continue on as they were in the Jahiliyyah. So He followed this with a statement that there is in this an explanation and guidance, so that the law of this community would not fall short of the laws of the nations before it, but would surpass them in the orderliness of its affairs. Thus this served as a kind of justification for what was mentioned of the prohibited things. So His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ is a ground (ta'lil) for the detailed explanation of the rulings in situations of doubt, so that they do not go astray as those before them went astray. Therein is the indication that this Shari'ah is more guided than what came before it.

His saying: ﴿and to guide you to the ways of those before you﴾ is a statement of the purpose of joining this community to the excellences of the nations that came before it.

صفحة ١٩
Al-iradah (will) means intent and resolve to act, and it is also applied to the divine attribute that particularizes the possible with some of what is permissible for it. The bestowal of favour through what Allah has legislated for the Muslims in clarifying the rulings has already had His will applied to it in the past, but the present tense is used here to indicate the renewal and continuity of that clarification, since these legislations are lasting and continuous, serving as clarification for those addressed and for those who come after them, and to indicate that Allah keeps sending down successive clarification after them.

His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾: the verb "yubayyina" (to make clear) is governed by an elided "an" (that, the verbal particle), and the resulting verbal noun is the object of "yurid" (desires), meaning: Allah desires for you clarification, guidance and repentance. The original usage was to mention "an" (that), and for this reason the lam here serves to emphasize the meaning of the verb preceding it. The addition of this lam after the root of "irada" (desire) and after the root of "amr" (command) has become common, replacing the verbal "an". You say: "uridu an taf'ala" (I want that you do) and "uridu li-taf'ala." The Most High said: ﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32], and He said: ﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ [al-Saff: 8] (with li), and He said: ﴿And I have been commanded that I should submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ghafir: 66], and He said: ﴿And I have been commanded to act justly between you﴾ [al-Shura: 15] (with li). When they come with the lam, it resembles the lam of causation, so they estimated an "an" after the emphasizing lam, just as they estimated it after the lam of "kay" (in order that), because it resembles it in form. For this reason al-Farra' said: the lam is a substitute for the verbal "an." And to this approach the author of al-Kashshaf inclined.

Sibawayh said: it is the lam of causation, i.e., the lam of "kay," and what follows it is the cause, and the object of the verb preceding it is elided and is determined by the context, i.e., Allah desires the legislation of what is lawful and what is unlawful in order to clarify. Some of them affirmed Sibawayh's view by saying that the elided object is indicated by the causation mentioned, so it is estimated as: Allah desires clarification in order to clarify, so the statement becomes an intensification by making the cause itself the caused.

Al-Khalil, and Sibawayh in one narration from him, said: the lam is a fixed adverbial complement, a predicate of the preceding verb, and that verb is estimated as a verbal noun without the fusion of "an," on the pattern of "You hear of al-Mu'aydi as better than that you see him," i.e., Allah's will is directed toward clarification. Perhaps their speech is understood as hyperbole, as if Allah's will were restricted to that. A small group said: this lam is for emphasis, contrary to the basic usage, because the lam of emphasis is only brought when the governing verb is weakened by being secondary or by being placed later. The best of these views is Sibawayh's, as evidenced by the entry of the lam upon "kay" in the verse of Qays ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah al-Khazraji:

"I wanted, in order that people might know that it is the trousers of Qays, and the delegations are witnesses."

صفحة ٢٠
From al-Nahhas: some of the reciters named this lam the lam of "an."

The meaning of: ﴿and to guide you to the ways of those before you﴾: guidance to the foundations of what set right the condition of the nations that preceded us, from the universal principles of the laws and their objectives. Al-Fakhr said: although the laws and obligations differ in themselves, they agree in the matter of benefits. I say: this is like His saying: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13], to the end of the verse.

His saying: ﴿and turn to you in forgiveness﴾, meaning: He accepts your repentance when you believed and cast aside what the people of polytheism were upon: marrying the wives of fathers, marrying the mothers of your wives, marrying stepdaughters, and combining two sisters.

The meaning of ﴿and turn to you in forgiveness﴾ is: He accepts your complete repentance by following Islam, so do not undo that by committing what is forbidden. And the meaning of ﴿and turn to you﴾ is not "He enables you to repent," which would raise the objection that the will of Allah does not fail, since enabling repentance is not constant among all people. Rather, the verse is an exhortation to repentance by way of metonymy, because the promise of accepting it entails encouraging it, like what is in the hadith: "He says: Is there any who seeks forgiveness, that I may forgive him? Is there any who calls upon Me, that I may respond to him?" This is the proper way of interpreting it, and al-Fakhr and others have here far-fetched elaborations for which there is no need.

His saying: ﴿and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ is fitting to the clarification, the guidance, and the encouragement to repentance by way of promising its acceptance, for all of that is the effect of knowledge and wisdom in guiding the community and bringing it closer to right conduct.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 27:

﴿And Allah desires to turn in forgiveness toward you, while those who follow the desires desire that you deviate into a tremendous deviation.﴾

He repeated His saying ﴿And Allah desires to turn in forgiveness toward you﴾ in order to build upon it His saying ﴿while those who follow the desires desire that you deviate into a tremendous deviation.﴾ It is therefore not a verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi, repetition of a word for emphasis). This is like the repetition of a word in the apodosis, in an attribute, and similar constructions, as in the saying of al-Ahwas in al-Hamasa:

Page 21

"So when he moves, he moves away from a raging one, whose outbursts are feared by his equals."

And like His exalted saying: ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ [al-Qasas: 63].

The purpose of mentioning the desire of those who follow the desires is to alert the Muslims to the hidden intentions of their enemies, so that they may know the difference between what Allah desires for creation and what the helpers of the devils desire, namely those who follow the desires. For this reason he placed the subject (musnad ilayh) before the verbal predicate (khabar fi'li) in His saying ﴿And Allah desires to turn in forgiveness toward you﴾, to indicate restriction relative to a particular comparison (takhsis idafi), i.e., Allah alone is the One who desires to turn in forgiveness toward you, that is, to urge you to repentance and to abandon sins. As for those who follow the desires, they desire that you turn away from the truth and incline away from it toward sins.

The use of the term "desire" (iradah) for the wish of the people of desires that the Muslims should incline away from the truth is by way of mushakalah (agreement in wording), in relation to ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26]. The intended meaning is: "and those who follow the desires love that you incline." Since their wish for the Muslims to incline away from the truth is a wish that is not free of their striving to bring that about, their wish resembles the desire of one who wills an act. A parallel to this is His exalted saying after this verse: ﴿They buy error and desire that you should go astray from the way﴾ [al-Nisa': 44].

The object of "tamilu" (you incline) is omitted because it is clear from the contextual indicator (qarinah al-maqam). By "those who follow the desires" he means those whose desires overpower them so that they oppose what Allah has prescribed for them, from among those who have no religion. These are the ones who do not consider the consequences of sins, their corruptions, and their punishment, but rather satisfy their desires which summon them to these sins. Mentioning this relative clause here serves to disparage their condition; thus the relative clause hints at the cause of the predicate. The intended ones here are the polytheists, who desired that the Muslims would follow them in marrying the wives of fathers; and the Jews, who desired that the Muslims would follow them in marrying paternal sisters, marrying paternal aunts, and combining two sisters in marriage. The great inclination (al-mayl al-'azim) is distance from the rulings of the Law and disparaging them. The polytheists used to make fornication appealing to the Muslims and offer them prostitutes. The Magians used to challenge the prohibition of marrying a brother's daughter and a sister's daughter, saying: "Why has your religion permitted the daughter of a paternal aunt and the daughter of a maternal aunt?" The Jews used to say: "The sister from the father is not forbidden, nor is the paternal aunt, nor the maternal aunt, nor the paternal uncle, nor the maternal uncle." He expressed all of this by the word "desires," because the coming of Islam has made clear the end of the permissibility of what was permitted in the other laws, let alone what was forbidden in all the laws and what the people of polytheism had been lax about.

Page 22

﴿Allah wants to lighten [the burden] for you, and man was created weak.﴾

This follows the excuse mentioned earlier, in His words: ﴿Allah wants to make [things] clear for you and to guide you to the ways of those before you﴾ [an-Nisa: 26]. It reminds the reader that Allah continues to show gentleness toward this community and intends ease for it, not hardship. It also points to the fact that this religion established the preservation of benefits (maslahah) and the averting of harms (mafsadah) in the easiest and most gentle manner. For this reason, the Shari'ah may set aside some harms when prohibiting them would bring hardship or the neglect of a benefit, just as it set aside the harms of marrying slave-women out of consideration for the hardship on one who lacks the means (dhu al-tawl). The verses that establish this meaning reach the level of certainty, such as His words: ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], His words: ﴿Allah wants ease for you and does not want hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and His words: ﴿and He removes from them their burdens and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. In the authentic hadith: "Verily this religion is ease, and no one will overburden this religion but it will overcome him." Likewise, he (ﷺ) used to instruct his companions whom he sent to spread the religion. He said to Mu'adh and Abu Musa: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult," and he said: "You were only sent as bringers of good news, not as repellers." He also said to Mu'adh when some who prayed behind him complained about his lengthening [of the prayer]: "Are you one who causes trial (fattan)?" Thus ease was one of the foundations of the Islamic Shari'ah, and from it branched out the concessions (rukhas) in their two types.

His words ﴿and man was created weak﴾ are a concluding statement (tadhyil) and a guiding justification for the lightening [of the burden], and a demonstration of the excellence of this religion, that it is the most suitable of religions for people in every time and place. For this reason, the earlier religions took into account one state over another. Among this meaning is His exalted words: ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knew that among you there is weakness﴾ [al-Anfal: 66], the verse in Surat al-Anfal. Some have interpreted the weakness mentioned here as weakness with regard to women. Tawus said: "A person is never weaker in any matter than in the matter of women." His intention is not to restrict the meaning of the verse to this, but it is certainly among what was taken into account in the verse, since among the rulings mentioned earlier is a concession regarding marriage.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 29–30:

Page 23
﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you.﴾
This is a new beginning (isti'naf) of the legislation intended in this surah. The mark of a new beginning is its opening with ﴿O you who have believed﴾. Its connection (munasabah) to what precedes it is that the rulings on inheritance and marriage contained commands to give the rightful holder his right in wealth, such as His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their properties﴾, and His saying: ﴿So give them their compensation as an obligation﴾ [4:24], and His saying: ﴿And if they give you willingly something of it, then consume it with pleasure and satisfaction﴾ [4:4], and so on. From this it moved to a general legislation concerning wealth and lives.

It has already been mentioned that "consuming" (al-akl) is a metaphor for benefiting from a thing in a complete way, such that it does not return to another. Thus "consuming wealth" is taking possession of it with the intention of not returning it to its owners, and the usual sense of this is possession by wrongdoing, a metaphor that has become like a literal meaning. It may also be applied to permitted benefit, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they give you willingly something of it, then consume it with pleasure and satisfaction﴾ [4:4], and His saying: ﴿And whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is reasonable﴾ [4:6]. For this reason, the forbidden form of it has commonly been restricted by the qualifier (unjustly) and similar terms.

The pronoun subject of (do not consume) and the pronoun attached to (wealth) refer to those who have believed. It is evident that a person is not forbidden from consuming his own wealth, and his benefiting from his own wealth is not called "consuming." So the meaning is: one of them should not consume the wealth of another. "Unjustly" (al-batil) is the opposite of the truth, and it is what Allah has not legislated and is not by His permission; the "ba'" in it denotes accompaniment (mulabasah).

The exception in His saying: ﴿except that it be trade﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), because trade is not among consuming wealth unjustly. So the meaning is: "but the fact that trade is not forbidden." The placement of the disjunctive exception here is clear and follows the Arabic manner, since in istidrak (a corrective "but") it is not necessary that the preceding statement include what is then corrected, and the istidrak does not imply restriction. Accordingly, it is what the context requires. It is also permissible to regard the qualifier "unjustly" as nullified in the case of the exception, so that it becomes an exception from the consumption of wealth and is connected (muttasil). This would imply that the exception restricts the permission to consume wealth to trade, which is not the case. Whichever it is, singling out trade by the istidrak or the exception is because it is the strongest kind of consuming wealth in resemblance to the unjust,

Page 24
for all gifts (tabarru'at) are consumption of wealth by pleasure of soul, and exchanges (mu'awadat) other than trades are likewise, because the taking by each of the two contracting parties of a consideration for what he gave to the other, equal to its value in his view, gratifies his soul. As for trade, because of what it contains of the seller of goods taking more wealth than the value of what he gave to the buyer, it may resemble consuming wealth unjustly, and therefore it was singled out for istidrak or exception. The wisdom in permitting the consumption of the surplus wealth in it is that upon it depends the circulation of goods needed and of those for embellishment, and were it not for the merchants' undertaking and bringing goods, the one in need would not find what fills his need when he requires it. This is indicated by what is in the Muwatta' from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, that he said concerning the hoarding of food: "But whatever importer imports at the cost of his liver in winter and summer, he is the guest of 'Umar; let him sell as he wishes and withhold as he wishes."

Al-Jumhur read ﴿except that it be trade﴾ with the raising of (trade) as the subject of kana in its complete sense, i.e., "it occurs." 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with the accusative (tijaratan), as the predicate of the incomplete kana, its subject estimated as: "except that the wealth be trade," i.e., wealth of trade.

His saying: ﴿by mutual consent among you﴾ is an attribute of "trade," and (an) in it denotes departure (mujawazah), i.e., proceeding from mutual consent, which is contentment from both sides by what indicates it of speech or custom. In the verse there is what may serve as evidence for Malik's view of denying the option of the meeting place (khiyar al-majlis), because Allah made the basis of concluding the contract to be mutual consent, and mutual consent is achieved at the time of trading by offer and acceptance.

This verse is a great principle regarding the sanctity of wealth. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The wealth of a Muslim man is not lawful except with the good pleasure of his soul." And in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed your blood and your wealth are sacred to you."

The placing of the prohibition on consuming wealth before the prohibition on killing souls, though the latter is graver, is either because the connection of what precedes led to the prohibition on consuming wealth, so it deserved precedence for that reason, or because the addressees were recent in their acquaintance with the Jahiliyyah, and consuming wealth was easier for them, and they were more casual about it than about killing souls, since it occurred in places of weakness where the owner does not defend himself, such as the orphan, the woman, and the wife. So the one who consumes the wealth of these is safe from consequences

Page 25
unlike killing a soul, for none is spared its consequences, however great his courage and might among his people; nor was anyone more protected than Kulayb ibn Wa'il, because the tribes did not waive the blood of their slain.
* * *
﴿And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you.﴾ ﴿And whoever does that in aggression and injustice, We will drive him into a Fire, and that is ever easy for Allah.﴾
His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ is a prohibition against a man killing another; the two pronouns in it are distributive, since it is known that no one kills himself so as to be prohibited from it. Yet a man killing himself falls within the prohibition, because Allah did not permit a person to destroy himself as He permitted him to dispose of his wealth. As for whether the intended meaning here is specifically the prohibition on a man killing himself, then no. As for what is in the Musnad of Abu Dawud: "that 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with him, performed tayammum on a day of severe cold without bathing, and that was during the expedition of Dhat al-Salasil, and he led the people in prayer; the news reached the Messenger of Allah, and he asked him, and he said: O Messenger of Allah, indeed Allah says ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾; and the Prophet did not reprimand him," that is an argument from the generality of the pronoun in "kill" rather than the specific occasion.

His saying: ﴿And whoever does that﴾ refers to what was mentioned: consuming wealth unjustly and killing. It has been said that the reference is to what was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by force﴾ [4:19], because all of that was not followed by a threat, whereas a threat preceded it; this was said by al-Tabari. He restricted it by "aggression and injustice" so that consuming wealth by a right way is excluded, and killing a soul likewise, as in killing a killer. In a hadith: "When they say it, they have protected their blood and their wealth from me, except by its right."

"Aggression" (al-'udwan), with a damma on the 'ain, is a verbal noun on the pattern of kufran, and it is said with a kasra on the 'ain, which is domination with force; it may be with injustice generally, and it may be with right. Allah said: ﴿There is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾ [2:193]. The conjunction of His saying "and injustice" to "aggression" is conjunction of the specific to the general.

(Sawfa) is a particle that enters upon the present tense and confines it to the future; it is synonymous with the sin (the particle sa-) according to the most correct view. Some grammarians said that sawfa indicates a distant future and named it al-taswif (procrastination), but there is no usage that supports this. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿And they will burn in a blaze﴾ [4:10] in this surah. (Nusallihi) means we make him burn or be scorched; the verb sali has also passed, and the reason for the accusative of "fire" was noted there. The verse indicates two of the universal aims of the Sharia: the preservation of wealth and the preservation of souls, of the category of the necessary and appropriate (al-munasib al-daruri).
