Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 31:

﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to an honorable entrance.﴾

This is a parenthetical statement (i'tiraD), whose mention was appropriate after the mention of two major sins: the killing of a soul, and consuming wealth wrongfully. This follows the Qur'an's habit of varying its style from one mode to another, and of seizing opportunities to deliver legislation right after exhortations, and vice versa.

The idafa of "kaba'ir" (major sins) to "ma tunhawna 'anhu" (that which you are forbidden) indicates that prohibited acts are of two kinds: major sins, and what falls short of them, which are called minor sins (saghair), described by way of contrast. Here they are called misdeeds (sayyi'at). He promised that He would forgive the misdeeds for those who avoid the major sins of what is forbidden. In the verse of al-Najm He said: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾ [al-Najm: 32], so He called the major sins "fawahish" (grave immoralities) and called their counterpart "al-lamam" (minor lapses). Thereby it is established that sins before Allah are of two kinds: grave major sins, and sins below that level, to which a believer may often be prone. For this reason the early scholars (al-salaf) differed in specifying the major sins.

From 'Ali: they are seven: associating partners with Allah, killing a soul, slandering chaste women, consuming the property of orphans, fleeing on the day of battle, and reverting to the desert as an apostate after emigration (ta'arrub ba'da al-hijra). He cited for all of them the evidence of the Qur'an's decisive prohibitions concerning them. In the hadith of al-Bukhari from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Avoid the seven destructive sins," and he mentioned those that 'Ali mentioned, except that he put sorcery in place of ta'arrub.

'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: they are nine, with the addition of profanity in the Sacred Mosque (al-ilhad fi al-masjid al-haram) and disobedience to parents ('uquq al-walidayn).

Ibn Mas'ud said: they are what has been forbidden from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to here.

From Ibn 'Abbas: every matter for which a threat of Fire, or punishment, or curse is stated is a major sin.

Also from Ibn 'Abbas: the major sins are what Allah has forbidden in His Book.

The best definition of the major sin is the statement of Imam al-Haramayn: it is every offence which indicates that its perpetrator has little concern for religion and a weakness in his faith.

Among the early scholars there was one who said: all sins are equal, if committed deliberately. And from Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini: all sins are equal absolutely, and he denied minor sins. These two views are baseless, because the textual evidence testifies to dividing sins into two categories, and because the corruptions contained in sins also vary. The authentic hadiths also affirm the category of major sins and the greatest of major sins.

Upon the establishment of major and minor sins follow legal obligations (ahkam taklifiyya): among them, the addressee is commanded to avoid major sins strictly; among them, repentance from them is obligatory upon committing them; among them, abandoning major sins counts as repentance from minor sins; among them, the perpetrator of major sins loses his standing of justice ('adala); among them, a judge's ruling by one who is engaged in them is overturned; among them, it is permissible to shun one who openly commits them; and among them, the wrong is to be changed by one who is engaged in it. Upon them also follow matters of the fundamentals of religion: among them, the takfir of the perpetrator of a major sin according to a group of the Kharijites, who distinguish between major and minor sins; and his being placed in an intermediate position between disbelief and Islam according to the Mu'tazila, contrary to the majority of the scholars of Islam.

It is strange that someone should say: Allah did not distinguish the major sins from the minor sins so that this would deter people from committing any sin. A parallel to this is concealing the middle prayer among the prayers, the Night of Decree among the nights of Ramadan, and the hour of answered prayer during the hours of Friday. Thus al-Fakhr related it in his tafsir. The folly of this speaker, and al-Fakhr's failure to refute it, has become clear, because the matters they cited relate to the virtues of acts, to which no obligation attaches. So concealing them is intended to encourage seeking them out, so that people will increase in doing good. But concealing a matter that one is obligated to is leading to misguidance, and this does not occur from the Lawgiver.

The word "madkhal" with a fatha on the mim is a noun of place of entering, and it may also be a mimi verbal noun. The meaning is: We will admit you to an honorable place, or We will admit you to an honorable entering. "Karim" means what is precious in its kind. So the intended sense is either Paradise or entering into it, and what is meant is Paradise. "Mudkhal" with a damma on the mim is likewise a place or the verbal noun of "adkhala." Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read (madkhalan) with a fatha on the mim, and the rest of the ten readers read it with a damma on the mim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 32:

Page 28
﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you excel over others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things.﴾
This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause: "Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood," and upon: "Do not kill yourselves."

The connection between the two conjoined clauses is that wishing (tamannī) makes the thing wished for beloved to the one who wishes; when he loves it, his soul follows it, he strives to obtain it and becomes captivated by it. This captivation may then drive him to devise stratagems to obtain it if it is not in his hand, and to seize it for himself against the rightful owner, so that he turns a blind eye to the duty of giving the right to its owner and to the prohibitions of the Sharia contained in the sentences conjoined to it. In our time this wishing has become a trial for groups of Muslims, who have absorbed from the extremists in the pursuit of equality the manners that have led many nations to the creed of Communism, so that they flounder in seeking equality in everything and suffer an exhaustion from which they have gained nothing.

The prohibition of wishing and of the soul's longing for what is not its own comes in this verse in a general form. Thus it serves as a concluding summary (tadhyīl) of the preceding rulings, to block their means and the means of other things, and it is among the comprehensive expressions (jawami' al-kalim) in averting evils. Wishing has been among the greatest means of crimes, for it leads to envy, and the first crime committed on earth arose from envy. Wealth has often been plundered and souls killed out of desire for expanded provision, or the temptation of women, or the attainment of rule, and history is full of incidents of this kind.

What appears is that this wishing is the wishing for the wealth of the wealthy, the wishing for the shares of heirs, the wishing to seize the property of orphans, male and female, and the wishing to deprive women of inheritance, in harmony with what preceded concerning giving orphans their property and doing justice to women in their dowries, and not harming them, compelling them to waive them, and giving the heirs their shares as God has apportioned to them. All of this is from the excelling of some people over others in provision.

Page 29
Al-Qaffal has indicated a connection for the conjunction that falls within what I have mentioned. In the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi, from Mujahid, from Umm Salama, that she said: "O Messenger of Allah, men fight and women do not fight, and we only have half of the inheritance." So Allah revealed: ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you excel over others.﴾ al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a mursal hadith." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "All its narrations are fair (hisan), but they do not reach the level of soundness." I say: Since it is mursal, the statement "So Allah revealed: ﴿And do not wish﴾ etc." is from the words of Mujahid, and its meaning is that the revelation of this verse was close in time to the saying of Umm Salama, so its generality included what answers Umm Salama and others.
Narrations have been reported: some that this verse was revealed concerning women's wishing for jihad; some that it was revealed concerning the statement of a woman: "Indeed, the male has the like of the share of two females, and the testimony of two women equals that of one man; are we then in deeds likewise?"; some that men said: "The reward of our deeds is double the reward of women"; and some that women asked for the reward of martyrdom in the way of Allah and said: "If fighting were prescribed for us, we would fight." All of these are particular instances and examples of what the generality of "that by which Allah has made some of you excel over others" encompasses.

Wishing (tamannī) is seeking the attainment of what is difficult for the seeker to attain. It has states: among them is that one wishes for what is from Allah's bounty without looking toward anything in the hand of another, and without any obstacle preventing it from the Sharia or custom, whether it is attainable, like wishing for martyrdom in the way of Allah, or unattainable, like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I would love to be killed in the way of Allah, then be brought to life, then be killed, then be brought to life, then be killed." And his saying ﷺ: "Would that we could see our brothers," meaning the Muslims who will come after him.

Among them is that one wishes for what cannot be attained due to an customary or legal impediment, like the wish of Umm Salama that women should fight as men fight, and that a woman should be equal to a man in inheritance. Among them is that one wishes in a manner that indicates dissatisfaction with what Allah has decreed and irritation with it, or agitation and disquiet, or non-acceptance of the legal rulings. Among them is that one wishes for a blessing similar to a blessing in the hand of another, while it is possible for the wisher to attain it without it being removed from the one who has it, like wishing for knowledge like that of the mujtahid, or wealth like the wealth of Qarun. 

Page 30
Among them is that one wishes for that, but its like cannot be attained except by stripping the one blessed with it, like wishing for the possession of a specific town or the wife of a specific man. Among them is that one wishes for the removal of a blessing from another without intending that it pass to the wisher.

The sum of the meaning of the prohibition in the verse is that it is either a prohibition of disapproval (nahy tanzih), to educate the believers not to occupy their souls with what they have no capacity to obtain, since it is called wishing, lest they be in the state described in the hadith: "He wishes wishes upon Allah." And his saying: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾ is guidance toward seeking what is possible, since they know that asking and supplicating Allah is in what is hoped to be attained, otherwise it would be bad manners.

Or it is a prohibition of prohibition (nahy tahrim), which is the apparent sense from its conjunction with the forbidden matters, so it is a manifest or inward transgression, like envy, by the indication of its mention after his saying: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Nisa: 29] ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa: 29].

So the first and fourth types of wishing are not forbidden. Al-Bukhari has entitled a chapter in his Sahih: "Chapter on wishing for martyrdom in the way of Allah," and "Chapter on envying (ighbita) in knowledge and wisdom," and he mentioned the hadith: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom Allah gave wealth and empowered him to spend it in the truth, and a man whom Allah gave wisdom, so he judges by it and teaches it to people."

As for the second and third types of wishing, they are forbidden because there follow from them agitation of the soul, non-acceptance of what Allah has apportioned, and doubt about the wisdom of the legal rulings.

As for the fifth and sixth types of wishing, they are unquestionably forbidden, and they are of envy. In the hadith: "A woman should not ask for the divorce of her sister so that she empties her bowl." For this reason one is forbidden to propose upon the proposal of his brother, unless his wishing in the fifth state is a wish for that to be his after the one who holds it, without hastening his death. Abu Bakr, when he appointed Umar as successor, said to the Muhajirun: "Each of you has his nose swollen, wishing that the matter be his instead of him."

The sixth is more severe, and it is the worse of the two envies, unless the possessor of the blessing is using it for harm that affects the religion or the nation, or for harming the one who wishes.

Page 31
Then the locus of the prohibition in the verse is wishing, which is seeking what no one has the capacity to attain by his own earning, because that is what drives one to walk the paths of hostility. As for seeking what one can attain without harming others, there is no prohibition against it, because by seeking it he turns toward attaining it and thereby gains a religious or worldly benefit. As for seeking what one has no capacity to attain, if it returns to otherworldly benefits, there is no harm in it.

The wisdom of the prohibition of the prohibited types of wishing is that they corrupt relations among people in their dealings, and envy arises from them, and envy was the first sin by which Allah was disobeyed, when Iblis envied Adam. Then from envy arise anger and rage, which lead to harming the envied one. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies﴾ [al-Falaq: 5]. The cause of the first crime in the world was envy, when the son of Adam envied his brother and killed him. Furthermore, the wishing of the prohibited states arises in souls first as a bare thought, then it grows in the soul gradually until it becomes a habit, prompting a person to commit crimes to quench his rancor. Therefore they were forbidden from it, so that they would restrain their souls at the arising of these wishes with the restraint of religion and wisdom, and not allow them to grow in the souls. The revolutions and propaganda seeking to extort wealth under various titles have arisen only from wishing for what Allah has favored some people with over others, or are only an effect of what Allah has favored some people with over others.

His saying: ﴿some of you over others﴾ is suitable to mean individuals of people, and also to mean their categories.

His saying: ﴿For men is a share of what they have earned﴾ etc. If by mentioning men and women here is meant the generalization of people, like when one mentions the east and the west, the land and the sea, the highland and the lowland, then the preceding prohibition is in its generality. This sentence is brought as a cause (ta'lil) for the prohibition of wishing, definitively cutting off the excuse of those who wish, and giving comfort with the prohibition; for this reason it is separated (fussilat). If by men and women is meant each of the two kinds specifically, meaning that men are特 specified by what they have earned and women are specified by what they have earned of wealth, then the preceding prohibition relates to the wishing that leads to consuming the wealth of orphans and women, meaning it is not permissible for guardians to consume the property of their wards and dependents, since each of these has what he has earned. This sentence is a cause for an omitted sentence which it indicates, its estimated form being: "And do not wish, so that you consume the property of your wards."

Page 32
The share (naṣīb): portion and measure, and it applies both to the share in the Hereafter and the share in this world, and this has been mentioned just above.

The iktisab (acquisition): striving to earn, and it may be used figuratively for the attainment of a thing even without effort and treatment. The "min" is either partitive or for origin, and the meaning may be that men and women each deserve their portion of the reward and recompense accomplished for them by their deed, so there is no benefit in one group wishing to do the deed of another group, because reward is not restricted to a specific deed, for the means of reward are many; so the prohibition of wishing for what Allah has favored some of you over others shall not trouble you. It may also be that the meaning is: each person, whether man or woman, deserves his portion of worldly benefits accomplished for him from what he strove for with his effort, or which is part of what he strove for; so wishing that one obtain something he did not strive for and which was not among his rights is an unjust wish, and it is rightly prohibited. Or the meaning is: those people deserve their share of what they have earned, that is, of what has been legislated for them of inheritance and the like, so let no one envy another for what has been made his right, because Allah knows best who among you is more deserving than another.

His saying: "And ask Allah of His bounty." If it is a conjunction upon his saying: ﴿For men is a share of what they have earned﴾ etc., which is the cause of the prohibition of wishing, then the meaning is: for men are their merits and rights, and for women are their merits and rights; so whoever wishes for what has not been prepared for his category has transgressed, but let him ask Allah of His bounty that He give him what has been prepared for his category of merits, and make his reward equal to the reward of deeds that were not prepared for his category, as the Prophet ﷺ said to the women: "For you, the best jihad is a hajj accepted (hajj mabrur)." If it is a conjunction upon the prohibition in his saying: ﴿And do not wish﴾, then the meaning is: do not wish for what is in the hand of another, ﴿and ask Allah of His bounty﴾, for the bounty of Allah is wide enough to bestow favor on all, so wishing has no effect except the weariness of the soul. The majority (al-Jumhur) read: "wa-s'alu" with the hamza retained after the sukun of the sin, which is the root letter of the verb; Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on the sin and the hamza dropped, after transferring its vowel to the preceding quiescent sin, for lightening.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾ is a fitting concluding summary (tadhyil) for this obligation, because it relates to the action of the soul, in which one watches none but his Lord.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 33:

Page 33
﴿To each We have appointed heirs of what the parents and the close relatives leave, and those with whom your oaths have bound you—give them their share. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Witness.﴾
This sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others﴾ [al-Nisa': 32], in terms of its comprehending the prohibition against coveting the property of the owner of wealth. Its purpose is to complete the clarification of those who have a right to the wealth.

The construction of (kull) (each), when what it is annexed to is omitted, is that tanwin replaces the omitted element. If something in the speech indicates the omitted annexed noun, the omitted element is estimated from its wording or its meaning, as has passed in the Lord's saying: ﴿For each there is a direction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148] in Surat al-Baqarah. Likewise here, it is permissible that the omitted element be drawn from what his saying before it indicates: (﴿For men there is a share﴾ [al-Nisa': 32]) (﴿and for women there is a share﴾ [al-Nisa': 32]). So it is estimated: "For each of men and women We have appointed heirs," or "For each heir We have appointed heirs."

It is also permissible to estimate: "For each person or thing We have appointed heirs."

The appointing (ja'l) in His saying (ja'alna) is the legislative appointing, i.e., "We have legislated for each heir, who has a right in his property," as in the Lord's saying: ﴿We have certainly given his heir authority﴾ [al-Isra': 33].

Al-mawali is the plural of mawla, which is the place of wilayah, i.e., nearness. It is a figurative place and a figurative nearness, and al-wala' is the verbal noun for the figurative wilayah.

In the arrangement of the verse there are estimations worthy of consideration, comprising meanings of legislation:

The first: "For each one who leaves [property], We have appointed heirs," i.e., those who have wala' to him, i.e., nearness, i.e., heirs. (Mimma taraka) (of what he left) is connected to what is in (mawali) of the meaning of "those who stand close to him," i.e., who inherit from him. (Min) is partitive, i.e., they inherit from what he left. The referent of the relative (ma) is the property, and the relative clause is an indication that what is meant by (mawali) is inheritance, and that the omitted annexed noun of "kull" is the deceased or the one who leaves. "Li-kullin" is connected to (ja'alna), placed before its complement for emphasis.

Page 34
His saying "al-walidan" (the parents) is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani) by which it clarifies what is meant by "mawali." It may also clarify the omitted annexed noun of "kull," estimated as "for each one who leaves." Both expressions are the same in meaning, because the one who leaves is a parent or a relative, and the mawali are parents or kinsfolk. Mentioning "al-walidan" suffices without mentioning the children, due to their mutual correlation: if the parents are among the heirs, then the deceased is a child; otherwise the deceased is a parent. The definite article in (﴿al-walidan wa al-aqrabun﴾) is a substitute for an omitted annexed noun, i.e., "their parents and their close relatives," and the omitted annexed noun is indicated by "mawali." This estimation suits being derived from His saying: ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned﴾ [al-Nisa': 32], i.e., "For each of the two categories We have appointed heirs who inherit from him," and this is the appointing found in the verses of inheritance.

The second estimation: "For each thing of what the parents and close relatives leave, We have appointed heirs," i.e., a people who stand close to it by inheritance, i.e., who inherit it, i.e., it becomes an inheritance for them. Thus the omitted annexed noun is a general indefinite noun whose kind the context specifies, (mimma taraka) is an explanation of the ambiguity in the tanwin of (kull), and (﴿al-walidan wa al-aqrabun﴾) is the subject of (taraka).

This estimation suits being derived from His saying: ﴿what Allah has made some of you exceed others by﴾ [al-Nisa': 32], i.e., in property: "For each of those whom We have made some exceed others, We have appointed heirs to whom the property reverts, so do not wish for what is not yours to have a right to during the lifetime of its owners, nor for what We have made for the heirs after the death of its owners."

The third estimation: "For each of you We have appointed heirs," i.e., agnatic heirs (asabah) from among those left by the parents, such as paternal uncles, grandfathers, and maternal uncles, for they are relatives of both parents; and of those left by the close relatives, such as the sons of paternal uncles and their sons however many they are, and the sons of sisters likewise, for they are relatives of the closest relatives. Thus the verse points to the return of property to the agnates according to the majority, and to the dhawu al-arham (distant kindred) according to some jurists, and that applies when the heirs mentioned in the preceding verse of inheritance are absent. This is a general ruling, clarified by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Give the fixed shares to their people, and what remains goes to the nearest male." And his saying: "The son of a sister of a people is one of them, or of themselves," narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i; and his saying: "The maternal uncle is the heir of one who has no heir," related by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi; and the Lord's saying: ﴿And those of blood relationship are nearer to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. Abu Hanifah and Ahmad adopted this view. Accordingly, (ma) the relative in His saying (mimma taraka) has the meaning of (man) the relative, and there is no novelty in that. This estimation suits being derived from His saying, after the verse of inheritance: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 13], so that it is a completion of the verse of inheritance.

The fourth estimation: "For each of you, O addressees by Our saying ﴿and do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others﴾ [al-Nisa': 32], We have appointed heirs," i.e., We have legislated the rulings of wala' for those who are clients (mawali) of you. Thus the ruling of wala' that your families left for you—the parents and the close relatives—i.e., the people of ancient wala' in the tribe arising from an old alliance, or by the ruling of the wala' established by oaths, i.e., the confederates between you and them, O addressees. This is the new wala', comprising adoption newly instituted and newly made alliance, like the brotherhood the Prophet ﷺ imposed between the Emigrants and the Helpers. Wala' is of two kinds: an ancient wala' among the tribes, and that which the present parties contract, as Abu Tammam indicated:

You gave me the blood-money of the slain, though I have no kinship nor an ancient alliance there.

On this estimation, (﴿and those with whom your oaths have bound you﴾) is conjoined to (﴿the parents and the close relatives﴾). This estimation suits being derived from His saying: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 13], so that this verse is a completion of the verses of inheritance.

The commentators have other estimations which fit some parts of the arrangement only with strain, so it is not appropriate to dwell on them.

As for His saying: "those with whom your oaths have bound you," it is said to be conjoined to His saying "the parents and the close relatives." It is also said to be a resumptive explanatory sentence, as if it were said: "Who are the mawali?" and it was answered: "The parents and the close relatives, etc.," with His saying ﴿give them their share﴾ being the predicate of His saying "those with whom [your oaths] bound." The fa' was introduced into the predicate because the relative pronoun includes the meaning of a conditional, and this is preferred because the commonly known pause is at "al-aqrabun" and not at "aymanukum."

Mu'aqadah is the occurrence of a contract from both sides, i.e., those with whom you have contracted that they be in the position of sons, or in the position of brothers, or in the position of paternal cousins. Al-ayman is the plural of yamin: either in the sense of the hand, the contract being attributed to the hands figuratively because they accompany the contracting parties, as they place the hands of some into the hands of others as a sign of the binding of the contract; for this reason the contract is also called (safqah), since the hand is clapped upon the hand in it. This is of the type of (aw ma malakat aymanukum); or in the sense of oath, because that was accompanied by an oath,

Page 36
and for this reason it was called hilf (alliance), and its party halif (ally). Attributing the contract to the oaths in this sense is also figurative, because the oath is the cause of the conclusion of the alliance.

What is meant by (﴿those with whom your oaths have bound you﴾) is said to be the clients of the alliance that the Arabs practiced in the Jahiliyyah, which was that a man would make an alliance with another and say to him: "My blood is your blood, my destruction is your destruction," i.e., the dropping by one of them of the blood-claim he is entitled to against the other, "my vengeance is your vengeance, my war is your war, my peace is your peace, you inherit me and I inherit you, you seek [blood-price] through me and I seek through you, you pay the blood-money for me and I pay for you." Al-Husayn ibn al-Humam, one of the poets of the Hamasah, combined these two types of clients in his saying:

Your clients: the client by birth from among you, and the client by oath, the restrained one, who has been divided [in shares].

It was said: they used to give the client a sixth of the estate of the deceased, and this verse confirmed it; then the verse of al-Anfal abrogated it: ﴿And those of blood relationship are nearer to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Jubayr, and perhaps their meaning is that the Muslims made the sixth for the client a bequest, since the people of the Jahiliyyah had no fixed inheritances. It was also said: this verse was revealed concerning the inheritance of the brothers whom the Prophet ﷺ paired between, from the Emigrants and the Helpers at the beginning of the Hijrah, for they used to inherit from one another to the exclusion of the distant kindred; then Allah abrogated that by the verse of al-Anfal, so this verse is abrogated. In the Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi, on the authority of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, it was revealed concerning the adoption that existed in the Jahiliyyah: the adopted son would inherit from the adopter, like the adoption of the Prophet ﷺ of Zayd ibn Harithah al-Kalbi, the adoption of al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth of al-Miqdad al-Kindi, known as al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, the adoption of al-Khattab ibn Nufayl of 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah, and the adoption of Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah of Salim ibn Ma'qil al-Istakhri, known as Salim, mawla of Abu Hudhayfah; then it was abrogated by the inheritances. On the view that (﴿and those with whom your oaths have bound you﴾) is a resumptive sentence, the verse is not abrogated. Ibn 'Abbas, in a narration of Ibn Jubayr from him in al-Bukhari, said: it abrogates the inheritance of those bound in brotherhood among the Emigrants and the Helpers, because His saying ﴿what the parents and the close relatives leave﴾ restricts inheritance to kinship; so on this view His saying ﴿give them their share﴾ means the share of those with whom your oaths bound you of support and aid, or ﴿give them their share﴾ by bequest, since inheritance has gone.

Page 37
Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it was revealed concerning adoption, commanding a bequest to the adopted son. It is narrated from al-Hasan that it concerns the beneficiary of a bequest who dies before the testator, that the bequest be made obligatory for his relatives.

The majority read (\*'aqadat*) with an alif after the 'ayn; Hamzah, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ('aqadat) without alif and with the qaf lightened.

The fa' in His saying ﴿so give them their share﴾ is the fa' of explanation (fa' al-fasihah), on the basis that His saying ﴿those with whom your oaths have bound you﴾ is conjoined to ﴿the parents and the close relatives﴾; or it is an extra fa' in the predicate, if (﴿those with whom [your oaths] bound﴾) is made the subject, with the relative including the meaning of the conditional. The matter of the pronoun in the genitive is clear on both views.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Men are in charge of women, because God has made some of them to excel others, and because they spend of their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in secret what God has guarded. As for those women from whom you fear disobedience, admonish them, forsake them in their beds, and strike them. But if they obey you, then seek no way against them. Indeed, God is ever Most High, Most Great.﴾

This is a fresh (ibtida'i) resumptive statement (isti'naf) that introduces a legislation concerning the rights of men, the rights of women, and the family society. It is mentioned following what precedes it because of the connection between the rulings on the family order, especially those concerning women. Thus His saying, ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾, is a universal legislative principle (asl tashri'i kulli) from which the rulings in the verses after it branch out. It is therefore like an introduction.

His saying, ﴿So righteous women﴾, is a branching (tafri') from it, and it also corresponds to what was mentioned as the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of His saying, ﴿And do not wish for that by which God has made some of you excel others﴾ [al-Nisa: 32], earlier on.

The ruling in this verse is a general ruling brought to give the reason (ta'lil) for a specific legislation.

Page 38

Therefore, the definite article in "the men and the women" (al-rijal wa al-nisa') is for comprehensive inclusion (istighraq). It is a customary comprehensive inclusion (istighraq 'urfi), based on considering the reality, like the definite article in people's saying, "The man is better than the woman." It amounts to customary comprehensive inclusion, because rulings derived from realities are rulings of the majority, so when a comprehensive inclusion is built upon them, it is a customary comprehensive inclusion. The statement is an informative sentence (khabar) used in the sense of a command, like much of the informative language in the legal texts.

Al-qawwam is one who stands over the affair of a thing, takes charge of it, and sets it right. It is said: qawwam, qayyam, and qayyum. This is because the one who cares about a matter and attends to it must stand up to manage it. So "standing" (al-qiyam) was used for "caring" by way of necessary association ('alaqat al-luzum), or the one who cares was likened to one standing for the matter by way of representation (tamthil). Thus, by "the men" is meant those who are individuals of the reality of "man," that is, the known category of the human species, which is the category of males. Likewise, by "the women" is meant the category of females of the human species. What is meant is not "men" as the plural of "rajul" in the sense of a woman's husband, since that meaning is not used. Nor is "the women" meant as the plural that denotes wives, although this has been used in some places, such as His saying, ﴿from your women with whom you have consummated [marriage]﴾ [al-Nisa: 23]. Rather, what is meant is what the word denotes by its basic coinage, as in His saying, ﴿and for women is a share of what they have earned﴾ [al-Nisa: 32], and in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Nor my women until they die as free women,"

he means his wives, his daughters, and his clients.

So the placement of ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ is that of an introduction to the ruling, presenting its evidence first out of concern for the evidence, since a misinterpretation may occur, or may already have occurred. It is reported that the occasion of revelation of the verse was the saying of women: "Would that we were equal to men in inheritance and shared with them in military campaigns."

The standing of men over women is the standing of protection and defense, and the standing of earning and financial production. For this reason He said, ﴿because God has made some of them to excel others and because they spend of their wealth﴾, meaning: by God's making some of them excel others and by their spending of their wealth. This is if "mā" in both clauses is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya). Or it means: by that with which God made some of them excel, and by that which they spent of their wealth, if "mā" in both is a relative pronoun (mawsula). The two returning pronouns in the two relative clauses are then omitted: as for the genitive one, because the relative noun is governed by a preposition like that by which the omitted pronoun is governed; and as for the accusative returning pronoun in the clause of ﴿and because they spend﴾, because it is very common to omit the accusative returning pronoun from the relative clause. What is meant by "some" in His saying, "God has made some of them to excel," is the group of men, as is evident from the conjunction in His saying, ﴿and because they spend of their wealth﴾, since both pronouns refer to men.

The excellence (tafdil) is the innate qualities that necessitate the woman's need for the man in defending her and guarding her so that her self may persist, as 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"They would hand over our horses and say, 'You are not our husbands if you do not protect us.'"

This excellence has shown its effects across the ages and generations, so it became a right acquired by men. This is a demonstrative proof (hujjah burhaniyya) that men are in charge of women, since women's need for men in this respect continues, although it may grow stronger or weaker.

His saying, ﴿and because they spend﴾, is in the past tense to indicate a matter that has been established in human societies since antiquity. Men are the ones who provide for the women of the household, wives and daughters. The wealth was attributed to the pronoun of the men because earning is the business of men. In the ages of nomadism it was by hunting, raiding, spoils of war, and farming, and these were men's work. In the ages of civilization, men's earnings increased through planting, trade, hiring, construction, and the like. This is a rhetorical argument (hujjah khitabiyya), since it refers to the common usage of most people, especially the Arabs. Women rarely take charge of earning activities, though this is rare compared with men's work, such as a woman hiring a wet-nurse herself or developing wealth she inherited from her relatives.

Among the marvels of inimitability (i'jaz) is the formulation of His saying, ﴿by that by which God made some of them to excel others and by that which they spent of their wealth﴾, in a form suitable for both the verbal-noun reading and the relative reading. The verbal-noun reading indicates that the standing has as its cause God's excelling and their spending; the relative reading indicates that its cause is what people know of the men's excellence and their spending. Thus the address suits both groups, the learned among them and the ignorant, as in the saying of as-Samaw'al or al-Harithi:

"Ask, if you are ignorant of people about us and about them, for the knowledgeable and the ignorant are not equal."

Page 40

Also, using "mā" with the verb, given the possibility of the verbal-noun reading, gives an eloquence that would not be found in our saying, "by God's excelling and by spending," because the Arabs prefer verbs over nouns in modes of expression.

It is also reported regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse that it was the saying of women, among them Umm Salama, mother of the believers: "Do men go out to fight while we do not, and we have only half of the inheritance?" Then God revealed His saying, "And do not wish for that by which God has made some of you excel others," up to this verse, as a completion of what relates to that wish. It was also said: "This verse was revealed because of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' al-Ansari: his wife Habiba bint Zayd ibn Abi Zuhayr rebelled against him, so he struck her. Her father complained about him to the Prophet ﷺ, and he commanded her to strike him as he had struck her. Then the verse was revealed immediately, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'I wanted one thing, and God wanted another,'" and he abrogated his first ruling. There is no sound report for this second occasion, nor one traced back to the Prophet ﷺ. Rather, it is among what was narrated from al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Qatada.

The fa' in His saying, ﴿So righteous women﴾, is an explanatory fa' (fa' fasiha), meaning: since men are in charge of women, it is important to detail the conditions of wives and how they keep company with their husbands, and this is the purpose. God therefore described the righteous among them with a description indicating His pleasure, so it carries the sense of legislation, meaning: let them be righteous women. "Qanitat" means those who are obedient to God.

Devout obedience (qunut) is the worship of God. He placed it first here, although it is not from the context of the discourse, to indicate the close association between their fear of God and their guarding of their husbands' right. For this reason He said, ﴿guarding in secret﴾, meaning: guarding their husbands during their absence. He linked "secret" (al-ghayb) with "guarding" by way of metaphorical attribution (majaz 'aqli), because it is its time. "Al-ghayb" is the verbal noun of "ghaba," the opposite of "hadara" (to be present). What is meant is the absence of their husbands. The lam is for transitivity because the operative word is weak, not being a verb, so "al-ghayb" is in the sense of a passive object. It has been made an object of "guarding" by extension, because in reality it is a time-frame for guarding, so it stands in the place of the object in order to include everything that is liable to cause a lapse in guarding during its period: everything concerning a woman's honor and property that her husband would guard if present. When he is present, there are two restraints: he restrains her himself, and her occupation with her husband also restrains her. As for the state of absence, it is one of forgetfulness and carelessness, so a woman may display what does not please her husband if she is unrighteous or foolish in judgment. Thus, by putting the time-frame in place of the object, a marvelous concision is achieved. Bashshar followed this when he said:

"And he guards your absence even if he has traveled far."

Page 41

The "bi" in ﴿by what God has guarded﴾ is for accompaniment (mulabasa), meaning: guarding that accompanies what God has guarded. "Mā" is a verbal-noun particle, meaning: by God's guarding. God's guarding is His command to guard, so what is meant is the obligatory guarding (hifz taklifi). The sense of accompaniment is that they guard their husbands in a way that conforms to God's command. God's command refers to what contains a right for husbands alone, or together with God's right. It thus includes what the husband dislikes, provided it entails no hardship for the woman. Excepted from this is what God has permitted women, as "the Prophet ﷺ permitted Hind bint 'Utba to take from Abu Sufyan's property what would suffice her and her child, in a reasonable manner." For this reason Malik said: a woman may bring witnesses into her husband's house in his absence and have them testify to whatever she wishes. And as the Prophet ﷺ permitted women to go out to the mosques and to call Muslims to faith.

His saying, ﴿As for those women from whom you fear disobedience﴾: this describes some of the states contrary to righteousness, namely nushuz (disobedience or rebellion), meaning dislike of the husband. This may be due to the woman's bad character, or because she desires to marry another, or because of harshness in the husband's character. Such cases are many. Nushuz in the language means rising up and elevation, and what returns to the meaning of disturbance and distancing. From it comes "nashaz al-ard," meaning the elevated part of the land.

The majority of jurists said: nushuz is a woman's disobedience to her husband, her rising above him, and her display of dislike for him, meaning a display of dislike that was not customary from her, that is, after she had lived with him, as in His saying, ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband nushuz or aversion﴾ [al-Nisa: 128]. They made the permission to admonish, forsake, and strike contingent upon this disobedience, and they argued from what has come in some reports regarding the permission for a husband to strike his rebellious wife, and from reports that some Companions did so in cases other than the manifestation of indecency. In my view, the permission in those reports and narrations is to be understood as follows: account was taken of the customs of some classes of people or some tribes, since people differ in this. The people of the desert do not regard striking a woman as aggression, nor do the women regard it as aggression. 'Amir ibn al-Harith al-Namari, known as Jiran al-'Awd, said:

"I went to a camel and stripped its neck skin, and wisdom is more effective and more successful in matters."

"Take care, O my two companions, for I have seen the neck of the camel has almost become suitable [for a whip]."

"Iltahaytu" means: I peeled, that is, I cut off, in the sense that he took a piece of skin from the inner part of a camel's neck and made it into a whip to strike his two wives, threatening them that the whip had dried out and was fit to be struck with.

It is firmly established in the Sahih that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "We, the emigrants, were a people who dominated our women. When we came to the Ansar, we found they were a people whose women dominated them, so our women began to take on the manners of the women of the Ansar." Thus, when striking is permitted for husbands and not for those in authority, and its cause is merely disobedience and dislike rather than indecency, it is certainly permitted for a people who do not regard its issuance from husbands as harmful, shameful, or an innovation in household treatment, and whose women do not feel the measure of their anger except through something of this kind.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 34 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, ﴿So admonish them, forsake them in the beds, and beat them﴾, is intended to express sequence (al-tartib), as the order in which the three are mentioned requires. It is evident, however, that the three are not meant to be combined. Sequence is the original and immediately understood meaning of the conjunction "wa" (and). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He admonishes her. If she complies, well; otherwise he forsakes her. If she complies, well; otherwise he beats her. The same is transmitted from 'Ali.

Know that the conjunction "wa" here is intended to express division (al-taqsim), according to the categories of wives in cases of nushuz (ill-conduct, defiance).

His saying, ﴿And if they obey you, then seek no way against them﴾, the pronoun of address in it may be read in the same way as the pronouns in "takhafun" (you fear) and what follows it. The meaning is obedience after nushuz, that is, if they return from nushuz to the known obedience. The meaning of ﴿then seek no way against them﴾ is: do not seek a means to impose those deterrents upon them. The address is applicable to everyone who has been granted authority over wives in a state of nushuz, as already explained.

The original meaning of "sabil" (way) is a road, and here it is used figuratively for a means, a cause, or a pretext for obtaining one's right. It will recur at his saying, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no way (sabil) against the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91] in Surah al-Tawbah, and see his later saying ﴿And if they offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way (sabil) against them﴾ [al-Nisa': 90].

"'Alayhinna" (against them) is connected to "sabilan" (way), because it has been treated as implying the meaning of authority and dominion, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no way against the good-doers﴾.

His saying, ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Most High, Most Great﴾, is a closing statement (tadhyil) that reinforces the warning. That is, Allah is Most High over you, Governing over you, so He is just between you. He is Great, that is, Mighty and Capable. By the attribute of loftiness, obedience to His command and prohibition is required; by the attribute of power, His seizure is to be feared when His command and prohibition are disobeyed.

[p. 43]

The meaning of ﴿whose nushuz you fear﴾ is: whose evil consequences you fear. The meaning, then, is that nushuz has occurred together with signs of an intention to disobey and a determination upon it, not mere displeasure or non-compliance. For such a state rarely fails to occur between spouses, since displeasure and disobedience befall both women and men and then pass away. In this way the meaning of fear remains in its literal sense, namely the anticipation that something harmful may occur. The command to admonish, forsake, and beat then becomes graded according to the degree of fear of this nushuz and its mixing with transgression and ill intent.

The addressee of the pronoun in "takhafun" (you fear) may be either the husbands. In that case the transitive use of "khafa" (to fear) is in its original form of taking a direct object, as in ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 175], and the attribution of "fa'izuhunna" (admonish them), "uhjuruhunna" (forsake them), and "idribuhunna" (beat them) is in its literal sense.

It is also permissible that the addressees be the whole group of those fit for this task among the rulers (wulat al-umur) and the husbands, so that each party undertakes what pertains to it. This is like His saying in Surah al-Baqarah, ﴿It is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], etc. Here the address "lakum" (for you) is to the husbands, and the address in ﴿if you fear﴾ [al-Nisa': 3] is to the rulers, as in al-Kashshaf. He said: Such usage is not rare in the Qur'an or elsewhere. He means that it is of the same kind as His saying in Surah al-Saff, ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Saff: 11] up to His saying ﴿and give good news to the believers﴾ [al-Saff: 13]. There he treated "wa bashshir" (and give good news) as coordinated with "tu'minun" (you believe). So the address is to all, but because the giving of good news can only come from the Messenger, it was restricted to him.

It was by this interpretation that 'Ata' took, when he said: A husband does not beat his wife, but he may become angry with her. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is from the jurisprudence and understanding of 'Ata' and his grasp of the Sharia, and his standing at the places where ijtihad is exercised (mazanni al-ijtihad). He knew that the command to beat here is a command of permission (amr ibaha), and he recognized disapproval (karahiyya) from another route, such as the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And the best of you will never beat." I, however, see in 'Ata' a broader view than what Ibn al-'Arabi attributed to him: namely, that he placed these matters in their proper places according to the contextual indications. A group of scholars agreed with him. Ibn al-Furs said: They denied the reports concerning beating. I say: Or they interpreted them. The apparent meaning is that the permission to beat is for the sake of considering subtle circumstances between the spouses. He permitted the husband to beat his wife a corrective beating, with the aim of restoring companionship between them. If he exceeds what the state of her nushuz requires, he is then a transgressor.

For this reason the meaning of ﴿And those whose nushuz you fear﴾ is: whose evil outcome of nushuz you fear. This requires, with respect to the rulers, that the nushuz was brought to them by the complaint of the husbands, that the attribution of "fa'izuhunna" (admonish them) is in its literal sense, and that the attribution of ﴿and forsake them in the beds﴾ is in the sense of the husbands being permitted to forsake them. The attribution of "idribuhunna" (beat them) is as you have known.

[p. 44]

The pronoun of address in His saying, ﴿And if they obey you﴾, follows the distribution (al-tawzi'), and likewise the pronoun in ﴿then seek no way against them﴾.

The conclusion is that forsaking and beating are not permitted merely upon the expectation of nushuz before it has occurred, by consensus. If the addressees are the husbands, this is a permission for them to treat their defiant wives with one of these three qualities, and the husbands are entrusted with discerning where each of these qualities should be applied according to the strength of the nushuz and the extent of its corruption. As for admonition, it has no limit. As for forsaking, its condition is that it must not reach the point of harm through the distress (kamad) the woman feels. Some have set its maximum at one month. As for beating, it is grave and its limit is difficult to define. Yet it was permitted in the state of manifest corruption, because the woman has by then transgressed. But a limit must be fixed for it, which is explained in jurisprudence, because if it were left absolutely to the husbands to carry out, while they are in a state of soothing their anger, that would be a likely occasion for exceeding the limit, since few punish in proportion to the offence. Moreover, the fundamental principles of the Sharia do not permit anyone to judge in his own favour except in necessity. Nevertheless, the majority restricted it to being free of harm and to its being inflicted by one among whom beating is not regarded as humiliation or injury.

So we say: when the rulers know that the husbands do not handle the legal penalties well, nor observe their limits, it is permissible for them to restrain the hands of the husbands from using this punishment, and to announce to them that whoever beats his wife will be punished, lest the matter of harm between spouses escalate, especially when the restraint of conscience is weak.

Conjunction with the clause ﴿And those [women] from whom you fear rebelliousness﴾ [al-Nisa: 34]. This ruling concerns other circumstances that arise between the spouses, namely situations of discord (shiqaq) involving quarrelling, resentment, disobedience, and the like, that is, without rebellion (nushuz) on the part of the wife.

[Page 45]

The addressees here are certainly the rulers and those in authority (wulat al-umur), which makes it likely that they were the addressees in the preceding verse as well.

Shiqaq is a verbal noun like mushaqqah, derived from shiqq (with a kasra on the shin), meaning a side or direction, because each of the two parties goes to one side, in the manner of figurative expression (takhyil). They said the same about the etymology of 'aduww (enemy), that it derives from 'adwat al-wadi (the side of the valley). In my view, however, it derives from shaqq (with a fatha on the shin), meaning a crack or split and a branching off. From this comes their saying: "He split the staff of obedience (shagga 'asa al-ta'ah)," and "dissent is shiqaq." This was discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqarah at the words of the Exalted: ﴿But if they turn away, they are only in schism﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137].

He attached shiqaq to bayn (between). This is either to remove the word bayn from its adverbial (zarfiyyah) sense and give it the meaning of the separation that two things put between themselves, that is, a schism of distancing, of withdrawal; or it is by way of extended usage (tawassu'), as in His words: ﴿Rather, the scheming of night﴾ [Saba': 33], and the verse of the poet:

O thief of the night, of the people of the house!

Whoever holds that the genitive construction occurs with the implied sense of "in" (fi) takes this as evidence for it, as in the expression "This is the parting between me and you." The Arabs use this adverbial usage very extensively, and the Qur'an contains much of it, including His words: ﴿Certainly your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94] in the reading with raf' (nominative).

The pronoun in bayniHima refers to the two spouses who are understood from the context of the discourse beginning with His words: ﴿Men are the protectors of women﴾ [al-Nisa: 34].

Al-hakam, with two fathas, is the arbiter (hakim) who is accepted for judgement without any prior authority. It is an adjective of the pattern sifah mushabbahah derived from their saying: "They made him an arbiter (hakkamuhu), so he judged (fahakama)." It is an old term in Arabic. The Arabs did not appoint judges and did not refer their disputes to anyone except the sword, but they might accept one of their wise men as an arbiter in some of their disputes. 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and 'Alqamah ibn 'Ullathah had recourse to Hiram ibn Sinan al-'Absi, and this is the arbitration that al-A'sha mentioned in his rhyming ode in which he says:

Alqama, you are no match for 'Amir,
the breaker of bonds and the one who holds a grudge.

The sons of Nizar ibn Ma'add ibn 'Adnan also referred to al-Af'a al-Jurhumi, as was mentioned earlier in this surah.

[Page 46]

The two pronouns in His words "from his people" (min ahlihi) and "from her people" (min ahliha) refer to two notions understood from the discourse: namely the husband and the wife. It is stipulated for the two arbiters that one of them be from the man's people and the other from the woman's people, so that they will be more knowledgeable about the inner circumstances of their affair (dakhaliyyat amrihima) and more perceptive regarding what may be hoped for in their condition. It is also known that the qualities which entitle them to judge in disputes between spouses are stipulated for them. Malik said: If it is impossible to find two arbiters from their own people, then they are appointed from outsiders. Ibn al-Furs said: If the judge appoints two outsiders while relatives are available, it is likely to be said that the ruling is nullified for contravening the text; and it is likely to be said that it stands, as if the spouses themselves had referred the matter to them. I say: The first view is more apparent. According to the Shafi'is, it is recommended that they be from the two families, so if they are sent from outsiders while relatives are available, it is valid.

The verse indicates the obligation to send two arbiters when the spouses have a continuous dispute, expressed as shiqaq. Its apparent meaning is that the one who sends them is the judge and the ruler, not the spouses, because the verb ub'athu (send) indicates that they are directed towards the spouses; if the two were designated by the spouses, the act of sending would have no meaning. The plain sense of the verse is that the two who are sent are arbiters (hakamani), not agents (wakilani). This is the view of the leading scholars among the Companions and the Successors, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib judged accordingly, and Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and Ishaq said it. According to the view of the majority of scholars, whatever the two arbiters decide, whether separation, continuation, or khul' (divorce for compensation), takes effect, and the spouses have no objection to it, because that is the meaning of arbitration (tahkim). Yes, this does not prevent these scholars from allowing the spouses to appoint two men to look after their affairs, nor from having them appoint two arbiters in the manner of the judge's appointment. Rabi'ah disagreed with this and said: Only the judge may judge, not the spouses. On the manner of their judgement and its conditions there is detail in the books of jurisprudence.

A small group interpreted this verse as meaning that the purpose of sending two arbiters is to reconcile the spouses and to determine means of restraining whichever of them is the wrongdoer, such as cutting off maintenance from the wife for a period until her condition improves; and that the arbiters do not have the right to divorce except with the consent of the spouses, so they become agents (wakilayn). This is the view of Abu Hanifa and is also one opinion of al-Shafi'i. So they mean that the two are in the position of the agent whom the judge appoints on behalf of an absent person. This is a diversion of the word "two arbiters" from its apparent meaning, and so it is an interpretation (ta'wil). What prompted this interpretation according to Abu Hanifa is that the basic principle is that divorce is in the hand of the husband; so if the two arbiters saw divorce imposed on him while he was unwilling, that would be

[Page 47]

a contravention of the evidence of the basic principle, which necessitated interpreting the meaning of "two arbiters." This is a distant interpretation, because divorce is not always in the hand of the husband, since the judge divorces when there is a cause that requires it.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿if they desire reconciliation﴾ — the apparent meaning is that this refers to the two arbiters, since they are the ones addressed by the discourse. He limited it to the desire for reconciliation because it is the aim that must be the purpose of the rulers and the arbiters. So it is obligatory for the arbiters to examine the affair of the spouses with a view that proceeds from the intention of reconciliation. If reconciliation is achieved, well and good; otherwise they proceed to separation. God has promised them that He will grant success between them (yuwaffiq baynahuma) if they intend reconciliation. The meaning of "granting success between them" is guiding them to hit upon the truth and the reality, since agreement is more reassuring to them in their judgement than disagreement. There is nothing in the verse indicating that God restricted the arbiters to the desire for reconciliation, so that it would serve as a basis for Abu Hanifa's interpretation that the arbiters are emissaries for reconciliation and not for separation. For God, exalted is He, only informed that the intention of reconciliation will be a cause of success between them in their judgement. Were anyone to understand a meaning other than this, he would be deviating from the sense of the construction.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the spouses. This is the interpretation of those who said that the two arbiters are sent by the spouses as their agents. That is, if the spouses desire, by sending the two arbiters, the reconciliation of their affair, God will grant success between them, meaning He will facilitate the return of their marital life to its best state. Even on this interpretation there is no proof that the arbiters are restricted to striving for union between the spouses rather than separation, because the condition only indicates that the spouses' desire for reconciliation will bring it about, while their desire for discord and strife will increase them in it. How far is this from determining the policy of the two arbiters according to the view of the Law!

This verse is a foundation for the permissibility of arbitration (tahkim) in all rights, and the question of arbitration is mentioned in jurisprudence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 36:

Page 48
﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, and to relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbour who is a relative, the neighbour who is a stranger, the companion at your side, the wayfarer, and those whom your right hands possess. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is self-deluded and boastful.﴾

This is a conjunctive legislation (ʿaṭf tashrīʿ) specific to dealings with relatives and the weak. He placed before it the command to worship Allah and the prohibition of associating partners with Him, by way of incorporation (al-idmāj), because this matter is of the greatest importance and is what a Muslim should most seek, renewing the meaning of tawhid in the souls of the Muslims, just as he had preceded this at the opening of the surah with His saying: ﴿Fear your Lord, who created you from one soul﴾ [al-Nisa larr: 1]. The connection (al-munasaba) is what is intended to be gathered in this surah of rulings on the bonds of kinship in lineage, religion and close association.

The address is to the believers, and for this reason he placed the command to worship before the prohibition of associating partners, because the negation of shirk among them had already been established, and what was desired from them was the continuance of worship of Allah and seeking more of it; and they were forbidden from shirk as a warning against what they had been upon in the Jahiliyya. The two clauses together are, in effect, a form of restriction (ḥaṣr), since their meaning is: worship Allah and do not worship other than Him; so it comprises an affirmation and a negation, as if it were said: Worship none but Allah. Deviating from the method of restriction in such a case is an Arabic practice, as in the verse of al-Samaw'al, or ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm al-Ḥārithī:

Our souls flow over the edges of the swords, and they do not flow over anything other than the swords.

It is resorted to when the primary aim is the affirmation of the one side, and then the intention afterward is to negate the ruling from what is other than that to which it is affirmed; for when restriction is employed, the primary aim becomes the negation of the ruling from what is other than what is mentioned, and that is not what the context requires here. For this reason, when the Children of Israel were addressed with a parallel of this verse, they were addressed by way of restriction in His saying: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: You shall not worship except Allah, and be good to parents﴾ [al-Baqara: 83], etc., because the primary aim there was to awaken them to the nullification of the worship of other than Allah, since they said to Musa: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 138], and because they worshipped the calf during the period of Musa's private conversation with his Lord; so He took from them the covenant to refrain from worshipping other than Allah.

Page 49
And likewise the verse of the poet, for the chief aim there is praise of them, that they are killed in war and their souls depart by the swords; then it occurred to him, and he followed it with the statement that this is an inherent disposition among them that does not fail, and there is no exaggeration in it.

"شَيْئًا" is in the accusative as an object of "تُشْرِكُوا", meaning: do not make a partner of anything that is worshipped, like His saying: ﴿And we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾ [al-Jinn: 2]. It may also be accusative as an infinitive of emphasis, meaning: any association at all, even a little, like His saying: ﴿They will not harm you at all﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42].

His saying: ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ shows concern for the matter of parents, since He placed the command to be good to them directly after the command to worship, as in His saying: ﴿Be grateful to Me and to your parents﴾ [Luqman: 14], and His saying: ﴿O my son, do not associate others with Allah; indeed, shirk is a great injustice. And We have enjoined upon man regarding his parents﴾ [Luqman: 13]. For this reason he placed the object of "إحسانًا" before it, as a means of emphasis, since there is no sense of restriction here, because goodness is prescribed for everything. The infinitive took the place of the verb. The verb "ihsan" was made transitive with the preposition "bi" only because it implies the meaning of righteousness (birr). Its transitivity with "bi" is widespread in the Qur'an in such contexts. In my view, ihsan is only transitive with "bi" when what is meant is goodness connected with dealing with a person's self, honouring and esteeming him, which is the meaning of birr; and for this reason it came in ﴿and He was good to me when He took me out of the prison﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. When what is meant is the delivery of material benefit, it is transitive with "ila", as you say: "ahsana ila fulan" when one provides him with money or the like.

"﴿وذِي القُرْبى﴾" means the possessor of kinship; al-qurbā is a form like al-ruj'ā, a noun for nearness, the verbal noun of qariba, and what is meant by it is kinship by lineage, as is most common in this genitive construction, namely their saying: dhu al-qurba. He commanded goodness to such a person only to preserve the bonds of affection among relatives, since the Arabs in the Jahiliyya had distorted the rights of kinship, making them a cause of rivalry, envy and fighting. Their statements on this are numerous in their poetry. Artah ibn Suhayya said:

We are sons of one paternal uncle, and between us, over that, are carpets in which there is hatred and rivalry.

It is enough to recall what occurred between Bakr and Taghlib in the war of al-Basus, though they were relatives and in-laws; and the Muslims at that time were Arabs recently departed from the Jahiliyya. For this reason He urged them to goodness toward kin. They used to be good to the neighbour, but if he was of their kin they did not concern themselves with being good to him; and He emphasised this by repeating the preposition after the conjunction. For this reason, in the narration of the charge to the Children of Israel, "﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾" [al-Baqara: 83] up to His saying "(﴿وذِي القُرْبى﴾ [al-Baqara: 83])", the preposition was not emphasised with "bi", because Islam emphasised the bonds of kinship more than any other. In the command to be good to relatives there is an admonition that it is among the baseness of character for someone to belittle a relative merely because he is his relative, and to feel secure from his harms, and to direct his kindness and affection toward strangers in order to be spared their evil, or to be mentioned among the tribes with good remembrance. For the soul that evil bends and severity brings low is a base soul; and as has been transmitted: the worst of people is the one whom people avoid for fear of his evil. So we say likewise: the worst of people is one who honours someone out of fear of his evil.

His saying "﴿واليَتامى والمَساكِينِ﴾": these are two weak categories who lack a helper, and for this reason they are enjoined.

The neighbour (al-jar) is the resident near your dwelling, and it is applied to a resident among a tribe in its protection. So what is meant by "﴿الجارِ ذِي القُرْبى﴾" is the neighbour who is a kinsman from the tribe, and by "﴿الجارِ الجُنُبِ﴾" is the neighbour who is a stranger, who has settled among the people and is not of the tribe; so he is "junub", that is, distant, derived from "al-janib" (the side), and it is a descriptive adjective on the pattern fu'ul, like their saying: a she-camel "ujud" (hard-hoofed). It was also said that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason it does not agree with the word it modifies. Bal'a' ibn Qays said:

Let no neighbour who is a stranger or a relative ever make us uneasy.

This meaning is confirmed by the saying of ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada in his poem by which he sought intercession with the king al-Harith ibn Jabala al-Ghassani, so that he would release his brother Shasa for him, when he fell into the captivity of al-Harith:

Do not deprive me of a gift because of a crime, for I am a man who is a stranger among the tents.

Some interpreted "al-jar dhi al-qurba" as the neighbour near in dwelling, and "al-junub" as the one far in dwelling, but this is remote, because kinship (qurba) is not known in terms of physical nearness; and the Arabs are famous for guarding the neighbour's rights and being good to the neighbour, and their statements on this are numerous. So this was emphasised in Islam, because it is among the praiseworthy qualities of the Arabs which Islam came to complete from the noble characters; and among them is goodness to the neighbour.

The Sunna also emphasised the charge concerning the neighbour in many hadiths. In al-Bukhari, from ʿA'isha, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Jibril continued to enjoin upon me concerning the neighbour until I thought he would make him an heir." And in it, from Abu Shurayh, that the Prophet (ﷺ) came out saying: "By Allah, he does not believe; by Allah, he does not believe; by Allah, he does not believe." It was said: "Who, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "One whose neighbour is not safe from his evils." And in it, from ʿA'isha: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have two neighbours; to which of them should I send a gift?" He said: "To the one whose door is nearer to you." And in Sahih Muslim: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Abu Dharr: "When you cook a broth, add plenty of water to it and look after your neighbours." The limit of the neighbourhood was disputed: Ibn Shihab and al-Awza'i said: forty houses from every side, and a hadith has been related on this; but there is no fixed limit from Malik on this, and the apparent view is that it is left to what people customarily recognise.

His saying: "﴿والصّاحِبِ بِالجَنْبِ﴾" is the companion who is constant in the place, from which is the guest, and from which is the travelling companion, and everyone who is attached to you seeking that you benefit him. It was also said: he meant the wife.

"ابْنِ السَّبِيلِ" is the stranger passing through a people without intending to stay, for whoever stays is the distant neighbour. The word "ابن" in it is used in the sense of attribution and association, as in their saying: "Abu al-Layl," and their proverb: "her father and her measurer." When he enters a tribe he is not one of its sons, so they called him "son of the road", as if the road had cast him upon them, so he is like their child. The charge concerning him is because he is weak in resources, scarce in helpers, since he cannot find his way to the conditions of a people other than his own, nor a land other than his own.

Both attributes are the source of harshness and rudeness, and so they contradict the goodness commanded, because what is meant is goodness in dealing and abandoning haughtiness toward one who may be suspected of having a reason that prevents him from retaliating.

The meaning of the negation of Allah's love is the negation of His pleasure and drawing near to whoever has this attribute; and this is an allusion to the characters of the people of shirk, for they were known for harshness and rudeness; so it carries the sense of a warning against remnants of the characters they were upon.

His statement "evil is that companion" is the answer to the condition. If the concealed pronoun in "sa'a" refers to Satan, then "sa'a" has the sense of "bi'sa" (evil is), the pronoun is its subject, and "qarinan" is a specifying accusative (tamyiz) for the pronoun, like His statement: "Evil is the example of the people who denied Our signs" [al-A'raf: 177], meaning "evil is a companion for him," so that the connection between the condition and its answer is established. It is also permissible that "sa'a" remain in its original sense, the opposite of "husuna" (was good), with a pronoun raised referring back to "man," and "qarinan" being a specifying accusative of relation, as in their saying "sa'a sam'an, fa-sa'a ijabatan" (bad in hearing, bad in response), meaning "evil is he whose companion is Satan, in respect of the companion." On both possibilities the intended meaning is the evil condition of whoever has Satan as a companion, by affirming the evil of his companion; for a man is known by his companion, as 'Adi ibn Zayd said:

"Every companion follows the example of his associate."

"'Ala" is for figurative elevation, with the meaning of burden and hardship, as in their saying: "'Alayka an taf'ala kadha" (it is incumbent upon you to do such-and-such). "Law amanu" is a conditional whose answer has been omitted because the preceding words indicate it; the indicator of the answer has been placed first for the sake of emphasis on the interrogation, as in the words of Qatilah bint al-Harith:
