The speech thus alludes to an omitted threat, which is of the kind of punishment, and that it is just with regard to them, because they deserved it through their disbelief. This implied meaning is also indicated by its contrast with His saying: ﴿And if it is a good deed﴾. Since what is negated is injustice, and "the weight of an atom" is a measure of the least injustice, this shows that the intended meaning is that Allah does not hold the evildoer accountable for more than the recompense of his evil deed.

"Mithqala dharratin" (the weight of an atom) is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (naib 'an al-maf'ul al-mutlaq); that is, He does not wrong with an injustice measured by the weight of an atom. The "mithqal" (weight) is that by which heaviness becomes apparent, and therefore it is formed on the pattern of the instrument noun (ism al-alah), and what is meant by it is the quantity.

The "dharra" (atom) is applied to the egg of an ant and to what scatters from dust when blown upon; this is the most insignificant thing by which something is measured, so it is known by a fortiori that what is greater than it is negated. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read "hasanatun" (a good deed) with a nominative ending, taking "takun" as the complete verb kana (to exist), meaning: if a good deed exists. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with the accusative "hasanatan," taking "takun" as the defective kana with "hasanatan" as its predicate, and the hidden subject of kana refers back to "mithqal dharratin." The verb of being is in the feminine form in deference to the word "dharra," to which "mithqal" is annexed, because the word "mithqal" is vague and is specified only by the word "dharra," so it is as though it were dispensed with.

Al-Mudá'afa (doubling) is the attribution of "al-di'f" (with a kasra on the dad), meaning the like or equivalent. It is said: dā'afa, da''afa and ad'afa; and they have one meaning according to verification, in the view of the linguists such as Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. Abu 'Ubayda said that "da'afa" implies more than a single multiple, and "da''afa" implies two multiples. This is refuted by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The punishment will be doubled for her, double﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. As for the indication of one of the three forms regarding the quantity of multiplication, it is derived from the contextual evidence, in accordance with the wisdom of the form. The majority read "yudā'if-hā" (He multiplies it), while Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read "yudha''if-hā" (He multiplies it) without an alif after the 'ayn and with a shadda on the 'ayn.

"Al-ajr al-'azim" (the great reward) is that which is added beyond the doubling; for this reason Allah, Exalted is He, attributed it to the pronoun of majesty, saying "min ladunhu" (from Himself), an attribution of honour. He called it "ajr" (reward) because it is a recompense for righteous deeds. It has been narrated that this was revealed concerning the reward of emigration (hijra).

[p. 57]

The *fa'* (ف) may be an eloquent *fa'* (*fa' fasīḥa*, a particle indicating an unstated condition), pointing to a suppressed condition that arises from the threat in His words ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ [4:37] and His words ﴿and evil is the companion he has been given﴾ [4:38]; and from the rebuke in His words ﴿And what would it have harmed them﴾ [4:39]; and from the promise in His words ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] an atom's weight﴾ [4:40], and so on. The implied sense is: "If you are certain of this, then what will be the state of all those when the witnesses come and the requirement of testimony becomes manifest concerning righteous deeds and concerning evil deeds?" On this reading, the pronoun in "*bika*" (بِكَ, "with you") is not a pronoun in place of a noun that should have been stated explicitly. The *fa'* may also be a consequence (*tafrī'*) of His words ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] an atom's weight; and if there is a good deed, He doubles it﴾ [4:40], meaning that from this there branches off a question about the state of people when We bring from every nation a witness. People will then be divided between one who rejoices and one who grieves. On this reading, the pronoun "*bika*" stands in the place of the explicit noun, because the requirement of this is that the speech be directed to the whole nation, so it would be expected to say: "and We bring the Messenger as a witness over them." Instead, He turned to direct address, to honour the Messenger (ﷺ) with the dignity of presence and of being attended to.

[p. 57, continued]

The state indicated by the interrogative used for amazement (*ta'jīb*) signals a terrifying condition for the polytheists and proclaims their bewilderment and their attempt to escape punishment by taking the path of denying that they were warned, in light of what the coming of a witness against them implies. For this reason, the subject being asked about is omitted, and it is to be understood as something like: "how are those (the people)?" or "how is the scene?" It should not be understood as "how is their state" specifically, since their states are many, and each of them is made clearer by the state of its opposite: the one who is saved grows in joy by witnessing the state of his opposite, and the one who is destroyed grows in grief by witnessing the state of his opposite. Each person's certainty is strengthened by what has happened to him, through the testimony of those who speak the truth about him, for or against him. For this reason, when He mentioned the witness, He did not mention with it its complement introduced by *'alā* (عَلى, "over") or by the *lām* (لِ, "for"), so that it would encompass both meanings. The interrogative is used in a secondary meaning of its sense, that of amazement, and a parallel to this has already occurred at His words, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾ [3:25], in Surat Al 'Imran.

"*Idhā*" (إذا, "when") is an adverbial of future time, added to the clause "*ji'nā*" (جِئْنا, "We came/bring"), meaning the time of Our bringing a witness. The content of the clause is known from other verses that were revealed earlier, such as the verse in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And [mention] the Day We will raise up from every nation a witness against them from among themselves, and We will bring you as a witness against these people﴾ [16:89]. Therefore, it is appropriate for the time noun to be made definite by being added to that clause. The adverbial is governed by "*kayfa*" (كَيْفَ, "how") because of the meaning of a verb it contains, namely the meaning of amazement, just as it is put in the accusative by the meaning of anguish in the words of Abu al-Tamhan:

*"And before tomorrow, O woe of my heart, from a tomorrow / when my companions depart, and I am not one who departs."*

The two prepositional phrases in His words ﴿from every nation﴾ and His words "(*bi-shahīd*)" (بِشَهِيدٍ, "with a witness") are attached to "*jī'nā*" (جِئْنا). The discussion of their parallel in His words ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾ [3:25] has already been given briefly.

The witness of every nation is its Messenger, by the indication of His words: ﴿and We bring you as a witness against these people﴾.

"*Hā'ulā'*" (هَؤُلاءِ, "these") is a demonstrative referring to those whom the Prophet (ﷺ) called to mind, so that they are present in the listener's mind when he hears the demonstrative. The original use of a demonstrative is for something that is visibly present in existence, or something placed in its position. The Qur'an has established the usage of the demonstrative "*hā'ulā'*" to mean the polytheists. This is a meaning we were inspired to, and which we arrived at by inductive study, and it fits. It is also possible that the demonstrative refers to ﴿those who are stingy and enjoin people to be stingy﴾ [4:37], who are the polytheists and the hypocrites, since their having been mentioned previously makes them as if present, so they are pointed to. Because of their extensive rebuke and dispute, they have become as though specified in the eyes of the Muslims. Among the weakest possibilities is that "*hā'ulā'*" refers to the witnesses, indicated by His words ﴿from every nation a witness﴾. Although there is a sound hadith that fits this in the testimony of Nuh (Noah) against his people, and that they deny him, so Muhammad (ﷺ) testifies to his truthfulness, it does not necessarily follow that this is the intended meaning of this verse.

The complement of the second "*shahīd*" (شَهِيدًا, "witness") is mentioned governed by "*'alā*" (عَلى, "over"), to threaten the disbelievers that the testimony will be against them, since they are the intended referent of the demonstrative.

In Sahih al-Bukhari: that 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to me, "Recite the Qur'an to me." I said, "Shall I recite it to you when it was revealed to you?" He said, "I love to hear it from others." So I recited Surat al-Nisa' to him, until I reached ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ He said, "Stop." And behold, his eyes were shedding tears.

As I have said, it expresses that state concisely through the word "*kayfa*." Likewise I say here: there is no verb more comprehensive in meaning for the totality of feeling at this moment than the weeping of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for it indicates a combined feeling in which there are great meanings: the joy at Allah's honouring him in that great scene; the believers' affirmation of him in conveying the message; the seeing of the good that was accomplished for them through him; the sorrow over the punishment that befell the rest of his nation because of their denial of him; and the witnessing of their regret for disobeying him. Weeping is an interpreter of mercy, joy, sorrow and delight.

His words ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them﴾, and the rest of the verse, form a explanatory resumption (*isti'nāf bayānī*), because the listener asks about the obscure state indicated by His words ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?﴾ and seeks its explanation. So this clause comes to explain part of that astonishing state: the state of those who disbelieved when they see the signs of evil, from the testimony of the witnesses of the nations over their believers and their disbelievers, and they become certain that those testified against for disbelief are being taken to punishment. Thus fear overtakes them, and they wish, because of it, that the earth were leveled over them.

The clause ﴿that the earth were leveled over them﴾ explains the clause "*yawaddu*" (يَوَدُّ, "wishes"): that is, they wish a wish that His words ﴿that the earth were leveled over them﴾ make clear. Because its content conveys the meaning of the object wished for, the conditional clause takes the place of the object of "*yawaddu*," so its verb takes the place of a verbal noun, and "*law*" (لَوْ, "if/that") takes the place of the particle of the verbal noun. This has already been explained at His words: ﴿One of them wishes he could live a thousand years﴾ [2:96] in Surat al-Baqarah.

His words "(*tasawwā*)" (تَسَوّى) were read by Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far with an open *ta'* and a doubled *sin*. It is the imperfect of *tasawwā*, the intransitive form (*muṭāwi'*) of *sawwāhu*, meaning to make it equal to something else, that is, similar, since *sawā'* means the like. One of the two *tā'*s has been assimilated into the *sīn*. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with an open *tā'* and a light *sīn*, with the same meaning as the previous reading, but with one of the two *tā'*s dropped for lightness. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read "(*tusawwā*)" (تُسَوّى) with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and a light *sīn*, in the passive, meaning "be made level/equal." The sameness indicated by the leveling may be sameness in essence, so the meaning is that they become dust like the earth, since it is evident that it is not meant that the earth becomes people. On this reading, the meaning is the same as His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Oh, I wish I had been dust"﴾ [78:40]. This is the view of the majority of exegetes. On this reading, the speech is an expansion (*iṭnāb*), whose expansion is intended to adopt the manner of metonymy (*kināya*) for their becoming dust, by a metonymy in which the attribution is what is intended, like their saying: "Glory is between his two garments," and the words of Ziyad al-A'jam:

*"Indeed generosity, manliness and liberality / are in a tent pitched over Ibn al-Hashraj."*

That is: he is generous, possesses manliness, and is noble. The sameness may also be sameness in quantity, so it has been said: they wish they had not been raised and had remained level with the earth in its belly. It has also been said: they wish to be buried at that time as they were before resurrection.

My own preference is that the meaning is leveling in emerging and appearing, that is, that the earth rises up so that it is levelled in height with their bodies, so that they do not appear. This is a metonymy for the intensity of their fear and humiliation, so they shrink and make themselves small until they wish to become unseen on the earth. This is like the description by one of the Bedouins who mocks a people of Tayy, which al-Mubarrad recited in *al-Kamil*:

*"When it is said, 'Which of them is which?' the shoulders and heads become alike."*

This is better for the meaning of the verse and more suitable to the metonymy.

His words ﴿and they do not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ may be a new independent clause, with the *wāw* as a conjunction joining it to the clause "*yawaddu*." It may also be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāliyya*), that is: they wish that the earth were leveled over them while they are not concealing. It is as though, when they saw the testimony of the messengers, and saw the reward of those testified against from the earlier nations, and saw the end of the disbelief of those to whom messengers were sent, to the point that the witnessing of their messengers became necessary, they knew that the turn had come to them, and it occurred to them to conceal their affair from Allah if He asked them, but their souls did not help them to confess the truth, because of what they saw of the consequences of the confirmation of disbelief, from the intensity of their panic. So they stood between the pull and the restraint, and they wished to be hidden and not appear, so they would not be asked, and would not be forced into a destructive confession nor into a destructive concealment.

**Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 4, verse 43 (Part 1 of 3)**

﴿O you who have believed, do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying.﴾

This verse is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic) that explains two rulings concerning the prayer. What called for its revelation right after the preceding verses was that the time had come to legislate this ruling on wine, and to pair it with an established ruling that also concerns the prayer. It appears that its occasion of revelation arose during the revelation of the verses before it and after it, so it came in its place at the time it was revealed and came as an interjection between those verses. It contains a first ruling that concerns the prayer directly, and this is also intended for its own sake according to its ultimate purpose. This is His saying: ﴿do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated.﴾ This is because wine had been permitted, and God Most High had not prohibited it, so it remained under its original permissibility, and among the Muslims there were those who drank it. Then God Most High sent down His saying: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219] early in the period of the Hijrah. A group of the Muslims said: "We drink it for its benefits, not for its sin," and they knew that what was meant by sin is hardship, harm and corruption. That verse was a notice to them that wine was close to becoming forbidden, because what contains sin is characterized by an attribute suitable for prohibition. However, God kept its permissibility as a mercy to them in their customary practice, together with preparing souls to accept its prohibition. Then, after three years, there occurred what al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf prepared a meal for us, invited us, and gave us wine to drink. The time of prayer came, and they put me forward, and I recited: *Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, and we worship what you worship*. So God Most High revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated.﴾" Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (good and sound)."

[Page 61 continues]

The word *qurb* (approaching) is used here in its metaphorical meaning, which is being engaged in the act, because *qaraba* is literally about drawing near in place or in essence. It is said: *qaruba minhu* with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ*, and *qaribahu* with a *kasra* on the *rāʾ*, and both have the same meaning. Some people claimed that the form with a *kasra* on the *rāʾ* is used only for metaphorical nearness, and this is not correct.

The verb was chosen over *lā tuṣallū* (do not pray) and similar forms in order to indicate that this condition is incompatible with the prayer, and that the one who is in it deserves to keep away from the best act in Islam. For this reason, the verse was a notice of a change in the status of wine and of a turning away from it, because the people addressed at that time were the most complete of people in faith and the most attached to the prayer, so they would look at nothing that prevents them from the prayer except with a look of contempt. Some exegetes interpreted the prayer here as the mosque, by way of using the name of the place for the thing located in it, as in His saying: ﴿And monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan, who said: "A group of the Companions used to drink wine and then come to the mosque for the prayer with the Messenger of God, so God forbade them from that." Its remoteness and its contradiction of the well-known reports are not hidden.

His saying: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾ is a limit (*ghāyah*) for the prohibition and an allusion to its reason. He settled on the word "you are saying" rather than "you are doing," because it is evident that this degree of intoxication may lead to disruption of the acts of the prayer, since an act is quickly subject to disruption when the intellect is disrupted before speech is disrupted. In the verse there is a notice that light intoxication does not prevent the prayer at that time. Or it is intended by the limit that it is the state of the end of intoxication, so that the remaining exhilaration (*nashwah*) continues after it.

*Sukārā* is the plural of *sakrān* (intoxicated), and the *sakrān* is the one whose intellect has begun to close, derived from *sakr*, which means closing or shutting. From it come *sakr al-ḥawḍ* (the closing of the pool), *sakr al-bāb* (the closing of the door), and ﴿our eyes have been dazzled﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 15].

When this verse was revealed, the Muslims avoided drinking wine during the times of the prayers, so they used to drink only after the 'Isha' prayer and after the Subh prayer, because of the length of time between these two prayers and what follows them. Then, together with the prohibition on approaching the prayer while intoxicated, there was added the prohibition on approaching it without purification.

* * *

[Page 62]

﴿Nor while in a state of janābah (major ritual impurity), except as travellers, until you have washed. And if you are sick, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then take clean earth and wipe your faces and hands. Indeed, God is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾

This is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) on the clause ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾, because it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). This accusative case after the conjunction is clear evidence that a circumstantial clause is considered to be in the accusative position.

*Junub* is on the pattern *fuʿul*. It was said to be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and it was said to be an adjective like *uʿud*. The discussion of this has already passed, at His saying: ﴿and the neighbour who is a stranger﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. What is meant by it is one who is kept away from worship, that is, from the prayer, when he has lain with his wife, until he washes.

The description *junub* is a description by a verbal noun, and therefore it was not made plural, since it is predicated of a plural, from His saying: ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾. The use of *janābah* with this meaning dates from the pre-Islamic era, since washing from *janābah* was known among them. It is perhaps from the remnants of the *ḥanīfiyyah* (the original monotheistic religion of Abraham), or from what they took from the Jews, since the command to wash from *janābah* came in chapter 15 of the Book of Leviticus in the Torah. Ibn Ishaq mentioned in the *Sīrah* that Abu Sufyan, when he returned defeated from Badr, swore that no ritual washing for *janābah* should touch his head until he raided Muhammad. I have not come across anything from the speech of the Arabs that indicates mention of washing for *janābah*.

The meaning is: do not pray while in a state of *janābah* until you wash, and so on. The intended purpose of His saying ﴿nor while in a state of janābah﴾ is to pave the way to the legislation of *tayammum* (dry ablution with clean earth), since the ruling on the ritual bath (*ghusl*) for *janābah* was established earlier, so mentioning it here is an incorporation (*idmāj*, embedding one matter within another). *Tayammum* was legislated during the Battle of al-Muraysi' according to the correct view, and that was in the sixth year or the fifth year according to the more sound view. The apparent meaning of the hadith of Malik from 'A'ishah is that the verse that was revealed at the Battle of al-Muraysi' is the verse of *tayammum*, so it appears that this is the verse in Surah al-Nisa', since nothing from it is mentioned except *tayammum*. In the hadith of 'Amr from 'A'ishah there is a report that the verse that was revealed was His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to pray﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], which is in Surah al-Ma'idah. Al-Bukhari recorded it, and

[Page 63]

al-Qurtubi affirmed that the verse revealed at the Battle of al-Muraysi' is the verse of Surah al-Nisa'. He said: "Because the verse of Surah al-Ma'idah is called the verse of ablution (*āyat al-wuḍū'*)." Likewise, al-Wahidi cited in *Asbāb al-Nuzūl* (Occasions of Revelation) the hadith of 'A'ishah concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse of Surah al-Nisa'. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is a problem for which I have not found a cure; we do not know which of the two verses 'A'ishah meant." Surah al-Ma'idah is said to have been revealed before Surah al-Nisa', and it is said to have been after it. The matter is easy, and the more correct view is that Surah al-Nisa' was revealed before Surah al-Ma'idah.

The exception in His saying ﴿except as travellers﴾ is an exception from the general range of states derived from the occurrence of *junuban* (in a state of janābah), which is an indefinite circumstantial word in the context of negation. A "traveller" (*ʿābir al-sabīl*), in the speech of the Arabs, is one who is travelling while on his journey. It is derived from *ʿabr*, which means crossing and passing through; it is said: *ʿabara al-nahr* (he crossed the river) and *ʿabara al-ṭarīq* (he crossed the road). Among the scholars there are those who interpreted *ʿābirī sabīl* as "passing through a path," and said: what is meant by it is the path to the mosque, based on interpreting the prayer in His saying ﴿do not approach the prayer﴾ as the mosque. They made the verse a concession for a person in a state of *janābah* to pass through the mosque when his intention is to pass through and not to stay. This was said by those who interpreted the prayer as the mosque. It was also attributed to Anas ibn Malik, Abu 'Ubaydah, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', Mujahid, Masruq, al-Nakha'i, Zayd ibn Aslam, 'Amr ibn Dinar, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Shihab and Qatadah, who said: "That was in the days when many of the Emigrants and the Helpers had doors of houses opening onto the mosque. Then this was abrogated (*nusikha*, cancelled by a later ruling) after all the doors were closed except the small door (*khawkhah*) of Abu Bakr, so passing through in this way remained a concession for the Prophet (ﷺ) and for Abu Bakr. In another report, it was for 'Ali as well." It was also said: "The small door of the house of 'Ali was left open into the mosque," but this is not authentically established.

The benefit of this exception, according to the one who interpreted ﴿do not approach the prayer﴾ as entering the mosque and interpreted ﴿travellers﴾ as those passing through the mosque, is clear. It is a true exception from the general range of states of the one in *janābah*, by excepting travellers. The "traveller" taken from the exception is unrestricted, and according to the proponents of this interpretation it remains on its unrestricted sense without any restriction. But according to the majority, who took the verse on its apparent meaning as "approaching the prayer" and as "travellers," no benefit appears for it, since it is dispensed with by His saying after it ﴿or on a journey﴾, and because the general scope of the restriction involves specification. What appears to me is that it was placed first here because it is the most common of the circumstances that come between a person and washing, by way of the traveller's need to conserve water, and because the onset of illness is rare. The exception, on the majority's interpretation, may be considered a connected exception according to the one who holds that the one performing *tayammum* is still in a state of *janābah*, and that *tayammum* does not remove the ritual impurity but permits the prayer out of necessity within the time. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, for whom it is a necessary substitute (*badal ḍarūrī*) that is assessed by the measure of necessity, and its evidence is the apparent meaning of the exception. And it may be considered a disconnected exception according to the one who holds that the one performing *tayammum* is not in a state of *janābah*, and that *tayammum* removes the ritual impurity until it is nullified by a nullifier and its cause is removed. This is the view of Abu Hanifah. Therefore, when the one in *janābah* performs *tayammum* and prays, and then a minor impurity that nullifies ablution occurs to him, he performs ablution again, because his *tayammum* is a substitute for the ritual bath in every respect. This is the apparent meaning according to the sense, and there is nothing in the Sunnah that requires otherwise.

There are two reports from Malik on this matter. The well-known report from Ibn al-Qasim is that *tayammum* permits the prayer and does not remove the minor impurity, so the one who performs *tayammum* prays only one obligatory prayer with it. If someone performs *tayammum* for *janābah* due to an excuse that prevents washing, and then his ablution is nullified, he performs *tayammum* in place of ablution. And there is a report from Malik, in the narration of the Baghdadis, that the sick person who cannot touch water performs *tayammum* and prays more than one prayer until his *tayammum* is nullified by a nullifier of ablution. Likewise for the one who has missed prayers, he prays them with one *tayammum*. Based on this, renewing *tayammum* for the other two cases is only because he does not know whether he might find water, so the intention for *tayammum* was not firm in its continuation. No view has been transmitted from Malik that the one who performs *tayammum* for *janābah* due to an excuse that prevents washing must perform ablution if his ablution is nullified.

Regarding the implication (*mafhūm*) of this exception, according to those among the majority who hold to implications, on this interpretation there is a detail. The "traveller" is unrestricted, and his restriction is His saying ﴿and you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾. The general scope of His saying ﴿nor while in a state of janābah﴾ remains for other than the traveller, because a general term that has been specified remains general in what is other than what was specified. The condition specified it a second time in His saying ﴿And if you are sick﴾. Then, if it had been established among the Muslims that the prayer may occur without purification, His saying ﴿except as travellers﴾ would remain ambiguous (*mujmal*), because they await the explanation of the ruling on approaching the prayer without purification for the traveller. Then His saying ﴿And if you are sick, or on a journey﴾ would be an explanation of this ambiguity. And if that had not occurred to their minds, there would be no ambiguity, and His saying ﴿And if you are sick, or on a journey﴾ would be a fresh beginning of the rulings of *tayammum*.

The placement of the excepted element in His saying ﴿except as travellers﴾ before the completion of the intended statement, which is restricted by His saying ﴿until you have washed﴾, is for emphasis. This is practised in a rare usage, like the saying of Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi, who was an Umayyad:

*I do not desire, O people, except unwillingly:*
*the gate of the governor, nor the protection of the chamberlain.*

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 4, verse 43 (part 2 of 3):

His saying, ﴿until you wash yourselves﴾, is a limit (ghayah) to the prohibition of prayer when they are in a state of janabah (ritual impurity from sexual intercourse or emission). It is thus a legislation of ghusl (full ritual bathing) from janabah and an obligation to perform it, because the obligation of prayer never lapses under any circumstance. Once they were forbidden to approach it without ghusl, it became known from this that ghusl is obligatory. The wisdom behind prescribing ghusl is cleanliness, and it was linked to the performance of prayer so that the worshipper would be in a state of bodily completeness, just as he would then be in a state of inner completeness through intimate supplication and humility. Among the most wonderful of the legal wisdoms is that the obligation of cleaning was not tied to a state of dirtiness, because the degree of dirt that calls for bathing and cleaning varies among people according to their perceptions, customs and conditions. Thus the obligation of ghusl was tied to a state that does not cease to accompany human strength throughout the usual span of human life, namely the state of discharging the surplus of human vigor. Between that state and the intensity of vigor there is a perfect proportion, for in proportion to the strength the excess is expelled. Likewise, between the intensity of vigor and the appearance of these excesses on the outer surface of the body, expressed as dirt, there is a perfect proportion. Tying ghusl to janabah was therefore tying it to an outward, definable attribute, and this was made the ratio (illah) or the cause (sabab). At the same time it secured the purpose that calls for legislation, namely the removal of filth when it reaches a degree that warrants removal, while linking this to the greatest act of worship, prayer. Thus purification became an act of worship in the same way. The same applies to the legislation of wudu'. Moreover, in ghusl from janabah there is another wisdom: the renewal of the vigor of the nervous system, which becomes lethargic through the expenditure of the strength derived from the froth of the blood, as physicians have observed. Thus great wisdoms were established by this regulation.

The attribution of the act of washing to the persons in His saying, ﴿until you wash yourselves﴾, indicates that ghusl is the envelopment of the body in water. This is agreed upon. There is disagreement regarding the obligation of dalk (rubbing the body with the hand over its parts). Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, made it a condition, on the basis that it is the familiar meaning of ghusl in the Arabic language, and because wudu' is not valid without rubbing, by consensus, so ghusl is likewise.

The majority of scholars said: in ghusl it suffices to envelop the body with water, by pouring or by immersion. They argued with the hadith of Maymunah and 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them both, concerning the description of the Prophet's ghusl (ﷺ), that he poured water over his body. There is no proof in it, because they did not mention that he did not rub, but they were silent about it, so their silence may have been because it was what was understood. This is also a narration from Malik, related from him by Abu al-Faraj and Marwan ibn Muhammad al-Tatari, but it is weak.

His saying, ﴿and if you are ill﴾ etc., mentions the situation of dispensation in abandoning ghusl and abandoning wudu', which is not mentioned in this surah but is mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah, and that was revealed before this surah. The aim, therefore, is to explain the ruling of tayammum in its entirety, and bringing these matters together in one sequence achieves this aim, and it also specifies the generality of His saying, ﴿nor in a state of janabah﴾, as has preceded.

His saying, ﴿or on a journey﴾, is an explanation of the ambiguity in His saying, ﴿except as travelers﴾, if there is ambiguity in it; otherwise it is the introduction of a new ruling, as has preceded.

His saying, ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾, is an addition to the ruling of tayammum in place of ghusl, by mentioning the tayammum that replaces wudu', to complete both types of tayammum. Other causes of it are taken by analogy to what is mentioned. The sick person here refers to one whose health has been disturbed such that bathing would harm him or increase his illness. "Came from the gha'it" is a euphemism for relieving the human need. Euphemizing with this became common in their speech because of the ugliness of the explicit term.

"Al-gha'it" means the low part of the land and what is hidden from sight. One says ghat fi al-ard when he disappears into the earth (yaghuts), so its hamzah is converted from a waw. The Arabs, when relieving themselves, would go to a low place away from the tribe's dwellings, and so they would euphemize it, saying "he went to the gha'it" or "he defecated." This was a subtle euphemism, and then people used it so often that it came to equal the literal meaning and became crude, so the jurists began to apply it to the very minor impurity itself and attach to it rulings that suit it.

His saying, ﴿or you have touched women﴾, was read as (lamastum) in the form of mufa'alah, and read as (lamastum) in the form of the simple verb, as will come, and both have the same meaning in verification. Whoever tries to detail the difference does not bring anything of substance. The original sense of al-lams is direct contact with the hand or with some part of the body, and it has been used figuratively and metaphorically for seeking, as Allah the Exalted said, ﴿and we have touched the sky﴾ [al-Jinn: 8], and for descending, as al-Nabighah said:

"He would search with the army the abode of the warrior"

and for sexual intercourse, because it is a synonym of masass, and from this is the saying:

"So-and-so does not turn away the hand of one who touches,"

and its counterpart is ﴿and if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. The mulamasah here may be understood in its apparent sense, namely touching by direct contact of the hand or some part of the body with the woman's body, so that it would be a second cause among the causes of wudu' which require tayammum when water is absent. On this basis al-Shafi'i explained it, making a man's touching his wife's body with his hand invalidate wudu'. This is a remote interpretation, since touching the body does not invalidate wudu'; rather wudu' is for what issues forth in the usual manner. The correct interpretation is therefore that mulamasah is a euphemism for intercourse, and the enumeration of these causes is to gather what commonly invalidates minor and major purity. The reason it did not dispense with "you have touched women" by His saying earlier, "nor in a state of janabah," is that the latter was mentioned in the context of commanding ghusl, while this is mentioned in the context of permitting tayammum as a dispensation, and the setting calls for legislation, which suits not relying on implication (dalalat al-iltizam). By this, mentioning it has a sound purpose. As for al-Shafi'i's interpretation and that of those who followed him, there would be no great importance in mentioning a second cause among the causes of wudu'. The majority inclined to this, and therefore according to Malik and Abu Hanifah, wudu' is not obligatory from a man touching his wife so long as nothing issues from him. However, Malik said: if the toucher experiences pleasure or intends pleasure, his wudu' is nullified. He understood mulamasah in this verse in both its euphemistic and literal senses, but this applies with the condition of experiencing pleasure, and a group of the early scholars also said so. I think Malik relied in this on the reports transmitted from the leading early authorities, and I do not think he took it to be what is meant by the verse.

The majority read (lamastum) in the form of mufa'alah. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (lamastum) without an alif.

His saying, ﴿and you find no water﴾, is a conjunction upon the conditional verb, and it is a restriction on the traveler, on the one who comes from the ghā'it, and on the one who has touched women. As for the sick person, his tayammum is not restricted to not finding water, because he performs tayammum unconditionally, and this is known from the meaning of illness. Thus the implication of the restriction in his case is rendered inoperative by the meaning. Nor is the intended sick person one who is chronically ill, since a chronically ill person is seldom without someone to bring him water.

His saying (﴿then perform tayammum﴾) is the answer of the conditional, and tayammum means intending. Al-sa'id means the surface of the earth. Dhu al-Rummah describes a young wild cow among the oryx, sleeping in the sun and hardly waking:

"As if in the forenoon the dabbabah (insect) strikes the surface of the earth with it, with a proboscis in the bones of the head"

And al-tayyib means the pure, that which has not been defiled by impurity or filth. Thus al-sa'id includes dust, sand and stones. He expressed it by al-sa'id only to turn the Muslims away from the folly of seeking dust or sand from beneath the surface of the earth, out of excess in ensuring its purity.

The ruling of tayammum has been legislated by this verse, or its earlier legislation in Surah al-Ma'idah has been confirmed, according to the more correct view. The legislation of tayammum occurred in the sixth year in the expedition of al-Muraysi'. The cause of its legislation is what is in the Sahih from 'A'ishah, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah on some of his journeys, until when we were at al-Bayda' or Dhat al-Jaysh, my necklace broke, and the Messenger of Allah stayed to search for it, and the people stayed with him, though they were not near water and had no water with them. So the people came to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and said: 'Do you not see what 'A'ishah has done? She has kept the Messenger of Allah and the people, and they are not near water and have no water with them.' Abu Bakr came while the Messenger of Allah was resting his head on my thigh, asleep, and he said: 'You have detained the Messenger of Allah and the people, and they are not near water and have no water with them?' He rebuked me and said what Allah willed him to say, and he began to strike me with his hand in my side, and nothing prevented me from moving except the position of the Messenger of Allah on my thigh. Then the Messenger of Allah rose when morning came, without water, and Allah the Exalted revealed the verse of tayammum. Usayd ibn al-Hudayr said: 'This is not your first blessing, O family of Abu Bakr.' By Allah, no matter ever befell you that you disliked but Allah made it, for you and for the Muslims, a good in it." She said: "We sent the camel I was riding and found the necklace beneath it."

Tayammum is among the distinctive features of the law of Islam, as in the hadith of Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things that were not given to anyone before me," and he mentioned among them: "the earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification."

Tayammum is a substitute that the law has prescribed in place of purification. I have not seen any scholar give an explanation of the wisdom of making tayammum a substitute for purification with water, and this was a concern of mine for a long time during the period of seeking, until the wisdom of it was opened to me.

And I think the wisdom behind its legislation is to affirm the obligation of purity in the hearts of the believers, to affirm the sanctity of prayer (ṣalāh), and to elevate its standing in their hearts, so that they are never left in a state in which they regard themselves as praying without purity, out of reverence for intimate communion with Allah, exalted is He. For this reason He prescribed for them an act resembling a gesture toward purity, so that they would sense themselves to be purified. He made this act consist of placing the two hands upon the surface of the earth, which is the source of water. And because dust is used for cleansing vessels and the like, by which they clean whatever filth has clung to their garments, bodies and utensils, and because istijmar (cleaning after relieving oneself with stones or the like) is only a type of this, there is also in this the renewal of the search for water for one who lacks it, and a reminder that he is required to use it once the impediment is removed.

Since tayammum (dry ablution) is a symbolic purification, the Law has been satisfied in it with the face and the two hands, in both the minor and the major purification, as the ḥadīth of 'Ammār ibn Yāsir indicates. This objective is supported by the fact that when the Muslims lacked water during the expedition of al-Muraysī', they prayed without wuḍū' (ablution), and then the verse of tayammum was revealed.

This is the furthest that has occurred to me of the wisdom in the prescription of tayammum, after long inquiry and reflection, into a wisdom that is convincing upon consideration. I had considered tayammum to be the only type among the legal rulings in which worship is in its very kind (i.e., the act itself is the object of worship). As for worship in certain modes and measures among other kinds of acts of worship, there are many, such as the number of rak'ahs in the prayers. It seems that al-Shāfi'ī, when he stipulated that tayammum must be with dust specifically, and that the one performing tayammum must transfer it from the dust to his face and hands, took into account the meaning of cleansing, as in istijmar. However, this view was not transmitted from any of the early generations (al-salaf), and it is what did not occur to the mind of 'Ammār ibn Yāsir when he rolled himself in the dust when he could not perform ghusl. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is sufficient for you to do this: the face and the two palms."

For this same reason the early scholars differed regarding the ruling on tayammum. 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ūd said: tayammum is only valid as a substitute for wuḍū', not for ghusl, and the one in a state of janābah (ritual impurity from sexual intercourse or emission) may not pray until he performs ghusl, whether that is in a settled place or while traveling. Abū Mūsā al-Ash'arī and 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd debated this matter. Al-Bukhārī narrated in the Book of Tayammum: Abū Mūsā said to Ibn Mas'ūd: "What do you say if a man becomes junub and does not find water, how does he act?" 'Abd Allāh said: "He does not pray until he finds water." Abū Mūsā said: "Then how will you act regarding the statement of 'Ammār when the Prophet said to him: 'It would have sufficed you to do this,' and he struck his palms upon the earth, then wiped them over his face and hands?" Ibn Mas'ūd said: "Did you not see that 'Umar was not satisfied with that?" Abū Mūsā said: "Then leave aside the statement of 'Ammār. How will you act with this verse: ﴿And if you are ill or on a journey﴾?" So 'Abd Allāh did not know what to say, and he said: "If we were to grant them this concession, it would soon happen that when the water became cold for one of them, he would leave it and perform tayammum."

There is no doubt that 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ūd interpreted the verse of al-Nisā' by making His statement ﴿except for those passing through [the mosque]﴾ a concession for passing through the mosque, and they made ﴿or you have contacted women﴾ refer to touching that nullifies wuḍū', in the manner of al-Shāfi'ī's interpretation. The whole community of scholars disagreed with 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ūd on this. The majority said: one who lacks water may perform tayammum, as may one who fears for his life, or illness, or the worsening of illness, even if it be a mild cold or fever. Al-Shāfi'ī said: only one who lacks water, or one who fears for his life from destruction, may perform tayammum, not one who fears illness or its worsening, because the increase of illness is not certain. This is refuted by the fact that both matters are not certain to occur, and that God did not burden creation with what involves hardship.

It is related that 'Amr ibn al-'Āṣ (may Allah be pleased with him) performed tayammum on a cold night during the expedition of Dhāt al-Salāsil and led the people in prayer. They mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he asked him. 'Amr said: "I heard Allah say: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever merciful to you﴾ [al-Nisā': 29]." The Prophet (ﷺ) smiled and did not object to him.

As for His statement ﴿then wipe over your faces and your hands﴾, it confined tayammum to wiping the face and the two hands, and dropped the wiping of anything beyond them of the limbs of wuḍū', let alone the limbs of ghusl. This is because the purpose of it is not physical purification, nor the renewal of vigor, but merely the consciousness of completing the state for prayer. Some of the Companions thought that this was a tayammum substituting for wuḍū', and that tayammum substituting for ghusl is not valid unless the whole body is wiped with the dust. So the Prophet (ﷺ) taught him that tayammum for janābah is like tayammum for wuḍū'. It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from 'Ammār ibn Yāsir, who said: "I was on a journey and became junub, so I rolled in the dust (i.e., I rubbed myself in it) and prayed. Then I came to the Prophet and mentioned that, and he said: 'It is sufficient for you: the face and the two palms.'" This has already been mentioned above.

The letter bā' (ب) here is for emphasis, like His statement ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ [Maryam: 25], and like the verse of al-Nābigha, lamenting al-Nu'mān ibn al-Mundhir:

"There is goodness for you if the earth has covered you, one [man]; and the fortune of people has become one that limps and stumbles."

He meant: if the earth has covered you with the covering of burial. The meaning is: wipe your faces and your hands. This bā' has been mentioned with the wiped part both in wuḍū' and in tayammum, to indicate the thoroughness of the wiping, lest one concession be added to another concession.

[Page 71]

His statement ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ is a conclusion (tadhyīl) to the ruling of the concession, since He pardoned the Muslims, so He did not burden them with ghusl or wuḍū' when ill, nor with waiting for the presence of water when it is absent, lest the prayers accumulate upon them and making up (qaḍā') become difficult for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 44–45:

﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Book, who purchase error and want you to stray from the way?﴾ ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies, and sufficient is Allah as an ally, and sufficient is Allah as a helper.﴾

This is a resumed discourse returning to the course of the verses that preceded it, from His saying: ﴿And worship Allah and associate nothing with Him﴾ [al-Nisa: 36]. After warning the polytheists, it directed the warning to the People of the Book. The verses forbidding wine at the time of prayer occurred, and the verses legislating purification for it lie between them. There is a connection between them and the command to abandon wine at the times of the prayers and the command to purify oneself, because that is from the guidance which the Jews had not been given the like of. So they envied the Muslims for it, because they had been deprived of its like and had neglected a great guidance, and they wished to lead the Muslims astray out of enmity toward them.

The sentence ﴿Have you not considered﴾ up to ﴿the Book﴾ is one whose purpose is to express wonder. The interrogative in it is affirmative (taqriri), concerning the negation of an act which the addressee would not wish to be negated from him, so that this serves to urge him to acknowledge that it occurred. It also conveys wonder. A parallel to it occurred previously in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Book, who are called to the Book of Allah that it may judge between them?﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 23] in Surat Al 'Imran.

The sentence ﴿who purchase﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), so it is a restriction on the clause ﴿Have you not considered﴾. The state of their purchasing error, although it is not seen with the eye, has been placed in the position of what is seen, because the fame of a thing and its certainty make it like the thing seen.

The word nasib (portion) was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿For men is a portion﴾ [al-Nisa: 7] in this surah. Its choice here conveys the possibility of its scarcity in the minds of the listeners; otherwise it would have been said: "those who were given the Book." This is similar to His saying, exalted is He, after this: ﴿If there is for you a conquest from Allah, they say: "Were we not with you?" And if there is a portion for the disbelievers, they say: "Did we not gain mastery over you?"﴾ [al-Nisa: 141], meaning a portion of the conquest or of the victory.

By "the Book" is meant the Torah, because the Jews were the ones who were mixed with the Muslims in Medina, and there was no one among the Christians there.

The word ishtira' (purchase) is a metaphor for choosing and striving to obtain a thing, because the buyer is the one who takes the desired thing from the two parties to the transaction, and the seller is the one who gives up the desired thing out of his need for its price. This is how the common usage on which the language is built regards it; otherwise, both parties to the transaction are buyers and sellers. So it is inevitable that ishtira' was applied metaphorically to choosing. A parallel to it occurred earlier in His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who purchased error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] in Surat al-Baqarah. This indicates that they plunged into error deliberately, due to the weakness of their faith in their own Book and the little benefit their knowledge had for them.

His saying: ﴿and want you to stray from the way﴾ means they want for the believers error, so that they would not surpass them in guidance, like His saying: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your belief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109]. So the wanting here means love, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah wants to make clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you﴾ [al-Nisa: 26]. You may also take the wanting in its predominant meaning, which is the inner impulse toward action, meaning they strive that you go astray, by casting doubts and working to turn the Muslims away from faith. His saying previously has already passed: ﴿And those who follow desires want you to incline a great inclination﴾ [al-Nisa: 27].

The sentence ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, and it is an allusion, since their wanting the believers to go astray arises from hostility and envy.

The sentence ﴿And sufficient is Allah as an ally, and sufficient is Allah as a helper﴾ is a concluding statement, to reassure the souls of the believers in Allah's help. The report about the Jews, that they want the Muslims to go astray and that they are enemies of the Muslims, is by nature something that instills fear in the hearts of the Muslims, since the Jews neighboring the Muslims were numerous and well equipped, had wealth in hand, and were scattered throughout Medina and its surroundings: Qaynuqa', Qurayza, al-Nadir and Khaybar. So their enmity and evil intentions are not a matter to be taken lightly. Therefore His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as an ally﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿and want you to stray from the way﴾, meaning: if they are concealing evil for you, then Allah is your ally who guides you and takes charge of your affairs, as is the way of an ally with his master. And His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a helper﴾ corresponds to ﴿your enemies﴾, meaning: Allah will give you victory.

The verb (kafa, "suffices") in His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as an ally, and sufficient is Allah as a helper﴾ is used to strengthen the attribution to its agent of a quality indicated by the specification (tamyiz) mentioned after it, meaning that the agent of kafa is most worthy of being described by that quality. To indicate this, it became common in speech to introduce a ba' before the agent of the verb kafa, and it is a superfluous ba' used to emphasize sufficiency, so that a vagueness arises which makes the listener eager to know its detail, and so they bring a noun that specifies the type of that relation, so that the meaning becomes firmly established in the listener's mind.

The agent of kafa may also come without the ba', as in the saying of 'Abd Bani al-Hisḥas:

Old age and Islam suffice a man as a restrainer
Al-Zajjaj considered the ba' here not superfluous and said: the verb kafa was made to include the meaning of "be content" (iktafi), and Ibn Hisham approved this.

The superfluous ba' occurred irregularly with the object, as in the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik or Hassan ibn Thabit:

So sufficient for us is superiority over those other than us ∗∗∗ the love of the Prophet Muhammad for us
Al-Wahidi, in explaining the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

Sufficient for my body is emaciation, that I am a man ∗∗∗ were it not for my addressing you, you would not see me
decided that it is an irregularity.

The ba' is not added to the agent of "kafa" in the sense of "ajza'" (suffice), nor to the one in the sense of "waqa" (protect), so as to distinguish between its figurative usage and its literal usage, which is the meaning of being content with the thing itself, as in:

It sufficed me, and I did not seek, a little of wealth.
