Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 46:

Page 74
﴿Among those who are Jews are some who distort words from their places, and say, "We hear and disobey," and "Hear, without being made to hear," and "Ra'ina," twisting their tongues and slandering the religion. And if they had said, "We hear and obey, and hear, and look at us," it would have been better for them and more upright. But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they believe not, except a few.﴾
It is permissible that this be an independent statement.

The "min" (from/some of) here is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and it is the predicate of an omitted subject, indicated by its qualifier, which is the clause "yuharrifuna" (they distort). The estimated sense is: "a people who distort the words."

Omitting the subject in such a construction is common in Arabic speech, by means of the qualifier standing in for the qualified. This occurs when the subject is qualified by a clause or an adverbial phrase, and when it is a part of a noun governed by the preposition "min", and that noun precedes the subject. Among the well-known Arabic sayings is: "Minna za'ana wa minna aqama," meaning: "Some of us departed, and some of us stayed," i.e., a group of us departed and a group of us stayed. From the same usage is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"So they remained, and among them is one whose tears overcome him, and another who sheds the tear of the eye freely."
i.e., and among them is a group, as evidenced by his saying "and another" in the coordination. And the verse of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

"Fate is but two turns: of them, one I die, and another I seek life, striving."

The plural pronoun in "yuharrifuna" indicates that this is the deed of a group among them. It has been said that the intended one is Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut from among the Jews. Perhaps the one who says this means that he is among this group, since it is not permissible that the intended be one person while a plural pronoun is used, and the context is not one of concealment, so that it would be in the manner of his saying, peace be upon him, "What is the matter with people who stipulate...", etc.

It is also permissible that "min alladhina hadu" be a qualifier of "alladhina utu nasiban mina al-kitab", and "min" be explanatory (bayaniyyah), i.e., "they are those who are Jews," so that the clause "yuharrifuna" becomes a circumstantial clause (hal) from his saying "alladhina hadu". On both views, attributes of distortion, misguidance, and love of misguiding the Muslims are affirmed for them.

Page 75
Distortion (tahrif) is inclining a thing toward its edge (harf), which is its side and border. It will come later, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], in Surah al-Ma'idah. Here it is used to mean deviating from the plain and clear sense toward false interpretation, as one says: "He deviated from the path" or "from the way," when he erred from the correct and went toward misunderstanding or misleading. Thus it is the distortion of Allah's intended meaning in the Torah into false interpretations, as the people of desires do in distorting the meanings of the Qur'an with corrupt interpretations. It is also possible that tahrif is derived from harf, which is a word or writing, so that it means changing the words of the Torah and replacing them with other words to suit the desires of the people of appetites in supporting what they hold of corrupt deeds. The apparent view is that both of these matters were committed by the Jews in their book. As for what is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, that tahrif is the corruption of interpretation, and that people do not deliberately alter their book, it looks to their general condition. So on the first possibility, the use of "'an" in His saying, ﴿from its places﴾, is metaphorical, with no "transgression" and no "places". On the second, it is literal, since tahrif then means transfer and removal.

His saying "and they say" is coordinated with "yuharrifuna", mentioning the evil of their deeds and the evil of their sayings which they directed at the Messenger, peace be upon him: they say, "We heard your call and disobeyed you." This is a display of their adherence to their religion, so that the Messenger's hope in their faith would disappear. For this reason they did not see in this saying any harm to the Messenger, so they followed it with their saying to him, ﴿Hear, without being made to hear﴾, as a display of courtesy toward him.

The meaning of ﴿Hear, without being made to hear﴾ is that they say to the Messenger, peace be upon him, when he reviews with them the matter of Islam: "Hear from us." Then they follow that with "without being made to hear," giving the impression that they intended the apparent, immediate sense of "without being made to hear", i.e., "not commanded to hear", in the sense of the Arabs' saying: "Do, without being commanded." It has also been said that its meaning is "without hearing anything disliked," for the Arabs used to say "asmahahu" meaning "insulted him." The summary is that this expression was well known among the Arabs in the sense of honour and gentleness, as a common usage. But when they said it to the Messenger, they intended by it another meaning that they derived from something its construction allows, namely that he should not hear a voice from a speaker, by becoming deaf, or that his supplication not be answered. What showed that they intended this is His saying afterward, ﴿And if they had said﴾, up to His saying ﴿and hear, and look at us﴾, which removed for them the expression ﴿without being made to hear﴾. Their purpose in uttering a double-meaning speech was to please the Messenger and the believers, while pleasing themselves with their evil intention toward the Messenger, peace be upon him, and pleasing their people, so that they would find no proof against them.

As for their saying ﴿Ra'ina﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104], they used a word whose apparent meaning is requesting consideration (mura'ah), i.e., gentleness. Mura'ah is a form of reciprocal construction used for intensifying care, in the common metonymic manner that equals the original sense, since herding (ra'y) entails gentleness toward the one herded, seeking good pasture for him, and warding off harm from him. They intended by "Ra'ina" [al-Baqarah: 104] a word in Hebrew that indicates what the word "ru'unah" (foolishness) indicates in Arabic. It has been transmitted that the word was "ra'unah," and that its meaning is foolishness. Perhaps they used to say it, presenting the appearance that they were glorifying the Prophet, peace be upon him, with the plural pronoun, and what supports this is that Allah forbade the Muslims from following them in that out of deception, saying in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina," but say "Unzurna" [look at us]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104].

Al-layy originally means bending and turning, from which ﴿and do not turn back for anyone﴾ [Al 'Imran: 153]. It may be understood literally in both words, "layy" and "al-alsinah" (the tongues), i.e., they twist their tongues so that the speech resembles two languages, by elongating vowels, shortening elongated ones, emphasizing light sounds, or lightening emphatic ones, so that the word gives in the hearing an image resembling another word, for a word may shift from one pattern to another, and from one language to another, in this way. It is also possible that "layy" is meant metaphorically and "al-alsinah" is meant metaphorically: "layy" meaning altering the word, and "al-alsinah" a metaphor for speech, i.e., they produce in their speech what is not purely for good.

"Layyan" is in the accusative as an absolute object of "yaqulun", because "layy" is a manner of speaking.

"Wa taʿnan fi al-din" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), so it is coordinated with another object. There is no harm in it; you may also make both of them absolute objects, or both objects of purpose. Their saying "and slandering the religion" was because they concealed a wicked intention in their speech, saying to their brethren and to those near them of recent converts to faith: "If Muhammad were a messenger, he would know what we intended by our saying." For this reason Allah exposed them with this verse and its like.

Page 77
His saying: ﴿And if they had said, "We hear and obey"﴾ means: if they had said what is acceptance of Islam, it would have been better. The saying "We hear and obey" appears to be among the things that became a proverb, said by one who is commanded to do something and complies: "Hearing and obedience," i.e., my condition is hearing and obedience. It is among those where omitting the subject is obligatory, because it has become a proverb. In Surah al-Nur His saying, exalted is He, will come: ﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is only that they say, "We hear and obey"﴾ [al-Nur: 51].

His saying "(wa aqwam)" is a comparative derived from al-qiyam, which means clarity and manifestness, as in their saying: "The proof stood (qama) on such-and-such," and "the argument of so-and-so stood." It was "more upright" because it indicates a meaning that admits no ambiguity, unlike their saying.

The contrast in His saying ﴿But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾ arises from His saying ﴿it would have been better for them﴾: i.e., but the effect of the curse fell upon them, so they were deprived of what is good, and their souls produce nothing but the traces of what is hidden within them of evil deed and foul speech, which they cannot turn away from.

The meaning of ﴿so they believe not, except a few﴾ is that they never believe, so this is the emphasis of a thing by what resembles its opposite. "Few" (qillah) is used for non-existence, and the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran is interpreted accordingly:

"Little complaining of the anxious one who afflicts him, much of desire, scattered in separations and paths."

Al-Jahiz said in al-Bayan, at the saying of 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ud describing the land of Nasibin: "Many scorpions, few relatives," they use "qalil" in the place of "laysa" (there is not), as in their saying: "So-and-so has little shame," not meaning that there is shame, even if little. I say: from this is the Arabs' saying: "Few a man says that," meaning that he does not exist. The author of al-Kashshaf said, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is there a god with Allah? Little do you remember﴾ [al-Naml: 62]: the meaning is negation of remembrance, and "qillah" is used with the sense of negation. The Arabs used "qillah" in place of negation out of a kind of caution and moderation, as though the speaker fears that the universality of his negation will be met with denial, so he retreats to affirming a little, while he intends negation.

[Page 78]

﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them back on their backs, or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath. And the command of Allah is ever fulfilled.﴾

He turned to address the People of the Book, those intended by them being the Jews, after mentioning the wonders of their misguidance and establishing the proof against them, which contains a restraint for them if there were any restraint in them. Likewise, it is the way of the Qur'an not to let pass any opportunity of admonition and guidance that arises without seizing it. Likewise, it is the way of sincere advisers, from among the wise and the orators, to watch for the signs that the souls of their addressees are receptive, and the places where they may turn away from falsehood and perceive the truth, and then to aid them at that moment with the striking admonitions and guidance, as al-Hariri indicated in the eleventh maqama (a rhymed prose narrative), when he said: "When they had buried the dead, and the words 'if only' had passed, an old man appeared from a mound, leaning on his staff, and said: 'For the like of this, let the workers work,' etc." For this reason, the verse ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾ was brought after what preceded it.

This is the reason for the difference of the relative clause here from the relative clause in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ [al-Nisa: 44], because that came in a context of wonder and reproach, so it suited it a relative clause that signals the belittling of their knowledge of what was given them of the Book. What is here came in a context of encouragement, so it suited it a relative clause that signals that they were honored with the giving of the Torah, to stir their resolve to adopt the mark of those firmly grounded in knowledge, in the course of their deeds in accordance with what suits that. There is no real difference between the two relative clauses, because they were given the whole Book in actuality, in terms of its being in their hands, and they were given a portion of it in terms of their deeds running contrary to what their Book brought. So what they did not act upon of it is as if they had not been given it.

The two relative clauses were brought in His saying ﴿what We have sent down﴾ and His saying (confirming what is with you), rather than the two proper names, which are the Qur'an and the Torah: because of what is in His saying ﴿what We have sent down﴾ of reminding of the great status of the Qur'an, that it was sent down by the sending down of Allah; and because of what is in His saying (confirming what is with you) of an allusion against them, that the Torah is a book kept in their possession, of which they do not know its true knowledge and do not act upon what is in it, in the manner of His saying: ﴿like the example of a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 5].

[Page 79]

His saying ﴿before We obliterate faces﴾ is a threat or a warning. The meaning of ﴿before We obliterate﴾ is: believe at a time that begins before the obliteration, i.e., before the time of obliteration upon the faces. This is a threat that a great matter will befall them. It admits of being taken in the literal sense of obliteration, by Allah imposing upon them what corrupts their countenances, for the power of Allah is capable of that. And it may be that the obliteration is a figurative expression for removing what makes a human being's perfection, namely the soundness of the faculties, for the faces are the gathering places of the senses.

A threat does not require that the threatened thing occur. And in a hadith: "Does not he who raises his head before the imam fear that Allah will make his face the face of a donkey?"

The original meaning of obliteration is the removal of visible traces. Ka'b said:

Its breadth is a desert of effaced landmarks, unknown.

The term obliteration is also sometimes used figuratively for the nullification of the familiar properties of a thing, and from it comes the obliteration of hearts, i.e., the nullification of the traces of discernment and knowledge from them.

His saying ﴿and turn them back on their backs﴾ is a conjunction merely for sequence, not for causation; i.e., before both matters occur: the obliteration and the turning back upon their backs, i.e., the inversion of their heads backward. Although the obliteration here is figurative, and that is the apparent meaning, it is a warning of the loss of the prominence of the Jews in the lands of the Arabs, and their being cast into humiliation after they had been there mighty, possessors of wealth and means. Among them was al-Samaw'al before the mission, and among them was Abu Rafi', merchant of the people of the Hijaz, and among them was Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, chief of his region in the time of the Hijra.

The turning back upon their backs, on this interpretation, may be figurative, meaning retreat backward, i.e., their being driven to the evil destination; and it may be literal, meaning their being returned from where they came, i.e., their expulsion from the lands of the Arabs to al-Sham.

The fa' (then) on this interpretation is for both sequence and causation, and the statement is a warning, and the warning has been realized: Allah cast them into abasement, then the Prophet (ﷺ) expelled them, and Umar ibn al-Khattab expelled them to Adhruat.

[Page 80]

His saying ﴿or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾: by cursing is meant here disgrace, which is other than obliteration. So if obliteration is meant as transformation (maskh), then cursing is meant as abasement, and if obliteration is meant as abasement, then cursing is meant as transformation.

﴿The people of the Sabbath﴾ are those in His saying: ﴿And you had certainly known those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: "Be apes, despised and driven away."﴾ [al-Baqara: 65]. This has been discussed in Surat al-Baqara.

[Page 80]

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly fabricated a tremendous sin.﴾

It is possible that this sentence is connected to what precedes it, the threat to the Jews with punishment in this world. The discourse then aims to encourage the Jews toward Islam and to inform them that Allah would overlook them upon their coming to faith, even if the punishment of obliteration (ʿadhāb al-ṭamsh) were descending upon them. Accordingly, forgiveness (al-ghufrān) here means overlooking, in this world, the requital they deserve for the enormity of their disbelief and sins, that is, by lifting the punishment from them. The verse also contains a threat to the polytheists of a punishment of this world that will befall them, such that faith will not benefit them after the punishment has come down, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed and its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus [Yunus: 98]﴾, and so on. On this reading, the particle ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) is in the position of causation and cause, meaning: "Believe in the Qur'an before the punishment descends upon you, because Allah forgives what is less than associating others with Him." This is like His saying: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them [al-Anfal: 33]﴾, meaning, that He would not punish them with the punishment of this world. Then He said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them [al-Anfal: 34]﴾, meaning in this world, which is the punishment of hunger and the sword. And His saying: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings forth a visible smoke, enveloping the people; this is a painful punishment [al-Dukhan: 10]﴾, meaning the smoke of the year of famine among Quraysh. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief] [al-Dukhan: 15]﴾, ﴿On the day We will strike the greatest striking; indeed, We will take retribution [al-Dukhan: 16]﴾, meaning the striking of the Day of Badr.

Or the meaning of forgiveness may be leniency (al-tasāmuḥ), for Islam accepted from the People of the Two Scriptures entry under the protection (dhimma) of Islam without entering the religion of Islam itself, and that is the ruling of the jizya (poll tax). But it did not accept from the polytheists anything except faith, not the jizya, on account of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So kill the polytheists wherever you find them [al-Tawbah: 5]﴾, up to His saying: 

[Page 81]

﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go on their way [al-Tawbah: 5]﴾. And He said concerning the People of the Scripture: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and who do not prohibit what Allah and His Messenger have prohibited, and who do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled [al-Tawbah: 29]﴾.

It is also possible that the sentence is a fresh statement (mustaʾnafa), placed as an interjection (iʿtirāḍ) between the calamities and admonitions addressed to the People of the Scripture. In that case the particle ﴿إنَّ﴾ (inna) serves to emphasize the assertion, with the aim of removing the possibility of metaphor or exaggeration in the threat. This is either a preparation for what follows, to shock the hearer at the enormity of the crime of associating others with Allah, so that it serves as a preparation for condemning the state of those who preferred polytheism over faith, and to show the extent of amazement at their affair that comes later in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in idols and false deities, and say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe, in the way [al-Nisa: 51]﴾, meaning: how, then, would you be content with the state of one with whom Allah is not pleased? On this reading, forgiveness may be understood as worldly overlooking, and also as overlooking in the Hereafter in a general sense.

Or the verse may be a fresh teaching of rulings concerning the forgiveness of the sins of the disobedient. It begins with the muḥkam (the clear, unambiguous), which is His saying: ﴿does not forgive that He be associated with﴾, and is concluded with the mutashābih (the ambiguous), which is His saying: ﴿but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾. Thus forgiveness here is meant as overlooking in the Hereafter. Al-Qurtubi said: "This is among the mutashābih about which the scholars have spoken." He means that its apparent meaning implies several problematic matters:

First: that it implies Allah may forgive disbelief which is not association, such as the disbelief of the Jews.

Second: that He forgives the perpetrator of sins even if he does not repent.

Third: that He may not forgive the disbeliever after his faith, nor the sinner after his repentance, because He has entrusted forgiveness to will (mashīʾa), and will admits of both occurrence and non-occurrence. All three of these have been contradicted by abundant evidence, and the community has agreed on disregarding their apparent meaning, so the verse is among the mutashābih for all Muslims. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This verse is the decisive one in clarifying what appears to conflict among the verses of promise and threat. The summary of the matter is that people are of four categories: a disbeliever who dies in his disbelief, who is eternally in the Fire by consensus; a believer who is righteous, who never sinned and died in that state, who is certainly destined for Paradise by Allah's promise, by consensus; a penitent who died in his repentance, who according to the Ahl al-Sunna and the majority of the jurists of the community joins the righteous believer; and a sinner who died before repenting, and this is the locus of disagreement."

[Page 82]

The Murji'a said: he is in Paradise by his faith, and his misdeeds do not harm him, and they made all verses of threat specific to disbelievers and the verses of promise general to believers. The Mu'tazila said: if he is a person of a major sin, he is in the Fire without doubt. The Khawarij said: if he is a person of a major or minor sin, he is eternally in the Fire and has no faith, and they made all verses of promise specific to the righteous believer and the penitent believer, and made all verses of threat general to the disobedient, whether disbelievers or believers. The Ahl al-Sunna said: the verses of promise have an apparently general wording, but it is not valid to enforce all of them in their apparent sense, because of their conflict, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿None will enter it except the most wretched, who denied and turned away [al-Layl: 15-16]﴾, and His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then for him is the fire of Hell [al-Jinn: 23]﴾. Therefore it is necessary to say that the verses of promise are general in wording but specific in meaning: to the righteous believer, and to those whom Allah in His knowledge has decided to pardon without punishment among the disobedient. And the verses of threat are general in wording but specific in meaning: to the disbelievers, and to those whom Allah in His knowledge has decided to punish among the disobedient. The verse ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ removed the doubt, because His saying ﴿but He forgives what is less than that﴾ refutes the Mu'tazila, and His saying ﴿for whomever He wills﴾ refutes the Murji'a, indicating that forgiveness of what is less than association is for some people and not others. Perhaps he founded his speech on interpreting association (al-shirk) so as to include all disbelief, or he founded it on the view that the Jews committed association when they said: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians committed association when they said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah." This is the interpretation of al-Shafiʿi as reported by Fakhr al-Din, but it is a distant interpretation. Thus association has its meaning in the Sharia, and disbelief lower than it has its own meaning.

The Mu'tazila interpreted the verse in the way indicated in al-Kashshaf: that His saying ﴿for whomever He wills﴾ is a complement governed by both the negated ﴿does not forgive﴾ and the affirmed ﴿forgives﴾. The realization of his words is that the meaning would be: "Indeed, Allah does not forgive association for whomever He wills, and forgives what is less than association for whomever He wills." And the meaning of "does not forgive for whomever He wills" becomes that He does not will forgiveness for him, for if He willed to forgive him He would forgive him, because the will of Allah regarding what is possible is not prevented by anything, and it does not relate to the impossible. So when He said "does not forgive," we know that "whomever He wills" means "He does not will to forgive." Thus the speech falls under the category of kināya (metonymy), like the saying: "I will not find you doing such a thing," meaning: "Do not do it, so that I find you doing it." This interpretation is a clear artificiality (taʿassuf).

I suppose the interpretation of the Khawarij is close to this. As for the Murji'a, they interpreted it by what Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted from them: that the object of ﴿for whomever He wills﴾ is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿that He be associated with﴾, meaning: and He forgives what is less than association for whomever He wills faith, that is, for whoever believes. These are artificialities that force the Qur'an into the service of their doctrines.

In my view, this verse, if the intent is to inform about the states of forgiveness of sins, is a verse in which only the principal matter is stated, which is the grave nature of associating others with Allah, and everything else is left in a remarkably general form, in that all its forms are included in His saying ﴿for whomever He wills﴾, which implies forgiveness for an unspecified group and requital for an unspecified group. The reference for explaining this general matter is to the other evidences drawn from the Book and the Sunna. And if this verse had been revealed at the beginning of the mission, one could have said that the verses after it abrogated (naskh) what it contained. And we are not troubled by its being a statement, because it is a statement intended to convey a legal (taklīfī) ruling. Rather, it was revealed after most of the Qur'an, so it is necessarily the case that it looks to everything that preceded it. By this, all groups of Muslims are spared the artificiality in interpreting it, each according to what supports his school, and it becomes suitable for the interpretations of all. The reference in its interpretation is to the clarifying evidences. On this basis, it is necessary to understand association in a sense that includes Judaism and Christianity. Perhaps he considered in this the saying of Ibn ʿUmar concerning the prohibition of marrying a Jewish or Christian woman, that they are both mushrikāt (associators). He said: "What association is greater than calling a son to Allah?"

The texts of the Sharia are explicit regarding the difference in the concept of these two descriptions. That a group of Jews said "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians said "The Messiah is the son of Allah," does not necessitate making them associators, since they did not, along with that, ascribe to these two a divinity that shares with Allah, exalted is He. And the difference in legal rulings between the two types of disbelief is evidence that this term is not to be understood in the sense of the general concept of disbelief. Moreover, what benefit is there in this interpretation if some disbelievers do not hold the divinity of anything other than Allah, like the majority of the Jews?

All Muslims agree that repentance from disbelief, that is, faith, necessitates its forgiveness, whether it was disbelief of association or disbelief in Islam. There is no doubt about this, either by the promise of Allah according to the Ahl al-Sunna, or by rational obligation according to the Mu'tazila. They also agree that dying upon disbelief in an absolute sense is certainly not forgiven, either by the threat of Allah or by rational obligation. And they agree that a sinner who repents has his sin definitely forgiven, either by the promise of Allah or by rational obligation. They differ regarding a sinner who dies upon his sin without repenting, or who does not have good deeds sufficient to cover his sins. The Ahl al-Sunna said: he is punished but not eternally in the torment, by the explicit text of the Sharia, not by obligation; and this is the meaning of will (mashīʾa), for Allah has willed that, and has made known His will through the evidences of the Book and the Sunna.

[Page 84]

The Mu'tazila and the Khawarij said: he is in the Fire eternally by rational obligation. The Murji'a said: he is not punished in any case. All these categories are included in the general expression ﴿for whomever He wills﴾.

His saying: ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly fabricated a tremendous sin﴾ is an addition to the condemnation of the state of association. Al-iftirā' (fabrication) is a lie about which the liar has no excuse, because it is derived from al-fary, which is cutting the skin. This is like their use of the term al-ikhtilāq (fabrication) derived from al-khalq (creation), which is also cutting of the skin; and this was mentioned under His saying: ﴿He said: "Thus Allah creates what He wills" [Ali ʿImran: 47]﴾ in Surat Al ʿImran. And al-ithm al-ʿaẓīm (the tremendous sin) is an extremely grave transgression.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 4, verses 49–50:**

﴿Have you not seen those who attribute purity to themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged even as much as a fatil.﴾ ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah, and that is sufficient as a manifest sin.﴾

This is an expression of wonder at the state of the Jews, when they say: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 18), and say: ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew﴾ (al-Baqarah: 111), and similar baseless claims of their own excessive self-regard.

His saying ﴿Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾ is a refutation of their belief by affirming its opposite, which is that purification is a testimony from Allah, and that a person's declaring himself pure does not benefit anyone. In beginning the sentence with *bal* (بَلْ, "rather"), there is an explicit nullification of their self-purification. Those who declared themselves pure have no share in Allah's purification, and they are not among those whom Allah wills to purify. Had *bal* not been mentioned, and it had said "and Allah purifies whom He wills," they would have had a hope of being among those whom Allah has purified.

The meaning of ﴿and they will not be wronged even as much as a fatil﴾ is that Allah has not withheld from them what they deserve, and that Allah's purifying others than them is not considered an injustice to them, because Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way, and He does not wrong anyone.

*Al-fatil* (الفَتِيلُ) is like a thread in the split of a date-stone, and its use as a metaphor for a small amount has become widespread, since it is of no benefit and has no clear appearance.

[p. 85]

The word ﴿fatilan﴾ (فَتِيلًا) is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*, the object that repeats or restricts the verbal noun), because it carries the sense of comparison. The implied meaning is: "wronging" (*zulman*) "like the fatil," that is, in its measure, so the particle of comparison has been omitted. It is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ (al-Nisa': 40).

His saying ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾ makes their inventing of lies, because of the strong certainty of its occurrence, as if it were a visible matter that people see with their eyes, though it is in fact something heard and understood. The phrase ﴿and that is sufficient as a manifest sin﴾ is an expression of the utmost extent of sin, as is indicated by the construction *kafa bihi* (كَفى بِهِ) followed by "such-and-such." The discussion of *kafa* (كَفى, "is sufficient") has already been presented at His saying earlier: ﴿and sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ (al-Nisa': 79).

Ibn ʿAshur's commentary on Surah 4, verses 51–52:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a share of the Scripture? They believe in *jibt* and *taghut*, and they say of those who disbelieve, "These are better guided in the way than those who have believed." Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, and whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper.﴾

The wonder expressed about the Jews, ﴿those who were given a share of the Scripture﴾, is repeated, now with something more astonishing than their condition mentioned in His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a share of the Scripture, who purchase error?﴾ [An-Nisa: 44]. Their belief in *jibt* and *taghut*, and their declaring the polytheists correct, is a far remove from the foundations of their own law, by vast distances. The first of the rules of the Torah and the first of its Ten Words are: "You shall have no other gods before Me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image. You shall not bow down to them or serve them." The structure of ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a share of the Scripture﴾ was explained earlier, in Surah Al ʿImran.

*Jibt*: a word arabicized from Ethiopic (Habashi), meaning the devil and sorcery. Since the root *j-b-t* is unused (*muhmal*) in Arabic, it is necessary that this word be a loanword (*dakhil*). It has been said that its origin is *jibs*, meaning that which contains no good. The *sin* was then changed to *ta'*, as it was changed in the verse of ʿIlbaʾ ibn Arqam:

"O may Allah curse the sons of al-Saʿlat, ʿAmr ibn Yarbuʿ, the worst of the people,
They are neither chaste nor shrewd."

That is, "the worst of people, and not shrewd." Similarly, they said *al-jatt* with the meaning of *al-jass* (touching).

[Page 87 continues below the marker]

*Taghut*: the idols. This is how the majority of scholars explained it here, and it is transmitted from Malik ibn Anas. It is a noun that applies to both the singular and the plural: one says *taghut* for an idol and *taghut* for idols, so it is like *tifl* and *fulk*. Perhaps the constant pairing of this word with the definite article of genus (*lam al-jins*) is what permitted its use for both singular and plural, like *al-kitab* and *al-kutub*. Then, when this became widespread, they extended its use even in the state of being stripped of the article. The Exalted said: ﴿They desire to seek judgment before the *taghut*, while they were commanded to reject it﴾ [An-Nisa: 60], where He used it in the singular. He also said: ﴿And those who avoid the *taghut* from worshipping it﴾ [Az-Zumar: 17], and: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the *taghut*; they bring them out﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 257], and so on.

This noun is derived from *taghā yaṭghū*, meaning to become great and exalted. Its original form is a verbal noun on the pattern *faʿalūt*, for intensification, like *rahabūt*, *malakūt*, *rahamūt*, and *jabarūt*. Its original form was *ṭaghwūt*, and a metathesis (*qalb makānī*) occurred by moving the third radical before the second, so it became *ṭawaghūt*, on the pattern *falaʿūt*. The purpose of this metathesis is to make possible the substitution of the *waw* by an *alif* when it is vocalized and the letter before it is open. They sometimes transpose the letters of a word so that substitution becomes possible, as they transposed *arʾām*, the plural of *rīm*, into *ārām*, so that the second hamza, which is unvocalized, could be substituted by an *alif* after the first, which is open. They sometimes treat this noun as if it were singular and form its broken plural as *ṭawāghīt*, on the pattern *faʿālīl*. A hadith has been transmitted: "Do not swear by the *ṭawāghīt*." And in the words of Ibn al-Musayyab in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: "The *baḥīrah* is the animal whose milk is withheld for the *ṭawāghīt*."

The term *taghut* may also be applied to the great leaders of the polytheists, such as the soothsayer (*kāhin*), because they venerate him on account of their idols, as will come in His words: ﴿They desire to seek judgment before the *taghut*﴾ [An-Nisa: 60] in this same surah.

The verse alludes to what occurred from some of the Jews, among whom were Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab. After the Battle of Uhud they hoped to work toward the extermination of the Muslims, so they went out to Mecca to form an alliance with the polytheists for fighting the Muslims. Kaʿb stayed with Abu Sufyan, and the rest of them stayed in the houses of Quraysh. The polytheists said to them: "You are People of the Book, and perhaps you are closer to Muhammad and his followers than we are, so we do not trust your deception." They said to them: "The worship of idols is more pleasing to Allah than what Muhammad calls to, and you are more rightly guided in the way." The polytheists said to them: "Then prostrate to our gods, so that we may be reassured by you." So they did, and this verse was revealed as an announcement from Allah to His Messenger of what the Jews and the people of Mecca had plotted.

The *lām* in His words ﴿to those who disbelieve﴾ is the *lām* of cause (*lām al-ʿillah*), meaning: they say on account of those who disbelieve, and it is not the *lām* of transitivity for the verb of saying. By "those who disbelieve" is meant the polytheists of Mecca, and that is the Qur'an's usage of the attribute of disbelief to mean polytheism.

[Page 87 marker is followed by the continuation above.]

The reference in His words ﴿these are more rightly guided﴾ is to those who disbelieve. This is a reporting of the statement by its meaning, because they only said: "You are more rightly guided than Muhammad and his companions." Or, some Jews said to others concerning the people of Mecca, "These are more rightly guided," that is, when they conferred privately and fabricated what they would say. Likewise His words ﴿of those who have believed﴾ are a reporting of their statement by its meaning, as a declaration of their error, because they only said: "These are more rightly guided than Muhammad and his followers." Since Muhammad and his followers are believers, it follows from their statement that the polytheists are more rightly guided than the believers. This is the place of the wonder.

He followed the wonder with His words ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed.﴾ The placement of the demonstrative here is at the height of elegance, because whoever reaches this degree in the description of his condition becomes as if he were witnessed. So after His words "Have you not seen," it was fitting that this group, claimed to be visible, be pointed to with "those." The demonstrative also contains an alert that those pointed to deserve what will be mentioned of the judgment, because of what has preceded concerning their conditions.

The relative clause in His words ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾ does not imply that the addressees know these people to be characterized by it, in the way that one known for it is characterized. Rather, the intended meaning is that these are the ones: if you hear of a people whom Allah has cursed, then they are them.

It is possible that the Muslims already knew that the Jews were cursed, so the purpose of the relative clause is what is joined to it by His words ﴿and whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper.﴾ The relative construction under both possibilities contains an allusion to the reason for the implicit report about them, that they have no helper, because Allah has cursed them, and whomever Allah curses has no helper. This is the counterpart of His words concerning the Muslims: ﴿And Allah knows best your enemies, and sufficient is Allah as a protector, and sufficient is Allah as a helper﴾ [An-Nisa: 45].

"O may Allah curse the sons of al-Saʿlat, ʿAmr ibn Yarbuʿ, the worst of the people,
They are neither chaste nor shrewd."

That is, "the worst of people, and not shrewd." Similarly, they said *al-jatt* with the meaning of *al-jass* (touching).

[Page 87 continues below the marker]

*Taghut*: the idols. This is how the majority of scholars explained it here, and it is transmitted from Malik ibn Anas. It is a noun that applies to both the singular and the plural: one says *taghut* for an idol and *taghut* for idols, so it is like *tifl* and *fulk*. Perhaps the constant pairing of this word with the definite article of genus (*lam al-jins*) is what permitted its use for both singular and plural, like *al-kitab* and *al-kutub*. Then, when this became widespread, they extended its use even in the state of being stripped of the article. The Exalted said: ﴿They desire to seek judgment before the *taghut*, while they were commanded to reject it﴾ [An-Nisa: 60], where He used it in the singular. He also said: ﴿And those who avoid the *taghut* from worshipping it﴾ [Az-Zumar: 17], and: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the *taghut*; they bring them out﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 257], and so on.

This noun is derived from *taghā yaṭghū*, meaning to become great and exalted. Its original form is a verbal noun on the pattern *faʿalūt*, for intensification, like *rahabūt*, *malakūt*, *rahamūt*, and *jabarūt*. Its original form was *ṭaghwūt*, and a metathesis (*qalb makānī*) occurred by moving the third radical before the second, so it became *ṭawaghūt*, on the pattern *falaʿūt*. The purpose of this metathesis is to make possible the substitution of the *waw* by an *alif* when it is vocalized and the letter before it is open. They sometimes transpose the letters of a word so that substitution becomes possible, as they transposed *arʾām*, the plural of *rīm*, into *ārām*, so that the second hamza, which is unvocalized, could be substituted by an *alif* after the first, which is open. They sometimes treat this noun as if it were singular and form its broken plural as *ṭawāghīt*, on the pattern *faʿālīl*. A hadith has been transmitted: "Do not swear by the *ṭawāghīt*." And in the words of Ibn al-Musayyab in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: "The *baḥīrah* is the animal whose milk is withheld for the *ṭawāghīt*."

The term *taghut* may also be applied to the great leaders of the polytheists, such as the soothsayer (*kāhin*), because they venerate him on account of their idols, as will come in His words: ﴿They desire to seek judgment before the *taghut*﴾ [An-Nisa: 60] in this same surah.

The verse alludes to what occurred from some of the Jews, among whom were Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab. After the Battle of Uhud they hoped to work toward the extermination of the Muslims, so they went out to Mecca to form an alliance with the polytheists for fighting the Muslims. Kaʿb stayed with Abu Sufyan, and the rest of them stayed in the houses of Quraysh. The polytheists said to them: "You are People of the Book, and perhaps you are closer to Muhammad and his followers than we are, so we do not trust your deception." They said to them: "The worship of idols is more pleasing to Allah than what Muhammad calls to, and you are more rightly guided in the way." The polytheists said to them: "Then prostrate to our gods, so that we may be reassured by you." So they did, and this verse was revealed as an announcement from Allah to His Messenger of what the Jews and the people of Mecca had plotted.

The *lām* in His words ﴿to those who disbelieve﴾ is the *lām* of cause (*lām al-ʿillah*), meaning: they say on account of those who disbelieve, and it is not the *lām* of transitivity for the verb of saying. By "those who disbelieve" is meant the polytheists of Mecca, and that is the Qur'an's usage of the attribute of disbelief to mean polytheism.

[Page 87 marker is followed by the continuation above.]

The reference in His words ﴿these are more rightly guided﴾ is to those who disbelieve. This is a reporting of the statement by its meaning, because they only said: "You are more rightly guided than Muhammad and his companions." Or, some Jews said to others concerning the people of Mecca, "These are more rightly guided," that is, when they conferred privately and fabricated what they would say. Likewise His words ﴿of those who have believed﴾ are a reporting of their statement by its meaning, as a declaration of their error, because they only said: "These are more rightly guided than Muhammad and his followers." Since Muhammad and his followers are believers, it follows from their statement that the polytheists are more rightly guided than the believers. This is the place of the wonder.

He followed the wonder with His words ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed.﴾ The placement of the demonstrative here is at the height of elegance, because whoever reaches this degree in the description of his condition becomes as if he were witnessed. So after His words "Have you not seen," it was fitting that this group, claimed to be visible, be pointed to with "those." The demonstrative also contains an alert that those pointed to deserve what will be mentioned of the judgment, because of what has preceded concerning their conditions.

The relative clause in His words ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾ does not imply that the addressees know these people to be characterized by it, in the way that one known for it is characterized. Rather, the intended meaning is that these are the ones: if you hear of a people whom Allah has cursed, then they are them.

It is possible that the Muslims already knew that the Jews were cursed, so the purpose of the relative clause is what is joined to it by His words ﴿and whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper.﴾ The relative construction under both possibilities contains an allusion to the reason for the implicit report about them, that they have no helper, because Allah has cursed them, and whomever Allah curses has no helper. This is the counterpart of His words concerning the Muslims: ﴿And Allah knows best your enemies, and sufficient is Allah as a protector, and sufficient is Allah as a helper﴾ [An-Nisa: 45].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 53–55:

Page 88
﴿Or do they have a share in the kingdom? Then they would not give the people even a speck (naqir).﴾ ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? We had already given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.﴾ ﴿Among them were those who believed in him, and among them were those who turned away from him. Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.﴾

(Am) is for the transitional (intiqali) idrab (change of subject), and it indicates an omitted interrogative hamza after it, i.e.: "Rather, do they have a share in the kingdom, so that they do not give the people a speck?"

The interrogation is denunciatory (inkari), and its ruling is the ruling of negation. The conjunction with the fa' is upon the clause "they have a share," and likewise "idhan" (then) is a response (jaza') to the clause "they have a share." The interrogation is understood as entering upon the whole clause together with its response, because their giving the people a speck is negated on the assumption that the kingdom is established for them, not on the assumption that it is negated. This statement is a mockery of them in their expectation that the kingdom of Israel would return to them, and a branding of them with stinginess, which does not help anyone who hopes for kingship. As Abu al-Fath al-Busti said:

If a king is not generous, leave him, for his dynasty is passing away.
Their miserliness and stinginess are well known and widely recognized.
The naqir is a mark on the date-pit resembling a circle, and it is proverbially used for something very small.

For this reason, this statement is followed by His words: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾

The interrogation implied after (am) here is a denunciation of their envy, and it does not serve to negate envy, because envy has occurred. By "the people" is meant the Prophet (ﷺ), and the bounty is prophethood; or it is meant the Prophet and the believers, and the bounty is guidance and faith.

His words: ﴿We had already given the family of Abraham the Book﴾ are a conjunction upon something implied from the meaning of the denunciatory interrogation, and a justification for the denunciation against them, i.e.: there is no novelty in what they envy, since We have given the family of Abraham the Book, wisdom and kingdom.

The family of Abraham (Al Ibrahim) are his sons, his offspring and his descendants, and this is included in the ruling, because they were given it only on account of his honour with Allah and Allah's promise to him of it. The definition of "the Book" is the definition of genus, so it applies to the many, and it includes the scrolls of Abraham, the scrolls of Moses, and what was revealed after that. Wisdom is prophethood. Kingdom is what Allah promised Abraham, that He would give it to his descendants, and what Allah gave to David, Solomon and the kings of Israel. The pronoun in "minhum" may refer to what the pronoun in "yahsudun" refers to. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "the people," meant as Muhammad (ﷺ): i.e., among those who were given a share of the Book, some believed in Muhammad and some turned away. The branching in His words "minhum" according to this interpretation arises from His words: ﴿Or do they envy the people﴾. It is also possible that the pronoun in "minhum" refers to the family of Abraham, and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to Abraham, i.e.: We had given them what has been mentioned. Among "his family" are those who believed in him, and among them are those who disbelieved, like his father Azar and the wife of his nephew Lot. That is, the denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) by the Jews is no more astonishing than that: ﴿the practice of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [al-Isra: 77], so that the argument against them is established on both matters, in refuting the basis of their denial, by affirming that the coming of prophethood is no novelty, and that Muhammad is of the family of Abraham, so his sending is no more astonishing than the sending of Moses. In reminding them that this is the practice of the prophets, so that they do not regard their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) as a flaw in his prophethood, since no messenger is known whose community unanimously affirmed him from Abraham onward.

His words: ﴿Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire﴾ are a threat and warning to those who believe in the idol (jibt) and the false deity (taghut). The explanation of this construction has already been given in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is sufficient as a protector﴾ [an-Nisa: 45] earlier in this surah.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 56–57:**

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs – We will surely expose them to a Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. For them therein are purified spouses, and We will admit them to a shade, deep and extended.﴾ This is a threat and a warning addressed to all the disbelievers. It is more general than what precedes it, so it has the ruling of the concluding statement (al-tadhyil, a closing sentence that generalizes the preceding message), and for this reason it is separated from what came before. Al-isla' (causing to be exposed to fire) is the verbal noun of "asla-hu," and it is said: "salah-u salyan," meaning roasting the meat over the fire.

Page 90

The discussion of (ṣalā) has already been covered in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they will burn in a blaze﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], and His words: ﴿So We will expose him to a Fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 30], in this surah. The discussion of (sawfa) has also been covered in the last verse. (Nusliihim), with a damma on the nun, is from al-isla'. (Nadajat) means it reached its completion of cooking. It is said: "nadija al-shiwa'" when the roasted meat reaches the point of being roasted, and it is said: "nadija al-tabikh" when the cooked dish reaches the point of being cooked. The meaning is: whenever their skins are burned, so that no life or sensation remains in them, (badaln-ahum) – that is, We replace them with other skins. Substitution (al-tabdil) requires difference, as was explained previously in His words in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. Therefore His words "other (ghayra-ha)" are an emphasis on what the verb of substitution already indicates. "Nāran" is in the accusative as a second object, because it belongs to the pattern of "a'ṭā" (to give).

His words: ﴿so that they may taste the punishment﴾ are a causal clause (ta'lil) explaining His words ﴿We replaced them﴾, because the skin is what conveys the sensation of punishment to the soul according to Allah's customary creation. Had the skin not been replaced after it was burned, the torment of the Fire would not reach the soul. The replacement of the skin while the person's own soul remains does not contradict justice, because the skin is merely the means of delivering the punishment and is not itself the intended object of torment. Moreover, it arises from the first skin, just as the re-creation of bodies on the Day of Gathering after they have decayed does not mean they are different people from those who merited reward and punishment. For when the souls that acquired good and evil are placed in them, they become the same. This is especially so when their re-creation comes from a growth from the coccyx (a'jaz al-adhnab, the small bone at the base of the spine), as reported in the tradition (athar), because that which arises from a thing is part of it, like the palm tree from its seed.

His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ are in the position of a causal explanation for what precedes. Might (al-'izza) accounts for the completeness of power in punishing the one who dares against Allah, and wisdom (al-hikma) accounts for that specific manner of exposing them to the Fire.

His words: ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ are mentioned here for contrast and to increase the rage of the disbelievers. From the delights of the Hereafter, He mentioned only the pleasure of the gardens and the righteous spouses, because these two are the most beloved of the familiar pleasures to the listeners. A righteous wife is the most pleasing thing to a person, and the gardens are the place of bliss and the delight of sight.

His words: ﴿and We will admit them to a shade, deep and extended﴾ are part of the excellences of the gardens, because shade exists only with the sun. This is the beauty of the gardens and the pleasure of bliss, seeing the light while its heat is absent. It is described as (zalil) with a derived description from the name of the described thing, to indicate that it has reached the utmost limit in its kind. Such descriptions come in the pattern (fa'il), as here, and as in the saying "dā'un dawiyyun" (a deep disease). They also come in the pattern (af'al), such as the saying "laylun alyal" (a very dark night) and "yawmun aywam" (a very windy day), and they come in the pattern (fa'il), such as the saying "shi'run sha'ir" (very poetic poetry) and "naṣabun naṣib" (a very fixed standing stone).
