**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 4, verse 58 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent is what God admonishes you with. Indeed, God is ever Hearing, Seeing.﴾

This is an initial resumptive statement (istinaf ibtida'i), intended to elaborate on the rules of justice, judgment, and the order of obedience. These are among the major legislative aims that this surah contains. It is not necessary to seek a connection (munasabah) between it and what precedes it, since munasabah (the thematic link between passages) is simply the transition from one set of legal rulings to another set on different aims. Here, however, there is a connection. The digression about the People of the Book, their distortion of words from their places, their twisting of their tongues with expressions that carry insult, their fabrication of lies against God, and their envy by denying God's favour that He gave to the Messenger and the believers, all of this involves betrayal of the trust of religion, knowledge, truth, and blessing. These are moral trusts (amanat ma'nawiyyah). So it was fitting to follow this with the command to discharge the concrete trust to its people, and to move from there to this legislation.

The clause ﴿Indeed, God commands you﴾ is explicit in command and obligation, just as the prohibition is explicit in the saying in the hadith: "Indeed God forbids you to swear by your fathers." The emphasis with "indeed" here serves only to draw attention to the statement, since it is evident that such a statement does not admit doubt and so needs no emphasis. It is a report about bringing something into being, not about its existence, so it is equivalent to a performative utterance (insha').

The address is to everyone who is fit to receive this address and to act upon it, from every person entrusted with anything, and from everyone who has assumed judgment between people regarding rights.

Al-ada' (discharging, rendering) is in its real sense the handing over of a thing to one who deserves it. It is said: "adda ilayhi kadha," meaning he delivered and handed it over to him, and from this comes the payment of a debt (ada' al-dayn). It has already been mentioned in the words of God, ﴿Of whom, if you entrust him with a qintar, he will return it to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], in Surah Al 'Imran. [p. 92] The original form of "adda" is that it should be the doubled form of "adda" (from the root meaning to convey), in the sense of "awsala" (to cause to arrive). However, they neglected the undoubled "adda" and dispensed with it in favour of the doubled form.

Al-ada' is used metaphorically for acknowledging and fulfilling something. On this basis, the discharge of a trust is applied to speaking the truth, acknowledging it, and conveying knowledge and the law as it is due. The intended meaning here is the first of the two meanings. The ruling on the other meaning, or on one of them, is known by analogy to it, an analogy from the lesser to the greater (qiyas al-adwan).

Al-amanah (trust) is the thing that its owner places with a person to keep until he asks for it back. This has already been discussed at the words of God, ﴿Let him who has been entrusted discharge his trust﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], in Surah al-Baqarah.

Al-amanah is also used metaphorically for whatever a responsible person must convey to its owners and rightful recipients, whether special or general, such as religion, knowledge, covenants, protection of a neighbour, sincere counsel, and the like. Its opposite is betrayal (khiyanah), in both senses. The command is for obligation.

The word "amanat" (trusts) is one of the forms of generality. For this reason, the majority of scholars said regarding a person who has entrusted a man with something, while the trustee has a right against the one who holds the trust and that person denies it to him: it is not permissible for him to take the trust in exchange for his right, because that is betrayal. Malik prohibited it in al-Mudawwanah. But from Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam: it is permissible for him to deny him the equivalent of what he is owed. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i.

Al-Tabari said, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and Makhul, that the addressees are the rulers of affairs, whom He commanded to render trusts to their owners. It was also said that the verse was revealed concerning the matter of 'Uthman ibn Talha ibn Abi Talha.

The people of a trust (ahl al-amanah) are those who deserve it. It is said: "ahl al-dar," meaning its owners. Al-Wahidi mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul, with a weak chain, that the verse was revealed on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, when 'Uthman ibn Talha ibn Abi Talha al-'Abdari al-Hajabi handed the key of the Ka'bah to the Prophet (ﷺ). The custodianship (sidanah) of the Ka'bah was in his hand, and he was from the Banu 'Abd al-Dar, among whom the custodianship was held. Then al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib asked the Messenger of God to give him the custodianship of the Ka'bah, to combine it with the provision of water (siqayah), which was in his hand and belonged to the Banu Hashim. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) called 'Uthman ibn Talha and his cousin Shayba ibn 'Uthman ibn Abi Talha, gave them the key of the Ka'bah, and recited this verse. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I had not heard it from him before that." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Uthman ibn Talha: "Take it, as a perpetual and inherited possession; none will take it from you except a wrongdoer." The Prophet's (ﷺ) taking the key of the Ka'bah from 'Uthman ibn Talha was not a taking by seizure. Rather, he took it while awaiting revelation concerning the matter, because the key being in the hand of 'Uthman ibn Talha was an established state from before Islam, and Islam did not change his possession of it. When the verse was revealed, the right of the Banu 'Abd al-Dar in it was confirmed by the ruling of Islam. So the custodianship of the Ka'bah remained with the Banu 'Abd al-Dar, and 'Uthman ibn Talha yielded it to his cousin Shayba ibn 'Uthman. Custodianship had been among the offices of the Quraysh in the pre-Islamic period, and the Prophet (ﷺ) abolished part of it in his sermon on the day of the Conquest or during the Farewell Pilgrimage, except for the provision of water and the custodianship.

So the use of the name "amanah" in the verse is literal, because 'Uthman handed the key of the Ka'bah to the Prophet (ﷺ) without giving up his right.

At that point, al-ada' is used in its literal meaning, because the right here is a concrete thing that can actually be delivered to those who deserve it. The verse therefore commands all kinds of delivery and fulfilment, and among these is the return of concrete trusts. So there is no metaphor in the word "tu'addu" (render).

His words ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾: "an tahkumu" (to judge) is coordinated (ataf) upon "an tu'addu" (to render), and the adverbial phrase ("bayna al-nas," between people) separates the conjunction from the conjoined element. This is permissible, as in His words, ﴿And in the Hereafter, good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201]. Likewise in coordinating verbs on the sound reading, as in ﴿And you build fortresses so that you may live forever? And when you seize, you seize as tyrants﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 129].

Al-hukm (judgment) is the verbal noun of "hakama bayn al-mutanazi'ayn," meaning he took care to show which of the two was in the right and which in the wrong, or to show the truth to one of them and declare it. It is derived from al-hukm, with a fatha on the ha', which means restraining from doing what is not fitting. From this comes the name "hakamah" for the bridle, the iron piece placed in a horse's mouth. It is said: "ahkim fulanan," meaning restrain him.

Al-'adl (justice) is the opposite of injustice (jawr). Linguistically it means equalization. It is said: "'adala kadha bi-kadha," meaning he made it equal to it and balanced it with it in equality. [God says]: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve set up equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. Then its use became common for delivering the right to its people and for repelling the transgressor against the right from its rightful holder. This usage arose from what people were accustomed to: that injustice comes from tyrants who do not consider themselves equal to the general population. They, if they wish, act justly and fairly, and if they wish, they oppress and wrong. Labid said:

*"And one who divides, giving the clan its due, and one who withholds from its rights, crushing them."*

So the word "justice," which is equalization, is applied to a beneficial equalization by which goodness and security are achieved. This is the removal of a thing from the hand of the transgressor, because equalization appears in it between the disputants. It is therefore a predominant metonymy (kinayah ghalibah). Its manifestation is judgment in favour of the rights-holder, taking his right from the one who wronged him. For this reason God says here, ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾. Then the usage was widened until it came to be applied to conveying the right to its owner even where there was no transgression or dispute.

Justice is equality among people, or among the members of a community, in determining things for their rightful holders, and in enabling every holder of a right to obtain his right without delay. It is therefore equality in the entitlement to things, and in the means of placing them in the hands of their owners. The first is justice in determining rights, and the second is justice in execution. Justice is not in distributing things equally among people without entitlement.

Justice is thus a mean between two extremes: excess in giving the rights-holder his right, that is, giving him more than his right, and deficiency in it, that is, diminishing his right. Both extremes are called injustice (jawr). Likewise, excess and deficiency in executing the giving, by bringing it forward before its time, such as giving property into the hand of a foolish person, or delaying it, such as keeping property in the hand of a guardian after maturity. For this reason God says, ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ [al-Nisa': 5], to His words ﴿But if you perceive in them maturity, then hand over to them their property﴾ [al-Nisa': 6]. So justice enters into all transactions. It is good by nature, because just as it restrains the transgressor from his transgression, it also restrains others from transgressing against him, as God says: ﴿You do not wrong, nor are you wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279].

[p. 95] Since justice, considered in these respects, is subject to mistaken understandings in its definition, it became necessary to enact laws to regulate it according to the perceptions of the legislators and the terms of the one who legislates for them. Yet most of these laws have not been free from distortion of the reality of justice in some cases.

Some laws were founded on the impulse of anger and self-interest, and so they contained grave errors, such as the laws that revolutionaries impose out of anger against those who held authority before them. Some laws branch from imaginations and illusions, such as the laws of the people of the Jahiliyyah and of the ancient idolatrous nations.

We find that the laws enacted by the wise were more effective in realizing the benefits of justice, such as the laws of Athens and Sparta. The highest laws are the divine legislations, because of their suitability to the circumstances of those for whom they were enacted. The greatest of them is the Shari'ah of Islam, because it is founded on pure or predominant benefit, turns away from the desires of nations and from corrupt customs, is not concerned with self-interest and desire or with customs of corruption, and is not founded on the interests of a particular tribe or a particular land, but on the interests of the human species, its refinement, and its guidance to the right path. For this reason, the righteous leaders have never ceased to record the statement of rights in order to preserve justice as far as possible, especially the divine legislations.

God says: ﴿We have sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance, that people may uphold justice﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], meaning justice. Among these rulings are those stated explicitly upon the tongue of the Messenger of humanity, and among them are those deduced by the scholars of that Shari'ah. These are incorporated into it and attached to it.

The command to justice has been restricted to the situation of undertaking judgment between people, whereas the command to return trusts to their owners has been stated without restriction. This is because every person may, at some point, come to hold a trust belonging to another, especially if the meaning of "trusts" is generalized to include whatever a person is obliged to convey to its rightful recipient, as has already been mentioned. Justice, by contrast, is commanded only of those who rule and judge between people, and not everyone is fit to assume that role. This is the reason behind His words, ﴿And when you judge between people﴾.

Al-Fakhr [al-Razi] said: His words ﴿And when you judge﴾ are as if they explicitly state that it is not for all people to begin judging, but that this belongs to some of them. The verse is therefore general as to the manner by which a person becomes a judge. Since the proofs establish that the community necessarily needs an imam, and that he appoints judges and governors, these proofs apply to this verse.

[p. 96] The clause ﴿Indeed, excellent is what God admonishes you with﴾ stands in the position of exhortation to comply with the command, so it functions as a justification. The initial "indeed" at the beginning of the clause dispenses with the need for the particle of consequence (fa'), as is the case when "inna" comes for emphasis of attention rather than for affirmation.

"Ni'imma" is originally "ni'ma ma" (excellent is what). "Ni'ma" was compounded with "ma" after the vowel of the first mim was dropped and the two were treated as a single word. The two mims were assimilated, and the unvocalized ayn was given a kasra to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized consonants.

Translation note: Ibn 'Ashur's "the excellence (ni'ima) of what" in this passage is rendered above as "excellent is what," following the grammatical explanation he gives.

Here is the translation:

And (mā) — the grammarians permitted that it be a relative pronoun (ismun mawsūl), or a qualified indefinite noun (nakira mawṣūfa), or a complete indefinite noun (nakira tāmma). The clause that follows (mā) proceeds in accordance with what suits the meaning of (mā). It has also been said that (mā) is a superfluous (zā'ida) particle that is "restrictive" (kāffa), stopping (nِʿma) from governing (the "ʿamal" of) the verb.

Al-waʿẓ (admonition) is reminding and advising, and it may also include rebuke and warning.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾ means: knowing of what you do and what you say. This is both good news and a warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 59 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and most suitable in outcome.﴾

When Allah commanded the Ummah to judge with justice, He followed that with addressing them with the command to obey their rulers, the holders of authority over them, because obedience to them is the manifestation of the enforcement of the justice by which their rulers judge. Obedience to the Messenger includes respecting the justice that is prescribed for them and implementing it, and obedience to the holders of authority is the implementation of justice. By this sequence, He indicated that the obedience commanded is obedience in what is right (al-ma'ruf). For this reason 'Ali said: "It is a duty upon the Imam to judge with justice and to render the trust, and when he does that, it is a duty upon the subjects to listen and obey."

Allah commanded obedience to Allah and His Messenger, and this means obedience to the Shari'a (the sacred law), for Allah is the One who sent down the Shari'a, and His Messenger is the one who conveys it and who judges by it in his presence.

[Page 97]

The verb "obey" is repeated with "obey the Messenger" even though the conjunction would suffice without repeating it, in order to show concern for achieving obedience to the Messenger, so that it would be of a higher rank than obedience to those in authority, and to alert to the obligation of obeying him in what he commands, even if his command is not accompanied by indications that he is conveying revelation. This prevents the listener from supposing that obedience to the Messenger that is commanded refers only to obeying Allah in what he conveys from Allah, and not what he commands in matters other than legislation, since complying with all his commands is good. Do you not see that the Prophet ﷺ called Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla while he was praying, and he did not answer him. When he finished his prayer, he came to him and said: "What prevented you from answering me?" He said: "I was praying." He said: "Did not Allah say: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾ [al-Anfal 8:24]?"

For this reason, when they did not know the Messenger's purpose in his command, they would sometimes ask him: "Is it a command of legislation, or is it opinion and judgment?" Just as al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir said to him on the Day of Badr when the army of the Muslims had descended: "Is this a place Allah caused you to alight, which we are not permitted to pass beyond, or is it opinion, war and strategy?" He said: "Rather, it is opinion, war and strategy." The hadith continues.

When he spoke to Barira about returning to her husband Mughith after she had been freed, she said to him: "Are you commanding, O Messenger of Allah, or are you interceding?" He said: "Rather, I am interceding." She said: "I will not remain with him."

For this reason, the verb "refer it" is not repeated in His saying "and the Messenger", because that [reference] concerns adjudication among them, and adjudication is only for taking up the judgment of Allah in His Law. For this reason we do not find repetition of the verb of obedience in similar verses in which those in authority are not conjoined, such as His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear﴾ [al-Anfal 8:20], and His saying: ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute, lest you lose courage﴾ [al-Anfal 8:46], and: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger and fears Allah and is conscious of Him, those are the attainers of success﴾ [al-Nur 24:52].

Because obedience to the Messenger is equal to obedience to Allah, since the Messenger is the one who conveys from Allah, so the command of Allah is received only from him, and he is the one who executes the command of Allah himself. Thus his obedience is obedience of reception (taláqqī) and obedience of compliance (imtithāl), since he is both conveyer and executor. By contrast, those in authority are executors of what the Messenger has conveyed, so their obedience is obedience of compliance only. For this reason, when he commanded them with an action in matters other than legislation, they would ask him: "Is this a command or an opinion and suggestion?" For when he said to the people who pollinated the palm trees: "If you did not do it, it would be better," [they did not do it].

His saying "those in authority" means their possessors, that is, those who hold authority and are entrusted with it. Al-amr (the matter) is the affair, that is, what is of concern in circumstances and affairs. So those in authority among the Ummah and among the people are those to whom people attribute the management of their affairs and on whom they rely in that, so that the matter becomes as if it were among their distinctive features. For this reason they are called "possessors of the matter" and "those in authority," and the opposite is said: "He has no share of the matter."

When Allah commanded obedience to those in authority, we know that those in authority, in the view of the Shari'a, are a specific group, and they are the exemplars of the Ummah and its trustees. So we know that this attribute is established for them by legitimate means, since the affairs of Islam do not go outside the legal sphere.

The means by which this attribute is established for them is either the appointment (wilāya) assigned to them by the Caliph or the like, or by the communities of Muslims if they have no sultan, or the qualities of perfection that make them the object of the Ummah's emulation, which are Islam, knowledge and justice. So scholars who are just are among those in authority by their very nature, because the attribute of knowledge does not require appointment. Rather, it is an attribute established in its possessors, who are famous among the Ummah for it, because of what has been tested of their knowledge and their mastery in giving legal opinions (fatwa) and teaching. Malik said: "Those in authority are the People of the Qur'an and knowledge," meaning the people of knowledge of the Qur'an and of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning).

So those in authority here are everyone other than the Messenger, from the Caliph down to the wali al-ḥisba (the market inspector), and from military commanders to the jurists of the Companions and the mujtahids, and to the people of knowledge in later times. Those in authority are also those who are called ahl al-ḥall wa al-'aqd (the people who loosen and bind), that is, those whose consensus and decisions are binding.

The command to this came after the command to justice and the rendering of trusts, because these two matters are the foundation of the order of the Ummah, which is the sincere counsel of the rulers and the subjects, and the spread of trust among them.

Since events do not escape the occurrence of disagreement among the subjects and between them and those who are in charge of their affairs, Allah guided them to the method of settling disputes: referring them to Allah and to the Messenger. The meaning of referring to Allah is referring to His Book, as indicated by His saying in a similar context: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down"﴾ [al-Nisa 4:61].

The meaning of referring to the Messenger is submitting matters to him during his life and presence, as indicated by His saying in a similar context: ﴿and to the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa 4:61]. As for after his death or in his absence, referring to him means returning to his sayings and actions and following his Sunnah.

Abu Dawud related from Abu Rafi', from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Let me not find any one of you reclining on his couch, to whom a matter comes from what I have commanded or forbidden, and he says: 'We do not know; whatever we find in the Book of Allah, we follow it.'"

In another narration from al-'Irbad ibn Sariya, that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ giving a sermon saying: "Does one of you suppose, while reclining on his couch, that Allah has not forbidden anything except what is in this Qur'an? Indeed, by Allah, I have commanded, admonished and forbidden things that are like the Qur'an or more." It was also related by al-Tirmidhi from the hadith of al-Miqdam. Presenting events to the standard of his conduct and the explicit part of the Sunnah is part of this.

Al-tanāzu' (dispute) is intense disagreement. It is a reciprocal form derived from al-nazʿ, meaning taking. Al-A'sha said:

"I contended with them over the shoots of basil, reclining, and over wine, sharp, its strainer moist."

He applied the word tanāzu' to intense disagreement by way of metaphor (isti'āra), because intense disagreement resembles the pulling between two persons, and this usage became so common that it equaled the literal sense. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and do not dispute, lest you lose courage﴾ [al-Anfal 8:46], and ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves and concealed their private counsel﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:62].

The pronoun in "you disagree" refers to those who have believed, so it includes everyone among whom dispute is possible, that is, everyone other than the Messenger, since believers do not dispute with him. It includes the dispute of the general public among themselves, the dispute of those in authority among themselves, such as the dispute of the ministers with the amir or among themselves, and the dispute of the subjects with those in authority over them, and the dispute of the scholars among themselves concerning matters of religious knowledge.

If we consider what was mentioned as the occasion of revelation, we find that the primary intended meaning is the disagreement between the leaders and the Ummah. For this reason the exegetes explained it with some of these forms, but their aim was not to restrict the verse to what they explained. The best of their expressions on this is al-Tabari's statement: "That is, if you disagree, O believers, among yourselves, or you and those in authority among you disagree about it." And from Mujahid: "If the scholars dispute, they should refer it to Allah."

The word "thing" (shay') is an indefinite noun extremely broad in indefiniteness, so it falls within the scope of the conditional and conveys generality, that is, in every matter. It thus applies to disputes over rights in litigation, and it applies to disagreement over opinions during consultation or when undertaking some action, such as the dispute of those in authority over the implementation of the affairs of the Ummah.

The generality of the word "thing" here has produced an excellent effect in generalizing the events and kinds of disagreement, and it was among the graceful usages in the classification of 'Abd al-Qahir. The verification of the usages of the word "thing" was already discussed in its occurrence in His saying: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [al-Baqara 2:155] in Surat al-Baqara.

[Page 100]

The word "refer" (radd) here is a metaphor for going to the judge for judgment and for appointing a person of opinion when opinions differ. Its literal meaning is returning a thing to its owner, like a loan or something usurped. Then it was applied to abandoning the claim to redress by entrusting the ruling to the judge, and to refraining from correcting one's opinion by entrusting its correction to another, as a metaphorical application, and this usage became so common in speech that it equaled the literal sense.

The generality of the word "thing" in the context of the conditional requires the generality of the command to refer to Allah and the Messenger, and the generality of the situations of dispute, following the generality of the matters disputed. Among these are litigations and claims concerning rights, which is what is most immediately understood from the verse, by the indication of His saying after it: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, yet they desire to seek judgment from the tyrant?﴾ [al-Nisa 4:60]. This is like an introduction to that, so it resembles an occasion of revelation, and for this reason it is the most immediately understood. But this does not prevent the generality of the general term. Among these is also disagreement over the means of implementing general commands, as occurs between individual soldiers and some of their commanders.

It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning a dispute that arose between the commander of the Ansar's detachment, 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafa al-Sahmi, as will come later. Among these is also the disagreement among the people of loosening and binding concerning the affairs of the Muslims' interests and what they wish to impose on the people.

Among these also is the disagreement of the people of knowledge concerning the legal rulings whose method is ijtihad and reflection on the evidences of the Shari'a.

So all this disagreement and dispute is such that its parties are commanded to refer their matter to Allah and the Messenger. The referral of each kind of this must be of a kind that allows the hope of removing the disagreement, and that is by exerting full effort in reaching the clear truth in those situations.

What is narrated from Mujahid and Maymun ibn Mihran in explaining the dispute as the dispute of the people of knowledge is only an alert to the least obvious individual instance among the instances of the general term, and not a restriction of the general term.

Mentioning referral to Allah in this context is intended to make people mindful of Allah the Exalted in seeking the clarification of the truth at the points of contention, out of glorification of Allah the Exalted, since referral to the Messenger achieves referral to Allah, because the Messenger is the one who informs of the intent of Allah the Exalted. So mentioning the name of Allah here is in the position of its mention in His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal 8:41], and so on.

[Page 101]

Then referral to the Messenger during his life and presence is manifest and is what is most immediately understood from the verse. As for referral to him in his absence or after his death, it is by seeking judgment from the judges whom the Messenger appointed or commanded to be appointed, and from the judges whom those in authority designated to judge among the people by the Shari'a, from among those believed to have knowledge of the aspects of the Shari'a and its various applications.

The authority of the rulers, the conditions for holding office, and the methods of appointing them, as established by the evidences from the Messenger about the qualities of rulers, take the place of specifying the individuals themselves. By reflecting on his conduct and Sunnah, and then on what becomes clear from circumstances that one judges to be what the Messenger would intend if he were asked about them, in all cases of dispute over understanding the Shari'ah and deriving rulings that the Messenger left unstated, or whose ruling was unknown to him.

His saying ﴿If you believe in God and the Last Day﴾ is both an exhortation and a warning. Belief in God and the Last Day restrains a person from violating the Shari'ah, and from exposing the interests of the community to ruin, and from pursuing immediate advantages while knowing that they do not please God and harm the community. Therefore, it is necessary that the practice of the sincere Muslim be to advance when the interests are clear, to deliberate when the matter is ambiguous, and to hold back after presenting the problems to the principles of the Shari'ah.

The meaning of ﴿If you believe﴾, even though they were addressed as ﴿O you who believe﴾, is: if you truly believe, and you adhere to the obligations of the believer. For this reason God the Exalted said ﴿that is better﴾, where the demonstrative is used to emphasize it, and it refers to the referral mentioned in "then refer it" (fa-ruddūhu).

(Khayr) means that which contains benefit, and is the opposite of evil. It is a comparative form stripped of comparison, and what is meant is the existence of good and the strength of beauty.

Ta'wil (interpretation, here: the act of returning something to its origin) is the verbal noun of awwala al-shay' when one returns it, derived from āla ya'ūlu, meaning "to return". Here it means "better in returning and turning back."

Al-Bukhari reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The verse ﴿Obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah ibn Qays ibn 'Adi, when the Prophet sent him on a sariyya (a small military expedition).

And he reported in the Book of Campaigns (Kitab al-Maghazi) from 'Ali who said: "The Prophet sent a sariyya and appointed over it a man from the Ansar, and commanded them to obey him. He became angry and said: Did not the Prophet command you to obey me? They said: Yes. He said: Gather wood. They gathered it. He said: Light a fire. They lit it. He said: Enter it. They hesitated, and some of them began holding others back, saying: We fled to the Prophet from the fire. They kept on until the fire died down and his anger subsided. This reached the Prophet, and he said: If they had entered it, they would not have come out of it until the Day of Resurrection. Obedience is only in what is right."

So Ibn 'Abbas's saying "it was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah" may mean that it was revealed at the time of his appointment as commander of the sariyya, and that the matter in it was what caused the people of the sariyya to hesitate about entering the fire. *Za'm* (claim) is a statement that is false, or mixed with error, or one for which people accuse the speaker of such. When al-A'sha praised Qays ibn Ma'd Yakrib al-Kindi, he said:

"I was informed of Qays, though I had not tested him,
as they claimed: the best of the people of Yemen."

Qays became angry and said: "It is nothing but *za'm* (mere claim)." Allah also says ﴿Those who disbelieved claim that they will never be resurrected﴾ [At-Taghabun: 7]. A narrator, speaking of a strange *hadith*, says: "*Fa-za'ama fulan anna Rasul Allah (ﷺ) qala kadha*" ("So-and-so claimed that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said such-and-such"), meaning that he thereby places the responsibility for the report on the one who relates it. From this is what occurs in Sibawayh's book, such as his saying "*za'ama al-Khalil*" ("al-Khalil claimed"). For this reason they said: "*Al-za'm* is the mount of falsehood."

*Za'm* is also used for a report that is confirmed by context, as in his words:

"The blamers claimed that I am in a deep flood (of troubles),
they spoke truly, but my flood will not clear."

His words "they spoke truly" are the context (*qarina*) indicating confirmation. Its present-tense form may have the vowel of the middle letter as *a*, *i*, or *u*, and the most eloquent is with *fatha*.

Those who intended to seek judgement before the *taghut* were, as is evident, hypocrites. So applying the term *za'm* to their faith is clear.

His words ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾ are conjoined (*'utifa*) because these hypocrites were from among the Jews, and the conjoined element has entered the scope of the claim. This shows that their belief in what was revealed before was not consistent. Therefore their assertion of that was a claim, because their belief in the Torah was absent in many situations like this one, for if they truly believed in it, they would not have sought judgement before the soothsayers, and the law of Musa (peace be upon him) warns against them.

His words "*yuridun*" (they desire) mean: they love with a love that drives them to do what is loved.

The *taghut* here is the idols, as shown by His words ﴿though they were commanded to reject it﴾. But they interpreted it as the soothsayer, or as the great man among the Jews, as you have seen in the occasion of revelation. If this is so, then it is a metaphorical usage (*majaz*), by likening the great unbelief to the worshipped idol, because of the excessive sanctification of it by its people; or because the soothsayer translates the words of the idol according to their claim. The derivation of *taghut* has already been discussed at His words ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in *jibt* and *taghut*?﴾ [An-Nisa: 51] in this surah.

He said ﴿And Satan desires to lead them astray, far astray﴾, meaning: he loves that and makes it attractive to them, because he cast into their souls the call to judgement by soothsayers and turning away from the ruling of the Messenger. Or the meaning is: he desires to lead them astray in the future because of this deed of theirs, were it not that Allah awakened them and they repented of what they had done.

*Al-dalal al-ba'id* (far astray) is unbelief. Describing it as "far" is a metaphor for the intensity of misguidance, by treating it as a kind of thing having distance, so that this instance of it has reached the utmost limit of distance. The poet said:

"I wasted my resolve in pursuing my hope far away."

His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come"﴾ ... the verse means: when they are told, "Come forward" or "Come to it." The word *ta'ala* is a term that indicates a command to come and approach, so its meaning is that of the particle of calling, except that it contains no alerting force. The grammarians differed on whether it is a verb or a verb-name (*ism fi'l*), and the more correct view is that it is a verb, because it is derived from the root of height (*'uluw*).

For this reason al-Jawhari said in *al-Sihah*: "*Al-ta'alli* and *al-irtifa'* (raising), you say from it when you command: *Ta'al ya rajul*," and the same is in *al-Qamus*. Also, because pronouns of the nominative case attach to it, and it is a verb built on *fatha* contrary to the usual pattern of the imperative verb. That structure is what led a group of Arabic grammarians to say it is a verb-name, and that view is not far-fetched. Nothing has come from the Arabs except the *fatha* of the *lam*, so the *kasra* of the *lam* in the verse of Abu Firas is considered a grammatical error:

"O neighbour of mine, fate has not been fair between us,
*ta'ali* (come), I will share my worries with you, *ta'ali*."

[The *kasra* is on the *lam* of the rhyme, which is a *kasra* rhyme, reckoned as a solecism.]

In *al-Kashshaf*, it is reported that the people of Mecca, in the time of al-Zamakhshari, say *ta'ali* to a woman. That is one of the solecisms that entered the Arabic language because of the spread of foreigners among them.

The reason *ta'ala* is derived from the root of height is that they imagined the caller to be on high and the one called (in the *fath* case) to be low, because they used to make their houses on elevated ground, as it is safer for them. For this reason its original purpose is to indicate a request for attendance for a benefit.

Ibn 'Atiyya said in his commentary on His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers doing"﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 104] in Surat al-Ma'ida: *Ta'al* is a call to righteousness, this is its origin, then it was used both for righteousness and for its opposite.

He said in his commentary on the verse of An-Nisa: It is a word derived from height. When it was used in calling a person and bringing him, it was formed from height as a refinement of manners, as you say: "*Irtafi' ila al-haqq*" (rise up to the truth) and similar.

Know that since *ta'ala* is a rigid verb, it is not possible to form any form from it other than the imperative. So you do not say *ta'alaytu* meaning "I attended," nor do you forbid it, so you do not say *la tata'al*. In *al-Sihah* he said: "It is not permissible to say *ta'alaytu* from it, nor to forbid it."

In *al-Sihah*, after this he says: "You say: '*Qad ta'alaytu*' (I have indeed come), and '*Ila ayy shay'in ata'ala*' (to what thing do I rise)," meaning that it is conjugated in the specific case of responding to a request from someone who said to you "*Ta'al*." The author of *al-Lisan* followed him in this, but neglected the statement before it.

As for the author of *Taj al-'Arus*, he perhaps erred when he said: "Al-Jawhari said: 'It is not permissible to say from it: *ta'alaytu* or *ila ayy shay'in ata'ala*.'" Perhaps there is a lacuna or an error in the manuscript made by the copyist, who thought the expression was a repetition. I have pointed this out only so that you do not fall into errors and confusion.

And *(ta'alaw)* is used here metaphorically, since there is no actual attendance or coming. It is a metaphor for calling to judgement by the Book of Allah and for calling to judgement by the Messenger in his presence. For this reason He said ﴿to what Allah has revealed﴾, since Allah does not judge except through His speech. As for judgement by the Messenger, what is meant is judgement by his person, because the people referred to were hypocrites who were in Medina during the lifetime of the Messenger (ﷺ).

*Sududan* (turning away) is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) for emphasis. The purpose of the indefinite nunation on *sududan* is to indicate that it is a nunation of magnification (*ta'zim*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 62–63:

Page 107
﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forward, and then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation"?﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves.﴾

This is a branch (tafri') from His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger"﴾ [an-Nisa': 61], because turning away from that brings upon them the anger of Allah, so it is likely that Allah will afflict them with a disaster without any act of anyone's, such as the exposure of their condition to the believers so that they are recognized as disbelievers and become threatened; or a disaster from the command of Allah to His Messenger and the believers, by their showing them enmity and killing them because of their hypocrisy. Then they come making excuses, saying that they intended by seeking judgment from the people of the tyrant (taghut) only the goodness toward them, winning them over to faith, and bringing about agreement between them and the believers.

This is a threat (wa'id), because (idha) refers to the future, so the two verbs after it, namely (asabat-hum) and (ja'uka), are both in the future. It is like His saying: ﴿If the hypocrites do not desist, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in Medina, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbors therein except briefly﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60], ﴿Cursed; wherever they are found, they will be seized and slain with [intense] slaughter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61].

And (kayfa) is the predicate of an omitted subject known from the context of the speech: i.e., how will their state be when a disaster strikes them because of what they did, so that they come to you apologizing.

The interrogative is used here to express awe and dread (al-tahwil), as was discussed earlier in His saying, ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ [an-Nisa': 41].

The construction "kayfa bika" is said when good news or a threat is intended, as an expression of wonder or dread. From the first type is the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Suraqa ibn Malik: "How will you be when you wear the bracelets of Kisra?" — as good news that the bracelets of Kisra would fall into the hands of the army of the Muslims. When the bracelets of Kisra were brought among the spoils of the conquest of Persia, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab put them on Suraqa ibn Malik, confirming the miracle of the Prophet ﷺ.

Page 108
From the second type is His saying: ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾ [Al 'Imran: 25]. And His saying: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you as a witness against these﴾ [an-Nisa': 41] combined both meanings.

His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ came with the demonstrative (ulaika) to distinguish them for the listeners in the most complete way, since their description had already been mentioned, making them as if present before the eyes. By "what is in their hearts" He means the disbelief which they concealed, and He commanded His Messenger to turn away from them.

The real meaning of i'rad (turning away) is not paying attention to a thing with the intention of distancing oneself from it. It is derived from al-'arad (with a damma on the ayn), which is the side. Perhaps the original sense of the hamza in the verb a'rada is entering into a thing, i.e., he entered the side of the place; or the hamza indicates becoming, i.e., he became one having a side, meaning he showed his side to another and did not show him his face. Then it came to be commonly used for abandoning and refraining from association and conversation, because it generally includes turning away.

It is said: a'rada 'anhu just as it is said: sadda 'anhu, as in His saying: ﴿And when you see those who engage in mocking Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in another topic﴾ [al-An'am: 68]. For this reason this word frequently occurred in the poetry of lovers as a counterpart to sudud (aversion). This is the closest of the meanings to the literal meaning, so it is a metonymy (majaz mursal) by the relation of necessary association (lazum). This usage became widespread in speech, and then it was applied to pardon and non-punishment, by likening the state of one who pardons to the state of one who does not turn to a thing and so turns the side of his face away from it.

Likewise safah was used in this sense, derived from the surface of the face, i.e., its side; it is further from the literal meaning than the first, since it is based on comparison (tashbih).

Al-wa'z (admonition) is commanding the doing of good and abandoning evil in a manner that includes warning and softening that move one to comply. Its noun is al-maw'izah. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah instructs you with what is excellent﴾ [an-Nisa': 58].

So this turning away is turning away with pardon, or turning away without grief over their aversion from you; i.e., do not concern yourself with their aversion, for Allah will recompense them, as is shown by His saying: ﴿and admonish them and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves﴾. That is a conveying to them concerning the excuse, and a hope for the amendment of their state, as is the conduct of the sincere advisor who strives by every means toward guidance and right direction.

Al-baligh is fa'il in the sense of bali'h, reaching with intense force, i.e., reaching into their souls, penetrating within them. His saying "concerning themselves" may be connected to "baligh," and the prepositional phrase was placed first for the sake of concern with the reform of their souls, together with observing the rhyme (fasilah). It may also be connected to the verb "qul lahum," i.e., say to them a word concerning the matter of their souls; the adverbial sense of "fi" is then figurative, as their souls were likened to a container for the speech.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 62–63:

Page 107
﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forward, and then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation"?﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves.﴾

[Page 109]

﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the leave of God.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (*jumlah mu'taridah*, a clause inserted into the middle of a narrative) within the account of the hypocrite who sought judgment from the *taghut* (false judge). It returns to the main theme, which is the censure of them for turning away from seeking judgment from the Messenger, and that this turning away indicates their hypocrisy. It does so by showing that the meaning of faith is contentment with the ruling of the Messenger, since the Messenger was sent only to be obeyed, so how can one turn away from him?

His words "by the leave of God" (*bi-idhni Allah*) are in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun in "to be obeyed" (*yuta'a*), meaning: while being invested in that by the leave of God, that is, by His command and His charge, since the benefit of the laws does not appear without their being followed. Among the messengers, some were obeyed and some were disobeyed, either occasionally or constantly. Moses was disobeyed on several occasions, and Jesus was disobeyed in most of his affair. Muhammad was not disobeyed by the sincere believers in him except through an interpretation (*ta'wil*), such as what occurred on the day of Uhud, when God the Exalted said, "and you disobeyed" (Q. 3:152). That was disobedience only by way of interpretation, but it was counted as disobedience because it was in reality an opposition to the command of the Messenger. For this reason, the most perfect manifestation of the message was the Messenger's being supported by authority (*sultan*), and that authority residing in his person so that he would not be in need of anyone else. This manifestation was fully realized in the message of Muhammad ﷺ, and for this reason he was described as "the Prophet of the Battles" (*nabi al-malahim*, the prophet of the great wars). The glimmers of this had begun in the message of Moses, peace be upon him, but were not completed; they were perfected for Muhammad ﷺ. God the Exalted said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance, that people may uphold justice. And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for people, and that God may know who helps Him and His messengers unseen﴾ (Q. 57:25). I do not think that by "His messengers" He meant anyone but His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, and he was the one intended by the plural, because he is the most perfect of them.

[Page 110]

﴿And if they, when they had wronged themselves, had come to you and asked God's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found God Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾.

This is coordinated (*'atf*) upon the clause ﴿So how will it be when a calamity strikes them because of what their hands have sent forward﴾ (Q. 4:62), as a rebuke to them for their seeking judgment, since that was disobedience upon disobedience. For they were not content with turning away from the judgment of the Messenger, but went further and obstructed those who said to them: ﴿Come to what God has sent down and to the Messenger﴾ (Q. 4:61). So if they had come to their senses at that point from their obstinacy, they would have known that their wish to seek judgment from the disbelievers and soothsayers was a transgression from which they must seek forgiveness. But they persisted and were arrogant. In the mention of "if" (*law*) and in making ﴿they would have found God Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾ its answer, there is an indication that, since they did not do this, they were deprived of forgiveness.

The act of this hypocrite was a wrong to himself, because he thrust himself into disobedience of God and disobedience of the Messenger, thereby bringing upon himself the punishment of the Hereafter and exposing himself to the calamities of retribution in this world.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 65:

﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not truly believe until they make you judge in what is disputed among them, and then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided, and submit with full submission.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾ [al-Nisa: 60] and what follows it, since that implies that they did what they did while claiming that they were believers. So the claim was an indication of the negation of their faith. Then it was followed by something more explicit, namely that their actions contradict their being believers, by His saying "they will not believe," and He emphasized it with an oath and with verbal emphasis (al-tawkid al-lafzi).

The original wording is: "fa-wa-Rabbika la yu'minun." The Arabs place the negative particle before the oath when the answer to the oath is negative, for the sake of rapidity (al-ta'jil) by conveying that what follows the conjunction is an oath upon the negation contained in the sentence it is conjoined to. So the fronting of the negation serves to draw attention to the negation, as in the verse of Qays ibn 'Asim:

fa-la wallahi ashrabuha sahihan / wa-la ushfa biha abadan saqimā
And they often use, after the conjunction, a negative particle of the same kind in the answer, so that emphasis is achieved together with the attention, as in this verse, and this is the more common usage. I have not seen in the speech of the Arabs the placing of (la) before the conjunction in order to nullify the preceding speech. There occurs in the verse of Abu Tammam:

la wal-ladhi huwa 'alimun anna al-nawa ∗∗∗ sabrun wa-anna Abi al-Husayn karimu
This "la" is not the one that occurs with the verb of swearing as an extra particle with an affirmative sentence after it, such as la uqsimu, nor in non-oath contexts such as li-la ya'lama ahl al-kitab [al-Hadid: 29], because in those the sentence is not negative, whereas here the sentence with it is negative. So it is an emphasis for it, according to what most verifiers have chosen, in disagreement with the author of al-Kashshaf. It does not follow that the positions of a single particle must be uniform in closely related positions.

The negation of being believers, as they claim, was made about these hypocrites in a state where people think they are believers and do not perceive their disbelief. Therefore the statement required emphasis by oath and verbal emphasis, because it is an unveiling of the hidden reality of their state. The matter sworn to is: the limit (al-ghayah) and what is conjoined to it with "thumma," together. So if they make someone other than the Messenger judge in what is disputed among them, they are not believers.

That is: if their turning away from the Messenger's judgment was out of fear of his injustice, as is known from the context, then their disbelief was exposed. God informed the community that these people will not be believers until they make the Messenger judge and find within themselves no discomfort (haraj) at his judgment, that is, no discomfort that turns them away from judging by him, or that angers them at his judgment after they have made him judge. It is known from this that believers do not turn away from the Messenger's judgment and do not find within themselves discomfort at his decision, by way of analogical reasoning a fortiori.

The intended discomfort is not the unease the one judged feels at being obliged to something he dislikes, when no doubt has touched him about the justice of the Messenger and his hitting the mark of the truth. God the Exalted has explained in Surat al-Nur how turning away from the Messenger's judgment becomes disbelief, whether it comes from a hypocrite or from a believer, when He said concerning the hypocrites: ﴿And when they are called to God and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away﴾ [al-Nur: 48] ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly﴾ [al-Nur: 49] ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts, or do they have doubt, or do they fear that God and His Messenger will wrong them?﴾ [al-Nur: 50].

Then He said: ﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to God and His Messenger that he may judge between them, is only that they say: We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Nur: 51], because the judgment of the Messenger by what God has legislated of rulings does not admit of injustice, since God legislates only the truth, and the Messenger does not oppose the Shari'ah of God in his judgment.

For this reason this verse is specific to the judgment of the Messenger ﷺ. As for turning away from the judgment of someone other than the Messenger, it is not disbelief if the one turning away allows that the judge may fail to hit the judgment of God the Exalted, or may be unjust in the ruling.

al-'Abbas and 'Ali disliked the judgment of Abu Bakr and the judgment of 'Umar in the matter of what the Prophet ﷺ left of the land of Fadak, because they held that the ijtihad of Abu Bakr and 'Umar in that was not correct.

'Uyayna ibn Hisn said to 'Umar: "You do not divide equally and you do not act justly in the matter," and his criticism of 'Umar's judgment was not counted as disbelief from him.

Furthermore, turning away from litigation before a judge who rules by the Shari'ah of Islam may be for the purpose of disparaging the Islamic rulings whose being the judgment of God the Exalted is established, and that is disbelief, since it falls under His saying ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts, or do they have doubt﴾ [al-Nur: 50]. It may be merely for following desire, when the ruling that opposes the Shari'ah suits the desire of the one in whose favor it is given, and this is wickedness (fisq) and misguidance (dalal), like the case of every violation by which the accountable person opposes the rulings of the Shari'ah in order to follow worldly aims.

It may also be out of disparagement of the judge and suspicion of injustice on his part, if he is not infallible (ma'sum). This has degrees according to the ability to obtain redress from the judge and correct him. The explanation of this will come at His saying ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44] in Surat al-'Uqud.

The meaning of (shajara) is: became intermingled and disputed, and the matter was not clarified with fairness. Its root is from al-shajar (trees), because part of it entwines with another, and its branches intertwine. They said: "shajara amruhum," meaning there was evil among them. And haraj means: severe constriction ﴿He makes his breast tight and constricted (haraj)﴾ [al-An'am: 125].

The consequence of His saying ﴿fa-la wa-Rabbika la yu'minun﴾ and the verse upon what precedes it implies that the cause of revelation of this verse is the matter of the dispute between the Jew and the hypocrite, and the hypocrite's seeking judgment in it from the soothsayer (al-kahin). This is what the arrangement of the speech requires, and it is the view of the majority of exegetes, and it was said by Mujahid, 'Ata' and al-Sha'bi.

In al-Bukhari, from al-Zubayr: "I think this verse was revealed concerning a dispute between me and one of the Ansar over a watercourse (shiraj) from al-Harra, that is, a channel of water, plural of sharj, with a fatha and then a sukun, which is the channel of water coming from the lava-field of Madinah to the orchards that are in it, to the Messenger of God ﷺ. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Irrigate, O Zubayr, then send the water to your neighbour.' The Ansari said: 'Because he is the son of your paternal aunt!' The face of the Prophet ﷺ changed and he said: 'Irrigate, O Zubayr, until the water reaches the jadr, then send it to your neighbour, and take your full right.' The jadr is the earth that is built around the palm trees, like a wall."

His first judgment was a reconciliation (sulh), and his second judgment was taking the right. It seems that this Ansari thought the Prophet ﷺ intended reconciliation between them in a way that gave Zubayr's right its full measure to placate him, and he did not see in that anything contrary to infallibility, for the Companions varied in knowledge of the realities of the attributes of the Messenger, and were restrained in probing souls by what they were accustomed to of inclinations and accommodations. So God the Exalted alerted them that this leads to impugning infallibility.

This Ansari was not a hypocrite nor one who doubted the Messenger, for they described him as "the Ansari," which is a description of the best of the believers, and they did not describe him as a hypocrite. But he was ignorant and heedless, so the Messenger of God pardoned him and did not require him to repent.

This matter returns to the examination of takfir by the necessary implication of speech and action, and there is a fine distinction by Ibn Rushd in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil in the Book of Funerals and the Book of Apostates. Its summary: it is necessary to alert the one who says such a thing to the necessary consequence of his words of disbelief; if he adopts it and does not retract, he is counted a disbeliever, because a person may be heedless of the implication of necessity (dalalat al-iltizam).

This interpretation of the cause of revelation is taken from the style of the verse, from His saying "they will not believe" up to His saying "submission." So the Ansari was alerted that he had become involved in a state that contradicts faith in a hidden way, and if he persisted in it after being alerted to its consequence, he would not be a believer.

As for the Ansari, it is said he is unknown, and it would be best to leave him unnamed. It is also said he is Tha'labah ibn Hatib. In the Kashshaf it occurs that he is Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, and this is an error by its author. It is also said: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas.

On this narration of the cause of revelation, the meaning of His saying "they will not believe" is that their faith does not persist. But the apparent view to me is that the two incidents occurred at close times, and the verse was revealed concerning the incident of Bishr the hypocrite, and al-Zubayr supposed it was revealed concerning his incident with the Ansari.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 66–68:

﴿Had We prescribed for them, "Kill yourselves" or "Leave your homes," they would not have done it, except a few of them. But had they done what they were admonished to do, it would have been better for them and firmer in establishing them.﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾

The connection of this passage with what precedes it is not evident, such that it could be joined to it by a conjunction, because what is mentioned here is not more deserving of the ruling than what was mentioned before it; that is, it is not more deserving of compliance, such that one would say: "Had We obligated them to accept what is less than severing rights, they would not have accepted it." Rather, what is supposed here is harder on the souls than what they disobeyed in. A group of the exegetes said: the connection of this verse is that the hypocrite, when he did not accept the judgment of the Prophet ﷺ and wanted to go to judgment before the taghut (false judge).

And the Jews said: "How foolish these people are! They believe in Muhammad, yet they do not accept his judgment. Our prophet commanded us to kill ourselves, so we did, and the number of our dead reached seventy thousand." Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas said: "Had that been prescribed for us, we would have done it." So this verse was revealed confirming Thabit ibn Qays. Its remoteness from the context is not hidden, for if it were so, it would not have been said ﴿except a few of them have done it﴾; rather it would have been said: "a group of them would have done it."

Al-Fakhr said: it is a rebuke to the hypocrites, meaning: had We imposed strict obligation upon them, it would not have been strange for their obstinacy to appear; but We showed them mercy by imposing ease upon them, so let them abandon obstinacy. On this interpretation, it is suitable to be an incitement to the believers to obey the Messenger and a removal of hardship from them regarding his rulings, for he did not impose upon them except ease. All of this is based on the understanding that the meaning of "killing of souls" is that one of them kills himself by himself.

In my view, the mention of this here is from the excellence of the transition (bara'at al-maqta'), preparing for the shift of discourse to the incitement to jihad that comes in His saying ﴿O you who believe, take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa': 71], and that the meaning of ﴿kill yourselves﴾ is: let some of you kill others, for the believers fight their people and their relatives among the polytheists in the jihad that they were commanded, as evidenced by His saying ﴿and had they done what they were admonished to do﴾, etc.

By "leaving the homes" is meant emigration (hijrah), that is, We prescribed for them emigration from Medina; and in this there is an honoring of the emigrants and the strivers (in jihad).

The majority of readers read ﴿except a few﴾ with the nominative (raf'), as a substitute (badal) from the waw in ﴿fa'aluhu﴾ on the basis of the exception. Ibn 'Amir read it with the accusative (nasb), on one of the two modes of exception from a negative statement.

The meaning of ﴿what they are admonished with﴾ is known from His saying ﴿so turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63]; that is, what they are commanded with as a command of warning and softening, that is, the content of what they are admonished, because al-wa'z (admonition) is speech and command, and the object is the thing commanded; that is, had they done everything the Messenger conveys to them, and among that is jihad and emigration. And its being "better" is that in it is the good of this world, because Allah knows and they do not know.

As for its being "firmer in establishing": it may mean firmness in faith, and this is how they explained it; and it may mean in my view that it is firmer in establishing them, that is, for their remaining among their enemies and for their honor and their true life, for they only dislike fighting out of concern for their own selves, and dislike emigration out of love for their homelands; so Allah taught them that jihad and being estranged in it or elsewhere is firmer in establishing them, because it repels their enemies from them, as al-Husayn ibn al-Hammam said:

"I held back, seeking to preserve life, but I found for myself no life like advancing forward."

Among what indicates that the intended "good" is the good of this world, and "establishment" is establishment therein, is His saying, conjoined to it: ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾

The clause ﴿And then We would have given them from Us﴾ is conjoined to the response of "law" (lau), and the sense is: "it would have been better and firmer, and We would have given them..." etc. The presence of the lam which falls in the response of "law" indicates this. As for the conjunctive waw, it is for linking the conjoined clause to the clause it is conjoined to. As for "idhan," it is a particle of response and consequence, that is, in the sense of a reply to a statement preceding it, and it is not restricted to a question. So it was inserted into the response of "law" by conjoining it to the response, as an emphasis on the meaning of the consequence. Thus "law" in the verse has been answered with two responses in meaning, because what is conjoined to a response is a response, and the combination of two responses is not good except with the presence of a conjunctive particle. Close to what is in this verse is the statement of al-'Anbari in the Hamasa:

"Had I been of Mazin, the sons of Laqit of Dhuhl ibn Shayban would not have plundered my camels;
then a rough company would have arisen to support me in the moment of wrath, if a lame one were to be present."

Al-Marzuqi said: it is permissible that "idhan la-qama" be the response of "law kunta min Mazin" in the preceding verse, as if it were answered with two responses. Al-Zamakhshari made His saying ﴿And then We would have given them﴾ a response to an implied question, as if it were said: "And what would be theirs after firmness?" So it was said: "And then We would have given them."

Al-Taftazani said: on the basis that the waw is for resumption (isti'naf), that is, because conjunction contradicts assuming a question. The truth is that what az-Zamakhshari arrived at in the Kashshaf is an artificiality for which there is no need, except the obligation that "idhan" be a particle answering a questioner; the correct view is that a response is that to which another statement is addressed, whether it be a question, a condition, or something else.

His saying ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path﴾ means: We would have opened for them the ways of knowledge and guidance, because their readiness to comply with what they were commanded is the beginning of emptying the souls of attachment to their illusions and habits which veil them from grasping the realities. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 66–68:

﴿Had We prescribed for them, "Kill yourselves" or "Leave your homes," they would not have done it, except a few of them. But had they done what they were admonished to do, it would have been better for them and firmer in establishing them.﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾

The connection of this passage with what precedes it is not evident, such that it could be joined to it by a conjunction, because what is mentioned here is not more deserving of the ruling than what was mentioned before it; that is, it is not more deserving of compliance, such that one would say: "Had We obligated them to accept what is less than severing rights, they would not have accepted it." Rather, what is supposed here is harder on the souls than what they disobeyed in. A group of the exegetes said: the connection of this verse is that the hypocrite, when he did not accept the judgment of the Prophet ﷺ and wanted to go to judgment before the taghut (false judge).

And the Jews said: "How foolish these people are! They believe in Muhammad, yet they do not accept his judgment. Our prophet commanded us to kill ourselves, so we did, and the number of our dead reached seventy thousand." Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas said: "Had that been prescribed for us, we would have done it." So this verse was revealed confirming Thabit ibn Qays. Its remoteness from the context is not hidden, for if it were so, it would not have been said ﴿except a few of them have done it﴾; rather it would have been said: "a group of them would have done it."

Al-Fakhr said: it is a rebuke to the hypocrites, meaning: had We imposed strict obligation upon them, it would not have been strange for their obstinacy to appear; but We showed them mercy by imposing ease upon them, so let them abandon obstinacy. On this interpretation, it is suitable to be an incitement to the believers to obey the Messenger and a removal of hardship from them regarding his rulings, for he did not impose upon them except ease. All of this is based on the understanding that the meaning of "killing of souls" is that one of them kills himself by himself.

In my view, the mention of this here is from the excellence of the transition (bara'at al-maqta'), preparing for the shift of discourse to the incitement to jihad that comes in His saying ﴿O you who believe, take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa': 71], and that the meaning of ﴿kill yourselves﴾ is: let some of you kill others, for the believers fight their people and their relatives among the polytheists in the jihad that they were commanded, as evidenced by His saying ﴿and had they done what they were admonished to do﴾, etc.

By "leaving the homes" is meant emigration (hijrah), that is, We prescribed for them emigration from Medina; and in this there is an honoring of the emigrants and the strivers (in jihad).

The majority of readers read ﴿except a few﴾ with the nominative (raf'), as a substitute (badal) from the waw in ﴿fa'aluhu﴾ on the basis of the exception. Ibn 'Amir read it with the accusative (nasb), on one of the two modes of exception from a negative statement.

The meaning of ﴿what they are admonished with﴾ is known from His saying ﴿so turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63]; that is, what they are commanded with as a command of warning and softening, that is, the content of what they are admonished, because al-wa'z (admonition) is speech and command, and the object is the thing commanded; that is, had they done everything the Messenger conveys to them, and among that is jihad and emigration. And its being "better" is that in it is the good of this world, because Allah knows and they do not know.

As for its being "firmer in establishing": it may mean firmness in faith, and this is how they explained it; and it may mean in my view that it is firmer in establishing them, that is, for their remaining among their enemies and for their honor and their true life, for they only dislike fighting out of concern for their own selves, and dislike emigration out of love for their homelands; so Allah taught them that jihad and being estranged in it or elsewhere is firmer in establishing them, because it repels their enemies from them, as al-Husayn ibn al-Hammam said:

"I held back, seeking to preserve life, but I found for myself no life like advancing forward."

Among what indicates that the intended "good" is the good of this world, and "establishment" is establishment therein, is His saying, conjoined to it: ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾

The clause ﴿And then We would have given them from Us﴾ is conjoined to the response of "law" (lau), and the sense is: "it would have been better and firmer, and We would have given them..." etc. The presence of the lam which falls in the response of "law" indicates this. As for the conjunctive waw, it is for linking the conjoined clause to the clause it is conjoined to. As for "idhan," it is a particle of response and consequence, that is, in the sense of a reply to a statement preceding it, and it is not restricted to a question. So it was inserted into the response of "law" by conjoining it to the response, as an emphasis on the meaning of the consequence. Thus "law" in the verse has been answered with two responses in meaning, because what is conjoined to a response is a response, and the combination of two responses is not good except with the presence of a conjunctive particle. Close to what is in this verse is the statement of al-'Anbari in the Hamasa:

"Had I been of Mazin, the sons of Laqit of Dhuhl ibn Shayban would not have plundered my camels;
then a rough company would have arisen to support me in the moment of wrath, if a lame one were to be present."

Al-Marzuqi said: it is permissible that "idhan la-qama" be the response of "law kunta min Mazin" in the preceding verse, as if it were answered with two responses. Al-Zamakhshari made His saying ﴿And then We would have given them﴾ a response to an implied question, as if it were said: "And what would be theirs after firmness?" So it was said: "And then We would have given them."

Al-Taftazani said: on the basis that the waw is for resumption (isti'naf), that is, because conjunction contradicts assuming a question. The truth is that what az-Zamakhshari arrived at in the Kashshaf is an artificiality for which there is no need, except the obligation that "idhan" be a particle answering a questioner; the correct view is that a response is that to which another statement is addressed, whether it be a question, a condition, or something else.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 69–70:

Page 116

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the steadfast in truth (al-siddiqin), the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾ ﴿That is the bounty from Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower.﴾

This is an appendage (tadhyil) to the sentence ﴿And had We then given them from Us a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa: 67]. It is conjoined (ʿutifat) by virtue of its being attached to the sentence ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger﴾ which is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And if they had done what they were admonished with﴾ [al-Nisa: 66]. The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) is used in the apodosis of the conditional sentence to draw attention to their worthiness of the content of the predicate, referring by the demonstrative to the content of the speech that precedes the demonstrative. The meaning of "with" (maʿiyya) is the companionship of rank in Paradise, even though the degrees differ.

The meaning of "whoever obeys" (man yuti') is one who is characterised by the complete meaning of obedience, that is, who does not disobey Allah and His Messenger. The particle "with" (maʿa) indicates that the station of what follows it is firmer and better known.

In the authentic hadith: "You are with the one whom you love." The siddiqun are those who affirmed the prophets from the outset, such as the Disciples (al-Hawariyyun) and the foremost early believers among the faithful. As for the martyrs (shuhada'), they are those who were killed in the cause of raising the word of Allah. The righteous (salihun) are those to whom steadfastness (istiqama) is firmly attached.

And ﴿ḥasuna﴾ is a verb used to express praise, assimilated to ni'ma and implying a sense of wonder at their excellence. This is the characteristic of the form fa'ula (with a dammed ʿayn) from the triliteral root, that it indicates praise or blame according to its root, together with wonder. The original form of the verb is ḥasana (with two fathas), which was changed to fa'ula (with a dammed ʿayn) to convey praise and wonder. ﴿Ulaʾika﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of ﴿ḥasuna﴾. And ﴿rafiqan﴾ is a specifier (tamyiz), meaning: how excellent they are, they are excellent as to the kind of companions.

The word "rafiq" applies to both the singular and the plural, and in the hadith of death: "the Most High Companion" (al-rafiq al-aʿla). The definiteness of the two parts in the phrase ﴿That is the bounty from Allah﴾ conveys restriction (hasr), and it is a claimed restriction (hasr idda'i), because the bounty of Allah comes in types and kinds, but the purpose is to emphasise the greatness of this bounty; it is like their saying: "You are the man."

The appendage with the phrase ﴿and sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾ is to indicate that those who are endowed with this virtue, even if people do not know them, Allah knows them, and the recompense is in His hand; He will give them their recompense according to what He knows of them. A similar instance has already been mentioned in this surah.
