[Page 117]

﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution and go forth in small groups or go forth all together.﴾ ﴿And indeed, among you is he who will surely lag behind. So if a disaster strikes you, he says, "Allah has bestowed favor upon me in that I was not present with them as a witness."﴾ ﴿But if a bounty from Allah comes to you, he will surely say, as if there had never been between you and him any affection, "Oh, I wish I had been with them so I could have achieved a great achievement."﴾

This is a new section, and a transition to exhorting jihad, connected by a subtle link. He moved from obedience to the Messenger to mentioning the most demanding of obligations, then to mentioning those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. The situation called for emphasizing the rank of martyrdom above the other qualities mentioned with it, which are attainable.

This verse undoubtedly refers to the preparation for one of the military expeditions (ghazawat) of the Muslims. The early scholars (al-salaf) did not mention the occasion of its revelation. There is no doubt that it was not the first expedition, because the Battle of Badr took place before the revelation of this surah, and likewise the Battle of Uhud, in which the surah of Al 'Imran was revealed. Nor was it revealed concerning the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), because His saying ﴿go forth in small groups﴾ requires that they be the ones attacking, not the ones attacked.

Perhaps it was revealed merely as a reminder of the principles of preparing to fight the enemy, and as a warning against the hidden enemy and the scheming enemy. And perhaps it is a preparation for the Conquest (ghazwat al-Fath), since this surah was revealed in the year six, and the conquest of Makkah took place in the year eight. There is no doubt that this period was one of intensifying the alliance of all the Arabs to support the polytheists of Quraysh and to defend their gods.

What indicates this is His saying after it ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the cause of Allah and for the oppressed men﴾ [al-Nisa: 75], etc., and His saying ﴿And if you have a victory from Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 141], for the term "victory" (fath) is intended to refer to the conquest of Makkah in many places, like His saying ﴿so He brought about from that a near victory﴾ [al-Fath: 27].

He began with the command to take precaution (al-hadhar). It is the greatest principle of fighting, for guarding against the enemy's deceptions. Al-hadhar is guarding against what is disliked.

[Page 118]

The meaning of that is that they should not be deceived by the truce between them and the enemy, the truce of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah. For the enemy and its helpers await misfortunes for them, and among them are hypocrites who are enemies in the form of allies. These are the ones referred to by His saying ﴿And indeed, among you is he who will surely lag behind﴾ up to ﴿a great achievement﴾.

The word "take" (khudhu) is a metaphor (isti'ara) for the meaning of intense caution and constancy in it. The literal sense of taking is grasping a thing that was far from you. Since forgetfulness and heedlessness resemble distance and casting away, remembrance and alertness resemble taking a thing after it has been cast away, like His saying ﴿Take what is pardoned﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], and the saying "he took from him a covenant and a pledge."

Caution is not a metaphor for weapons, as many have supposed, for Allah the Exalted said in another verse ﴿and let them take their precaution and their weapons﴾ [al-Nisa: 102], so He conjoined weapons to it.

His saying ﴿so go forth in small groups or go forth all together﴾ is a branch from taking precaution, because when they have taken their precaution they choose methods of fighting according to the condition of the enemy. "Infiru" means go forth to war, and its verbal noun is al-nafr. This is unlike "nafara, yanfuru" with a dhamma on the fa' in the imperfect, whose verbal noun is al-nufur.

"Thubat" with a dhamma on the tha' is the plural of "thubah," also with a dhamma on the tha', which means a group. Its original form is either thubayah or thubawah, with ya' or waw. The more apparent is that it is with waw, because words whose roots retain two letters and end in the feminine ta' have the waw as their root, such as 'izzah and 'idhah, so their pattern is fi'ah.

As for thubat al-hawd, which is its middle where the water gathers, it is from thaba, yathubu, meaning to return. Its original form is thuwabah, which was lightened, becoming of the pattern of fulah. They cited as evidence for this that it is diminutive as thuwaybah, while thubah meaning group is diminutive as thubayyah. Al-Nahhas said: "Sometimes the weak in language supposes that the two are one, although there is a difference between them." Nevertheless, the author of al-Qamus (the lexicon) placed them in one category, and this is good, since thubat al-hawd may be derived from gathering, unless a difference in diminutive form is established by sound transmission.

"Thubat" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), because it is in the sense of "scattered," and the meaning of "jami'an" is a single army.

His saying ﴿And indeed, among you is he who will surely lag behind﴾ means "from among your group and your reckoning." The report concerning them makes it apparent that they were not believers in their privacy, because a believer, if he lagged behind from jihad, would not say ﴿Allah has bestowed favor upon me in that I was not present with them as a witness﴾. So these are hypocrites, and Allah has informed about them of the like of this explicitly at the end of this surah in His saying ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Nisa: 138], up to His saying

[Page 119]

﴿those who wait for you, so if you have a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" And if the disbelievers have a portion, they say, "Did we not gain control over you and protect you from the believers?"﴾ [al-Nisa: 141].

On the basis that the intended meaning of "man layubatti'anna" is the hypocrites, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj interpreted the verse. It was also said that what is intended by them are the weak among the believers, who are slow to go out until the matter of victory becomes clear. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "This is the choice of a group of commentators (mufassirun)." On this view, "minkum" means "from among the people of your religion." On both opinions the report has been emphasized with the strongest emphases, because this report is of a kind that is received with astonishment.

"Battaa" with the doubling of the letter is intransitive, meaning he became sluggish within himself regarding a matter, and it is lagging behind going out, lagging by the impulse of hypocrisy or cowardice. The report of this entails rebuke for him and an allusion to him, while the report remains on its literal meaning, because the implications of constructions are not described as metaphor.

His saying ﴿But if a disaster strikes you﴾ is a branch from ﴿will surely lag behind﴾, since this lagging sometimes leads to rejoicing at safety, and sometimes leads to regret and remorse.

(Al-musibah) is the name for what befalls a person of harm, and what is meant here is the disaster of war, namely defeat, with killing and captivity.

The meaning of ﴿Allah has bestowed favor upon me﴾ is the bestowal of safety. If he is from among the hypocrites, then describing that as a blessing is evident, because killing for them is a pure disaster, since they do not hope for reward from it. And if he is from among the weak believers, then he counted the blessing of remaining better than the blessing of the excellence of martyrdom, because of intense cowardice. This is from the preponderance of the innate impulse over the legal impulse.

The "shahid" (witness) on the first interpretation is either in the sense of one present, witnessing the fighting, or it is a mockery by him toward the believers, like His saying ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah"﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. On the second interpretation, "shahid" has its legal meaning, which is one killed in jihad. His saying ﴿and if a bounty from Allah comes to you, he will surely say﴾ is emphasized with the lam preceding the oath, the lam of the answer to the oath, and the nun of emphasis, to alert to the strangeness of his condition, until the hearer is brought to the position of one who denies that this proceeds from him.

What is meant by "bounty" is victory and spoils. This lagger wishes that he had been with the army, so that he might achieve a great achievement, which is

[Page 120]

the achievement of spoils and the achievement of the reward of jihad, when safety and the attainment of the Messenger's pleasure occur. For this reason he followed "uffaza" with a verbal noun and with the description "great."

He likened their condition at the time of this saying to the condition of one between whom and those addressed there was no real or formal affection before, so the comparison implies that there had been affection between him and them before this saying.

The aspect of this comparison is that when he wished he had been with them and grieved over the loss of his achievement had he been present with them, his condition in neglecting his companions resembles the condition of one who had no connection with them, such that he does not witness what they had resolved upon of going forth for jihad. This comparison is brought for the sake of increasing his blame and regret, meaning that he is the one who wasted for himself the cause of benefiting from what came to his companions of good, that is, he had the association with the warriors that should have been a cause of his going out with them, and benefiting from the reward of victory, its pride, and the blessing of spoils.

[Page 117]

﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution and go forth in small groups or go forth all together.﴾ ﴿And indeed, among you is he who will surely lag behind. So if a disaster strikes you, he says, "Allah has bestowed favor upon me in that I was not present with them as a witness."﴾ ﴿But if a bounty from Allah comes to you, he will surely say, as if there had never been between you and him any affection, "Oh, I wish I had been with them so I could have achieved a great achievement."﴾

This is a new section, and a transition to exhorting jihad, connected by a subtle link. He moved from obedience to the Messenger to mentioning the most demanding of obligations, then to mentioning those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. The situation called for emphasizing the rank of martyrdom above the other qualities mentioned with it, which are attainable.

This verse undoubtedly refers to the preparation for one of the military expeditions (ghazawat) of the Muslims. The early scholars (al-salaf) did not mention the occasion of its revelation. There is no doubt that it was not the first expedition, because the Battle of Badr took place before the revelation of this surah, and likewise the Battle of Uhud, in which the surah of Al 'Imran was revealed. Nor was it revealed concerning the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), because His saying ﴿go forth in small groups﴾ requires that they be the ones attacking, not the ones attacked.

Perhaps it was revealed merely as a reminder of the principles of preparing to fight the enemy, and as a warning against the hidden enemy and the scheming enemy. And perhaps it is a preparation for the Conquest (ghazwat al-Fath), since this surah was revealed in the year six, and the conquest of Makkah took place in the year eight. There is no doubt that this period was one of intensifying the alliance of all the Arabs to support the polytheists of Quraysh and to defend their gods.

What indicates this is His saying after it ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the cause of Allah and for the oppressed men﴾ [al-Nisa: 75], etc., and His saying ﴿And if you have a victory from Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 141], for the term "victory" (fath) is intended to refer to the conquest of Makkah in many places, like His saying ﴿so He brought about from that a near victory﴾ [al-Fath: 27].

He began with the command to take precaution (al-hadhar). It is the greatest principle of fighting, for guarding against the enemy's deceptions. Al-hadhar is guarding against what is disliked.

[Page 118]

The meaning of that is that they should not be deceived by the truce between them and the enemy, the truce of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah. For the enemy and its helpers await misfortunes for them, and among them are hypocrites who are enemies in the form of allies. These are the ones referred to by His saying ﴿And indeed, among you is he who will surely lag behind﴾ up to ﴿a great achievement﴾.

The word "take" (khudhu) is a metaphor (isti'ara) for the meaning of intense caution and constancy in it. The literal sense of taking is grasping a thing that was far from you. Since forgetfulness and heedlessness resemble distance and casting away, remembrance and alertness resemble taking a thing after it has been cast away, like His saying ﴿Take what is pardoned﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], and the saying "he took from him a covenant and a pledge."

Caution is not a metaphor for weapons, as many have supposed, for Allah the Exalted said in another verse ﴿and let them take their precaution and their weapons﴾ [al-Nisa: 102], so He conjoined weapons to it.

His saying ﴿so go forth in small groups or go forth all together﴾ is a branch from taking precaution, because when they have taken their precaution they choose methods of fighting according to the condition of the enemy. "Infiru" means go forth to war, and its verbal noun is al-nafr. This is unlike "nafara, yanfuru" with a dhamma on the fa' in the imperfect, whose verbal noun is al-nufur.

"Thubat" with a dhamma on the tha' is the plural of "thubah," also with a dhamma on the tha', which means a group. Its original form is either thubayah or thubawah, with ya' or waw. The more apparent is that it is with waw, because words whose roots retain two letters and end in the feminine ta' have the waw as their root, such as 'izzah and 'idhah, so their pattern is fi'ah.

As for thubat al-hawd, which is its middle where the water gathers, it is from thaba, yathubu, meaning to return. Its original form is thuwabah, which was lightened, becoming of the pattern of fulah. They cited as evidence for this that it is diminutive as thuwaybah, while thubah meaning group is diminutive as thubayyah. Al-Nahhas said: "Sometimes the weak in language supposes that the two are one, although there is a difference between them." Nevertheless, the author of al-Qamus (the lexicon) placed them in one category, and this is good, since thubat al-hawd may be derived from gathering, unless a difference in diminutive form is established by sound transmission.

"Thubat" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), because it is in the sense of "scattered," and the meaning of "jami'an" is a single army.

His saying ﴿And indeed, among you is he who will surely lag behind﴾ means "from among your group and your reckoning." The report concerning them makes it apparent that they were not believers in their privacy, because a believer, if he lagged behind from jihad, would not say ﴿Allah has bestowed favor upon me in that I was not present with them as a witness﴾. So these are hypocrites, and Allah has informed about them of the like of this explicitly at the end of this surah in His saying ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Nisa: 138], up to His saying

[Page 119]

﴿those who wait for you, so if you have a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" And if the disbelievers have a portion, they say, "Did we not gain control over you and protect you from the believers?"﴾ [al-Nisa: 141].

On the basis that the intended meaning of "man layubatti'anna" is the hypocrites, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj interpreted the verse. It was also said that what is intended by them are the weak among the believers, who are slow to go out until the matter of victory becomes clear. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "This is the choice of a group of commentators (mufassirun)." On this view, "minkum" means "from among the people of your religion." On both opinions the report has been emphasized with the strongest emphases, because this report is of a kind that is received with astonishment.

"Battaa" with the doubling of the letter is intransitive, meaning he became sluggish within himself regarding a matter, and it is lagging behind going out, lagging by the impulse of hypocrisy or cowardice. The report of this entails rebuke for him and an allusion to him, while the report remains on its literal meaning, because the implications of constructions are not described as metaphor.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 74–76:

Page 121

﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or achieves victory – We will give him a great reward.﴾ ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you fight not in the way of Allah and for the oppressed among men, women, and children who say, "Our Lord, take us out of this city whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector and appoint for us from Yourself a helper."﴾ ﴿Those who believe fight in the way of Allah, and those who disbelieve fight in the way of Taghut. So fight against the allies of Shaytan. Indeed, the plot of Shaytan is ever weak.﴾

The fa' (ف) here is either for sequence (tafri'), linking the command to what precedes it, meaning: this command is derived from ﴿Take your precaution and go forth﴾ [al-Nisa': 71], or it is the fa' of eloquence (fa' fasiha), which makes explicit what is implied by what came before, namely His words ﴿Take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa': 71] and ﴿And indeed among you is he who will lag behind﴾ [al-Nisa': 72], because all of that required the command to take precaution, which prepares for the call to fight and the command to mobilise, and the informing about those whose state is that of the hesitant and reluctant. That is: when you know all of that, then those who fight in the way of Allah are ﴿those who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter﴾, not everyone.

"Yashrūna" (يَشْرُونَ) means "they sell," for shara (شرى) is the opposite of ishtara (اشترى), like baa'a (باع) and ibtaa'a (ابتاع), and aknā (أكرى) and iktara (اكترى). Its detailed treatment has already been given at His words ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] in Surat al-Baqarah.

So those who sell the worldly life are those who expend it and desire the share of the Hereafter. The attribution of the command to fight to the people of this relative clause, namely ﴿who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter﴾, serves to praise those who fight in the way of Allah,

because the relative clause contains an allusion to the cause of the predicate, meaning: their expending of their worldly lives in pursuit of eternal life moves them to fight in the way of Allah, and it also shames the matter of those who lag behind, so that they desist from staying back, and so that the hypocrites reveal what is hidden in their hearts. Thus the meaning of the statement is:

Page 122

"So let the believers in truth fight in the way of Allah, for they sell the worldly life for the Hereafter."

No one should understand from His words ﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell﴾ that the command to fight is restricted to one group rather than another, because the expending of life in pursuit of the reward of the Hereafter is not something apparent such that the obligation could be attached to it; rather it is a matter of hearts between the servants and their Lord. Therefore it is established that attributing the command to the people of this relative clause is intended to praise the mujahidin and to belittle those who lag behind, as a speaker says, "This is not your nest, so depart." This is the interpretation of the verse in a way that is free from difficulty.

Included in His words ﴿or achieves victory﴾ are all kinds of victory over the enemy, by killing them, taking them captive, or seizing their property.

He limited the statement to "is killed or achieves victory" in ﴿is killed or achieves victory﴾ and did not add "or is taken captive," out of reluctance to mention for them a condition that is blameworthy and that Allah does not approve for the believers, namely the state of captivity; so He remained silent about it, lest He mention it in the context of encouragement, although there is also a great reward for the Muslim in it if he exerts his effort in the war and is overcome, since war is not free of that. And he is not commanded to cast himself into destruction when he knows that daring courage will not avail him, for among the benefits of Islam is the preservation of its men for the defence against the enemy.

The address in His words ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you fight not﴾ is an iltifat (التفات) from the third-person form, which is the form of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter﴾, to the form of direct address.

The meaning of ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you fight not﴾ is: what prevents you from fighting? The original construction is: "What is it that is right for you while you are not fighting?", so the clause ﴿you fight not﴾ is a circumstantial clause (حال) from the pronoun in the genitive, to indicate what the interrogation is about.

The interrogation is denunciatory (إنكاري), meaning: there is nothing right for you in a state of not fighting, and the intended sense is that what is right for you is that you fight. It is thus in the position of a command, meaning: fight in the way of Allah; let nothing turn you away from fighting. A similar expression was given earlier at His words ﴿And why should we not fight in the way of Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of "in the way of Allah" is for the sake of His religion and to seek His pleasure, so the particle (في) here is causal, and "for the oppressed" means for their benefit and for repelling the polytheists from them.

"Al-mustad'afun" (المستضعفون) are those whom people regard as weak; the sin and ta' in it indicate reckoning. By them is meant those believers remaining in Mecca among the men whom the polytheists prevented from emigrating under the terms of the treaty concluded between the Messenger (ﷺ) and the envoy of Quraysh, Suhayl ibn 'Amr. For among the conditions on which the treaty was concluded was that whoever came to Mecca from the Muslims as an apostate from Islam would not be returned to the Muslims, and whoever came to Medina fleeing from Mecca as a believer would be returned to Mecca.

Among the mustad'afun were al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salamah ibn Hisham, and 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah. As for the women, they were those who were married, or the wards of polytheist guardians, whose husbands and guardians prevented them from emigrating, such as Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and Umm al-Fadl Lubabah bint al-Harith, the wife of al-'Abbas, for they were being harmed and humiliated.

As for the wildan (الولدان), they are the young children of the believing men and women, for they would suffer from witnessing the torture of their fathers and relatives and the harming of their mothers and nurses. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I and my mother were among the mustad'afun."

Fighting in the way of these people is evident, for the rescue of them from the trial of the polytheists, and the rescue of the children from growing up in states of disbelief or ignorance of faith.

"Al-qaryah" (القرية) is Mecca. They asked to leave it because of the oppression that had defiled its sanctity, that is, the oppression of polytheism and the oppression of the believers. [p. 125]

The context was ready for a reminder about a group of Muslims whose condition changed from its beginning to its end. Ibn 'Ashur (the author) therefore digresses here to express wonder at their state, in the form of an interjection (i'tiradh) in the middle of the exhortation to jihad. These are a group who wished to be given permission to fight, but when fighting was prescribed for them at its appointed time, they became cowardly. The meaning of their eagerness for fighting before it was enjoined on them is already known from His words ﴿It was said to them: restrain your hands﴾, because restraining the hand here means abstaining from fighting, as in His words ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah﴾ [Al-Fath: 24].

This sentence (al-jumlah) is an interjection between the sentence ﴿And why do you not fight in the way of Allah?﴾ [An-Nisa: 75] and the sentences that follow it, and between the verse ﴿Let those who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter fight in the way of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 74]. The relevance of drawing a lesson from the condition of this group and its shifting state required this interjection.

[p. 126]
Those who were told this were all the Muslims, and the reason for the statement addressed to them was the question put by a group among them. The object of the wonder is only the condition of that group of Muslims.

The meaning of ﴿fighting was prescribed for them﴾ is that it was prescribed for you, meaning for the Muslims in general who were able. The sudden "idha" (إذا الفجائية, "suddenly") indicates that this group was not expected to be in this state, because they used to appear among the most eager for fighting.

The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: this verse was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who had encountered severe harm from the polytheists in Makkah. They said to the Prophet ﷺ, "O Messenger of Allah, we were in honour while we were polytheists; when we believed, we became humiliated," and they asked his permission to fight the polytheists. He said to them, "I have been commanded to pardon, so restrain your hands, establish the prayer, and give the zakah." When the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah and jihad was enjoined, a group among those who had asked his permission to fight became cowardly, and the verse was revealed concerning them.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that among these were 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, Qudamah ibn Maz'un, and their companions. On this view, His words ﴿as they fear people, or with even greater fear than the fear of Allah﴾ are said as a rebuke to them, because they preferred to delay acting on Allah's command to fight out of fear of the might of the polytheists. The comparison is therefore in the manner of hyperbole, since taking these words as a literal report does not fit their condition of virtue in faith and migration.

Al-Suddi said: ﴿those to whom it was said, restrain your hands﴾ are a people who had embraced Islam before fighting was enjoined, and who asked that fighting be enjoined upon them; but when fighting was enjoined, ﴿suddenly a group of them fear people﴾.

The exegetes differed about who is meant by the "group" in His words, ﴿suddenly a group of them fear people﴾. It was said that they are a group of those who had asked permission in Makkah to fight the polytheists. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and al-Kalbi, and it is the apparent meaning of the verse.

Perhaps what turned their resolve was that they came to be in security and safety from humiliation and harm, so the necessity to defend themselves was removed. Al-Qurtubi relates that it was said that this group were the hypocrites (munafiqun).

On this view, the wording of the verse must be interpreted as follows: the Muslims who had asked permission to kill the polytheists while they were in Makkah, when they migrated to Madinah, repeated their desire to fight the polytheists; the Prophet ﷺ repeated calming them for a time; and the hypocrites pretended to desire that, as a cover for their hypocrisy. Then when fighting was prescribed for the Muslims, the hypocrites became cowardly,

[p. 127]
and this is what fits the report about them that they fear people as with the fear of Allah or more.

The interpretation of their description by His words "from among them" is: that is, from among those to whom it was said, "restrain your hands." Although this is obscure, it is the one that harmonises with the style of the rest of the discourse in His words ﴿If good befalls them, they say, "This is from Allah"﴾ [An-Nisa: 78] and what follows it, as will come. As for al-Suddi's view, there is no need to interpret the verse this way.

The interrogative in His words ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is for wonder, and its parallels have already been mentioned. The ones being wondered at are not all of those who were told in Makkah, "restrain your hands," but a different group, whose attribute is that they fear people as they fear Allah. The wonder was attached to all of those who were told this only on the basis that a group among them was in the state described. The implied meaning is: have you not seen a group of those who were told, "restrain your hands"?

On the construction of His words ﴿with a fear like the fear of Allah or greater﴾, what is said is the same as what is said about its parallel, His words ﴿Remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with greater remembrance﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 200] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Their words ﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?﴾ are only what they said within themselves, in the sense of failing to grasp the wisdom behind the command to fight, and their thinking that it was a trial. "Al-ajal al-qarib" (the near term) is a late period that gives them time to complete their preparation, like His words ﴿Then one of you would say, "My Lord, if only You had delayed me for a near term, so I could give charity"﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 10].

It was also said that the intended meaning of "ajal" is the lifespan, meaning: "if only You had delayed us until our lifespans ended without fighting." Then it becomes a wish that fighting had not been prescribed. This is far-fetched, because it does not fit the context, since death in battle is no different from death at one's appointed term; and because it does not fit describing it as "near," since a person's term is not known to be near or far unless the intention is to make all of life short.

On both interpretations, the fighting referred to here is the first fighting they were commanded to do, and the verse, at the time of its revelation, reminded them of that when they were being prepared for the command to conquer Makkah.

Al-Suddi said: the "group" refers to some of the tribes of the Arabs who had recently entered Islam before fighting became one of its obligations; they used to wish to fight, but when fighting was prescribed for them they became cowardly because of the weakness of their faith. The fighting they feared would be the campaign against Makkah, because they feared the might of the polytheists.

Their words ﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?﴾ may be words within themselves, and they may also be words spoken aloud. The latter appears to be the definite meaning if the "group" is the group of hypocrites, for they say, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?" openly with their tongues, in order to spread weakness into the hearts of those who were preparing for it,

[p. 128]
while they do not believe that Allah has prescribed fighting for them.

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid: it was revealed concerning the Jews. On this view the verse is an example that Allah set for the Muslims whom He had obliged to fight, as a warning against falling into the same thing. It would then be in the manner of His words "Have you not seen the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, 'Send us a king'?" [Al-Baqarah: 246], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The seeing (al-ru'yah) is visual. On some of the reported views it is literally visual, and on others it is visual in the sense of being made known (tanzili), to emphasise how well known this is.

The word "khashyah" (fear) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz, a grammatical term meaning a noun clarifying the comparison) after "ashadd" (greater), as was mentioned before in His words ﴿as you remember your fathers or with greater remembrance﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 200]; what is said about it was already covered in Surat al-Baqarah.

The answer is given by His words ﴿Say: the enjoyment of this world is little﴾, which is an answer to their words ﴿Why did You not delay us to a near term?﴾, whether their statement was spoken aloud, which is clear, or was within themselves, so that they would know that Allah had informed His Messenger of what their souls concealed. That is, delay does not benefit, and clinging to delay in order to preserve life does not equal the share of the Hereafter. By this the trial they intended by their words ﴿Why did You not delay us to a near term?﴾ is nullified.

The position of His words ﴿and you will not be wronged a whit (fatilan)﴾ is that of adding to the rebuke required by His words ﴿Say: the enjoyment of this world is little﴾. That is: "and you will not have any of your written lifespans reduced, so there is no reason to fear and seek to delay the prescription of fighting." If "ajal" in ﴿Why did You not delay us to a near term?﴾ is explained as the lifespan, which is the far-fetched view, then the meaning of ﴿and you will not be wronged a whit﴾ is a correction of their belief that killing hastens the term. This would require that this be a belief of the believers, if they were the ones addressed before the details of the creed of Islam were firmly established in them, or that this is the belief of the hypocrites, if they were the ones addressed.

It was also said that the meaning of negating wrong here is that they will not be wronged by a reduction in the reward for their jihad. Its position is then that of encouragement, to remove fear, and its accusative form is as a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq, the cognate object). It was also said that the meaning is that they will not be wronged by a reduction of even the least part of their terms.

On this explanation, "tuzlamun" may be understood in the sense of "tunqasun" (you will be diminished), as in His words ﴿and did not wrong (tadhlim) anything of it﴾ [Al-Kahf: 33], meaning both gardens yielded their fruit. Then "fatilan" is the direct object, meaning: you will not be diminished in your lifespans by a moment, so there is no cause for cowardice.

[p. 128 continued]
The majority read "wa la tuzlamun" with the taa of address, on the basis that He commanded the Messenger to say it to them. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, Rawh from Ya'qub, and Khalaf read it with the yaa of the third person, on the basis that it is something Allah informed His Messenger ﷺ of, so that he might convey it to them.

"Fatil" (a thread in a date-stone's split) was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿Nay, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged a whit (fatilan)﴾ [An-Nisa: 49].

The sentence ﴿Wherever you are, death will overtake you﴾ [An-Nisa: 78] may be part of the statement related by the words ﴿Say: the enjoyment of this world is little﴾. It was not conjoined to the sentence ﴿the enjoyment of this world is little﴾ because the two aims differ: the sentence ﴿the enjoyment of this world is little﴾ and what is conjoined to it are a rebuke to them for seeking delay to a near term, whereas the sentence ﴿wherever you are﴾ [An-Nisa: 78] and so on is brought to make them aware that cowardice was what led them to seek delay to a near limit, because they imagined that the places of fighting bring death closer to people.

It is also possible that the statement has ended, and that the sentence ﴿wherever you are﴾ [An-Nisa: 78] is an address directed to them from Allah the Exalted, or an address directed to the whole community. In both cases it is an interjection between parts of the discourse.

"Aynama" (wherever) is a conditional particle that covers all places. The "wa law" (even if) in His words ﴿even if you were in towers﴾ [An-Nisa: 78] is concessive (wasliyyah). Its meaning and usage were already explained in detail at His words in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿Never will be accepted from any of them the earth full of gold, even if he offered it in ransom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91].

"Burudj" is the plural of "burj," which is a strong building or fortress. "Mushayyadah" means built with "shid," which is gypsum (jiss). It is also applied to what is raised and high, because when they extended a building, they built it with gypsum. So the description with it is meant in the allusive sense (kinaʼi, a figurative meaning by implication). The word "burudj" is also applied to the mansions of the stars in the sky, as in His words ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky burudj﴾ [Al-Furqan: 61] and His words ﴿By the sky with its burudj﴾ [Al-Buruj: 1]. It is related from Malik that he said: the "burudj" here are the burudj of the stars, meaning: even if you reached the sky. On this view the description "mushayyadah" would be a metaphor for height, which is far-fetched.

[Page 129]

﴿When good comes to them, they say, "This is from God," and when evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you." Say, "All is from God." What is the matter with these people that they can barely understand any statement?﴾ ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. We have sent you to the people as a messenger, and God is sufficient as a witness.﴾ [an-Nisa: 78–79]

It is necessary, according to the preferred view among what has been related about identifying the group mentioned in His words, ﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands"?﴾ [an-Nisa: 77], that they were a group of the emigrant believers, that the plural pronoun in His words ﴿When good comes to them﴾ refers to the hypocrites. This is because they are known from the context, and because they were mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿And among you is one who will surely lag behind﴾ [an-Nisa: 72]. The sentence then is connected as one narrative following another, since what is related in this verse befits none but the hypocrites.

The purpose then shifts from urging fighting to describing those who do not respond to fighting, because they do not believe in what the Prophet (ﷺ) conveys to them of God's promise of victory to the believers.

As for the narration of al-Suddi, it is possible that these were people from the Arab tribes who had recently entered Islam, who were on the brink of doubt. When misfortune or hardship befell them, they took it as an omen against Islam, saying, "This bad state is from the evil of Islam."

It has also been said that some of the Bedouins, when they embraced Islam and emigrated to Medina, saw their livestock multiply and their condition improve, and they praised Islam. But when illness or death struck their livestock, they took it as an omen against Islam and apostatized. From this is the report of the Bedouin who fell ill in Medina and asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to release him from his pledge of allegiance. The Prophet (ﷺ) said about him, "Medina is like a bellows: it expels its impurities and its good remains pure."

The saying intended in His words, ﴿they say, "This is from God"﴾ and ﴿they say, "This is from you"﴾, is an inner saying, because they did not dare to say that openly to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while they were displaying faith in him.

Or it is a saying they uttered among their hypocrite brethren,
[Page 130]
saying, "This is from Muhammad." In that case, the use of the second-person address (kaf al-khitab), "from you," is in the manner of reporting their speech by its essential meaning according to the situation of the reporter and the one addressed. This is a well-known mode in reporting the speech of someone absent to the person addressed when one relates his words to that person.

From this is His words, related about Jesus: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]. What was commanded was: "Worship God, your Lord and their Lord." It is reported that those who said this were the Jews. So the pronoun refers to something not mentioned in the preceding discourse, because those intended were known at the time of the revelation of the verse.

Long ago it was said to their predecessors: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they take it as an omen from Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131]. The meaning of "good" and "evil" here is what the Arabs customarily understood them to mean, before the technical usage of the Shari'ah, namely, the occurrence that is agreeable and the occurrence that is disagreeable. Like His words: ﴿But when good comes to them, they say, "This is ours." And if evil befalls them, they take it as an omen from Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131]. And His words: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201]. The fact that the verb of "befalling" is connected to both of them is evidence for this. As for "good" and "evil" in the technical sense of the Shari'ah, namely the act that earns reward and the act that earns punishment, they have no place here, because they cannot be things that befall a person, and their befalling cannot be perceived, since they are legal evaluations.

It was said: The Jews used to say, "When Muhammad came to Medina, the fruits became scarce and prices rose." So they made the Messenger's presence in Medina the cause of the occurrence of evils, and held that, were it not for him, all events would have proceeded in accordance with what suited them.

For this reason, in reporting their speech, there was used what indicates that they intended this meaning: the word "ʿinda" ("from") in both places: ﴿This is from God﴾ and ﴿This is from you﴾. For the sense of "ʿinda" here is the sense of complete causal influence, as shown by the parallelism in the expression. So if what comes "from God" means that it comes from His decree and the influence of His power, then likewise its counterpart, what comes "from the Messenger," means the same.

In al-Bukhari, it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And among the people is one who worships God on the edge﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]: "A man would come to Medina, and if his wife bore a son and his mares foaled, he would say, 'This is a good religion.' But if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say, 'This is a bad religion.'" This indicates that such a saying was made by the Arab emigrants, who were people of coarseness and harshness, when they wished to apostatize. So perhaps among them there were those who addressed the Messenger directly with words like their saying, ﴿This is from you.﴾

The meaning of ﴿from God﴾ in their belief is that He is the One who brought it to them and bestowed it upon them, as is His customary generosity toward them, especially if the one saying this was a Jew. And the meaning of "from you" is: from the ill omen of your coming, because God does not treat them except with honor. But He has begun to test them with evil in order to harm the Muslims, so that the evil reaches the Jews through the Muslims, in the manner of His words, ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who do wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25], and so on.
[Page 131]
God taught him to answer that all is from God, because there is no meaning in something being "from God" except that He is the One who decreed it and prepared its causes, since He does not directly lead them to good things.

If this is so, then just as good is from Him, so likewise evil is from Him in this sense, setting aside what He intended by good and evil. Making a distinction between them in this respect comes only from a mind lacking in disciplined reasoning, because they made some events from God and others not from God. For this reason He said, ﴿What is the matter with these people that they can barely understand any statement?﴾ That is, they are close to not understanding any statement, that is, they are almost incapable of understanding what is said to them. This is the implication of the verb "kāda" (to be on the verge of) when it occurs in a negative context, as was explained earlier at His words, ﴿and they barely did it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71].

"Iṣābah" (befalling) is the occurrence of a state or a thing upon a thing. One says: an illness befell him (aṣābahu marad), a blessing befell him (aṣābatu niʿmah), an arrow struck him (aṣābahu sahm). It is derived from the word ṣawb, which means rain, and for this reason the forms of "iṣābah" convey a sudden or overpowering occurrence.

After God commanded His Messenger with what to answer these misguided people, He taught him the reality of the distinction in the befalling of good and evil, in terms of whether the attribution is purely to God Most High or is mixed with attribution to the servant. So He said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.﴾ The address is directed to the Messenger because he is the one who conveys from God, and because this answer is meant to refute what those misguided people attributed to him, namely that he is the source of the evils that befall them.

Know that every event has an effective cause, a concurrent cause, and indications that point to it and to its consequences. These are three things that no event is free of, whether it is involuntary or voluntary, like the acts of servants. God decreed benefits and harms by His knowledge and His decree, and He created their effective causes and their means. This part belongs to God alone, by His words, ﴿Say, "All is from God."﴾

God established existence by His subtle kindnesses: He brought things into being, facilitated for them the means of survival and benefit through what He placed in them of intellects and inspirations, and surrounded all of them in every state with many kindnesses. Without these the species would not have persisted. He brought them to the principles of suitability and repelled from them, for the most part, the causes of pain. God is Subtle toward His servants. This part too belongs to God alone, by His words, ﴿Say, "All is from God."﴾
[Page 132]
God set up proofs for people concerning the benefits and harms that are acquired through the various kinds of proofs: the necessary, the rational, the customary, and the legal. He taught the ways of reaching them and the ways of turning away from them, and He pointed out the obstacles to their effect for whoever wished to prevent them. He sent the messengers and legislated the laws. Through all of this He taught us the states of things, their benefits and harms, and the consequences of these, both apparent and hidden, in this world and the next. Thus He perfected His favor, established the proof, and cut off excuses. He guided and warned by this, having created the intellects and the means of knowledge, nurtured them through reflection and inspiration, and created the incentives for teaching and learning. This part too belongs to God alone.

As for the concurrent causes of the good and evil events, and of the consequences they bring when they befall a person, these consist of the guidance to means of attaining benefits, ignorance of those means, and overlooking the obstacles to falling into them, whether in good or evil. This is in proportion to what a person acquires of the means of right guidance, and to his choice of what is good for gathering benefit, and in proportion to the opposite: the dominance of ignorance, or the dominance of desire, and throwing oneself into ruin without insight.

That is a small part in comparison with the parts we have mentioned. God gave the human a share in this part, granting him power over it. So when a good thing comes to someone, its coming to him is by God's creation without any doing of the servant in it, or by what God guided the servant through, until he knew the way to gather the good, that is, the agreeable thing, and God created in him the readiness to choose the right in what lies within his own choice of beneficial acts, according to what God Most High guided him to. Thus the favor in it belongs to God alone, for were it not for His subtle kindness, His guidance, and His direction, the person would be in bewilderment. So it is correct that the good is from God, because the greatest of its causes, or all of them, come from Him.

As for evil, although it comes by the influence of God Most High, the befalling of most of it upon a person comes from his ignorance, his negligence, his poor judgment of consequences, or his giving precedence to his desire over his right guidance. And there are evils that befall a person without his causing them, like what befell nations of earthquakes and plagues. But that is rare compared to most evils. Moreover, some of these were a recompense for an evil deed. So it is inevitable that the greater share in evil befalling a person is due to his causing it, directly or indirectly. So it is correct to attribute its causation to him, since the part of it that belongs to God alone is the smaller part.

This meaning is confirmed by what is reported in the Sahih. In the hadith of al-Tirmidhi: "No servant is afflicted with a calamity, great or small, except because of a sin, and God pardons much."
[Page 133]
The terms "good" and "evil" include things that are substances, like rain and thunderbolts, fruit and locusts, and things that are accidents, like health, the blowing of the east wind, and profit in trade, and their opposites, like sickness, deadly poisonous winds, and loss. In this category was the occasion of revelation of this verse. It also includes what is among the acts of servants, like acts of obedience that benefit the one who performs them and others, and acts of disobedience that harm the one who commits them and others. On this matter came His words: ﴿Say, "If I go astray, I go astray only to my own detriment, and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me"﴾ [Saba': 50]. This is similar in meaning to this verse, though it was not revealed concerning it.

Because this matter is subtle in understanding, God drew attention to their lack of understanding of hidden meanings by His words: ﴿What is the matter with these people that they can barely understand any statement?﴾

His words ﴿they can barely﴾ may be read in accordance with its parallels in the inversion of meaning (al-qalb), that is, "they are close to not understanding," as was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿so they slaughtered it, though they barely could have﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71]. In that case there is some sparing of them from blame. It may also be read according to the original structure of the expression, that is, "they do not come close to understanding the statement, which only the discerning comprehend," and in that case the blame is more severe.

"Fiqh" (deep understanding) is the comprehension of what requires the exertion of thought. Al-Raghib said: it is reaching a hidden knowledge through an evident knowledge, and it is more specific than "ʿilm" (knowledge). Others defined it as grasping hidden things.

The address in His words ﴿What has befallen you﴾ is directed to the Messenger, and this is the most fitting reading given the coherence of the pronouns; yet it is then acknowledged that others are like him in this respect.

The argument from this verse has become widespread for the claim that the actions of servants are created by God, according to the method of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, based on His words ﴿Say: all is from God﴾. Likewise the Mu'tazilah's argument from it has become widespread, that God does not create disobedience and evil, based on His words ﴿Whatever misfortune befalls you is from yourself﴾. Abu al-Hasan Shabib ibn Haydarah al-Maliki said in the book Hazz al-Ghalasim: The argument from it in both matters is ignorance, since it rests on the assumption that the good deed (hasanah) and the bad deed (sayyi'ah) are obedience and disobedience, and they are not so.

I say: The People of the Sunnah only argued from it by way of conceding the Mu'tazilah's argument from it, in distinguishing between the acquisition (iktisab) of good and of evil; and the general meaning of hasanah and sayyi'ah, as I have explained just now, makes the verse fit for argument. It is an approximate argument, because the fundamentals of religion are not established by apparent (zahir) texts such as general expressions (umum).

In the reporting of their saying ﴿They say: this is from God﴾ and ﴿They say: this is from you﴾, the word "'inda" ("with/from") is used to indicate the strength of the attribution of the good deed to God and of the bad deed to the Prophet (peace be upon him); that is, they said what conveys their certainty in that attribution.

When God commanded His Messenger to answer them, He said ﴿Say: all is from God﴾, in conformity with their words (mushakalah), and to express the eternal decree (al-taqdir al-azali) with God.

As for His words ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, the word "'inda" is not used in it, indicating that the beginning of the coming of the good deed is from God, while the beginning of the coming of the evil deed is from the self of the addressee, being the beginning of the one who causes the occasion of the act, not the beginning of the one who produces the effect.

His words ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, as a response to their saying: the evil is from Muhammad. That is, you were sent as a conveyor of the law and a guide, and you are not an influencer of events; and the coincidence of painful events does not indicate the falsity of the message. So the meaning of "We sent you" is "We dispatched you," like His words ﴿And We sent the winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22] and similar.

"Lil-nas" (to mankind) is connected to "arsalnaka" (We sent you), and His words "rasulan" (as a Messenger) are a circumstantial clause (hal) from "arsalnaka." The term "rasul" here means its technical religious sense known among the people of the religions: the prophet who conveys from God Most High. It is thus a titular term indicating this meaning, and it is not intended in its linguistic sense as a passive participle. For this reason its coming as a qualifying circumstantial clause for "arsalnaka" is apt, because the two meanings differ: that is, We dispatched you as a conveyor, not an influencer of events, nor a sign of the occurrence of evil events.

By this the difficulty is removed of this clause coming without any purpose other than emphasis, to the point that they were compelled to make the prepositional phrase connected to "rasulan," and that it was placed before it to indicate restriction (hasr) on account of the generality derived from the definiteness, as in the Kashshaf; that is, for all people and not for some of them. But this is an artificial interpretation for which there is no need, and the context is not one of such restriction.

That is a small part in comparison with the parts we have mentioned. God gave the human a share in this part, granting him power over it. So when a good thing comes to someone, its coming to him is by God's creation without any doing of the servant in it, or by what God guided the servant through, until he knew the way to gather the good, that is, the agreeable thing, and God created in him the readiness to choose the right in what lies within his own choice of beneficial acts, according to what God Most High guided him to. Thus the favor in it belongs to God alone, for were it not for His subtle kindness, His guidance, and His direction, the person would be in bewilderment. So it is correct that the good is from God, because the greatest of its causes, or all of them, come from Him.

As for evil, although it comes by the influence of God Most High, the befalling of most of it upon a person comes from his ignorance, his negligence, his poor judgment of consequences, or his giving precedence to his desire over his right guidance. And there are evils that befall a person without his causing them, like what befell nations of earthquakes and plagues. But that is rare compared to most evils. Moreover, some of these were a recompense for an evil deed. So it is inevitable that the greater share in evil befalling a person is due to his causing it, directly or indirectly. So it is correct to attribute its causation to him, since the part of it that belongs to God alone is the smaller part.

This meaning is confirmed by what is reported in the Sahih. In the hadith of al-Tirmidhi: "No servant is afflicted with a calamity, great or small, except because of a sin, and God pardons much."
[Page 133]
The terms "good" and "evil" include things that are substances, like rain and thunderbolts, fruit and locusts, and things that are accidents, like health, the blowing of the east wind, and profit in trade, and their opposites, like sickness, deadly poisonous winds, and loss. In this category was the occasion of revelation of this verse. It also includes what is among the acts of servants, like acts of obedience that benefit the one who performs them and others, and acts of disobedience that harm the one who commits them and others. On this matter came His words: ﴿Say, "If I go astray, I go astray only to my own detriment, and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me"﴾ [Saba': 50]. This is similar in meaning to this verse, though it was not revealed concerning it.

Because this matter is subtle in understanding, God drew attention to their lack of understanding of hidden meanings by His words: ﴿What is the matter with these people that they can barely understand any statement?﴾

His words ﴿they can barely﴾ may be read in accordance with its parallels in the inversion of meaning (al-qalb), that is, "they are close to not understanding," as was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿so they slaughtered it, though they barely could have﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71]. In that case there is some sparing of them from blame. It may also be read according to the original structure of the expression, that is, "they do not come close to understanding the statement, which only the discerning comprehend," and in that case the blame is more severe.

"Fiqh" (deep understanding) is the comprehension of what requires the exertion of thought. Al-Raghib said: it is reaching a hidden knowledge through an evident knowledge, and it is more specific than "ʿilm" (knowledge). Others defined it as grasping hidden things.

The address in His words ﴿What has befallen you﴾ is directed to the Messenger, and this is the most fitting reading given the coherence of the pronouns; yet it is then acknowledged that others are like him in this respect.

The argument from this verse has become widespread for the claim that the actions of servants are created by God, according to the method of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, based on His words ﴿Say: all is from God﴾. Likewise the Mu'tazilah's argument from it has become widespread, that God does not create disobedience and evil, based on His words ﴿Whatever misfortune befalls you is from yourself﴾. Abu al-Hasan Shabib ibn Haydarah al-Maliki said in the book Hazz al-Ghalasim: The argument from it in both matters is ignorance, since it rests on the assumption that the good deed (hasanah) and the bad deed (sayyi'ah) are obedience and disobedience, and they are not so.

I say: The People of the Sunnah only argued from it by way of conceding the Mu'tazilah's argument from it, in distinguishing between the acquisition (iktisab) of good and of evil; and the general meaning of hasanah and sayyi'ah, as I have explained just now, makes the verse fit for argument. It is an approximate argument, because the fundamentals of religion are not established by apparent (zahir) texts such as general expressions (umum).

In the reporting of their saying ﴿They say: this is from God﴾ and ﴿They say: this is from you﴾, the word "'inda" ("with/from") is used to indicate the strength of the attribution of the good deed to God and of the bad deed to the Prophet (peace be upon him); that is, they said what conveys their certainty in that attribution.

When God commanded His Messenger to answer them, He said ﴿Say: all is from God﴾, in conformity with their words (mushakalah), and to express the eternal decree (al-taqdir al-azali) with God.

As for His words ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, the word "'inda" is not used in it, indicating that the beginning of the coming of the good deed is from God, while the beginning of the coming of the evil deed is from the self of the addressee, being the beginning of the one who causes the occasion of the act, not the beginning of the one who produces the effect.

His words ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, as a response to their saying: the evil is from Muhammad. That is, you were sent as a conveyor of the law and a guide, and you are not an influencer of events; and the coincidence of painful events does not indicate the falsity of the message. So the meaning of "We sent you" is "We dispatched you," like His words ﴿And We sent the winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22] and similar.

"Lil-nas" (to mankind) is connected to "arsalnaka" (We sent you), and His words "rasulan" (as a Messenger) are a circumstantial clause (hal) from "arsalnaka." The term "rasul" here means its technical religious sense known among the people of the religions: the prophet who conveys from God Most High. It is thus a titular term indicating this meaning, and it is not intended in its linguistic sense as a passive participle. For this reason its coming as a qualifying circumstantial clause for "arsalnaka" is apt, because the two meanings differ: that is, We dispatched you as a conveyor, not an influencer of events, nor a sign of the occurrence of evil events.

By this the difficulty is removed of this clause coming without any purpose other than emphasis, to the point that they were compelled to make the prepositional phrase connected to "rasulan," and that it was placed before it to indicate restriction (hasr) on account of the generality derived from the definiteness, as in the Kashshaf; that is, for all people and not for some of them. But this is an artificial interpretation for which there is no need, and the context is not one of such restriction.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 80–81:

Page 135
﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah; and whoever turns away — We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Obedience." But when they leave your presence, a faction of them plans by night other than what you say. But Allah records what they plan by night. So turn away from them and rely upon Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾

This is like a complement to His saying ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾ [an-Nisa: 79], in terms of what it contains of refuting their belief that the Messenger is the source of the evils that afflict them, and then from His saying ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾ [an-Nisa: 79], and so on.

It indicates that there is a difference between the Creator and the created in terms of causation, and that the Message is another meaning. By His saying ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ He guarded against the listeners' supposing a distinction between Allah and His Messenger in matters of legislation. So He affirmed that the Messenger, in his conveying, only conveys from Allah; his command is Allah's command, his prohibition is Allah's prohibition, and his obedience is Allah's obedience. His saying ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ indicates all of this, because it includes the affirmation of his being a messenger and implies that he commands and forbids, and that this is a conveying of the intent of Allah the Exalted. So whoever is aware of this, or is heedless of it, Allah has made clear to him the variation of the Messenger's positions.

As for whoever turns away or refuses and persists in obstinacy, ﴿We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾, i.e., a protector for them and one responsible for their turning away. This is an allusion to them and a threat to them that He has diverted him from concerning himself with them, so it is known that Allah will take charge of their punishment.

The root meaning of tawalli is turning away and retreating. It has preceded in His saying ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the earth to cause corruption therein﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205] and in His saying ﴿What turned them away from their qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here it is used metaphorically for disobedience and not listening to the call.

"Then He explained that, because of the weakness of their souls, they do not openly turn away, but rather display obedience. So when the Messenger commands them or forbids them, they say to him: "Ta'ah" — i.e., our matter is obedience — a word by which they indicate compliance. Perhaps it is said: "Sam'un wa ta'ah" (we hear and obey). It is a verbal noun in the nominative, being the predicate of an omitted subject,

Page 136
i.e., our affair or our state is obedience, as in His saying ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ [Yusuf: 18]. It is not a substitute for the absolute object which is replaced for the verb, which is changed from the accusative to the nominative to indicate permanence, like "qala salamun" (Peace said). For the intent here is not the bringing about of obedience; rather the intent is that we will obey and there will be no disobedience from us.

"Baraza" means "they went out"; the original meaning of al-buruz is appearance, and its use for going out became common as a metonymy.

"Bayyata" here means to plan a matter secretly and conceal it, because the original sense of al-bayat is doing something at night, and the Arabs borrow this to the meaning of secrecy, since the night is the best concealer of secrets. For this reason they say: "This is a matter decided by night," meaning no one became aware of it. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

They resolved their matter by night, and when they awoke, a clamour was theirs.

Abu Sufyan said: "This is a matter decided by night." And He, the Exalted, said ﴿We will surely attack him and his family by night﴾ [an-Naml: 49], i.e., we will kill them by night. And He said ﴿And He is with them when they plan by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾ [an-Nisa: 108]. The taa' of the present tense in ﴿other than what you say﴾ is for the feminine third person, referring to the faction; it is also permissible that the address be to the Prophet ﴿ﷺ﴾, i.e., other than what you say to them, and they respond to it with their saying: "Ta'ah."

The meaning of ﴿But Allah records what they plan by night﴾ is a threat, informing them that He will not let them escape His punishment, so the delay of the punishment for a period should not deceive them. By the present-tense form in His saying "yaktub" (records) it indicates the continual renewal of this, and that nothing of it is lost.

His saying ﴿So turn away from them﴾ is a command to disregard them and that their opposition is not to be feared, and that he should rely upon Allah ﴿and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾, i.e., one relied upon, and he should not rely on the obedience of these people, nor should their opposition grieve him.

The majority read ﴿bayyata ta'ifatun﴾ with the taa' of bayyata made distinct from the ta' of ta'ifatun. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read it with the assimilation of the taa' into the ta' for lightness, because their places of articulation are close.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 82:

Page 137
﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.﴾

The fa' (فاء) here is a continuation (tafri') of the preceding discourse, which concerns these hypocrites, or the open disbelievers, and their turning away from what was addressed to them concerning him in the words ﴿And whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ [an-Nisa': 80], and in their saying "obedience," then their plotting disobedience regarding what they had been promised of obedience concerning him. Since all of that was a consequence of concealing disbelief, or doubt, or preferring what in their view was better than what they were commanded, and since their persistence in that, despite the manifest proofs of the religion, indicated their scant understanding of the Qur'an and their weak benefit from it, the context called for following with a question about their lack of understanding. The interrogation is therefore a rebuke (inkari) for censure and wonder at their persistence in ignorance despite the abundance of the means of reflection available to them.

Allah challenged these people with the meanings of the Qur'an, just as He challenged them with its wording, on account of its eloquence. The hypocrites had doubted that the Qur'an was from Allah; therefore they would show obedience to whatever it commanded them, but when they left the gathering of the Prophet (ﷺ) they would oppose what he had commanded them, due to their lack of trust. They would raise doubts and be doubtful whenever some apparent contradiction appeared to them. So Allah commanded them to reflect upon the Qur'an, as He said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is allegorical﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 7], and so on.

Tadabbur (تدبّر) is derived from dubur (دُبُر), meaning the back. The Arabs formed a verb from dubur, saying tadabbara when one looked at the dubur of a matter, i.e., its hidden side or its outcome. It is among the verbs derived from solid nouns. Tadabbur is transitive to the one who contemplates it directly, as one says tadabbara al-amr (تدبّر الأمر).

So the meaning of ﴿they reflect upon the Qur'an﴾ is that they contemplate its significance. This admits two meanings: first, that they contemplate the indication of the details of its verses upon the aims to which it guided the Muslims, i.e., reflection upon its details; second, that they contemplate the indication of the Qur'an as a whole, by its eloquence, that it is from Allah and that the one who brought it is truthful. The context of these verses favours taking tadabbur here in the first sense, i.e., "If they had contemplated and reflected upon the guidance of the Qur'an, they would have obtained great good, and they would not have remained in their trial, which is the cause of their concealing disbelief while displaying Islam." Both meanings suit their situation, but the first is more closely connected with what is related of their conditions.

His saying "﴿Had it been from other than Allah﴾ etc." may be a conjunction (atf) upon the interrogative sentence, so that they are commanded to reflect upon its details and informed of what indicates that it is from Allah, namely the absence of discrepancy from it. Then the command to reflect is general, and this is a particular instance of reflection, mentioned here to seize the opportunity of the occasion to overwhelm them with evidence for the truthfulness of the Messenger. It is then an addition to the rebuke for which the speech was brought, mentioned because it is important with respect to them, since they were in doubt about their affair. This construction is most fitting with the first of the two meanings of tadabbur here. It is also possible that the sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the Qur'an, and then it is a qualifier of tadabbur, i.e., "Do they not reflect upon the absence of discrepancy in it, so that they would know that it is from Allah?" This is most fitting with the second of the two meanings of tadabbur.

As support for the first construction, one may note that this addition is not mentioned in the similar verse in Surat Muhammad, where He says: ﴿And when a decisive surah is sent down and fighting is mentioned therein … Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24]. These are subtle points of the interpretation of this verse which all the exegetes have neglected.

As for "ikhtilaf" (اختلاف), it appears that what is intended is discrepancy of part with part, i.e., its inconsistency. It may also be its discrepancy with their conditions: that is, "they would find in it a discrepancy between what it mentions of their conditions and the reality," so let them suffice with that in knowing that it is from Allah, since it describes what is in their hearts with the description of one who has knowledge of the unseen. This is a brief and remarkable argument, intended to cut off their excuse for persisting in disbelief. The discrepancy is described as "much" (كثيرًا) in the case that is impossible to occur, by the implication of (لو). This is so that the one who reflects knows that the absence of discrepancy from it altogether is the greatest proof that it is from Allah. This restriction is not considered in the opposite clause of the answer to (لو), so that clause is not to be understood as restricted by the word "much"; rather it is to be understood thus: "But it is from Allah, so there is no discrepancy in it at all."

[Page 139]

﴿When news comes to them concerning security or fear, they spread it about. If they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those among them who seek to draw out its meaning would have known it. And were it not for the grace of God upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few.﴾

This is a continuation of the clause ﴿And they say: "Obedience"﴾ [al-Nisa larr: 81]. The plural pronoun refers back to the pronouns preceding it, which point to the hypocrites (munafiqun). This fits the context, and the only thing that disturbs this reading is His words "and to those in authority among them," which you will understand when its interpretation is explained. It has also been said that this pronoun refers to a group of weaker believers, those with little experience and weak resolve. This suits His words "and to those in authority among them" on the surface, and in that case the referent of the pronoun is omitted from the speech, relying on the contextual indication of the circumstances of revelation, as in His words ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32].

The discourse is directed as a rebuke to the hypocrites and a reproach to those Muslims, naive as they were, who accept such spreading of news.

The meaning of ﴿came to them a matter﴾ is that they were informed of it. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And that is from a report that came to me."

So "coming" is a conventional metaphor (majaz 'urfi, a metaphor fixed by common usage) for hearing news, like its counterparts: "reached," "arrived at him," and "came to him." al-Nabigha said:

"Does it come to me, may you not be cursed, that you have blamed me?"

The word "matter" here means "thing," and here it means "news," by the indication of His words "spread it about."

The meaning of "spread" (adha'u) is "disseminated." It takes the news as a direct object and also with the preposition bi-, so one says adhaʿahu and adha'a bihi. The bi- here emphasizes adherence, as in ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

The meaning is: when they heard news about the expeditions of the Muslims, whether of security, that is, victory that brings security to the Muslims, or of fear, that is, what causes fear to the Muslims, namely the enemy's increasing power over them,

[Page 140]

they hastened to spread it. Or, when they heard news from the Messenger, peace be upon him, and his companions concerning the management of the affairs of the Muslims, whether in circumstances of security or fear, they spoke of those reports in both situations and spread them among the people. Their aim was to discourage preparation: when news of security came, so that the believers would be caught off guard, and their aim was to cause cowardice when news of fear came; and they varied their excuses to prepare for staying behind from the campaign when they were called to it. So God warned the believers against the schemes of these people, and alerted these people to their inner intentions, and cut off their excuse in their plotting, through His words "And if they had referred it to the Messenger," and so on. That is: were it not that they intended evil, they would have sought to verify the news from the Messenger and from the people of judgment.

On the view that the pronoun refers to the believers, the verse is a reproach to the believers for this hastiness in spreading news, and a command to them to bring such news to the Messenger and to the leaders of the Companions so that they may place it in its proper context and teach them its implications.

It has also been said: the hypocrites would fabricate reports of security or fear, contrary to reality, so that the Muslims would think there was security when there was fear and would thus not take precautions, or fear when there was security, so that their affairs would be thrown into disorder and their social conditions broken. So when the common Muslims heard this from the hypocrites, it spread among them and they spread it.

Thus the hypocrites' ploy succeeded and their scheme worked. God rebuked them and taught them to bring the matter to the Messenger and the foremost of his Companions before spreading it, so that they would know the reality of the report and its condition, whether true or false, and take precautions for each situation, thus the believers would be safe from the hypocrites' deceit, which they intended. This is distant from His words "came to them." On this view, His words "would have known it" are the indication of the response to "if" (law) and its cause. The response has been replaced by this and the caused element has been omitted, since the intended meaning is: "those among them who seek to draw out its meaning from those in authority would have known it, and they would have explained it to them in its correct form."

It is also permissible that the meaning be: "If they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, the hypocrites who fabricated the report would have known that, and they would have been frustrated, since they would be certain that their trick had not succeeded against the Muslims." On this reading, the relative pronoun refers to those who fabricated, by the indication of the context, and the second "among them" pronoun refers to the hypocrites, by the indication of the context.

"Return" (radd) in its literal sense is sending something back to the place or hand it was in. It is used here metaphorically for conveying the news to those most entitled to knowledge of it. "Those in authority" (uli al-amr) are the senior Muslims and the people of judgment

[Page 141]

among them.
