If the ones being spoken of are the hypocrites, then describing those in authority as "among them" follows the apparent sense and the loosening of the reins, that is: those in authority who make themselves part of them. If the ones being spoken of are the believers, then the partitive sense is clear.

"Istinbat" (drawing out) in its literal sense means seeking nabat, with a vowel on the first letter. This is the first water that comes out of a well when it is dug. Here it is a metaphor for knowing the reality of a thing and recognizing its consequences. Its origin is an implicit metaphor (makniyyah): the occurring news is compared to a pit from which water is sought, and mentioning "drawing out" is an imaginative element (takhyil). This metaphor became so common that it became a conventional literal meaning, so that istinbat came to mean explanation and clarification, and the verb is made to take the matter as its object according to the conventional meaning. Were it not for this, one would say "they draw out from it," as is obvious; or it is with the preposition omitted.

If you follow the possibility that "they draw out" (yastanbitun) means "they fabricate" (yakhtaliqun), as mentioned earlier, then "they draw it out" becomes a subordinate metaphor: the fabricated report is compared to water dug out from it, and "draw out" is used in the sense of "fabricate," and the verb is extended to the pronoun for the report because it is what is extracted. The Arabs use the metaphor of water conditions very often, as in their saying "he sends forth and brings to the watering place," and their saying "he struck fifths for sixths," and their saying "he inclines toward such-and-such," and His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed for those who did wrong is a portion like the portion of their companions﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 59]. And 'Abdah ibn al-Tabib said:

"So Sha's is entitled to a share of your generosity."

From this comes their saying: "The people drew water in turns" (tasajal al-qawm), its origin being from the sajl, which is the bucket.

Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"When I drink in the morning four times, my waistcloth loosens, and I follow my bucket with its rope in generosity."

So he mentions the bucket and the rope. al-Nabigha said:

"Hooks of curved iron on strong ropes, pulled by hands toward you, drawing."

And he said:

"Were it not for Abu al-Shaqra, a drawer would not have ceased, working with a hook at one of the ropes."

[Page 142]

They also say: "He seized the opportunity" (intahaza al-fursa), and "opportunity" (al-fursa) is the turn at drinking. They also say: "The people departed from the opinion of so-and-so and came to his opinion."

His words "among them" describe those who draw it out, and they are specifically the leaders among the Muslims, that is: they bring it to the group of those in authority, so that those among them who understand will grasp it; and if all of them understand it, that is even more fitting.

His words "And were it not for the grace of God upon you and His mercy" are a favor in guiding them to kinds of benefit, and a warning against plots, snares of Satan, and his helpers.

The exception "except for a few" is from the general sense of circumstances implied by "you would have followed." That is: except in a few circumstances. If by God's grace and mercy is meant what includes the mission and what follows it, then the "few" refers to the situations in which souls are led by intellectual or habitual restraint. If by grace and mercy is meant the counsel and guidance, then the "few" refers to what is known from the rules of Islam. It is also possible to take it as an exception from the pronoun in "you followed," that is: except a few of you, so that following means following such plots that do not succeed against the people of judgment among the believers.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, verse 84:**

﴿So fight in the way of God; you are not charged except with yourself. And urge the believers. Perhaps God will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve. God is greater in violence and greater in punishment.﴾

This is a consequential connection (*tafrīʿ*) to what preceded: the command to fight, the description of those who discourage others from it, those who complain about it, and those who try to tempt the believers concerning it. All of this has given emphasis to the matter of fighting and to urging it, so the discourse was prepared for the consequential command to fight.

You may also take the *fāʾ* as an eloquent *fāʾ* (*fāʾ faṣīḥa*), after those many sentences, meaning: "If the matter is as you have known, then fight in the way of God." This returns to the earlier exhortation to jihad, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (*iʿtirāḍ*). Thus the verse obligated the Messenger ﷺ to fight, and obligated him to convey to the believers the command to fight and to urge them to it. So it expressed this by His saying, ﴿you are not charged except with yourself﴾ and ﴿urge the believers﴾. This style is one of the ways of inciting and urging someone other than the one addressed, because the obligation of fighting falls upon the Messenger, and its obligation upon all the believers is already known from His saying, ﴿So let those fight in the way of God who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter﴾ (Q. 4:74). So this is a command addressed to the exemplar, in what people must follow him in. It also clarified to them the reason for the command, which is the hope of restraining the violence of the polytheists. Here *ʿasā* (perhaps) is used figuratively to mean a promise. The intended people here are the disbelievers of Mecca, so these verses prepare for the conquest of Mecca.

The clause ﴿God is greater in violence and greater in punishment﴾ is a concluding phrase (*tadhyīl*) confirming the hope or the promise. The meaning is that He is greater in violence when He wills to manifest that. Among the indications of this will is obedience to His commands, among which is preparation and awaiting the causes together with their means.

*Al-Tankīl* is a punishment by which the one who sees it is deterred, not only the one who is punished with it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 4, verse 85:**

﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will bear a portion of it. And Allah is ever Controlling over all things.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh clause without grammatical dependence on what precedes it), which carries the sense of a concluding statement (*tadhyil*, a sentence that sums up and affirms the preceding meaning) and of causal explanation (*ta'lil*, giving the reason for what was said). It follows His saying ﴿You are not charged except with yourself, and urge the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 84]. It is good news to the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, that the struggle of those who fight through his call will bring him a great share of reward, for his urging them is a means of conveying them to great goods. So this verse came with this general ruling, in keeping with the Qur'an's habit of seizing opportunities for guidance.

From its generality it is known that urging to fight in the way of Allah is among the good intercessions, and that the efforts of those who discourage people are among the evil intercessions. The verse therefore informs both groups of their respective states. The intended purpose, along with this, is to encourage mediation in good and to warn against its opposite.

*Shafa'ah* (intercession) means mediation in bringing about a benefit or averting a harm, whether it is by a request from the one who benefits or not. It has been mentioned in His saying ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48] in Surah al-Baqarah. In a hadith: "Intercede, and you will be rewarded."

Describing it as *hasanah* (good) is a clarifying description, because *shafa'ah* is used only for mediation in good. As for applying *shafa'ah* to striving to bring about harm, it is a figure of speech by association (*mushakalah*, using a word for something else because it is paired with the word in the same context), and its indicator is its description as *say'ah* (evil), since one does not say "he interceded for the one who strove to bring evil."

*Nasib* (share): the portion of anything, whether good or bad. It was mentioned in His saying ﴿For them is a share of what they have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 202] in Surah al-Baqarah.

*Kifl*, with a kasra on the *kaf* and a sukun on the *fa'*, is likewise a portion or share. I have not clearly determined the derivation of this word. *Kifl* is also used in the sense of "equivalent," so from the two explanations it is taken that *kifl* is a share equivalent to another share.

The author of *Lisan al-Arab* said: "One does not say 'this is the *kifl* of so-and-so' until a like of it has been prepared for another." He did not attribute this to a source, and al-Fakhr attributed it to Ibn al-Muzaffar. As far as I know, no one other than these two has mentioned this, and perhaps usage does not support it. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾.

Can what Ibn al-Muzaffar said be relied upon? Ibn al-Muzaffar is Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Muzaffar al-Hatimi, the man of letters and contemporary of al-Mutanabbi. In *Mufradat* of al-Raghib, *kifl* is the share of evil and of severity, and it is borrowed from *kifl*, which means a bad thing. Thus the reward in the case of good intercession is described as *nasib*, as a hint that he may receive a greater reward than the reward of the one he interceded for.

The clause ﴿And Allah is ever Controlling over all things﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) to the clause ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession﴾ and the verse, to convey that Allah recompenses every deed with what suits it, whether good or evil.

*Muqit* means the Preserver, the Watchful, the Witness, and the Capable. According to Abu 'Ubaydah its original meaning is "the Preserver." It is an active participle from *aqat*, meaning to provide sustenance, so its form is *muf'il* and its middle radical is a waw. It has been used figuratively in the meanings of preservation and witnessing through the relation of necessity, because whoever provides sustenance for someone has preserved them from want or from destruction. Here it is used in the sense of "overseeing," or it implies that meaning, as is indicated by its construction with the preposition *'ala* (over).

Among the names of Allah the Exalted is *al-Muqit*. Al-Ghazali explained it as "the One who conveys sustenance," which returns to the meaning of the Provider, though it is more specific. It also means "the One who has dominion over a thing and is capable of it," and His saying ﴿And Allah is ever Controlling over all things﴾ points to this. Thus it returns to power and knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 86:

Page 145

﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with one better than it, or return it. Indeed, Allah is ever a Reckoner over all things.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession [will have a share of it]﴾ [al-Nisa: 85], in terms of what the preceding clause aims at, namely encouragement toward good intercession and warning against evil intercession. This includes encouragement to accept good intercession and to reject evil intercession.

Since it is the nature of the intercessor to enter upon the one whose intercession is sought with a greeting of peace, to make him feel at ease so that he will accept the intercession, the connection in this conjunction is that intercession requires the presence of the intercessor before the one being petitioned, and that the manner in which the petitioned person receives the intercessor indicates the degree of his readiness to accept the intercession, and that the first signs of meeting are the greeting of peace and its return.

So God taught the Muslims the etiquette of acceptance and meeting in intercession and in other matters, and intercessions had a great standing among them.

In the hadith: "A man passed by, and the Messenger of Allah said: What do you say about him? They said: He is worthy, if he intercedes, to be interceded for..." the hadith [continues]. When the one petitioned accepts the intercession, he has pleased the heart of the intercessor; and when he does not accept it, the goodness of the greeting is in general a source of satisfaction for him. This is the way of the Qur'an in seizing opportunities for guidance and discipline.

By this explanation, the perplexity that arose regarding the coherence of this verse with what precedes it is dispelled for you, and you are spared from resorting to the weak connections to which people have turned.

His saying ﴿greet with one better than it﴾ indicates the command to return the greeting, and the obligation of returning it, because the original form of the imperative is for obligation, according to the position of the majority regarding the force of the imperative form. For this reason, the jurists agreed on the obligation of returning the greeting.

Then they differed when those greeted are a group: Does the return become obligatory upon each one of them? Malik said: it is obligatory upon the group as a collective obligation (wujub al-kifaya); so if one of the group returns it, it suffices for them. A sound hadith has been narrated on this; however, if the group is large, returning it by all becomes confused noise.

Abu Hanifa said: the return is an individual obligation (fard) upon each person of the group by himself. Perhaps his evidence in this is analogy (qiyas).

Page 146

His saying ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting﴾ indicates that initiating the greeting is something known among them, and its evidence is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their inhabitants﴾ [al-Nur: 27], which will come in Surat al-Nur.

His saying ﴿with one better than it, or return it﴾ conveys the choice between the two states, and it is known from the placing of ﴿with one better than it﴾ first that this is more excellent.

The root of "hayyā" (to greet) linguistically means to invoke life for him, and it is perhaps of the kind of nahṭ (word-formation by contraction) from the saying of the speaker: "ḥayyāka Allāh," i.e., God granted you long life. Thus one says to a king: "ḥayyāka Allāh." For this reason it occurs in the supplication of the tashahhud: "al-taḥiyyātu lillāh," i.e., He is the one deserving of them, not the kings of people. Al-Nabigha said:

They are greeted with basil on the day of the sabasib — i.e., they are greeted, with basil being presented, on the day of the festival of Palm Sunday. The greeting was specific to kings with the formula "ḥayyāka Allāh" usually; therefore they applied the term "taḥiyya" to kingship, in the saying of Zuhayr ibn Janab al-Kalbi:

And everything the young man attained, I have attained, except the taḥiyya.

He means that he reached the peak of glory except kingship. And this is what al-Ma'arri meant by his saying:

The greeting of Kisra and Tubba' in praise — for your quarter I do not accept the greeting of the four.

This verse is among the etiquettes of Islam: God taught by it that they should return the greeting to the one who greets with something better than his greeting or with its equivalent, so as to nullify what existed in the Jahiliyya of disparity between nobles and commoners.

The greeting is "better" through an increase in meaning; therefore they said regarding His saying ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 25]: the greeting of Ibrahim was better, since he expressed it with what is stronger in Arabic speech, namely the nominative of the verbal noun, to indicate permanence and to make one forget the occurrence which the accusative of the verbal noun implies. Ibrahim's language did not have anything like this, but it is of the wondrous rendering.

"For this reason the Islamic greeting is: 'as-salamu 'alaykum,' and its return: 'wa 'alaykumu as-salam,' because fronting the prepositional phrase there serves to give importance to the addressed pronoun."

Some people said: the waw in the return of the greeting conveys the meaning of addition; so if the greeter had reached the furthest extent of greeting by saying:

Page 147

"as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh," then when the one returning says "wa 'alaykumu as-salam" etc., he has returned it with something better by the addition of the waw. But this is an error.

The meaning of "ruddūhā" is "return its like," and this is like their saying: "I have a dirham and its half," because of the evident impossibility of returning the greeting itself; and like His saying: ﴿If a man dies leaving no child and has a sister, she has half of what he left, and he inherits from her﴾ [al-Nisa: 176], where the pronoun of "huwa" and the "ha'" of "yarithuha" refer to the two words, not to the two persons.

The command indicates the obligation of returning the greeting. There is no indication in the verse regarding the ruling on initiating the greeting; that is established by the Sunna, for encouragement toward it. They mentioned that the Arabs did not put the name of the one greeted, governed by 'ala, before the greeting at the beginning except in elegy, as in the saying of 'Abda ibn al-Tabib:

Upon you is the peace of God, Qays ibn 'Asim, and His mercy, as much as He willed to show mercy.

And in the saying of al-Shammakh:

Upon you is peace from the commander, and the hand of God has blessed that torn hide.

He laments 'Uthman ibn 'Affan or 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Abu Dawud narrated that "Jabir ibn Sulaym greeted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying: 'Upon you is peace, O Messenger of Allah.' He said to him: 'Indeed, "upon you is peace" is the greeting of the dead; say: "as-salamu 'alayka."'"

The concluding phrase, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever a Reckoner over all things﴾, is for the purpose of expressing favor through these beneficial instructions.

Al-Hasib: the Knower. It is an adjectival form (sifa mushabbaha) from ḥasiba with a kasra on the sin, which is one of the verbs of the heart; it was transferred to the pattern fa'ula with a damma on its ʿayn, when it is intended that knowledge is an essential attribute of Him. With this, its transitivity decreased, so it is restricted to one object; then it was made to imply the meaning of "counting/reckoning," so it takes "ʿalā" to it. It may also be of the forms of intensification. It has been said: al-Hasib here means "al-muhasib" (the Reckoner), like al-akil and al-shari b. According to their statement, the concluding phrase is a promise of reward in proportion to the excellence of returning the greeting, or a threat of evil recompense for abandoning the return altogether. The description of God as ḥasib is emphasized by two emphatics: the particle inna and the verb kana, which indicate that this is a firmly established, eternal attribute.

Surah 4, verse 87 — Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir

Page 148

﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him. He will surely gather you for the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾

This is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), which gathers together the glorification of Allah, a threat, a warning against disobeying His command, an affirmation of belief in the Day of Resurrection (ba'th), and a rebuttal of the polytheism of some of the hypocrites (munafiqin) and their denial of resurrection.

The word Allah (ism al-jalalah) is the subject (mubtada'). The clause ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah) between the subject and its predicate, for the glorification of Allah.

The clause "He will surely gather you" (la-yajma'anna-kum) is the answer to an elided oath (qasam mahdhuf), and the whole of it occupies the position of the predicate (khabar) of the subject Allah. This predicate is emphasised by the oath particle (lam al-qasam), the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid), and by placing the subject-noun before the verbal predicate, in order to strengthen the certainty of this predicate, as a refutation of the denial of those who denied resurrection.

The phrase ﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ means a negation that doubt, in its generic sense, could touch it, i.e., regarding its coming. The intended meaning is that there is no real doubt concerning it; or that the doubting of the doubters, due to its weakness, has been treated as though it were the non-existent category.

The interrogative "who is more truthful than Allah" is a denying interrogative (istifham inkari). "Hadithan" (in statement) is a specifier (tamyiz) for the comparative form (fi'l al-tafdil) in terms of its relation.

**Translation:**

This is a consequence (*tafri'*, a derived ruling or implication) of the reports about the hypocrites that came before, since what has been described of their conditions leaves no doubt among the believers about the corruption of their inner intentions and their disbelief. Alternatively, it is a consequence of His saying: ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾. Since Allah has spoken about them with what He described in the preceding verses, there is no room for hesitation about the evil of their intentions and their disbelief. So the position of the *fa'* (the connecting "then/so") here is like its position in His saying ﴿So fight in the cause of Allah﴾ [4:84] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The interrogative is for expressing wonder and reproach. The definite article in *al-munafiqin* (the hypocrites) is for a known reference (*al-'ahd*). *Fi'atayn* (two groups) is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) referring to the pronoun governed by the preposition *lam* (to you), so it is a qualifier of its governing element, which is the rebuke. It is therefore understood that the object of the rebuke is the division. *Fi al-munafiqin* (regarding the hypocrites) is connected to *fi'atayn* because it is interpreted as meaning "divided," and its meaning is: regarding the matter of the hypocrites, because the ruling does not attach to the persons of the hypocrites themselves.

*Al-fi'ah* (group) means a company or party. Its form is *fi'lah*, and it is derived from *al-fay'* (return), because some of them return to others in their affairs. Its original form was *fay'*, and they deleted the *yā'* from its middle because of frequent use and compensated for it with the *hā'*.

It is known that the division into two groups is only a division within one of two states, and the context of the speech concerns faith and disbelief. That is: what is the matter with you, dividing between one who declares them disbelievers and one who excuses them? It also concerns applying the rulings of faith or disbelief to them. It was said: this verse was revealed concerning those who withdrew on the day of Uhud, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his followers. The Muslims disagreed about describing them as believers or disbelievers because of that action.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: Some people from among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from Uhud, and the people were divided into two groups regarding them. One group said: Kill them. Another group said: No. So the verse was revealed: ﴿What is the matter with you regarding the hypocrites, [that you are] two groups?﴾

He also said: [the city] is good (*taybah*), it expels impurity just as fire expels the dross of silver. That is, the Prophet (ﷺ) did not kill them, going by their outward state of professing Islam. So the verse serves to show that there should have been no hesitation about their matter.

From Mujahid: it was revealed concerning a people from Makkah who showed faith, emigrated to Madinah, and then asked permission to return to Makkah to bring merchandise they would trade in, claiming that they had remained believers all along. The Muslims disagreed about their status: were they polytheists or Muslims?

What clarifies this is what is reported "from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning a people from Makkah who concealed polytheism and showed Islam to the Muslims, so that they would be safe from being attacked by the Muslims when they went out on trade or the like. It reached the Muslims that they had set out from Makkah on a trade mission. A group of the Muslims said: We will ride out against them and fight them. Another group said: How can we kill them when they have pronounced Islam? The Muslims disagreed about this, and the Messenger of Allah did not pronounce judgment on either of the two groups until the verse was revealed."

From al-Dahhak: it was revealed concerning a people who showed Islam in Makkah without emigrating, and who used to support the polytheists against the Muslims. These are the ones of whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, [the angels] will say: "In what [condition] were you?"﴾ [4:97], and the rest of the verse.

I think that all these groups were known at the time the verse was revealed, so they were examples of its generality. The verse is general concerning them and concerning others: everyone who was known for hypocrisy at that time, from the people of Madinah and the people of Makkah.

The apparent view is that the verse was revealed after the time for fighting them had passed, with the intention of not confronting them at the time of their departure, leading them on (*istidraj*) until the day of the conquest of Makkah.

According to all the possibilities, the locus of the blame is the error in *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning, the exertion of judgment) due to the weakness of the evidence of those who erred, because the indications of the disbelief of those spoken about were stronger than the evidence of their Islam, which was merely the utterance of the words of Islam, without showing loyalty to the Muslims.

This verse is evidence that a *mujtahid* (one who exercises ijtihad) who relies on weak evidence, of the kind that a scholar would not normally rely on, is not far from blame in this world, in that he errs in a matter in which people of knowledge do not err in such a case.

The clause ﴿And Allah has returned them [to their former state] because of what they earned﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). That is: if you have disagreed about them, Allah has already returned them to their evil state, because the meaning of *arkasa* is to return someone to *al-riks*, and *al-riks* is close to *al-rijs* (filth).

In the sound hadith about the dung: "Indeed, this is *riks*." It was also said that the meaning of *arkasa* is *nakkasa* (to overturn, to cause to fall back), that is, to return them in a shameful manner, and this is close to the first meaning. Allah made their return to disbelief a recompense for the badness of their belief and the scarcity of their sincerity with His Messenger (ﷺ), for deeds generate similar deeds: a good deed brings more good deeds, and an evil deed brings the extreme of sins. For this reason the Qur'an repeatedly mentions that a deed is a cause for reaching its ends of the same kind.

His saying ﴿Do you want to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ is a explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*), arising from the rebuke and wonder in His saying ﴿What is the matter with you regarding the hypocrites, [that you are] two groups?﴾, because the listeners await an explanation of the reason for the rebuke and ask what they should do regarding these hypocrites.

The denunciatory interrogative mixed with reproach indicates a omitted clause, which is the locus of the explanatory resumption, and its estimated form is: Indeed Allah has sent them astray. ﴿Do you want to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ This is based on the premise that His saying ﴿And Allah has returned them﴾ does not mean that He sent them astray, but rather that He made their condition evil. Evil condition is a general matter that requires explanation, so the separation of the clause is the separation of resumption.

If you take the meaning of ﴿And Allah has returned them﴾ to be that He returned them to disbelief, then the clause ﴿Do you want...﴾ is a new independent sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*), and the reason for the separation is that it turns to reproach and denunciation after the clause ﴿And Allah has returned them﴾, which is declarative. So the separation is due to complete disconnection because the two aims differ.

The most apparent view is that the pronoun in "they wish" refers to the hypocrites mentioned in His saying ﴿So what is [the matter] with you regarding the hypocrites, [that you have become] two groups?﴾ [al-Nisa': 88]. God exposed this group, and informed the Muslims that they conceal disbelief and that they seek to turn back to disbelief any of the Muslims whom they are able to turn back.

Accordingly, His saying ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of God﴾, if it is taken in the apparent sense of emigration (hijrah), fits only what preceded regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) transmitted from Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas, and does not fit what is in the Sahih (the authentic collection of Bukhari and Muslim) from Zayd ibn Thabit. Therefore the interpretation of emigration as striving in the way of God (jihad) is determined. So God forbade the Muslims from their allegiance until they go out in the way of God in a military campaign (ghazwah) that takes place after the revelation of the verse, because the battle of Uhud, from which 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions withdrew, had already taken place before the revelation of this surah.

How eloquent is the expression regarding the endeavour of the believers by the verb "will," in His saying ﴿Do you wish to guide those whom God has led astray?﴾ [al-Nisa': 88], and regarding the endeavour of the hypocrites by "wish" (wudd), because will gives rise to action. The believers consider the attainment of faith by the hypocrites to be near, because faith is close to the natural disposition (fitrah) of people, while the hypocrites know that the believers do not turn back from their religion, and they see the believers' love for them. Therefore their seeking the disbelief of the believers was nothing but a wishful desire (tamanni), so it was expressed by bare wudd.

[p. 152]

The clause ﴿so you would be alike﴾ serves to emphasize the content of His saying "as they disbelieved," and its purpose is to warn the Muslims against falling into the snare of the hypocrites.

His saying ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of God﴾ is a sign God established for the Muslims by which to recognize the disbelief of those who display Islam, so that no disagreement among them regarding their status remains. It is a clear sign, and there remains no hidden hypocrisy except the hypocrisy of the hypocrites of Medina.

Emigration in the way of God is the departure from Mecca to Medina with the intention of separating from the people of Mecca. For this reason He said ﴿in the way of God﴾, meaning for the sake of reaching God, that is, reaching His religion which He willed.

His saying ﴿But if they turn away﴾ means they turn away from emigration. This is a warning to them before they are taken to account, since the meaning is: convey this ruling to them, and if they turn away from it and do not accept it, then seize them and kill them. This indicates that whoever says something that may imply disbelief is not held accountable for it until he is approached, informed of what he has said, and given an excuse; if he then persists in it, he is held accountable and then asked to repent. This is the ruling given by Sahnun.

The walī (ally) is the one who is loyal, to whom his protégé entrusts his secret and his counsel. The nasir (helper) is the one who defends his ally and assists him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 90:

﴿Except those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant, or who come to you with their hearts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people. And had Allah willed, He would have empowered them over you, and they would have fought you. So if they keep away from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you any way against them.﴾

The exception is from the command in His words ﴿So take them and kill them﴾ [al-Nisa': 89], meaning: except those who believed but did not emigrate. Or: except those who turned back on their heels to Makkah after having emigrated. These ones join a people from among those with whom you have made a covenant, so do not attack them with killing, lest you break your covenants concluded with their people.

The meaning of yasilun ("join", "be affiliated with") is like the meaning of ittasala (to be connected) in the verse of one of the Banu Nabhan:

"Ala balligha khullati Rashidan wa sinwi qadiman idha ma ittasala"

That is, "became affiliated." It may also carry the meaning of iltahaqa (to attach oneself), that is: except those who attach themselves to a people between whom and you there is a covenant, so they enter into their pact. On the first interpretation they are originally among the covenant-partners; on the second interpretation they are like covenant-partners, because the covenant-partner of a covenant-partner is like a covenant-partner. The intended sense of "those who join" is not a specific people, but rather anyone who connects himself to a people who have a covenant with the Muslims. For this reason Mujahid said: "These are from the people about whom it was revealed: 'Why are you divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?'"

As for His words ﴿to a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾, what is meant are the tribes that had a covenant with the Muslims. Mujahid said: When ﴿Why are you divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ [al-Nisa': 88] was revealed, those about whom it was revealed became afraid, so they went with their goods to Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami, who had made an alliance with the Prophet ﷺ that he would not aid him nor aid against him, and that whoever took refuge with Hilal, from his people or others, would have the same protection as he had.

It has also been said: what is meant by the people between whom and you there is a covenant is Khuza'ah. It was also said: the Banu Bakr ibn Zayd Manat, who were in truce and armistice with the Muslims, and had not yet become Muslims on that day. It was also said: they are the Banu Mudlij, since Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji had concluded a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on behalf of his people, the Banu Mudlij, after the day of Badr, on the condition that they would not aid against the Messenger of Allah, and that if Quraysh embraced Islam they would embrace Islam, and if Quraysh did not embrace Islam they would not embrace Islam, so that the hearts of Quraysh would not harden against them. The more likely view is that all these tribes are included in the verse.

The meaning of ﴿or who come to you with their hearts constricted from fighting you﴾ etc.: or who came to Madinah as emigrants, but stipulated that they would not fight alongside the believers against their own people, and so they were accepted from them in this regard. This was a concession for them at the beginning of Islam, when the Muslims had made truces with some Arab tribes to win their hearts, and with those who entered into their covenant. When Islam grew strong, fighting alongside the believers became obligatory upon everyone who entered Islam. As for the early Muslims among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who embraced Islam without making this stipulation, the concession does not cover them; they are the ones who fought the polytheists of Makkah and others.

The majority read ﴿ḥaṣirat﴾ in the form of the past tense verb with the feminine ending attached to the verb. Ya'qub read ḥaṣiratan, in the form of an adjective with the feminine ending of the adjective at its end, in the accusative and with tanwin.

"Ḥaṣirat" means "became constricted" and "distressed."

"An yuqatilukum" is in the genitive by the omission of ʿan, meaning: their hearts were constricted from fighting you, because they are believers who do not wish to fight their brothers, and from fighting their own people, because they are of one lineage, so fighting them weighed heavily upon them. His words ﴿their hearts were constricted﴾ indicate that this was from sincerity on their part.

By "these" is meant the Banu Mudlij, who made this covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Allah excused them for this because they were truthful. Allah the Exalted made clear to the believers the benefit of this subjugation which He had arranged for them from a people who had been enemies to them, so that they became peaceful toward them and loved them, yet they refused to fight their own people. So He said ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have empowered them over you, and they would have fought you﴾. For this reason He commanded the believers to hold back their hands from these people if they withdrew from them and did not fight them; and this is the meaning of His words ﴿then Allah has not made for you any way against them﴾, that is, a permission, after He had commanded the believers to fight others wherever they found them.

Here "sabil" (way) is used metaphorically for the means of blame or taking to account, and for this reason its predicate came with the preposition of elevation ('ala) rather than the preposition of limit (ila). The discussion of it will come at His words, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no way against the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91], in Surat Bara'ah.

﴿You will find others who want to be safe from you and safe from their own people. Whenever they are returned to disorder, they are plunged back into it. If they do not withdraw from you, offer you peace, and restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. Against these We have given you clear authority.﴾

These are another group, whose only concern is for themselves and who care nothing for others. They show affection to the Muslims so that they may be safe from their raid, and they show affection to their own people so that they may be safe from their harm. They sincerely love neither party. For this reason they are described as wanting to be safe from both the believers and their own people. They have no aim except the fulfilment of their own desires. They join the Muslims in their affairs, [to achieve] their trivial ends, and so they profess faith. Then they return to their people and revert to disbelief.

This is the meaning of His words ﴿whenever they are returned to disorder, they are plunged back into it﴾. The meaning of "urkisu" (plunged back) has already been explained shortly before. These people were Ghatafan and Banu Asad, from among those who lived around Madinah before their Islam became sincere, and Banu Abd al-Dar from the people of Makkah. They used to come to Madinah and profess Islam, then return to Makkah and worship idols.

The command God gave the believers regarding the treatment of these people and the treatment of the earlier group in His words ﴿except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾ [al-Nisa: 90] is one command: they are left alone if they leave the believers and make peace with them, and they are fought if they show hostility.

However, God made the condition required of the first group that they withdraw from the Muslims, offer them peace, and not fight them. He made the condition required of these people that they do not withdraw from the Muslims, do not offer them peace, and do not restrain their hands from them. This is in view of the state expected from each of the groups mentioned.

This is a wonderful arrangement, in which no difference in ruling remains, but the difference in the two circumstances is made explicit, along with a description of what lies in the hearts of the two groups.

The word "wijdan" (finding) in His words ﴿you will find others﴾ means discovering and coming upon. That is, you will come upon other people. It is from the usage of wajada, which takes one object. His words "﴿want﴾" form a clause in the position of a hal (circumstantial clause). The various usages of wijdan in their speech will be explained when He says ﴿you will surely find the most hostile of people toward those who believed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 82] in Surat al-Ma'idah.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿against these We have given you﴾ is used to add to their distinction.

"Al-sultan al-mubin" (clear authority) is the clear proof that indicates their hypocrisy, so the Muslims need not fear being accused of aggression in fighting them or of dividing the community.

[Page 155]

**[Page 156]**

The transition of purpose (*intiqal al-gharad*) renews the listener's attention through variety of topics. He moved from specifying the conduct of the Muslims toward the enemy to the rulings on how Muslims deal with one another: the obligation to restrain aggression among themselves.

The connection between the purpose transitioned from and the purpose transitioned to is this: the discussion had been about fighting those who displayed Islam while their hypocrisy had become apparent. Naturally, the soul becomes eager to learn the ruling on killing sincere believers.

It is narrated that an incident occurred in Medina in which a believer was killed by mistake, arising from old enmities during the days of fighting against polytheism. The killer erred because he thought the victim was a disbeliever. There was also an incident in which a believer was killed deliberately by someone who had professed faith. The incident referred to in His words ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the way of God, verify carefully﴾ [al-Nisa': 94] and it is said that these verses were revealed concerning that. The connection becomes clearer, because this verse serves as an introduction to the rulings on killing that follow.

God Most High magnified the matter of a Muslim killing his Muslim brother and placed it in the category of what should not happen. He said ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾. He used the form of intensified negation, which is the form of denial, meaning: it is not found for a believer to kill a believer in any state except in the state of mistake, or to kill a killing of any kind except the killing by mistake.

So the statement is a restriction (*hasr*), and it is an assertive restriction (*hasr idde'a'i*) intended for emphasis, as if the quality of faith in the killer and the killed is incompatible with being together with killing in reality, like the incompatibility of opposites. The purpose is to announce that when a believer kills a believer, faith has been removed from him, and he is not a believer, in the manner of the saying: "A person does not drink wine while he drinks it, being a believer."

Therefore this sentence is independent of what follows. It is not intended as legislation; rather it serves as an introduction to legislation, aiming to express the gravity of a believer killing a believer in a way other than by mistake. It is declarative in both wording and meaning, and the exception (*istithna'*) is genuine, drawn from the generality of states: that is, the killing of a believer by a believer is negated in every state except the state of lack of intention. This is the best apparent meaning of the verse.

You may also take His words ﴿It is not for a believer﴾ as a declarative statement intended to mean a prohibition. The compound is used in its implied meaning by way of the figurative metonymy of illustration (*majaz mursal tamthili*), and you take His words ﴿except by mistake﴾ as a supporting element for the figure (*tarshih*), in the manner we established in the first aspect. This yields the warning that the form of mistake is not something to which a prohibition applies, since everyone knows that a mistake is not subject to command or prohibition.

That is to say: if a kind of killing of a believer were permitted to the believer, it would be killing by mistake. And it is known that one who errs does not perform his act intending obedience or disobedience. Thus the statement returns to the meaning: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer with a killing that is ever subject to will and intention in any state." The sentence then becomes the starting point of legislation, and what follows it is its detailed explanation. On both of these readings, the exception in His words ﴿except by mistake﴾ presents no difficulty.

The exegetes held that ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer﴾ is intended as a prohibition, that is, a declarative statement with the meaning of an imperative. They resorted to taking the exception as disjunctive (*munqati'*), meaning "but" (*lakin*), to escape the implication of the exception, which would permit a believer to kill a believer by mistake. You have understood that this is not an assumption here.

The qualifier in His words ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake﴾ was introduced because His words ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾ are intended either as an assertion of restriction or as a prohibition, as you have learned. Had the statement been on its literal footing, it would not need the qualifier, since the killing of a believer would by its implication be confined to killing by mistake, and so there would be no need to specify it.

Al-Tabari and al-Wahidi narrated concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse: "'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi had embraced Islam and migrated to Medina before the Prophet's migration (ﷺ). He was the maternal half-brother of Abu Jahl. Abu Jahl went out, along with his brother al-Harith ibn Hisham and al-Harith ibn Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah, in pursuit of him. They came to him in Medina and said to him: 'Your mother has sworn that no shade will cover her until she sees you. So return with us so that she may look at you, and then you may come back.'

They gave him a covenant from God that they would not harm him, nor prevent him from his religion. So he went out with them. When they had passed beyond Medina, they bound him and entered Mecca with him, and said: 'We will not release you from your bonds until you disbelieve in the One in whom you have believed.'

Al-Harith ibn Zayd used to beat him and torment him. 'Ayyash said to al-Harith: 'By God, if I ever meet you alone, I will kill you.' He remained in Mecca until he went out to Medina on the day of the Conquest. He met al-Harith ibn Zayd at Quba', and al-Harith had embraced Islam, but 'Ayyash did not know of his Islam. 'Ayyash struck him and killed him.

When he was informed that the man was a Muslim, 'Ayyash returned to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him of what he had done, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake.﴾" Therefore this verse was revealed after the Conquest of Mecca.

In Ibn 'Atiyyah: it is said that it was revealed concerning al-Yaman, the father of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, when the Muslims killed him by mistake on the day of Uhud.

In a narration of al-Tabari: it was revealed concerning the case of Abu al-Darda', when he was in a military detachment (*sariyyah*). He turned aside to a mountain pass and found a man with his sheep. Abu al-Darda' attacked him with a sword. The man said: "There is no god but God," but he struck him and killed him, and brought his sheep to the detachment. Then he felt something in his soul and went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and then the verse was revealed.

His words ﴿then [the penalty is] the freeing of a believing neck﴾: the *fa'* is the connecting particle for the response of the conditional clause. The word *tahrir* (freeing) is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject from the response clause, because the meaning is evident: "then its ruling or its matter is the freeing of a neck," like His words ﴿so patience is fitting﴾. *Tahrir* is a form of *tafil* from *hurriyyah* (freedom), meaning making the neck free. The word *raqabah* (neck) is used to refer to the whole person, by the figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole, as people say: "the *jizyah* is levied on heads, four dinars for every head."

Among the secrets of the Islamic Law is its concern to spread freedom among Muslims in an orderly manner. When God sent His Messenger with the religion of Islam, slavery was widespread among humanity, and vast wealth was built upon it. Its causes were numerous: capture in wars, reduction to servitude through debts, abduction in raids, parents selling their children, hostages taken under threat, and indebtedness.

Islam abolished all of its causes except capture, and retained capture for the sake of encouraging the brave and deterring the rebellious from rising against Muslims, because the Arab feared nothing among the consequences of war as much as captivity. An-Nabighah said:

"Out of fear that my leadership and my women should not be seized, until they die as free women."

Then the Law healed these human wounds by establishing the causes of freedom in numerous religious circumstances: some obligatory and some recommended. Among the obligatory causes is the expiation for killing mentioned here.

The expiation for killing by mistake has been made of two parts. The first is the freeing of a believing neck. This freeing has been made a substitute for the loss of God's right in the person of the victim, for the victim is a servant of God, and it is hoped that from his offspring there would arise one who worships God and obeys His religion. The killer therefore could not be free of having, by his killing, deprived God of that quality. The Law has indicated through this that freedom is life and that servitude is death. Whoever causes the death of a living soul must strive to bring to life a soul that is like a dead one, namely the enslaved person.

We will expand on this explanation at His words, Most High, ﴿And when Moses said to his people: "O my people, remember God's blessing upon you, when He made among you prophets and made you kings"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20], in Surah al-Ma'idah, for its interpretation is that God delivered them from the enslavement of Pharaoh, so they became like kings, not ruled by anyone else.

The second part is the *diyah* (blood-money). The *diyah* is the wealth paid to the family of the victim of an accidental killing, as consolation for their calamity, in the form of livestock, gold or silver, or the like, as will come.

The *diyah* is well known among the Arabs in its meaning and its measures, so for this reason the Qur'an did not detail it. The Arabs had made the *diyah* in various forms. It was a substitute for the blood of the victim both in deliberate and accidental killing. As for deliberate killing, they used to be ashamed of accepting it. Al-Hamasi said:

"If a living people accepted wealth as ransom, we would have driven to them a generous portion of wealth, filled up.
But a people whose brother was struck refused the satisfaction of shame, and chose blood over milk."

When the heirs of the victim agreed to a *diyah* through the intercession of the chiefs of the tribe, they fixed it by what they mutually agreed upon. Zuhayr said:

"The wounds are healed with hundreds, and it has become that one who is not guilty pays it in installments."

As for accidental killing, they did not refuse to accept the *diyah*. It is said that it was ten camels, and that the first to make it one hundred camels was 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, when he ransomed his son 'Abd Allah after he had vowed to sacrifice him to the Ka'bah, for one hundred camels. This became the custom among the Quraysh, and then the Arabs followed them. It is also said that the first to make the *diyah* one hundred camels was Abu Sayyarah 'Umaylah al-'Adwani. The *diyah* of a king was a thousand camels, the *diyah* of a chief two hundred camels, and the *diyah* of an ally half the *diyah* of a full member of the tribe. The first person to be paid *diyah* in camels was Zayd ibn Bakr ibn Hawazin, when his brother Mu'awiyah, the ancestor of Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, killed him.

The most common *diyah* stated in the Sunnah is one hundred camels, divided into five categories of twenty each: twenty *hiqqah* (four-year-old females), twenty *jadha'ah* (five-year-old females), twenty *bint makhad* (one-year-old females), twenty *bint labun* (two-year-old females), and twenty *ibn labun* (two-year-old males).

The *diyah* for deliberate killing, when the heirs of the victim agree to it, is quadrangular: twenty-five from each of the first four categories.

The *diyah* is made more severe when a parent kills their child by mistake, in terms of category rather than number: thirty *jadha'ah*, thirty *hiqqah*, and forty *khalifah*, meaning she-camels with fetuses in their wombs.

When the family of the victim are not camel-owners, the *diyah* is converted approximately into the value of camels: for the gold-owners it is one thousand dinars, and for the silver-owners twelve thousand dirhams.

It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he made the *diyah* for cattle-owners two hundred cows, and for sheep-owners two thousand sheep. In the hadith of Abu Dawud, the *diyah* is "for the people of *hulal*," meaning the people of woven cloth, like the people of Yemen, one hundred *hullah*. A *hullah* is two garments of one type.

The standard for fixing blood-money, across different eras and regions, is returning to the value of its equivalent in camels as specified in the Sunnah. The *diyah* for a female victim is half the *diyah* for a male.

The *diyah* for a People of the Book is half the *diyah* of a Muslim. The *diyah* for a female People of the Book is half the *diyah* of a male People of the Book.

The *diyah* is paid in installments over three years, one installment after each year. The beginning of those installments is from the time of the judgment concerning the killing, or the agreement reached between the heirs of the victim and the paternal kin (*'aqilah*) of the killer.

The word *diyah* with the Ya' lightened is the verbal noun of *wada*, meaning "gave," like *rama* (threw). Its verbal noun is *wad'*, like *wa'd*, the first letter of the root (waw) was dropped for lightness, because the waw is heavy, as it was dropped in *'iddah*, and the *ha'* was added at the end of the word as compensation, like *shiyah* from *al-washy*.

Ibn 'Ashur's words: "His saying ﴿delivered to his family﴾ indicates that the blood-money (diyah) is a placating of the victim's family. The 'family' is mentioned in a general way, from which it is understood that the most entitled to it are the nearest of people to the slain, for 'family' means the close relative, and the most entitled to it is the nearest."

"In Islamic law it is taken by the heirs of the slain according to the shares of inheritance, except that the one who killed by mistake, if he is an heir of the slain, does not inherit from his diyah. It is in the position of compensation for destroyed property: it is made a substitute for the life of the one whose killing the slayer caused. Perhaps this meaning was the intended one in the pre-Islamic era, and for this reason they said: 'the blood-money is measured out' (takayul al-dima'), and they said: 'they are a bawa'' (bawa'), meaning equals in blood, and they increased the diyah for their chieftains."

"The pardoning of the victim's family from taking the diyah was made a charity (sadaqah) on their part, as an encouragement to pardon."

"The Qur'an mentioned in general who is obliged to pay the diyah, and the Sunnah clarified it, that they are the 'aqilah (kin who bear the obligation), and this is a confirmation of what the matter was before Islam."

"The 'aqilah are the kinsmen from the tribe. It is obligatory upon the nearest and then the nearest, according to the order of precedence in agnatic relationship (ta'sib)."

"His saying ﴿But if he was from a people hostile to you, and he is a believer﴾ (the verse), meaning: if the slain was a believer and his family were disbelievers, with enmity between them and the Muslims, then the expiation is limited to freeing a slave, without paying a diyah to them, because the diyah: if we consider it a consolation for the victim's guardians, then since they were enemies there is no wisdom in consoling their hearts; and if we consider it a compensation for the benefits of their slain, like the values of destroyed property, then withholding it from the disbelievers is because a disbeliever does not inherit from a Muslim, and because we do not give them our wealth by which they would strengthen themselves against us."

"This ruling is agreed upon among the jurists, if the believing slain was still in the abode of his people who were disbelievers. As for if the slain was in the lands of Islam and his guardians were disbelievers, Ibn 'Abbas, Malik and Abu Hanifah said: the diyah is not dropped from the slayer, and it is paid to the public treasury of the Muslims."

"al-Shafi'i, al-Awza'i and al-Thawri said: the diyah is dropped, because the cause of its dropping is that its entitled recipients are disbelievers. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿from a people hostile﴾ is that the consideration is for the slain's family, not the place of his residence, since the place of residence has no effect in this ruling, even if his residence there was not excused."

"He referred to a people using the word 'enemy' (ʿaduww) in the singular, because fa'ul in the sense of fa'il is common in their speech to be singular, masculine, not agreeing with its described noun, as in His saying ﴿Indeed the disbelievers have been to you an manifest enemy﴾ [al-Nisa: 101], ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], ﴿And thus We made for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind﴾ [al-An'am: 112], and 'a woman is an enemy (ʿaduww)'. And their saying ʿaduwwah (feminine) is anomalous."

"In the speech of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in Sahih al-Bukhari, that he said to the women who were in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ"

"When 'Umar entered, they hastened to the curtain when they saw him: 'O enemies of themselves!' And it is pluralized frequently as a'da', He said, the Exalted: ﴿And the Day We gather the enemies of Allah to the Fire﴾ [Fussilat: 19]."

"His saying ﴿And if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾ meaning: if the slain was a believer. So He made for the people who are between the Muslims and them a covenant, that is a pact from the people of disbelief, the diyah for their believing slain, in consideration of the covenant that is between us. This indicates that the diyah is a consolation for the victim's guardians, and is not inherited wealth from the slayer, since a disbeliever does not inherit from a Muslim. So there is no need to interpret the verse as meaning that the believing slain had a believing heir among a people with a treaty, or that the slain was a covenanted person and not a believer, based on the view that the pronoun in 'kana' refers to the slain without the attribute of belief; and this is a remote interpretation, because the subject of the verse concerns one who kills a believer by mistake."

"Do not let the explicit description of the attribute in His saying 'and he is a believer' alarm you, for that is a safeguard and a prevention of an assumption, when the statement about him, ﴿from a people hostile to you﴾, might lead someone to think that he is also an enemy to us in religion. The condition that the slain be a believer in this ruling is understood by carrying its unrestricted mention here upon its restricted mention there, 'and he is a believer', and the subject of this detail is the Muslim slain by mistake, given that the verse opens with His saying ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake﴾. This is the view of Malik and Abu Hanifah."

"Some have gone to leaving the unrestricted here upon its generality, and they interpreted the meaning of the verse as referring to the dhimmi and the covenanted person who is killed by mistake, so the diyah and freeing of a slave are obligatory. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and al-Shafi'i. But they said: this was a ruling concerning the polytheist Arabs who had a truce with the Muslims up to a term, until they either embrace Islam or declare war; and this ruling has been abrogated."

"His saying ﴿then fasting two consecutive months﴾: the two months are described as consecutive, and what is intended is the consecutiveness of their days, because the succession of days necessitates the succession of the two months."

"His saying ﴿a repentance from Allah﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlih), with the implied meaning: Allah legislated fasting as a repentance from Him. Here 'tawbah' is a verbal noun of tāba in the sense of 'accepted repentance', indicated by its being construed with 'min', since tāba is used both in the sense of 'regretted' and in the sense of 'accepted from him', as previously mentioned in His saying ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 17] in this surah; that is, Allah lightened the burden on the slayer, so He legislated fasting in order to accept his repentance concerning what he erred in, because he erred in a grave matter."

"You may also make 'tawbah' an object of purpose referring to the freeing of the slave and the diyah and their substitute, which is fasting, meaning: Allah legislated the whole as a repentance from Him upon the slayer; for had He not legislated that for him, He would have punished him for the causes of the error, and these return to neglecting caution and failing to take precaution. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of 'siyam', meaning: a cause of repentance, so it is a figurative (majazi) metaphorical hal."

This is the intended purpose of the legislation on killing, since it is the killing that is most likely to occur among people. It was placed last to magnify its gravity. He began with the mention of accidental killing under the heading of His words, ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾ [al-Nisa': 92].

The intentional killer (al-muta'ammid) is one who intends to kill. The word is derived from 'amada ila kadhā, meaning qasada wa dhahaba (he intended and set out). All acts fall into two states, intentional and mistaken. Intention is recognised by an act that no one performs against another person unless he intends specifically to take that person's life by means that are commonly used to take lives, and this is not hidden from any sensible person.

For this reason, the majority of jurists (al-Jumhur min al-fuqaha') said: killing is of two kinds, intentional and mistaken, and this is what accords with the verse. Some jurists made a third kind, which they named quasi-intentional (shibh al-'amd). They relied on transmitted reports, and if these are authentic, their interpretation is necessary and they are to be restricted to the specific cases in which they were narrated.

Ibn Jarir and al-Wahidi mention that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that Miqyas ibn Subabah and his brother Hisham came as Muslim emigrants. Hisham was found slain among the Banu al-Najjar, and his killer was not known. The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to give his brother Miqyas one hundred camels as the blood-money (diyah) for his brother, and he sent with them a man of Fihr to deliver this. When Miqyas took the camels, he attacked the Fihri and killed him, drove off the camels, and returned to Makkah as an unbeliever. He recited concerning his brother:

I killed for him a man of Fihr, and I carried his blood-money
To the chiefs of the Banu al-Najjar, the lords of Fari'.
I have settled through him my blood-debt, and I have attained my revenge,
And I was the first to return to the idols.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had declared his blood lawful to be shed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, and he was killed in the market of Makkah.

As for His words, "abiding therein" (khālidan fīhā), according to the majority of the scholars of the Sunnah, they are to be understood as a long duration of staying in the Fire because of the killing of a believer intentionally. This is because killing a soul is not disbelief in Allah and His Messenger, and according to our scholars among the people of the Sunnah, eternal abiding in the Fire is only for disbelief. Therefore the meaning of khulūd must be interpreted as an intensification of the length of stay, and this is an Arabic usage. Al-Nabighah said concerning the illness of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir:

We, in his presence, ask Allah to grant him long life,
That He may return to us a kingdom, and the land be prosperous.

Its meaning is understood differently by those who declare the major sins to be disbelief, the Khawarij, and by those who make eternal abiding obligatory for the people of major sins, following the same course as the obligation of eternal abiding through committing a major sin.

Both groups agree that repentance (tawbah) applies to the crime of intentionally killing a soul, as it applies to other major sins. However, a small group among the people of the Sunnah strayed clearly in the interpretation of this verse. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas that the repentance of one who intentionally kills a soul is not accepted. This became well known from Ibn 'Abbas and he was known for it, relying on this verse.

Al-Bukhari reports that Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "It is a verse about which the people of Kufa disagreed, so I travelled to Ibn 'Abbas and asked him about it. He said: 'This verse, ﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ — it is the last of what was revealed, and nothing abrogated it.'" So he did not take the path of interpretation.

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed in interpreting the words of Ibn 'Abbas. A group took his words at face value, saying that their basis is that this verse is the last of what was revealed, so it abrogated (naskh) the preceding verses that indicate the general acceptance of repentance, such as His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. So the killer is among those whom Allah has not willed to forgive. Likewise His words, ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving to whoever repents and believes and does righteousness and then remains guided﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82].

Likewise His words, ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse — and whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein humiliated﴾ [al-Furqan: 69], ﴿Except for one who repents and believes and does righteous work﴾ [al-Furqan: 70].

The truth is that the locus of interpretation is not whether a verse was revealed earlier or later, but rather in applying the absolute wording of this verse to the evidences that restrict all the evidences for otherworldly punishments to the condition of not repenting.

As for the ruling of eternal abiding, whether it is to be taken literally or figuratively, meaning a long duration of punishment, is a separate question, and there is no need to go into it when discussing the repentance of the intentional killer. How can he be deprived of acceptance of repentance, when repentance from disbelief, which is the greatest of sins, is accepted? So how much more so for what is less than it of sins?

A group understood Ibn 'Abbas's intention as aiming at magnifying and deterring, so that people would not dare to kill a soul intentionally, while still hoping for repentance. They support this by the report that a man came to Ibn 'Abbas and asked: "Is there repentance for one who intentionally kills a believer?" He said: "No, except the Fire." When the man left, his companions said to him: "Is this how you used to issue fatwas for us? You used to say that his repentance is accepted." He said: "I think the questioner is a man in anger who wants to kill a believer." They sent people after him and found him to be so. Ibn Shihab, when someone asked him about this and he understood from him that he had killed a soul, would say to him: "Your repentance is accepted." And when someone asked him who had not killed, and he perceived from his condition that he was trying to kill a soul, he would say to him: "There is no repentance for the killer."

I say: this is a position in which the statements of the commentators have become confused, as you have known. Its essence is that what Allah mentions here in the threat against the killer of a soul has exceeded the usual limit of severity. So some of the early scholars held that this requires taking the threat in the verse at face value without interpretation, because of the intensity of its emphasis, which prevents taking eternal abiding figuratively, and so it establishes for the killer eternal abiding in its literal sense, unlike the rest of the verses of threat. It seems that this meaning is what led them to dispute whether this verse is decisive (muhkam) or abrogated (mansukh), because they found no other refuge to which they could turn in interpreting it in the way that the other verses of threat are interpreted, whether by the various modes of figurative interpretation or by reconciling conflicting texts. So they took refuge in the claim that its text was abrogated by the words of the Exalted in Surat al-Furqan, ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], up to His words, ﴿except one who repents﴾, because His words ﴿and whoever does that﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] either refer to the totality of the sins mentioned, and if the doer of all of them can benefit from repentance, then the doer of some of them, which is killing intentionally, is more deserving; or they refer to the doer of one of them, and killing intentionally is among those counted with them.

For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "The verse of al-Nisa' is the last verse revealed, and nothing abrogated it." It is strange that such a statement should be made, and then lengthened, and that people should pass it on and generations should go by it, while there is no contradiction between this verse, which is a threat against the killer of a soul, and the verses on the acceptance of repentance. One group answered that it was abrogated by the verse ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], on the basis that the generality of "whom He wills" abrogated the particularity of killing.

Another group answered that the verse was revealed concerning Miqyas ibn Subabah, who was an unbeliever, so the eternal abiding is because of disbelief. This answer is based on an error, because the wording of the verse is general, since it is in the form of a conditional, so "whoever" (man) is a conditional particle, which is among the forms of generality, and so it cannot be restricted to a specific person, except according to one who holds that the cause of a general text restricts it to its cause only. This is not worth paying attention to.

All these are refuges for which there is no need, because the verses of repentance are established, agreed upon, and their apparent meanings are mutually supporting, to the point of reaching the level of a definitive text. Therefore the verses threatening all sins, including disbelief, are to be understood in their light.

Moreover, the emphasis of the threat in the verse only removes the possibility of figurative meaning regarding it being a threat, not regarding the determination of what is threatened, which is eternal abiding. For the emphatic particles here have different meanings, so it is not correct to consider one of them as emphasizing the meaning of another. Rather, they emphasize the purpose, which is the threat, not its types. This is the decisive answer to this perplexity, and it is the one to which one must resort and rely upon.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 94:

﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who gives you [the greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life; for with Allah are abundant gains. Thus were you before, and Allah bestowed His favor upon you. So investigate carefully. Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾.

This is a new, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), addressed to the believers, to intensify the warning against killing a believer, by mentioning circumstances in which one may be lax and in which doubts may arise.

The occasion of revelation (al-munasaba) is what al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A man had a small flock of sheep, and the Muslims caught up with him. He said, "As-salamu 'alaykum," but they killed him and took his flock. So Allah revealed this verse concerning that. In another narration he said, "La ilaha illa Allah, Muhammad Rasul Allah." In another narration, "The Prophet (ﷺ) sent his blood-money to his family and returned his flock."

[Page 167]

There is disagreement about the names of the killer and the killed, although there is agreement that this occurred during a sariyya (a small military detachment). Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that the killer was Usama ibn Zayd and the one killed was Mirdas ibn Nahik al-Fazari, from the people of Fadak. In the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq, the killer was Muhallam ibn Jathama and the one killed was 'Amir ibn al-Adbat. It is also said that the killer was Abu Qatada, and it is said Abu al-Darda'. And the Prophet (ﷺ) rebuked the killer and said to him: "Why did you not split open his belly so that you would know what was in his heart?" Addressing them with "O you who have believed" hints that the motive for killing one who has manifested Islam is forbidden.

If the killer's intention was to be certain that the quality of faith was present in the one killed, then this certainty is not what the Shari'ah requires. The attribute of Islam has been linked to the saying "La ilaha illa Allah, Muhammad Rasul Allah," or to the greeting of Islam, which is "As-salamu 'alaykum."

Al-darb means travel (al-sayr). It was discussed earlier, at His saying ﴿And they say to their brothers when they travel in the land﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], in Surat Al 'Imran. His saying "in the cause of Allah" (fi sabil Allah) is a stable adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqirr) functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "daraftum." It is not connected to "daraftum," because travel (al-darb, i.e., the going) cannot be "in the way of Allah," since "the way of Allah" is a designation for military expedition (al-ghazw). Do you not see His saying ﴿And they say to their brothers when they travel in the land or are engaged in military campaigns﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], and so on.

Al-tabayyun means intense seeking of clarification, that is, strong deliberation, as the form tafa''ul requires. The attachment of the fa' (then) to the verb "tabayyanu" is due to the conditional sense that "idha" generally carries. The majority of readers recited "fa-tabayyanu" with a taa' on top, then a baa', then a ya' underneath, then a nun, from al-tabayyun, which is the tafa''ul form. That means: be steadfast and seek the clarification of matters, so do not hasten and follow fleeting, mistaken impulses. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited it as "fa-tathabbatu" (with a fa', then a taa' on top, then a thaa' with three dots, then a baa', then a taa' on top), meaning seek what is firm, that is, what does not change and does not admit the opposite of what has appeared to you.

His saying ﴿and do not say to one who gives you [the greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer"﴾: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and Khalaf read "al-salam" without an alif after the lam, meaning the opposite of war. The sense of "alqa al-salam" is that he manifested peace among you, as if he threw it among them. The rest read "al-salam" with an alif, which is shared between the meaning of peace as the opposite of war, and the meaning of the greeting of Islam, which is the statement "As-salamu 'alaykum." That is, whoever addresses you with the greeting of Islam as a sign that he is a Muslim.

[Page 168]

The clause ﴿You are not a believer﴾ is the content of the saying "do not say." The majority read "mu'minan" with a kasra on the second mim, in the form of the active participle, meaning: do not deny him faith, when he manifests it to you. Ibn Wardan, from Abu Ja'far, read it with a fatha on the second mim, in the form of the passive participle, meaning: do not say to him, "You have not obtained our security for you," that is, you are going to be killed or taken captive.

"'Arad al-hayat" means the goods of life, and what is meant is the spoils of war. He expressed them as "'arad al-hayat" to belittle them, since they are a fleeting, passing benefit.

The clause ﴿seeking﴾ is a circumstantial clause, that is, you examined his faith out of fear that he intended to secure his property, so your not believing him led to seeking the spoils of his property, and you were held accountable for the outcome. The purpose of this qualifier is therefore to add to the rebuke, along with knowledge that if one had said to someone who had manifested Islam, "You are not a believer," and killed him without taking any property from him, his ruling would have been more fitting than for one who intended to take spoils. The qualifier looks to the cause of revelation, while the ruling is more general than that.

Likewise His saying ﴿For with Allah are abundant gains﴾, meaning Allah has not confined your gains to this spoil.

His saying ﴿Thus were you before﴾ adds to the rebuke: that is, you were disbelievers, then you entered Islam by the word of Islam. So if someone had refused to believe you about your Islam, would that have pleased you? This is a great discipline (tarbiyah): that a person, when holding another accountable, should sense that he himself was once in states similar to those of the one he is holding accountable. This is like a teacher holding a student accountable for a bad performance when the student has not fallen short in exerting his effort.

Likewise, this is an admonition for those who test students of knowledge, who become accustomed to being harsh with them and seeking out their slips. Likewise for rulers and senior officials in dealing with junior officials under their authority, and likewise for parents with their children, when foolishness leads them to scold them for customary play or for impatience with pains.

The verse has indicated a great wisdom in preserving the religious community, which is spreading trust and security among the members of the nation, and casting aside whatever might introduce suspicion. For if this door is opened, it becomes difficult to close.
