Just as the accused accuses others, so others may accuse the one who accused them, and by that trust is lifted, and it becomes easy for those weak in faith to apostatize, since accusation has come to overshadow both the truthful and the hypocrite. Consider the Prophet's (ﷺ) treatment of the hypocrites, which was the treatment of Muslims.

Moreover, this religion spreads quickly into hearts, so its adherents are content with those who enter it without interrogation, since they will soon become accustomed to it,

[Page 169]

and its sweetness will mingle with their hearts. They rush into it with doubt and hesitation, and then it becomes firm faith. Among what helps in this is the trust of the earlier adherents in the later ones who join them.

Because of this, Allah repeated the command, saying "fa-tabayyanu," as emphasis for the earlier mentioned "tabayyanu," and He concluded it with His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾, which combines both a warning and a promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 95–96:

﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm, are not equal to those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit at home by a degree. And to each Allah has promised the best reward. But Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit at home with a great reward, degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

When Allah rebuked some of the strivers for what proceeded from them of excessive probing into the purpose of jihad, He followed that with an explanation of the virtue of the strivers, so that this rebuke would not give the impression that their excellence had declined in some of their circumstances. This follows the Qur'an's usual practice of following warning (indhar) with glad tidings (bishara), to repel despair of mercy from the souls of the Muslims.

The Arabs say: "la yastawi" and "laysa sawaan" (they are not equal), meaning that one of the two mentioned is superior to the other. They rely in this on the indicator (qarina) that determines which is the one preferred, since it is by nature the superior one. Al-Samaw'al or someone else said:

"So the scholar and the ignorant are not equal."

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are not equal﴾ [Al 'Imran: 113]. They sometimes follow it with something that makes explicit the aspect of the negation of equality, either because it is obscure, as in His saying: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest; those are greater in degree than those who spent and fought afterward﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. Or the explicitness may be merely for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal; the companions of Paradise are the victorious﴾ [al-Hashr: 20]. Since the aspect of preference was known in most occurrences of such constructions, such constructions have come to be used in most cases with the sense of a kinaya (allusion), namely an oblique reproach of the one who is deficient in neglecting and renouncing what is better while able to attain it. This is also the case here, since it is evident that the one who sits out of jihad is not equal to the striver in the virtue of supporting the religion, nor in its reward. Thus the oblique reproach of those who sit out and the condemnation of their state is determined.

With this, the placement of the exception in His saying ﴿other than those with a harm﴾ becomes clear, lest those with a harm think that they are intended by the exhortation and so go out with the Muslims, burdening them with the cost of transporting and protecting them to no benefit; or lest they think that they are intended by the oblique reproach, so that their souls are broken by it, in addition to their being broken by their incapacity. Also, in their exception there is equity toward them and an excuse, that had they been able they would not have sat out; and that is the assumption one should make about a believer. Had the intended meaning been the explicit sense, the exception would have had no place. So hold to this: the exception is intended, and it has a place in eloquence that must not be wasted. Even if the exception were not mentioned, it would be known from the context of the speech that the oblique reproach does not extend to those with a harm; so the exception is a shift away from relying on the indicator to explicit wording.

This is supported by what is in the Two Sahihs, from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "Revelation descended upon the Messenger of Allah while I was beside him. Then he was relieved of it and said: 'Write.' So I wrote on a shoulder-blade: ('Not equal are those who sit at home among the believers and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives') — and behind the Prophet was Ibn Umm Maktum — and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if I were able to strive, I would strive.' So there was revealed in its place: ﴿Not equal are those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm, and those who strive in the way of Allah﴾, the verse."

So Ibn Umm Maktum understood the intended meaning of the negation of equality and thought that the oblique reproach included him and those like him, since he is among those who sit at home. Because of this assumption he shifted from guarding the context to the explicitness of the speech. These two are equal states in the usage of eloquent speakers: the state of considering the address to the intelligent and the address to the dull. Therefore the addition of the exception did not forfeit a requirement of eloquence, but rather compensated for it with its counterpart, since the hearers are many kinds.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read (ghayra) with a fatha on the ra', as a circumstantial (hal) qualifier of "al-qa'iduna." Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with a damma as an attributive (na't) of "al-qa'iduna."

For ghayra both the raf' (as an attribute) and the nasb (as a circumstantial) are permissible, because "al-qa'iduna" is definite in the sense of a genus, so both regard for the wording and regard for the meaning are allowed.

Al-darar: the illness or defect, such as blindness, lameness, or chronic disability, because this form is for the sources of afflictions and the like. Its most common use is for blindness, and for this reason the blind man is called "darir," and it is not said of the lame or the chronically ill. I think that what is intended in this verse is specifically blindness, and that other conditions are analogous to it.

Al-darar is the verbal noun of darira (with kasra on the ra'), like marida, and this pattern occurs for defects and the like, such as 'amiya, 'urija and hasira. Its verbal noun has a fatha on the 'ayn, like al-'araj. Because of its lightness with a fatha on the 'ayn, the idgham of the two identical letters is blocked in it, so it is said darar with the fakk (unassimilated form). By contrast, al-durr, which is the verbal noun of darrahu, is obligatorily assimilated, since there is no reason for fakk.

We do not know in the speech of the Arabs of the application of al-darar to anything other than harmful defects. As for what is narrated in the hadith "la darar wa la dirar," it is either rare or follows the pattern of pairing (ittiba' wa muzawaja) because it is joined to the word "dirar," which is unassimilated. al-Jawhari claimed that darar is the noun of the verbal noun of al-durr, but there is scrutiny in this; it has not been transmitted from anyone else and there is no evidence for it.

His saying "with their wealth and their lives": jihad requires both matters, the expending of the self and the expending of wealth. However, jihad in its true sense is the expending of oneself in the way of Allah, even if one spends nothing, and even if one is a burden on the believers. Just as one who spends wealth to aid the fighters, without striving himself, is not called a striver, even if he has a great reward. Likewise, one who is held back by an excuse and wishes for the removal of his excuse and to join the strivers has a great virtue; but the virtue of actual jihad is not equaled by the virtue of others.

The clause ﴿Allah has preferred the strivers﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿not equal are those who sit at home among the believers﴾.

The real meaning of a darajah is a part of a place that is higher than another part adjoining it, such that the foot reaches it by ascending from the place where it was, by climbing; like the degrees of a high room or the rungs of a ladder.

Here darajah is used metaphorically for moral elevation, as in His saying ﴿And men have a degree over them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]. The elevation meant here is the elevation of virtue and abundance of reward.

Darajah is used here in the singular form, and its singularity is not for unity, because darajah here is a moral genus without individual instances. For this reason the expression is repeated in the clause that follows, as an emphasis on it, in the plural form in His saying "darajat minhu," because the plural is stronger than the singular.

The tanwin of darajatan is for magnification, and it corresponds to the meaning of the plural in His later saying "darajat minhu."

Darajatan is in the accusative by way of standing in for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) specifying the type of the verb "faddala," since the degree here is an addition to the meaning of preference. The sense is: Allah preferred the strivers with a preference that is a degree, i.e., a degree of preference.

The clause ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best reward﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah). The tanwin of kullan is the tanwin of substitution for an omitted genitive complement, and the sense is: "And each of the strivers and the sitters."

The clause ﴿But Allah has preferred the strivers over those who sit at home with a great reward﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Allah has preferred the strivers﴾, although the meaning of the two clauses is one, in view of the addition of "a great reward" in the second clause; by this, the conjoined clause differs from the clause conjoined to it with a difference that justifies the conjunction, along with the emphasis produced by repeating most of its wording.

By "al-mujahidin" is meant "those who strive with their wealth and their lives," so mention of the qualifier is dispensed with, due to its prior mention in the preceding parallel. Ajran 'azima is in the accusative by way of standing in for the absolute object specifying the type, since the reward is that preference, and it is described as great.

Darajat is in the accusative either as a substitute for "ajran 'azima," or as a circumstantial qualifier, considering that darajat is described as "from Him," i.e., from Allah.

Darajat is plural to indicate the magnification of the degree, since the plural, because of the meaning of multiplicity in it, has its form borrowed for the meaning of strength. Do you not see that 'Alqamah, when he recited to al-Harith ibn Jabalah, king of Ghassan, his verse seeking intercession for his brother Shaas ibn 'Abdah:

"In every tribe you have dealt out a favor, so Shaas deserves a draught (dhanub) of your generosity"

the king said to him: "And adhnabah (a multitude of draughts)?"

Its verbal noun has a fatha on the 'ayn, like al-'araj. Because of its lightness with a fatha on the 'ayn, the idgham of the two identical letters is blocked in it, so it is said darar with the fakk (unassimilated form). By contrast, al-durr, which is the verbal noun of darrahu, is obligatorily assimilated, since there is no reason for fakk.

We do not know in the speech of the Arabs of the application of al-darar to anything other than harmful defects. As for what is narrated in the hadith "la darar wa la dirar," it is either rare or follows the pattern of pairing (ittiba' wa muzawaja) because it is joined to the word "dirar," which is unassimilated. al-Jawhari claimed that darar is the noun of the verbal noun of al-durr, but there is scrutiny in this; it has not been transmitted from anyone else and there is no evidence for it.

His saying "with their wealth and their lives": jihad requires both matters, the expending of the self and the expending of wealth. However, jihad in its true sense is the expending of oneself in the way of Allah, even if one spends nothing, and even if one is a burden on the believers. Just as one who spends wealth to aid the fighters, without striving himself, is not called a striver, even if he has a great reward. Likewise, one who is held back by an excuse and wishes for the removal of his excuse and to join the strivers has a great virtue; but the virtue of actual jihad is not equaled by the virtue of others.

The clause ﴿Allah has preferred the strivers﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿not equal are those who sit at home among the believers﴾.

The real meaning of a darajah is a part of a place that is higher than another part adjoining it, such that the foot reaches it by ascending from the place where it was, by climbing; like the degrees of a high room or the rungs of a ladder.

Here darajah is used metaphorically for moral elevation, as in His saying ﴿And men have a degree over them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]. The elevation meant here is the elevation of virtue and abundance of reward.

Darajah is used here in the singular form, and its singularity is not for unity, because darajah here is a moral genus without individual instances. For this reason the expression is repeated in the clause that follows, as an emphasis on it, in the plural form in His saying "darajat minhu," because the plural is stronger than the singular.

The tanwin of darajatan is for magnification, and it corresponds to the meaning of the plural in His later saying "darajat minhu."

Darajatan is in the accusative by way of standing in for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) specifying the type of the verb "faddala," since the degree here is an addition to the meaning of preference. The sense is: Allah preferred the strivers with a preference that is a degree, i.e., a degree of preference.

The clause ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best reward﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah). The tanwin of kullan is the tanwin of substitution for an omitted genitive complement, and the sense is: "And each of the strivers and the sitters."

The clause ﴿But Allah has preferred the strivers over those who sit at home with a great reward﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Allah has preferred the strivers﴾, although the meaning of the two clauses is one, in view of the addition of "a great reward" in the second clause; by this, the conjoined clause differs from the clause conjoined to it with a difference that justifies the conjunction, along with the emphasis produced by repeating most of its wording.

By "al-mujahidin" is meant "those who strive with their wealth and their lives," so mention of the qualifier is dispensed with, due to its prior mention in the preceding parallel. Ajran 'azima is in the accusative by way of standing in for the absolute object specifying the type, since the reward is that preference, and it is described as great.

Darajat is in the accusative either as a substitute for "ajran 'azima," or as a circumstantial qualifier, considering that darajat is described as "from Him," i.e., from Allah.

Darajat is plural to indicate the magnification of the degree, since the plural, because of the meaning of multiplicity in it, has its form borrowed for the meaning of strength. Do you not see that 'Alqamah, when he recited to al-Harith ibn Jabalah, king of Ghassan, his verse seeking intercession for his brother Shaas ibn 'Abdah:

"In every tribe you have dealt out a favor, so Shaas deserves a draught (dhanub) of your generosity"

the king said to him: "And adhnabah (a multitude of draughts)?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 97–99 (part 1 of 2):

Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, [the angels] will say, "In what [condition] were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." They will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination. Except the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children who are unable to devise a plan and are not guided to a way, for those, perhaps Allah will pardon them, and ever is Allah Pardoning and Forgiving.

When the mention came, in the previous verse, of those who stayed away from jihad among the believers, with or without excuse, the state of those who stayed away from openly displaying their Islam, from among those who had resolved upon it in Makkah, or who had followed it and then the people of Makkah had barred them from it and tempted them until they returned them to the worship of idols, with or without excuse, [became such that] it would occur to the hearer's mind to ask about their fate if they persisted in that until they died.

So this verse came answering what surges in the souls of the hearers of questioning about the fate of those. Its position is therefore an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) for a hesitant questioner, and for this it is detached (fuṣṣilat), and for this it is introduced by the emphatic particle (inna), since their state makes it necessary to doubt that they are joined with the disbelievers, how so, when their inclination toward Islam has become apparent, and among them are those who had actually entered it and then were barred from it or tempted on its account.

The relative pronoun (alladhina) here has the force of the definite article of genus (lam al-jins), and the intended referent is not a specific person or group, but the category of those who died wronging themselves. And because of the implication in the relative clause of the reason for the ruling, which is His saying, "For those, their refuge is Hell," meaning: because they wronged themselves.

The meaning of "tawaffahum" is "cause them to die and seize their souls." So the meaning is: those who die wronging themselves. He turned away from "yamutuna" or "yutawaffawna" to "tawaffahumu al-malaʾika" in order to make it a means of showing the enormity of their temptation at death.

"Al-malaʾika" is a plural intended in the sense of genus, and the plural in this sense conveys the meaning of genus just as the singular does, as in His saying, "Say: the Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you" [al-Sajdah: 11]. So it is permissible that the Angel of Death, who seizes the souls of people, is one, with a power from him that reaches every person who perishes; and it is permissible that for every person who perishes there is an angel who seizes his soul, and this is clearer, and His saying, "Indeed, those whom the angels take in death," up to His saying, "In what [condition] were you?" supports it.

"Tawaffahum" is a past-tense verb; one says "tawaffahu Allah" and "tawaffahu malak al-mawt." It was not joined with a feminine marker for the subject of the verb, because the feminine form of broken-plural patterns is a grammatical (lafzi) and not a real feminine, so it is permissible to attach the feminine ta' to its verb: one says "ghazat al-ʿarab" and "ghaza al-ʿarab."

The wronging of oneself is for a person to do an act that leads to his own harm; so he is a wrongdoer to himself, because he did to himself what is not the business of rational people to do, due to the gravity of its consequence. Wrongdoing (zulm) is the thing whose doing is not right and which sound souls and the sacred laws do not accept. The usage of "wronging oneself" in the Qur'an has become well known for disbelief and for disobedience.

The meaning intended by it in this verse has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: what is intended by it is disbelief, and that it was revealed concerning a group of people from Makkah who had embraced Islam when the Messenger ﷺ was in Makkah; when he emigrated, they remained with their people in Makkah, and they were tempted and apostatized, and they went out on the day of Badr with the polytheists, and they increased the numbers of the polytheists, so they were killed at Badr as disbelievers. The Muslims said: "These companions of ours were Muslims, but they were compelled to disbelief and to going out," so this verse was revealed concerning them.

Al-Bukhari narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. They said: among them were Abu Qays ibn al-Fakih, al-Harith ibn Zamʿah, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, ʿAli ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and al-ʿAs ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj; these were killed.

Al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, and ʿAqil and Nawfal, the two sons of Abu Talib, were among those who went out with them, but these three were taken captive and ransomed themselves, and embraced Islam after that. This is the most correct of the opinions concerning this verse.

It has been said: what is intended by the wrongdoing is not emigrating, since some people from Makkah had embraced Islam and held back from emigration. al-Suddi said: whoever embraced Islam but did not emigrate was considered a disbeliever until he emigrated, meaning even if he displayed his Islam and left the state of polytheism.

Others said: rather, emigration was obligatory, and one who abandons it does not become a disbeliever. According to al-Suddi's view, the wrongdoing is also intended as disbelief, because it is considered disbelief in the view of the Sharia, meaning that the Sharia did not suffice with faith when its possessor did not emigrate while being able to do so; and this is far-fetched, for God the Exalted said: "And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship over them of anything until they emigrate; and if they seek your help in religion, then upon you is help," [al-Anfal: 72], so He obligated the Muslims to help them in religion if they sought their help, and this is a state that differs from the state of the disbelievers.

According to the view of the others: the wrongdoing is a grave disobedience, and the threat in this verse is suitable for both matters, on the basis that the Muslims did not count those who had not emigrated before the conquest of Makkah among the companions. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: because those among them who died in Islam and those who died in disbelief were not distinguished, so they did not count what they knew of them before the Prophet's emigration ﷺ.

The clause "They said, 'In what [condition] were you?'" is the predicate of "inna." The meaning: they said to them a statement of reproach and threat, with the threat, and as a preparation for refuting their excuse in their saying, "We were oppressed in the land," so they said to them, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?"

It is also permissible that the clause "They said, 'In what [condition] were you?'" occupies the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from the clause "tawaffahumu," since the angels' taking of them that is related here includes their saying to them, "In what [condition] were you?"

As for the clause "They said, 'We were oppressed in the land,'" it is detached from the conjunction, following the manner of the exchange of speech in dialogue, as we explained at His saying, "They said: Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?" in Surat al-Baqarah. Likewise the clause "They said: Was not the earth of Allah spacious?"

The predicate of "inna" is His saying, "For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination," with the particle fa' entering the predicate because the subject of "inna" is a relative pronoun, for it is treated like conditional nouns often, and its parallels have already been mentioned. The use of fa' here is more fitting because of the long separation between the subject of "inna" and its predicate by the exchange of speech, so that the predicate became like the result of that exchange, as the demonstrative noun also indicates.

The interrogative in His saying "In what [condition] were you?" is used for confirmation and reproach.

"Fi" is for figurative location. "Ma" is an interrogative about a state, as indicated by "fi." The questioned ones knew that the state asked about was the state of their remaining upon disbelief or not emigrating. So they replied, offering an excuse: "We were oppressed in the land."

The "mustad'af" is one counted as weak, so he is not regarded in whatever is done to him; he is not in a strength that enables him to openly display his Islam, so for this he is compelled to conceal his Islam. "The land" is Makkah.

They meant: "We were compelled to disbelief as long as we stayed in Makkah." This is a truthful answer, since there is no hope of lying in the realm of reality; and they thought this an excuse that permits remaining in polytheism, or permits staying away from emigration, according to the difference between the two interpretations. Therefore the angels refuted them with their saying, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?" that is, you could leave the land in which you are oppressed, and by that you would manifest faith; or, the earth has become spacious, so you will not lack a land where you can settle.

The apparent sense of the verse is that going out to any land other than the land of temptation counts as emigration; but His saying "emigrating to Allah and His Messenger" indicates that the intended emigration is to Madinah, which was the obligatory one. As for the emigration of the believers to Abyssinia, it was before the obligation of emigration, because the Prophet and a group of the believers were still in Makkah, and it was by the permission of the Prophet ﷺ. This is a decisive refutation of them.

Emigration (muhajarah) is leaving one's homeland and abandoning one's people; it is a form of mufa'alah from "hajara," meaning he abandoned. The term "muhajarah" was derived for leaving the homeland because it is generally from aversion between the one departing and those remaining, since each party seeks the other's abandonment. Then its use spread to departing from the homeland without this condition.

The "fa'" in His saying "For those, their refuge is Hell" is a consequence of what was related of the angels' reproach and threat toward them.

The demonstrative noun in His saying "For those, their refuge is Hell" is used to alert that they are deserving of the ruling that follows the demonstrative because of the attributes mentioned before it, since they were capable of escaping the temptation of polytheism by leaving its land.

His saying "Except the oppressed" is an exception from the threat. The meaning: except the truly oppressed, that is, those unable to leave Makkah due to lack of means, or due to the polytheists' coercing them and binding them to remain, like 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, whose report was mentioned earlier at His saying, "And it is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake" [al-Nisa': 92], and like Salamah ibn Hisham and al-Walid ibn al-Walid.

In al-Bukhari: "That the Messenger of Allah used to supplicate
in the 'Isha' prayer: O Allah, deliver ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah. O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid. O Allah, deliver Salamah ibn Hisham. O Allah, deliver the oppressed among the believers." And from Ibn ʿAbbas: "I and my mother were among the oppressed."

The specification by "among the men, the women, and the children" is for the purpose of generalization. The intention is to draw attention to the fact that among the men there are oppressed ones; therefore they were mentioned first, then the women and the children were attached to their mention, because their presence in the household serves as an excuse for their guardian when he cannot find a way out. Their mention was made earlier in His saying, "And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah and [for] the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children" [al-Nisa': 75]; and repeating their mention here reinforces that all these verses were revealed in preparation for the conquest of Makkah.

The clause "who are unable to devise a plan and are not guided to a way" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the oppressed," clarifying the oppression, so that it becomes evident that it is other than the oppression that those who wronged themselves claimed: "We were oppressed in the land." That is: they are unable to devise a plan for leaving, either because the people of Makkah prevented them, or because of their poverty; and they are not guided to a way, meaning they lack knowledge of the path, like the blind.

The clause "For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them" has the fa' in it as a fa' of explanation (fa' fasihah), and the use of the demonstrative is to alert that they are deserving of the ruling mentioned, namely forgiveness.

The verb "ʿasa" in His saying "For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them" implies that Allah hopes to pardon them. Since Allah is the doer of pardon and He knows that He will pardon them, or some of them by specification, it is necessary that the meaning of hope derived from "ʿasa" here be a figurative meaning: that His pardon for their sin is a pardon difficult to obtain, so the state of pardoning them is represented by the state of one who is not certain of obtaining pardon.

The purpose of this is to tighten the verification of their excuse, lest they be lax in its conditions relying on Allah's pardon, for Allah's excuse for them due to their oppression is a concession and a widening from Allah the Exalted, because remaining while openly displaying polytheism is a grave matter, and the obligatory course was resoluteness: that they be required to proclaim faith among the polytheists even if that brought upon them torment and destruction, as Sumayyah, the mother of ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, did.

This usage is the proper interpretation of the occurrences of "ʿasa" and "laʿalla" when they are attributed to the name of Allah the Exalted, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, "And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, perhaps you would be guided" [al-Baqarah: 53] in Surat al-Baqarah,

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 4, verses 97–99 (Part 2 of 2)

This is the meaning of the saying of Abu 'Ubayda: "'Asā from Allah is an obligation (ījāb)." And the saying of many scholars: that 'asā and la'alla in the Qur'an are for certainty (li-l-yaqīn). Their intention, when it is attributed to Allah the Exalted, is different from something like His saying: ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer to right conduct than this."﴾

Similar to this is what they said regarding the occurrence of the conditional particle "in" (if) in the speech of Allah the Exalted, even though its original use is for a condition whose occurrence is doubtful.

The scholars have agreed that the ruling of this verse ended on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, because emigration (hijra) was obligatory for the sake of separating oneself from the people of polytheism and the enemies of the religion, and for the ability to worship Allah without any obstacle preventing that. So when Mecca became a land of Islam, it was equal to other lands. This is supported by the hadith: "There is no hijra after the Conquest, but there is jihad and intention." So the believers remained in their homelands, except that the emigrants (muhājirūn) were forbidden to return to Mecca.

In the hadith: "O Allah, complete the emigration of my Companions and do not turn them back on their heels," which he (ﷺ) said after Mecca had been conquered. However, analogy (qiyās) based on the ruling of this verse opens to the jurists (mujtahidūn) a consideration of the rulings on the obligation to leave a land where the believer is tested in his religion, and these rulings are comprised of six situations.

The first situation: a believer is in a land where he is tested in his faith, forced into disbelief, and he is able to leave. His ruling is the ruling of those about whom this verse was revealed. Muslims emigrated from al-Andalus when the Christians compelled them to convert to Christianity, so they departed in every direction, leaving their wealth and homes, saving themselves and their faith, and a group of them perished on the way. That was in the year 902 (AH) and after, until the final expulsion in the year 1016.

The second situation: a believer is in a land of disbelief, not tested in his faith, but exposed to harm to his person or property through captivity, killing, or confiscation of wealth. This person has exposed himself to harm, and it is unlawful without dispute. This is what is called residing in a land of war, interpreted as the land of the enemy.

The third situation: a believer is in a land dominated by non-Muslims, but they do not test people in their faith, their worship, their persons, their wealth, or their honor. However, by residing there, the rulings of non-Muslims apply to him when some incident occurs with one of the people of that land who are non-Muslims. This is like one who lives today in the Christian lands of Europe.

The apparent meaning of Malik's saying is that residing in such a case is strongly disliked (makrūh karāha shadīda), because the rulings of non-Muslims apply to him. This is the apparent meaning of the Mudawwana in the book on trade to the land of war, and of al-'Utbiyya.

Thus the jurists of Qayrawan interpreted Malik's saying, and it is the apparent meaning of al-Risala, and it is the explicit statement of al-Lakhmi in the introduction to the book on trade to the land of war in his Tabsira. Ibn Muhriz and 'Abd al-Haqq approved it. Sahnun and Ibn Habib interpreted it as prohibition (ḥurma), as did 'Abd al-Hamid al-Sa'igh and al-Mazari. Sahnun added, saying that residing there is a blemish on one's integrity ('adāla), and al-Mazari and 'Abd al-Hamid agreed with him. On this basis the discussion proceeds concerning travel on Christian ships to the Hajj and other purposes.

Al-Barzali related from Ibn 'Arafa: if the ruler of Tunis is strong against the Christians, travel is permitted; otherwise it is not permitted, because they humiliate the Muslims.

The fourth situation: disbelievers overcome a land whose people are Muslims, and they do not test them in their religion, their worship, or their property, but they have the authority of power over them alone, and the rulings among them proceed according to the principles of the Islamic law, as occurred in Sicily when Rujayr al-Narmandi seized it.

And as occurred in the lands of Granada when the tyrant of the Galicians (al-Jallaqa) seized it on conditions, among them respect for their religion. Its people remained there for a period, and their scholars remained among them, holding the judiciary, fatwa, justice, trustworthiness, and similar offices. A group of them emigrated, and the emigrant did not blame the one who stayed, nor the one who stayed blame the emigrant.

The fifth situation: non-Muslims have influence and authority over some lands of Islam, while Muslim kings remain in them, their rulers continue to manage their people, their governors are appointed from among them, and their religions and all their rites are respected. But the conduct of the princes is under the supervision of non-Muslims and with their approval. This is what is called protection (ḥimāya), occupation (iḥtilāl), guardianship (wiṣāya), and mandate (intidāb), as occurred in Egypt during the occupation by the French army, then the period of the British occupation, and as occurred in Tunisia and the Far Maghrib under French protection, and as occurred in Syria and Iraq during the Mandate period. Regarding these there is no doubt that emigration from them is not obligatory.

The sixth situation: a land in which vices and innovations abound, and many rulings are applied contrary to the clear teaching of Islam, such that good deeds are mixed with evil ones, and the Muslim is not compelled therein to commit what is contrary to the Shari'a, but he is unable to change them except by speech, or he is entirely unable to do so.

Regarding this, it is narrated from Malik that emigration from it is obligatory; Ibn al-Qasim related it. However, this happened in Qayrawan during the time of the Banu 'Ubayd, and it is not known that any of its righteous jurists called the people to emigrate. It is enough for you that Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd and those like him remained there. And it occurred in Egypt during the period of the Fatimids as well, and none of its righteous scholars left it.

Below these six situations are many other situations which are more deserving of permissibility of residence, and these are degrees. Indeed, for the remaining of Muslims in their homelands, when they are not tested in their religion, there is a great benefit for the Islamic community (al-jāmi'a al-islāmiyya).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 97–99 (part 1 of 2):

Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, [the angels] will say, "In what [condition] were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." They will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination. Except the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children who are unable to devise a plan and are not guided to a way, for those, perhaps Allah will pardon them, and ever is Allah Pardoning and Forgiving.

When the mention came, in the previous verse, of those who stayed away from jihad among the believers, with or without excuse, the state of those who stayed away from openly displaying their Islam, from among those who had resolved upon it in Makkah, or who had followed it and then the people of Makkah had barred them from it and tempted them until they returned them to the worship of idols, with or without excuse, [became such that] it would occur to the hearer's mind to ask about their fate if they persisted in that until they died.

So this verse came answering what surges in the souls of the hearers of questioning about the fate of those. Its position is therefore an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) for a hesitant questioner, and for this it is detached (fuṣṣilat), and for this it is introduced by the emphatic particle (inna), since their state makes it necessary to doubt that they are joined with the disbelievers, how so, when their inclination toward Islam has become apparent, and among them are those who had actually entered it and then were barred from it or tempted on its account.

The relative pronoun (alladhina) here has the force of the definite article of genus (lam al-jins), and the intended referent is not a specific person or group, but the category of those who died wronging themselves. And because of the implication in the relative clause of the reason for the ruling, which is His saying, "For those, their refuge is Hell," meaning: because they wronged themselves.

The meaning of "tawaffahum" is "cause them to die and seize their souls." So the meaning is: those who die wronging themselves. He turned away from "yamutuna" or "yutawaffawna" to "tawaffahumu al-malaʾika" in order to make it a means of showing the enormity of their temptation at death.

"Al-malaʾika" is a plural intended in the sense of genus, and the plural in this sense conveys the meaning of genus just as the singular does, as in His saying, "Say: the Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you" [al-Sajdah: 11]. So it is permissible that the Angel of Death, who seizes the souls of people, is one, with a power from him that reaches every person who perishes; and it is permissible that for every person who perishes there is an angel who seizes his soul, and this is clearer, and His saying, "Indeed, those whom the angels take in death," up to His saying, "In what [condition] were you?" supports it.

"Tawaffahum" is a past-tense verb; one says "tawaffahu Allah" and "tawaffahu malak al-mawt." It was not joined with a feminine marker for the subject of the verb, because the feminine form of broken-plural patterns is a grammatical (lafzi) and not a real feminine, so it is permissible to attach the feminine ta' to its verb: one says "ghazat al-ʿarab" and "ghaza al-ʿarab."

The wronging of oneself is for a person to do an act that leads to his own harm; so he is a wrongdoer to himself, because he did to himself what is not the business of rational people to do, due to the gravity of its consequence. Wrongdoing (zulm) is the thing whose doing is not right and which sound souls and the sacred laws do not accept. The usage of "wronging oneself" in the Qur'an has become well known for disbelief and for disobedience.

The meaning intended by it in this verse has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: what is intended by it is disbelief, and that it was revealed concerning a group of people from Makkah who had embraced Islam when the Messenger ﷺ was in Makkah; when he emigrated, they remained with their people in Makkah, and they were tempted and apostatized, and they went out on the day of Badr with the polytheists, and they increased the numbers of the polytheists, so they were killed at Badr as disbelievers. The Muslims said: "These companions of ours were Muslims, but they were compelled to disbelief and to going out," so this verse was revealed concerning them.

Al-Bukhari narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. They said: among them were Abu Qays ibn al-Fakih, al-Harith ibn Zamʿah, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, ʿAli ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and al-ʿAs ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj; these were killed.

Al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, and ʿAqil and Nawfal, the two sons of Abu Talib, were among those who went out with them, but these three were taken captive and ransomed themselves, and embraced Islam after that. This is the most correct of the opinions concerning this verse.

It has been said: what is intended by the wrongdoing is not emigrating, since some people from Makkah had embraced Islam and held back from emigration. al-Suddi said: whoever embraced Islam but did not emigrate was considered a disbeliever until he emigrated, meaning even if he displayed his Islam and left the state of polytheism.

Others said: rather, emigration was obligatory, and one who abandons it does not become a disbeliever. According to al-Suddi's view, the wrongdoing is also intended as disbelief, because it is considered disbelief in the view of the Sharia, meaning that the Sharia did not suffice with faith when its possessor did not emigrate while being able to do so; and this is far-fetched, for God the Exalted said: "And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship over them of anything until they emigrate; and if they seek your help in religion, then upon you is help," [al-Anfal: 72], so He obligated the Muslims to help them in religion if they sought their help, and this is a state that differs from the state of the disbelievers.

According to the view of the others: the wrongdoing is a grave disobedience, and the threat in this verse is suitable for both matters, on the basis that the Muslims did not count those who had not emigrated before the conquest of Makkah among the companions. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: because those among them who died in Islam and those who died in disbelief were not distinguished, so they did not count what they knew of them before the Prophet's emigration ﷺ.

The clause "They said, 'In what [condition] were you?'" is the predicate of "inna." The meaning: they said to them a statement of reproach and threat, with the threat, and as a preparation for refuting their excuse in their saying, "We were oppressed in the land," so they said to them, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?"

It is also permissible that the clause "They said, 'In what [condition] were you?'" occupies the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from the clause "tawaffahumu," since the angels' taking of them that is related here includes their saying to them, "In what [condition] were you?"

As for the clause "They said, 'We were oppressed in the land,'" it is detached from the conjunction, following the manner of the exchange of speech in dialogue, as we explained at His saying, "They said: Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?" in Surat al-Baqarah. Likewise the clause "They said: Was not the earth of Allah spacious?"

The predicate of "inna" is His saying, "For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination," with the particle fa' entering the predicate because the subject of "inna" is a relative pronoun, for it is treated like conditional nouns often, and its parallels have already been mentioned. The use of fa' here is more fitting because of the long separation between the subject of "inna" and its predicate by the exchange of speech, so that the predicate became like the result of that exchange, as the demonstrative noun also indicates.

The interrogative in His saying "In what [condition] were you?" is used for confirmation and reproach.

"Fi" is for figurative location. "Ma" is an interrogative about a state, as indicated by "fi." The questioned ones knew that the state asked about was the state of their remaining upon disbelief or not emigrating. So they replied, offering an excuse: "We were oppressed in the land."

The "mustad'af" is one counted as weak, so he is not regarded in whatever is done to him; he is not in a strength that enables him to openly display his Islam, so for this he is compelled to conceal his Islam. "The land" is Makkah.

They meant: "We were compelled to disbelief as long as we stayed in Makkah." This is a truthful answer, since there is no hope of lying in the realm of reality; and they thought this an excuse that permits remaining in polytheism, or permits staying away from emigration, according to the difference between the two interpretations. Therefore the angels refuted them with their saying, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?" that is, you could leave the land in which you are oppressed, and by that you would manifest faith; or, the earth has become spacious, so you will not lack a land where you can settle.

The apparent sense of the verse is that going out to any land other than the land of temptation counts as emigration; but His saying "emigrating to Allah and His Messenger" indicates that the intended emigration is to Madinah, which was the obligatory one. As for the emigration of the believers to Abyssinia, it was before the obligation of emigration, because the Prophet and a group of the believers were still in Makkah, and it was by the permission of the Prophet ﷺ. This is a decisive refutation of them.

Emigration (muhajarah) is leaving one's homeland and abandoning one's people; it is a form of mufa'alah from "hajara," meaning he abandoned. The term "muhajarah" was derived for leaving the homeland because it is generally from aversion between the one departing and those remaining, since each party seeks the other's abandonment. Then its use spread to departing from the homeland without this condition.

The "fa'" in His saying "For those, their refuge is Hell" is a consequence of what was related of the angels' reproach and threat toward them.

The demonstrative noun in His saying "For those, their refuge is Hell" is used to alert that they are deserving of the ruling that follows the demonstrative because of the attributes mentioned before it, since they were capable of escaping the temptation of polytheism by leaving its land.

His saying "Except the oppressed" is an exception from the threat. The meaning: except the truly oppressed, that is, those unable to leave Makkah due to lack of means, or due to the polytheists' coercing them and binding them to remain, like 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, whose report was mentioned earlier at His saying, "And it is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake" [al-Nisa': 92], and like Salamah ibn Hisham and al-Walid ibn al-Walid.

In al-Bukhari: "That the Messenger of Allah used to supplicate
in the 'Isha' prayer: O Allah, deliver ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah. O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid. O Allah, deliver Salamah ibn Hisham. O Allah, deliver the oppressed among the believers." And from Ibn ʿAbbas: "I and my mother were among the oppressed."

The specification by "among the men, the women, and the children" is for the purpose of generalization. The intention is to draw attention to the fact that among the men there are oppressed ones; therefore they were mentioned first, then the women and the children were attached to their mention, because their presence in the household serves as an excuse for their guardian when he cannot find a way out. Their mention was made earlier in His saying, "And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah and [for] the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children" [al-Nisa': 75]; and repeating their mention here reinforces that all these verses were revealed in preparation for the conquest of Makkah.

The clause "who are unable to devise a plan and are not guided to a way" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the oppressed," clarifying the oppression, so that it becomes evident that it is other than the oppression that those who wronged themselves claimed: "We were oppressed in the land." That is: they are unable to devise a plan for leaving, either because the people of Makkah prevented them, or because of their poverty; and they are not guided to a way, meaning they lack knowledge of the path, like the blind.

The clause "For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them" has the fa' in it as a fa' of explanation (fa' fasihah), and the use of the demonstrative is to alert that they are deserving of the ruling mentioned, namely forgiveness.

The verb "ʿasa" in His saying "For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them" implies that Allah hopes to pardon them. Since Allah is the doer of pardon and He knows that He will pardon them, or some of them by specification, it is necessary that the meaning of hope derived from "ʿasa" here be a figurative meaning: that His pardon for their sin is a pardon difficult to obtain, so the state of pardoning them is represented by the state of one who is not certain of obtaining pardon.

The purpose of this is to tighten the verification of their excuse, lest they be lax in its conditions relying on Allah's pardon, for Allah's excuse for them due to their oppression is a concession and a widening from Allah the Exalted, because remaining while openly displaying polytheism is a grave matter, and the obligatory course was resoluteness: that they be required to proclaim faith among the polytheists even if that brought upon them torment and destruction, as Sumayyah, the mother of ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, did.

This usage is the proper interpretation of the occurrences of "ʿasa" and "laʿalla" when they are attributed to the name of Allah the Exalted, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, "And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, perhaps you would be guided" [al-Baqarah: 53] in Surat al-Baqarah,

This is the meaning of the saying of Abu 'Ubayda: "'Asā from Allah is an obligation (ījāb)." And the saying of many scholars: that 'asā and la'alla in the Qur'an are for certainty (li-l-yaqīn). Their intention, when it is attributed to Allah the Exalted, is different from something like His saying: ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer to right conduct than this."﴾

Similar to this is what they said regarding the occurrence of the conditional particle "in" (if) in the speech of Allah the Exalted, even though its original use is for a condition whose occurrence is doubtful.

The scholars have agreed that the ruling of this verse ended on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, because emigration (hijra) was obligatory for the sake of separating oneself from the people of polytheism and the enemies of the religion, and for the ability to worship Allah without any obstacle preventing that. So when Mecca became a land of Islam, it was equal to other lands. This is supported by the hadith: "There is no hijra after the Conquest, but there is jihad and intention." So the believers remained in their homelands, except that the emigrants (muhājirūn) were forbidden to return to Mecca.

In the hadith: "O Allah, complete the emigration of my Companions and do not turn them back on their heels," which he (ﷺ) said after Mecca had been conquered. However, analogy (qiyās) based on the ruling of this verse opens to the jurists (mujtahidūn) a consideration of the rulings on the obligation to leave a land where the believer is tested in his religion, and these rulings are comprised of six situations.

The first situation: a believer is in a land where he is tested in his faith, forced into disbelief, and he is able to leave. His ruling is the ruling of those about whom this verse was revealed. Muslims emigrated from al-Andalus when the Christians compelled them to convert to Christianity, so they departed in every direction, leaving their wealth and homes, saving themselves and their faith, and a group of them perished on the way. That was in the year 902 (AH) and after, until the final expulsion in the year 1016.

The second situation: a believer is in a land of disbelief, not tested in his faith, but exposed to harm to his person or property through captivity, killing, or confiscation of wealth. This person has exposed himself to harm, and it is unlawful without dispute. This is what is called residing in a land of war, interpreted as the land of the enemy.

The third situation: a believer is in a land dominated by non-Muslims, but they do not test people in their faith, their worship, their persons, their wealth, or their honor. However, by residing there, the rulings of non-Muslims apply to him when some incident occurs with one of the people of that land who are non-Muslims. This is like one who lives today in the Christian lands of Europe.

The apparent meaning of Malik's saying is that residing in such a case is strongly disliked (makrūh karāha shadīda), because the rulings of non-Muslims apply to him. This is the apparent meaning of the Mudawwana in the book on trade to the land of war, and of al-'Utbiyya.

Thus the jurists of Qayrawan interpreted Malik's saying, and it is the apparent meaning of al-Risala, and it is the explicit statement of al-Lakhmi in the introduction to the book on trade to the land of war in his Tabsira. Ibn Muhriz and 'Abd al-Haqq approved it. Sahnun and Ibn Habib interpreted it as prohibition (ḥurma), as did 'Abd al-Hamid al-Sa'igh and al-Mazari. Sahnun added, saying that residing there is a blemish on one's integrity ('adāla), and al-Mazari and 'Abd al-Hamid agreed with him. On this basis the discussion proceeds concerning travel on Christian ships to the Hajj and other purposes.

Al-Barzali related from Ibn 'Arafa: if the ruler of Tunis is strong against the Christians, travel is permitted; otherwise it is not permitted, because they humiliate the Muslims.

The fourth situation: disbelievers overcome a land whose people are Muslims, and they do not test them in their religion, their worship, or their property, but they have the authority of power over them alone, and the rulings among them proceed according to the principles of the Islamic law, as occurred in Sicily when Rujayr al-Narmandi seized it.

And as occurred in the lands of Granada when the tyrant of the Galicians (al-Jallaqa) seized it on conditions, among them respect for their religion. Its people remained there for a period, and their scholars remained among them, holding the judiciary, fatwa, justice, trustworthiness, and similar offices. A group of them emigrated, and the emigrant did not blame the one who stayed, nor the one who stayed blame the emigrant.

The fifth situation: non-Muslims have influence and authority over some lands of Islam, while Muslim kings remain in them, their rulers continue to manage their people, their governors are appointed from among them, and their religions and all their rites are respected. But the conduct of the princes is under the supervision of non-Muslims and with their approval. This is what is called protection (ḥimāya), occupation (iḥtilāl), guardianship (wiṣāya), and mandate (intidāb), as occurred in Egypt during the occupation by the French army, then the period of the British occupation, and as occurred in Tunisia and the Far Maghrib under French protection, and as occurred in Syria and Iraq during the Mandate period. Regarding these there is no doubt that emigration from them is not obligatory.

The sixth situation: a land in which vices and innovations abound, and many rulings are applied contrary to the clear teaching of Islam, such that good deeds are mixed with evil ones, and the Muslim is not compelled therein to commit what is contrary to the Shari'a, but he is unable to change them except by speech, or he is entirely unable to do so.

Regarding this, it is narrated from Malik that emigration from it is obligatory; Ibn al-Qasim related it. However, this happened in Qayrawan during the time of the Banu 'Ubayd, and it is not known that any of its righteous jurists called the people to emigrate. It is enough for you that Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd and those like him remained there. And it occurred in Egypt during the period of the Fatimids as well, and none of its righteous scholars left it.

Below these six situations are many other situations which are more deserving of permissibility of residence, and these are degrees. Indeed, for the remaining of Muslims in their homelands, when they are not tested in their religion, there is a great benefit for the Islamic community (al-jāmi'a al-islāmiyya).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 97–99 (part 1 of 2):

Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, [the angels] will say, "In what [condition] were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." They will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination. Except the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children who are unable to devise a plan and are not guided to a way, for those, perhaps Allah will pardon them, and ever is Allah Pardoning and Forgiving.

When the mention came, in the previous verse, of those who stayed away from jihad among the believers, with or without excuse, the state of those who stayed away from openly displaying their Islam, from among those who had resolved upon it in Makkah, or who had followed it and then the people of Makkah had barred them from it and tempted them until they returned them to the worship of idols, with or without excuse, [became such that] it would occur to the hearer's mind to ask about their fate if they persisted in that until they died.

So this verse came answering what surges in the souls of the hearers of questioning about the fate of those. Its position is therefore an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) for a hesitant questioner, and for this it is detached (fuṣṣilat), and for this it is introduced by the emphatic particle (inna), since their state makes it necessary to doubt that they are joined with the disbelievers, how so, when their inclination toward Islam has become apparent, and among them are those who had actually entered it and then were barred from it or tempted on its account.

The relative pronoun (alladhina) here has the force of the definite article of genus (lam al-jins), and the intended referent is not a specific person or group, but the category of those who died wronging themselves. And because of the implication in the relative clause of the reason for the ruling, which is His saying, "For those, their refuge is Hell," meaning: because they wronged themselves.

The meaning of "tawaffahum" is "cause them to die and seize their souls." So the meaning is: those who die wronging themselves. He turned away from "yamutuna" or "yutawaffawna" to "tawaffahumu al-malaʾika" in order to make it a means of showing the enormity of their temptation at death.

"Al-malaʾika" is a plural intended in the sense of genus, and the plural in this sense conveys the meaning of genus just as the singular does, as in His saying, "Say: the Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you" [al-Sajdah: 11]. So it is permissible that the Angel of Death, who seizes the souls of people, is one, with a power from him that reaches every person who perishes; and it is permissible that for every person who perishes there is an angel who seizes his soul, and this is clearer, and His saying, "Indeed, those whom the angels take in death," up to His saying, "In what [condition] were you?" supports it.

"Tawaffahum" is a past-tense verb; one says "tawaffahu Allah" and "tawaffahu malak al-mawt." It was not joined with a feminine marker for the subject of the verb, because the feminine form of broken-plural patterns is a grammatical (lafzi) and not a real feminine, so it is permissible to attach the feminine ta' to its verb: one says "ghazat al-ʿarab" and "ghaza al-ʿarab."

The wronging of oneself is for a person to do an act that leads to his own harm; so he is a wrongdoer to himself, because he did to himself what is not the business of rational people to do, due to the gravity of its consequence. Wrongdoing (zulm) is the thing whose doing is not right and which sound souls and the sacred laws do not accept. The usage of "wronging oneself" in the Qur'an has become well known for disbelief and for disobedience.

The meaning intended by it in this verse has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: what is intended by it is disbelief, and that it was revealed concerning a group of people from Makkah who had embraced Islam when the Messenger ﷺ was in Makkah; when he emigrated, they remained with their people in Makkah, and they were tempted and apostatized, and they went out on the day of Badr with the polytheists, and they increased the numbers of the polytheists, so they were killed at Badr as disbelievers. The Muslims said: "These companions of ours were Muslims, but they were compelled to disbelief and to going out," so this verse was revealed concerning them.

Al-Bukhari narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. They said: among them were Abu Qays ibn al-Fakih, al-Harith ibn Zamʿah, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, ʿAli ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and al-ʿAs ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj; these were killed.

Al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, and ʿAqil and Nawfal, the two sons of Abu Talib, were among those who went out with them, but these three were taken captive and ransomed themselves, and embraced Islam after that. This is the most correct of the opinions concerning this verse.

It has been said: what is intended by the wrongdoing is not emigrating, since some people from Makkah had embraced Islam and held back from emigration. al-Suddi said: whoever embraced Islam but did not emigrate was considered a disbeliever until he emigrated, meaning even if he displayed his Islam and left the state of polytheism.

Others said: rather, emigration was obligatory, and one who abandons it does not become a disbeliever. However, by residing there, the rulings of non-Muslims apply to him when some incident occurs with one of the people of that land who are non-Muslims.
