The apparent meaning of Malik's saying is that residing in such a case is strongly disliked (makrūh karāha shadīda), because the rulings of non-Muslims apply to him. This is the apparent meaning of the Mudawwana in the book on trade to the land of war, and of al-'Utbiyya.

Thus the jurists of Qayrawan interpreted Malik's saying, and it is the apparent meaning of al-Risala, and it is the explicit statement of al-Lakhmi in the introduction to the book on trade to the land of war in his Tabsira. Ibn Muhriz and 'Abd al-Haqq approved it. Sahnun and Ibn Habib interpreted it as prohibition (ḥurma), as did 'Abd al-Hamid al-Sa'igh and al-Mazari. Sahnun added, saying that residing there is a blemish on one's integrity ('adāla), and al-Mazari and 'Abd al-Hamid agreed with him. On this basis the discussion proceeds concerning travel on Christian ships to the Hajj and other purposes.

Al-Barzali related from Ibn 'Arafa: if the ruler of Tunis is strong against the Christians, travel is permitted; otherwise it is not permitted, because they humiliate the Muslims.

The fourth situation: disbelievers overcome a land whose people are Muslims, and they do not test them in their religion, their worship, or their property, but they have the authority of power over them alone, and the rulings among them proceed according to the principles of the Islamic law, as occurred in Sicily when Rujayr al-Narmandi seized it.

And as occurred in the lands of Granada when the tyrant of the Galicians (al-Jallaqa) seized it on conditions, among them respect for their religion. Its people remained there for a period, and their scholars remained among them, holding the judiciary, fatwa, justice, trustworthiness, and similar offices. A group of them emigrated, and the emigrant did not blame the one who stayed, nor the one who stayed blame the emigrant.

The fifth situation: non-Muslims have influence and authority over some lands of Islam, while Muslim kings remain in them, their rulers continue to manage their people, their governors are appointed from among them, and their religions and all their rites are respected. But the conduct of the princes is under the supervision of non-Muslims and with their approval. This is what is called protection (ḥimāya), occupation (iḥtilāl), guardianship (wiṣāya), and mandate (intidāb), as occurred in Egypt during the occupation by the French army, then the period of the British occupation, and as occurred in Tunisia and the Far Maghrib under French protection, and as occurred in Syria and Iraq during the Mandate period. Regarding these there is no doubt that emigration from them is not obligatory.

The sixth situation: a land in which vices and innovations abound, and many rulings are applied contrary to the clear teaching of Islam, such that good deeds are mixed with evil ones, and the Muslim is not compelled therein to commit what is contrary to the Shari'a, but he is unable to change them except by speech, or he is entirely unable to do so.

Regarding this, it is narrated from Malik that emigration from it is obligatory; Ibn al-Qasim related it. However, this happened in Qayrawan during the time of the Banu 'Ubayd, and it is not known that any of its righteous jurists called the people to emigrate. It is enough for you that Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd and those like him remained there. And it occurred in Egypt during the period of the Fatimids as well, and none of its righteous scholars left it.

Below these six situations are many other situations which are more deserving of permissibility of residence, and these are degrees. Indeed, for the remaining of Muslims in their homelands, when they are not tested in their religion, there is a great benefit for the Islamic community (al-jāmi'a al-islāmiyya).

[Page 181]

The clause ﴿Whoever migrates in the way of Allah will find on earth many a refuge and abundance﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves [will be asked, "In what condition were you?"]﴾ [al-Nisa, 4:97]. The word "man" (whoever) is a conditional particle. Migration in the way of Allah (al-muhajara fi sabil Allah) is migration for the sake of the religion of Allah.

"Sabil" (way, path) is a well-known metaphor (isti'ara). What made it more acceptable is that migration is a kind of journeying, so mentioning "way" alongside it carries a type of double meaning (tawriya).

"Muraghaman" is a noun of place from "raghama," which means to go off into the earth. The verb "raghama" is derived from "al-raghaam," with a fatha on the ra, which means dust. Or it comes from "raghama ghayrahu," meaning he overcame him and subdued him. Its original sense may be that he left him on the raghaam, that is, the dust, so that he finds a place where he can humble (yurghim) those who humbled him, that is, where he can overcome his people by being independent of them, just as they humiliated him by forcing him into disbelief. Al-Harith ibn Wa'la al-Dhuhli said:

"Do not feel safe from a people whom you have wronged,
and whom you have begun with insult and humiliation.
If they pollinate palms that belong to others,
and a thing you belittle may grow."

That is, they would become a help to the enemy against their own people.

The description of "muraghaman" as "kathiran" (many) is because what is meant is the genus of places. "Sa'a" (abundance, expanse) is the opposite of narrowness. It is the literal meaning of the expansion of places, and it is also used for ease of living, so it is a figurative expanse. If "muraghaman" means going off into the earth, then the conjunction of "sa'a" to it is an explanatory conjunction (atf tafsir). If it means a place of anger and resentment, then the conjunction of "sa'a" indicates that he finds it suitable both in terms of satisfying the self and in terms of comfort of residence.

Then Allah honored the matter of migration by making its reward attained merely by leaving the land of disbelief, even if he does not reach the land to which he migrates, through His saying: ﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger﴾, and so on.

The meaning of "migration to Allah" is migration to the place that Allah is pleased with. "The Messenger" is conjoined to the name of Allah (ism al-jalala) to point to the particular migration to Madina, for joining the Messenger and strengthening his side, because one who migrates to somewhere other than Madina has been spared the oppression of disbelief but has not gained the support of the Messenger. For this reason, the people who migrated to Abyssinia (al-Habasha) hastened to join the Messenger when news of his migration to Madina reached them.

The meaning of ﴿then death overtakes him﴾ is: on the road. It is also possible that the meaning is: then death overtakes him as a migrant, that is, he does not return after his migration to the lands of disbelief, and this is the more correct view.

There is disagreement about the migration intended by this verse. It was said: it is migration to Madina. It was said: it is migration to Abyssinia. There is also disagreement about who is meant by the relative clause in His saying ﴿whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger﴾. Among those who said that the intended migration is to Madina, they said that what is meant by "whoever leaves" is a man from among the Muslims who remained behind after the Prophet (ﷺ) migrated to Madina. When the saying of the Exalted ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves; [the angels] say, "In what condition were you?"﴾ [4:97] down to His saying ﴿And Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ [4:99] was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote it to the Muslims of Makkah. This man was ill, and he said: "Indeed, I have wealth and slaves." He called his sons and said to them: "Carry me to Madina." They carried him on a litter, and when he reached al-Tan'im he died, and this verse was revealed concerning him. It includes those like him, so it is general in the context of the conditional, and the occasion of revelation does not restrict it.

This man was from Kinana. It was said he was from Khuza'a, and it was said from Jundu'. His name differs across ten statements: Jundub ibn Hamza al-Jundu'i; Hunduj ibn Damra al-Laythi al-Khuza'i; Damra ibn Baghid al-Laythi; Damra ibn Jundub al-Damri; Damra ibn Damra ibn Nu'aym; Damra from Khuza'a (thus); Damra ibn al-'Is; al-'Is ibn Damra ibn Zinba'; Habib ibn Damra; Akthan ibn Sayfi.

Those who said that the intended migration is to Abyssinia said: the one meant by "whoever leaves his home" is Khalid ibn Hizam ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi, nephew of Khadija, mother of the believers. He left as a migrant to Abyssinia, and a snake bit him on the road, and he died. The context of the conditional rejects this interpretation.

[Page 183]

This is a transition to another ruling, prompted by the mention of travel as a means of leaving the authority of disbelief, in keeping with the Qur'an's practice of varying its topics and seeking out their occasions. The sentence is coordinated with the preceding sentence. *Al-darb fi al-ard* means travel.

*Idha* is here implicitly carrying the meaning of a conditional, as is most common in its usage, which is why the *fa'* entered the verb that functions like the apodosis of a condition. *Idha* is governed by the verb of the apodosis.

*Qasr al-salah* (shortening of the prayer) means reducing it. It is known that the parts of the prayer are its units (*rak'at*) with their prostrations and recitations, so it is necessarily understood that shortening the prayer means reducing the number of units. The Prophet ﷺ clarified this by his practice, when he made the four-unit prayer into a two-unit prayer. The verse was general and did not specify which prayers may be shortened, so the Sunnah clarified that they are the Dhuhr, the 'Asr and the 'Isha'. The Subh was not shortened because it would become a single unit and thus would not be a prayer, and the Maghrib was not shortened so that it would not become an even number, since it is the odd-numbered prayer of the day, and so that it would not become a single unit, as we have said regarding the Subh.

This verse refers to the shortening of the four-unit prayers while travelling, and its style suggests that it was revealed concerning this. It has been said that the shortening of the prayer during travel was legislated in the fourth year after the Hijrah, and this is the most sound view. It has also been said that it was in Rabi' al-Akhir of the second year, and it has been said that it was forty days after the Hijrah.

The people of the authentic collections have related the statement of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "The prayer was prescribed as two units, then the travelling prayer was left as it was and the resident prayer was increased." This is a clear and evident report. The meaning of the verse, in accordance with it, is that when Allah the Exalted prescribed the prayer as two units, and it was established in that form, then when the Dhuhr, the 'Asr and the 'Isha' became four units, the earlier number was abrogated (*nusikha*).

This was at the beginning of the Hijrah. Since the normal state of people was residence, which was the predominant condition for them, the performance of the mentioned prayers as two units was discontinued. When they went out to fight, Allah lightened the burden for them and permitted them to perform those prayers as two units each. For this reason Allah said "there is no blame upon you" and said "that you shorten the prayer". 'A'ishah's words "the travelling prayer was left as it was" refer to the fact that it did not change from its original state. This indicates that they did not perform it in full while travelling after the Hijrah, so there is no contradiction between her statement and the verse.

His saying ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you﴾ is a condition which indicates that the permission to shorten is restricted to the state of fear of the polytheists gaining power over them and invalidating their prayer, and that Allah permitted shortening so that the prayer might be performed in tranquillity.

Therefore this verse is specific to shortening the prayer in a state of fear, which is the shortening that has a special form in congregational prayer. This is the opinion of Malik, and what he transmitted in the *Muwatta'* supports it: "A man from the family of Khalid ibn Usayd asked 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar: 'We find the prayer of fear and the prayer of residence in the Qur'an, but we do not find the prayer of travel.' Ibn 'Umar said: 'O son of my brother, Allah sent Muhammad to us and we know nothing, so we only do as we have seen him doing.'"

He means that Ibn 'Umar confirmed the questioner and informed him that the travelling prayer was established by the Sunnah. Likewise 'A'ishah and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas held that this verse was specific to fear, so they would complete the prayer while travelling.

This interpretation is the clearest regarding the meaning of this verse. Thus the shortening during travel without fear and the shortening of the prayer in residence during fear are both established by the Sunnah, and one of them is earlier than the other, as Ibn 'Umar said.

[Page 184]

It is also reported from Ya'la ibn Umayyah that he said: "I said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: 'Allah the Exalted says: ﴿if you fear﴾, and the people are now safe.' He said: 'I wondered at what you wondered at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah about that, and he said: "It is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity."'"

There is no doubt that the meaning of this report is that the Prophet ﷺ confirmed 'Umar in his understanding that this verse restricts shortening to the case of fear. So shortening because of fear was a concession to remove hardship. His saying "it is a charity" and so on means that shortening during travel without fear is a charity from Allah, that is, a lightening, and it is less than a concession, so do not reject His concession.

There is no need for the strained interpretations used to explain the qualifier in His saying ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you﴾, and the verse is restricted to the prayer of fear. The scholars who hold that shortening is obligatory in travel, such as Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hanifah, Muhammad ibn Sahnun and Isma'il ibn Ishaq among the Malikis, and those who hold that the shortening is a strongly affirmed Sunnah, such as Malik ibn Anas and most of his companions, would be spared from interpreting His saying ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ in a way that does not suit the apparent sense of such wording.

His saying ﴿And when you travel in the land﴾ is a repetition of the legislation of the concession of shortening during travel, for the purpose of preparing for His saying ﴿And when you are among them﴾ and the verses that follow.

As for shortening the prayer during travel, it is indicated by the practical Sunnah, and most of the Companions followed it, except 'A'ishah and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. Those who held that it was obligatory went so far, on the basis of 'A'ishah's report in the *Muwatta'* and the two *Sahihs*, because it indicates that the travelling prayer remained in its original prescribed form, so if one were to perform it in four units it would be an addition to the prayer.

Also, there is the saying of 'Umar, related by al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah: "The prayer of travel is two units, complete, not shortened." Malik only said it was a Sunnah because nothing was transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the travelling prayer except shortening, and likewise the caliphs after him.

'Uthman ibn 'Affan only completed the prayer during the Hajj out of fear that the Bedouins would suppose that all prayers are two units. However, Malik did not say it was obligatory because of His saying ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, since that is incompatible with the forms of obligation. He indeed did well in reconciling the implications of the evidences.

He speaks of ﴿the disbelievers﴾, which is plural, with the word ''aduwwan'' (enemy), which is singular. We have already mentioned this at His saying ﴿and if he was from a people hostile to you﴾ [An-Nisa': 92].

[Page 185]

His saying ﴿And when you are among them and establish the prayer for them﴾ describes the form of the prayer of fear in congregation, by His saying ﴿and establish the prayer for them﴾. The scholars agreed that this verse prescribed the prayer of fear. Most reports indicate that its prescription was at the battle of Dhat al-Riqa', in a place called Nakhlah between 'Usfan and Dajnan in Najd, when they met the forces of Ghatafan: Muharib, Anmar and Tha'labah. This was between the sixth and seventh years after the Hijrah, and the first prayer performed in this way was the 'Asr prayer.

Its cause was that when the polytheists saw the eagerness of the Muslims for the prayer, they said: "This prayer is an opportunity for us. If we raid them, we would strike them while they are unaware." So Allah informed His Prophet of that, and the verse was revealed.

However, Allah began the ruling on the prayer with His saying ﴿And when you are among them﴾, which at first sight implies that the prayer of fear does not take this form except when it is with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so it is a particularity of his leadership.

This was the view of Isma'il ibn 'Ulayyah, and Abu Yusuf, the companion of Abu Hanifah, in one of his opinions. They explained the particularity by saying that it is due to the eagerness of people for the merit of congregation with the Messenger, unlike other imams, so that each group could follow a different imam.

This is a weak view, because it contradicts the practice of the Companions, and because the purpose of the legislation of congregation is the gathering of the Muslims in one place, so this purpose is observed to the extent possible. Moreover, Abu Yusuf does not accept the implication of the opposite (*mafhum al-mukhalafah*), so the verse does not indicate that the rule is restricted to the Prophet's leadership. For this reason, the majority of scholars affirmed that this verse prescribed the prayer of fear for the Muslims for all time.

The scope of this condition, according to them, is in accordance with the general circumstances of the Muslims at that time, namely that the Prophet ﷺ remained with their military expeditions and detachments unless there was necessity, as in the hadith: "Were it not that there are people who would not stay behind after me, and I did not have anything to mount them upon, I would never stay behind any detachment that went out in the way of Allah."

So the intention is not to guard against the presence of others among them, but rather to emphasise the presence of the Prophet among them. Since the commanders were in his place in the campaigns, what Allah permitted for the Muslims with him, He permits for them with his commanders. This is like His saying ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾.

In the arrangement of the verse there is a wonderful concision, for when He said ﴿So let a group of them stand with you﴾, it is understood that there is another group. So the pronoun in His saying ﴿and let them take their arms﴾ refers to the group in terms of its individuals. Likewise the pronoun in His saying ﴿and when they have prostrated﴾ refers to the group which is with the Prophet, because the "being with" is the being with in prayer, and He has said ﴿when they have prostrated﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿then let them be behind you﴾ refers to the other group implied by the contrast, since it is evident that the answer, which is ﴿then let them be behind you﴾, is necessarily for the group facing the enemy.

His saying ﴿and let another group come who have not prayed﴾ is the counterpart of His saying ﴿so let a group of them stand with you﴾.

The verse has summarised what each group does in the rest of the prayer, but it indicates that the Prophet's prayer is one, because He said ﴿and let them pray with you﴾. So He made them followers of his prayer, and this indicates that his prayer is one. If he were to pray a separate prayer with each group, He would have said ﴿so let him pray with them﴾. By this, the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri is refuted: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed two units with each group." This is because it would make him complete the prayer and not shorten it, or else he would have prayed the obligatory prayer with one of the two groups and a supererogatory prayer with the second group, which would be obligatory for the believers. Unless al-Hasan commits to that and holds that it is permissible for one performing an obligatory prayer to follow one performing a supererogatory prayer. It appears that such following is not valid, although there is no evidence in the Sunnah for its invalidity.

The majority of scholars held that the imam prays one unit with each group. They differed only concerning how the prayer is divided with respect to the followers. The decisive statement on this is what Malik transmitted in the *Muwatta'*, from Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah, that he prayed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the prayer of fear on the day of Dhat al-Riqa'. A group lined up behind him and another group stood facing the enemy. He prayed one unit with those who were with him, then he stood up and they completed one unit for themselves. Then they departed and stood facing the enemy, and the other group came, and he prayed with them the unit that remained for him, then he gave the salam. Then they completed the unit that they had missed and gave the salam. This form is more in accordance with the wording of the verse. The other reports are numerous.

The *ta'ifah* (group) is a number of people with many members. The truth is that it is not applied to one or two, although some early exegetes said so. It may exceed a thousand, as in His saying, "between two groups from before us." Its root is derived from *ta'ifat al-shay'*, which is a part of a thing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 101–102 (part 2 of 2):

His saying ﴿and let them take their precautions and their weapons﴾: the verb "take" (al-akhdh) is used both in its literal and figurative senses. Taking precaution (akhdh al-hadhar) is figurative, since the literal meaning of "taking" is to grasp, whereas it is used figuratively for being engaged in something and persisting in it. Taking up weapons is literal. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and those who had homes [in Medina] and [adopted] the faith before them﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], for the "settling" (tabawwu') in the faith means entering into it and attaining it after leaving disbelief. The command is given in the imperative form rather than saying, "There is no blame upon you if you take your weapons," because taking up weapons contains a legislated benefit (maslahah shar'iyyah).

His saying ﴿The disbelievers wish﴾ etc.: this wish of theirs is well known, for it is the nature of every combatant. So that well-known meaning is not what is intended by the verse. What is intended is that they wished a wish that they regarded as attainable, because they supposed that the Muslims' occupation with the affairs of their religion would keep them away from the interests of their worldly life. This was out of ignorance on the part of the polytheists regarding the reality of the religion, so they hoped that the prayer would distract them from preparing against their enemies. God therefore alerted the believers to this, so that they would not be in accordance with the supposition of the polytheists, and so that He would train them to adopt resolve in all matters, and show them that the wellbeing of religion and of worldly life are twin companions (sinwan).

Al-asliha (weapons) is the plural of silah, which is a collective noun for all instruments of war made of iron, namely the sword, the spear, the arrow, and the lance. The shield, the coat of mail and the helmet are not counted as weapons (silah). It may be masculine or feminine, though the masculine is more eloquent, and for this reason they formed its plural as asliha, which is among the patterns of the sound masculine plural.

Al-amti'ah is the plural of matA', which is everything that may be benefited from, of goods and furnishings, and it includes whatever aids in war, such as saddles and the war gear, like coats of mail and helmets. "So they incline" (fa-yamiluna) is a branch of His saying "if you were heedless" etc., and it is the object of the wish, meaning: they wished for your heedlessness so that they might incline upon you. Al-mayl (inclining) is turning away from the middle to the side, and it is also used for turning away from something one was with to something else, as here, meaning: they turn away from their camp toward your army. Since the intended sense of inclining here is charging and attacking, it is governed by "upon" (ʿalā), meaning: they will rush upon you while you are heedless.

The phrase ﴿a single inclination﴾ (mayylatan) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) explaining the number, meaning: a single, unified assault. The form of the single occurrence is used here as a metaphor (kinayah) for strength and force, because a forceful and powerful act achieves its aim swiftly without repeated treatment, so the action is not repeated to attain its purpose. The word "single" (wahidah) reinforces the sense of single occurrence derived from the pattern fa'lah, so as to draw attention to the metaphorical intent, lest it be supposed that the infinitive is merely for emphasis of His saying "they will incline."

His saying ﴿There is no blame upon you if rain causes you discomfort﴾ etc.: this is a concession (rukhsah) granted to them to lay down their weapons in cases of hardship. The more complete form in performing the prayer has become here a concession, because actions are judged by their intentions and by the benefits and harms that result from them, and for this reason the concession was restricted together with taking precaution. The cause of the concession is that rain distracts both parties equally, whereas illness necessitates the concession specifically for the one who is ill.

His saying ﴿Indeed God has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ is an appended conclusion (tadhyil) to encourage the Muslims. When He repeated the command to take up weapons and precaution, it was feared that fear of the enemy might arise in the souls of the Muslims because of the intensity of the warning against him, so He followed this with the statement that God has prepared for them a humiliating punishment, namely the punishment of defeat, killing and capture, like that in His saying, ﴿Fight them, and God will punish them at your hands﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14]. The command to take precaution and weapons is only to bring about the causes of what God has prepared for them, for when God wills a matter He prepares its causes. In this is a teaching to the Muslims that they should seek effects from their causes, meaning: if you take your precaution, you will be safe from your enemy.

It is also reported from Ya'la ibn Umayyah that he said: "I said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: 'Allah the Exalted says: ﴿if you fear﴾, and the people are now safe.' He said: 'I wondered at what you wondered at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah about that, and he said: "It is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity."'"

There is no doubt that the meaning of this report is that the Prophet ﷺ confirmed 'Umar in his understanding that this verse restricts shortening to the case of fear. So shortening because of fear was a concession to remove hardship. His saying "it is a charity" and so on means that shortening during travel without fear is a charity from Allah, that is, a lightening, and it is less than a concession, so do not reject His concession.

There is no need for the strained interpretations used to explain the qualifier in His saying ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you﴾, and the verse is restricted to the prayer of fear. The scholars who hold that shortening is obligatory in travel, such as Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hanifah, Muhammad ibn Sahnun and Isma'il ibn Ishaq among the Malikis, and those who hold that the shortening is a strongly affirmed Sunnah, such as Malik ibn Anas and most of his companions, would be spared from interpreting His saying ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ in a way that does not suit the apparent sense of such wording.

His saying ﴿And when you travel in the land﴾ is a repetition of the legislation of the concession of shortening during travel, for the purpose of preparing for His saying ﴿And when you are among them﴾ and the verses that follow.

As for shortening the prayer during travel, it is indicated by the practical Sunnah, and most of the Companions followed it, except 'A'ishah and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. Those who held that it was obligatory went so far, on the basis of 'A'ishah's report in the *Muwatta'* and the two *Sahihs*, because it indicates that the travelling prayer remained in its original prescribed form, so if one were to perform it in four units it would be an addition to the prayer.

Also, there is the saying of 'Umar, related by al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah: "The prayer of travel is two units, complete, not shortened." Malik only said it was a Sunnah because nothing was transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the travelling prayer except shortening, and likewise the caliphs after him.

'Uthman ibn 'Affan only completed the prayer during the Hajj out of fear that the Bedouins would suppose that all prayers are two units. However, Malik did not say it was obligatory because of His saying ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, since that is incompatible with the forms of obligation. He indeed did well in reconciling the implications of the evidences.

He speaks of ﴿the disbelievers﴾, which is plural, with the word ''aduwwan'' (enemy), which is singular. We have already mentioned this at His saying ﴿and if he was from a people hostile to you﴾ [An-Nisa': 92].

[Page 185]

His saying ﴿And when you are among them and establish the prayer for them﴾ describes the form of the prayer of fear in congregation, by His saying ﴿and establish the prayer for them﴾. The scholars agreed that this verse prescribed the prayer of fear. Most reports indicate that its prescription was at the battle of Dhat al-Riqa', in a place called Nakhlah between 'Usfan and Dajnan in Najd, when they met the forces of Ghatafan: Muharib, Anmar and Tha'labah. This was between the sixth and seventh years after the Hijrah, and the first prayer performed in this way was the 'Asr prayer.

Its cause was that when the polytheists saw the eagerness of the Muslims for the prayer, they said: "This prayer is an opportunity for us. If we raid them, we would strike them while they are unaware." So Allah informed His Prophet of that, and the verse was revealed.

However, Allah began the ruling on the prayer with His saying ﴿And when you are among them﴾, which at first sight implies that the prayer of fear does not take this form except when it is with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so it is a particularity of his leadership.

This was the view of Isma'il ibn 'Ulayyah, and Abu Yusuf, the companion of Abu Hanifah, in one of his opinions. They explained the particularity by saying that it is due to the eagerness of people for the merit of congregation with the Messenger, unlike other imams, so that each group could follow a different imam.

This is a weak view, because it contradicts the practice of the Companions, and because the purpose of the legislation of congregation is the gathering of the Muslims in one place, so this purpose is observed to the extent possible. Moreover, Abu Yusuf does not accept the implication of the opposite (*mafhum al-mukhalafah*), so the verse does not indicate that the rule is restricted to the Prophet's leadership. For this reason, the majority of scholars affirmed that this verse prescribed the prayer of fear for the Muslims for all time.

The scope of this condition, according to them, is in accordance with the general circumstances of the Muslims at that time, namely that the Prophet ﷺ remained with their military expeditions and detachments unless there was necessity, as in the hadith: "Were it not that there are people who would not stay behind after me, and I did not have anything to mount them upon, I would never stay behind any detachment that went out in the way of Allah."

So the intention is not to guard against the presence of others among them, but rather to emphasise the presence of the Prophet among them. Since the commanders were in his place in the campaigns, what Allah permitted for the Muslims with him, He permits for them with his commanders. This is like His saying ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾.

In the arrangement of the verse there is a wonderful concision, for when He said ﴿So let a group of them stand with you﴾, it is understood that there is another group. So the pronoun in His saying ﴿and let them take their arms﴾ refers to the group in terms of its individuals. Likewise the pronoun in His saying ﴿and when they have prostrated﴾ refers to the group which is with the Prophet, because the "being with" is the being with in prayer, and He has said ﴿when they have prostrated﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿then let them be behind you﴾ refers to the other group implied by the contrast, since it is evident that the answer, which is ﴿then let them be behind you﴾, is necessarily for the group facing the enemy.

His saying ﴿and let another group come who have not prayed﴾ is the counterpart of His saying ﴿so let a group of them stand with you﴾.

The verse has summarised what each group does in the rest of the prayer, but it indicates that the Prophet's prayer is one, because He said ﴿and let them pray with you﴾. So He made them followers of his prayer, and this indicates that his prayer is one. If he were to pray a separate prayer with each group, He would have said ﴿so let him pray with them﴾. By this, the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri is refuted: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed two units with each group." This is because it would make him complete the prayer and not shorten it, or else he would have prayed the obligatory prayer with one of the two groups and a supererogatory prayer with the second group, which would be obligatory for the believers. Unless al-Hasan commits to that and holds that it is permissible for one performing an obligatory prayer to follow one performing a supererogatory prayer. It appears that such following is not valid, although there is no evidence in the Sunnah for its invalidity.

The majority of scholars held that the imam prays one unit with each group. They differed only concerning how the prayer is divided with respect to the followers. The decisive statement on this is what Malik transmitted in the *Muwatta'*, from Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah, that he prayed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the prayer of fear on the day of Dhat al-Riqa'. A group lined up behind him and another group stood facing the enemy. He prayed one unit with those who were with him, then he stood up and they completed one unit for themselves. Then they departed and stood facing the enemy, and the other group came, and he prayed with them the unit that remained for him, then he gave the salam. Then they completed the unit that they had missed and gave the salam. This form is more in accordance with the wording of the verse. The other reports are numerous.

The *ta'ifah* (group) is a number of people with many members. The truth is that it is not applied to one or two, although some early exegetes said so. It may exceed a thousand, as in His saying, "between two groups from before us." Its root is derived from *ta'ifat al-shay'*, which is a part of a thing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 101–102 (part 2 of 2):

His saying ﴿and let them take their precautions and their weapons﴾: the verb "take" (al-akhdh) is used both in its literal and figurative senses. Taking precaution (akhdh al-hadhar) is figurative, since the literal meaning of "taking" is to grasp, whereas it is used figuratively for being engaged in something and persisting in it. Taking up weapons is literal. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and those who had homes [in Medina] and [adopted] the faith before them﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], for the "settling" (tabawwu') in the faith means entering into it and attaining it after leaving disbelief. The command is given in the imperative form rather than saying, "There is no blame upon you if you take your weapons," because taking up weapons contains a legislated benefit (maslahah shar'iyyah).

His saying ﴿The disbelievers wish﴾ etc.: this wish of theirs is well known, for it is the nature of every combatant. So that well-known meaning is not what is intended by the verse. What is intended is that they wished a wish that they regarded as attainable, because they supposed that the Muslims' occupation with the affairs of their religion would keep them away from the interests of their worldly life. This was out of ignorance on the part of the polytheists regarding the reality of the religion, so they hoped that the prayer would distract them from preparing against their enemies. God therefore alerted the believers to this, so that they would not be in accordance with the supposition of the polytheists, and so that He would train them to adopt resolve in all matters, and show them that the wellbeing of religion and of worldly life are twin companions (sinwan).

Al-asliha (weapons) is the plural of silah, which is a collective noun for all instruments of war made of iron, namely the sword, the spear, the arrow, and the lance. The shield, the coat of mail and the helmet are not counted as weapons (silah). It may be masculine or feminine, though the masculine is more eloquent, and for this reason they formed its plural as asliha, which is among the patterns of the sound masculine plural.

Al-amti'ah is the plural of matA', which is everything that may be benefited from, of goods and furnishings, and it includes whatever aids in war, such as saddles and the war gear, like coats of mail and helmets. "So they incline" (fa-yamiluna) is a branch of His saying "if you were heedless" etc., and it is the object of the wish, meaning: they wished for your heedlessness so that they might incline upon you. Al-mayl (inclining) is turning away from the middle to the side, and it is also used for turning away from something one was with to something else, as here, meaning: they turn away from their camp toward your army. Since the intended sense of inclining here is charging and attacking, it is governed by "upon" (ʿalā), meaning: they will rush upon you while you are heedless.

The phrase ﴿a single inclination﴾ (mayylatan) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) explaining the number, meaning: a single, unified assault. The form of the single occurrence is used here as a metaphor (kinayah) for strength and force, because a forceful and powerful act achieves its aim swiftly without repeated treatment, so the action is not repeated to attain its purpose. The word "single" (wahidah) reinforces the sense of single occurrence derived from the pattern fa'lah, so as to draw attention to the metaphorical intent, lest it be supposed that the infinitive is merely for emphasis of His saying "they will incline."

His saying ﴿There is no blame upon you if rain causes you discomfort﴾ etc.: this is a concession (rukhsah) granted to them to lay down their weapons in cases of hardship. The more complete form in performing the prayer has become here a concession, because actions are judged by their intentions and by the benefits and harms that result from them, and for this reason the concession was restricted together with taking precaution. The cause of the concession is that rain distracts both parties equally, whereas illness necessitates the concession specifically for the one who is ill.

His saying ﴿Indeed God has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ is an appended conclusion (tadhyil) to encourage the Muslims. When He repeated the command to take up weapons and precaution, it was feared that fear of the enemy might arise in the souls of the Muslims because of the intensity of the warning against him, so He followed this with the statement that God has prepared for them a humiliating punishment, namely the punishment of defeat, killing and capture, like that in His saying, ﴿Fight them, and God will punish them at your hands﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14]. The command to take precaution and weapons is only to bring about the causes of what God has prepared for them, for when God wills a matter He prepares its causes. In this is a teaching to the Muslims that they should seek effects from their causes, meaning: if you take your precaution, you will be safe from your enemy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 103:

﴿So when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides. And when you are secure, establish the prayer. Indeed, the prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times.﴾

Al-qada' (qadaʾ, completion): the completion of a thing, as in His saying: ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200]. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾ is that the remembrance intended here is the voluntary acts, or the remembrance of the tongue such as tasbih (glorifying Allah) and tahmid (praising Allah). They used to sit in times of safety until they finished from tasbih and the like, so He permitted them, at the time of fear, to remember Allah in every state. What is meant by standing, sitting, and lying on the sides is what occurs of that in the circumstances of war, not for the sake of rest.

His saying ﴿And when you are secure, establish the prayer﴾ is a consequence of His saying ﴿And when you travel through the earth, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear﴾ [al-Nisa': 101] to the end of the verse. So "security" (i'tmi'nan) here means returning from the raid, because in returning to the homeland there is calm from the turmoil of travel and the agitation of the body. Applying the term "security" to it is likely to be literal, and the intended meaning is not the security that is the absence of fear, since that does not fit here. The discussion of i'tmi'nan has already been made at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿but so that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260] in Surat al-Baqarah.

And the meaning of ﴿establish the prayer﴾ is: perform it complete and do not shorten it. This is the saying of Mujahid and Qatadah, so it stands in contrast to His saying ﴿there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾ [al-Nisa': 101], and it agrees with what preceded, that what is mentioned in the Qur'an is the ruling on shortening the prayer in a state of fear, not shortening it on a journey without fear. Thus iqamah (establishing) here means bringing a thing standing, i.e., complete, in a figurative manner, as in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And establish the balance with justice﴾ [al-Rahman: 9], and His saying ﴿that you establish the religion and do not divide over it﴾ [al-Shura: 13]. This is the saying of the majority of the imams: Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Sufyan. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: the fighter does not perform the prayer until the fear is gone, because he regarded direct engagement in fighting as an action that invalidates the prayer. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when you travel through the earth﴾ up to His saying ﴿So when you are secure﴾ supports the view of the majority, because His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, the prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times﴾ is brought as a reason for eagerness to perform it at its times.

Al-mawqut: that which is limited by times, and that which is apportioned to fixed portions; it may also be used in the sense of "obligatory" by way of metaphor. The first meaning is more apparent here.

ولا تَهِنُوا في ابْتِغاءِ القَوْمِ إنْ تَكُونُوا تَأْلَمُونَ فَإنَّهم يَأْلَمُونَ كَما تَأْلَمُونَ وتَرْجُونَ مِنَ اللَّهِ ما لا يَرْجُونَ وكانَ اللَّهُ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا

[It is] an conjunction to the sentence "And take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment" [an-Nisa: 102], as an addition to encouraging them to fight the enemies, and to making the enemies seem insignificant in the hearts of the Muslims, because the polytheists were more numerous than the Muslims and better equipped. The legislation of shortening the prayer and the forms of the prayer of fear were only a means of realizing the negation of weakness in jihad.

Page 190

The word ibtigha' (seeking, pursuit) is the verbal noun of abtagha, with the meaning of the transitive baghā, i.e., "to seek" (talab). It was discussed earlier at His saying "Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?" in Surah Al 'Imran.

What is meant here is taking the initiative in attacking, and not being lax, so that the polytheists are the ones who begin the attack. The Arabs say: "We pursued the sons of so-and-so," meaning, "we raided them." The one who initiates the attack has terror in the hearts of his enemies. He was further encouraged to pursue the enemy by the fact that the pain of the two warring parties is equal, since each fears the might of the other, and by the fact that the believers have a distinction over the disbelievers: they hope from Allah for what the disbelievers do not hope for. That is the hope of martyrdom if they are killed, the hope that His religion will prevail through them if they are victorious, and the hope of reward in all circumstances. His saying "from Allah" is connected to "you hope." The returning pronoun governed by "min" is omitted from the clause "what they do not hope," because the preposition by which the relative pronoun is governed indicates it. You may also take what they do not hope for to be victory, so that it is a promise to the Muslims that Allah is their helper, and good news that the polytheists do not hope for victory for themselves, and that they despair of it because of the terror Allah has cast into their hearts, and this weakens their resolve. On this reading, His saying "from Allah" is a parenthetical clause or a circumstantial phrase placed before the prepositional phrase, and the meaning on this is like His saying: "That is because Allah is the protector of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no protector."

[p. 191]

The connection of this verse with what precedes it goes back to the earlier description of the conditions of the hypocrites and their supporters. It then moved from that to preparation for fighting those who oppose Islam, from His saying: ﴿O you who believe, take your precautions and go forth in companies or go forth all together﴾ (4:71). In the course of this, there was a discussion of the hypocrites' waiting for misfortunes to befall the Muslims, of the various conditions of the tribes in their relations with the Muslims, and of a digression on accidental and intentional killing. It then moved to the mention of emigration (hijrah), and was followed by the mention of the prayer while traveling and the prayer in fear. After that, the discourse returned to the conditions of the people of hypocrisy.

The sentence is a fresh, independent beginning (istinaf ibtida'i).

The majority of the exegetes hold that this verse was revealed because of an incident related by al-Tirmidhi, the essence of which is: "Three brothers, called Bishr, Bashir and Mubashshir, the sons of Ubayriq, (and it is said: the sons of Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq; and it is said: Bashir was one of them, and he was known by the kunyah Abu Tu'mah), were from the Banu Zafar of the people of Madinah. Bishr was the worst of them. He was a hypocrite who satirized the Muslims in poetry, which he spread and attributed to others. These brothers were in poverty, and they were neighbors of Rifa'ah ibn Zayd. A caravan had arrived from Syria carrying durmak, which is fine wheat flour (al-hawwari, i.e., the finest flour). Rifa'ah ibn Zayd bought a load of durmak from it for his food. The people of Madinah used to eat barley flour, and when durmak came, the head of a household would buy some of it for his meals. Rifa'ah placed the durmak in a storehouse (mashrabah) he had, in which there were weapons. The Banu Ubayriq attacked it, broke into his storehouse, and stole the flour and the weapons. When Rifa'ah awoke in the morning and found that his storehouse had been robbed, he informed his nephew Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man of this, and Qatadah began to investigate. He was informed that the Banu Ubayriq had lit a fire that night, and it was perhaps over some of Rifa'ah's food. When the Banu Ubayriq were exposed, they threw the stolen goods into the house of Abu Mulayl al-Ansari. (It is also said: into the house of a Jew named Zayd ibn al-Samin; and it is also said: Labid ibn Sahl.) Some of the Banu Zafar came to the Prophet ﷺ and complained to him that Rifa'ah and his nephew had accused a household of faith and righteousness of theft. Qatadah said: 'I came to the Messenger of Allah, and he said to me: "You have deliberately targeted a household of Islam and righteousness and accused them of theft without clear evidence."' They spread among the people that the stolen goods were in the house of Abu Mulayl or the house of the Jew. Shortly after, this verse was revealed, and Allah informed His Messenger of the clear truth of the matter as a miracle for him, so that no one would hope to deceive the Messenger with falsehood."

This is the correct form of this report. What is recorded in the book Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, and in some narrations of al-Tabari, differs somewhat from what I have mentioned: that the Banu Zafar asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to argue on behalf of their companions so that they would not be exposed, and that the Jew would be cleared. The Messenger of Allah was inclined to do so, and then this verse was revealed.

In some narrations, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rebuked the Jew and cleared the accused. This narration is weak, and this addition is a clear error by storytellers who have no knowledge or insight into the meanings of the Qur'an. The apparent meaning is that the beginning of the verse is a preface alluding to the story, but it is not specific to it, since that statement contains nothing that clearly points to it. The starting point of the allusion to the story is from His saying: ﴿And do not dispute on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾.

As for His saying ﴿by what Allah has shown you﴾, the bā' here is the bā' of instrumentality. It makes what Allah has shown him into a means for judgment, because it is a way of reaching justice and truth and eliminating injustice, since the knowledge of Allah does not admit error. The seeing in His saying "what Allah has shown you" is cognitive (irfaniyyah), and its literal sense is visual seeing. It was applied to what is perceived with certainty because of its resemblance to the thing witnessed. Visual seeing governs one object; when the causative hamzah is added to it, it governs two objects, as here. The second object has been omitted because it is a pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun, and the relative pronoun has substituted for it. This omission is common. The estimated form is: "by what Allah has shown you it (hu)."

So whatever Allah has made true in His Book, He has commanded judgment by it among the people. The intended meaning is not that He informs him of the truth regarding a specific person, such as saying to him: "So-and-so is in the right," because this cannot be a consistent principle, and because it cannot be found as the referent of all the verses of the Qur'an, even though it may be suitable to interpret this verse that way. Rather, the intended meaning is that He sent down the Book to him so that he would judge by the methods and principles that indicate the descriptions of conditions by which justice is established, and thus judge among the people according to that, by bringing the particular details of their cases, at the time of litigation, under the general descriptions stated in the Book. An example is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ (33:4). He nullified the rule of adoption that existed in the pre-Islamic period, and informed us that a man's saying to one who is not his son, "This is my son," does not give the one so attributed any right to his inheritance.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ does not err in bringing particulars under their universals, though error may befall others. The intended meaning is not that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reaches the truth from outside the ways in which matters are established among the people. This is why he said: "I am only a human being, and you bring your disputes to me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I judge for him according to what I hear. Whoever I give to him something of his brother's right, let him not take it, for I am only cutting off for him a piece of Fire."

Others besides the Messenger err in applying the general to the particular. Therefore, it is obligatory to exert effort and to exhaust the evidence, and for this reason our scholars have used this verse as evidence for the obligation of ijtihad (independent reasoning) in understanding the Sharia.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "No one should say: 'I have judged by what Allah has shown me,' for Allah, may He be exalted, has not granted that except to His Prophet. As for one of us, his opinion is conjecture (zann), not knowledge ('ilm).'" Its meaning is what we have previously mentioned: that error may enter understanding for someone other than the Messenger, not for the Messenger ﷺ.

The lam in His saying ﴿for the treacherous﴾ is the lam of causation (lam al-'illah), not the lam of reinforcement (lam al-taqwiyah). The object of khasim (here, "a disputant") is omitted, indicated by the mention of its counterpart, which is "for the treacherous." That is, do not be a disputant on behalf of those who dispute for the treacherous; that is, do not dispute on their behalf. So khasim here means "one who defends and supports," as in His saying: "I will be their adversary on the Day of Resurrection" (a hadith in the sense: "I will be his opponent on the Day of Resurrection"). The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the intended audience is the community, because dispute on behalf of the treacherous cannot be expected from the Prophet ﷺ. The intended purpose is to warn those whom zeal had driven to defend the children of Ubayriq.

The command to seek forgiveness from Allah follows the style of directing the address to the Messenger, while the intended addressees are others. He guided them to what is more beneficial for them, which is to seek forgiveness from Allah for what they have committed. Or it may mean: "And seek forgiveness from Allah for the treacherous, so that by the blessing of your seeking forgiveness for them, Allah may inspire them to repentance. That is more fitting than the defense of those who defend them."

This is similar to His saying: ﴿If they had come to you when they wronged themselves, and sought forgiveness from Allah﴾ (4:64). The command does not mean that the Prophet should seek forgiveness for himself, as one erred in thinking, who then constructed upon this the notion that the Prophet ﷺ had something in mind that required his command to seek forgiveness, namely his intention to argue on behalf of the children of Ubayriq, while knowing that they had stolen, out of fear that they would be exposed. This is one of the misunderstandings of the weak and of the poor quality of their reports, used to support their defective understanding.

The address in His saying "and do not dispute" is to the Messenger, but what is meant is the prohibition of the community from this, because such a thing is not expected from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, as indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾.

[p. 194]

Yakhtanuna means yakhununa (they betray). It is an ifti'al form, indicating effort and exertion for the purpose of intensifying the betrayal. Their betrayal of themselves means that by committing what harms themselves, they were like one who betrays another, as in His saying: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾ (2:187). You may also take anfusahum here to mean "their own sons," that is, their own people, as in His saying: ﴿You kill your own people and expel a group of you from their homes﴾ (2:85), and His saying: ﴿So greet one another (lit. yourselves)﴾ (24:61), meaning those who betray people of their own family and tribe. The Arabs say: "He is a Tamimi of their own (min anfusihim)," meaning he is not a client (mawla) nor an attached outsider.

Mujadalah is a form from al-jadal, which is the capacity for contention and argument in it, and it is a dispute by speech to persuade another of your opinion. From it the rules of debate and argumentation in jurisprudence are called 'ilm al-jadal (the science of disputation), and it was mixed with the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), the science of the ethics of inquiry, and the science of logic.

No primary unaugmented verb form of jadal has been heard; what has been heard is jadala, because contention requires two disputants. As for the saying jadalahu, it means "he overcame him in disputation," so it is not a primary verb in derivation. The verbal noun of mujadalah is al-jidal, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and there is no disputing during the pilgrimage﴾ (2:197).

As for al-jadal with two fathas, it is the verbal noun (ism al-masdar), and its root is derived from al-jadal, which is throwing someone to the ground, because the ground is called al-jadalah with a fatha on the jim. It is said: jadalahu, so he is majdul (thrown down).

The sentence "they hide from the people" is an explanation of "they betray." The sentence "and they do not hide from Allah" is a circumstantial clause (hal), and this is the point of astonishment about their condition and their betraying themselves. Hiding from Allah is used figuratively for shame (haya'), since no one who believes in Allah believes that he can hide from Allah.

The sentence "and He is with them" is a circumstantial clause from the name of Allah (ism al-jalalah), and the "being with" here is being with knowledge and awareness. The majority of the exegetes hold that this verse was revealed because of an incident related by al-Tirmidhi, the essence of which is: "Three brothers, called Bishr, Bashir and Mubashshir, the sons of Ubayriq, (and it is said: the sons of Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq; and it is said: Bashir was one of them, and he was known by the kunyah Abu Tu'mah), were from the Banu Zafar of the people of Madinah. Bishr was the worst of them. He was a hypocrite who satirized the Muslims in poetry, which he spread and attributed to others. These brothers were in poverty, and they were neighbors of Rifa'ah ibn Zayd. A caravan had arrived from Syria carrying durmak, which is fine wheat flour (al-hawwari, i.e., the finest flour). Rifa'ah ibn Zayd bought a load of durmak from it for his food. The people of Madinah used to eat barley flour, and when durmak came, the head of a household would buy some of it for his meals. Rifa'ah placed the durmak in a storehouse (mashrabah) he had, in which there were weapons. The Banu Ubayriq attacked it, broke into his storehouse, and stole the flour and the weapons. When Rifa'ah awoke in the morning and found that his storehouse had been robbed, he informed his nephew Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man of this, and Qatadah began to investigate. He was informed that the Banu Ubayriq had lit a fire that night, and it was perhaps over some of Rifa'ah's food. When the Banu Ubayriq were exposed, they threw the stolen goods into the house of Abu Mulayl al-Ansari. (It is also said: into the house of a Jew named Zayd ibn al-Samin; and it is also said: Labid ibn Sahl.) Some of the Banu Zafar came to the Prophet ﷺ and complained to him that Rifa'ah and his nephew had accused a household of faith and righteousness of theft. Qatadah said: 'I came to the Messenger of Allah, and he said to me: "You have deliberately targeted a household of Islam and righteousness and accused them of theft without clear evidence."' They spread among the people that the stolen goods were in the house of Abu Mulayl or the house of the Jew. This is the correct form of this report. What is recorded in the book Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, and in some narrations of al-Tabari, differs somewhat from what I have mentioned: that the Banu Zafar asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to argue on behalf of their companions so that they would not be exposed, and that the Jew would be cleared. The Messenger of Allah was inclined to do so, and then this verse was revealed.

In some narrations, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rebuked the Jew and cleared the accused. This narration is weak, and this addition is a clear error by storytellers who have no knowledge or insight into the meanings of the Qur'an. The apparent meaning is that the beginning of the verse is a preface alluding to the story, but it is not specific to it, since that statement contains nothing that clearly points to it. The starting point of the allusion to the story is from His saying: ﴿And do not dispute on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾.

As for His saying ﴿by what Allah has shown you﴾, the bā' here is the bā' of instrumentality. It makes what Allah has shown him into a means for judgment, because it is a way of reaching justice and truth and eliminating injustice, since the knowledge of Allah does not admit error. It was applied to what is perceived with certainty because of its resemblance to the thing witnessed. Visual seeing governs one object; when the causative hamzah is added to it, it governs two objects, as here. The second object has been omitted because it is a pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun, and the relative pronoun has substituted for it. This omission is common. The estimated form is: "by what Allah has shown you it (hu)."

So whatever Allah has made true in His Book, He has commanded judgment by it among the people. The intended meaning is not that He informs him of the truth regarding a specific person, such as saying to him: "So-and-so is in the right," because this cannot be a consistent principle, and because it cannot be found as the referent of all the verses of the Qur'an, even though it may be suitable to interpret this verse that way. Rather, the intended meaning is that He sent down the Book to him so that he would judge by the methods and principles that indicate the descriptions of conditions by which justice is established, and thus judge among the people according to that, by bringing the particular details of their cases, at the time of litigation, under the general descriptions stated in the Book. An example is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ (33:4). He nullified the rule of adoption that existed in the pre-Islamic period, and informed us that a man's saying to one who is not his son, "This is my son," does not give the one so attributed any right to his inheritance.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ does not err in bringing particulars under their universals, though error may befall others. The intended meaning is not that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reaches the truth from outside the ways in which matters are established among the people. This is why he said: "I am only a human being, and you bring your disputes to me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I judge for him according to what I hear. Whoever I give to him something of his brother's right, let him not take it, for I am only cutting off for him a piece of Fire."

Others besides the Messenger err in applying the general to the particular. Therefore, it is obligatory to exert effort and to exhaust the evidence, and for this reason our scholars have used this verse as evidence for the obligation of ijtihad (independent reasoning) in understanding the Sharia.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "No one should say: 'I have judged by what Allah has shown me,' for Allah, may He be exalted, has not granted that except to His Prophet. As for one of us, his opinion is conjecture (zann), not knowledge ('ilm).'" Its meaning is what we have previously mentioned: that error may enter understanding for someone other than the Messenger, not for the Messenger ﷺ.

The lam in His saying ﴿for the treacherous﴾ is the lam of causation (lam al-'illah), not the lam of reinforcement (lam al-taqwiyah). The object of khasim (here, "a disputant") is omitted, indicated by the mention of its counterpart, which is "for the treacherous." That is, do not be a disputant on behalf of those who dispute for the treacherous; that is, do not dispute on their behalf. So khasim here means "one who defends and supports," as in His saying: "I will be their adversary on the Day of Resurrection" (a hadith in the sense: "I will be his opponent on the Day of Resurrection"). The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the intended audience is the community, because dispute on behalf of the treacherous cannot be expected from the Prophet ﷺ. The intended purpose is to warn those whom zeal had driven to defend the children of Ubayriq.

The command to seek forgiveness from Allah follows the style of directing the address to the Messenger, while the intended addressees are others. He guided them to what is more beneficial for them, which is to seek forgiveness from Allah for what they have committed. Or it may mean: "And seek forgiveness from Allah for the treacherous, so that by the blessing of your seeking forgiveness for them, Allah may inspire them to repentance. That is more fitting than the defense of those who defend them."

This is similar to His saying: ﴿If they had come to you when they wronged themselves, and sought forgiveness from Allah﴾ (4:64). The command does not mean that the Prophet should seek forgiveness for himself, as one erred in thinking, who then constructed upon this the notion that the Prophet ﷺ had something in mind that required his command to seek forgiveness, namely his intention to argue on behalf of the children of Ubayriq, while knowing that they had stolen, out of fear that they would be exposed. This is one of the misunderstandings of the weak and of the poor quality of their reports, used to support their defective understanding.

[p. 194]

Their betrayal of themselves means that by committing what harms themselves, they were like one who betrays another, as in His saying: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾ (2:187). You may also take anfusahum here to mean "their own sons," that is, their own people, as in His saying: ﴿You kill your own people and expel a group of you from their homes﴾ (2:85), and His saying: ﴿So greet one another (lit. yourselves)﴾ (24:61), meaning those who betray people of their own family and tribe. The Arabs say: "He is a Tamimi of their own (min anfusihim)," meaning he is not a client (mawla) nor an attached outsider.

The sentence "they hide from the people" is an explanation of "they betray." The sentence "and they do not hide from Allah" is a circumstantial clause (hal), and this is the point of astonishment about their condition and their betraying themselves. Hiding from Allah is used figuratively for shame (haya'), since no one who believes in Allah believes that he can hide from Allah.

The sentence "and He is with them" is a circumstantial clause from the name of Allah (ism al-jalalah), and the "being with" here is being with knowledge and awareness. "When they plot (idh yubayyitun)" is a temporal adverb. Tabyit means making something occur at night (bayat), like tasbih (making something occur in the morning). It is said: "The enemy attacked them by night (bayyatahum al-'aduw)" and "the enemy attacked them in the morning (sabbahahum al-'aduw)." In the Qur'an: ﴿We will surely attack him and his family by night﴾ (27:49), meaning we will come to them at night and kill them. Here, the "plotted" is what does not please in speech, meaning they devised and fabricated it at night for the purpose of concealment, as the Arabs say: "This matter was decided at night," or "it was deliberated upon at night." The meaning here is the planning of their scheme to throw the innocent with the accusation of theft.

[p. 195]

His saying ﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf﴾ is a new sentence (istinaf) prompted by His saying ﴿and do not dispute on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾, and the addressee is everyone among the Muslims who is fit to be addressed. The speech runs as a hypothetical supposition and estimation, or as an allusion to some of the Banu Zafar who argued on behalf of the Banu Ubayriq.

The discussion of the structure "Here you are, you people" has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then you are those who kill your own selves﴾ (2:85), and a similar one preceded in Al 'Imran: ﴿Here you are, you love them but they do not love you﴾ (3:119).

As for wakil (guardian/trustee), the discussion of it has already passed at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Trustee"﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran.

Interposed clause (*i'tiraḍ*) with a concluding remark, placed between the verse ﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf﴾ [an-Nisa': 109] and the verse ﴿Were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved to mislead you﴾.

The "doing evil" (*'amal al-su'*) is disobedience and violation of what the Law has commanded and forbidden. The "wronging of oneself" (*zulm al-nafs*) has commonly been used in the Qur'an for polytheism and disbelief, and it is also applied to committing acts of disobedience. The best of what has been said in explaining this verse is that "doing evil" is meant as wrongdoing against people, namely transgressing upon their rights, while "wronging oneself" refers to acts of disobedience that return to a person's violation, in his own personal affairs, of what he has been commanded or forbidden.

By *istighfār* (seeking forgiveness) is meant repentance (*tawba*) and asking Allah for pardon for the sins committed before repentance. The phrase ﴿finds Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ means that this is realized. The verb "finds" (*yajid*) is used metaphorically (*isti'āra*) for realization, because the basic meaning of "to find" (*wajada*) is to obtain a thing and see it, so it is applied to the actual realization of pardon and forgiveness. The meaning of "Forgiving and Merciful" is "greatly forgiving and greatly merciful," and this is an allusion (*kināya*) to generality and promptness. The meaning thus becomes: he finds Allah forgiving him and having mercy upon him, because His forgiveness and mercy are all-encompassing, so none who seeks His forgiveness and turns to Him is excluded from them, and the comprehensiveness of His forgiveness and mercy does not lag behind for any length of time. Thus the form "Forgiving and Merciful" together with "finds" indicates the acceptance of every penitent by the bounty of Allah.

The mention of *khaṭī'a* (a lesser error) and *ithm* (a sin) here indicates that they are distinct; by *khaṭī'a* is meant a minor disobedience, and by *ithm* a major sin.

The basic meaning of *ramy* (throwing) is casting something from the hand, and it is used figuratively for attributing a report or a quality to its owner, whether truthfully or falsely. Its most common usage is for attributing what did not occur. Among their proverbs is "she threw her ailment at me and slipped away." And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [an-Nur: 4]. It is so here as well, and similarly *qadhf* (accusation) is used both literally and figuratively.

The meaning of ﴿throws it upon an innocent person﴾ is that he attributes it to him and contrives to spread that accusation, as though he removes that sin from himself and throws it upon the innocent. *Buhtān* (slander) is a gross lie. The throwing of a fault and of a sin have been placed at one level in being "a clear sin," because accusing an innocent person of a crime is in itself a major sin, since it involves transgression upon the right of another. The greatness of this slander is indicated by the phrase "has taken upon himself," as an image of the condition of its doer to the condition of one who labours under a heavy load. *Mubīn* (clear) is that which shows to everyone that it is a sin, that is, an evident sin with no doubt about its being a sin.

His saying ﴿Were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved to mislead you﴾ is coordinated with "do not be a disputant for the treacherous."

The bounty and mercy meant here is the blessing of the sending down of the Book, which details the aspects of truth in judgment, and protection from error in it. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the resolve of a group of those who were betraying themselves, to mislead the Messenger, did not occur at all, let alone that they actually misled him.

The meaning of this is that their knowledge of his trustworthiness restrained them from attempting to pass falsehood off on him, since it was well known among people, believers and disbelievers alike, that Muhammad (ﷺ) was trustworthy, so they could not but recount the truth to him.
