﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or reconciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward.﴾

The events that the preceding verses pointed to, and the situations they warned against, were not free of secret consultation and private conversation, whether in private or in public, for plotting betrayals, concealing them and devising them by night. Therefore the context was fitting for following all of this with a mention of secret talk (najwa) and what it involves, because in that there is instruction, education and legislation. Secret talk is among the most common conditions that arise among people in their communities, especially at the time when the Muslims were emerging in Medina, for there were the hypocrites, the Jews and the weak believers. Secret talk was widespread for various purposes, so it often stirred suspicion (shakk), meaning fear, in the minds of those who witnessed such private conferences, since the believers were in a state of hostility from the polytheists and the People of the Book. Therefore the prohibition of secret talk was repeated in the Qur'an, such as ﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret talk?﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8] and the verses that follow it, and His saying ﴿when they listen to you, and when they are in secret talk﴾ [al-Isra': 47], and His saying ﴿and when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed we are with you"﴾ [al-Baqara: 14]. For this reason Allah also censured secret talk here, saying ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk.﴾ So the sentence is a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new independent resumption) to convey the ruling on secret talk, and the connection has become clear.

Najwa is a verbal noun, meaning private whispering in speech. It is derived from najw, which is a hidden place to which one withdraws to escape a pursuer. The term najwa is also applied to those who converse in secret. In the Qur'an there is ﴿when they listen to you, and when they are in secret talk﴾ [al-Isra': 47], and this is a description using the verbal noun, and the verse admits both meanings. The pronoun to which najwa is attached refers to all the people together, like His exalted saying ﴿Surely they fold their breasts to hide from Him﴾ [Hud: 5] up to His saying ﴿and what they proclaim﴾ [Hud: 5] in Surat Hud. It does not refer back to what the pronouns before it referred to in His saying ﴿They hide from people﴾ [al-Nisa': 108] up to here, because the context prevents its returning to that group, since their secret talk concerned only their own affair, so it has no generality with which the exception in His saying ﴿except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or reconciliation between people﴾ can be consistent. On this basis, the purpose of the verse is a social education called for by the context, for the nature of conversations and discussions is that they should be open, because frankness is among the finest of morals, as it indicates the speaker's confidence in his opinion and his courage in revealing what he wishes to reveal of his thinking. Therefore one does not resort to secret talk except in unusual circumstances that call for concealing the conversation. Whoever engages in secret talk in other than those circumstances is accused of having a base affair, and of concealing what he is ashamed to reveal, as Salih ibn 'Abd al-Quddus said:

"Concealment is for indecencies; let there be no concealment shrouding you from goodness."

Allah has forbidden the Muslims from secret talk on more than one occasion, because secret talk was a characteristic of the hypocrites. He said: ﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret talk, then they return to what they were forbidden?﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8], and He said ﴿Secret talk is only from Satan, to grieve those who believe﴾ [al-Mujadila: 10].

It has become clear from the Prophet's ﷺ prohibition that two should not converse in secret without a third person, that secret talk arouses doubt about the intentions of those who converse privately. We therefore learn from this that it does not prevail except among people of doubt and suspicion, such that it does not become a habit except for them. For this reason Allah negated good from most secret talk.

The meaning of "there is no good" is that it is evil, based on the common usage in negating a thing, where what is intended is affirming its opposite, since the intermediate state is not considered, as in His exalted saying ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus: 32], and because the context of legislation is only to explain good and evil.

He negated good from much of their secret talk, or from those who converse in secret among them, so it is understood from the implication of the attribute (mafhum al-sifa) that a little of their secret talk contains good, since people's speech is never free of private conversation about what is beneficial. The exception in His saying ﴿except for one who enjoins charity﴾ is either by way of an implied omission, meaning "except the secret talk of one who enjoins," or without an omission if najwa means those who converse in secret, and it is an exception from "much." Thus from the implication of the attribute and the implication of the exception there result two types of secret talk to which good is affirmed, and yet these two are a small part of their secret talk. As for the type excluded by the attribute, it is general, and in reality it applies to every secret talk issuing from them which has benefit and no harm, such as private consultation about who is suitable for companionship, or marriage, or the like.

[Page 199]

As for the type excluded by the exception, it is specified in three matters: charity, what is right, and reconciliation between people. If these three had not been mentioned, they would have entered into the small part of their secret talk to which good is affirmed. But since they were mentioned by way of exception, we know that the composition of the speech follows a wonderful style: it first removed from their secret talk what contains good by the implication of the attribute, then it intended to emphasize some of this small portion of their secret talk, so it was excluded from their much secret talk by way of exception. What remains of their secret talk, which is the much, is described as having no good in it. By this it becomes clear that the exception is connected (muttasil) and that there is no need to make it disconnected (munqati'). The purpose of all this is to give attention and honour to the importance of these three matters, even if someone whose general affair is the intention of evil converses about them.

His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾ and so on is a promise of reward for doing the things mentioned, if it is for seeking the pleasure of Allah. This shows that their being good is an attribute established for them because of the benefits in them, and because they are commanded in the Law. However, the reward is not obtained except from doing them seeking the pleasure of Allah, as in the hadith, "Actions are only by intentions."

Al-Jumhur read ﴿nu'tihi﴾ with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama, the royal "we"), as a shift (iltifat) from the third person in His saying ﴿the pleasure of Allah﴾ to the first person.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Khalaf read it with the ya' (third person), in accordance with the apparent sense of His saying ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 115:

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him, and follows other than the way of the believers, We will leave him to what he has chosen, and We will burn him in Hell, and it is an evil destination.﴾

This is a coordination with ﴿And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 114], because of the contrast between the two states. Al-musharaqah (deliberate opposition) is the intentional contrary action. It is derived from al-shiqq (the side), because the one who opposes seems to choose a side that is other than the side of the one he opposes.

His words ﴿after guidance has become clear to him﴾ may mean "after he has believed in the Messenger," so the verse is a warning to the apostate. Its relevance here is that Bashir ibn Ubayriq, the subject of the earlier story, when his deception was exposed, apostatised and joined Makkah. It may also mean "after the truth of the Messenger has become evident through the miracles, but he opposed him out of obstinacy and enmity toward Islam."

The way (sabil) of every people is the path they follow in their particular characteristics. Thus sabil is used metaphorically for beliefs, actions and customs to which a person adheres and from which he does not seek to turn away, just as a traveller keeps to a road that brings him to his destination. Allah said ﴿Say: This is my way﴾ [Yusuf: 108]. The meaning of this verse is similar to the meaning of His words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah and oppose the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them will not harm Allah at all, and He will render their deeds void﴾ [Muhammad: 32]. Whoever follows the way of the believers in faith, and follows the way of others in matters other than disbelief, such as following the way of the Jews of Khaybar in planting palm trees or building fortresses, cannot rightly be described as having "followed other than the way of the believers."

It seems that the purpose of coordinating the following of other than the way of the believers with opposing the Messenger is caution, to preserve the Islamic community after the Messenger. Some Arabs apostatised after the Messenger ﴿ﷺ﴾.

Al-Hutay'ah said about this:

"We obeyed the Messenger of Allah while he was among us, so, O servants of Allah, what is with Abu Bakr?"

Those (who apostatised) were among those who followed other than the way of the believers, but they did not oppose the Messenger.

His words ﴿We will leave him to what he has chosen﴾ mean turning away from him, that is, We leave him to himself because He cares little for him, as occurs in the hadith: "As for the other, he turned away, so Allah turned away from him."

Many scholars of usul al-fiqh (legal theory) have widely argued from this verse that the consensus (ijma') of the scholars of Islam on a ruling is a proof (hujjah). The first to argue from it in this way was al-Shafi'i.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: It is reported that al-Shafi'i was asked about a verse in the Book of Allah that indicates that consensus is a proof, so he recited the Qur'an three hundred times until he found this verse.

The structure of the argument is that following other than the way of the believers is forbidden, so following the way of the believers must be obligatory. The explanation of the first premise is that Allah attached the threat to the one who opposes the Messenger and follows other than the way of the believers. Opposing the Messenger alone necessitates this threat. So if following other than the way of the believers did not necessitate it, then this would add to the threat something that has no effect on it, to something that by itself necessitates that threat, and this is impermissible. Therefore it is established that following other than the way of the believers is forbidden, and once this is established, it follows that following their way is obligatory.

Others have argued from the verse for the authority of consensus by other methods, and all of them, despite their weakness in approximation, namely the implication of the proof for the claim, have been subjected to objections, which Ibn al-Hajib pointed out in his Mukhtasar. The leading verifiers agreed, namely al-Ghazali, the Imam in al-Ma'alim, and Ibn al-Hajib, on weakening the use of this verse as evidence for the authority of consensus.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly gone far astray.﴾.

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), and it serves as an introduction to what follows: a description of the states of their polytheism (*shirk*). Following the previous verse with this one indicates that what is meant by "following other than the way of the believers" is following the way of disbelief, which includes *shirk* and other things. So it follows that with a warning against *shirk*, and it is emphasized to indicate the removal of the possibility of exaggeration or metaphor.

The discussion of a verse like this has already come up recently, but the previous verse says in it ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah has fabricated a great sin.﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], while in this one He says ﴿has certainly gone far astray.﴾. He said in the previous one ﴿has fabricated a great sin﴾ [al-Nisa': 48] because the addressees there are the People of the Book, by His words ﴿O you who were given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾ [al-Nisa': 47]. So they were alerted that *shirk* is a kind of fabrication, as a warning to them against fabrication and as a denunciation of its category.

As for this verse, the speech is addressed to the Muslims, so they were alerted that *shirk* is a kind of going astray, as a warning to them against opposing the Messenger and against the conditions of the hypocrites, for these are of the same kind as going astray. The report is emphasized here with the particle *"qad"* (indeed, certainly), out of concern for it, because those being addressed here are the believers, and they have no doubt about the realization of that.

By "*al-ba'id*" (far, distant) is meant the strong in its kind, for which its possessor is not hoped to be guided. So "far" is used figuratively for it, because distance keeps the one in it from returning to the place from which he set out.

[Page 203]

﴿They invoke, besides Him, only females, and they invoke only a rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿Allah has cursed him, and he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion.﴾ ﴿And I will mislead them, and I will arouse in them desires, and I will command them, so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will command them, so they will alter the creation of Allah." And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss.﴾ ﴿He promises them and arouses desires in them, but Satan promises them nothing except delusion.﴾ ﴿Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will not find an escape from it.﴾

His saying ﴿They invoke﴾ is an explanation of His saying ﴿He has certainly strayed into far error﴾ [An-Nisa: 116]. And what error is more severe than that someone associates with Allah other than Him, and then claims that His partners are females, although they know that the female is the weaker of the two kinds in every species?

What is more astonishing than this is that it should come from the Arabs, although people knew the condition of women among them, and they deprived them of many rights and regarded them as weak. The restriction in His saying ﴿They invoke, besides Him, only females﴾ is a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i), because it is the most astonishing of their forms of associating partners, and because the greatest of their gods they believed to be female, namely al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and Manat. This is like your saying, "No scholar except Zayd." Al-'Uzza belonged to Quraysh, and Manat belonged to the Aws and the Khazraj. It is not hidden that most of the opponents of the Muslims at that time were from these two tribes: the polytheists of Quraysh were the most hostile of people toward Islam, and the hypocrites of Medina and its polytheists were the most troublesome of people within Islam.

The meaning of ﴿They invoke only a rebellious devil﴾ is that their invocation of the idols is an invocation of Satan. What is intended is the species of Satan. They were made to invoke Satan because he is the one who adorned for them the worship of idols.

Al-Marid is one who is disobedient and who departs from the king. In the proverb, "The rebel Marid has rebelled, and al-Ablaq has grown strong," the two are names of two fortresses belonging to al-Samaw'al. So al-Marid is an adjectival form derived from marada (with a damma on the ra), when one becomes extreme in disobedience.

The clause ﴿Allah has cursed him﴾ is a description of Satan, meaning He has distanced him. It may also be taken as a supplication against him, but the context rejects the objection of supplication in a context like this. Its conjunction with ﴿And he said, "I will surely take﴾ increases the likelihood of the supplication's remoteness.

[Page 204]
The context of this verse is like the context of its sister in His saying ﴿Go out, for you are of the debased﴾ [Al-A'raf: 13], ﴿He said, "Grant me respite until the Day they are resurrected"﴾ [Al-A'raf: 14], ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are of those granted respite"﴾ [Al-A'raf: 15], ﴿He said, "Because You have sent me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path"﴾ [Al-A'raf: 16], and the verse, for all of these are reports. They point to what existed at the beginning of the creation of mankind of the discord between satanic states and human states, and the arising of enmity from that discord; and to what Allah established as means of protecting the interests of mankind, so that satanic forces would not obtain them to destruction, through depriving the devils of the pleasure of Allah the Exalted, and through their intruding into the places of goodness, except to the extent that those forces seize upon the inclination of human forces toward satanic forces and their attraction to them. Those are stealthy moments in which the devils carry out their work. This is what His saying the Exalted indicates: ﴿He said, "This is a path upon Me, straight"﴾ [Al-Hijr: 41], ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ [Al-Hijr: 42]. Those are kindnesses from Allah which He deposited in the order of human life at creation, so that goodness prevailed by means of them over the community of mankind in every age, and there remained with them a small portion of evils in which Satan contends with his contenders. Allah entrusted the task of repelling them to human will, after equipping them with counsel and guidance through the legislations and wisdom.

So the meaning of the reporting of Satan by His saying ﴿I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion﴾ is that Allah created in Satan a necessary knowledge, by the requirement of which he was certain that he had the capacity to tempt mankind and subjugate them, and that in the order of mankind there were openings into which the effects of Satan's temptation could enter. That is the appointed portion, that is, what was made by Allah's decree and His destiny in the basic disposition. The saying ﴿from among Your servants﴾ is not a denial by Satan of his servitude to Allah, but it is the coarseness of speech arising from the wickedness of thought rooted in his disposition, so that he does not bring to mind from the meanings implied except what has an appetite in it for him, and he does not perceive the harshness that surrounds that, nor the courtesy and beautiful meanings that escape him. So every share that Satan had in human conduct, whether in their inward acts, such as beliefs and evil thoughts, or in their outward acts, such as corruption in the earth, the public declaration of serving Satan, such as worshipping idols, drawing near to them, and giving their wealth for their misguidance, all of that is part of the appointed portion.

The meaning of ﴿And I will mislead them﴾ is their misguidance away from the truth. The meaning of ﴿And I will arouse in them desires﴾ is: I will give them false promises which I cast into their souls, making them wish, that is, estimate what is not real to be real, by immersing them in imagination, so that through that he may assist in making light the spread of misguidance among them. It is said: manna, when he promised him false promises and made him hope for the occurrence of what he loves that does not occur. Ka'b said:

"So let not what she wished and what she promised deceive you."

From this is named tamanni (wishing), the seeking of what there is no hope for, or what there is difficulty in.

The meaning of ﴿And I will command them, so they will slit the ears of cattle﴾ is: I will command them to slit the ears of cattle, so they will slit them; that is, he commands them and finds them obedient. So the object of "commanded" is omitted, being dispensed with by what is arranged upon it. Tabtik means cutting. Ta'abbata Sharran said:

"He makes his two eyes a sentinel of his heart, toward a knife of sharpened edge, cut through."

Here he mentions something of what Satan commands which pertains to the conditions of the Arabs, since they used to slit the ears of the cattle which they dedicated to their idols, as a sign that they were freed for the idols. So they would split the ears of the bahira, the sa'iba, and the wasila. This splitting was thus a work of Satan, since the motive for it was a satanic purpose.

His saying ﴿And I will command them, so they will alter the creation of Allah﴾ is an allusion to what the people of the Jahiliyya used to do of altering the creation of Allah for foolish motives. Among that is what relates to the legislation of the idols, such as cutting the eye of the hami, which is the camel that protected its back from riding because of its abundant offspring, and it was left free for the idols. And among it is what relates to base aims, such as tattooing, when they intended by it adornment, though it is a disfigurement; and likewise branding the faces with fire.

Included in the meaning of altering the creation of Allah is placing created things in other than the purpose for which Allah created them, and that is from the superstitious misguidances, such as making the stars gods, and making eclipses of the sun and moon indicators of the conditions of people.

Included in it is the enticement to turn away from the religion of Islam, which is the religion of the innate nature (fitra), and the fitra is the creation of Allah. So deviating from Islam to something else is an alteration of the creation of Allah.

Not included in altering the creation of Allah is dealing with created things in what Allah has permitted, nor what falls within the meaning of beauty. For circumcision is from the alteration of the creation of Allah, but it is for health benefits. Likewise shaving the hair for the benefit of averting some harms, and trimming the nails for the benefit of facilitating work with the hands, and likewise piercing the ears of women for placing earrings and for adornment.

[Page 206]
As for what has come in the Sunna of the curse upon women who join hair (al-wasilat), those who tattoo or are tattooed, and those who file the teeth for beauty (al-mutafallijat), it is among what has been difficult to interpret. I think its interpretation is that the purpose of it is the prohibition of marks which were considered marks of prostitutes in that era, or marks of polytheistic women. Otherwise, if we supposed these to be forbidden, the prohibition would not have reached the degree of cursing those who do them.

The essence of the matter is that altering the creation of Allah is only sinful when it contains a share of obedience to Satan, by being made a sign of a satanic creed, as is the context of the verse and the connection of the speech to it. We have clarified that in my book called: Al-Nazar al-Fasih 'ala Mushkil al-Jami' al-Sahih.

The clause ﴿And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾ is a concluding phrase indicating that what Satan called them to, of slitting the ears of cattle and altering the creation of Allah, he called them to only because of what it requires as an indication of their taking on his emblem and adopting his call. Otherwise, Satan does not benefit by anyone slitting the ear of his she-camel, or altering anything of its creation, unless that is for being influenced by his call.

His saying ﴿He promises them and arouses desires in them﴾ is a resumption explaining that he has carried out his resolve: he promised and aroused desires, and he still continues to promise and arouse desires. Therefore the present tense is used. He did not mention that he commands them so they slit the ears of cattle and alter the creation of Allah, because its occurrence is evident to everyone.

The demonstrative is used in His saying ﴿Those—their refuge is Hell﴾ to draw the attention of the listeners to what follows the demonstrative of the report, and that those referred to are deserving of it after what was mentioned before of their attributes.

Al-Mahis means a place of escape and refuge, from haasa, when one flees and turns aside. In the hadith of Heraclius: "So they fled the flight of wild asses toward the gates." Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi said:

"We did not know, if we escaped from death by a flight, how much life remains while the span is long."

It is narrated: "hisna" and "haysa," with the unpointed ha and sad. It is also said: jada, with the jim and the dotted dad, and both forms are narrated in Ja'far's verse as well.

The saying ﴿from among Your servants﴾ is not a denial by Satan of his servitude to Allah, but it is the coarseness of speech arising from the wickedness of thought rooted in his disposition, so that he does not bring to mind from the meanings implied except what has an appetite in it for him, and he does not perceive the harshness that surrounds that, nor the courtesy and beautiful meanings that escape him. So every share that Satan had in human conduct, whether in their inward acts, such as beliefs and evil thoughts, or in their outward acts, such as corruption in the earth, the public declaration of serving Satan, such as worshipping idols, drawing near to them, and giving their wealth for their misguidance, all of that is part of the appointed portion.

The meaning of ﴿And I will mislead them﴾ is their misguidance away from the truth. The meaning of ﴿And I will arouse in them desires﴾ is: I will give them false promises which I cast into their souls, making them wish, that is, estimate what is not real to be real, by immersing them in imagination, so that through that he may assist in making light the spread of misguidance among them. It is said: manna, when he promised him false promises and made him hope for the occurrence of what he loves that does not occur. Ka'b said:

"So let not what she wished and what she promised deceive you."

From this is named tamanni (wishing), the seeking of what there is no hope for, or what there is difficulty in.

The meaning of ﴿And I will command them, so they will slit the ears of cattle﴾ is: I will command them to slit the ears of cattle, so they will slit them; that is, he commands them and finds them obedient. So the object of "commanded" is omitted, being dispensed with by what is arranged upon it. Tabtik means cutting. Ta'abbata Sharran said:

"He makes his two eyes a sentinel of his heart, toward a knife of sharpened edge, cut through."

Here he mentions something of what Satan commands which pertains to the conditions of the Arabs, since they used to slit the ears of the cattle which they dedicated to their idols, as a sign that they were freed for the idols. So they would split the ears of the bahira, the sa'iba, and the wasila. This splitting was thus a work of Satan, since the motive for it was a satanic purpose.

His saying ﴿And I will command them, so they will alter the creation of Allah﴾ is an allusion to what the people of the Jahiliyya used to do of altering the creation of Allah for foolish motives. Among that is what relates to the legislation of the idols, such as cutting the eye of the hami, which is the camel that protected its back from riding because of its abundant offspring, and it was left free for the idols. And among it is what relates to base aims, such as tattooing, when they intended by it adornment, though it is a disfigurement; and likewise branding the faces with fire.

Included in the meaning of altering the creation of Allah is placing created things in other than the purpose for which Allah created them, and that is from the superstitious misguidances, such as making the stars gods, and making eclipses of the sun and moon indicators of the conditions of people.

Included in it is the enticement to turn away from the religion of Islam, which is the religion of the innate nature (fitra), and the fitra is the creation of Allah. So deviating from Islam to something else is an alteration of the creation of Allah.

Not included in altering the creation of Allah is dealing with created things in what Allah has permitted, nor what falls within the meaning of beauty. For circumcision is from the alteration of the creation of Allah, but it is for health benefits. Likewise shaving the hair for the benefit of averting some harms, and trimming the nails for the benefit of facilitating work with the hands, and likewise piercing the ears of women for placing earrings and for adornment.

[Page 206]
As for what has come in the Sunna of the curse upon women who join hair (al-wasilat), those who tattoo or are tattooed, and those who file the teeth for beauty (al-mutafallijat), it is among what has been difficult to interpret. I think its interpretation is that the purpose of it is the prohibition of marks which were considered marks of prostitutes in that era, or marks of polytheistic women. Otherwise, if we supposed these to be forbidden, the prohibition would not have reached the degree of cursing those who do them.

The essence of the matter is that altering the creation of Allah is only sinful when it contains a share of obedience to Satan, by being made a sign of a satanic creed, as is the context of the verse and the connection of the speech to it. We have clarified that in my book called: Al-Nazar al-Fasih 'ala Mushkil al-Jami' al-Sahih.

The clause ﴿And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾ is a concluding phrase indicating that what Satan called them to, of slitting the ears of cattle and altering the creation of Allah, he called them to only because of what it requires as an indication of their taking on his emblem and adopting his call. Otherwise, Satan does not benefit by anyone slitting the ear of his she-camel, or altering anything of its creation, unless that is for being influenced by his call.

His saying ﴿He promises them and arouses desires in them﴾ is a resumption explaining that he has carried out his resolve: he promised and aroused desires, and he still continues to promise and arouse desires. Therefore the present tense is used. He did not mention that he commands them so they slit the ears of cattle and alter the creation of Allah, because its occurrence is evident to everyone.

The demonstrative is used in His saying ﴿Those—their refuge is Hell﴾ to draw the attention of the listeners to what follows the demonstrative of the report, and that those referred to are deserving of it after what was mentioned before of their attributes.

Al-Mahis means a place of escape and refuge, from haasa, when one flees and turns aside. In the hadith of Heraclius: "So they fled the flight of wild asses toward the gates." Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi said:

"We did not know, if we escaped from death by a flight, how much life remains while the span is long."

It is narrated: "hisna" and "haysa," with the unpointed ha and sad. It is also said: jada, with the jim and the dotted dad, and both forms are narrated in Ja'far's verse as well.

[Page 203]

﴿They invoke, besides Him, only females, and they invoke only a rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿Allah has cursed him, and he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion.﴾ ﴿And I will mislead them, and I will arouse in them desires, and I will command them, so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will command them, so they will alter the creation of Allah." And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss.﴾ ﴿He promises them and arouses desires in them, but Satan promises them nothing except delusion.﴾ ﴿Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will not find an escape from it.﴾

His saying ﴿They invoke﴾ is an explanation of His saying ﴿He has certainly strayed into far error﴾ [An-Nisa: 116]. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 122:

Page 207

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿Those – their abode is Hell﴾ [al-Nisa: 121], following the Qur'an's customary practice of coupling warning with glad tidings and threat with promise.

His words ﴿promise of Allah﴾ are an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar muʾakkid) for the content of the clause ﴿We will admit them into gardens, beneath which rivers flow﴾ and so on, and it has the same meaning as that clause. For this reason the grammarians call such a construction "an emphasis of itself" (muʾakkid li-nafsihi), meaning an emphasis of what has the same meaning as it.

His words ﴿ḥaqqan﴾ ("truly") are an emphatic infinitive for the content of ﴿We will admit them into gardens﴾, since this carries the sense of a promise; that is, "This is a promise which I will indeed bring to fulfilment, truly, meaning it will not fail." Since the content of the clause preceding it was free of the notion of bringing to fulfilment, this infinitive is among those which the grammarians call an emphatic infinitive emphasising something other than itself (muʾakkid li-ghayrihi).

The clause ﴿and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyīl) to the promise and a confirmation of it: that is, this is from the promise of Allah, and the promises of Allah are promises of truth, since none is more truthful than Allah in statement. The waw is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyyah), because the tadhyīl is one of the types of parenthetical insertion, and it is an insertion at the end of the speech. The word ﴿qīlan﴾ ("in statement") is in the accusative as a specifier of relation (tamyīz nisbah) from ﴿more truthful than Allah﴾.

The interrogative is one of denial (istifhām inkārī).

Qīl means "qawl" (saying). It is a verbal noun (ism maṣdar) on the pattern fiʿl, and it occurs for both evil and good.

[Page 208]

The more apparent view is that His saying ﴿Not by your wishful thinking﴾ is a new, independent sentence (*istina' ibtida'i*, a resumptive sentence that begins a new topic), serving to highlight the excellence of good deeds and to disfigure evil deeds. The pronoun in *laysa* refers to the recompense understood from His saying ﴿he will be recompensed for it﴾. The meaning is: recompense does not follow people's wishes and desires, but is a matter decreed by God, Exalted is He, according to their deeds.

What supports the view that His saying ﴿Not by your wishful thinking﴾ is a new independent sentence is that it comes after a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) that implies finality, namely His saying ﴿And who is more truthful than God in speech?﴾ [al-Nisa: 122].

Another point that favors this view is that on this reading there is an ambiguity in the pronoun, followed by its clarification in the sentence after it, which is ﴿whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾. Also, the sentence ﴿Not by your wishful thinking﴾ is placed ahead of its expected position at the end of the speech, and this fronting shows concern for it and prepares for the ambiguity of the pronoun. All of these are features of the means of inimitability (*i'jaz*) in the composition.

The sentence ﴿whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ is an explanatory resumptive sentence (*istina' bayani*) arising from the sentence ﴿Not by your wishful thinking﴾, because the listener asks for an explanation of this general negation. This resumption has a rhetorical position and a distinction that would be lost without the composition we have explained.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* took the hidden pronoun to refer to the promise of God. That is, "Not is the promise of God by your wishful thinking." In that case the sentence is a continuation of the previous speech, serving as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) for "the promise of God," and the sentence ﴿whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ is a purely independent resumptive sentence.

Al-Wahidi related in *Asbab al-Nuzul* (Occasions of Revelation), with his chain going back to Abu Salih, and Ibn Jarir related with his chain going back to Masruq, Qatadah, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak, and some reports add to others, that the occasion of its revelation was that a dispute took place between the Muslims and the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. Each group said to the others, "We are better than you," and argued for this, saying, "None will enter Paradise except those who follow our religion." So God revealed ﴿Not by your wishful thinking nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾ and the following verses. He explained that everyone who follows the guidance of God is among the people of Paradise, and everyone who goes astray and opposes the command of God will be recompensed for the evil of his deeds. Thus those Jews who believed before the mission of Jesus and did righteous deeds are among the people of Paradise, even if they were not upon the religion of Jesus. This refutes the claim of the Christians: "None will enter Paradise except those who follow our religion." And those who believed in Moses and Jesus before the mission of Muhammad, peace be upon him and them, and did righteous deeds, will enter Paradise. This refutes the claim of the Muslims and the Jews: "None will enter Paradise except those who follow our religion." So this verse was a decisive judgment between the groups, and an instruction to them to examine whether the reality of true faith and the presence of righteous deeds together are fulfilled. For this reason God combined the wishful thinking of the three groups in His saying ﴿Not by your wishful thinking nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾.

Then God alluded to the victory of the argument of the Muslims by the indication in His saying ﴿while he is a believer﴾. If a faith lacks some of what the true religion brought, it is as if it did not exist. From Ikrimah: The Jews and the Christians said, "None will enter Paradise except those who are of us." The polytheists said, "We will not be resurrected."

*Al-amani* (wishful thinkings) is the plural of *umniyyah* (a wish, desire), which is a noun for wishing, meaning the supposing of what is not real to be real. *Umniyyah* follows the pattern *uf'uulah*, like *u'juubah* (marvel). This was already discussed in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they know not the Book except wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78] in Surat al-Baqarah. It seems that the mention of the Muslims within "wishful thinkings" aims at generalization in entrusting affairs to what God has decreed and promised, and that whatever is contrary to that is not to be relied upon, while whatever agrees with it is the truth. The principal intended point is His saying ﴿nor the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾, in the manner of His saying ﴿Indeed we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba: 24]. The Jews were in delusion, saying, ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]. It has been said that the address is to the disbelievers of the Arabs, meaning: not by the wishful thinking of the polytheists, who made the idols their intercessors with God, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book, who claimed that their prophets and forefathers would avail them against the punishment of God. This is one interpretation of the verse.

His saying ﴿and he will not find for himself besides God any protector or helper﴾ is an added emphasis, to refute the belief of one who imagines that anyone can avail against the punishment of God.

*Al-wali* (protector) is the *mawla*, that is, one who shares in the lineage of the tribe, and what is meant by it is one who defends his relative. *Al-nasir* (helper) is one who, when you call upon him for aid, helps you, or an ally (*halif*). Support in the pre-Islamic period was by one of these two types.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 125–126:

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good and follows the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf (one who turns away from polytheism). And Allah took Ibrahim as a khalīl (intimate friend).﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever encompassing of all things.﴾

The most apparent view is that the *wāw* is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿they will enter Paradise﴾ [4:124], whose referent is the righteous believers. So when He mentioned the reward of the believers, He followed it with the praise of their religion. The interrogative is one of denial (istifhām inkārī). *Dīnan* is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz).

The phrase "submitting the face" (islām al-wajh) is a metonymy (kināyah) for complete obedience and acknowledgment of servitude. It is the most excellent of metonymies, because the face is the noblest of the limbs, and in it is what makes a human a human. In the Qur'an: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah, and so have those who follow me﴾ [3:20]. The Arabs mention things of this kind, as in His saying ﴿We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾ [96:15], and they say: "He took him by the shin," meaning he gained control over him, as if it were a figure for the way shepherds hold their livestock.

In a hadith: "Divorce belongs to the one who takes hold of the shin." They also say: "He threw the reins to him" (alqā ilayhi al-qiyād), and "He threw the halter to him" (alqā ilayhi al-zimām). Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said:

*He says: "My nose is humbled before you, a subdued one who is submitting."*

And they say: "My hand is pledged to so-and-so." By "submitting the face" he meant the acknowledgment of Allah's existence and His oneness. What is relevant to this has already been explained under His saying ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [3:19] and His saying ﴿And Ibrahim instructed his sons with it﴾ [2:132].

[Page 211]

The clause ﴿and he is a doer of good﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) intended to describe him as characterized by goodness at the time he submitted his face to Allah. That is, he cast off polytheism while intending goodness, meaning he was desirous of Islam because of what he saw in it of the call to goodness. The meaning of ﴿and followed the religion of Ibrahim as a ḥanīf﴾ is that he followed the law of Islam, which is founded on the foundations of the religion of Ibrahim. These are three attributes by which the meaning of entering into Islam is completed, and perhaps they are: faith (īmān), goodness (iḥsān), and submission (islām). You may also take the meaning of ﴿submitted his face to Allah﴾ to be that he entered Islam, that ﴿and he is a doer of good﴾ means sincere and desirous of good, and that following the religion of Ibrahim refers to monotheism (tawḥīd). It has been mentioned that ḥanīf means inclining away from polytheism or devoted to worship. If you take the meaning of ﴿and he is a doer of good﴾ to be "one who performs righteous deeds," then ﴿and followed the religion of Ibrahim as a ḥanīf﴾ would be in the position of a synonymous conjunction (ʿaṭf al-murādif), and that is far-fetched.

His saying ﴿and Allah took Ibrahim as a khalīl﴾ joins the praise of Ibrahim to the praise of whoever follows his religion, as an added honoring of the religion of Ibrahim. So He informs that Allah took Ibrahim as a khalīl. In the speech of the Arabs, the khalīl is the close companion who constantly stays with his friend, to whom nothing about his friend's affairs is hidden. It is derived from *khilāl*, which means the spaces that are interspersed within a place: ﴿You see the rain coming out from between it﴾ [24:43], ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾ [18:33]. This is the most apparent of the views on the derivation of *khalīl*. It is said *khil* and *khul*, with the *kh* vowelled with kasra or damma, and its feminine is *khullah* with damma on the *kh*, and it is not said with kasra. Ka'b said:

*How noble is this intimate friendship, if only it were true.*

Its plural is *khalā'il*. The term *khullah*, with damma on the *kh*, is applied to pure companionship: ﴿There is no trading in it, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾ [2:254], and its plural is *khilāl*: ﴿before a day comes in which there is no trading nor friendship﴾ [14:31]. The meaning of Allah taking Ibrahim as a khalīl is the intensity of Allah's pleasure with him, since everyone knows that true friendship is impossible for Allah, so what is meant are its necessary implications, which are pleasure, answering his supplication, mentioning him with goodness, and the like.

His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ and so on is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl) placed as a precautionary clause (iḥtirās), to indicate that by "khalīl" what is meant is the necessary implication of the meaning of khullah, and that it is not like the friendship of people, which entails equality or preference. So what is meant by it is a metonymy for the servitude of Ibrahim within the clause ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. *Al-Muḥīṭ* means *al-ʿAlīm* (the All-Knowing).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 127:

Page 212
﴿They ask you concerning women. Say, "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan girls to whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them and whom you desire to marry, and concerning the oppressed among the children, and that you should maintain justice for orphans. And whatever good you do – indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of it."﴾.

Legislation has been conjoined to faith, wisdom and admonition. Perhaps this inquiry (istiftaʾ) occurred at the time the preceding verses were revealed, so He mentioned its ruling after them in conjunction. This inquiry came from the Muslims after the revelation of His saying, ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 3], etc.

The best of what has been related in the interpretation of this verse is what al-Bukhari narrated from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr that he asked ʿAʾisha about the saying of Allah, ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 3]. She said: "O son of my sister, this is the orphan girl who is in the guardianship of her guardian, sharing with him his property, and he is attracted to her wealth and beauty, so he wants to marry her without giving her a fair dowry, giving her what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them and give them the highest of their customary dowry, and they were commanded to marry other women of their choice besides them." And the people asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after this verse, so Allah revealed, ﴿They ask you concerning women﴾. ʿAʾisha said: And the saying of Allah, ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ refers to the aversion of one of you from his orphan when she is little in wealth and beauty. She said: So they were forbidden to marry those whose wealth and beauty they desired from among the orphan women, except with justice, because of their aversion to them when they were little in wealth and beauty. The guardian would be averse to marrying her, and would dislike to marry her to a man who would share his property with her, since she shared with him; so he would hold her back (yaʿḍulhā). So this verse was revealed.

Thus the meaning is: "They ask you concerning the rulings about women," since it is known that the inquiry does not relate to the persons themselves; it is like His saying, ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 23]. The rulings most specific to women are the rulings of their guardianship and the rulings of their mutual dealings with men. The concern here is not the inheritance of women, since it does not come to mind here.

His saying, ﴿Say, "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them"﴾, is a promise to complete the answer to the inquiry, and is a kind of giving good news to the perplexed questioner that he has found what he sought, like the saying: "You have fallen upon one who knows" (ʿalā al-khabīr saqaṭ).

Page 213
And His saying, ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. The placing of the Name of Majesty first serves to draw attention to the importance of this ruling.

His saying, ﴿and what is recited to you﴾, is conjoined to the Name of Majesty, meaning: "and He gives you a ruling concerning them through what is recited to you in the Book," i.e., the Qurʾan. Attributing the giving of the ruling to what is recited is a metaphorical attribution, because what is recited indicates Allah's ruling, so it is a cause of it. The meaning thus becomes: "Say, Allah gives you a ruling concerning them through what is recited to you in the Book." What is meant by this is what was recited to them from the beginning of the sura and what will be recited after it, for reminding of it and repeating it is a ruling given once more, and the rulings that follow it are also rulings. The verse touches upon a summary of what preceded, from His saying, ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 2] to His saying, ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 6]. Likewise, this verse alludes to a section of what preceded: by His saying here, ﴿concerning the orphan girls to whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them﴾, it alludes to His saying, ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 3] up to His saying, ﴿then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 4].

The omission of the preposition after targhabūn ("you desire") here has a great effect of brevity and abundance of meaning: that is, "you desire to turn away from marrying some of them" and "you desire to marry others." The verb raghiba takes ʿan for the thing that is not loved, and fī for the thing that is loved. When the preposition is omitted, it allows both meanings, provided they are not contradictory, and this is covered by His saying in the preceding verse, ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 3], etc. By His saying here, ﴿and the oppressed among the children﴾, he alludes to His saying there, ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 2] up to "great," and to His saying, ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 5] up to "reasonable."

By His saying, ﴿and that you should maintain justice for orphans﴾, he alludes to His saying there, ﴿And test the orphans﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 6] up to "Reckoner."

There is no doubt that what is recited in the Book is from Allah's giving of rulings; however, since it preceded the time of the inquiry, it was different from the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾, and therefore its conjunction to it is valid as the conjunction of cause to effect. The new ruling (al-ifta' al-unuf) is from His saying, ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 128] up to ﴿Expansive and Wise﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 130].

The "fī" in His saying, ﴿concerning the orphan girls﴾, is for figurative location, i.e., "regarding their affairs," or for causation, i.e., "for their sake." The meaning of ﴿was prescribed for them﴾ is "was imposed for them," either from the property of those whom they inherit from, or from the dowries which you pay them, so that you do not give them the dowries of their equals; and both are considered "prescribed for them," as the hadith of ʿAʾisha – may Allah be pleased with her – indicates. On both interpretations the estimation comes in His saying, ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾. You may also make both possibilities in His saying, ﴿what was prescribed for them﴾ and in His saying, ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ intended, in the manner of using a homonym in both its meanings.

His saying, ﴿and the oppressed﴾ is conjoined to ﴿orphan women﴾, and it is a completion and inclusion (idmaj), because the inquiry was concerning women specifically, while the intended meaning is the oppressed men and the oppressed women; but the masculine form is used by way of predominance (taghlib), and likewise "al-wildan" (the children). In the pre-Islamic period they used to consume the property of the young children under their care.

His saying, ﴿and that you should maintain﴾ is conjoined to ﴿orphan women﴾, meaning: "and what is recited to you concerning standing for the orphans with justice." The meaning of "standing for them" (al-qiyam lahum) is managing their affairs, and that includes the orphan women.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 128–130:

﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion, there is no blame upon them both if they make terms of settlement between themselves; and settlement is best. And souls are present with stinginess. But if you do good and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you should strive to do so. So do not incline completely [away from one] and leave her as if suspended. And if you amend and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance. And ever is Allah All-Encompassing and Wise.﴾

This is a continuation of Allah's rulings, and it concerns the case of the breakdown of marital companionship between spouses. Part of it was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿And those from whom you fear arrogance [i.e., nushuz]...﴾ [al-Nisa': 34] in this surah. That passage gives the ruling on the judicial resolution between them, whereas this passage gives the ruling on separation through reconciliation between them. That passage mentioned the nushuz of the woman, and here the nushuz of the husband is mentioned. Al-ba'l (the husband) is the husband of the woman. The reason for applying this name to him has already been explained in His saying ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The form "fa-la junah" (there is no blame) is, on its apparent reading, one of the forms of permission, so this indicates permission for the spouses to conclude a settlement between them. It is known that permission is only mentioned where prohibition is presumed; so the intended meaning is permission for a settlement that takes the form of khul', i.e., a financial compensation given by the woman, or a relinquishment of some of her rights.

Thus the implication of this verse is more general than the implication of His saying ﴿It is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. There He called it iftida' (ransom), and here He called it sulh (settlement). The use of sulh to denote mutual consent between two disputants to waive some of a right has become widespread, and this is the more apparent meaning here.

The Malikī jurists have conventionally applied the term iftida' (ransom) to a woman's separation from her husband in exchange for property she gives, and the term khul' (divorce by redemption) to separation in which she waives the remainder of the dowry, or maintenance for herself or for her children.

It is possible that the phrase "la junah" is used here to encourage settlement, i.e., the reform of their affair through reconciliation and good companionship. Thus the negation of blame is a metaphorical figure of speech (isti'arah tamlihiyyah): it likens the state of one who abandons settlement and persists in nushuz and aversion to the state of one who deliberately abandons settlement, supposing that there is blame in it. So the intended meaning of sulh is reform of the relationship (islah dhat al-bayn), and the more common term for this is islah. The intended purpose is the command to adopt the causes of reconciliation, namely overlooking faults and meeting harshness with gentleness; and this is more fitting and appropriate to what follows it, His saying ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾.

Nushuz and aversion have many states: they grow stronger and weaker, and their consequences differ according to the conditions of souls; and His saying ﴿fears from her husband nushuz or aversion﴾ encompasses them all. Settlement too has many states: among them is khul', and so it includes what has been transmitted in reports indicating incidents of this kind. In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of 'A'ishah, she said regarding His saying ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband nushuz﴾: "The man has a wife with whom he is not overly content, and he wishes to part from her, so she says to him, 'I make you free of my duty [toward me].' Then this verse was revealed." And al-Tirmidhi transmitted, with a good chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, that Sawdah, the Mother of the Believers, gave her day to 'A'ishah. And in Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi:

That the daughter of Muhammad ibn Maslamah was with Rafi' ibn Khadij, and he disliked something in her, namely her age, so he wished to divorce her. She said to him: "Keep me and divide [your attention] for me as you wish." Then the verse was revealed concerning that.

The majority read "an yaṣṣālaḥā" with a doubled ṣād, a fatḥah on the lām, and its origin is yatasālaḥā, the tā' being assimilated into the ṣād. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "an yuṣliḥā" with a ḍammah on the yā' and a light ṣād and a kasrah on the lām, meaning that each of them reforms their affair by what manifests of the ways of reconciliation.

The definite article in His saying ﴿and settlement is best﴾ is the article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins) and not the article of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), because the intent is to affirm that the reality of settlement is good for people. So it is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) to the command to settle and the encouragement toward it. The intent is not that the settlement mentioned just before, namely khul', is better than conflict between the spouses; for although this meaning is correct, the benefit of the first aspect is greater, and because in it is avoidance of the problem of preferring settlement over conflict in goodness, when conflict has no goodness in it at all.

Whoever takes the second settlement to be identical with the first has been deceived by the widespread rule among some grammarians: that a indefinite noun, when repeated as a definite with the lām, is the same as the first. This rule was mentioned by Ibn Hisham al-Ansari in Mughni al-Labib in the sixth chapter, where he said: "They say: an indefinite noun, when repeated as indefinite, is other than the first; and when repeated as definite, or when a definite is repeated as definite or indefinite, the second is the same as the first."

Then he mentioned that the Qur'an contains verses that refute these four rulings, such as His saying ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54], and His saying ﴿an yaṣṣālaḥā baynahumā ṣulḥan wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr﴾, and ﴿We have increased them in punishment upon punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 88], and "a thing cannot be above itself," and "the soul for the soul" [al-Ma'idah: 45], and ﴿The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from the heaven﴾ [al-Nisa': 153].

And that in the speech of the Arabs there is also what refutes that. The truth is that there is no disagreement about this when there is an indication that the speech is for the definition of the genus and not for the definition of reference, as here. The discussion of repeating a definite noun as indefinite has already been given at His saying ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193] in Surat al-Baqarah.

It will also come at His saying ﴿And they said, "Why was there not sent down to him a sign from his Lord?"﴾ [al-An'am: 37] in Surat al-An'am.

His saying "khayr" (good) is not a comparative (tafdil); rather it is an adjective in the form of the sifah mushabbahah, of the pattern fa'l, like their saying "samh" and "sahl," and its plural is khuyur. Or it is a masdar corresponding to evil, in which case it is a report using the masdar. As for the case where it is intended as a comparative, its original pattern is af'al, which was lightened by dropping the hamzah and then transposing its vowel and sukun; its plural is akhyar, meaning that settlement in itself is a great good. Taking it as a comparative requires that the thing compared against be nushuz and aversion, and there is no great meaning in that.

This verse indicates the intensity of encouragement toward this settlement through three emphases: the emphatic masdar in His saying "ṣulḥan," the use of the noun in place of the pronoun in His saying "wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr," and the reporting about it by a masdar or by the sifah mushabbahah, for the latter indicates a fixed natural disposition.

The meaning of ﴿and souls are present with stinginess﴾ is that stinginess is constantly attached to human souls, to the point that it is as if present with them. Because it is among the acts of innate disposition, its verb is built in the passive, following the Arabic manner of building every verb whose agent is unknown into the passive, as in their saying "shughifa bi-fulanah" and "udturra ila kadha." So "al-shuḥḥa" is in the accusative as a second object of "uḥḍirat," since it belongs to the category of a-'ṭā.

The original meaning of shuḥḥ in the speech of the Arabs is stinginess with wealth; and in the hadith: "That you give charity while you are healthy and miserly, fearing poverty and hoping for wealth." And Allah said ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, those are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]. It is also applied to the soul's greed for rights and its scarcity of leniency regarding them, from which comes al-mushahhah (haggling), and its opposite is al-samahah (generosity) in both respects.

So it is permissible that the intended meaning of settlement in this verse is settlement of property, which is the ransom; and the stinginess is stinginess with property. The sequence of His saying "and settlement is best" with His saying "and souls are present" in this sense is like the speech of people, after commanding what contains benefit in an admonition or the like: "And I do not think you will do it," for the purpose of encouragement.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning of stinginess is what souls are created upon: haggling, lack of tolerance, and difficulty of restraint. Then the intended meaning of settlement would be settlement of property and other matters, and the purpose of following it with this is to warn people against being afflicted with this haggling that stands between them and reconciliation.

The discussion of stinginess has already been given at His saying ﴿And let not those who withhold of what Allah has given them from His bounty think it is good for them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 180] in Surat Al 'Imran. Dispraise of stinginess with wealth and of one who lacks generosity is well known among the Arabs, so this sequence was a warning against the obstacles that prevent generosity and settlement. For this reason it was concluded with His saying ﴿And if you do good and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾, because of what it contains of encouragement toward goodness and piety.

Then He excused people regarding the matter of women, saying ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives﴾, i.e., complete justice.

"Lan" (never) was used for emphasis in negation, because the matter of women overpowers the soul, since Allah made a woman's beauty and character have the strongest influence. Many a woman is intelligent and light of spirit, while another is heavy and foolish, so their difference in this and the lack of it in some of them inevitably produces a difference in the husband's love for some of his wives, even if he is eager to show justice among them. Therefore He said ﴿even if you should strive to do so﴾.

Allah set the balance of justice by His saying ﴿So do not incline completely﴾, i.e., do not excessively display your inclination toward one of them to the extent that the other is hurt, so that the other becomes like one suspended. It is clear that the object of "tamilu" is implied as "ihdahunna," and that the pronoun in "tadharuhā," which is in the accusative, refers to something other than the implied object, by the indication of context; and this is a wonderful brevity.

Al-mu'allaqah is the woman whom her husband abandons for a long time, so she is neither divorced nor a wife. In the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is al-'Ashannaq; if I speak he divorces me, and if I remain silent he leaves me suspended." And the daughter of al-Himarith said:

It is nothing but neglect or divorce, or arrogance, or something between that: suspension.

His saying "And you will never be able to..." up to "So do not incline completely" indicates that love is something compulsory, and that attachment to a woman has causes which necessitate it, which may not be present in some women; so the husband is not charged with what is beyond his capacity of love and approval.

However, there is a share of love that is voluntary: that the husband train himself to do good to his wife, and to bear as much as he can what does not suit him of her character or her characters, and to treat her well in companionship, until through long repetition and habituation he acquires, by choice, the familiarity and tenderness toward her that stands in place of natural inclination. That is the inclination toward her enjoined in His saying ﴿So do not incline completely﴾, i.e., toward one of them or away from one of them.

Then Allah widened the way for both of them if reconciliation does not succeed between them, and permitted them separation by His saying ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾.

In His saying ﴿Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ there is an indication that separation may be better for them, because separation is better than bad companionship. The meaning of Allah's enriching each of them is His enriching each of them from the other. And in the verse there is an indication that Allah's enriching each of them occurs only after separation that was preceded by striving for reconciliation.

His saying ﴿And ever is Allah All-Encompassing and Wise﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) and closure of the discussion on the ruling concerning women.
