His saying "And you will never be able to..." up to "So do not incline completely" indicates that love is something compulsory, and that attachment to a woman has causes which necessitate it, which may not be present in some women; so the husband is not charged with what is beyond his capacity of love and approval.

However, there is a share of love that is voluntary: that the husband train himself to do good to his wife, and to bear as much as he can what does not suit him of her character or her characters, and to treat her well in companionship, until through long repetition and habituation he acquires, by choice, the familiarity and tenderness toward her that stands in place of natural inclination. That is the inclination toward her enjoined in His saying ﴿So do not incline completely﴾, i.e., toward one of them or away from one of them.

Then Allah widened the way for both of them if reconciliation does not succeed between them, and permitted them separation by His saying ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾.

In His saying ﴿Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ there is an indication that separation may be better for them, because separation is better than bad companionship. The meaning of Allah's enriching each of them is His enriching each of them from the other. And in the verse there is an indication that Allah's enriching each of them occurs only after separation that was preceded by striving for reconciliation.

His saying ﴿And ever is Allah All-Encompassing and Wise﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) and closure of the discussion on the ruling concerning women.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 128–130:

﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion, there is no blame upon them both if they make terms of settlement between themselves; and settlement is best. And souls are present with stinginess. But if you do good and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you should strive to do so. So do not incline completely [away from one] and leave her as if suspended. And if you amend and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance. And ever is Allah All-Encompassing and Wise.﴾

This is a continuation of Allah's rulings, and it concerns the case of the breakdown of marital companionship between spouses. Part of it was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿And those from whom you fear arrogance [i.e., nushuz]...﴾ [al-Nisa': 34] in this surah. That passage gives the ruling on the judicial resolution between them, whereas this passage gives the ruling on separation through reconciliation between them. That passage mentioned the nushuz of the woman, and here the nushuz of the husband is mentioned. Al-ba'l (the husband) is the husband of the woman. The reason for applying this name to him has already been explained in His saying ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The form "fa-la junah" (there is no blame) is, on its apparent reading, one of the forms of permission, so this indicates permission for the spouses to conclude a settlement between them. It is known that permission is only mentioned where prohibition is presumed; so the intended meaning is permission for a settlement that takes the form of khul', i.e., a financial compensation given by the woman, or a relinquishment of some of her rights.

Thus the implication of this verse is more general than the implication of His saying ﴿It is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. There He called it iftida' (ransom), and here He called it sulh (settlement). The use of sulh to denote mutual consent between two disputants to waive some of a right has become widespread, and this is the more apparent meaning here.

The Malikī jurists have conventionally applied the term iftida' (ransom) to a woman's separation from her husband in exchange for property she gives, and the term khul' (divorce by redemption) to separation in which she waives the remainder of the dowry, or maintenance for herself or for her children.

It is possible that the phrase "la junah" is used here to encourage settlement, i.e., the reform of their affair through reconciliation and good companionship. Thus the negation of blame is a metaphorical figure of speech (isti'arah tamlihiyyah): it likens the state of one who abandons settlement and persists in nushuz and aversion to the state of one who deliberately abandons settlement, supposing that there is blame in it. So the intended meaning of sulh is reform of the relationship (islah dhat al-bayn), and the more common term for this is islah. The intended purpose is the command to adopt the causes of reconciliation, namely overlooking faults and meeting harshness with gentleness; and this is more fitting and appropriate to what follows it, His saying ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾.

Nushuz and aversion have many states: they grow stronger and weaker, and their consequences differ according to the conditions of souls; and His saying ﴿fears from her husband nushuz or aversion﴾ encompasses them all. Settlement too has many states: among them is khul', and so it includes what has been transmitted in reports indicating incidents of this kind. In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of 'A'ishah, she said regarding His saying ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband nushuz﴾: "The man has a wife with whom he is not overly content, and he wishes to part from her, so she says to him, 'I make you free of my duty [toward me].' Then this verse was revealed." And al-Tirmidhi transmitted, with a good chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, that Sawdah, the Mother of the Believers, gave her day to 'A'ishah. And in Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi:

That the daughter of Muhammad ibn Maslamah was with Rafi' ibn Khadij, and he disliked something in her, namely her age, so he wished to divorce her. She said to him: "Keep me and divide [your attention] for me as you wish." Then the verse was revealed concerning that.

The majority read "an yaṣṣālaḥā" with a doubled ṣād, a fatḥah on the lām, and its origin is yatasālaḥā, the tā' being assimilated into the ṣād. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "an yuṣliḥā" with a ḍammah on the yā' and a light ṣād and a kasrah on the lām, meaning that each of them reforms their affair by what manifests of the ways of reconciliation.

The definite article in His saying ﴿and settlement is best﴾ is the article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins) and not the article of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), because the intent is to affirm that the reality of settlement is good for people. So it is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) to the command to settle and the encouragement toward it. The intent is not that the settlement mentioned just before, namely khul', is better than conflict between the spouses; for although this meaning is correct, the benefit of the first aspect is greater, and because in it is avoidance of the problem of preferring settlement over conflict in goodness, when conflict has no goodness in it at all.

Whoever takes the second settlement to be identical with the first has been deceived by the widespread rule among some grammarians: that a indefinite noun, when repeated as a definite with the lām, is the same as the first. This rule was mentioned by Ibn Hisham al-Ansari in Mughni al-Labib in the sixth chapter, where he said: "They say: an indefinite noun, when repeated as indefinite, is other than the first; and when repeated as definite, or when a definite is repeated as definite or indefinite, the second is the same as the first."

Then he mentioned that the Qur'an contains verses that refute these four rulings, such as His saying ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54], and His saying ﴿an yaṣṣālaḥā baynahumā ṣulḥan wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr﴾, and ﴿We have increased them in punishment upon punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 88], and "a thing cannot be above itself," and "the soul for the soul" [al-Ma'idah: 45], and ﴿The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from the heaven﴾ [al-Nisa': 153].

And that in the speech of the Arabs there is also what refutes that. The truth is that there is no disagreement about this when there is an indication that the speech is for the definition of the genus and not for the definition of reference, as here. The discussion of repeating a definite noun as indefinite has already been given at His saying ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193] in Surat al-Baqarah.

It will also come at His saying ﴿And they said, "Why was there not sent down to him a sign from his Lord?"﴾ [al-An'am: 37] in Surat al-An'am.

His saying "khayr" (good) is not a comparative (tafdil); rather it is an adjective in the form of the sifah mushabbahah, of the pattern fa'l, like their saying "samh" and "sahl," and its plural is khuyur. Or it is a masdar corresponding to evil, in which case it is a report using the masdar. As for the case where it is intended as a comparative, its original pattern is af'al, which was lightened by dropping the hamzah and then transposing its vowel and sukun; its plural is akhyar, meaning that settlement in itself is a great good. Taking it as a comparative requires that the thing compared against be nushuz and aversion, and there is no great meaning in that.

This verse indicates the intensity of encouragement toward this settlement through three emphases: the emphatic masdar in His saying "ṣulḥan," the use of the noun in place of the pronoun in His saying "wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr," and the reporting about it by a masdar or by the sifah mushabbahah, for the latter indicates a fixed natural disposition.

The meaning of ﴿and souls are present with stinginess﴾ is that stinginess is constantly attached to human souls, to the point that it is as if present with them. Because it is among the acts of innate disposition, its verb is built in the passive, following the Arabic manner of building every verb whose agent is unknown into the passive, as in their saying "shughifa bi-fulanah" and "udturra ila kadha." So "al-shuḥḥa" is in the accusative as a second object of "uḥḍirat," since it belongs to the category of a-'ṭā.

The original meaning of shuḥḥ in the speech of the Arabs is stinginess with wealth; and in the hadith: "That you give charity while you are healthy and miserly, fearing poverty and hoping for wealth." And Allah said ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, those are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]. It is also applied to the soul's greed for rights and its scarcity of leniency regarding them, from which comes al-mushahhah (haggling), and its opposite is al-samahah (generosity) in both respects.

So it is permissible that the intended meaning of settlement in this verse is settlement of property, which is the ransom; and the stinginess is stinginess with property. The sequence of His saying "and settlement is best" with His saying "and souls are present" in this sense is like the speech of people, after commanding what contains benefit in an admonition or the like: "And I do not think you will do it," for the purpose of encouragement.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning of stinginess is what souls are created upon: haggling, lack of tolerance, and difficulty of restraint. Then the intended meaning of settlement would be settlement of property and other matters, and the purpose of following it with this is to warn people against being afflicted with this haggling that stands between them and reconciliation.

The discussion of stinginess has already been given at His saying ﴿And let not those who withhold of what Allah has given them from His bounty think it is good for them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 180] in Surat Al 'Imran. Dispraise of stinginess with wealth and of one who lacks generosity is well known among the Arabs, so this sequence was a warning against the obstacles that prevent generosity and settlement. For this reason it was concluded with His saying ﴿And if you do good and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾, because of what it contains of encouragement toward goodness and piety.

Then He excused people regarding the matter of women, saying ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives﴾, i.e., complete justice.

"Lan" (never) was used for emphasis in negation, because the matter of women overpowers the soul, since Allah made a woman's beauty and character have the strongest influence. Many a woman is intelligent and light of spirit, while another is heavy and foolish, so their difference in this and the lack of it in some of them inevitably produces a difference in the husband's love for some of his wives, even if he is eager to show justice among them. Therefore He said ﴿even if you should strive to do so﴾.

Allah set the balance of justice by His saying ﴿So do not incline completely﴾, i.e., do not excessively display your inclination toward one of them to the extent that the other is hurt, so that the other becomes like one suspended. It is clear that the object of "tamilu" is implied as "ihdahunna," and that the pronoun in "tadharuhā," which is in the accusative, refers to something other than the implied object, by the indication of context; and this is a wonderful brevity.

Al-mu'allaqah is the woman whom her husband abandons for a long time, so she is neither divorced nor a wife. In the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is al-'Ashannaq; if I speak he divorces me, and if I remain silent he leaves me suspended." And the daughter of al-Himarith said:

It is nothing but neglect or divorce, or arrogance, or something between that: suspension.

However, there is a share of love that is voluntary: that the husband train himself to do good to his wife, and to bear as much as he can what does not suit him of her character or her characters, and to treat her well in companionship, until through long repetition and habituation he acquires, by choice, the familiarity and tenderness toward her that stands in place of natural inclination. That is the inclination toward her enjoined in His saying ﴿So do not incline completely﴾, i.e., toward one of them or away from one of them.

Then Allah widened the way for both of them if reconciliation does not succeed between them, and permitted them separation by His saying ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾.

In His saying ﴿Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ there is an indication that separation may be better for them, because separation is better than bad companionship. The meaning of Allah's enriching each of them is His enriching each of them from the other. And in the verse there is an indication that Allah's enriching each of them occurs only after separation that was preceded by striving for reconciliation.

His saying ﴿And ever is Allah All-Encompassing and Wise﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) and closure of the discussion on the ruling concerning women.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 131–133:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. We had already enjoined upon those who were given the Scripture before you, and upon you, to fear Allah. And if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever Free of need, Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Trustee.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others. And Allah is ever capable of that.﴾

The clause ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is an interjection (i'tiraD) between the preceding clauses, which contain the exhortation to piety, beneficence and the rectifying of deeds, from His saying ﴿And if you do good and fear Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 128] and His saying ﴿And if you rectify and fear Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 129], and the clause ﴿And We had already enjoined﴾ (the verse).

This clause contains concluding statements (tadhyil) for those preceding clauses. Yet at the same time it is a preparation (tamhid) for what is mentioned after it, His saying ﴿And We had already enjoined those who were given the Scripture﴾ etc., since it is evidence for the obligation of fearing Allah.

The connection between this clause and the one preceding it, namely His saying ﴿Allah will enrich each of them from His bounty﴾ [An-Nisa: 130], is that the One to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth is capable of enriching each person from His bounty. This is a glorification of Allah, a reminder that He is Lord of the worlds, and a metaphorical expression (kinayah) for the greatness of His dominion and His deserving to be feared.

The clause ﴿And We had already enjoined those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with partners﴾ [An-Nisa: 116].

The command to piety was made a wasiyyah (a charge or testament) because a wasiyyah is a statement containing a command to something beneficial that gathers much good. Therefore it is the norm for a wasiyyah to be concise, since its purpose is that the listener be mindful of it and keep its words present in all his circumstances. Piety (taqwa) gathers all goods, because it is the carrying out of commands and the avoidance of prohibitions. For this reason they said: no word is repeated in the Qur'an as often as the word taqwa, meaning other than proper names, such as the name of Allah (ism al-jalalah).

In the hadith from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition by which the hearts trembled and the eyes shed tears. We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, it is as if it were the admonition of one who bids farewell, so give us a charge.' He said: 'I charge you to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to hear and obey.'"

Thus the mention of taqwa in ﴿that fear Allah﴾ etc. is an explanation (tafsir) of the clause "We enjoined," so "an" therein is explanatory (tafsiriyyah). The report that Allah enjoined those who were given the Scripture before them to have taqwa is intended to stir the resolve of the Muslims to strive for the fear of Allah, lest the nations before them among the People of the Scripture surpass them, for emulation (al-i'tisa') has a profound effect on souls, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 183].

By "those who were given the Scripture" are meant the Jews and the Christians, and the definite article in "al-Kitab" is the definite article of genus, so it applies to the plural.

The taqwa commanded here is considered with regard to its foundation, which is faith in Allah and His messengers. For this reason it is contrasted with the clause ﴿And if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.

By this He shows that He has no need of the piety of people, but it is for the good of their own souls, as He said: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need from you, and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [Az-Zumar: 7].

So His saying ﴿then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a metaphorical expression (kinayah) for the fact that He is not harmed by the disobedience of those who disobey Him. For this reason He made it the answer to the condition, the implied sense being "then indeed He is Free of need from you." This intention is reinforced by concluding it with His saying ﴿and Allah is ever Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾, meaning Free of need from your obedience, praised in His essence, whether those who praise Him obey Him or those who disbelieve disobey Him.

It has become clear from this that the clause ﴿And if you disbelieve﴾ is coordinated upon the clause ﴿that fear Allah﴾, so it is part of the charge, that is, part of the speech expressed by "We enjoined." Therefore it is good to pause at His saying "Praiseworthy."

As for the clause ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾, it is coordinated upon the clause ﴿We had already enjoined﴾. It was brought as a preparation for His saying ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾. Its intended meaning is its metaphorical sense, which is the capacity to exercise control through bringing into existence and annihilation. For this reason it is not good to pause at His saying "Trustee."

Thus the clause ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ has been repeated here three times in succession, identical in wording and literal meaning, but differing in the metaphorical purposes intended from it. Preceding them was a similar clause, His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever encompassing of all things﴾ [An-Nisa: 126], so its repetition occurred four times in a harmonious discourse.

As for the first, the preceding one, it stands in the position of giving the reason (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with partners, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 116], and for His saying ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly strayed far astray﴾ [An-Nisa: 116], and it serves as a concluding statement for both of them, and as a safeguard (ihtiras) against the clause ﴿And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾ [An-Nisa: 125], as we mentioned just above.

As for the second, which follows it, it stands in the position of giving the reason for the clause ﴿Allah will enrich each of them from His bounty﴾ [An-Nisa: 130].

As for the third, which follows that, it is a reason for the omitted answer, which is the answer to His saying ﴿And if you disbelieve﴾. The estimate is: "And if you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need from your piety and your faith, for to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He was and still is Free of need, Praiseworthy."

As for the fourth, which follows that, it is coordinated upon an implied element which is itself coordinated upon the answer of the condition. Its estimate is: "And if you disbelieve in Allah and His messenger, then indeed Allah is a Trustee over you and a Trustee on behalf of His messenger, and sufficient is Allah as Trustee."

The clause ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾ stands in the position of a consequence (tafri') from His saying ﴿Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾. The address in His saying ﴿O people﴾ is to all people who hear the address, as an alert to them through this call. The meaning of ﴿and bring others﴾ is: He will bring into existence other people who will be better than you in receiving the religion.

It is known from the contrast of His saying ﴿O people﴾ with His saying "others" that the meaning is "other people, not disbelievers." This is in accordance with what is common in describing with the word "other" (akhar) or "another" (ukhra), after mention of a counterpart to the described noun, that the noun described by "other" should be a part of the same kind as that upon which it is coordinated, according to what the speaker has made a kind in his speech, whether explicitly or by estimation.

Some grammarians went to the necessity of this, and al-Hariri elaborated on this question in Durrat al-Ghawwas. Its summary is that al-Akhfash al-Saghir, al-Hariri, al-Radi, Ibn Ya'un, al-Siqilli, and Abu Hayyan held the condition that the kind of the noun described by "other," and its derivatives, must be the same as the kind of that upon which it is coordinated.

So they do not permit saying: "I rode a horse and another donkey." They gave as examples of what fulfills the condition His saying ﴿days numbered﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 184], then He said ﴿then an equal number of other days﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 184], and His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [An-Najm: 19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾ [An-Najm: 20], where Manat is described as "the other" because it is of the same kind as al-Lat and al-'Uzza in being an idol. They said: similar to the word "other" in this are the words: "remainder" (sa'ir), "rest" (baqiyyah), and "some" (ba'd), so you do not say: "I honored a man and left aside the remainder of the women."

Some of these grammarians went to extremes, requiring agreement between the noun described by "other" and that upon which it is coordinated even in singularity and its opposite. This was said by Ibn Ya'un and al-Siqilli, and Ibn Hisham refuted it in al-Tadhkirah, arguing with the saying of Rabi'ah ibn Mukaddam:

And indeed I paired the two of them with another, a third, and my generosity refused to flee for me this morning.

And with the saying of Abu Hayyah al-Numayri:

And I used to walk upon two legs, upright, so I came to walk upon another from among the trees.

Other people held that agreement is required in masculinity and its opposite, and Ibn Jinni chose this, while al-Mubarrad disagreed with them, and al-Mubarrad argued with the saying of 'Antarah:

And the horses plunge through the dust, grim, between a swift-running one (shaythamah) and another swift-running one.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah went to the view that agreement between the noun described by "other" and that upon which it is coordinated is not required, and for this reason they both permitted in this verse that the meaning be: "and bring creatures other than humankind."

They agreed that it is not permissible to describe a noun with the word "other" if no counterpart to it has been mentioned at all before it. So you do not say: "Another came to me," without having said anything before. This is because the meaning of "other" is a meaning different in essence but similar in attribute. As for the saying of Kuthayyir:

Allah has blessed 'Azzah the Merciful and her daughter Lubna, and has blessed her other neighbors.

It is interpreted as meaning that he made her daughter a neighbor, or that he intended: "May Allah bless my beloved ones: 'Azzah, her daughter, and her other neighbors, my beloved ones."

Abu al-Hasan said that this is not permissible except in poetry, and he brought no proof for it.

Abu al-Hasan said: Something prohibited of that may be permitted with interpretation, such as: "I saw a horse and another donkey," with the interpretation that it is an animal. And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

When I say, "This is my companion," and I am pleased with him, and both eyes are cooled by him, I have been changed for another.

I say: The verse of Kuthayyir may be taken as an instance of this, and the reliance would be upon the context.

Among this category is counted the Arabs' saying: "May the right hand of the other be dusted (taribat yamin al-akhar)." And in the hadith: "A Bedouin said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Indeed the other had intercourse with his wife in Ramadan,'" as a metaphorical reference to himself, and it seems to be of the kind of tajrid (abstraction), meaning he abstracted from himself a person, in order to exonerate himself from speaking about himself with what he mentioned.

In the hadith of al-Aslami in the Muwatta': that he said to Abu Bakr: "Indeed the other has committed fornication," and some people of hadith vocalize it with a short vowel and a kasrah on the kha', and the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) have preferred this.

In the verse there is an indication that Allah will replace from the polytheists a people other than them who are believers, for Allah destroyed some of the polytheists for their polytheism after the revelation of this verse, and He did not will to destroy all of them. In the hadith: "Perhaps Allah will bring forth from their loins one who worships Him."

Therefore it is the norm for a wasiyyah to be concise, since its purpose is that the listener be mindful of it and keep its words present in all his circumstances. Piety (taqwa) gathers all goods, because it is the carrying out of commands and the avoidance of prohibitions. For this reason they said: no word is repeated in the Qur'an as often as the word taqwa, meaning other than proper names, such as the name of Allah (ism al-jalalah).

In the hadith from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition by which the hearts trembled and the eyes shed tears. We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, it is as if it were the admonition of one who bids farewell, so give us a charge.' He said: 'I charge you to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to hear and obey.'"

Thus the mention of taqwa in ﴿that fear Allah﴾ etc. is an explanation (tafsir) of the clause "We enjoined," so "an" therein is explanatory (tafsiriyyah). The report that Allah enjoined those who were given the Scripture before them to have taqwa is intended to stir the resolve of the Muslims to strive for the fear of Allah, lest the nations before them among the People of the Scripture surpass them, for emulation (al-i'tisa') has a profound effect on souls, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 183].

By "those who were given the Scripture" are meant the Jews and the Christians, and the definite article in "al-Kitab" is the definite article of genus, so it applies to the plural.

The taqwa commanded here is considered with regard to its foundation, which is faith in Allah and His messengers. For this reason it is contrasted with the clause ﴿And if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.

By this He shows that He has no need of the piety of people, but it is for the good of their own souls, as He said: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need from you, and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [Az-Zumar: 7].

So His saying ﴿then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a metaphorical expression (kinayah) for the fact that He is not harmed by the disobedience of those who disobey Him. For this reason He made it the answer to the condition, the implied sense being "then indeed He is Free of need from you." This intention is reinforced by concluding it with His saying ﴿and Allah is ever Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾, meaning Free of need from your obedience, praised in His essence, whether those who praise Him obey Him or those who disbelieve disobey Him.

It has become clear from this that the clause ﴿And if you disbelieve﴾ is coordinated upon the clause ﴿that fear Allah﴾, so it is part of the charge, that is, part of the speech expressed by "We enjoined." Therefore it is good to pause at His saying "Praiseworthy."

As for the clause ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾, it is coordinated upon the clause ﴿We had already enjoined﴾. It was brought as a preparation for His saying ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾. Its intended meaning is its metaphorical sense, which is the capacity to exercise control through bringing into existence and annihilation. For this reason it is not good to pause at His saying "Trustee."

Thus the clause ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ has been repeated here three times in succession, identical in wording and literal meaning, but differing in the metaphorical purposes intended from it. Preceding them was a similar clause, His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever encompassing of all things﴾ [An-Nisa: 126], so its repetition occurred four times in a harmonious discourse.

As for the first, the preceding one, it stands in the position of giving the reason (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with partners, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 116], and for His saying ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly strayed far astray﴾ [An-Nisa: 116], and it serves as a concluding statement for both of them, and as a safeguard (ihtiras) against the clause ﴿And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾ [An-Nisa: 125], as we mentioned just above.

As for the second, which follows it, it stands in the position of giving the reason for the clause ﴿Allah will enrich each of them from His bounty﴾ [An-Nisa: 130].

As for the third, which follows that, it is a reason for the omitted answer, which is the answer to His saying ﴿And if you disbelieve﴾. The estimate is: "And if you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need from your piety and your faith, for to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He was and still is Free of need, Praiseworthy."

As for the fourth, which follows that, it is coordinated upon an implied element which is itself coordinated upon the answer of the condition. Its estimate is: "And if you disbelieve in Allah and His messenger, then indeed Allah is a Trustee over you and a Trustee on behalf of His messenger, and sufficient is Allah as Trustee."

The clause ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾ stands in the position of a consequence (tafri') from His saying ﴿Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾. The address in His saying ﴿O people﴾ is to all people who hear the address, as an alert to them through this call. The meaning of ﴿and bring others﴾ is: He will bring into existence other people who will be better than you in receiving the religion.

It is known from the contrast of His saying ﴿O people﴾ with His saying "others" that the meaning is "other people, not disbelievers." This is in accordance with what is common in describing with the word "other" (akhar) or "another" (ukhra), after mention of a counterpart to the described noun, that the noun described by "other" should be a part of the same kind as that upon which it is coordinated, according to what the speaker has made a kind in his speech, whether explicitly or by estimation.

Some grammarians went to the necessity of this, and al-Hariri elaborated on this question in Durrat al-Ghawwas. Its summary is that al-Akhfash al-Saghir, al-Hariri, al-Radi, Ibn Ya'un, al-Siqilli, and Abu Hayyan held the condition that the kind of the noun described by "other," and its derivatives, must be the same as the kind of that upon which it is coordinated.

So they do not permit saying: "I rode a horse and another donkey." They gave as examples of what fulfills the condition His saying ﴿days numbered﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 184], then He said ﴿then an equal number of other days﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 184], and His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [An-Najm: 19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾ [An-Najm: 20], where Manat is described as "the other" because it is of the same kind as al-Lat and al-'Uzza in being an idol. They said: similar to the word "other" in this are the words: "remainder" (sa'ir), "rest" (baqiyyah), and "some" (ba'd), so you do not say: "I honored a man and left aside the remainder of the women."

Some of these grammarians went to extremes, requiring agreement between the noun described by "other" and that upon which it is coordinated even in singularity and its opposite. This was said by Ibn Ya'un and al-Siqilli, and Ibn Hisham refuted it in al-Tadhkirah, arguing with the saying of Rabi'ah ibn Mukaddam:

And indeed I paired the two of them with another, a third, and my generosity refused to flee for me this morning.

And with the saying of Abu Hayyah al-Numayri:

And I used to walk upon two legs, upright, so I came to walk upon another from among the trees.

Other people held that agreement is required in masculinity and its opposite, and Ibn Jinni chose this, while al-Mubarrad disagreed with them, and al-Mubarrad argued with the saying of 'Antarah:

And the horses plunge through the dust, grim, between a swift-running one (shaythamah) and another swift-running one.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah went to the view that agreement between the noun described by "other" and that upon which it is coordinated is not required, and for this reason they both permitted in this verse that the meaning be: "and bring creatures other than humankind."

They agreed that it is not permissible to describe a noun with the word "other" if no counterpart to it has been mentioned at all before it. So you do not say: "Another came to me," without having said anything before. This is because the meaning of "other" is a meaning different in essence but similar in attribute. As for the saying of Kuthayyir:

Allah has blessed 'Azzah the Merciful and her daughter Lubna, and has blessed her other neighbors.

It is interpreted as meaning that he made her daughter a neighbor, or that he intended: "May Allah bless my beloved ones: 'Azzah, her daughter, and her other neighbors, my beloved ones."

Abu al-Hasan said that this is not permissible except in poetry, and he brought no proof for it.

Abu al-Hasan said: Something prohibited of that may be permitted with interpretation, such as: "I saw a horse and another donkey," with the interpretation that it is an animal. And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

I say: The verse of Kuthayyir may be taken as an instance of this, and the reliance would be upon the context.

Among this category is counted the Arabs' saying: "May the right hand of the other be dusted (taribat yamin al-akhar)." And in the hadith: "A Bedouin said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Indeed the other had intercourse with his wife in Ramadan,'" as a metaphorical reference to himself, and it seems to be of the kind of tajrid (abstraction), meaning he abstracted from himself a person, in order to exonerate himself from speaking about himself with what he mentioned.

In the hadith of al-Aslami in the Muwatta': that he said to Abu Bakr: "Indeed the other has committed fornication," and some people of hadith vocalize it with a short vowel and a kasrah on the kha', and the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) have preferred this.

In the verse there is an indication that Allah will replace from the polytheists a people other than them who are believers, for Allah destroyed some of the polytheists for their polytheism after the revelation of this verse, and He did not will to destroy all of them. In the hadith: "Perhaps Allah will bring forth from their loins one who worships Him."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 134:

﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world — with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.﴾

Since the matter of taqwa (God-consciousness) is great upon souls, for the eagerness of people for the benefits of this world turns them away from it, toward the goods of the Hereafter, Allah alerted them that the good of this world is in the hand of Allah, and so is the good of the Hereafter. If they fear Him, they attain both goods.

It is also possible that the verse is an instruction to believers that faith should not prevent them from seeking the reward of this world, since everything is from the bounty of Allah. It is also possible that it is a reminder to believers that the pursuit of the good of this world should not distract them from the pursuit of the Hereafter, since combining the two is better, and both are from Allah, in the manner of His saying:

صفحة ٢٢٤
﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he has no share in the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200] ﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201] ﴿For those there is a share from what they have earned.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 202]

Or it is an instruction to believers that they should not seek the good of this world through unlawful means, for in what is lawful there is ample scope and sufficiency for them, and let them seek it through what is lawful, and Allah will facilitate its attainment for them, since all good is in the hand of Allah. Otherwise he is likely to be deprived of what he seeks, through a way that does not please Allah or in which He does not bless him.

By "reward" (thawab) in the verse is meant its linguistic sense, not the legal sense: it is good and that to which the seeker of benefit returns of the aspects of benefit. It is derived from thaba, meaning "returned" (raja'a). On all these possibilities, the answer of the conditional clause, "Whoever desires the reward of this world," is omitted, and its cause indicates it.

The estimate is: Whoever desires the reward of this world, let him not turn away from the religion of Allah; or let him not turn away from asking Him; or let him not limit himself to asking Him; or let him not obtain it through means that do not please Allah the Exalted, as the Banu Ubayriq and their like did; and let him seek it through the avenues of righteousness, because the bounty of Allah encompasses both goods, and all is from Him. This is like the saying of al-Qutami:

فَمَن تَكُنِ الحَضارَةُ أعْجَبَتْهُ فَأيُّ رِجالِ بادِيَةٍ تَرانا
(Whoever is captivated by urban civilization — what men of the desert are we, whom you see!)

The estimate is: let him not be deceived or delighted by civilization, for our condition is evidence of the nobility of the desert life.

[Page 225]

This is a transition from the command to act justly in particular circumstances concerning the affairs of orphans and women, to the command to act justly in all circumstances, together with the truthful testimony that accompanies it. Justice in judgment and giving testimony in truth are the foundation (*qiwam*, "upholding" or "sustaining") of the righteousness of the Islamic community. Deviation from this, even by a hair's breadth, leads to a chain of corruption.

The form *qawwamin* (ﷲ "those who steadfastly uphold") indicates intensity, and what is implied by it is that this upholding must not be neglected in any circumstance.

[Page 226]

*Al-qist* means justice. It was discussed earlier at the words of God, Exalted, ﴿standing firm in justice﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18], in Surat Ali 'Imran. The verse departs from the word *al-'adl* (justice) to the word *al-qist* because *al-qist* is a loanword (*mu'arrab*) that entered the speech of the Arabs due to its meaning, in the language from which it was taken, of justice in judgment. The word *al-'adl*, however, is more general than that. This is indicated by the verse's following it with the words ﴿witnesses for God﴾, since testimony is among the matters related to judicial rulings and judgment.

The phrase *lillah* ("for God") is a stationary adverbial phrase, a circumstantial element (*hal*) from the pronoun in *shuhada'* ("witnesses"), meaning "for the sake of God." It is not the *lam* that makes the verb *shuhada'* transitive to its object. The beneficiary of the testimony is not mentioned, nor is its connection to its complement, which is the qualifier of *shuhada'*, because the qualifier indicates its specification, that is, the one for whom testimony is given with the truth. The verse combines the two fundamental elements of adjudication, which are judgment and testimony.

The clause ﴿even against yourselves﴾ is circumstantial (*hali*), and the *law* in it is concessive (*wasliyyah*). The discussion of the precise function of the concessive *law* was already addressed at the words of God, Exalted, ﴿never will be accepted from any of them the earth full of gold, even if he should ransom with it﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 91], in Surat Ali 'Imran.

The phrase ﴿against yourselves﴾ is connected to both *qawwamin* and *shuhada'*, so that it includes both judgment and testimony.

*Al-anfus* is the plural of *nafs*. Its original usage is for the self (*dhat*), but the Arabs also use it for the core of a tribe, so they say: "He is from the Banu so-and-so from their own *anfus*."

It is permissible for *anfusikum* here to mean what it most commonly means, namely: "Uphold justice against yourselves, and bear witness for God against yourselves," meaning that the judgment and testimony should mostly go against your own interests. This is because the preposition *'ala* indicates that its object is something difficult and burdensome for the one governed by *'ala*. That is, even if the judge's ruling and the witness's testimony come from you and entail harm and displeasure for the judge and the witness.

This is the utmost extent of severity and hardship in what is required, because the hardest thing for a person is what harm and injury he suffers to his own self. Then the parents and relatives are mentioned after that, because the rulings of a judge and the testimony of a witness that inflict harm and hardship on one's parents and relatives are more numerous than those affecting oneself.

It is also permissible that what is meant is: "even against your tribe, or your parents and relatives." The emphasis derived from the concessive *law* lies in the fact that it was a custom of the Arabs to support their clients (*mawali*) from among the tribes, and to repel from them what they disliked. They regarded this as a matter of refusing humiliation, and they considered it a duty upon themselves, and they regarded neglect in this as a disgrace and shame, to a degree that is astonishing. Murrah ibn 'Adda al-Fiqsi said:

*I saw my clients, those who forsake me
in the times of calamity when fortune turns.*

[Page 227 continues, but as given in the passage, the following is the remainder of page 226 and beginning of the next discussion.]

They also regard concern for fathers and sons as secondary, to the point that they say in supplication: "May my father and mother be your ransom." The verse therefore nullifies this partisan zeal and urges Muslims to support the truth and defend the oppressed.

If you insist on taking *anfus* to mean the selves of the two witnesses, then make the conjunction of ﴿the parents and the relatives﴾ after that for the purpose of precaution, lest anyone think that he may bear witness for the truth against himself, because that is his right, since he is the master of himself in it; and that it is not appropriate for him to testify against his parents or relatives, because of the reproach and disgrace or sinfulness in that. On this view, *shahadah* (testimony) is used in a common meaning that includes both acknowledgment and testimony, as in the words of God: ﴿God bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge [affirm it], standing in justice﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18].

His words ﴿whether he is rich or poor﴾ form a resumptive clause (*isti'nafi*) standing in the position of a causal explanation for the entire statement ﴿be upholders of justice, witnesses for God﴾. That is: whether the one for whom justice is sought or the one for whom testimony is given is rich or poor, neither his wealth nor his poverty should be a reason for ruling in his favor or against him, or for testifying for him or against him.

The purpose of this is to warn against being influenced by circumstances in which falsehood becomes mixed with truth, because of surrounding factors which one imagines to be a form of safeguarding interests and guarding justice. When the preceding verse nullified being swayed by partisanship, this verse follows to nullify being swayed by appearances that attract souls to observe them, so that their gaze becomes fixed upon them, and because of them they overlook the distinction between truth and falsehood and become heedless of it. Some souls imagine that wealth elevates its possessor above taking the rights of others; one says to himself: "This man is free from consuming the rights of others, and God has blessed him with not needing them." 

Some people incline toward the poor out of tenderness for him, and so regard him as wronged, or they suppose that ruling in favor of the poor at the expense of the rich will not harm the rich in any way. God therefore forbade them from these influences with a comprehensive expression, namely His words: ﴿whether he is rich or poor, God is more entitled to both of them﴾. This disjunction applies to the adherents of each of these two illusions: the one who honors the rich dismisses the right of the poor for his sake, and the one who is tender toward the poor dismisses the right of the rich for his sake. Both are false, for the One who takes into account the condition of the rich and the poor and who determines the welfare of both groups is God, Exalted.

[Page 227]

His words ﴿God is more entitled to both of them﴾ are not the answer (*jawab*), but rather its evidence and cause. The implied meaning is: "Let their situation not concern you at the time of litigation, for God is more entitled to consider their affairs; and you are only obligated to consider the truth."

For this reason He made the following consequence of it: ﴿So do not follow desire lest you not be just﴾. He thus made inclination toward clients and relatives a form of desire, and considering poverty and wealth a form of desire.

*Al-ghaniyy* (the rich) is the opposite of *al-faqir* (the poor). Wealth is the absence of need for something, and it is predicated by degrees; it is known by its complement, as in the line:

*We are each independent of the other, in his life.*

It is also known by custom; one says "So-and-so is rich," meaning he has property with which he can obtain his needs without being indebted to anyone. Thus, receiving the wages of laborers is a form of wealth, even if the employer is in need of laborers, because receiving wages makes him like one who is not in need. Absolute wealth, however, belongs only to God, Exalted.

*Al-faqir* is the one in need, except that one says "he has become poor (*iftaqara*) in such-and-such," with specification. When one says "he is poor" (*faqir*), its meaning in common usage is that he is greatly in need of the bounty of people, or of patience in the face of need, due to the scarcity of his wealth. Every created being is poor in a relative sense. God, Exalted, said: ﴿And God is the Rich, and you are the poor﴾ [Muhammad: 38].

The subject of *yakun* ("he be") is a concealed pronoun referring to something known from the context, which is indicated by the words ﴿upholders of justice, witnesses for God﴾, which carry the sense of disputing and litigating. The implied meaning is: "If one of the two disputants is of this description or that description"; the intended meaning is the two categories, and *aw* ("or") is for division. The dual pronoun in ﴿God is more entitled to both of them﴾ refers to "rich and poor" in terms of their category, since the intent is not a specific individual who is wealthy, nor a specific individual who is poor, but rather any individual in this category and that category.

The phrase *an ta'diluu* ("that you be just") has the preposition deleted from it, as is customary with the verbal *an*. It may be that the deleted particle is the *lam* of purpose, so that it gives the reason for the prohibition, that is: "Do not follow desire in order that you may be just." It may also be that the deleted particle is *'an* ("from"), meaning: "Do not follow desire away from justice," that is, turning away from it.

I have known a judge whose trustworthiness and integrity are beyond reproach, but he was afflicted with the belief that those who possess power and authority are none other than oppressors: from among the wealthy or the men of influence. He would therefore regard these two categories as being in the wrong, and would not fully consider their arguments.

[Page 228]

After God, Exalted, had commanded, forbidden, and warned, He concluded all of that with a threat, saying: ﴿But if you distort or turn away, then indeed God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾.

The majority read *talwu* with a sukun on the *lam* and two *waws* after it, the first of which is vowelled with a damma, so it is the imperfect of *lawa* (to twist). *Al-layy* means twisting and bending. From this literal meaning are derived other meanings that became common and came to be equal to the literal sense. Among them: deviating from one side and turning toward another side. When it is followed by *'an*, it means turning away from the object governed by *'an*; when followed by *ila*, it means turning away from a side one was on and turning toward the object governed by *'ala*. God, Exalted, said: ﴿and do not turn back for anyone﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 153], meaning: do not incline toward anyone.

Among its meanings: *lawa 'an al-amr* means he hesitated or was slow regarding the matter; *lawa amrahu 'anni* means he concealed his matter from me. Another is *layy al-lisan*, meaning distorting speech either in its pronunciation or in its meanings. This was discussed earlier at the words of God, Exalted, ﴿who distort their tongues with the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 78], in Surat Ali 'Imran, and at His words ﴿distorting with their tongues﴾ [al-Nisa': 46], in this surah.

The use of the verb *talwu* here is eloquent, because it can take an implied complement governed by *'an* or governed by *'ala*, so it includes the senses of deviating from truth in judgment, deviating from honesty in testimony, slackening in enabling the one with the right to obtain his right and in giving testimony to the one who seeks it, or leaning toward one of the two disputants in judgment and testimony. As for *i'rad* (turning away), it means refusing to judge or to give testimony, and delaying judgment when the truth has become manifest. It is other than *layy*, as you have seen.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Khalaf read: *wa in tulu*, with a damma on the *lam* followed by a *waw* with a sukun. It was said that this is the imperfect of *wali al-amr*, meaning he took charge of it. The meaning then is: "And if you take charge of judgment between the litigants," which refers back to the phrase *an ta'diluu*, and this reference cannot apply to testimony, since giving testimony is not an office of authority. The correct view is that this reading is a lightened form of *talwu*, in which the vowel of the *waw* was transferred to the preceding consonant, so two consonantal *waws* came together and one was deleted. The meanings of the two readings are the same.

His words ﴿then indeed God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ are an allusion to a threat, because one who is Acquainted with the doer of evil, and who is All-Powerful, is not incapable of punishing him for it. The sentence is emphasized with *inna* ("indeed") and with *kana* ("is ever").

[صفحة ٢٢٩]

﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا آمِنُوا بِاللَّهِ ورَسُولِهِ والكِتابِ الَّذِي نَزَّلَ عَلى رَسُولِهِ والكِتابِ الَّذِي أنْزَلَ مِن قَبْلُ ومَن يَكْفُرْ بِاللَّهِ ومَلائِكَتِهِ وكُتُبِهِ ورُسُلِهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ فَقَدْ ضَلَّ ضَلالًا بَعِيدًا﴾ .

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding statement, one that adds a general principle after a preceding command). It follows the command to the believers to be ﴿upholders of justice, witnesses for God﴾ (Qur'an 4:135). After that command, God orders them to do what comprises the meanings of upholding justice and bearing witness for God: that they believe in God, His messengers and His books, that they persist in their faith, and that they guard against the paths that would undermine it.

Describing the addressees as "those who believed," and then following this with a command to believe in God, His messengers and so on to the end, guides the listener to an interpretation that makes it coherent to combine the fact that they have believed with the fact that they are commanded to believe.

In this interpretation there are five possible approaches.

The first approach: the faith mentioned in ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ is a deficient faith, lacking some of what faith requires. Accordingly, the address is to a group of Jews who had believed: ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, Asad and Usayd, the sons of Kaʿb, Thaʿlabah ibn Qays, Salam, the son of the sister of ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, Salamah, his brother's son, and Yamin ibn Yamin. They asked the Prophet ﷺ to let them believe in him and in his book, as they had believed in Musa and the Torah, and not to believe in the Gospel. This is related in the narration of al-Wahidi from al-Kalbi, and others transmitted it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second approach: the faith commanded is a complete faith, free from any aversion to some of God's books, and this is a warning against such aversion. The address is then to the Muslims, because the description "those who believed" has become like a title for the Muslims, and there is no doubt that the believers have believed in God and in what is joined to His name here.

The apparent purpose of commanding them in this way is either: to reinforce the affirmation of what must be believed and to repeat their calling it to mind, so that they do not neglect any part of it, out of concern for all of it; or: to forbid denying the Book revealed to Musa and denying his prophethood, lest the hatred of the Jews, and the enmity between them and the believers, drive the believers to respond in kind to what the Jews openly say, namely the denial of Muhammad ﷺ and the denial of the revelation of the Qur'an; or: it is intended as an allusion to those who claim that they believe in God and His messengers, [p. 230] and then deny the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and deny the Qur'an, out of envy from their own selves, and who hate some of the angels for this reason. These are the Jews. It is also a reminder that the Muslims are the most complete of the nations in faith and the most entitled of people to God's messengers and books, so they are worthy of leading others, because their faith is sound and free from denying the virtues of the people of virtue. This is supported by His saying after it: ﴿ومَن يَكْفُرْ بِاللَّهِ ومَلائِكَتِهِ وكُتُبِهِ﴾. It is further strengthened by His saying ﴿واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ﴾, which He joins to the things whose denial leads to going astray, even though He did not command the believers to believe in the Last Day among what He commanded them to believe, because the Jews share with them in belief in it. So He did not mention it among what must be believed, but He mentioned it afterwards as an allusion to the polytheists.

The third approach: the command to believe is meant as a command to persist in it, to make them firm in it and to warn them against apostasy. Then this command serves as a preparation and a groundwork for His saying ﴿ومَن يَكْفُرْ بِاللَّهِ ومَلائِكَتِهِ﴾ and for His saying ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا ثُمَّ كَفَرُوا﴾ (Qur'an 4:137), and so on.

The fourth approach: the address is to the hypocrites, meaning: O you who have professed faith, make your faith sincere in truth.

The fifth approach: it has been related from al-Hasan that the command in His saying ﴿آمِنُوا بِاللَّهِ﴾ is interpreted as a request for them to remain firm in the faith they already have. This was chosen by al-Jubba'i. It is also the common understanding among the scholars, and on this basis they took the verse as evidence for using the imperative form to request persistence.

By "the Book which He revealed before" (﴿الكِتابِ الَّذِي أنْزَلَ مِن قَبْلُ﴾) is meant the genus, and the definite article is for comprehensiveness, meaning: the books that God revealed before the Qur'an. This is supported by His saying after it, ﴿وكُتُبِهِ ورُسُلِهِ﴾.

Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisaʾi, Abu Jaʿfar, Yaʿqub and Khalaf read ﴿نَزَّلَ﴾ and ﴿أنْزَلَ﴾ both in the active voice. Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr read them in the passive voice.

The relative clause describing "the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger" uses the form ﴿نَزَّلَ﴾ (the intensive form), while the relative clause for "the Book which He revealed before" uses the form ﴿أنْزَلَ﴾ (the causative form). This variation is for stylistic variety, or because the Qur'an at that time was in the process of being revealed in installments, whereas the Torah had by then finished being revealed. As for the one who said that the Qur'an was revealed in installments, unlike the other books, he was mistaken, since no book is known to have been revealed all at once.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 137:

[Page 231]
﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief — Allah would never forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path.﴾ This is a resumption (istinaf) of His saying ﴿And whoever disbelieves in Allah﴾ [an-Nisa: 136], because if disbelief is as you know, then what do you think of a doubled disbelief, which its bearer returns to after having entered into belief and the impediments to acknowledging the truth have been removed from him? So his disbelief is the worst of disbelief.

It has been said that the verse refers to the Jews, because they believed in Musa, then disbelieved in him when they worshipped the calf; then they believed in Musa, then disbelieved in 'Isa, then increased in disbelief by [rejecting] Muhammad. Accordingly, the verse would be a censure directed at the community on account of the deeds of its predecessors. But this is remote, because the verse is a ruling, not a censure, as shown by His saying ﴿Allah would never forgive them﴾.

The earlier Jews did disbelieve when they worshipped the calf, but they repented, so they did not deserve non-forgiveness or non-guidance. How could they, when it was said to them ﴿So repent to your Creator﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54] up to His saying ﴿and He turned to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54]? Moreover, the later ones among them did not worship the calf, so that the first disbelief should be counted against them. Furthermore, the Jews disbelieved more than once in their history: they disbelieved after the death of Sulayman and worshipped idols, and they disbelieved in the time of Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar).

According to this interpretation, the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾ is not that they disbelieved in another instance of disbelief; rather the intended meaning is a general summary, i.e., "then they disbelieved after that," just as the one making an endowment says: "and their children and their children's children and their children's children's children," without intending to stop at the third generation. The intended meaning of the verse is that those who are known for their habit of levity toward rejecting the messengers and casting off the bond of religion are a people whose conduct will not be forgiven, since it stems from contempt for Allah and His messengers.

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to believe when they met the believers, and when they returned to their people they disbelieved, and at that time there was no intention to count the instances of belief and disbelief. In my view, it refers to groups of Arabs from the people of Makkah who used to trade with Madinah, and they would believe there; when they returned to Makkah they would disbelieve, and this recurred among them. These are the ones mentioned in the explanation of His saying ﴿So why have you become two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ [an-Nisa: 88].

[Page 232]
In all these views, the relative noun in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ refers to a specific, known group. The verse is therefore a threat to them and a warning that Allah has deprived them of guidance, so He would not forgive them, because He has deprived them of the cause of forgiveness. For this reason, the verse does not indicate that some states of disbelief are beyond the reach of faith after them. The Muslims have agreed that faith erases what came before it, even if a person disbelieved a hundred times, and that repentance from sins is likewise. A similar verse has already occurred in Al 'Imran, namely His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief, then increased in disbelief — their repentance will never be accepted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 90].

If you say: if this is so, then these people — Allah has known that they will not believe and has informed of the denial that He would guide them or forgive them. Then there is no benefit in calling them to believe after this statement. Are they then exempted from the general verses of the call?

I say: the individuals whom Allah knew would not believe, such as Abu Jahl, and whom He did not inform His Prophet would not believe, are addressed to believe along with the general community, because Allah's knowledge of their non-belief was not attached to any sign, as is known from the question of obligation to the impossible, which is an issue in the principles of jurisprudence. As for these, if they were known individually, this verse would be a deterrent from calling them to belief thereafter. If they were not known individually, then the matter concerning them is like the matter concerning one whose non-belief Allah knew but did not disclose; and there is no criterion by which it can be verified that they were called individually to belief after this verse and its like.

The negation in His saying ﴿Allah would never forgive them﴾ is more emphatic than "Allah does not forgive them," because the original function of this construction is to indicate that the subject of kana was not made such that its predicate should proceed from it; and there is no doubt that a thing not made for something is repugnant to it, because it is contrary to its nature. The grammarians have been inventive in naming the lam that comes after the negated kana: they call it lam al-juhud (the lam of denial).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 138–141 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 233]
﴿Announce to the hypocrites that there is a painful punishment for them,﴾ ﴿those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honor with them? Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah.﴾ ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different topic of conversation. Otherwise, you would be like them. Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell,﴾ ﴿those who wait and watch over you. If you achieve a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" And if the disbelievers have a share [of success], they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?" Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers.﴾

It is an independent resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i) arising from the description in ﴿Those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa: 137]. Those people were openly manifesting disbelief against Muhammad (ﷺ), and there was a group that concealed disbelief, namely the people of hypocrisy (ahl al-nifaq, the hypocrites). Since displaying faith and then following it with disbelief was a form of mockery of Islam and its people, their punishment was described with a threat appropriate to their mockery of the Muslims. It came in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum), when He said, "﴿Announce to the hypocrites﴾," for glad tidings (bishara) is news of what delights the one informed, and punishment is not of that kind. The Arabs have various styles of sarcasm, such as the words of Shaqiq ibn Sulaik al-Asadi:

A threat has come to me from Abu Anas,
so my body is drawn out in the anger of al-Dahhak.

And the words of al-Nabigha:

"You will surely become forbearing or desist,
when you grow old, or when the crow grows white."

And the words of Ibn Zayyaba:

"I was informed that Amr, sticking his head [into the ground],
threatens his maternal uncles in a year [of drought],
and such from him is not reliable,
that he will do the thing when he says it."

[Page 234]
The description of them in the form of a relative clause (al-mawsul) serves to give the reason for their deserving the painful punishment, meaning: because they took the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers, that is, they took them as allies for the sake of opposing the believers. The disbelievers here mean either the polytheists of Mecca or the rabbis of the Jews, because no open polytheists remained in Medina at the time this surah was revealed; there were only hypocrites and Jews. The clause ﴿Do they seek honor with them? Indeed, honor belongs to Allah﴾ is an explanatory resumptive statement (isti'naf bayani) in relation to the conjoined clause ﴿Indeed, honor belongs to Allah﴾, and His saying "Do they seek" is the source of the resumption. This implies that the hypocrites' allegiance to the polytheists was not due to similarity in religion and creed, since most of the hypocrites were from the Jews; rather, they took them so that they might gain strength through them over the believers. It also implies that the hypocrites felt weakness and so sought strength, and in this is the utmost ignorance and blame. The interrogative is one of denial and rebuke, and therefore the consequence ﴿Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah﴾ is valid as following from it, meaning there is no honor except through Him, because seeking strength from other than Him is void, as it is said: "Whoever seeks strength from other than Allah will be humiliated." If the disbelievers mean the Jews, the interrogative is sarcasm directed at both groups, like the proverb:

"Like one seeking help from the scorching sand by [falling into] the fire."

This statement conveys a warning against associating with them by way of metonymy (kinaya).

The clause ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book﴾ etc. may be conjoined to the clause ﴿Announce to the hypocrites﴾, as a reminder to the Muslims of what they had been informed of, which reinforces the warning against associating with them. In that case the pronoun of address is directed to the believers and the pronouns of absence to the hypocrites. It may also be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yattakhidhun" [they take], so that the pronoun of address in ﴿has been revealed to you﴾ is an address to the people of the relative clause ﴿those who take the disbelievers as allies﴾, by way of iltifat (shift of address), as if after the relative clause was applied to them they became specific and known, so He turned to them with address, because they know that they are the people of that relative clause, perhaps they will desist from allegiance to the disbelievers.

According to this, the pronoun of address is for the hypocrites and the pronouns of absence are for the disbelievers, and what was revealed in the Book refers to verses revealed before this surah in the Qur'an concerning the disbelief of the disbelievers and hypocrites and their mockery.

The exegetes said: what is referred to here is His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-An'am: ﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk about Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different topic of conversation﴾ [al-An'am: 68], because the state of the disbelievers spreads to those who take them as allies. The apparent meaning is that what Allah referred to is what was repeated in the Qur'an before the revelation of this surah, such as His saying in al-Baqara: ﴿When they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking"﴾ [al-Baqara: 14], which together establishes this meaning.

The "an" in ﴿that when you hear﴾ is explanatory (tafsiriyya), because "nuzzila" [was revealed] contains the meaning of a statement without the letters of saying, since he did not intend to quote the wording "what was revealed" but rather its essential meaning. Some made it a lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy "an" with a deleted pronoun of the matter (damir sha'n) as its subject, but this is far-fetched.

The two verbs "yukfaru" [is disbelieved] and "yustahza'u" [is mocked] are put in the passive so that, by omitting the agent, they may be applicable to be attributed to both the disbelievers and the hypocrites. In it is an indication that the hypocrites lean toward the polytheists and Jews, because these reject the verses and mock them, and thus the souls of the hypocrites are soothed by it, since the hypocrites cannot openly display this to the Muslims, so their rage is relieved by hearing the Muslims hear it from the disbelievers.

The time of their disbelief and mockery has been made the time when the believers hear the verses of Allah. The intended meaning is that it is the time of the revelation of the verses of Allah or the recitation of the verses of Allah, but He turned from that to "the hearing of the believers" to indicate the wondrous contrast of the two states: in the state of the hypocrites being characterized by disbelief in Allah and jesting at His verses, the believers are characterized by receiving His verses, listening to them, intending to understand them, and acting upon them.

This was followed by the consequence of prohibiting sitting with them in that state until they move to something else, lest Satan use this as a means to weaken the believers' eagerness to hear the Qur'an, for morals are contagious; and in the proverb: "Mangy camels infect healthy ones."

This prohibition entails the command to leave their gatherings when they engage in disbelief in the verses and mockery of them. In the prohibition against sitting with them there is another wisdom: the obligation to show anger for Allah's sake at that, as in His saying: ﴿You convey to them affection, while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth﴾ [al-Mumtahana: 1].

"Hatta" (until) is a particle that makes the end of a thing a conjunction to it, so the prohibition against sitting with them has as its end that they cease engaging in disbelief in the verses and mocking them.

This ruling is a gradual process in forbidding Muslims' allegiance to the disbelievers. Its starting point was made that they should not attend gatherings of their disbelief, so that the distinction between sincere Muslims and hypocrites would become evident; and they were permitted to sit with them when they engaged in a topic other than disbelief. Then this was abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith; and whoever among you allies with them, then it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Tawba: 23] ﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your clan, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear will decline, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings His command﴾ [al-Tawba: 24].

The answer to sitting with them, which is forbidden, was made to be that if they do not desist from sitting with them, they would be like them in treating the verses of Allah lightly, when He said: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them.﴾ "Idhan" is a particle of answer and consequence to a statement either spoken or implied. The consequence here is to an implied statement indicated by the prohibition against sitting with them; the implied sense is: if you sit with them, then indeed you are like them. The use of "idhan" as a consequence to an implied statement is common in Arabic speech, as in the words of al-Anbari:

"Had I been of Mazin, the sons of Laqita of Dhuhl ibn Shayban would not have plundered my camels;

The answer to sitting with them, which is forbidden, was made to be that if they do not desist from sitting with them, they would be like them in treating the verses of Allah lightly, when He said: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them.﴾ "Idhan" is a particle of answer and consequence to a statement either spoken or implied. The consequence here is to an implied statement indicated by the prohibition against sitting with them; the implied sense is: if you sit with them, then indeed you are like them. The use of "idhan" as a consequence to an implied statement is common in Arabic speech, as in the words of al-Anbari:

"Had I been of Mazin, the sons of Laqita of Dhuhl ibn Shayban would not have plundered my camels;
then a band of rough men would have risen to support me, when the protector is aggrieved, if one with a lapse [of judgment] were to be lenient."

Al-Marzuqi said in his commentary on al-Hamasa: The benefit of "idhan" is that he presented the second verse as an answer to someone who said to him: "And if they had plundered, what would the sons of Mazin have done?" He said: "Then a band of rough men would have risen to support me."

I say: From this is His saying: ﴿You did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted﴾ [al-Ankabut: 48]. The estimate is: "If you had recited and written, then the falsifiers would have doubted." It is known that the consequence in His saying "indeed you would then be like them" is of the forbidden act, not of the prohibition itself, like the words of the rajaz poet, which is among the evidences of language and grammar:

"Do not leave me among them as a stranger; indeed I would then perish or fly away."

Apparently a group of believers used to sit in these gatherings and did not undertake to change this, nor did they rise from them out of fear of them, so they were prohibited from that. This likeness to them is exceptional in manner, for emphasis, threat and intimidation, and a believer does not become a hypocrite by sitting with hypocrites; the likeness intended is in the sin, not in its degree, meaning that you would become like them in engaging in sins.

Tarabbus (waiting, watching) literally means remaining in a place, as has passed in His saying ﴿yatarabbasna bi-anfusihinna﴾ [al-Baqara: 228] in Surat al-Baqara. The meaning of ﴿Did we not gain mastery over you﴾ is: Did we not take charge of your affairs and encompass you with the encompassing of care and support, ﴿and protect you from the believers﴾, meaning from their might reaching you.
