His saying, ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾, is a reassurance (*tathbit*) for the believers. Reports of the hidden schemes of enemies and their conspiring, whether from an enemy who openly declares his disbelief or from one who flatters and shows brotherhood, and the explanation of these satanic acts that reach the utmost of cunning and scheming, stir fear in the souls of the Muslims and may make them imagine abysses of failure in their future. So, out of gentleness toward them, it was fitting that this warning be followed by bracing up (*al-shadd ʿala al-ʿadud*) and a promise of a good outcome. Allah therefore promised them that He will not give the disbelievers, however their factions band together and however their paths of disbelief differ, any way over the believers.

The meaning of *sabil* (way) here is the path of reaching the believers with defeat and dominance. This is indicated by its being followed by *ʿala* (over), and by the fact that an enemy's way to his enemy is striving to harm him. If the beloved said to you, "There is no way to you," you would grieve; if the enemy said to you, "There is no way to you," you would beam with joy. When it is followed by *ʿala*, it becomes explicit in the way of evil and harm. So the verse is a purely worldly promise. It is not part of legislation at all, nor of matters of the Hereafter, since the context is remote from both.

If you say: if it is a promise, it cannot be broken, yet we see the disbelievers clearly prevailing over the believers, and perhaps they take over their lands, and this lasts a long time. How, then, is this promise to be interpreted? I say: if by the disbelievers and believers are meant the two groups known from the context, the problem disappears, because Allah made the outcome of victory on that day belong to the believers and cut off the root of the people who did wrong. They were soon caught, seized and slain in slaughter, and their remnant entered Islam and became helpers of the religion. If the generality is meant, then by the believers is meant the sincere believers who are clothed in faith in all its states, foundations and branches. Had the believers remained steadfast in that, the disbelievers would not have attained any reach over them, and they would have warded off from themselves failure and ruin.

Since displaying faith and then following it with disbelief was a form of mockery of Islam and its people, their punishment was described with a threat appropriate to their mockery of the Muslims. It came in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum), when He said, "﴿Announce to the hypocrites﴾," for glad tidings (bishara) is news of what delights the one informed, and punishment is not of that kind. The Arabs have various styles of sarcasm, such as the words of Shaqiq ibn Sulaik al-Asadi:

A threat has come to me from Abu Anas,
so my body is drawn out in the anger of al-Dahhak.

And the words of al-Nabigha:

"You will surely become forbearing or desist,
when you grow old, or when the crow grows white."

And the words of Ibn Zayyaba:

"I was informed that Amr, sticking his head [into the ground],
threatens his maternal uncles in a year [of drought],
and such from him is not reliable,
that he will do the thing when he says it."

The disbelievers here mean either the polytheists of Mecca or the rabbis of the Jews, because no open polytheists remained in Medina at the time this surah was revealed; there were only hypocrites and Jews. Indeed, honor belongs to Allah﴾ is an explanatory resumptive statement (isti'naf bayani) in relation to the conjoined clause ﴿Indeed, honor belongs to Allah﴾, and His saying "Do they seek" is the source of the resumption. This implies that the hypocrites' allegiance to the polytheists was not due to similarity in religion and creed, since most of the hypocrites were from the Jews; rather, they took them so that they might gain strength through them over the believers. It also implies that the hypocrites felt weakness and so sought strength, and in this is the utmost ignorance and blame. The interrogative is one of denial and rebuke, and therefore the consequence ﴿Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah﴾ is valid as following from it, meaning there is no honor except through Him, because seeking strength from other than Him is void, as it is said: "Whoever seeks strength from other than Allah will be humiliated." This statement conveys a warning against associating with them by way of metonymy (kinaya).

In that case the pronoun of address is directed to the believers and the pronouns of absence to the hypocrites. [Page 239]

This is a resumptive (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that opens a fresh topic) that adds further explanation of their vices. The connection is evident. The emphasis of the sentence with *inna* serves to confirm their strange condition and to confirm what follows it, namely the words ﴿and He is their deceiver﴾.

The meaning of the hypocrites' deceiving God, exalted is He, was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah at the words ﴿they deceive God and those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:9].

This verse, with the words ﴿and He is their deceiver﴾, adds that He responds to them with the like of their conduct. Just as their action toward the believers who follow the command of God and His Messenger was a deception of God, so God's granting them respite in this world, until they felt secure and thought that their scheme and their plotting would prevail over the Muslims and that God would not support them, and His warning the believers about their plotting, so that their stratagems would not deceive them, and His decree to seize them in the end, are like the act of a deceiver, as a fitting requital. Thus, the application of the word *khida'* (deception) to God's gradual leading of them on (*istidraj*) is a figurative metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*, a metaphor built on a comparison of the whole scene), and it is made fitting by *mushakala* (figurative congruence, the use of a word for something else because it accompanies a word of similar form). *Mushakala* is nothing more than the borrowing of a word for a meaning other than its own, with a closer relationship to another word like the borrowed word. *Mushakala* thus returns to *tamlih* (witty allusion): when there is no link between the literal meaning of the word and the intended meaning except the imitation of the word, it is called *mushakala*, as in the verse of Abu al-Raqa'maq:

They said: "Propose something and we will cook it for you."
I said: "Cook for me a robe and a shirt."

*Kusala* is the plural of *kaslan* on the pattern *fu'ala*. *Kaslan* is one characterized by *kasal*, which is lethargy in actions due to weariness or aversion. Laziness in prayer indicates little concern on the part of the one praying and indifference to performing it, and therefore it is one of the characteristics of the hypocrites. For this reason the Law warned against exceeding the limit of energy in worship, out of fear of weariness. In a hadith: "Take upon yourselves of deeds only what you are able to do, for God does not tire until you tire."

He forbade prayer when a person has a pressing need, and prayer when food is present, all so that the believer's turning to prayer may be with eagerness and resolve, because when weariness of something creeps into the soul, its aversion to it creeps in gradually until aversion takes hold of it, and nothing endangers the soul more than coming to dislike good.

﴿Kusala﴾ is a necessary circumstantial clause (*hal lazimah*) from the pronoun in *qamu* (they stood), because *qamu* cannot stand alone as the answer to *idha* (when), whose condition is *qamu*. For if it stood alone, the answer would be the very condition, so a circumstantial phrase must be mentioned, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan 25:72], and the words of al-Ahwas al-Ansari:

So when he departs, he departs from a raging one,
whose outbursts are feared by his peers.

The clause ﴿they show off to the people﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, or an attribute of *kusala*, or a resumed sentence explaining the answer to one who asks: What is their purpose in this standing for prayer, and why did they not abandon this standing altogether? The explanation is that they show off their prayer to the people. *Yura'una* (they show off) is a verb that implies they show the people their prayer and the people show them likewise. That is not the case here, so the form *mufa'ala* here serves only to intensify the act of showing, and this is common in the *mufa'ala* pattern.

His words ﴿and they do not remember God except a little﴾ are conjoined to *yura'una* if *yura'una* is a circumstantial or attributive clause. If *yura'una* is a resumed sentence, then the clause ﴿and they do not remember﴾ is circumstantial, and the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance, meaning: and they do not remember God through prayer except a little. The exception is either from the times of remembrance, that is, except for a little time, which is the time of their presence with the Muslims when they stand for prayer with them, at which time they remember God by saying *takbir* and other words; or it is from the verbal noun of *yadhkurun*, that is, except a little remembrance in that prayer by which they show off, which is the remembrance that cannot be avoided, such as *ta'min* (saying "Amin"), *rabbana laka al-hamd* (saying "Our Lord, to You be praise"), and *takbir*. Anything beyond that they do not say, such as glorification in bowing and the recitation in silent prayers. You may also make the clause ﴿and they do not remember﴾ conjoined to the clause ﴿and when they stand﴾, in which case it is a report about their qualities, meaning: they do not remember God in all their states except in a little state or a little time, which is the remembrance that no servant is free of who needs his Lord in times of ease and times of hardship. That is, they are not like the Muslims who remember God in every state and remember Him often.

In any case, the verse conveys their servitude and their ingratitude for the blessing of their Lord, in addition to their disbelief in His Messenger and His Qur'an.

Then He brought a state that expresses the essence of their hypocrisy, namely His words ﴿wavering between that﴾, which is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *yura'una*.

[Page 241]

*Mudhabdhab* is a passive participle from *dhabdhabah*. One says: *dhabdhabahu* and he became *tadhabdhaba* (he was made to waver). *Dhabdhabah* is the intensity of agitation from fear or embarrassment. It is said that *dhabdhabah* is derived from the repetition of *dhabba*, meaning to drive away, because the one driven away hastens and is agitated. It is therefore one of the verbs that indicate abundance of the verbal noun through repetition, like *zalzala* (to shake), *lamlama bil-makan* (to gather together in a place), *salsala* (to rattle), and *kabkaba* (to overturn). There is also a form with two unpointed *dal*s, which is used in our common speech today; people say: *rajul mudabdab*, meaning one who does things incorrectly and without success. It has been said that it is derived from *dubbah*, with a *dal* vowelled with a *damma* and a doubled *ba'*, meaning path, in the sense that he takes this path at one time and that path at another.

The indication in His words ﴿between that﴾ refers to what was derived from His words ﴿they show off to the people﴾, because one who intends by his action to please people will not remain long before becoming *mudhabdhab*, for he finds among people groups of differing aims and desires.

It is also permissible to make the indication refer to something not mentioned, but to something that is suitable to be indicated, meaning: wavering between two extremes, such as faith and disbelief.

The clause ﴿neither to these nor to those﴾ is an attribute of *mudhabdhabin* (wavering), intended to reveal its meaning because of the hidden metaphor in it. Or it is an explanation of His words ﴿wavering between that﴾. *Hā'ulā'* (these), one of them, is an indication to the believers, and the other is an indication to the disbelievers, without specification, since in this context there are only two groups. Whichever of the two you make the object of reference by one of the demonstratives is correct. A parallel is His words ﴿and he found in it two men fighting, one of his own party and the other of his enemy﴾ [al-Qasas 28:15].

The sense is: neither they going to the Muslims nor they going to the disbelievers. *Ila* (to) is connected to an omitted element indicated by the meaning of arrival or destination: neither going to this group nor to the other group. The going indicated by *ila* is figurative, namely affiliation and attachment. That is, they have lost both affiliations: they are neither Muslims nor steadfast disbelievers. The Arabs use this construction containing the repeated negative *la* for two purposes: sometimes they intend by it the loss of both matters, as in the saying of one of the women in the story of Umm Zar': "neither easy to climb, nor fat enough to be carried off," and His words ﴿so he neither affirmed nor prayed﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:31], ﴿not a beast broken to plough the earth or water the field﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:71]. And sometimes they intend by it the affirmation of a middle state between two states, as in His words ﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [al-Nur 24:35], ﴿neither old nor virgin﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68], and the words of Zuhayr:

So he neither concealed it nor did he advance it.

In both usages, the meaning of the verse is obscure, since the intent is not to affirm a middle state for the hypocrites between faith and disbelief, for there is no benefit in that meaning. So it is determined that it belongs to the first usage: they are neither among the believers nor among the disbelievers, and in reality they are inclined toward the disbelievers, as many verses indicate, such as His words ﴿those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:139], and His words ﴿and if there is a portion for the disbelievers, they say: Did we not have mastery over you and protect you from the believers?﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:141]. It is therefore determined that the meaning is that they lost faith and affiliation with the Muslims, and they lost disbelief by abandoning the support of its people. That is, they were in a state of agitation, which is the meaning of *tadhabdhub*. The purpose of this is to belittle them and to repel both groups from their company, so that both groups may spurn them.

His words ﴿then you will not find for him a way﴾: the address is to an unspecified person, and the meaning is: you will not find for him a way to guidance, by the context of its contrast with His words ﴿and whomever God leads astray﴾.

[Page 239]

This is a resumptive (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that opens a fresh topic) that adds further explanation of their vices. The connection is evident. The emphasis of the sentence with *inna* serves to confirm their strange condition and to confirm what follows it, namely the words ﴿and He is their deceiver﴾.

The meaning of the hypocrites' deceiving God, exalted is He, was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah at the words ﴿they deceive God and those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:9].

This verse, with the words ﴿and He is their deceiver﴾, adds that He responds to them with the like of their conduct. Just as their action toward the believers who follow the command of God and His Messenger was a deception of God, so God's granting them respite in this world, until they felt secure and thought that their scheme and their plotting would prevail over the Muslims and that God would not support them, and His warning the believers about their plotting, so that their stratagems would not deceive them, and His decree to seize them in the end, are like the act of a deceiver, as a fitting requital. Thus, the application of the word *khida'* (deception) to God's gradual leading of them on (*istidraj*) is a figurative metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*, a metaphor built on a comparison of the whole scene), and it is made fitting by *mushakala* (figurative congruence, the use of a word for something else because it accompanies a word of similar form). *Mushakala* is nothing more than the borrowing of a word for a meaning other than its own, with a closer relationship to another word like the borrowed word. *Mushakala* thus returns to *tamlih* (witty allusion): when there is no link between the literal meaning of the word and the intended meaning except the imitation of the word, it is called *mushakala*, as in the verse of Abu al-Raqa'maq:

They said: "Propose something and we will cook it for you."
I said: "Cook for me a robe and a shirt."

*Kusala* is the plural of *kaslan* on the pattern *fu'ala*. *Kaslan* is one characterized by *kasal*, which is lethargy in actions due to weariness or aversion. Laziness in prayer indicates little concern on the part of the one praying and indifference to performing it, and therefore it is one of the characteristics of the hypocrites. For this reason the Law warned against exceeding the limit of energy in worship, out of fear of weariness. In a hadith: "Take upon yourselves of deeds only what you are able to do, for God does not tire until you tire."

He forbade prayer when a person has a pressing need, and prayer when food is present, all so that the believer's turning to prayer may be with eagerness and resolve, because when weariness of something creeps into the soul, its aversion to it creeps in gradually until aversion takes hold of it, and nothing endangers the soul more than coming to dislike good.

﴿Kusala﴾ is a necessary circumstantial clause (*hal lazimah*) from the pronoun in *qamu* (they stood), because *qamu* cannot stand alone as the answer to *idha* (when), whose condition is *qamu*. For if it stood alone, the answer would be the very condition, so a circumstantial phrase must be mentioned, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan 25:72], and the words of al-Ahwas al-Ansari:

So when he departs, he departs from a raging one,
whose outbursts are feared by his peers.

The clause ﴿they show off to the people﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, or an attribute of *kusala*, or a resumed sentence explaining the answer to one who asks: What is their purpose in this standing for prayer, and why did they not abandon this standing altogether? The explanation is that they show off their prayer to the people. *Yura'una* (they show off) is a verb that implies they show the people their prayer and the people show them likewise. That is not the case here, so the form *mufa'ala* here serves only to intensify the act of showing, and this is common in the *mufa'ala* pattern.

His words ﴿and they do not remember God except a little﴾ are conjoined to *yura'una* if *yura'una* is a circumstantial or attributive clause. If *yura'una* is a resumed sentence, then the clause ﴿and they do not remember﴾ is circumstantial, and the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance, meaning: and they do not remember God through prayer except a little. The exception is either from the times of remembrance, that is, except for a little time, which is the time of their presence with the Muslims when they stand for prayer with them, at which time they remember God by saying *takbir* and other words; or it is from the verbal noun of *yadhkurun*, that is, except a little remembrance in that prayer by which they show off, which is the remembrance that cannot be avoided, such as *ta'min* (saying "Amin"), *rabbana laka al-hamd* (saying "Our Lord, to You be praise"), and *takbir*. Anything beyond that they do not say, such as glorification in bowing and the recitation in silent prayers. You may also make the clause ﴿and they do not remember﴾ conjoined to the clause ﴿and when they stand﴾, in which case it is a report about their qualities, meaning: they do not remember God in all their states except in a little state or a little time, which is the remembrance that no servant is free of who needs his Lord in times of ease and times of hardship. That is, they are not like the Muslims who remember God in every state and remember Him often.

In any case, the verse conveys their servitude and their ingratitude for the blessing of their Lord, in addition to their disbelief in His Messenger and His Qur'an.

Then He brought a state that expresses the essence of their hypocrisy, namely His words ﴿wavering between that﴾, which is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *yura'una*.

[Page 241]

*Mudhabdhab* is a passive participle from *dhabdhabah*. One says: *dhabdhabahu* and he became *tadhabdhaba* (he was made to waver). *Dhabdhabah* is the intensity of agitation from fear or embarrassment. It is said that *dhabdhabah* is derived from the repetition of *dhabba*, meaning to drive away, because the one driven away hastens and is agitated. It is therefore one of the verbs that indicate abundance of the verbal noun through repetition, like *zalzala* (to shake), *lamlama bil-makan* (to gather together in a place), *salsala* (to rattle), and *kabkaba* (to overturn). There is also a form with two unpointed *dal*s, which is used in our common speech today; people say: *rajul mudabdab*, meaning one who does things incorrectly and without success. It has been said that it is derived from *dubbah*, with a *dal* vowelled with a *damma* and a doubled *ba'*, meaning path, in the sense that he takes this path at one time and that path at another.

The indication in His words ﴿between that﴾ refers to what was derived from His words ﴿they show off to the people﴾, because one who intends by his action to please people will not remain long before becoming *mudhabdhab*, for he finds among people groups of differing aims and desires.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 144:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do you wish to give Allah a clear case against yourselves?﴾.

He turned to the believers with a warning against allying with the disbelievers, after he had described their inner workings and their enlisting of the hypocrites for the purpose of harming the Muslims. So the listener understood that were it not for the enmity of the disbelievers toward this religion, there would have been no hypocrisy and no shifting stratagems of the hypocrites. Then He said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾. This is a fresh, initiating resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), since it is the directing of an address after finishing the report about the hypocrites in the third-person form (al-ghayba). This verse comprehensively warns against allying with the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and against falling into hypocrisy, because the hypocrites made a show of faith while allying with the disbelievers. Thus the warning against allying with the disbelievers is a warning against adopting the emblem of hypocrisy, and a warning against allying with the hypocrites, who are the allies of the disbelievers. It is also an exposure of the hypocrites' hypocrisy and a recording against them, so that they cannot say: "We did not know that Allah does not love the alliance with the disbelievers."

Page 243

The apparent meaning is that by "the disbelievers" here are meant the polytheists of Makkah and the People of the Book of Madinah, because the hypocrites were for the most part allied with the People of the Book.

His saying ﴿Do you wish to give Allah a clear case against yourselves?﴾ is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because the prohibition against taking the disbelievers as allies prompts people to ask about the consequence of this act, together with what we have mentioned of the purpose of exposing the hypocrites and recording against them. That is: if you persist in allying with the disbelievers, you will be giving Allah a clear case against you, i.e., a manifest proof against the corruption of your faith. This is an allusion (ta'ridh) directed at the hypocrites.

The interrogative is used here, by way of metonymy (majaz mursal), to express the meaning of warning and admonition.

This "sultan" (clear case) is the Messenger's proof against them that they are not believers, so the rulings of disbelief apply to them, because Allah knows what is in their souls and has no need of a proof against them. Or it is meant as the proof of their exposure on the Day of Reckoning through allying with the disbelievers, as in His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165]. From here it is also permissible that the intended meaning of "proof" is the cutting off of the argument of whoever commits this alliance, and the giving of excuse to him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 145–146:

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire, and you will not find for them a helper.﴾ ﴿Except those who repent, make amends, hold fast to Allah, and purify their religion for Allah. Those are with the believers, and Allah will give the believers a great reward.﴾

He followed the allusion to the hypocrites in His saying ﴿Do not take the disbelievers as allies﴾ [al-Nisa: 144] with an explicit statement, as previously mentioned, that the hypocrites are the most severely punished of the people of the Fire. The transition from the prohibition of taking disbelievers as allies to mentioning the state of the hypocrites indicates that those who took disbelievers as allies are counted among the hypocrites. For transitions between sentences carry meanings that the speech does not otherwise convey, because of the order in which thoughts arise in the mind.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites﴾ is a resumptive sentence of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), the second of its kind, since it returns to the states of the hypocrites. The emphasis of the report with "inna" serves to convey that there is no escape for them from it.

Al-darak (الدَّرَكُ) is the plural form of "darakah" (دَرَكَةٌ), the opposite of al-daraj (الدَّرَجُ), the plural of "darajah" (دَرَجَةٌ). A darakah is a station in descent. So for a thing whose bottom is intended, the stations of descending toward it are called darakat, and for a thing whose top is intended, the stations of ascending toward it are called darajat. Both terms may be applied to a single station depending on the perspective. The hypocrites were in the lowest darak, that is, in the most abased stations of punishment, because their disbelief is the worst kind of disbelief, given the vices that surround it.

The majority read (في الدَّرَكِ) with a fatha on the ra' (الرَّاءِ), as a plural form of "darakah," the opposite of "darajah." ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a sukun on the ra', and both are dialectal variants. The fatha on the ra' is the original form and the more well known.

The address in ﴿and you will not find for them a helper﴾ is to everyone capable of hearing the address. It is an affirmation of the threat and a cutting off of their hope, because the Arabs were accustomed to intercessions and rescue in times of hardship. Therefore, the Qur'an frequently concludes threats by cutting off hope of a helper, ransom, and the like.

Exempted from this threat are those hypocrites who believed, amended their condition, held fast to Allah rather than seeking strength through the disbelievers, and sincerely devoted their religion to Allah, so that it was not mixed with hesitation or waiting to see which of the two groups, the believers or the disbelievers, would prevail. He informed that whoever attains this good state is ﴿with the believers.﴾ In the word "with" (مَعَ) there is an indication of the virtue of those who believed from the outset and did not stain themselves with hypocrisy, because "ma'a" is used with the one who is followed, and he is the more excellent.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿Those are with the believers﴾ is used to further distinguish those who repented, and to draw attention to the fact that they are deserving of what will be mentioned after the demonstrative.

People already know what Allah has prepared for the believers through what has been repeated in the Qur'an, but He added emphasis here with His saying ﴿and Allah will give the believers a great reward.﴾ The particle of future (sawfa) here indicates that the intended reward is the reward of this world, which is victory and a good outcome, and the reward of the Hereafter, since all of it lies in the future, and that the intended meaning is not the recompense, because that has already been realized beforehand.

﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is ever Appreciative, All-Knowing.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil, an appended closing remark) for both the sentence ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 145] and the sentence that implies the exception of those among them who repent and believe, along with what it contains of honoring the believers in the words ﴿And Allah will give the believers a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa': 146].

The address (al-khitab) may be intended for the entire community, and it may also be directed at the hypocrites through a shift from the third person (al-ghayba) to the second person (al-khitab) known as iltifat, in order to be gentler with them.

The interrogative in His words ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment﴾ is intended to convey a negative answer, so it is a rhetorical denial (inkari), meaning: He does nothing with your punishment at all.

The meaning of yaf'alu is "does" or "benefits," as evidenced by its being followed by the preposition bi (with). The meaning is that the threat with which the hypocrites were warned applies only to disbelief and hypocrisy. So when they repent, make amends, and hold fast to Allah, He forgives them the punishment. Therefore they should not suppose that Allah punishes them out of aversion to their essence or to take revenge on them. Rather, it is a recompense for their evil, because the Wise one places things in their proper places: He rewards good with good and evil with evil. When the wrongdoer ceases his evil, Allah nullifies His requital of him with evil, since He does not benefit from punishing or rewarding, but rather effects (al-musabbabat) follow causes (al-asbab). And when the believers have remained steadfast in their faith and gratitude, and have avoided allying with the hypocrites and the disbelievers, then Allah does not punish them, since there is no cause for punishing them.

The clause ﴿And Allah is ever Appreciative, All-Knowing﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) at the end of the speech. It informs that Allah does not withhold good recompense from those who believe in Him and are grateful for His abundant blessings. Belief in Allah and His attributes is the first degree of a servant's gratitude to his Lord.

[p. 5]

﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged. And Allah is ever Hearing, Knowing.﴾ ﴿If you show good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent.﴾

The placement of this verse after the preceding verses is as follows. Allah had disfigured the condition of the hypocrites and exposed their disgraceful conduct at length. The preceding discourse was therefore likely to arouse in the hearers aversion to hypocrisy and its manifestations, and hatred for those accused of it. This was especially so after Allah described them as taking the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers, mocking the Qur'an, and forbidding the Muslims to sit with them. So Allah warned the Muslims that this anger might lead them to denounce, openly and with evil speech, those whom they suspected of hypocrisy. He granted a concession to any Muslim who had been wronged, permitting him to speak openly of evil against his oppressor, because that is a defence of himself.

Al-Bukhari narrated: "Some men gathered in the house of 'Attab ibn Malik for a meal that he had prepared for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. A speaker said: 'Where is Malik ibn al-Dukhshum?' Some of them said: 'That is a hypocrite who does not love Allah and His Messenger.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Do not say that. Do you not see that he has said: There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the Face of Allah?' He said: 'We see his face and his counsel toward the hypocrites.'" [The hadith continues.]

This speaker thought that Malik was a hypocrite because of his association with the hypocrites, and so he described him as a hypocrite who does not love Allah and His Messenger. Perhaps this verse was revealed to restrain rash accusations of hypocrisy against one who is not a hypocrite. Also, since one of the most distinctive traits of the hypocrites is displaying the opposite of what they conceal, their secret conspiracies and their showing off are mentioned in this sūrah, and many instances of their displaying the opposite of what is inwardly in them are mentioned in Sūrat al-Baqarah. This was likely to arouse in souls the fear that displaying what contradicts what is within might itself be hypocrisy. So Allah wished to make clear the distinction between the two conditions.

The clause "Allah does not like" (لا يُحِبُّ) is separated [from what precedes] because it is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'nāf ibtidā'ī) for the purpose explained above: "the public mention of evil speech" (الجَهْرَ بِالسُّوءِ مِنَ القَوْلِ). The Muslims know that love and hatred, in their literal reality, are impossible for Allah, the Exalted, since they are emotional states of the soul in response to approving the good and disapproving the evil. So what is meant is their necessary implications that suit divinity, namely approval and anger. The form "does not like" (لا يُحِبُّ), according to the rules of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl), is a form of negation of permission (ṣīghat nafy al-idhn), and its basis is prohibition. This is the meaning intended here, because "does not like" conveys the meaning of "dislikes," which reverts to the sense of a prohibition. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah is pleased with three things for you and dislikes three things for you, ... and He dislikes for you qīl wa qāl (idle talk), excessive questioning, and squandering of wealth." These are three matters, most of whose forms are prohibited or disliked.

By "public mention" (al-jahr) is meant what reaches the ears of people, since a speech that is kept secret within the speaker himself does not give rise to harm. Restricting it to "speech" is because speech is the weakest kind of harm, so it is known that evil in action is more gravely forbidden.

He made an exception with "one who has been wronged" (مَن ظُلِمَ), permitting him to speak openly of evil. The thing excepted from is the agent of the implied infinitive that occurs in a negative context, which implies generality. The sense is: Allah does not like anyone's public mention of evil, except the public mention of one who has been wronged. Or the excepted term is an omitted genitive construction, meaning: except the public mention of one who has been wronged. The intended meaning is clear, and the principle of brevity has been observed in the discourse.

Allah granted the wronged person permission to speak openly of evil speech so that he might relieve his anger, lest he resort to the sword or to striking with the hand. This permission is a widening of latitude for one who cannot control himself when injustice befalls him. The purpose of this is caution in the ruling "Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech." The verse indicates the permission for the wronged person in all kinds of open evil speech, but it is restricted to what does not exceed the bounds of seeking redress between him and his oppressor, or complaining of the injustice: saying to him, "You wronged me," or "You are an oppressor," and saying to people, "He is an oppressor." Among this is supplicating against the oppressor openly, because supplication against him is a public announcement of his injustice and a referral of the matter to the justice of Allah, the Exalted. Many instances of this meaning occur in the Qur'an. This is restricted to what does not lead to slander (qadhf). The evidences forbidding slander and protecting the self from exposure to the legal penalty for slander (ḥadd al-qadhf) or to discretionary punishment for backbiting (ghībah, ta'zīr) are established in the Sharī'ah. So this exception permits the open mention of evil speech from the side of the wronged person against his oppressor,

[p. 7]

and among this is the hadith: "Procrastination by the wealthy is injustice" (maṭl al-ghanī ẓulm). That is, the one who is kept waiting may say: "So-and-so is a procrastinator and an oppressor." And in another hadith: "The delay of the one who is able [to pay] makes his honour and his punishment permissible."

The clause "And Allah is ever Hearing, Knowing" (وكانَ اللَّهُ سَمِيعًا عَلِيمًا) is coordinated with "does not like." The intended meaning is that He knows all the utterances that issue forth, and knows all intentions and matters. "Knowing" (عَلِيمًا) is mentioned after "Hearing" (سَمِيعًا) to intend generality in knowledge, as a warning lest they suppose that Allah does not know some of what proceeds from them.

After forbidding and permitting, He urged those granted the concession toward pardon and speaking good, saying: "If you show good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent." Showing good (ibdā' al-khayr) means displaying it. He coordinated "or conceal it" (أوْ تُخْفُوهُ) with it to increase the encouragement, so that they would not suppose that reward is only for displaying good, as in His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271]. Pardoning an evil is by forgiveness and abandoning retaliation, and it is a negative matter (amr 'adamī).

The clause "then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent" is the answer (dalīl jawāb) to the conditional, and it is its cause. The estimated answer is: "He will pardon you when you have power over them, just as you have done good openly and secretly and have pardoned when you were able to take your right, because what is permitted by the Sharī'ah is considered within the power of the one permitted." So the answer to the conditional is a promise of forgiveness for them in some of what they commit, as recompense for doing good and for pardoning one who has committed a wrong. This is what I consider to be the meaning of the answer.

The commentators said: the clause of recompense is an exhortation to pardon, by showing that in it is an adoption of perfection, since the attributes of Allah are the ultimate of perfections. The estimated sense is: "If you show good, etc., you will be characterized by the attributes of Allah, for Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent." This estimate fits only "or pardon an evil," and does not fit His saying "If you show good or conceal it," unless that is specified as showing good to one who has wronged them, and concealing it from one who has wronged them. In a hadith: "That you pardon the one who has wronged you, give to the one who has deprived you, and maintain ties with the one who has severed them."

[p. 5]

﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged. And Allah is ever Hearing, Knowing.﴾ ﴿If you show good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent.﴾

The placement of this verse after the preceding verses is as follows. Allah had disfigured the condition of the hypocrites and exposed their disgraceful conduct at length. The preceding discourse was therefore likely to arouse in the hearers aversion to hypocrisy and its manifestations, and hatred for those accused of it. This was especially so after Allah described them as taking the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers, mocking the Qur'an, and forbidding the Muslims to sit with them. So Allah warned the Muslims that this anger might lead them to denounce, openly and with evil speech, those whom they suspected of hypocrisy. He granted a concession to any Muslim who had been wronged, permitting him to speak openly of evil against his oppressor, because that is a defence of himself.

Al-Bukhari narrated: "Some men gathered in the house of 'Attab ibn Malik for a meal that he had prepared for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. A speaker said: 'Where is Malik ibn al-Dukhshum?' Some of them said: 'That is a hypocrite who does not love Allah and His Messenger.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Do not say that. Do you not see that he has said: There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the Face of Allah?' He said: 'We see his face and his counsel toward the hypocrites.'" [The hadith continues.]

This speaker thought that Malik was a hypocrite because of his association with the hypocrites, and so he described him as a hypocrite who does not love Allah and His Messenger. Perhaps this verse was revealed to restrain rash accusations of hypocrisy against one who is not a hypocrite. Also, since one of the most distinctive traits of the hypocrites is displaying the opposite of what they conceal, their secret conspiracies and their showing off are mentioned in this sūrah, and many instances of their displaying the opposite of what is inwardly in them are mentioned in Sūrat al-Baqarah. This was likely to arouse in souls the fear that displaying what contradicts what is within might itself be hypocrisy. So Allah wished to make clear the distinction between the two conditions.

The clause "Allah does not like" (لا يُحِبُّ) is separated [from what precedes] because it is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'nāf ibtidā'ī) for the purpose explained above: "the public mention of evil speech" (الجَهْرَ بِالسُّوءِ مِنَ القَوْلِ). The Muslims know that love and hatred, in their literal reality, are impossible for Allah, the Exalted, since they are emotional states of the soul in response to approving the good and disapproving the evil. So what is meant is their necessary implications that suit divinity, namely approval and anger. The form "does not like" (لا يُحِبُّ), according to the rules of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl), is a form of negation of permission (ṣīghat nafy al-idhn), and its basis is prohibition. This is the meaning intended here, because "does not like" conveys the meaning of "dislikes," which reverts to the sense of a prohibition. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah is pleased with three things for you and dislikes three things for you, ... and He dislikes for you qīl wa qāl (idle talk), excessive questioning, and squandering of wealth." These are three matters, most of whose forms are prohibited or disliked.

By "public mention" (al-jahr) is meant what reaches the ears of people, since a speech that is kept secret within the speaker himself does not give rise to harm. Restricting it to "speech" is because speech is the weakest kind of harm, so it is known that evil in action is more gravely forbidden.

The thing excepted from is the agent of the implied infinitive that occurs in a negative context, which implies generality. The sense is: Allah does not like anyone's public mention of evil, except the public mention of one who has been wronged. Or the excepted term is an omitted genitive construction, meaning: except the public mention of one who has been wronged. The intended meaning is clear, and the principle of brevity has been observed in the discourse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 4, verses 150–152:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and want to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and want to adopt a way between that.﴾ ﴿They are the disbelievers in truth, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make a distinction between any of them—those, We will give them their rewards. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The Qur'an's practice, when addressing the condition of those who showed hostility toward the Muslims, is to shift from the attributes of the hypocrites, or the People of the Book, or the polytheists, to the attributes of others. Here, by "those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers" is meant the Jews and the Christians, as the exegetes (ahl al-tafsir, the scholars of tafsir, i.e. Qur'anic exegesis) have said. The more apparent view is that it refers specifically to the Jews, because they were the ones mixed with the Muslims and the hypocrites, and many of the hypocrites were Jews. He expressed them with the relative pronoun rather than a proper noun, because of the allusion within the relative clause to the reason for the predicate, and to the enormity of their conduct, so that it suits the subsequent reference to them with the demonstrative.

He used the plural "messengers" because the Jews disbelieved in 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, and the Christians disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). So He used the plural in view of the totality of the disbelievers. Or He intended by the plural the dual. Or He intended by the genitive construction the sense of the genus, so that the singular and plural forms are equal in it, because the intention is to censure those who have this attribute without specifying a group. The way of the Arabs in such a case is to express themselves with plural forms even if the one being referred to is singular, as in His saying, ﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾ (Surah al-Nisa, 4:54), and His saying, ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon the people﴾ (Surah al-Nisa, 4:37),

[p. 9]

﴿by which the prophets who submitted judge for those who are Jews﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 5:44), and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is the matter with people who stipulate conditions...?"

The imperfect verb is used here to indicate that this is a renewed and continuous matter among them, because if they had disbelieved in the past and then returned, they would not deserve censure.

The meaning of their disbelief in Allah is that when they believed in Him but attributed to Him qualities other than His own, such as anthropomorphism (tajsim), taking a consort and a son, incarnation (hulul), and the like, they believed in the name but not in the One named. In reality, they disbelieved in the One named. This is like when someone thinks he knows a certain person, and you say to him, "Describe him to me," and he describes him with qualities other than his own; you say to him, "You do not know him." Moreover, when they disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ), they disbelieved in what he brought of the Oneness of Allah and His transcendence above resemblance to created things, and so they disbelieved in His true divinity, since among them are those who anthropomorphized and among them are those who made Him a trinity.

His saying, ﴿and want to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers﴾, means that they try to do this, and so "wanting" is applied to "trying." In this there is an indication that the matter is difficult to attain, and that they had not reached what they wanted of it, because they were still trying it, as the imperfect verb in His saying "and want" indicates. Had they reached it, He would have said "and made a distinction between Allah and His messengers."

The meaning of making a distinction between Allah and His messengers is that they deny the truthfulness of some of the messengers whom Allah sent, and acknowledge the truthfulness of some messengers but not others, and claim that they believe in Allah. Thus they have made a distinction between Allah and His messengers, since they negated their messengership and thereby distanced them from Him. This is a representative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah): it likens the imagined matter in their souls to what the one who intends to separate friends and beloved ones harbors. It is a likening of one intellectual state to another intellectual state, and the purpose of the comparison is to disfigure the likened, since people know that separating those who are connected is blameworthy.

This verse is in the meaning of the verses that preceded it in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitters﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:136), ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:285),

[p. 10]

and in Surah Al 'Imran: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitters﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 3:84). However, those verses are a warning against making distinctions among the messengers, while this verse is a warning against making a distinction between Allah and some of His messengers. The final result of all is one, because making a distinction among the messengers necessarily entails making a distinction between Allah and some of His messengers.

The addition of the plural to the pronoun here is for a specific reference (al-'ahd), not for generality (al-'umum), by the presence of the indicator, which is His saying, ﴿and say, "We believe in some"﴾.

The clause ﴿and say, "We believe in some"﴾ stands in the sense of an explanatory resumptive clause (al-isti'naf al-bayani) for the making of a distinction between Allah and His messengers. However, it was conjoined because it is a specific aspect of their affairs, since what it signifies is a saying among their abominable sayings, while what "they want" signifies is a state resulting from their disbelief. Therefore conjoining was appropriate, given the difference, even if only in general terms. Had it been separated, it would have been correct. The meaning of "they say, 'We believe'" etc. is that the Jews say: "We believe in Allah and in Musa, and we disbelieve in 'Isa and Muhammad," and the Christians say: "We believe in Allah and in Musa and 'Isa, and we disbelieve in Muhammad." Thus they believed in Allah and some of His messengers outwardly, and made a distinction between Him and some of His messengers.

The wanting in His saying, ﴿and want to adopt a way between that﴾, is genuine wanting. "The way" may be understood as the way of salvation from accountability in the Hereafter, imagining that this is a stratagem that secures their safety if the believers are safe; or as the way of disowning disbelief in some of the messengers; or as a way between two religions. These last two aspects suit their transition from overt disbelief to hypocrisy, so they are, as it were, a preparation for hypocrisy.

This interpretation follows the apparent structure of the speech, which is that the conjunction particle links the conjoined elements in the ruling of the element conjoined to. Since the first conjoined element was a relative clause of ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who), what was conjoined to it are relative clauses of that relative pronoun, and that relative pronoun is the possessor of all those relative clauses.

[p. 11]

It has been attributed to some exegetes that he took the conjunctions (al-waw) in them to mean "or," and took the relative pronoun to include groups of disbelievers whose states of disbelief were varied, according to the distribution of the conjoined relative clauses. He took "those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers" to mean the polytheists; "those who want to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers" to mean a people who affirmed the Creator and denied all prophethoods; and "those who say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others'" to mean the Jews and the Christians. He remained silent about the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿and want to adopt a way between that﴾; had he wished, he would have made "those" a different group, namely the hypocrites who vacillate, who did not remain firm in faith or in disbelief, but were between the two states, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿wavering between that﴾ (Surah al-Nisa, 4:143). What led him to this interpretation is that he did not find a group that combined all these states in their apparent sense, because the Jews did not disbelieve in Allah and His messengers. You have learned that the interpretation of disbelief in Allah is disbelief in the attributes whose denial entails the negation of divinity.

This style is rare in eloquent speech, since if that were intended, the expected form would have been: "Those who want to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, and those who say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others,'" as He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated and strove with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah, and those who sheltered and helped—those are allies of one another. And those who believed but did not emigrate...﴾ (Surah al-Anfal, 8:72).

As for His saying, ﴿They are the disbelievers in truth﴾: the sentence is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), and the demonstrative refers to the holders of that previous relative clause. The placement of the demonstrative here serves to draw attention to the fact that those being pointed to, by virtue of these attributes being recalled, deserve the judgment that will be passed on them, which is the punishment associated with the demonstrative noun.

The definiteness of both parts of the sentence and the use of the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) served to emphasize the restriction (qasr) of the attribute of disbelief upon them. This is a figurative, claimed restriction (qasr idda'i majazi), by treating the disbelief of others, in comparison with their disbelief, as though it were nonexistent, like His saying about the hypocrites: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun, 63:4). Such a restriction indicates the perfection of the described in that restricted attribute.

[p. 12]

The reason for this exaggeration is that their disbelief comprised many states of disbelief, and a baseness of character or foolishness of opinion, by the totality of those relative clauses that were reported about them. Each one of those traits, if taken alone, is disbelief, so how much more so when they are combined.

"In truth" (haqqan) is an absolute object serving to emphasize the content of the preceding sentence, meaning: "Their disbelief is true, O listener, reaching the utmost limit of disbelief." A similar usage is their saying "jiddan" (truly). The emphasis in such a case is on the content of the preceding sentence as conveyed by the sentence, and it is not intended to remove figurative meaning. It is an emphasis on what the sentence conveys of the meaning of utmost limit, because the restriction is used in that sense. The emphasis was not intended to make the restriction literal, since it is evident that this is not correct. So the statement of some grammarians about the absolute object emphasizing the content of the sentence, that it conveys the removal of the possibility of figurative meaning, is based on the common function of emphasis.

"A'tadna" means "We prepared and decreed." The "ta'" in "a'tadna" is, according to many lexicographers, a substitution for "dal" (the root being 'a-d-d). Many of them said the "ta'" is original, and that it is a separate morphological form, different from the form of "'adda." Some said that "'atada" is the original, and that "'adda" was assimilated from it, the "ta'" being merged into the "dal." Both forms occur frequently in their speech and in the Qur'an.

The sentence ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾ to its end was introduced to contrast the wrongdoers with the good-doers, and warning with good tidings, in accordance with the Qur'anic practice.

By "those who believe" is meant all believers, and especially those among the People of the Book who believed, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam. They are intended primarily, because of what the position of this sentence after the mention of their misguidance suggests, and because of what the concluding phrase ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ requires, that is: forgiving to them whatever disbelief preceded, and merciful to them.

The discussion of the use of the relative pronoun and the demonstrative in this sentence is the same as the discussion of its counterpart.

As for His saying ﴿between any of them﴾, the discussion of its like has already passed in His saying ﴿We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitters﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:136), in Surah al-Baqarah.

[p. 13]

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read "nu'tihim" with the royal "we" (nun al-'azamah). Hafs, from 'Asim, read it with the "ya'" of the third-person masculine, and the pronoun refers to the divine name in His saying ﴿those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾.

Thus they believed in Allah and some of His messengers outwardly, and made a distinction between Him and some of His messengers.

"The way" may be understood as the way of salvation from accountability in the Hereafter, imagining that this is a stratagem that secures their safety if the believers are safe; or as the way of disowning disbelief in some of the messengers; or as a way between two religions. These last two aspects suit their transition from overt disbelief to hypocrisy, so they are, as it were, a preparation for hypocrisy.

[p. 11]

What led him to this interpretation is that he did not find a group that combined all these states in their apparent sense, because the Jews did not disbelieve in Allah and His messengers. You have learned that the interpretation of disbelief in Allah is disbelief in the attributes whose denial entails the negation of divinity.

This is a figurative, claimed restriction (qasr idda'i majazi), by treating the disbelief of others, in comparison with their disbelief, as though it were nonexistent, like His saying about the hypocrites: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun, 63:4). Such a restriction indicates the perfection of the described in that restricted attribute.

[p. 12]

In reality, they disbelieved in the One named. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 4, verses 153–154:**

﴿The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. But they had asked Moses for something greater than that, when they said, "Show us God openly," and the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf (for worship) after the clear signs had come to them, yet We pardoned that, and We gave Moses clear authority.﴾ ﴿And We raised the Mount above them by their covenant, and We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," and We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a firm covenant.﴾

When He mentioned the excuses of the People of the Two Scriptures for their denial of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), He followed it with mention of some of their demands for miracles that would come according to their own desires.

The sentence is a fresh, inceptive resumption (istinaf ibtida'i).

The use of the present tense here may be either to bring to mind their astonishing state in this request, so that the listener seems to see them, as in His saying ﴿and he was building the ark﴾ [Hud 38], His saying ﴿Rather, you are amazed, and they mock﴾ [al-Saffat 12], and His saying ﴿It is God who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [Fatir 9]. Or it may indicate that the request was repeated and renewed time after time, in that they persisted in this request with the aim of causing difficulty, like the saying of Tarif ibn Tamim al-'Anbari:

*"They sent to me their overseer, who keeps on examining (me)."*

That is, he keeps repeating the examining. The intended meaning under both possibilities is to express wonder at this request, and for this reason He said after it, ﴿for they asked Moses before.﴾

The askers are the Jews. They asked for a miracle like the miracle of Moses, namely that there be sent down to them something like what was sent down to Moses in the tablets containing the Ten Commandments. They did not mean the whole Torah, as some exegetes imagined, for the Book of the Torah was not sent down all at once. Thus the People of the Scripture here refers specifically to the Jews.

The word "Book" here is either a name for the written thing, as the tablets of Moses were sent down, or a name for a coherent piece made of written pages. In that case they would have asked for a miracle different from the miracle of Moses.

The fa' in His saying ﴿for they asked Moses before﴾ is the eloquent fa' (fa' al-fasihah), indicating a presumed clause that the present tense points to, whose purpose is wonder. That is: "Do not be amazed at this, for it is an old trait of their forefathers with their messenger, when they asked him for a miracle greater than this." Deducing their state from the state of their forefathers is of the kind of deducing the characteristics of nations and tribes to the conditions of their clans, and much of this has already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah.

In this statement there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and an indication of their audacity, and a demonstration that messengers do not come to fulfil the proposals of nations in asking for miracles. Rather, miracles come by the will of God, the Exalted, when prophets are challenged. Had God answered those who propose what they propose of miracles, He would have made His messengers like charlatans and practitioners of conjuring tricks and illusions, who receive the proposals of people in gatherings and public and private assemblies. This would diminish the status of the message.

In the Gospel of Matthew, a group said to the Messiah, "We want to see a sign from you," and he said, "An evil generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it." This was repeated in another incident. Such a request may be accepted from believers, as God related about Jesus: ﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?" He said, "Fear God, if you are believers."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 112] ﴿They said, "We want to eat from it, and that our hearts be at rest, and that we know you have spoken truly to us, and that we be witnesses to it."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 113] up to His saying ﴿God said, "I am sending it down to you. But whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will punish him with a punishment with which I shall not punish anyone among all the worlds."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 115]. And the Exalted said, ﴿Nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her. And We send not the signs except as a warning.﴾ [al-Isra' 59]

[p. 15]

As for them, when they asked Moses to show them God openly, they did not intend seeking blessing through God, nor enjoying the vision. Rather, they wanted a wonder to look at. That is why they said, ﴿Show us God openly,﴾ and did not say, "Would that we might see our Lord."

"Openly" (jahratan) is the opposite of "secretly" (khufyah), that is, publicly. It may be an adjective of the seeing derived from "show us," or it may be a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "show us," meaning: while you are openly showing us Him, not concealing His vision from us.

Here He digressed to what befell them as a consequence of their request for this vision and what followed from it, and He said, ﴿so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing.﴾ This is what the Exalted related in Surat al-Baqarah with His saying, ﴿Then the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ [al-Baqarah 55]. That was a terror and a rebuke for them, and for this reason He said, "for their wrongdoing."

The wrongdoing is what is mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah concerning their refusal to believe Moses until they should see God openly. The wrongdoing was not merely for asking for the vision, because Moses himself had asked a similar question once. God related it about him with His saying, ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, "My Lord, show me, that I may look at You."﴾ [al-A'raf 143], the verse in Surat al-A'raf.

He made clear that this did not deter them. They took the calf as a god after the clear signs had come to them, which indicate the oneness of God and the negation of any partner. The clause of their taking the calf is connected by the particle thumma ("then"), which, in conjoining clauses, conveys the meaning of a rank-based sequencing (al-taraakhi al-rutbi), that is, a delay in rank. For their taking the calf as a god is a greater crime than what was related before it. Despite this, God pardoned them and gave Moses clear authority, that is, a manifest proof against them in their rebellion, so that he could rebuke and reprimand them. Among his clear authority was that he burned the calf they had taken as a god.

Then He mentioned other signs that God showed them, namely: the raising of the Mount, the command to fight the people of Jericho (Ariha), their entering its gate prostrating, and the prohibition of hunting from the sea for them on the Sabbath. All of these have already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The word "gate" may be the gate of the city of Jericho, or it may be the gap or passage between mountains and the like, as will come in the explanation of His saying, ﴿Two men of those who feared (God) said, "Enter upon them through the gate"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 23], in Surat al-'Uqud.

[p. 16]

As for taking the covenant from them, what is meant is the pact, and describing it as "firm" (ghalizan) means strong. Ghilaz (thickness, coarseness) is an attribute of bodies, so it was borrowed for the strength of meaning, and it is used as a metaphor for the solidity of the pact, because thickness implies strength. What is meant is the category of the solemn covenant, with its many pacts that were taken from them, most of which were mentioned in the verses of Surat al-Baqarah. The purpose of this is to show how deeply rooted they were in obstinacy and stubbornness since the days of their prophets, as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he met from them, and as a preparation for His saying, ﴿So because of their breaking of their covenant﴾ [al-Nisa' 155].

As for His saying, "do not transgress" (la ta'addu): Nafi' recited it in the most authentic transmissions, and those are the transmission of Warsh from him and one of the two transmissions of Qalun from him, with a fatha on the 'ayn and a shadda on the dal with a damma, its original form being la ta'tadu. The verb i'tada is of the form (ifti'al) from 'adw, and one says i'tada 'ala fulan, meaning he exceeded the bounds of right with him. When the ta' was close to the articulation point of the dal and occurred vowelled after a sakin, its assimilation became possible. Its vowel was moved to the preceding sakin 'ayn, and it was assimilated into the dal for the purpose of lightening. For this reason it is permissible in Arabic speech to pronounce it clearly, so they say ta'tadu and ta'addu, because it occurred before the dal, and so it was not drawn toward its articulation point. Had it occurred after the dal, its assimilation would have been obligatory, as in "adda'ana." Al-Jumhur, and Qalun in one of his two transmissions, recited it as ﴿la ta'du﴾ with a sukun on the 'ayn and a lightened dal, a jussive present verb from 'adw, which is 'udwan, as in His saying ﴿when they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-A'raf 163], in Surat al-A'raf. In one of the two transmissions from Qalun it is with ikhtilas (a brief, partial pronunciation of) the fatha. Abu Ja'far recited it with a sukun on the 'ayn and a shadda on the dal, and this is also a transmission from Nafi', narrated by Ibn Mujahid.

Abu 'Ali said in al-Hujjah: Many grammarians deny the joining of two sakin letters when the second of them is assimilated and the first of them is not a soft letter (harf lin), as in dabbah. They say that the madd becomes a substitute for the vowel. He said: If something like duwaybbah is permissible even with the loss of the madd in it, it is not prohibited to join two sakin letters in something like ta'du, because the difference between a soft letter and other letters is slight, that is, given that pronouncing it is not impossible.
