﴿The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. But they had asked Moses for something greater than that, when they said, "Show us God openly," and the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf (for worship) after the clear signs had come to them, yet We pardoned that, and We gave Moses clear authority.﴾ ﴿And We raised the Mount above them by their covenant, and We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," and We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a firm covenant.﴾

When He mentioned the excuses of the People of the Two Scriptures for their denial of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), He followed it with mention of some of their demands for miracles that would come according to their own desires.

The sentence is a fresh, inceptive resumption (istinaf ibtida'i).

The use of the present tense here may be either to bring to mind their astonishing state in this request, so that the listener seems to see them, as in His saying ﴿and he was building the ark﴾ [Hud 38], His saying ﴿Rather, you are amazed, and they mock﴾ [al-Saffat 12], and His saying ﴿It is God who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [Fatir 9]. Or it may indicate that the request was repeated and renewed time after time, in that they persisted in this request with the aim of causing difficulty, like the saying of Tarif ibn Tamim al-'Anbari:

*"They sent to me their overseer, who keeps on examining (me)."*

That is, he keeps repeating the examining. The intended meaning under both possibilities is to express wonder at this request, and for this reason He said after it, ﴿for they asked Moses before.﴾

The askers are the Jews. They asked for a miracle like the miracle of Moses, namely that there be sent down to them something like what was sent down to Moses in the tablets containing the Ten Commandments. They did not mean the whole Torah, as some exegetes imagined, for the Book of the Torah was not sent down all at once. Thus the People of the Scripture here refers specifically to the Jews.

The word "Book" here is either a name for the written thing, as the tablets of Moses were sent down, or a name for a coherent piece made of written pages. In that case they would have asked for a miracle different from the miracle of Moses.

The fa' in His saying ﴿for they asked Moses before﴾ is the eloquent fa' (fa' al-fasihah), indicating a presumed clause that the present tense points to, whose purpose is wonder. That is: "Do not be amazed at this, for it is an old trait of their forefathers with their messenger, when they asked him for a miracle greater than this." Deducing their state from the state of their forefathers is of the kind of deducing the characteristics of nations and tribes to the conditions of their clans, and much of this has already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah.

In this statement there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and an indication of their audacity, and a demonstration that messengers do not come to fulfil the proposals of nations in asking for miracles. Rather, miracles come by the will of God, the Exalted, when prophets are challenged. Had God answered those who propose what they propose of miracles, He would have made His messengers like charlatans and practitioners of conjuring tricks and illusions, who receive the proposals of people in gatherings and public and private assemblies. This would diminish the status of the message.

In the Gospel of Matthew, a group said to the Messiah, "We want to see a sign from you," and he said, "An evil generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it." This was repeated in another incident. Such a request may be accepted from believers, as God related about Jesus: ﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?" He said, "Fear God, if you are believers."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 112] ﴿They said, "We want to eat from it, and that our hearts be at rest, and that we know you have spoken truly to us, and that we be witnesses to it."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 113] up to His saying ﴿God said, "I am sending it down to you. But whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will punish him with a punishment with which I shall not punish anyone among all the worlds."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 115]. And the Exalted said, ﴿Nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her. And We send not the signs except as a warning.﴾ [al-Isra' 59]

[p. 15]

As for them, when they asked Moses to show them God openly, they did not intend seeking blessing through God, nor enjoying the vision. Rather, they wanted a wonder to look at. That is why they said, ﴿Show us God openly,﴾ and did not say, "Would that we might see our Lord."

"Openly" (jahratan) is the opposite of "secretly" (khufyah), that is, publicly. It may be an adjective of the seeing derived from "show us," or it may be a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "show us," meaning: while you are openly showing us Him, not concealing His vision from us.

Here He digressed to what befell them as a consequence of their request for this vision and what followed from it, and He said, ﴿so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing.﴾ This is what the Exalted related in Surat al-Baqarah with His saying, ﴿Then the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ [al-Baqarah 55]. That was a terror and a rebuke for them, and for this reason He said, "for their wrongdoing."

The wrongdoing is what is mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah concerning their refusal to believe Moses until they should see God openly. The wrongdoing was not merely for asking for the vision, because Moses himself had asked a similar question once. God related it about him with His saying, ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, "My Lord, show me, that I may look at You."﴾ [al-A'raf 143], the verse in Surat al-A'raf.

He made clear that this did not deter them. They took the calf as a god after the clear signs had come to them, which indicate the oneness of God and the negation of any partner. The clause of their taking the calf is connected by the particle thumma ("then"), which, in conjoining clauses, conveys the meaning of a rank-based sequencing (al-taraakhi al-rutbi), that is, a delay in rank. For their taking the calf as a god is a greater crime than what was related before it. Despite this, God pardoned them and gave Moses clear authority, that is, a manifest proof against them in their rebellion, so that he could rebuke and reprimand them. Among his clear authority was that he burned the calf they had taken as a god.

Then He mentioned other signs that God showed them, namely: the raising of the Mount, the command to fight the people of Jericho (Ariha), their entering its gate prostrating, and the prohibition of hunting from the sea for them on the Sabbath. All of these have already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The word "gate" may be the gate of the city of Jericho, or it may be the gap or passage between mountains and the like, as will come in the explanation of His saying, ﴿Two men of those who feared (God) said, "Enter upon them through the gate"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 23], in Surat al-'Uqud.

[p. 16]

As for taking the covenant from them, what is meant is the pact, and describing it as "firm" (ghalizan) means strong. Ghilaz (thickness, coarseness) is an attribute of bodies, so it was borrowed for the strength of meaning, and it is used as a metaphor for the solidity of the pact, because thickness implies strength. What is meant is the category of the solemn covenant, with its many pacts that were taken from them, most of which were mentioned in the verses of Surat al-Baqarah. The purpose of this is to show how deeply rooted they were in obstinacy and stubbornness since the days of their prophets, as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he met from them, and as a preparation for His saying, ﴿So because of their breaking of their covenant﴾ [al-Nisa' 155].

As for His saying, "do not transgress" (la ta'addu): Nafi' recited it in the most authentic transmissions, and those are the transmission of Warsh from him and one of the two transmissions of Qalun from him, with a fatha on the 'ayn and a shadda on the dal with a damma, its original form being la ta'tadu. The verb i'tada is of the form (ifti'al) from 'adw, and one says i'tada 'ala fulan, meaning he exceeded the bounds of right with him. When the ta' was close to the articulation point of the dal and occurred vowelled after a sakin, its assimilation became possible. Its vowel was moved to the preceding sakin 'ayn, and it was assimilated into the dal for the purpose of lightening. For this reason it is permissible in Arabic speech to pronounce it clearly, so they say ta'tadu and ta'addu, because it occurred before the dal, and so it was not drawn toward its articulation point. Had it occurred after the dal, its assimilation would have been obligatory, as in "adda'ana." Al-Jumhur, and Qalun in one of his two transmissions, recited it as ﴿la ta'du﴾ with a sukun on the 'ayn and a lightened dal, a jussive present verb from 'adw, which is 'udwan, as in His saying ﴿when they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-A'raf 163], in Surat al-A'raf. In one of the two transmissions from Qalun it is with ikhtilas (a brief, partial pronunciation of) the fatha. Abu Ja'far recited it with a sukun on the 'ayn and a shadda on the dal, and this is also a transmission from Nafi', narrated by Ibn Mujahid.

Abu 'Ali said in al-Hujjah: Many grammarians deny the joining of two sakin letters when the second of them is assimilated and the first of them is not a soft letter (harf lin), as in dabbah. They say that the madd becomes a substitute for the vowel. He said: If something like duwaybbah is permissible even with the loss of the madd in it, it is not prohibited to join two sakin letters in something like ta'du, because the difference between a soft letter and other letters is slight, that is, given that pronouncing it is not impossible.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 155:

﴿So for their breaking their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, "Our hearts are uncovered," (No!) Rather, Allah has sealed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a few.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying (﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ [an-Nisa: 154]). The bā' is for causality (al-sababiyyah), governing "naqdihim" (their breaking). The "mā" is superfluous (zā'idah) after the bā', to emphasise the causation, and the superfluous "mā" after the bā' does not stop the bā' from its governing function in the genitive case. The same applies when "mā" is superfluous after "min" and after "'an".

However, when "mā" is superfluous after the kāf of comparison (kāf al-jarr) and after rubba, it stops the particle from governing the genitive case.

As for the object of His saying "bi-mā naqdihim": it may be elided, so that the listener's mind goes off in the directions of awe, and its estimate is: "We did to them what We did." It may also be connected to (﴿We forbade them good things which had been lawful for them﴾ [an-Nisa: 160]), with what lies between them being digressions (mustatradat), and His saying (﴿So because of the wrongdoing of those who judaized﴾ [an-Nisa: 160]) serving as a comprehensive summation (fadhlakah) of their enumerated crimes mentioned earlier. It is not suitable to connect the genitive phrase to "ṭaba'a" (sealed), because it came as a response to their saying "Our hearts are uncovered", and it belongs to the set of coordinated clauses that demand a connection; but "ṭaba'a" may be a proof for the elided answer.

The events mentioned here have already been explained in their places.

The object is placed first to convey restriction (ḥaṣr): namely, that the prohibition was only because of what they did. The meaning is: "We did not forbid them good things except because of their breaking [the covenant]." The meaning of restriction and causation is emphasised by the superfluous "mā", so the sentence conveys both restriction and emphasis.

His saying "Rather, Allah has sealed them" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) between the coordinated items (al-ma'atif). Ṭab' (sealing) is the firm closing of a lock by placing clay or the like over the sealed opening so that whoever wishes to extract what is within cannot reach it except after removing that sealing substance. They may also mark that lock with a mark that leaves an imprint on the sealed object; the instrument that makes the mark is called ṭābi' (with a fatha on the bā'), and it is synonymous with khatm (stamping). The meaning of "bi-kufrihim" is "because of it" (bi-sababihi): increasing disbelief increases the hearts' resistance to receiving guidance. By "bi-kufrihim" is meant their disbelief mentioned in His saying "and their disbelief in the signs of Allah."

The exception in His saying "except a few" is from the generality of the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq): that is, they do not believe with any belief except a small belief. This is emphasis of a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, since belief does not admit of few or many; so a little of belief is non-existence, and thus it is disbelief. This was discussed earlier in His saying (﴿Little is it that they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88]). It is also possible that the scarcity of belief is a metonymy (kinayah) for the scarcity of its adherents, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 4, verse 156:**

﴿And for their disbelief and their saying against Mary a tremendous slander,﴾ ﴿and for their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah." But they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; rather, it was made to appear so to them. Indeed, those who differ concerning him are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption.﴾ [An-Nisa: 157].

The phrase "wa-bi-kufrihim" (and for their disbelief) is conjoined a second time to his statement "fa-bi-ma naqdihim" (so for their breaking of the covenant). He did not dispense with it by his statement, "﴿and their disbelief in the signs of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 155]." Yet he repeated the preposition, which the conjunction would otherwise make unnecessary, for the purpose of emphasis. The conjunction is taken into account because of the distance between the two phrases, and because the context is one of amplifying the gravity of disbelief. The speaker mentions it and repeats it, to affirm it and to show that there is no doubt in attaching the judgment to it. A parallel to this repetition is the verse of Labid:

*So they contended over a flowing shade whose shadow stretches, like the smoke of a kindled fire whose blaze leaps up.*

*A mashmulah (a fire of mixed fuel), its fuel mingled with growing 'arfaj shrub, like the smoke of a fire whose tops rise high.*

He repeated the comparison with his words "like the smoke of a fire," to establish the meaning of the first comparison.

In the *Kashshaf* (by al-Zamakhshari): "Their disbelief was repeated because they disbelieved in Musa, then in 'Isa, then in Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all. So part of their disbelief was conjoined to another part." That is, the second disbelief is regarded as differing from the one before it, by virtue of the conjunction of his statement "﴿and their saying against Mary a slander﴾." A parallel to this is the verse of 'Uways al-Qawafi:

*Baseness is more noble than Wabr and his father; baseness is more noble than Wabr and what he fathered.*

Here he conjoined his statement "baseness is more noble than Wabr" with the second, on the basis that the second was conjoined to the first by his statement "and what he fathered."

*Al-buhtan* is the verbal noun of *bahatahu*, when one comes to him with a saying or an action that he does not anticipate and for which he finds no answer. One who deliberately does this is a *bahut*, and its plural is *buhut* and *buhtun*. The Jews fabricated whatever they wished in their lie against Mary, peace be upon her. As for their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam," the basis of blame against them for it is that they intended to count this sin among the glories of their forefathers, which return to breaking the clear covenant in the cause of supporting the religion.

"Al-Masih" was a title of 'Isa, peace be upon him, which the Jews gave him in mockery, because the meaning of *al-Masih* in the Hebrew language is "the king." This was mentioned earlier in the saying of the Exalted, "﴿his name is the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 45]," in Surah Aal 'Imran. It was a title they intended in mockery, and it became a title for him among them. Allah turned their intention of belittling him into a means of honoring him. A parallel to this is what some of the polytheists used to call the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the name *Mudhammam*. The wife of Abu Lahab said, "We have disobeyed Mudhammam, and we have rejected his command." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do you not wonder how Allah turns away from me the abuse and cursing of Quraysh? They abuse and curse Mudhammam, but I am Muhammad."

His statement "Rasul Allah (the Messenger of Allah)," if it is part of the quoted speech, its purpose is praise of him and an indication that those who boast of killing him deserve what Allah has ordained for them because of their saying. In this case, the accusative of "Rasul Allah" is by way of praise. If it is part of the reported statement, then their description of him is in mockery, like the saying of the polytheists to the Prophet ﷺ, "﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, indeed you are mad﴾ [Al-Hijr: 6]," and the saying of the people of Madyan to Shu'ayb, "﴿Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped or that we not do with our wealth what we please? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning﴾ [Hud: 87]." In this case, the accusative of "Rasul Allah" is as an attribute of the Messiah.

His statement "﴿and they did not kill him﴾ [An-Nisa: 157]" and so on: the apparent reading is that the *waw* in it is for the circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), meaning they said that while they had not killed him. It is not a report of the negation of killing, because if it were a report, the context would require strong emphasizing devices. But since it is a circumstantial clause of the subject of the saying conjoined to the causes of their curse and blame, those causes establish the affirmation of their lie. Furthermore, it is permissible that it be a report conjoined to the sentences reported about them. Its being stripped of emphasizing devices is either because the one addressed by it is the believers, or because this report is considered self-sufficient without emphasis, so omitting emphasis is a departure from what the apparent context requires, or because it was received only from Allah, the Knower of hidden matters, and so it was too great to be emphasized.

He conjoined "﴿and they did not crucify him﴾ [An-Nisa: 157]" because crucifixion may occur without killing. They sometimes crucified a criminal as punishment for him and then pardoned him. The Exalted said, "﴿The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is only that they be killed or crucified﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 33]."

The well-known usage of *al-salb* (crucifixion) is that the person designated for killing is tied to a wooden post so that he cannot move, and then he is stabbed with a spear or shot with an arrow. Likewise, they claimed that 'Isa was crucified and then stabbed with a spear in his heart.

The clause "but it was made to appear so to them" is an *istidrak* (a corrective exception, introducing a qualification that corrects what precedes). What it corrects is what "they did not kill him" implied, namely that this saying has no basis in doubt and is pure fabrication. By the *istidrak* he clarifies that the root of their assumption that they killed him was that they imagined they had killed him. This is a doubt that led the Jews to think they had killed the Messiah. It is what they saw openly: the occurrence of a killing and crucifixion upon a person whom they believed to be the Messiah himself. Reports have come concerning this interpretation of the meaning of *al-shabah* (resemblance).

His statement "shubbiha lahum" (it was made to appear to them) may mean: the Jews who claimed they killed the Messiah in their time had a resemblance made to them of someone who looked like the Messiah, and they killed him, while Allah saved the Messiah from the humiliation of killing. In this case, "shubbiha" is a verb in the passive voice, derived from *al-shabah*, which is similarity in form. The object which should be the deputy subject of "shubbiha" is omitted because the verb "shubbiha" indicates it. The estimated reading is: "a look-alike was made to resemble," so that the deputy subject is the one for them. The pronoun "lahum" in this sense refers to those who said, "﴿Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam﴾ [An-Nisa: 157]," who were the Jews of his time. That is, resemblance occurred to them. In this sense the *lam* means "in the view of," as when you say, "a suspicion arose for me about such-and-such." The *istidrak* is clear on this reading.

It may also mean: "but it was made to appear to the Jews, both earlier and later, that the news of the crucifixion of the Messiah was true," that is, the falsehood was confused with the truth for them. This is like the Arabic expression, "it was imagined to you," or "it became confused for so-and-so." There was no look-alike of 'Isa, but the lie about his news resembled the truth. In this sense the *lam* is the *lam* of cause: the report was made to appear true to them for their sake, that is, for their misguidance. That is, their elders invented it for them, so that they could cool their burning anger against 'Isa, since he had come to nullify their misguidance. Or the *lam* may mean *'ala* (upon), for figurative elevation, as in the Exalted's saying, "﴿and if you do evil, it is against yourselves﴾ [Al-Isra': 7]." The reason for shifting from a particle to including the meaning of "made" (*sun'a*) in the verb "shubbiha" is that the rabbis fabricated this report in order to introduce doubt among the common people.

In the reports, Yahudha al-Iskhariyuti (Judas Iscariot), one of the companions of the Messiah, had gone astray and become a hypocrite. He was the one who informed on 'Isa, peace be upon him, and Allah cast upon him the likeness of 'Isa, and he was the one who was crucified. This is its origin in the Gospel of Barnabas, one of the disciples of the Apostles. This agrees with the first possibility.

It is said that Pilate, governor of Palestine, was asked in Rome about the matter of the killing and crucifixion of 'Isa, and he answered that he had no knowledge of anything in this matter. By this the confusion of people concerning whether his killing and crucifixion occurred was strengthened, and it did not occur; the Jews only fabricated the report. This agrees with the second possibility.

What must be believed, by the text of the Qur'an, is that the Messiah was neither killed nor crucified, and that Allah raised him to Himself and saved him from those who sought him. As for everything beyond that, the matter is open to possibility. The discussion of his raising was mentioned earlier in the saying of the Exalted, "﴿Indeed, I will take you and raise you to Myself﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 55]," in Surah Aal 'Imran.

His statement "﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning him are in doubt about it﴾ [An-Nisa: 157]" indicates that there was disagreement about the matter of the killing of the Messiah. The disagreement about it exists among the Christians: most of them say, "The Jews killed him," while some of them say, "The Jews did not kill him, but they killed Yahudha al-Iskhariyuti, who was made to resemble the Messiah for them." This belief is recorded in the Gospel of Barnabas, which the Church today regards as a corrupted book. The meaning is that most of the Christians who differ concerning him do not believe in his crucifixion. Rather, doubt stirs within their souls, and they pretend to certainty, but it is not certainty. "﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾." Here the word "assumption" means doubt. Assumption has been used in this sense in many places in the speech of the Arabs, and in the Qur'an: "﴿Indeed, some assumption is sin﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 12]," and in the authentic hadith: "Beware of assumption, for assumption is the most false of speech." So the exception in the saying "except the following of assumption" is *munqati'* (disjunctive, not of the same kind as what precedes), like the verse of Nabigha:

*I swore an oath, not one open to reservation, and there is no knowledge except a good opinion of my companion.*

﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ وكانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا﴾ [And they did not kill him for certain. Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself. And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.]

It is permissible that this be coordinated (ma‘tuf) with His saying ﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ وما صَلَبُوهُ﴾ [And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him], and it is permissible that it be coordinated with His saying ﴿ما لَهم بِهِ مِن عِلْمٍ﴾ [They have no knowledge of it].

Al-yaqin (certainty): the firm knowledge that admits no doubt. It is an ism masdar (a noun functioning as a verbal noun). The masdar is al-yaqan with a vowelled middle letter, and it is said: yaqina, like fariha, yayqanu yaqanan. This masdar is rarely used. It is also said: ayqana yuqinu iqanan, and this is the common usage.

[صفحة ٢٣ / Page 23]

His saying (﴿يَقِينًا﴾) may be in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf‘ul al-mutlaq, the cognate object) that emphasises the content of a preceding clause. This is because the content of (﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا﴾), following His saying (﴿وقَوْلِهِمْ إنّا قَتَلْنا المَسِيحَ﴾) up to His saying ﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ وما صَلَبُوهُ ولَكِنْ شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ﴾ [But it was made to appear so to them], indicates that the negation of their killing him is a matter that is certain. Thus it is correct that yaqinan be an emphasis of this content.

It is also correct that it be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the waw in qatalūhu, meaning: they did not kill him while they were certain of his killing. In this case the negation falls upon both the condition and the conditioned together, by the indication of His saying before it (﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ وما صَلَبُوهُ﴾). That is: in their claim of having killed him, they were not certain of it, because of the confusion that arose concerning his person when those who seized him took hold of him. On this reading, the killing is used in its literal sense.

The object pronoun in qatalūhu refers to ‘Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him).

It is also permissible that qatl (killing) be used figuratively to mean gaining control over a thing and overcoming it, as in their saying: qatala al-khamr (he killed the wine), when he mixed it until he removed its strength, and their saying: qatala ardan ‘alimuha (he killed a land, whose knower...), meaning he thoroughly mastered its knowledge. From the poetry of the Hamasa (the anthology of Abu Tammam) in the chapter on satire:

"Its bodies startle you, of Sa‘d ibn ‘Amr, and you come to shun it when you have tested it by experience (khubr)."

And the saying of the poet:

"Thus do the knowing women tell of it, and I have, by my knowledge, surely mastered that certainty (yaqanan)."

And the saying of another:

"The days overcame me when I overcame them by experience; so I see a slayer who has been slain."

The object pronoun in qatalūhu may refer to the knowledge in His saying ﴿ما لَهم بِهِ مِن عِلْمٍ﴾ [They have no knowledge of it]. In that case (﴿يَقِينًا﴾) is, on this reading, a specifier (tamyiz) for the relation of qatalūhu.

Because of all this, the refutation follows with His saying ﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾ [Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself], meaning: they did not gain possession of him. Raf‘ (raising) means removing him far from this world to the world of the heavens. The particle (إلى) [ila, "to"] here expresses figurative limit, in the sense of honour. That is, Allah raised him with a raising of nearness and closeness.

[صفحة ٢٤ / Page 24]

The discussion of the meaning of this raising has already been covered, and of the disagreement over whether ‘Isa (peace be upon him) remained alive or whether Allah caused him to die, at His saying ﴿إنِّي مُتَوَفِّيكَ ورافِعُكَ إلَيَّ﴾ [Indeed, I will take you and raise you to Myself] [Al ‘Imran: 55] in Surat Al ‘Imran.

The concluding phrase ﴿وكانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا﴾ [And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise] is clearly appropriate in its placement, because when He is Mighty, it is fitting that by His might He honours His allies. And since He is Wise, He has perfected the making of this raising, so He made it a trial for the disbelievers, a insight for the believers, and a punishment for Yahudha (Judas) the traitor.

﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ وكانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا﴾ [And they did not kill him for certain. Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself. And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.]

It is permissible that this be coordinated (ma‘tuf) with His saying ﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ وما صَلَبُوهُ﴾ [And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him], and it is permissible that it be coordinated with His saying ﴿ما لَهم بِهِ مِن عِلْمٍ﴾ [They have no knowledge of it].

Al-yaqin (certainty): the firm knowledge that admits no doubt. It is an ism masdar (a noun functioning as a verbal noun). The masdar is al-yaqan with a vowelled middle letter, and it is said: yaqina, like fariha, yayqanu yaqanan. This masdar is rarely used. It is also said: ayqana yuqinu iqanan, and this is the common usage.

[صفحة ٢٣ / Page 23]

His saying (﴿يَقِينًا﴾) may be in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf‘ul al-mutlaq, the cognate object) that emphasises the content of a preceding clause. This is because the content of (﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا﴾), following His saying (﴿وقَوْلِهِمْ إنّا قَتَلْنا المَسِيحَ﴾) up to His saying ﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ وما صَلَبُوهُ ولَكِنْ شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ﴾ [But it was made to appear so to them], indicates that the negation of their killing him is a matter that is certain. Thus it is correct that yaqinan be an emphasis of this content.

It is also correct that it be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the waw in qatalūhu, meaning: they did not kill him while they were certain of his killing. In this case the negation falls upon both the condition and the conditioned together, by the indication of His saying before it (﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ وما صَلَبُوهُ﴾). That is: in their claim of having killed him, they were not certain of it, because of the confusion that arose concerning his person when those who seized him took hold of him. On this reading, the killing is used in its literal sense.

The object pronoun in qatalūhu refers to ‘Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him).

It is also permissible that qatl (killing) be used figuratively to mean gaining control over a thing and overcoming it, as in their saying: qatala al-khamr (he killed the wine), when he mixed it until he removed its strength, and their saying: qatala ardan ‘alimuha (he killed a land, whose knower...), meaning he thoroughly mastered its knowledge. From the poetry of the Hamasa (the anthology of Abu Tammam) in the chapter on satire:

"Its bodies startle you, of Sa‘d ibn ‘Amr, and you come to shun it when you have tested it by experience (khubr)."

And the saying of the poet:

"Thus do the knowing women tell of it, and I have, by my knowledge, surely mastered that certainty (yaqanan)."

And the saying of another:

"The days overcame me when I overcame them by experience; so I see a slayer who has been slain."

The object pronoun in qatalūhu may refer to the knowledge in His saying ﴿ما لَهم بِهِ مِن عِلْمٍ﴾ [They have no knowledge of it]. In that case (﴿يَقِينًا﴾) is, on this reading, a specifier (tamyiz) for the relation of qatalūhu.

Because of all this, the refutation follows with His saying ﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾ [Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself], meaning: they did not gain possession of him. Raf‘ (raising) means removing him far from this world to the world of the heavens. The particle (إلى) [ila, "to"] here expresses figurative limit, in the sense of honour. That is, Allah raised him with a raising of nearness and closeness.

[صفحة ٢٤ / Page 24]

The discussion of the meaning of this raising has already been covered, and of the disagreement over whether ‘Isa (peace be upon him) remained alive or whether Allah caused him to die, at His saying ﴿إنِّي مُتَوَفِّيكَ ورافِعُكَ إلَيَّ﴾ [Indeed, I will take you and raise you to Myself] [Al ‘Imran: 55] in Surat Al ‘Imran.

And since He is Wise, He has perfected the making of this raising, so He made it a trial for the disbelievers, a insight for the believers, and a punishment for Yahudha (Judas) the traitor.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 159:

﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the clause (wa-mā qatalūhu, "and they did not kill him"). This statement is a report about them, not a command to them, because the presence of the lam of emphasis (lam al-ibtidāʾ) in it calls out that it is informative (khabariyya). The particle (in) is negating, and (min ahl al-kitāb, "of the People of the Scripture") is a qualifier of an omitted noun whose estimated form is: aḥad ("anyone").

The pronoun in the genitive refers to ʿĪsā (Jesus): i.e., "he will surely believe in ʿĪsā." The pronoun in (mawtihi, "his death") may refer to one of the People of the Scripture, i.e., "before the People of the Scripture die," and this is supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: illā la-yuʾminunna bihi qabla mawtihim ("before their death"). The term People of the Scripture applies to the Jews and the Christians; as for the Christians, they already believe in ʿĪsā, so it is necessary that the intended meaning of the People of the Scripture be the Jews. The meaning is that the Jews, despite the intensity of their disbelief in ʿĪsā, none of them dies except that he believes in his prophethood before his death, i.e., this becomes evident to him at the time of approaching death before his soul departs. This is a favour from God upon ʿĪsā, since He made his enemies not leave the world except having believed in him, as a recompense to him for what he suffered from their denial, for he did not enjoy witnessing a community following him. It has been said: likewise the Christian, at his death, it becomes evident to him that ʿĪsā is the servant of God.

In my view, the pronoun in (bihi, "in him") refers to the lifting (al-rafʿ) derived from the verb (rafaʿahu Allāhu ilayh, "God raised him to Himself"), and the phrase (ahl al-kitāb) includes the Jews and the Christians, insofar as they are equal with the Jews in the belief that the crucifixion occurred.

Page 25
The apparent meaning is that God casts into the souls of the People of the Two Scriptures doubt concerning the validity of the crucifixion, so doubt continues to stir in their hearts and grows until it reaches the level of knowledge that the crucifixion was not valid, at the end of their lives, confirming what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, since he denied their reports and negated the crucifixion for ʿĪsā, peace be upon him.

It has been said that the pronoun in His saying (mawtihi) refers to ʿĪsā, i.e., "before the death of ʿĪsā." Those who held this view derived several consequences from it. Among them: his death will not occur except at the end of the world, so that the belief of all the People of the Scripture in him occurs before death takes place, because God made their belief future and made it before his death, so it follows that his death is future. Among them is what is reported in the hadith: that ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, will descend at the end of the period of the world so that the People of the Scripture believe in him. It is not hidden that the generality of His saying "﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture﴾" invalidates this interpretation, because those who believe in him according to this interpretation are those who will exist among the People of the Scripture, not all of them.

And (al-shahid) is the witness: he bears witness that he conveyed to them the call of their Lord and they turned away, and that the Christians altered (the message). The meaning of the verse is elaborated in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿On the Day when God gathers the Messengers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 109] and the verses that follow in Surat al-'Uqud.

[Page 26]

If the phrase "for their transgression" (﴿فَبِما نَقْضِهِمْ﴾ [An-Nisa 155]) is governed by a omitted element (mutaʿalliq mahdhuf) according to one of the two possibilities mentioned earlier, then his statement "for an injustice" (فَبِظُلْمٍ) is a consequence built upon the whole collection of their previous crimes. In that case, "their injustice" refers to another injustice, other than what was enumerated before. If, however, his statement "for their transgression" is attached to his statement "We forbade them" (﴿حَرَّمْنا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾), then his statement "for an injustice" and what follows is a corresponding substitute (badal muṭābiq) for the clause "for their breaking their covenant" (﴿فَبِما نَقْضِهِمْ مِيثاقَهُمْ﴾ [An-Nisa 155]), with the governing element repeated in the substitute because of the long separation. The benefit of this phrase is to make clear its connection to his statement "We forbade them good things" (﴿حَرَّمْنا عَلَيْهِمْ طَيِّباتٍ﴾), since the distance between it and its referent, namely his statement "for their breaking their covenant" (﴿فَبِما نَقْضِهِمْ مِيثاقَهُمْ﴾ [An-Nisa 155]), had grown, so that the connection of the speech be strengthened. In the substitute clause, a term comprehensive of the substituted element and what is joined to it was used, because breaking the covenant, disbelief, killing the prophets, their saying "our hearts are closed" (ghulf), their slandering of Maryam with a great calumny, and their saying "we killed the Messiah," all of these are injustice. So the last clause serves as a summary (fadhlaka) of what preceded, as if it were said: "For all of that We forbade them," but he turned to the word "injustice" because it is more varied in style and more beneficial than using a demonstrative noun.

This has been explained shortly before, at his statement, exalted is He, "for their transgression" (﴿فَبِما نَقْضِهِمْ﴾ [An-Nisa 155]).

It is also possible that it is another injustice that the Qur'an summarized.

The indefinite form of "injustice" (ظُلْمٍ) is for magnifying it, and the departure from saying "for their injustice," so that the pronouns come in succession from his statement "for their breaking their covenant and their disbelief" (﴿فَبِما نَقْضِهِمْ مِيثاقَهم وكُفْرِهِمْ﴾ [An-Nisa 155]) to its end, to the apparent noun, which is "those who were Jews" (الَّذِينَ هادُوا), is due to the distance of the pronoun in the clause that is substituted, which is "for their transgression" (﴿فَبِما نَقْضِهِمْ﴾ [An-Nisa 155]). And also because in the relative pronoun and its relative clause there is what requires their being free from injustice, if they were as they described themselves, when they said "we have turned to You" (﴿إنّا هُدْنا إلَيْكَ﴾ [Al-A'raf 156]). Therefore, the emergence of injustice from "those who were Jews" is a matter of surprise.

The verse implies that the forbidding of what was forbidden to them was only a punishment for them, and that those prohibited things did not contain such harms as would require forbidding their consumption; otherwise they would have been forbidden to them from the very beginning of the coming of the Law. It has been said that what is meant by these "good things" is what is mentioned in His statement, exalted is He: "And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws, and of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat" (Al-An'am 146), up to His statement: "That was a recompense We gave them for their rebellion" (Al-An'am 146) in Surat al-An'am. So this is the recompense for their injustice.

[Page 27]

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) reported in his commentary on the verse in Surat al-An'am that 'Abd al-Jabbar said: the prohibition itself cannot be a punishment for a crime committed by them, because obligation (taklif) is an exposure to reward, and exposure to reward is a favor, so it is not permissible for obligation to be a requital for a crime. Al-Fakhr said: the answer is that the prevention from benefiting may be for the purpose of earning reward, and it may be for the crime.

This answer is a begging of the question (muṣādara). What strengthens the difficulty is that punishment, by its nature, should be restricted to the criminals and then abrogated. What appears to me in the answer is this: either the cause of forbidding those good things is that what spread in their natures, because of their transgression and injustice, of hardness became a natural trait in their temperaments, so it required that God soften their natures by forbidding foods whose nature is to thicken dispositions; and for this reason, when 'Isa came to them, God permitted them some of what had been forbidden to them of that, since the cause of the prohibition had ceased. Or the forbidding of what was forbidden to them was a punishment for those who were unjust and rebellious, and then that remained upon those who came after them, so that it would be a reminder (dhikra) for them and so that the first ones would have a bad reputation, in the manner of His statement: "And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have wronged" (Al-Anfal 25), and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish killing." Or, because this prohibition is a worldly punishment that returns to deprivation of good things, so we do not consider what may occur to this prohibition at times of reward for the intention of obeying the prohibition, because such intention is rare in abstention.

As for their "hindering from the way of God" (وصَدُّهم عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ): if it is the intransitive verb's infinitive of ṣadda, whose present tense is yaṣiddu with a kasra on the ṣād, then the meaning is "by their turning away from the way of God." But if it is the infinitive of the transitive verb, whose analogical present is with a ḍamma on the ṣād, then perhaps they used to hinder the people from piety, saying: "We will be forgiven," from the time of Musa, before some good things were forbidden to them. After Musa, they hindered the people greatly, opposed the prophets, pressed them to conceal the admonitions, denied 'Isa, opposed the call of Muhammad ﷺ, and beautified for many of the people, openly or hypocritically, remaining in the state of ignorance, as was mentioned in

[Page 28]

His statement: "Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, who believe in jibt and taghut?" (An-Nisa 51), and what follows from the verses. For this reason, "greatly" (كَثِيرًا) is described as a state (ḥāl) of it.

As for their "taking usury, though they were forbidden it" (وأخْذُهُمُ الرِّبا الَّذِي نُهُوا عَنْهُ): it is that they took it from their own people specifically, and it was permissible for them to take it from non-Israelites, as in the chapter of the Book of Deuteronomy: "You shall not lend upon interest to your brother: interest on money, interest on food, interest on anything that is lent upon interest. To the foreigner you may lend upon interest."

Usury was forbidden to them by the explicit text of the Torah in the Book of Exodus, in the chapter: "If you lend money to My poor people who are with you, you shall not be to him as a usurer; do not impose upon him interest."

Their "eating the wealth of the people unjustly" (وأكْلُهم أمْوالَ النّاسِ بِالباطِلِ) is more general than usury, so it includes the bribe that was forbidden among them, and their taking ransom for captives from their own people, and other things.

The concessive transition (istidrak) with His statement "But those firm in knowledge among them" (﴿لَكِنِ الرّاسِخُونَ في العِلْمِ﴾) and so on arises from what the preceding speech may suggest from its beginning at His statement "The People of the Book ask you" (﴿يَسْألُكَ أهْلُ الكِتابِ﴾ [An-Nisa 153]), from their going deep into error, so that no good or righteousness is hoped for from any of them. So it was corrected: those firm in knowledge among them are not as was imagined; they believe in the Qur'an, like 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq.

The "firm" (al-rāsikh) in its basic meaning is one firm of foot in walking, who does not waver; and it is borrowed for the establishment of an attribute, such as knowledge, in such a way that doubts do not deceive him. This was mentioned earlier at His statement "And none knows its interpretation except God, and those firm in knowledge" (﴿وما يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ إلّا اللَّهُ والرّاسِخُونَ في العِلْمِ﴾ [Ali 'Imran 7]) in Surat Ali 'Imran.

The one firm in knowledge is far from over-elaboration and from obstinate hostility, so there is no barrier between him and the truth; they recognize the proofs of the truthfulness of the prophets and do not ask them for miracles that break the customary order.

The conjunction of "the believers" (المُؤْمِنُونَ) with "those firm" (الرّاسِخُونَ) is a praise of them, that they did not ask their Prophet to show them signs that break the customary order. Therefore he said "believe" (يُؤْمِنُونَ), that is, all of them, "in what was sent down to you" (﴿بِما أُنْزِلَ إلَيْكَ﴾), that is the Qur'an, which is sufficient for them as a sign, "and what was sent down before you" (﴿وما أُنْزِلَ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾) to the messengers, and they do not oppose the messengers of God out of partisanship and zeal.

[Page 29]

What is meant by "the believers" in His statement "and the believers" (والمُؤْمِنُونَ) are those whom God guided to faith from among the People of the Book, who were not among the firm in knowledge among them, like the Jew who used to serve the Messenger of God ﷺ and believed in him.

The conjunction of "those who establish" (المُقِيمِينَ) in the accusative case is established in the Imam Mushaf (the standard codex), and the Muslims in the regions read it without a change; from this we know that it is an Arabic method in conjoining nouns that indicate praiseworthy attributes to their like, so it is permissible in some conjoined words to use the accusative to single out for praise, and the nominative by resumption (istiʾnaf) for emphasis, as they did with successive descriptive attributes, whether without conjunction or with conjunction, like His statement: "But righteousness is in one who believes in God..." (﴿ولَكِنَّ البِرَّ مَن آمَنَ﴾ [Al-Baqara 177]) up to His statement "and the patient" (والصّابِرِينَ). Sibawayh said in his book, in the chapter "What is put in the accusative for exaltation and praise": "If you wish, you make it a description and it follows the first; if you wish, you break it off and begin it." He mentioned, of the same kind as what we are dealing with, this verse, and said: "If all of it were in the nominative it would be good," and similar to it is His statement: "And those who fulfill their covenant when they make it, and the patient in hardship and adversity" (Al-Baqara 177). The like of it is the saying of al-Khirniq:

"Let not my people be without harm, those who are the poison of enemies and the bane of the ruined..."

"The alighting ones in every battlefield, and the good ones at the knots of the waistcloths."

In the transmission of Yunus from the Arabs: the nominative for "the alighting ones" and the accusative for "the good ones," so that it would be like this verse. It appears that this is among what happens intentionally for variety when successive conjunctions are repeated, and for this reason it occurs repeatedly in the Qur'an in successive conjunctions, as in Surat al-Baqara and in this verse, and in His statement "and the sabians" in Surat al-Ma'ida.

It is narrated from 'A'isha and Aban ibn 'Uthman that the accusative of "those who establish" is an error from the scribe of the Mushaf, and they counted this verse among the errors, and His statement "But righteousness is in one who believes in God" (Al-Baqara 177) up to "and the patient in hardship" (Al-Baqara 177), and His statement "Indeed, these two are sorcerers" (﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾ [Ta-Ha 63]), and His statement "and the sabians" in Surat al-Ma'ida. 'A'isha, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, al-Jahdari, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read it as "those who establish" in the nominative. The reading of the majority, which is agreed upon, is not to be rejected by an irregular reading.

[Page 30]

Some people claimed that the accusative of "those who establish" and similar words is the manifestation of the interpretation of 'Uthman's statement to the scribes of the Mushafs, when they completed them and read them, that he said to them: "You have done well and beautifully, and I see a slight error that the Arabs will correct with their tongues." These are fancies and reports that were not authentically transmitted from those to whom they are attributed. It is very far-fetched that a scribe of the Mushaf would make an error in one word among its like and make it an error alone without its predecessor or follower, and even more remote is that the error should come in a group of similar words, which are those whose i'rab is by letters that substitute for the vowel marks of case in the dual and the sound plural. I do not think what was narrated from 'A'isha and Aban ibn 'Uthman about this is sound. I have known the Arabic justification in conjunctions, and as for the Arabic justification of "Indeed, these two are sorcerers" (﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾ [Ta-Ha 63]), it will come when discussing Surat Ta-Ha.

It appears that the interpretation of 'Uthman's statement is what occurred in the orthography of the Mushaf of the kind of omitted alifs. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "They were far more eager in zeal for Islam and in defending it against accusations than to leave in the Book of God a breach that those after them would have to mend, or a tear that those who come after them would have to patch." The like of this has been mentioned earlier at His statement "and the patient in hardship and adversity" (Al-Baqara 177) in Surat al-Baqara.

The promise of a great reward regarding the firm among the People of the Book is because they believed in their own messenger and in Muhammad ﷺ; and it has come in the sound hadith that they have two rewards. And regarding the believers from the Arabs, it is because they preceded others in faith. The majority read "We will give them" (سَنُؤْتِيهِمْ) with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness), and Hamza and Khalaf read it with the third-person yā', and the pronoun refers to the Name of Majesty in His statement "and the believers in God" (﴿والمُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ﴾).

This answer is a begging of the question (muṣādara). What strengthens the difficulty is that punishment, by its nature, should be restricted to the criminals and then abrogated. What appears to me in the answer is this: either the cause of forbidding those good things is that what spread in their natures, because of their transgression and injustice, of hardness became a natural trait in their temperaments, so it required that God soften their natures by forbidding foods whose nature is to thicken dispositions; and for this reason, when 'Isa came to them, God permitted them some of what had been forbidden to them of that, since the cause of the prohibition had ceased. Or the forbidding of what was forbidden to them was a punishment for those who were unjust and rebellious, and then that remained upon those who came after them, so that it would be a reminder (dhikra) for them and so that the first ones would have a bad reputation, in the manner of His statement: "And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have wronged" (Al-Anfal 25), and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish killing." Or, because this prohibition is a worldly punishment that returns to deprivation of good things, so we do not consider what may occur to this prohibition at times of reward for the intention of obeying the prohibition, because such intention is rare in abstention.

But if it is the infinitive of the transitive verb, whose analogical present is with a ḍamma on the ṣād, then perhaps they used to hinder the people from piety, saying: "We will be forgiven," from the time of Musa, before some good things were forbidden to them. After Musa, they hindered the people greatly, opposed the prophets, pressed them to conceal the admonitions, denied 'Isa, opposed the call of Muhammad ﷺ, and beautified for many of the people, openly or hypocritically, remaining in the state of ignorance, as was mentioned in

[Page 28]

His statement: "Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, who believe in jibt and taghut?" (An-Nisa 51), and what follows from the verses. For this reason, "greatly" (كَثِيرًا) is described as a state (ḥāl) of it.

The "firm" (al-rāsikh) in its basic meaning is one firm of foot in walking, who does not waver; and it is borrowed for the establishment of an attribute, such as knowledge, in such a way that doubts do not deceive him. [Page 29]

What is meant by "the believers" in His statement "and the believers" (والمُؤْمِنُونَ) are those whom God guided to faith from among the People of the Book, who were not among the firm in knowledge among them, like the Jew who used to serve the Messenger of God ﷺ and believed in him.

The conjunction of "those who establish" (المُقِيمِينَ) in the accusative case is established in the Imam Mushaf (the standard codex), and the Muslims in the regions read it without a change; from this we know that it is an Arabic method in conjoining nouns that indicate praiseworthy attributes to their like, so it is permissible in some conjoined words to use the accusative to single out for praise, and the nominative by resumption (istiʾnaf) for emphasis, as they did with successive descriptive attributes, whether without conjunction or with conjunction, like His statement: "But righteousness is in one who believes in God..." (﴿ولَكِنَّ البِرَّ مَن آمَنَ﴾ [Al-Baqara 177]) up to His statement "and the patient" (والصّابِرِينَ). Sibawayh said in his book, in the chapter "What is put in the accusative for exaltation and praise": "If you wish, you make it a description and it follows the first; if you wish, you break it off and begin it." He mentioned, of the same kind as what we are dealing with, this verse, and said: "If all of it were in the nominative it would be good," and similar to it is His statement: "And those who fulfill their covenant when they make it, and the patient in hardship and adversity" (Al-Baqara 177). The like of it is the saying of al-Khirniq:

"Let not my people be without harm, those who are the poison of enemies and the bane of the ruined..."

"The alighting ones in every battlefield, and the good ones at the knots of the waistcloths."

In the transmission of Yunus from the Arabs: the nominative for "the alighting ones" and the accusative for "the good ones," so that it would be like this verse. It appears that this is among what happens intentionally for variety when successive conjunctions are repeated, and for this reason it occurs repeatedly in the Qur'an in successive conjunctions, as in Surat al-Baqara and in this verse, and in His statement "and the sabians" in Surat al-Ma'ida.

It is narrated from 'A'isha and Aban ibn 'Uthman that the accusative of "those who establish" is an error from the scribe of the Mushaf, and they counted this verse among the errors, and His statement "But righteousness is in one who believes in God" (Al-Baqara 177) up to "and the patient in hardship" (Al-Baqara 177), and His statement "Indeed, these two are sorcerers" (﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾ [Ta-Ha 63]), and His statement "and the sabians" in Surat al-Ma'ida. 'A'isha, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, al-Jahdari, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read it as "those who establish" in the nominative. The reading of the majority, which is agreed upon, is not to be rejected by an irregular reading.

[Page 30]

Some people claimed that the accusative of "those who establish" and similar words is the manifestation of the interpretation of 'Uthman's statement to the scribes of the Mushafs, when they completed them and read them, that he said to them: "You have done well and beautifully, and I see a slight error that the Arabs will correct with their tongues." These are fancies and reports that were not authentically transmitted from those to whom they are attributed. It is very far-fetched that a scribe of the Mushaf would make an error in one word among its like and make it an error alone without its predecessor or follower, and even more remote is that the error should come in a group of similar words, which are those whose i'rab is by letters that substitute for the vowel marks of case in the dual and the sound plural. I do not think what was narrated from 'A'isha and Aban ibn 'Uthman about this is sound. I have known the Arabic justification in conjunctions, and as for the Arabic justification of "Indeed, these two are sorcerers" (﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾ [Ta-Ha 63]), it will come when discussing Surat Ta-Ha.

It appears that the interpretation of 'Uthman's statement is what occurred in the orthography of the Mushaf of the kind of omitted alifs. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "They were far more eager in zeal for Islam and in defending it against accusations than to leave in the Book of God a breach that those after them would have to mend, or a tear that those who come after them would have to patch." The like of this has been mentioned earlier at His statement "and the patient in hardship and adversity" (Al-Baqara 177) in Surat al-Baqara.

And regarding the believers from the Arabs, it is because they preceded others in faith. The majority read "We will give them" (سَنُؤْتِيهِمْ) with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness), and Hamza and Khalaf read it with the third-person yā', and the pronoun refers to the Name of Majesty in His statement "and the believers in God" (﴿والمُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ﴾).

In the substitute clause, a term comprehensive of the substituted element and what is joined to it was used, because breaking the covenant, disbelief, killing the prophets, their saying "our hearts are closed" (ghulf), their slandering of Maryam with a great calumny, and their saying "we killed the Messiah," all of these are injustice. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 163–165 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms.﴾ ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾ ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and as warners, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾

Page 31

These verses resume the response to the Jews' demand that a book be sent down to them from heaven, after they had been foolish in this matter, following the folly of their forefathers, with His saying ﴿For they had asked Moses for something greater than that﴾ [an-Nisa': 153]. Between the two, sentences concerning the opposition of their forefathers and what befell them as a consequence were interposed. Now He turns to explain that the sending down of the Qur'an upon Muhammad ﷺ was not an innovation, for it is the way of revelation to the messengers. Thus, the fact that no book was sent down to them from heaven did not discredit their messengerhood.

The emphasis with inna is either for the importance of this report, or to place those being refuted in the position of one who denies the manner of revelation to messengers other than Moses, since they did not act in accordance with the requirement of their knowledge, to the point that they denied the messengerhood of a messenger to whom no book had been sent down from heaven.

Revelation (wahy) is the conveying of a meaning by a way other than speech, such as a sign. Allah says: ﴿So he came out to his people from the sanctuary and signalled to them to glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 11]. Dawud ibn Jarir said:
They throw at [us] long sermons, and at times the revelation of glances, for fear of the watchers.

The comparison in His saying ﴿As We revealed to Noah﴾ is a comparison with the genus of revelation, even though its types differ. Revelation to the Prophet ﷺ occurred in various kinds, whose explanation is recorded in the hadith of 'A'isha in the Sahih, concerning al-Harith ibn Hisham's question to the Prophet ﷺ: "How does revelation come to you?" This differs from revelation to others whom Allah named, for some of its types may be conceivable for them. Moreover, revelation to the Prophet ﷺ included the Book, the Qur'an, whereas some of those mentioned with him had no book.

Here Allah enumerated a group of prophets and messengers and mentioned that He revealed to them, and the scholars did not differ that messengers and prophets are revealed to.

Page 32

The scholars' expressions differed only regarding the meaning of "messenger" and "prophet." In the statements of a group of our scholars we find no distinction, and that every prophet is a messenger, because revelation is made to him with something which does not fail to be conveyed, even if only to his household. The condition of a messenger may begin with prophethood, followed afterwards by his being sent, so that prophethood is a preparation for messengerhood, as was the case at the beginning of revelation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for he informed Khadija, and there descended upon him ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 214].

The correct view is that the messenger is more specific: he is one to whom revelation is made together with a command to convey, whereas the prophet is not commanded to convey, although he may convey by way of enjoining good and calling to good, meaning without warning and giving good news. Some hadiths state: "The prophets are one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and the number of messengers is three hundred and thirteen messengers." In the hadith of intercession in the Sahih it is recorded: "Noah, peace be upon him, is the first of the messengers." The verses of the Qur'an indicate that religion was known in the time of Adam and that recompense was known to them. The two sons of Adam offered an offering, and one said to the other: ﴿Allah only accepts from the righteous﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27], and he said to him ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 28] ﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and thus be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 29].

It indicates that there was not, at that time, among them anyone who would restrain the transgressor or give justice to the weak against the strong; rather, what they had learned was the method of admonition and instruction, and it was a familial mission.

Noah is the first of the messengers, and he is Noah son of Lamech. The Arabs say: Lamak son of Mutushalakh son of Akhnukh. The Egyptians call him Hermes, and the Arabs call him Idris son of Yard son of Mahalalel son of Qenan son of Anush son of Shith son of Adam, according to the words of the Torah. In his time the great Flood occurred. He lived nine hundred and fifty years, and it is said nine hundred and ninety years, and the Qur'an confirmed that. Noah died three thousand and nine hundred and seventy years before the Hijra, according to the reckoning of the Jews derived from their book.

Abraham is the Friend (al-Khalil), Abraham son of Terah, and the Arabs call him Azar son of Nahur son of Saruch son of Ar'u son of Falegh son of Eber son of Shelah son of Qenan son of Arphaxad son of Sam son of Noah. He was born in the year 2893 before the Hijra, in the land of Ur of the Chaldeans, and died in the land of the Canaanites, which is Syria, in Hebron, where his tomb now is, known as the city of al-Khalil, in the year 2718 before the Hijra.

Allah said: ﴿And mention in the Book Ishmael; he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 54].

Isaac is the son of Abraham by Sarah, his paternal cousin. He died before the Hijra in the year 2613. Isaac was a prophet confirming the law of his father Abraham and did not bring a law.

The Descendants (al-Asbat) are the descendants of Isaac, i.e., his grandchildren, and they are the twelve sons of Jacob: Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin, Manasseh, Dan, Asher, and Naphtali. As for the rest of the Descendants, each of them was a caller to the law of Abraham among his sons and people. Revelation to these varied.

It is said that he was a hundred years before Abraham.

The correct view is that he was after Abraham and before Moses, in the fifteenth century before Christ, that is, in the twenty-first century before the Hijra. It is said that the book attributed to him in the books of the Jews originally was composed in the Arabic language, and that Moses, peace be upon him, transferred it into Hebrew as an admonition. Therefore many researchers in history think that Job was from an Arab tribe. This is not far-fetched. Job was a messenger and a prophet. He had a companion named Elihu the Yemenite, who strengthened him in patience, as we shall mention in its place. His name was not declined because he was not from the Arabs of the Hijaz or Najd; for the Arabs regarded distant tribes as non-Arab, even if their origin was Arab, and for this reason they did not decline the name of Thamud when they dwelt in al-Hijr.

David, father of Solomon, is David son of Jesse. He died in the year 1626 before the Hijra. It is a verbal noun on the pattern fa'ul, like qabul. It is also said zubur with a damma on the zay, meaning a verbal noun like shukur; its meaning is writing, and the written thing is called zabur, plural zubur. Allah said: ﴿With clear proofs and scriptures﴾ [Al 'Imran: 184]. It has become, by dominance in the Arabic language, a proper name for the book of the Prophet David, and it is one of the books of the Holy Bible among the Jews.

The clause ﴿And to David We gave the Psalms﴾ is conjoined to (We revealed to you). The name David was not conjoined to the rest of the names mentioned before it, to hint that the Psalms was revealed in being a book.

Al-Jumhur read (zabura) with a fatha on the zay, and Hamza and Khalaf read it with a damma on the zay.

His saying ﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾ means in the verses of the Qur'an, such as: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Zechariah, John, Elias, Elisha, Lot, and Tubba'. His saying ﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾ means He did not mention them in the Qur'an. Among them are those whose mention does not occur in the Sunnah, such as Handhala ibn Safwan, prophet of the People of the Rass, and such as some of the sages of the Greeks according to some scholars of wisdom. Al-Suhrawardi said in Hikmat al-Ishraq: among them are the people of the embassy. Among them are those whom the Sunnah mentioned, such as Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi.

Allah mentioned here the prophets who were well known among the Children of Israel, because the purpose is to argue with them. Allah left out relating to the Prophet ﷺ the names of many messengers, being content with those He related to him, because those mentioned are the greatest of messengers and prophets in lessons-bearing narratives.

His saying ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾ changes the style, turning away from conjunction to mentioning another verb, because this kind of revelation has added importance, and it, with that distinction, is not the sending down of a book from heaven. So if there is no lesson except in sending down a book from heaven according to their demand, then what is other than the Ten Words inscribed on the tablets given to Moses, peace be upon him, is also invalidated.

The speech of Allah the Exalted is, according to us, an independent attribute. It concerns conveying the will of Allah to the angels and messengers, and this has been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) in the speech of the prophets and messengers, a transmission that is established

Page 36

among all the adherents of the religions. The speech of God (kalam Allah) is an attribute of Him established by revelation (al-shar'). On careful examination, rational proof does not establish it, since rational arguments do not show that God is obligated to convey His purpose to people. Rather, it is permissible for Him to bring existents into being and then leave them to their own affairs, so His knowledge would not be connected to driving them toward performing good deeds and avoiding their evils. Do you not see that He created the animals without commanding or forbidding them? Had He left people in disorder like the animals, that would not have been impossible.

And when He wishes to direct created beings toward something He desires, He originates them upon it, and they are drawn to it by their innate natures, as He made the bee to produce honey and trees to bear fruit. Had He willed, He could likewise have directed people to a nature from which they could not deviate. But since we know that He is All-Knowing and All-Wise, and knowledge requires the unveiling of the realities of things as they are in His sight, He knows the goodness and ugliness of actions, desires the attainment of benefits and the removal of harms, is pleased with the former and dislikes the latter. Since His wisdom and will required that He make humankind capable of learning and of righteousness, and made human intellects fit to reach the ultimate ends of good and of evil and to diversify in both, unlike the animal, which attains, in what it is created for, whether good or evil, only to a limit upon which it was originated and beyond which it does not go, it was to be expected that evil would prevail over good through the works of the faction of wicked people among mankind. It was then a requirement of wisdom that He direct people to doing the good He is pleased with and abandoning the evil He hates. Guiding them to this may occur through creating the excellent among people and innately disposing them to righteousness and goodness, so that they become callers to mankind. But the wisdom and grace of God required that He create the righteous who are receptive to good, and that He assist them in reaching what they were disposed to, through His guidance and direction. So He created souls receptive to prophethood and messengership and supported them with guidance indicating His purpose, expressed by revelation (wahy), as His saying, may He be exalted, requires: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. Thus He established messengership and the preparation of the messenger to accept it, and from here the attribute of speech is established.

We know from the mass-transmitted reports of the Shari'ah that God desired righteousness from mankind and commanded them to it, and that His command reached humankind across many eras. This indicates that God is pleased with some human actions and not pleased with others, and that this is called a precious speech (kalam nafis), and it is eternal (azali).

Then, the reality of the attribute of speech may be among the objects connected to the attribute of knowledge, or among the objects connected to the attribute of will, or an independent attribute distinct from the two others. [p. 37]

Some say: He knew the people's need for guidance, so He guided them; or He willed the guidance of the people, so He guided them. We say: divinity requires the establishment of the attributes of perfection, among which are good pleasure, displeasure, commanding and forbidding toward humans or angels. Thus there is established an independent attribute, namely the attribute of inner speech (kalam nafsi). All of this is close in meaning, and its detailed treatment belongs to the science of kalam (theology).

As for God's addressing (taklim) some of His servants among the angels or humans, it is the bringing into being of that by which the angel or messenger knows that God commands, forbids, or informs. So "addressing" is the connection of the attribute of speech to the one addressed, on the basis of making speech an independent attribute; or the connection of knowledge to conveying the known to the one addressed; or the connection of will to conveying the willed to the one addressed.

The Ash'ariyya said: God's addressing His servant is that He creates in the servant a perception through hearing by which he attains knowledge of God's speech, without letters or sounds. It has been illustrated that Moses heard something like thunder, from which he knew the meaning of the inner speech. I say: the Prophet (ﷺ) also illustrated it in the authentic hadith from Abu Hurayrah: "When God decrees a matter in heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon a smooth rock. When fear is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'" [Saba': 23]. According to this view, it is not necessary that what the messenger or angel hears be letters and sounds; rather it is a knowledge he attains through his hearing, connected to God's speech, and it is one of the connections of the attribute of inner speech to the speaker in what does not cease, so that connection is necessarily originated, like the connection of will.

The Mu'tazila said: God creates letters and sounds in the language of the Messenger, which the Messenger hears; he then knows, by a knowledge he finds in himself, that this came from God, and that it was sent to him from God, but not through an angel. They interpret it in the same way we interpret the descent of the Qur'an. Thus attributing speech to God is a metaphor in attribution according to their view, because God is exempt from letters and sounds. Speech in its literal sense is letters and sounds. This is sophistry in argument, for no one claims that the Essence, exalted be He, is characterized by letters and sounds. It is, according to us and according to them, other than the revelation that falls on the heart of the Messenger, and other than the conveyance that occurs through Jibril. It is what is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or from behind a veil﴾ [al-Shura: 51].

[p. 38]

As for God's speech that reaches the Messenger through an angel, which is expressed as the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms: these are words, letters and sounds, which God makes known to the angel in a manner we do not know, by which the angel knows that God, through the particular words cast to the angel, indicates the meanings of those words, so the angel casts them upon the Messenger as they are. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿or sends a messenger and reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 51], and He said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193], ﴿upon your heart, that you may be of the warners﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 194], ﴿in clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 195]. Concerning its being originated, no one who has a share of knowledge of religion doubts. However, some of the imams of Islam refrained from explicitly stating that it is originated, or that it is created, in assemblies of debate attended by the common people, or by the darkness of obstinacy and the eagerness to revile and harm. This was to avert misunderstanding, to preserve the attribution to Islam, and to disavow the rabble of the vulgar. So may God have mercy on souls that were tried, bodies that were hurt, and mouths that were silenced, who intended good, whether they were moderate or went to excess. God is the Reckoner of those who incited against them, gathered together, and provoked them, and evil is what they did.

His saying "addressing" (taklim) is a verbal noun (masdar) for emphasis (tawkid). Emphasis by the verbal noun returns to affirming and confirming the attribution, like "qad" and "inna". It is not intended to remove the possibility of metaphor. For this reason the Arabs emphasized with the verbal noun verbs that were used only metaphorically, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God only desires to remove from you the uncleanness, O people of the household, and to purify you with complete purification﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. He intended that He purifies them with spiritual purity, that is, perfection of the soul, so the emphasis did not serve to remove metaphor. Hind bint al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said, dispraising her husband Rawh ibn Zinba':

"The silk wept because of Rawh, and its skin denied it,
and the garments of Judham cried out with a loud cry."

But the crying is only metaphorical. So the verbal noun emphasizes, that is, it confirms the occurrence of the emphasized act in the meaning it had before the emphasis.

So the meaning of His saying "addressing" (taklaman) here is: Moses heard speech from God, in such a way that it is not possible that God sent Jibril to him with speech, or inspired it into his soul. As for the manner in which this speech issues from God's side, that is another matter, a field of disagreement among the sects. For this reason [p. 39]

the argument of many Ash'aris from this verse, that the speech Moses heard is the essential attribute subsisting in God, is a weak argument. Ibn 'Arafa related that al-Mazari said in his commentary on al-Talqin: this verse is a proof against the Mu'tazila in their saying that God did not address Moses directly, but through the creation of speech, because He emphasized it with the verbal noun. And that Ibn 'Abd al-Salam al-Tunisi, the teacher of Ibn 'Arafa, refuted this by saying that emphasis by the verbal noun serves to remove doubt about the report, not about the one who reports it. Ibn 'Arafa criticized him with what amounts to strengthening Ibn 'Abd al-Salam's refutation.

His saying "messengers" (rusulan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from those mentioned. He named them messengers for the reason we previously mentioned.
