It is a preparatory circumstantial (hal muwatti'ah) for its description, namely "bearers of good news and warners," because that is what is intended by the circumstantial.

His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ is a causal clause (ta'lil) for His saying "bearers of good news and warners." It cannot be taken as a cause for His saying ﴿We have revealed to you﴾, because that is directed toward explaining the validity of the message without the descent of a book from heaven, in response to their saying ﴿until you bring down upon us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra': 93]. So the placement of His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ is in the position of incidental inclusion (idmaj), teaching the community one of the wisdoms in God's sending of the messengers. Argument (hujjah) is what indicates the truthfulness of the claimant and the rightness of the one who makes an excuse, so it requires that one not be held accountable for sin or negligence. What is meant here is the clear excuse that necessitates disavowal of anger and punishment. So the sending of messengers is to cut off the excuse of mankind when they are questioned about their criminal deeds and deserve God's anger and punishment. From this it is known that people, before the sending of messengers, had an argument against God, that they could say: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs and be among the believers?﴾ [al-Qasas: 47].

The verse indicates that among people's actions are some that anger God and for which one is punished, namely the actions which sound intellects recognize as ugly because they lead to corruption and clear harms. The mode of this indication is that argument only opposes an attempt at some action; so when God sent the messengers to cut off argument, we know that when God sent the messengers He was about to hold accountable those to whom they were sent, and His mercy required that He cut off their argument by sending messengers, guiding them and warning them. For this reason He made the cutting off of argument the final cause of the good news and warning, since good news and warning only clarify the consequences of actions. That is why He did not give the reason for sending messengers as alerting to what pleases God and what angers Him.

[p. 40]

This verse thus obliges all the sects to hold that sending messengers is a precondition for being held accountable for sins, and its apparent sense is that all kinds of accountability depend upon it, whether the sins relate to belief or to action, and including the obligation of knowing God. Sending messengers, in our view, is part of God's complete justice, because if He had not sent them, punishment would have been mere absolute dominion, which the act of creating requires, since He is not questioned about what He does; yet it would have been justice in the broader sense.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 163–165 (part 3 of 3)**

As for the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the Sunni mainstream), whose positions are transmitted through the approach of al-Ash'ari (the Ash'ari school of theology), they generalized and said: no obligation is established, and no one is held accountable for abandoning or doing anything, except through the sending of the Messengers, including the knowledge of God, Exalted is He. They argued with this verse and others, such as ﴿We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15], and with consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement). However, there is scrutiny concerning the claim of consensus, there is a different scrutiny concerning using it as evidence for a foundation of religion, and there is a third scrutiny concerning using the verses, which are apparent (zawahir, texts with apparent meanings), as evidence for a foundation of religion. The exception would be if it were said that they are so numerous that they reach the level of certainty; but this too is open to debate. They are compelled to interpret this verse, because they hold that the people of the fatrah (the interval between prophets) are held accountable for their polytheism toward God.

The answer is to say: the word "Messengers" in the verse is a collective noun used distributively (kull ifradi), which applies to each single Messenger, and it varies according to the variation of the call. As for the call to the totality of faith and monotheism, it was established through the earlier Messengers, whose calls established, for human beings, the obligation of faith and monotheism. As for the call to the details of the signs and attributes and the branches of the sharia (the divine law), it is established through the coming of the Messengers who are specific to known nations.

As for the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilites), they established that good and evil are intrinsic (dhatiyyan) in the state in which no messenger has been sent. They said: reason establishes the obligation of many rulings and the prohibition of many, especially the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, because knowledge repels a presumed harm, which is the otherworldly harm of incurring punishment in the Hereafter, as a large number of people have reported it; and the fear of what results from the disagreement of sects over knowledge of the Creator before correct knowledge is worldly harm. Everything that repels a presumed or doubtful harm is obligatory by reason. Like someone who wants to take a road and is told that there is a predator on it: reason requires that he pause and investigate until he knows whether he should take that road or not. Likewise, it is obligatory to examine the miracle of the Messengers and all that leads to the establishment of the sharia. For this reason, they interpreted this verse in the way that al-Zamakhshari (author of al-Kashshaf) mentioned when he said: "If you ask, how can people have a proof against God before the Messengers, when they are held to account by the proofs God has set up, whose examination leads to knowledge, and the Messengers themselves did not reach knowledge by examining those proofs, i.e., before the prophethood?" I say: the Messengers are reminders against heedlessness and prompters to examination, together with conveying what they carried of the matters of religion and teaching the laws. Their sending was thus a removal of the excuse and a completion of the establishment of the proof. This means that the sending of the Messengers is a mercy from God, not a matter of justice; had He not sent them, holding people accountable for their vices would have been just. So the sending of the Messengers completes the proof regarding the very principle of accountability, and completes the proof regarding the increase in purification, so that people would not say: "Our Lord, why did You not guide us to what would raise our ranks among the sincere (siddiqin), and limit us to mere salvation from punishment, when we were guided to the principle of monotheism by our intellects?"

Al-Maturidi (the Maturidi school) agreed with the majority regarding everything except the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, when the intention is to silence the Messengers specifically, because he considered it the foundation of the principles of religion, as indicated by the words of Sadr al-Shari'ah in al-Tawdih: "That is, the act is a quality for which the doer of the act is praised and rewarded, or blamed and punished; because the obligation of affirming the Prophet, if it depended on the sharia, would lead to circularity (dawr)." He also explicitly stated that it is also known through the sharia.

The Mu'tazilah pressed the Ash'ari school on this matter, specifically regarding the obligation of knowledge. They said: if knowledge were not obligatory except through the sharia, it would necessarily lead to silencing the Messengers, and there would be no benefit in sending them. The basis of the necessity is that if a Messenger says to someone, "Look at my miracle until my truthfulness becomes clear to you," he can say: "I will not look, since it is not obligatory upon me, because abandoning what is not obligatory is permissible, and it is not obligatory upon me until the obligation is established for me through the sharia, and the sharia is not established as long as I have not looked, because the establishment of the sharia is theoretical, not necessary." The Maturidis and some Shafi'is supported this argument.

I have not found a convincing answer from the Ash'aris, except that Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni), in al-Irshad, responded that this objection is shared: the obligation to contemplate the miracle is undoubtedly theoretical, not necessary. So the one whom the Messenger calls may say: "I will not contemplate the miracle unless that is obligatory upon me by reason, and it is not obligatory upon me by reason until I have examined it, because it is a theoretical obligation, and the theoretical requires arranging premises, and I do not arrange them." All the later mutakallimun (theologians) among the Ash'aris followed him in this answer, such as al-Baydawi, al-Adud, and al-Taftazani. Ibn 'Arafah said in al-Shamil: "This is an acknowledgment of the necessity of silencing, so it does not remove the doubt; rather, it generalizes it between us and them, so the resolution of the problem has not been achieved." Ibn 'Arafah's statement is a firmly established objection.

The apparent intention of Imam al-Haramayn is to dismiss the Mu'tazilah's argument for the rational obligation, by confining the argument to the sharia proofs, which is our aim.

I hold that the answer should be given in one of two ways. The first is by denial: we deny that the obligation to hear the Messenger's call depends on listening to him and examining his miracle, and that if the obligation were not established by reason, the Messenger would be silenced. Rather, we claim that this is a matter established by the sharias that have succeeded one another among human beings, to the extent that everyone with any connection to human civilization knows that callers came to people in different eras, and their call was one: each says that he has been sent from God to call people to what God wants from them. Thus it became firmly rooted in the souls of all human beings that there is faith and disbelief, salvation and perdition, a firm settlement that they cannot find a way to dispel. So when the Messenger calls people to faith, the past reports and discussions present themselves to the listener's soul, and so it becomes obligatory upon him, by a compelling obligation, to listen to him and examine the matter that is established in human souls. For this reason God held the people of the fatrah accountable for polytheism, as many texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicate. Therefore, if we suppose someone who did not mix with human communities and had never had any awareness that people believed, disbelieved, affirmed, and denied, then listening to the Messenger would not be obligatory for him, because that compelling inclination is absent from him. On this view, the obligation is neither legal (shar'i) nor theoretical rational; rather, it is among the necessary matters that cannot be avoided, so it is no wonder that accountability falls upon one who deliberately opposes them.

The second of the two answers is by acceptance: even granting the objection, the inclination established in human nature to investigate events and new reports, and to listen to every bearer of a call, is a matter that moves everyone whom a Messenger calls to religion to listen to his words, to receive his call, his challenge, and his miracle. He does not realize it until his call has traveled into the soul of the one called, stirring in him the impulse to examine, so he is drawn gradually to receive the call, until he finds himself having grasped and known it with a knowledge after which he cannot say: "I do not look at the miracle," or "I do not listen to the call." If he turns away after that, he has chosen blindness over guidance, and so he is held accountable. Suppose someone passed by a Messenger who was calling people, and something occupied him from learning his affair, listening to his words, and examining his conduct; we would grant that he is not addressed, and that this individual and those like him, if they silence the Messenger, do not thereby nullify the mission. But he has lost his guidance and made his own soul foolish.

It is not an objection to us that one who hears the call of the Messenger, puts his fingers in his ears, and flees at that moment, is not subject to the obligation of knowledge, because he did not do this except after knowing that he was about to be held accountable if he heard and disobeyed. That is enough evidence of his awareness that the obligation is directed at him, and so he is held accountable for preferring blindness to guidance, as God said about the people of Noah: ﴿And indeed, whenever I called them﴾ [Nuh: 7], meaning to faith, ﴿that You might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments﴾ [Nuh: 7].

The use of the explicit noun in the phrase ﴿after the Messengers﴾ rather than saying "after them" is for emphasis on this matter, and for making it independent in its signification, so that it becomes like a proverb.

As for the concluding pairing of the two attributes in His words ﴿Mighty, Wise﴾: the appropriateness of the attribute "Wise" is evident, because all these reports are evidence of His wisdom, Exalted is He. As for the attribute "Mighty," it is because might suits His being overpowering in every respect: He is overpowering in terms of worship, so He is not questioned about what He does; and He is overpowering in terms of rational accountability, since He wills not to hold His servants accountable except after proofs, evidences, and signs. The attribute "Wise" is placed later because the execution of His might in this complete manner is itself among the forms of brilliant wisdom.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 163–165 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms.﴾ ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾ ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and as warners, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾

Page 31

These verses resume the response to the Jews' demand that a book be sent down to them from heaven, after they had been foolish in this matter, following the folly of their forefathers, with His saying ﴿For they had asked Moses for something greater than that﴾ [an-Nisa': 153]. Between the two, sentences concerning the opposition of their forefathers and what befell them as a consequence were interposed. Now He turns to explain that the sending down of the Qur'an upon Muhammad ﷺ was not an innovation, for it is the way of revelation to the messengers. Thus, the fact that no book was sent down to them from heaven did not discredit their messengerhood.

The emphasis with inna is either for the importance of this report, or to place those being refuted in the position of one who denies the manner of revelation to messengers other than Moses, since they did not act in accordance with the requirement of their knowledge, to the point that they denied the messengerhood of a messenger to whom no book had been sent down from heaven.

Revelation (wahy) is the conveying of a meaning by a way other than speech, such as a sign. Allah says: ﴿So he came out to his people from the sanctuary and signalled to them to glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 11]. Dawud ibn Jarir said:
They throw at [us] long sermons, and at times the revelation of glances, for fear of the watchers.

The comparison in His saying ﴿As We revealed to Noah﴾ is a comparison with the genus of revelation, even though its types differ. Revelation to the Prophet ﷺ occurred in various kinds, whose explanation is recorded in the hadith of 'A'isha in the Sahih, concerning al-Harith ibn Hisham's question to the Prophet ﷺ: "How does revelation come to you?" This differs from revelation to others whom Allah named, for some of its types may be conceivable for them. Moreover, revelation to the Prophet ﷺ included the Book, the Qur'an, whereas some of those mentioned with him had no book.

Here Allah enumerated a group of prophets and messengers and mentioned that He revealed to them, and the scholars did not differ that messengers and prophets are revealed to.

Page 32

The scholars' expressions differed only regarding the meaning of "messenger" and "prophet." In the statements of a group of our scholars we find no distinction, and that every prophet is a messenger, because revelation is made to him with something which does not fail to be conveyed, even if only to his household. The condition of a messenger may begin with prophethood, followed afterwards by his being sent, so that prophethood is a preparation for messengerhood, as was the case at the beginning of revelation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for he informed Khadija, and there descended upon him ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 214].

The correct view is that the messenger is more specific: he is one to whom revelation is made together with a command to convey, whereas the prophet is not commanded to convey, although he may convey by way of enjoining good and calling to good, meaning without warning and giving good news. Some hadiths state: "The prophets are one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and the number of messengers is three hundred and thirteen messengers." In the hadith of intercession in the Sahih it is recorded: "Noah, peace be upon him, is the first of the messengers." The verses of the Qur'an indicate that religion was known in the time of Adam and that recompense was known to them. The two sons of Adam offered an offering, and one said to the other: ﴿Allah only accepts from the righteous﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27], and he said to him ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 28] ﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and thus be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 29].

It indicates that there was not, at that time, among them anyone who would restrain the transgressor or give justice to the weak against the strong; rather, what they had learned was the method of admonition and instruction, and it was a familial mission.

Noah is the first of the messengers, and he is Noah son of Lamech. The Arabs say: Lamak son of Mutushalakh son of Akhnukh. The Egyptians call him Hermes, and the Arabs call him Idris son of Yard son of Mahalalel son of Qenan son of Anush son of Shith son of Adam, according to the words of the Torah. In his time the great Flood occurred. He lived nine hundred and fifty years, and it is said nine hundred and ninety years, and the Qur'an confirmed that. Noah died three thousand and nine hundred and seventy years before the Hijra, according to the reckoning of the Jews derived from their book.

Abraham is the Friend (al-Khalil), Abraham son of Terah, and the Arabs call him Azar son of Nahur son of Saruch son of Ar'u son of Falegh son of Eber son of Shelah son of Qenan son of Arphaxad son of Sam son of Noah. He was born in the year 2893 before the Hijra, in the land of Ur of the Chaldeans, and died in the land of the Canaanites, which is Syria, in Hebron, where his tomb now is, known as the city of al-Khalil, in the year 2718 before the Hijra.

Page 33

Ishmael is the son of Abraham by the Egyptian slave-girl Hagar. He died in Makkah in approximately the year 2686 before the Hijra. Ishmael was a messenger to his people, among whom he settled, from Jurhum and others, and to his sons and family. Allah said: ﴿And mention in the Book Ishmael; he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 54].

Isaac is the son of Abraham by Sarah, his paternal cousin. He died before the Hijra in the year 2613. Isaac was a prophet confirming the law of his father Abraham and did not bring a law.

Jacob is the son of Isaac, titled Israel. He died in the year 2586 before the Hijra. Jacob was a prophet confirming the law of Abraham; Allah said: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it, and [so did] Jacob﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], and he did not bring a new law.

The Descendants (al-Asbat) are the descendants of Isaac, i.e., his grandchildren, and they are the twelve sons of Jacob: Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin, Manasseh, Dan, Asher, and Naphtali. As for Joseph, he was a messenger to his people in Egypt. Allah said to the Children of Israel, through the words of a believer of the Children of Israel, or as direct address from Allah: ﴿And Joseph had already come to you before with clear evidences, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you, until when he died, you said, "Allah will never send after him a messenger"﴾ [Ghafir: 34]. As for the rest of the Descendants, each of them was a caller to the law of Abraham among his sons and people. Revelation to these varied.

Jesus is Jesus son of Mary; he was born without a father in the year 622 before the Hijra, and he was raised to heaven before it in the year 589. He is a messenger with a law that abrogates some rulings of the Torah. His call to Allah lasted three years.

Job is a prophet. It is said that he was of Arab origin from the land of Uz, in the lands of Edom, which is among the lands of Hauran. It is said that he was Job son of Nahur, the brother of Abraham; it is said that his name was 'Awad; and it is said that he was Yubab son of a grandson of Esau. It is said that he was a hundred years before Abraham.

Page 34

The correct view is that he was after Abraham and before Moses, in the fifteenth century before Christ, that is, in the twenty-first century before the Hijra. It is said that the book attributed to him in the books of the Jews originally was composed in the Arabic language, and that Moses, peace be upon him, transferred it into Hebrew as an admonition. Therefore many researchers in history think that Job was from an Arab tribe. This is not far-fetched. Job was a messenger and a prophet. He had a companion named Elihu the Yemenite, who strengthened him in patience, as we shall mention in its place. His name was not declined because he was not from the Arabs of the Hijaz or Najd; for the Arabs regarded distant tribes as non-Arab, even if their origin was Arab, and for this reason they did not decline the name of Thamud when they dwelt in al-Hijr.

Jonah is the son of Matthew, of the tribe of Zebulun, from the Children of Israel. Allah sent him to the people of Nineveh, capital of the Assyrians, after the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis, and that was around the eleventh century before the Hijra.

Aaron, brother of Moses son of 'Imran, died in the year 1972 before the Hijra, and he was a messenger with Moses to the Children of Israel.

Solomon is the son of David. He was a prophet ruling by the Torah and a great king. He died in the year 1597 before the Hijra. Among what Allah revealed to him is what is contained in the Book of Ecclesiastes (al-Jami'ah) and the Book of Proverbs (al-Amthal) of wisdom and admonitions, which are attributed to Solomon, but it was not said regarding them that Allah revealed them to him; thus we know that they were revealed in their meanings, not their wording.

David, father of Solomon, is David son of Jesse. He died in the year 1626 before the Hijra. Allah sent him to support the Children of Israel, and He revealed to him a book containing admonitions and proverbs, which the Children of Israel used to chant with its sections, and it is named the Psalms (az-Zabur). It is a verbal noun on the pattern fa'ul, like qabul. It is also said zubur with a damma on the zay, meaning a verbal noun like shukur; its meaning is writing, and the written thing is called zabur, plural zubur. Allah said: ﴿With clear proofs and scriptures﴾ [Al 'Imran: 184]. It has become, by dominance in the Arabic language, a proper name for the book of the Prophet David, and it is one of the books of the Holy Bible among the Jews.

Page 35

The clause ﴿And to David We gave the Psalms﴾ is conjoined to (We revealed to you). The name David was not conjoined to the rest of the names mentioned before it, to hint that the Psalms was revealed in being a book.

Al-Jumhur read (zabura) with a fatha on the zay, and Hamza and Khalaf read it with a damma on the zay.

His saying ﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾ means in the verses of the Qur'an, such as: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Zechariah, John, Elias, Elisha, Lot, and Tubba'. His saying ﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾ means He did not mention them in the Qur'an. Among them are those whose mention does not occur in the Sunnah, such as Handhala ibn Safwan, prophet of the People of the Rass, and such as some of the sages of the Greeks according to some scholars of wisdom. Al-Suhrawardi said in Hikmat al-Ishraq: among them are the people of the embassy. Among them are those whom the Sunnah mentioned, such as Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi.

Allah mentioned here the prophets who were well known among the Children of Israel, because the purpose is to argue with them. Allah left out relating to the Prophet ﷺ the names of many messengers, being content with those He related to him, because those mentioned are the greatest of messengers and prophets in lessons-bearing narratives.

His saying ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾ changes the style, turning away from conjunction to mentioning another verb, because this kind of revelation has added importance, and it, with that distinction, is not the sending down of a book from heaven. So if there is no lesson except in sending down a book from heaven according to their demand, then what is other than the Ten Words inscribed on the tablets given to Moses, peace be upon him, is also invalidated.

The speech of Allah the Exalted is, according to us, an independent attribute. It concerns conveying the will of Allah to the angels and messengers, and this has been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) in the speech of the prophets and messengers, a transmission that is established

Page 36

among all the adherents of the religions. The speech of God (kalam Allah) is an attribute of Him established by revelation (al-shar'). On careful examination, rational proof does not establish it, since rational arguments do not show that God is obligated to convey His purpose to people. Rather, it is permissible for Him to bring existents into being and then leave them to their own affairs, so His knowledge would not be connected to driving them toward performing good deeds and avoiding their evils. Do you not see that He created the animals without commanding or forbidding them? Had He left people in disorder like the animals, that would not have been impossible.

And when He wishes to direct created beings toward something He desires, He originates them upon it, and they are drawn to it by their innate natures, as He made the bee to produce honey and trees to bear fruit. Had He willed, He could likewise have directed people to a nature from which they could not deviate. But since we know that He is All-Knowing and All-Wise, and knowledge requires the unveiling of the realities of things as they are in His sight, He knows the goodness and ugliness of actions, desires the attainment of benefits and the removal of harms, is pleased with the former and dislikes the latter. Since His wisdom and will required that He make humankind capable of learning and of righteousness, and made human intellects fit to reach the ultimate ends of good and of evil and to diversify in both, unlike the animal, which attains, in what it is created for, whether good or evil, only to a limit upon which it was originated and beyond which it does not go, it was to be expected that evil would prevail over good through the works of the faction of wicked people among mankind. It was then a requirement of wisdom that He direct people to doing the good He is pleased with and abandoning the evil He hates. Guiding them to this may occur through creating the excellent among people and innately disposing them to righteousness and goodness, so that they become callers to mankind. But the wisdom and grace of God required that He create the righteous who are receptive to good, and that He assist them in reaching what they were disposed to, through His guidance and direction. So He created souls receptive to prophethood and messengership and supported them with guidance indicating His purpose, expressed by revelation (wahy), as His saying, may He be exalted, requires: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. Thus He established messengership and the preparation of the messenger to accept it, and from here the attribute of speech is established.

We know from the mass-transmitted reports of the Shari'ah that God desired righteousness from mankind and commanded them to it, and that His command reached humankind across many eras. This indicates that God is pleased with some human actions and not pleased with others, and that this is called a precious speech (kalam nafis), and it is eternal (azali).

Then, the reality of the attribute of speech may be among the objects connected to the attribute of knowledge, or among the objects connected to the attribute of will, or an independent attribute distinct from the two others. [p. 37]

Some say: He knew the people's need for guidance, so He guided them; or He willed the guidance of the people, so He guided them. We say: divinity requires the establishment of the attributes of perfection, among which are good pleasure, displeasure, commanding and forbidding toward humans or angels. Thus there is established an independent attribute, namely the attribute of inner speech (kalam nafsi). All of this is close in meaning, and its detailed treatment belongs to the science of kalam (theology).

As for God's addressing (taklim) some of His servants among the angels or humans, it is the bringing into being of that by which the angel or messenger knows that God commands, forbids, or informs. So "addressing" is the connection of the attribute of speech to the one addressed, on the basis of making speech an independent attribute; or the connection of knowledge to conveying the known to the one addressed; or the connection of will to conveying the willed to the one addressed.

The Ash'ariyya said: God's addressing His servant is that He creates in the servant a perception through hearing by which he attains knowledge of God's speech, without letters or sounds. It has been illustrated that Moses heard something like thunder, from which he knew the meaning of the inner speech. I say: the Prophet (ﷺ) also illustrated it in the authentic hadith from Abu Hurayrah: "When God decrees a matter in heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon a smooth rock. When fear is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'" [Saba': 23]. According to this view, it is not necessary that what the messenger or angel hears be letters and sounds; rather it is a knowledge he attains through his hearing, connected to God's speech, and it is one of the connections of the attribute of inner speech to the speaker in what does not cease, so that connection is necessarily originated, like the connection of will.

The Mu'tazila said: God creates letters and sounds in the language of the Messenger, which the Messenger hears; he then knows, by a knowledge he finds in himself, that this came from God, and that it was sent to him from God, but not through an angel. They interpret it in the same way we interpret the descent of the Qur'an. Thus attributing speech to God is a metaphor in attribution according to their view, because God is exempt from letters and sounds. Speech in its literal sense is letters and sounds. This is sophistry in argument, for no one claims that the Essence, exalted be He, is characterized by letters and sounds. It is, according to us and according to them, other than the revelation that falls on the heart of the Messenger, and other than the conveyance that occurs through Jibril. It is what is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or from behind a veil﴾ [al-Shura: 51].

[p. 38]

As for God's speech that reaches the Messenger through an angel, which is expressed as the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms: these are words, letters and sounds, which God makes known to the angel in a manner we do not know, by which the angel knows that God, through the particular words cast to the angel, indicates the meanings of those words, so the angel casts them upon the Messenger as they are. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿or sends a messenger and reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 51], and He said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193], ﴿upon your heart, that you may be of the warners﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 194], ﴿in clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 195]. Concerning its being originated, no one who has a share of knowledge of religion doubts. However, some of the imams of Islam refrained from explicitly stating that it is originated, or that it is created, in assemblies of debate attended by the common people, or by the darkness of obstinacy and the eagerness to revile and harm. This was to avert misunderstanding, to preserve the attribution to Islam, and to disavow the rabble of the vulgar. So may God have mercy on souls that were tried, bodies that were hurt, and mouths that were silenced, who intended good, whether they were moderate or went to excess. God is the Reckoner of those who incited against them, gathered together, and provoked them, and evil is what they did.

His saying "addressing" (taklim) is a verbal noun (masdar) for emphasis (tawkid). Emphasis by the verbal noun returns to affirming and confirming the attribution, like "qad" and "inna". It is not intended to remove the possibility of metaphor. For this reason the Arabs emphasized with the verbal noun verbs that were used only metaphorically, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God only desires to remove from you the uncleanness, O people of the household, and to purify you with complete purification﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. He intended that He purifies them with spiritual purity, that is, perfection of the soul, so the emphasis did not serve to remove metaphor. Hind bint al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said, dispraising her husband Rawh ibn Zinba':

"The silk wept because of Rawh, and its skin denied it,
and the garments of Judham cried out with a loud cry."

But the crying is only metaphorical. So the verbal noun emphasizes, that is, it confirms the occurrence of the emphasized act in the meaning it had before the emphasis.

So the meaning of His saying "addressing" (taklaman) here is: Moses heard speech from God, in such a way that it is not possible that God sent Jibril to him with speech, or inspired it into his soul. As for the manner in which this speech issues from God's side, that is another matter, a field of disagreement among the sects. For this reason [p. 39]

the argument of many Ash'aris from this verse, that the speech Moses heard is the essential attribute subsisting in God, is a weak argument. Ibn 'Arafa related that al-Mazari said in his commentary on al-Talqin: this verse is a proof against the Mu'tazila in their saying that God did not address Moses directly, but through the creation of speech, because He emphasized it with the verbal noun. And that Ibn 'Abd al-Salam al-Tunisi, the teacher of Ibn 'Arafa, refuted this by saying that emphasis by the verbal noun serves to remove doubt about the report, not about the one who reports it. Ibn 'Arafa criticized him with what amounts to strengthening Ibn 'Abd al-Salam's refutation.

His saying "messengers" (rusulan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from those mentioned. He named them messengers for the reason we previously mentioned. It is a preparatory circumstantial (hal muwatti'ah) for its description, namely "bearers of good news and warners," because that is what is intended by the circumstantial.

His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ is a causal clause (ta'lil) for His saying "bearers of good news and warners." It cannot be taken as a cause for His saying ﴿We have revealed to you﴾, because that is directed toward explaining the validity of the message without the descent of a book from heaven, in response to their saying ﴿until you bring down upon us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra': 93]. So the placement of His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ is in the position of incidental inclusion (idmaj), teaching the community one of the wisdoms in God's sending of the messengers. Argument (hujjah) is what indicates the truthfulness of the claimant and the rightness of the one who makes an excuse, so it requires that one not be held accountable for sin or negligence. What is meant here is the clear excuse that necessitates disavowal of anger and punishment. So the sending of messengers is to cut off the excuse of mankind when they are questioned about their criminal deeds and deserve God's anger and punishment. From this it is known that people, before the sending of messengers, had an argument against God, that they could say: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs and be among the believers?﴾ [al-Qasas: 47].

The verse indicates that among people's actions are some that anger God and for which one is punished, namely the actions which sound intellects recognize as ugly because they lead to corruption and clear harms. The mode of this indication is that argument only opposes an attempt at some action; so when God sent the messengers to cut off argument, we know that when God sent the messengers He was about to hold accountable those to whom they were sent, and His mercy required that He cut off their argument by sending messengers, guiding them and warning them. For this reason He made the cutting off of argument the final cause of the good news and warning, since good news and warning only clarify the consequences of actions. That is why He did not give the reason for sending messengers as alerting to what pleases God and what angers Him.

[p. 40]

This verse thus obliges all the sects to hold that sending messengers is a precondition for being held accountable for sins, and its apparent sense is that all kinds of accountability depend upon it, whether the sins relate to belief or to action, and including the obligation of knowing God. Sending messengers, in our view, is part of God's complete justice, because if He had not sent them, punishment would have been mere absolute dominion, which the act of creating requires, since He is not questioned about what He does; yet it would have been justice in the broader sense.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 163–165 (part 3 of 3)**

As for the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the Sunni mainstream), whose positions are transmitted through the approach of al-Ash'ari (the Ash'ari school of theology), they generalized and said: no obligation is established, and no one is held accountable for abandoning or doing anything, except through the sending of the Messengers, including the knowledge of God, Exalted is He. They argued with this verse and others, such as ﴿We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15], and with consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement). However, there is scrutiny concerning the claim of consensus, there is a different scrutiny concerning using it as evidence for a foundation of religion, and there is a third scrutiny concerning using the verses, which are apparent (zawahir, texts with apparent meanings), as evidence for a foundation of religion. The exception would be if it were said that they are so numerous that they reach the level of certainty; but this too is open to debate. They are compelled to interpret this verse, because they hold that the people of the fatrah (the interval between prophets) are held accountable for their polytheism toward God.

The answer is to say: the word "Messengers" in the verse is a collective noun used distributively (kull ifradi), which applies to each single Messenger, and it varies according to the variation of the call. As for the call to the totality of faith and monotheism, it was established through the earlier Messengers, whose calls established, for human beings, the obligation of faith and monotheism. As for the call to the details of the signs and attributes and the branches of the sharia (the divine law), it is established through the coming of the Messengers who are specific to known nations.

As for the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilites), they established that good and evil are intrinsic (dhatiyyan) in the state in which no messenger has been sent. They said: reason establishes the obligation of many rulings and the prohibition of many, especially the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, because knowledge repels a presumed harm, which is the otherworldly harm of incurring punishment in the Hereafter, as a large number of people have reported it; and the fear of what results from the disagreement of sects over knowledge of the Creator before correct knowledge is worldly harm. Everything that repels a presumed or doubtful harm is obligatory by reason. Like someone who wants to take a road and is told that there is a predator on it: reason requires that he pause and investigate until he knows whether he should take that road or not. Likewise, it is obligatory to examine the miracle of the Messengers and all that leads to the establishment of the sharia. For this reason, they interpreted this verse in the way that al-Zamakhshari (author of al-Kashshaf) mentioned when he said: "If you ask, how can people have a proof against God before the Messengers, when they are held to account by the proofs God has set up, whose examination leads to knowledge, and the Messengers themselves did not reach knowledge by examining those proofs, i.e., before the prophethood?" I say: the Messengers are reminders against heedlessness and prompters to examination, together with conveying what they carried of the matters of religion and teaching the laws. Their sending was thus a removal of the excuse and a completion of the establishment of the proof. This means that the sending of the Messengers is a mercy from God, not a matter of justice; had He not sent them, holding people accountable for their vices would have been just. So the sending of the Messengers completes the proof regarding the very principle of accountability, and completes the proof regarding the increase in purification, so that people would not say: "Our Lord, why did You not guide us to what would raise our ranks among the sincere (siddiqin), and limit us to mere salvation from punishment, when we were guided to the principle of monotheism by our intellects?"

Al-Maturidi (the Maturidi school) agreed with the majority regarding everything except the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, when the intention is to silence the Messengers specifically, because he considered it the foundation of the principles of religion, as indicated by the words of Sadr al-Shari'ah in al-Tawdih: "That is, the act is a quality for which the doer of the act is praised and rewarded, or blamed and punished; because the obligation of affirming the Prophet, if it depended on the sharia, would lead to circularity (dawr)." He also explicitly stated that it is also known through the sharia.

The Mu'tazilah pressed the Ash'ari school on this matter, specifically regarding the obligation of knowledge. They said: if knowledge were not obligatory except through the sharia, it would necessarily lead to silencing the Messengers, and there would be no benefit in sending them. The basis of the necessity is that if a Messenger says to someone, "Look at my miracle until my truthfulness becomes clear to you," he can say: "I will not look, since it is not obligatory upon me, because abandoning what is not obligatory is permissible, and it is not obligatory upon me until the obligation is established for me through the sharia, and the sharia is not established as long as I have not looked, because the establishment of the sharia is theoretical, not necessary." The Maturidis and some Shafi'is supported this argument.

I have not found a convincing answer from the Ash'aris, except that Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni), in al-Irshad, responded that this objection is shared: the obligation to contemplate the miracle is undoubtedly theoretical, not necessary. So the one whom the Messenger calls may say: "I will not contemplate the miracle unless that is obligatory upon me by reason, and it is not obligatory upon me by reason until I have examined it, because it is a theoretical obligation, and the theoretical requires arranging premises, and I do not arrange them." All the later mutakallimun (theologians) among the Ash'aris followed him in this answer, such as al-Baydawi, al-Adud, and al-Taftazani. Ibn 'Arafah said in al-Shamil: "This is an acknowledgment of the necessity of silencing, so it does not remove the doubt; rather, it generalizes it between us and them, so the resolution of the problem has not been achieved." Ibn 'Arafah's statement is a firmly established objection.

The apparent intention of Imam al-Haramayn is to dismiss the Mu'tazilah's argument for the rational obligation, by confining the argument to the sharia proofs, which is our aim.

I hold that the answer should be given in one of two ways. The first is by denial: we deny that the obligation to hear the Messenger's call depends on listening to him and examining his miracle, and that if the obligation were not established by reason, the Messenger would be silenced. Rather, we claim that this is a matter established by the sharias that have succeeded one another among human beings, to the extent that everyone with any connection to human civilization knows that callers came to people in different eras, and their call was one: each says that he has been sent from God to call people to what God wants from them. Thus it became firmly rooted in the souls of all human beings that there is faith and disbelief, salvation and perdition, a firm settlement that they cannot find a way to dispel. So when the Messenger calls people to faith, the past reports and discussions present themselves to the listener's soul, and so it becomes obligatory upon him, by a compelling obligation, to listen to him and examine the matter that is established in human souls. For this reason God held the people of the fatrah accountable for polytheism, as many texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicate. Therefore, if we suppose someone who did not mix with human communities and had never had any awareness that people believed, disbelieved, affirmed, and denied, then listening to the Messenger would not be obligatory for him, because that compelling inclination is absent from him. On this view, the obligation is neither legal (shar'i) nor theoretical rational; rather, it is among the necessary matters that cannot be avoided, so it is no wonder that accountability falls upon one who deliberately opposes them.

The second of the two answers is by acceptance: even granting the objection, the inclination established in human nature to investigate events and new reports, and to listen to every bearer of a call, is a matter that moves everyone whom a Messenger calls to religion to listen to his words, to receive his call, his challenge, and his miracle. He does not realize it until his call has traveled into the soul of the one called, stirring in him the impulse to examine, so he is drawn gradually to receive the call, until he finds himself having grasped and known it with a knowledge after which he cannot say: "I do not look at the miracle," or "I do not listen to the call." If he turns away after that, he has chosen blindness over guidance, and so he is held accountable. Suppose someone passed by a Messenger who was calling people, and something occupied him from learning his affair, listening to his words, and examining his conduct; we would grant that he is not addressed, and that this individual and those like him, if they silence the Messenger, do not thereby nullify the mission. But he has lost his guidance and made his own soul foolish.

It is not an objection to us that one who hears the call of the Messenger, puts his fingers in his ears, and flees at that moment, is not subject to the obligation of knowledge, because he did not do this except after knowing that he was about to be held accountable if he heard and disobeyed. That is enough evidence of his awareness that the obligation is directed at him, and so he is held accountable for preferring blindness to guidance, as God said about the people of Noah: ﴿And indeed, whenever I called them﴾ [Nuh: 7], meaning to faith, ﴿that You might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments﴾ [Nuh: 7].

The use of the explicit noun in the phrase ﴿after the Messengers﴾ rather than saying "after them" is for emphasis on this matter, and for making it independent in its signification, so that it becomes like a proverb.

As for the concluding pairing of the two attributes in His words ﴿Mighty, Wise﴾: the appropriateness of the attribute "Wise" is evident, because all these reports are evidence of His wisdom, Exalted is He. As for the attribute "Mighty," it is because might suits His being overpowering in every respect: He is overpowering in terms of worship, so He is not questioned about what He does; and He is overpowering in terms of rational accountability, since He wills not to hold His servants accountable except after proofs, evidences, and signs. The attribute "Wise" is placed later because the execution of His might in this complete manner is itself among the forms of brilliant wisdom.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 163–165 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms.﴾ ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾ ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and as warners, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾

Page 31

These verses resume the response to the Jews' demand that a book be sent down to them from heaven, after they had been foolish in this matter, following the folly of their forefathers, with His saying ﴿For they had asked Moses for something greater than that﴾ [an-Nisa': 153]. Between the two, sentences concerning the opposition of their forefathers and what befell them as a consequence were interposed. Now He turns to explain that the sending down of the Qur'an upon Muhammad ﷺ was not an innovation, for it is the way of revelation to the messengers. Thus, the fact that no book was sent down to them from heaven did not discredit their messengerhood.

The emphasis with inna is either for the importance of this report, or to place those being refuted in the position of one who denies the manner of revelation to messengers other than Moses, since they did not act in accordance with the requirement of their knowledge, to the point that they denied the messengerhood of a messenger to whom no book had been sent down from heaven.

Revelation (wahy) is the conveying of a meaning by a way other than speech, such as a sign. Allah says: ﴿So he came out to his people from the sanctuary and signalled to them to glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 11]. Dawud ibn Jarir said:
They throw at [us] long sermons, and at times the revelation of glances, for fear of the watchers.

The comparison in His saying ﴿As We revealed to Noah﴾ is a comparison with the genus of revelation, even though its types differ. Revelation to the Prophet ﷺ occurred in various kinds, whose explanation is recorded in the hadith of 'A'isha in the Sahih, concerning al-Harith ibn Hisham's question to the Prophet ﷺ: "How does revelation come to you?" This differs from revelation to others whom Allah named, for some of its types may be conceivable for them. Moreover, revelation to the Prophet ﷺ included the Book, the Qur'an, whereas some of those mentioned with him had no book.

Here Allah enumerated a group of prophets and messengers and mentioned that He revealed to them, and the scholars did not differ that messengers and prophets are revealed to.

Page 32

The scholars' expressions differed only regarding the meaning of "messenger" and "prophet." In the statements of a group of our scholars we find no distinction, and that every prophet is a messenger, because revelation is made to him with something which does not fail to be conveyed, even if only to his household. The condition of a messenger may begin with prophethood, followed afterwards by his being sent, so that prophethood is a preparation for messengerhood, as was the case at the beginning of revelation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for he informed Khadija, and there descended upon him ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 214].

The correct view is that the messenger is more specific: he is one to whom revelation is made together with a command to convey, whereas the prophet is not commanded to convey, although he may convey by way of enjoining good and calling to good, meaning without warning and giving good news. Some hadiths state: "The prophets are one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and the number of messengers is three hundred and thirteen messengers." In the hadith of intercession in the Sahih it is recorded: "Noah, peace be upon him, is the first of the messengers." The verses of the Qur'an indicate that religion was known in the time of Adam and that recompense was known to them. The two sons of Adam offered an offering, and one said to the other: ﴿Allah only accepts from the righteous﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27], and he said to him ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 28] ﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and thus be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 29].

It indicates that there was not, at that time, among them anyone who would restrain the transgressor or give justice to the weak against the strong; rather, what they had learned was the method of admonition and instruction, and it was a familial mission.

Noah is the first of the messengers, and he is Noah son of Lamech. The Arabs say: Lamak son of Mutushalakh son of Akhnukh. The Egyptians call him Hermes, and the Arabs call him Idris son of Yard son of Mahalalel son of Qenan son of Anush son of Shith son of Adam, according to the words of the Torah. In his time the great Flood occurred. He lived nine hundred and fifty years, and it is said nine hundred and ninety years, and the Qur'an confirmed that. Noah died three thousand and nine hundred and seventy years before the Hijra, according to the reckoning of the Jews derived from their book.

Abraham is the Friend (al-Khalil), Abraham son of Terah, and the Arabs call him Azar son of Nahur son of Saruch son of Ar'u son of Falegh son of Eber son of Shelah son of Qenan son of Arphaxad son of Sam son of Noah. He was born in the year 2893 before the Hijra, in the land of Ur of the Chaldeans, and died in the land of the Canaanites, which is Syria, in Hebron, where his tomb now is, known as the city of al-Khalil, in the year 2718 before the Hijra.

Page 33

Ishmael is the son of Abraham by the Egyptian slave-girl Hagar. He died in Makkah in approximately the year 2686 before the Hijra. Ishmael was a messenger to his people, among whom he settled, from Jurhum and others, and to his sons and family. Allah said: ﴿And mention in the Book Ishmael; he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 54].

Isaac is the son of Abraham by Sarah, his paternal cousin. He died before the Hijra in the year 2613. Isaac was a prophet confirming the law of his father Abraham and did not bring a law.

Jacob is the son of Isaac, titled Israel. He died in the year 2586 before the Hijra. Jacob was a prophet confirming the law of Abraham; Allah said: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it, and [so did] Jacob﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], and he did not bring a new law.

The Descendants (al-Asbat) are the descendants of Isaac, i.e., his grandchildren, and they are the twelve sons of Jacob: Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin, Manasseh, Dan, Asher, and Naphtali. As for Joseph, he was a messenger to his people in Egypt. Allah said to the Children of Israel, through the words of a believer of the Children of Israel, or as direct address from Allah: ﴿And Joseph had already come to you before with clear evidences, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you, until when he died, you said, "Allah will never send after him a messenger"﴾ [Ghafir: 34]. As for the rest of the Descendants, each of them was a caller to the law of Abraham among his sons and people. Revelation to these varied.

Jesus is Jesus son of Mary; he was born without a father in the year 622 before the Hijra, and he was raised to heaven before it in the year 589. He is a messenger with a law that abrogates some rulings of the Torah. His call to Allah lasted three years.

Job is a prophet. It is said that he was of Arab origin from the land of Uz, in the lands of Edom, which is among the lands of Hauran. It is said that he was Job son of Nahur, the brother of Abraham; it is said that his name was 'Awad; and it is said that he was Yubab son of a grandson of Esau. It is said that he was a hundred years before Abraham.

Page 34

The correct view is that he was after Abraham and before Moses, in the fifteenth century before Christ, that is, in the twenty-first century before the Hijra. It is said that the book attributed to him in the books of the Jews originally was composed in the Arabic language, and that Moses, peace be upon him, transferred it into Hebrew as an admonition. Therefore many researchers in history think that Job was from an Arab tribe. This is not far-fetched. Job was a messenger and a prophet. He had a companion named Elihu the Yemenite, who strengthened him in patience, as we shall mention in its place. His name was not declined because he was not from the Arabs of the Hijaz or Najd; for the Arabs regarded distant tribes as non-Arab, even if their origin was Arab, and for this reason they did not decline the name of Thamud when they dwelt in al-Hijr.

Jonah is the son of Matthew, of the tribe of Zebulun, from the Children of Israel. Allah sent him to the people of Nineveh, capital of the Assyrians, after the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis, and that was around the eleventh century before the Hijra.

Aaron, brother of Moses son of 'Imran, died in the year 1972 before the Hijra, and he was a messenger with Moses to the Children of Israel.

Solomon is the son of David. He was a prophet ruling by the Torah and a great king. He died in the year 1597 before the Hijra. Among what Allah revealed to him is what is contained in the Book of Ecclesiastes (al-Jami'ah) and the Book of Proverbs (al-Amthal) of wisdom and admonitions, which are attributed to Solomon, but it was not said regarding them that Allah revealed them to him; thus we know that they were revealed in their meanings, not their wording.

David, father of Solomon, is David son of Jesse. He died in the year 1626 before the Hijra. Allah sent him to support the Children of Israel, and He revealed to him a book containing admonitions and proverbs, which the Children of Israel used to chant with its sections, and it is named the Psalms (az-Zabur). It is a verbal noun on the pattern fa'ul, like qabul. It is also said zubur with a damma on the zay, meaning a verbal noun like shukur; its meaning is writing, and the written thing is called zabur, plural zubur. Allah said: ﴿With clear proofs and scriptures﴾ [Al 'Imran: 184]. It has become, by dominance in the Arabic language, a proper name for the book of the Prophet David, and it is one of the books of the Holy Bible among the Jews.

Page 35

The clause ﴿And to David We gave the Psalms﴾ is conjoined to (We revealed to you). The name David was not conjoined to the rest of the names mentioned before it, to hint that the Psalms was revealed in being a book.

Al-Jumhur read (zabura) with a fatha on the zay, and Hamza and Khalaf read it with a damma on the zay.

His saying ﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾ means in the verses of the Qur'an, such as: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Zechariah, John, Elias, Elisha, Lot, and Tubba'. His saying ﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾ means He did not mention them in the Qur'an. Among them are those whose mention does not occur in the Sunnah, such as Handhala ibn Safwan, prophet of the People of the Rass, and such as some of the sages of the Greeks according to some scholars of wisdom. Al-Suhrawardi said in Hikmat al-Ishraq: among them are the people of the embassy. Among them are those whom the Sunnah mentioned, such as Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi.

Allah mentioned here the prophets who were well known among the Children of Israel, because the purpose is to argue with them. Allah left out relating to the Prophet ﷺ the names of many messengers, being content with those He related to him, because those mentioned are the greatest of messengers and prophets in lessons-bearing narratives.

His saying ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾ changes the style, turning away from conjunction to mentioning another verb, because this kind of revelation has added importance, and it, with that distinction, is not the sending down of a book from heaven. So if there is no lesson except in sending down a book from heaven according to their demand, then what is other than the Ten Words inscribed on the tablets given to Moses, peace be upon him, is also invalidated.

The speech of Allah the Exalted is, according to us, an independent attribute. It concerns conveying the will of Allah to the angels and messengers, and this has been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) in the speech of the prophets and messengers, a transmission that is established

Page 36

among all the adherents of the religions. The speech of God (kalam Allah) is an attribute of Him established by revelation (al-shar'). On careful examination, rational proof does not establish it, since rational arguments do not show that God is obligated to convey His purpose to people. Rather, it is permissible for Him to bring existents into being and then leave them to their own affairs, so His knowledge would not be connected to driving them toward performing good deeds and avoiding their evils. Do you not see that He created the animals without commanding or forbidding them? Had He left people in disorder like the animals, that would not have been impossible.

And when He wishes to direct created beings toward something He desires, He originates them upon it, and they are drawn to it by their innate natures, as He made the bee to produce honey and trees to bear fruit. Had He willed, He could likewise have directed people to a nature from which they could not deviate. But since we know that He is All-Knowing and All-Wise, and knowledge requires the unveiling of the realities of things as they are in His sight, He knows the goodness and ugliness of actions, desires the attainment of benefits and the removal of harms, is pleased with the former and dislikes the latter. Since His wisdom and will required that He make humankind capable of learning and of righteousness, and made human intellects fit to reach the ultimate ends of good and of evil and to diversify in both, unlike the animal, which attains, in what it is created for, whether good or evil, only to a limit upon which it was originated and beyond which it does not go, it was to be expected that evil would prevail over good through the works of the faction of wicked people among mankind. It was then a requirement of wisdom that He direct people to doing the good He is pleased with and abandoning the evil He hates. Guiding them to this may occur through creating the excellent among people and innately disposing them to righteousness and goodness, so that they become callers to mankind. But the wisdom and grace of God required that He create the righteous who are receptive to good, and that He assist them in reaching what they were disposed to, through His guidance and direction. So He created souls receptive to prophethood and messengership and supported them with guidance indicating His purpose, expressed by revelation (wahy), as His saying, may He be exalted, requires: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. Thus He established messengership and the preparation of the messenger to accept it, and from here the attribute of speech is established.

We know from the mass-transmitted reports of the Shari'ah that God desired righteousness from mankind and commanded them to it, and that His command reached humankind across many eras. This indicates that God is pleased with some human actions and not pleased with others, and that this is called a precious speech (kalam nafis), and it is eternal (azali).

Then, the reality of the attribute of speech may be among the objects connected to the attribute of knowledge, or among the objects connected to the attribute of will, or an independent attribute distinct from the two others. [p. 37]

Some say: He knew the people's need for guidance, so He guided them; or He willed the guidance of the people, so He guided them. We say: divinity requires the establishment of the attributes of perfection, among which are good pleasure, displeasure, commanding and forbidding toward humans or angels. Thus there is established an independent attribute, namely the attribute of inner speech (kalam nafsi). All of this is close in meaning, and its detailed treatment belongs to the science of kalam (theology).

As for God's addressing (taklim) some of His servants among the angels or humans, it is the bringing into being of that by which the angel or messenger knows that God commands, forbids, or informs. So "addressing" is the connection of the attribute of speech to the one addressed, on the basis of making speech an independent attribute; or the connection of knowledge to conveying the known to the one addressed; or the connection of will to conveying the willed to the one addressed.

The Ash'ariyya said: God's addressing His servant is that He creates in the servant a perception through hearing by which he attains knowledge of God's speech, without letters or sounds. It has been illustrated that Moses heard something like thunder, from which he knew the meaning of the inner speech. I say: the Prophet (ﷺ) also illustrated it in the authentic hadith from Abu Hurayrah: "When God decrees a matter in heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon a smooth rock. When fear is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'" [Saba': 23]. According to this view, it is not necessary that what the messenger or angel hears be letters and sounds; rather it is a knowledge he attains through his hearing, connected to God's speech, and it is one of the connections of the attribute of inner speech to the speaker in what does not cease, so that connection is necessarily originated, like the connection of will.

The Mu'tazila said: God creates letters and sounds in the language of the Messenger, which the Messenger hears; he then knows, by a knowledge he finds in himself, that this came from God, and that it was sent to him from God, but not through an angel. They interpret it in the same way we interpret the descent of the Qur'an. Thus attributing speech to God is a metaphor in attribution according to their view, because God is exempt from letters and sounds. Speech in its literal sense is letters and sounds. This is sophistry in argument, for no one claims that the Essence, exalted be He, is characterized by letters and sounds. It is, according to us and according to them, other than the revelation that falls on the heart of the Messenger, and other than the conveyance that occurs through Jibril. It is what is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or from behind a veil﴾ [al-Shura: 51].

[p. 38]

As for God's speech that reaches the Messenger through an angel, which is expressed as the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms: these are words, letters and sounds, which God makes known to the angel in a manner we do not know, by which the angel knows that God, through the particular words cast to the angel, indicates the meanings of those words, so the angel casts them upon the Messenger as they are. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿or sends a messenger and reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 51], and He said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193], ﴿upon your heart, that you may be of the warners﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 194], ﴿in clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 195]. Concerning its being originated, no one who has a share of knowledge of religion doubts. However, some of the imams of Islam refrained from explicitly stating that it is originated, or that it is created, in assemblies of debate attended by the common people, or by the darkness of obstinacy and the eagerness to revile and harm. This was to avert misunderstanding, to preserve the attribution to Islam, and to disavow the rabble of the vulgar. So may God have mercy on souls that were tried, bodies that were hurt, and mouths that were silenced, who intended good, whether they were moderate or went to excess. God is the Reckoner of those who incited against them, gathered together, and provoked them, and evil is what they did.

His saying "addressing" (taklim) is a verbal noun (masdar) for emphasis (tawkid). Emphasis by the verbal noun returns to affirming and confirming the attribution, like "qad" and "inna". It is not intended to remove the possibility of metaphor. For this reason the Arabs emphasized with the verbal noun verbs that were used only metaphorically, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God only desires to remove from you the uncleanness, O people of the household, and to purify you with complete purification﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. He intended that He purifies them with spiritual purity, that is, perfection of the soul, so the emphasis did not serve to remove metaphor. Hind bint al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said, dispraising her husband Rawh ibn Zinba':

"The silk wept because of Rawh, and its skin denied it,
and the garments of Judham cried out with a loud cry."

But the crying is only metaphorical. So the verbal noun emphasizes, that is, it confirms the occurrence of the emphasized act in the meaning it had before the emphasis.

So the meaning of His saying "addressing" (taklaman) here is: Moses heard speech from God, in such a way that it is not possible that God sent Jibril to him with speech, or inspired it into his soul. As for the manner in which this speech issues from God's side, that is another matter, a field of disagreement among the sects. For this reason [p. 39]

the argument of many Ash'aris from this verse, that the speech Moses heard is the essential attribute subsisting in God, is a weak argument. Ibn 'Arafa related that al-Mazari said in his commentary on al-Talqin: this verse is a proof against the Mu'tazila in their saying that God did not address Moses directly, but through the creation of speech, because He emphasized it with the verbal noun. And that Ibn 'Abd al-Salam al-Tunisi, the teacher of Ibn 'Arafa, refuted this by saying that emphasis by the verbal noun serves to remove doubt about the report, not about the one who reports it. Ibn 'Arafa criticized him with what amounts to strengthening Ibn 'Abd al-Salam's refutation.

His saying "messengers" (rusulan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from those mentioned. He named them messengers for the reason we previously mentioned. It is a preparatory circumstantial (hal muwatti'ah) for its description, namely "bearers of good news and warners," because that is what is intended by the circumstantial.

His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ is a causal clause (ta'lil) for His saying "bearers of good news and warners." It cannot be taken as a cause for His saying ﴿We have revealed to you﴾, because that is directed toward explaining the validity of the message without the descent of a book from heaven, in response to their saying ﴿until you bring down upon us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra': 93]. So the placement of His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ is in the position of incidental inclusion (idmaj), teaching the community one of the wisdoms in God's sending of the messengers. Argument (hujjah) is what indicates the truthfulness of the claimant and the rightness of the one who makes an excuse, so it requires that one not be held accountable for sin or negligence. What is meant here is the clear excuse that necessitates disavowal of anger and punishment. So the sending of messengers is to cut off the excuse of mankind when they are questioned about their criminal deeds and deserve God's anger and punishment. From this it is known that people, before the sending of messengers, had an argument against God, that they could say: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs and be among the believers?﴾ [al-Qasas: 47].

The verse indicates that among people's actions are some that anger God and for which one is punished, namely the actions which sound intellects recognize as ugly because they lead to corruption and clear harms. The mode of this indication is that argument only opposes an attempt at some action; so when God sent the messengers to cut off argument, we know that when God sent the messengers He was about to hold accountable those to whom they were sent, and His mercy required that He cut off their argument by sending messengers, guiding them and warning them. For this reason He made the cutting off of argument the final cause of the good news and warning, since good news and warning only clarify the consequences of actions. That is why He did not give the reason for sending messengers as alerting to what pleases God and what angers Him.

[p. 40]

This verse thus obliges all the sects to hold that sending messengers is a precondition for being held accountable for sins, and its apparent sense is that all kinds of accountability depend upon it, whether the sins relate to belief or to action, and including the obligation of knowing God. Sending messengers, in our view, is part of God's complete justice, because if He had not sent them, punishment would have been mere absolute dominion, which the act of creating requires, since He is not questioned about what He does; yet it would have been justice in the broader sense.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verses 163–165 (part 3 of 3)**

As for the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the Sunni mainstream), whose positions are transmitted through the approach of al-Ash'ari (the Ash'ari school of theology), they generalized and said: no obligation is established, and no one is held accountable for abandoning or doing anything, except through the sending of the Messengers, including the knowledge of God, Exalted is He. They argued with this verse and others, such as ﴿We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15], and with consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement). However, there is scrutiny concerning the claim of consensus, there is a different scrutiny concerning using it as evidence for a foundation of religion, and there is a third scrutiny concerning using the verses, which are apparent (zawahir, texts with apparent meanings), as evidence for a foundation of religion. The exception would be if it were said that they are so numerous that they reach the level of certainty; but this too is open to debate. They are compelled to interpret this verse, because they hold that the people of the fatrah (the interval between prophets) are held accountable for their polytheism toward God.

The answer is to say: the word "Messengers" in the verse is a collective noun used distributively (kull ifradi), which applies to each single Messenger, and it varies according to the variation of the call. As for the call to the totality of faith and monotheism, it was established through the earlier Messengers, whose calls established, for human beings, the obligation of faith and monotheism. As for the call to the details of the signs and attributes and the branches of the sharia (the divine law), it is established through the coming of the Messengers who are specific to known nations.

As for the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilites), they established that good and evil are intrinsic (dhatiyyan) in the state in which no messenger has been sent. They said: reason establishes the obligation of many rulings and the prohibition of many, especially the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, because knowledge repels a presumed harm, which is the otherworldly harm of incurring punishment in the Hereafter, as a large number of people have reported it; and the fear of what results from the disagreement of sects over knowledge of the Creator before correct knowledge is worldly harm. Everything that repels a presumed or doubtful harm is obligatory by reason. Like someone who wants to take a road and is told that there is a predator on it: reason requires that he pause and investigate until he knows whether he should take that road or not. Likewise, it is obligatory to examine the miracle of the Messengers and all that leads to the establishment of the sharia. For this reason, they interpreted this verse in the way that al-Zamakhshari (author of al-Kashshaf) mentioned when he said: "If you ask, how can people have a proof against God before the Messengers, when they are held to account by the proofs God has set up, whose examination leads to knowledge, and the Messengers themselves did not reach knowledge by examining those proofs, i.e., before the prophethood?" I say: the Messengers are reminders against heedlessness and prompters to examination, together with conveying what they carried of the matters of religion and teaching the laws. Their sending was thus a removal of the excuse and a completion of the establishment of the proof. This means that the sending of the Messengers is a mercy from God, not a matter of justice; had He not sent them, holding people accountable for their vices would have been just.
