So the sending of the Messengers completes the proof regarding the very principle of accountability, and completes the proof regarding the increase in purification, so that people would not say: "Our Lord, why did You not guide us to what would raise our ranks among the sincere (siddiqin), and limit us to mere salvation from punishment, when we were guided to the principle of monotheism by our intellects?"

Al-Maturidi (the Maturidi school) agreed with the majority regarding everything except the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, when the intention is to silence the Messengers specifically, because he considered it the foundation of the principles of religion, as indicated by the words of Sadr al-Shari'ah in al-Tawdih: "That is, the act is a quality for which the doer of the act is praised and rewarded, or blamed and punished; because the obligation of affirming the Prophet, if it depended on the sharia, would lead to circularity (dawr)." He also explicitly stated that it is also known through the sharia.

The Mu'tazilah pressed the Ash'ari school on this matter, specifically regarding the obligation of knowledge. They said: if knowledge were not obligatory except through the sharia, it would necessarily lead to silencing the Messengers, and there would be no benefit in sending them. The basis of the necessity is that if a Messenger says to someone, "Look at my miracle until my truthfulness becomes clear to you," he can say: "I will not look, since it is not obligatory upon me, because abandoning what is not obligatory is permissible, and it is not obligatory upon me until the obligation is established for me through the sharia, and the sharia is not established as long as I have not looked, because the establishment of the sharia is theoretical, not necessary." The Maturidis and some Shafi'is supported this argument.

I have not found a convincing answer from the Ash'aris, except that Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni), in al-Irshad, responded that this objection is shared: the obligation to contemplate the miracle is undoubtedly theoretical, not necessary. So the one whom the Messenger calls may say: "I will not contemplate the miracle unless that is obligatory upon me by reason, and it is not obligatory upon me by reason until I have examined it, because it is a theoretical obligation, and the theoretical requires arranging premises, and I do not arrange them." All the later mutakallimun (theologians) among the Ash'aris followed him in this answer, such as al-Baydawi, al-Adud, and al-Taftazani. Ibn 'Arafah said in al-Shamil: "This is an acknowledgment of the necessity of silencing, so it does not remove the doubt; rather, it generalizes it between us and them, so the resolution of the problem has not been achieved." Ibn 'Arafah's statement is a firmly established objection.

The apparent intention of Imam al-Haramayn is to dismiss the Mu'tazilah's argument for the rational obligation, by confining the argument to the sharia proofs, which is our aim.

I hold that the answer should be given in one of two ways. The first is by denial: we deny that the obligation to hear the Messenger's call depends on listening to him and examining his miracle, and that if the obligation were not established by reason, the Messenger would be silenced. Rather, we claim that this is a matter established by the sharias that have succeeded one another among human beings, to the extent that everyone with any connection to human civilization knows that callers came to people in different eras, and their call was one: each says that he has been sent from God to call people to what God wants from them. Thus it became firmly rooted in the souls of all human beings that there is faith and disbelief, salvation and perdition, a firm settlement that they cannot find a way to dispel. So when the Messenger calls people to faith, the past reports and discussions present themselves to the listener's soul, and so it becomes obligatory upon him, by a compelling obligation, to listen to him and examine the matter that is established in human souls. For this reason God held the people of the fatrah accountable for polytheism, as many texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicate. Therefore, if we suppose someone who did not mix with human communities and had never had any awareness that people believed, disbelieved, affirmed, and denied, then listening to the Messenger would not be obligatory for him, because that compelling inclination is absent from him. On this view, the obligation is neither legal (shar'i) nor theoretical rational; rather, it is among the necessary matters that cannot be avoided, so it is no wonder that accountability falls upon one who deliberately opposes them.

The second of the two answers is by acceptance: even granting the objection, the inclination established in human nature to investigate events and new reports, and to listen to every bearer of a call, is a matter that moves everyone whom a Messenger calls to religion to listen to his words, to receive his call, his challenge, and his miracle. He does not realize it until his call has traveled into the soul of the one called, stirring in him the impulse to examine, so he is drawn gradually to receive the call, until he finds himself having grasped and known it with a knowledge after which he cannot say: "I do not look at the miracle," or "I do not listen to the call." If he turns away after that, he has chosen blindness over guidance, and so he is held accountable. Suppose someone passed by a Messenger who was calling people, and something occupied him from learning his affair, listening to his words, and examining his conduct; we would grant that he is not addressed, and that this individual and those like him, if they silence the Messenger, do not thereby nullify the mission. But he has lost his guidance and made his own soul foolish.

It is not an objection to us that one who hears the call of the Messenger, puts his fingers in his ears, and flees at that moment, is not subject to the obligation of knowledge, because he did not do this except after knowing that he was about to be held accountable if he heard and disobeyed. That is enough evidence of his awareness that the obligation is directed at him, and so he is held accountable for preferring blindness to guidance, as God said about the people of Noah: ﴿And indeed, whenever I called them﴾ [Nuh: 7], meaning to faith, ﴿that You might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments﴾ [Nuh: 7].

The use of the explicit noun in the phrase ﴿after the Messengers﴾ rather than saying "after them" is for emphasis on this matter, and for making it independent in its signification, so that it becomes like a proverb.

As for the concluding pairing of the two attributes in His words ﴿Mighty, Wise﴾: the appropriateness of the attribute "Wise" is evident, because all these reports are evidence of His wisdom, Exalted is He. As for the attribute "Mighty," it is because might suits His being overpowering in every respect: He is overpowering in terms of worship, so He is not questioned about what He does; and He is overpowering in terms of rational accountability, since He wills not to hold His servants accountable except after proofs, evidences, and signs. The attribute "Wise" is placed later because the execution of His might in this complete manner is itself among the forms of brilliant wisdom.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 166:

﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He has sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness. And Allah suffices as a witness.﴾

This is a istidrak (a corrective qualification, a "but" that retracts an impression raised by the preceding discourse). The reason is that what precedes His saying ﴿The People of the Book ask you...﴾ [al-Nisa: 153] is set in the context of explaining their obstinacy and stubbornness in refusing to bear witness to the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ and to the correctness of the attribution of the Qur'an to Allah the Exalted. This meaning implies that they refuse to testify to the truthfulness of the Messenger, and that this grieves the Messenger ﷺ. So the istidrak came with His saying (﴿But Allah bears witness﴾). The istidrak is a following of speech by lifting what might be assumed to be established or negated. The meaning is: the People of the Book did not bear witness, but Allah bore witness, and Allah's testimony is better than theirs.

It has already passed, at His saying the Exalted ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282] in Surah al-Baqarah, that the true reality of shahadah (testimony) is an informing to confirm one informant and to refute another informant. It was also mentioned that it is applied to a definite report that is not touched by doubt, at His saying the Exalted ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18] in Surah Ali 'Imran. So the shahadah in His saying (﴿But Allah bears witness﴾) is applied, metaphorically, to the informing about the descent of the Qur'an from Allah, because this report includes confirming the Messenger and refuting his opponents. This is an application by way of metaphor (isti'arah) and is different from the literal application in His saying ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18], for that one is in the manner of majaz mursal (metonymy by a related sense).

The testimony of the angels is conjoined to the testimony of Allah in order to strengthen this testimony by the multiplicity of witnesses, and because the testimony of Allah is figurative for knowledge while the testimony of the angels is literal. The verb (﴿yashhadūn﴾, "they bear witness") is expressed explicitly despite the presence of the conjunctive particle, for emphasis. The particle (لكن, "but") with a sakin nun is the lightened form of (لكنّ, "but") with a shaddah on the nun, which is among the sisters of (إنّ, "indeed"); when it is lightened, its government ('amal) is annulled.

His saying ﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾ may be read according to both possibilities.

His saying ﴿with what He has sent down to you; He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ involves a transposition in the structure of the sentence for the purpose of brevity (ijmal) which is followed by detail (tafsil), so that it falls more effectively upon the soul. The original wording of the speech is: He bears witness to the sending down of what He sent down to you with His knowledge, because His saying (﴿with what He has sent down to you﴾) does not convey the object of testimony except implicitly along with the subject of testimony, since the relative pronoun was brought so that it would connect with a relative clause containing an allusion to the intended meaning. Despite this, the intended object of the testimony, which is the true object of the preposition (ba') after the root shahida, was not mentioned, so the clause (﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾) completes the meaning of the testimony. This is close to the transposition that the Arabs use in tamyiz of the relation (tamyiz al-nisbah).

Al-Zamakhshari said: the position of His saying (﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾) relative to His saying ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾ is the position of an explanatory clause, because it is an explanation of the testimony, and His testimony to its correctness is that He sent it down with the inimitable composition. Perhaps he makes the clause ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾ self-standing in its benefit, and that the meaning of (بما أنزل إليك) is "to the correctness of what He sent down to you." What I have mentioned is more deeply rooted in eloquence.

The meaning of (﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾) is: that is, bound up with His knowledge, i.e., reaching the utmost limit in the domain of the heavenly books, as is the case with what comes from knowledge of Allah the Exalted. The meaning of that is that it is inimitable in wording and meaning; just as it defeated the eloquent among the people of language, it defeated the scholars among the people of lofty realities.

The ba' in His saying ﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾ is superfluous for emphasis, and its origin is: "Allah suffices as a witness," like the verse of poetry:

"Gray hair and Islam suffice a man as a restrainer"

Or (كفى) is taken to include the meaning of "be content," in which case the ba' is for transitivity.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 167:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and averted [others] from the way of Allah have certainly strayed far astray.﴾

Page 46

It is permissible that what is meant by "those who disbelieved" here is the People of the Book, namely the Jews. In that case the sentence serves as a summary (fadhlaka) of the preceding discourse that refuted the Jews, from the argument that came before it.

Their averting [others] from the way of Allah may be of the intransitive kind of ṣadda, whose present-tense form is analogically yaṣuddu with a kasra on the ṣād, meaning they turned away from the way of Allah, that is, Islam. Or it may be of the transitive ṣadda, whose present-tense form is analogically yaṣuddu with a ḍamma on the ṣād, meaning they averted people. The object has been omitted for the purpose of generalization (li-qaṣd al-takthīr). The Jews used to subject the Muslims to trials (fitna) and strengthen the delusions of the polytheists by denying the Prophet (ﷺ).

It is also permissible that what is meant by "those who disbelieved" is the polytheists, as is most common in the Qur'an's use of this description. In that case the sentence is an independent initial resumption (isti'nāf ibtidā'ī), moved to by way of the discussion of the Jews' hostility toward Islam. Their averting [others] from the way of Allah, that is, their averting people from entering Islam, is well known.

Al-ḍalāl (straying) here means disbelief (kufr), because it is a loss of faith, which is the path of good and happiness. Applying the term ḍalāl to kufr is a metaphor (isti'āra) built upon the metaphor of the straight path for faith.

Describing the straying as "far" (ba'īd), although distance is an attribute of spatial distances, is a metaphorical extension of distance to express the intensity and perfection of the straying within its kind, such that its measure cannot be grasped. This is a common figure in their speech: they liken the attainment of perfection to what indicates distances and extremes, as in their saying: "deep of bottom" (ba'īd al-ghawr), "deep of pit" (ba'īd al-qa'r), "without end" (lā nihāya lahu), "without limit" (lā ghāya lahu); "a man of lofty aspiration" (ba'īd al-himma), "far-reaching in aim" (ba'īd al-marmā); "its greatness has no terminus," and "a sea without shore"; and their saying: "this is an immersion (ighrāq) in such-and-such."

Among the subtle appropriateness of this expression here is that genuine straying occurs in deserts and wastelands. When bewilderment and straying intensify, the one afflicted moves far from the inhabited land. Thus describing it as "far" maintains the literal sense, and hints that its application to disbelief and ignorance is a conventional transfer (naql 'urfī).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 168–169:

[Page 47]
﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged [themselves], Allah would never forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path,﴾ ﴿except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ The sentence is an explanation (bayan) of the sentence (﴿They have certainly strayed, a far straying﴾ [An-Nisa: 167]), because the listener awaits knowledge of the recompense of this straying, so this sentence explains it.

The repetition of the relative pronoun and its clause without mentioning their pronoun serves to build upon it the clause "and wronged" (wa-zalamu), and because repeating the clause carries a rebuke against them. On both readings regarding the meaning of "those who disbelieved" in the preceding verse, the conjunction of "wronging" to "disbelief" in His saying "Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged" may be taken in one of the following ways. It may mean wronging the self and wronging the Prophet and the Muslims, and this is what is fitting for the People of the Book. Or it may mean polytheism (shirk), as is common in the Qur'anic usage, in His saying "Indeed, polytheism is a great wrong" [Luqman: 13], in which case it is the conjunction of the more specific to the more general in terms of types. Or it may mean transgression against people, such as their wronging the Prophet ﷺ by expelling him from his land, inciting people against him, and other things, and their wronging the believers by torturing them for Allah's sake, expelling them, confiscating their wealth, and dealing with them through hypocrisy, mockery and deception. Or it may mean committing corruptions and crimes that are established among people of intellect as wrongdoing and aggression.

And His saying "Allah would never forgive them" (lam yakuni Allahu liyaghfira lahum) is a form of negation of intention (ṣīghat judūd), and its explanation has already been given at His saying, exalted is He, "It is not for a human that Allah should give him the Book" [Aal 'Imran: 79] in Surat Aal 'Imran. It therefore implies the affirmation of the negation. The negation of Allah's forgiving them is given as a warning against remaining upon disbelief and wrongdoing, because this ruling is attached to the attribute and not to specific known persons; so if they desist from disbelief and wrongdoing, they will not be among those who disbelieved and wronged. As for the meaning of the negation of "that He guide them to a path": if the path is the path of the Day of Resurrection, it is clear, i.e., He does not guide them to any path that leads them to a place except a path that leads to Hell. It is permissible that by "the path" is meant the signs in this world, as in His saying "Guide us to the straight path" [Al-Fatiha: 6]. So the negation of His guiding them to it

[Page 48]
is a warning that disbelief and wrongdoing, by their nature, cover the heart with a veil that prevents guidance from reaching it, so as to caution the one afflicted with disbelief and wrongdoing against going deeper into them, lest he come to a state where there is no escape for him from them. The negation of Allah's guidance to them on this reading is a metaphorical rational attribution (majaz 'aqli), in the negation of facilitating the means of guidance according to the law by which the means come about and their effects follow after them. On either of the two possibilities, the repentance of the disbelieving wrongdoer through faith is accepted, and many disbelievers and wrongdoers have believed and their faith has become good; the verses on the acceptance of repentance, and the observation of reality, point to the interpretation of this verse. A parallel to this verse has preceded shortly, namely "Those who believed, then disbelieved" [An-Nisa: 137], and so on.

His saying "except the path of Hell" (illa tariqa jahannam) is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) if the path whose guidance He negated is the real path, and a disconnected exception (munqati') if the first path is intended as guidance. In this exception there is an emphasis of a thing by what resembles its opposite, because the speech is directed toward warning, and the exception in it carries a scent of raising hope; then when the excepted item is heard, it becomes clear that it belongs to the category of warning. It also contains mockery, because He made an exception from the path that is supposed to guide them, whereas driving them into the path of Hell is not guidance, since guidance is directing the one who has gone astray to the desired place.

Therefore He follows it with His saying "And that was" (wa-kana dhalika), i.e., driving them into the path of the Fire, "ever easy for Allah" (ʿala Allahi yasiran), since nothing can overpower Him, and since they are His servants whom He turns wherever He wills.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 170:

﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe, it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

After the discourse with the People of the Book had been fully concluded, and after addressing the disbelievers in terms that could also include the People of the Book, the address was directed to all of mankind.

[Page 49]

This serves as a concluding statement (tadhyil) and a reinforcement of what preceded it. The proofs of the earlier clear signs had been established, the argument was complete, and the path had been made broad. Thus the situation called for commanding them to follow the Messenger and to believe. This is the practice of the orator when hearts are prepared and dispositions are softened. This is called the purpose of the address (al-maqsid min al-khitab), and what precedes it is called its introduction (al-muqaddima). Moreover, the address with "O mankind" in general refers mostly to the polytheists, and this fits His saying, ﴿so believe, it is better for you﴾.

The definite article in "al-Rasul" (the Messenger) is for a known reference (al-'ahd), namely the one known to them as being among them. "Al-haqq" (the truth) refers to the Law (al-shari'a) and the Qur'an. "Min Rabbikum" (from your Lord) is connected to "jaa'akum" (has come to you), or is an adjective of "al-haqq." The "min" in both cases indicates a figurative starting point (li'l-ibtida' al-majazi). Making "jaa'" transitive to the pronoun of the addressees is an encouragement for them to believe, because one who comes out of concern for people is rightly owed their following. Also, in the construction of the possessive "Rabbikum" there is a second encouragement, in what it indicates of their being singled out for this religion that comes from their Lord. Therefore the command to believe is made to follow these clauses, in His saying, ﴿so believe, it is better for you﴾.

"Khayran" (better) is in the accusative because it is governed by a verb that is necessarily omitted in their speech due to frequent usage, so it has become like proverbs. This occurs in utterances that imply a command or prohibition, such as ﴿Desist, it is better for you﴾ [al-Nisa: 171], "wara'aka awsa'u lak" (behind you is more room for you, i.e., move back), and "hasbuka khayran laka" (what suffices you is better for you), and the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

"So promise him the two acacias of Malik, or the hills between them, the easy one."

Its accusative status is one on which there is no disagreement among the Arabs, and on which the grammarians agree. They differ only regarding the omitted element. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh made it a verb in the imperative, implied by the context of the speech, with the estimated meaning: "Come" or "intend." They said: when you said to him, "Desist," or "Do," or "Enough for you," you are directing him to something else that is better for him. Al-Farra', from the Kufans, said that in such cases it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and this cannot apply to what is in the accusative after a prohibition, nor to what is in the accusative after a non-inflecting term such as "wara'aka" and "hasbuka." Al-Kisa'i and the Kufans said it is in the accusative by an omitted "kana" (to be) together with its predicate, and the estimate is: "let it be better." My own view is that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the verbal noun contained in the verb alone, or together with the particle of prohibition. The estimate is: "so believe, with belief being better," "enough for you, with sufficiency being better," and "do not do such and such, with abstention being better." Making the circumstantial qualifier refer back to the verbal noun of the verb in such a case is like the pronoun referring back to it in His saying, ﴿Be just, that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8]. This is especially so since this usage has become like proverbs, and the nature of proverbs is brevity of expression. Some of the Kufans and Abu al-Baqa' have said this as well.

His saying "wa in takfuru" (but if you disbelieve) means: that you remain upon your disbelief.

His saying ﴿fa-inna lillahi ma fi as-samawati wa al-ard﴾ (then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth) is an indication of the answer to the conditional clause, and the answer itself is omitted, because the estimate is: "If you disbelieve, then Allah is free of need of your belief, because to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth." What is omitted here is stated explicitly in surah al-Zumar in His saying, ﴿If you disbelieve, then Allah is free of need of you﴾ [al-Zumar: 7]. In it there is an implicit warning (ta'rid) to the addressees, meaning: their disbelief will not let them escape His punishment, because they are His servants, since to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 4, verse 171 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion, and do not say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary, and a spirit from Him.﴾

It is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), addressed specifically to the Christians.

They are addressed with the title "People of the Scripture" as an allusion to the fact that they had gone against their own Scripture.

The indication that they are the intended audience is the statement "The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of Allah," up to His saying ﴿that he should be a servant of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 172]. It explains what is meant by the general statement "do not commit excess in your religion, and do not say about Allah except the truth." Their admonition begins with the prohibition of excess (ghuluww) because the Christians exaggerated in glorifying Jesus, so they attributed to him sonship of Allah and made him the third of the gods.

Ghuluww is going beyond the familiar limit. It is derived from ghalwat al-sahm (the range of an arrow), which is the furthest point it reaches. It is used figuratively for exceeding what is required, whether in rational matters, in what is prescribed in beliefs, in perceptions, or in actions. Excess in religion is for the religious person to display what goes beyond the limit that religion has set for him. He (Allah) forbade excess because it is the root of much of their misguidance and their denial of the truthful messengers. The excess of the People of the Scripture is their going beyond the limit that their religion required of them. The Jews were required to follow the Torah and to love their messenger, but they went beyond this to hatred of the messengers, such as Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. The Christians were required to follow the Messiah, but they exceeded the limit regarding him by claiming his divinity or that he was the son of Allah, together with disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ.

His saying ﴿and do not say about Allah except the truth﴾ is a specific statement following a general one, for the sake of emphasizing the prohibition of the monstrous fabrication. When the verb "to say" is followed by the preposition ʿalā ("about"), it indicates that the speaker's attribution of the saying to what is governed by ʿalā is a false attribution. He, exalted is He, said ﴿and they say about Allah the lie﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]. The meaning of "saying about Allah" here is that they say something they claim is part of their religion, since religion is by nature something to be received from Allah.

His saying ﴿The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary﴾ is a clause that explains the limit at which the excess occurred, since that limit was general (mujmal). It also explains what is meant by "the truth."

Because this clause stands in the place of explanation with respect to the preceding one, it is detached from it (fusilat ʿanha). The clause restricts the Messiah to three attributes: the attribute of messengerhood, the attribute of being a word of Allah directed to Mary, and the attribute of being a spirit from Allah. This is a restriction of a subject to an attribute (qasr mawsuf ʿala sifa). The purpose of this restriction is to refute what their excess introduced into these attributes, an excess that took them out of their true reality. These attributes are established for Jesus, and they affirm them, so it is not objected to them that they describe Jesus with them. But they went beyond the limit set for them: they made messengerhood into sonship, and they made the word into the union of the reality of divinity with Jesus in the womb of Mary. They made Jesus a son of Allah, and Mary a consort of Allah, exalted is He, and they made the meaning of the spirit, by which the reality of the Messiah came to be in the womb of Mary, to be from the very essence of divinity.

The restriction is relative (idafi), and it is a restriction of exclusion (qasr ifrad). That is, Jesus is restricted to the attributes of messengerhood, word, and spirit, and does not go beyond these to what is added to them, such as the Messiah being a son of Allah, the union of divinity with him, or Mary being a consort.

The description of the Messiah as the word of Allah is a description whose use occurs in the Gospels. At the beginning of the Gospel of John: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and then he said, "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." The Qur'an has related this and affirmed it, which indicates that it is among the Gospel's expressions. So this means that he is an effect of the word of Allah. The "word" is the act of bringing into being (takwin), which is expressed in technical terminology by "Be" (kun). So applying the term "word" to the act of bringing into being is a metaphor, and it is not in fact a word; rather, it is the attachment of power (taʿalluq al-qudra). The description of Jesus with this is because his coming into being did not have the apparent, well-known effect that appears in the formation of embryos. So his origin occurred through the attachment of power. Thus in His saying "his word" in the verse there are two figurative usages: a metaphor by omission (majaz hadhf), and a metaphor by borrowing (majaz isti'ara) which became a customary literal meaning (haqiqa 'urfiyya).

The meaning of "which He directed to Mary" is that He conveyed it to Mary. The pronoun has been made feminine in agreement with the grammatical form of the word "word" (kalima). Otherwise, the intended meaning is Jesus, or it refers to the word of the command of bringing into being. The description of Jesus as "a spirit of Allah" is a description that occurred in the Gospels. Allah has confirmed it here, so it is among the things that were truly revealed.

The meaning of Jesus being "a spirit from Allah" is that his spirit is one of the spirits which are the elements of life, but it is attributed to Allah because it reached Mary without being formed in a drop of semen. By this he was distinguished from the rest of the spirits. He is described as originating from the side of Allah. It has also been said that because the angelic nature (malakiyya) overcame his self, he was described as a spirit, as if the portions of animality were stripped from him. It has also been said: the spirit is the breath. The Arabs call the soul a spirit and breath a spirit. Dhu al-Rumma says, addressing his companion to light a fire with firewood:

*So I said to him: raise it toward yourself, then revive it with your spirit, and blow upon it a small measure of fuel for it.*

That is, with your breath.

The naming of Jesus as "the Spirit" is found plainly in the expressions of the Gospels. The "min" (from) is for origin (ibtida'iyya) under all the interpretations.

If you ask: what is the wisdom in these two descriptions occurring here, despite the confusion by which the Christians were misled? And why was the Messiah not described, in the restrictive clause, with the same description with which Muhammad ﷺ was described in His saying, ﴿Say: I am only a human like you, to whom it is revealed﴾ [al-Kahf: 110], which would have been clearer in explaining servanthood and more effective in negating misguidance?

I answer: The wisdom in that is that these two descriptions occurred in the language of the Gospel, or in the speech of the disciples, as descriptions of Jesus, peace be upon him. They were understood in the language of those addressed at that time. But when the styles of languages changed, and understanding of the distinction between the literal and the figurative became confused, misguidance crept into the Christians through their misplacement of these two descriptions. So it was intended to point out this error in interpretation. That is, the most that came to you from the words of the Gospels is the description of the Messiah as the word of Allah and the spirit of Allah, and nothing in any of that leads to the belief that he is the son of Allah or that he is a god.

The opening of the restrictive clause with "he is a messenger of Allah" proclaims the attribute of servanthood, since Allah does not send a god who is like Himself. Therefore in it there is sufficient alerting to the meaning of "word" and "spirit."

﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say "Three." Desist; it is better for you. Allah is only one God. Glory be to Him that He should have a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾

The "fa" (so) is for a consequence (tafri') of the restrictive clause and what it is built upon. That is: when all that Allah has made clear of His oneness, His transcendence, and the truthfulness of His messengers has become evident, it follows that I command you to believe in Allah and His messengers. They were commanded to believe in Allah even though they are believers, that is, the Christians, because when they described Allah with what is not fitting, they had corrupted faith. The command to believe in Allah serves as a preparation for the command to believe in His messengers, which is the intended aim. This is what appears to me to be correct. By "the messengers" is meant all of them, that is: do not disbelieve in any one of His messengers. This is in the position of a precaution against anyone imagining that they might turn away from belief in the messengership of Jesus, peace be upon him, in exaggerated negation of divinity from him.

His saying ﴿and do not say "Three"﴾ means: do not utter this word. It was perhaps a slogan of the Christians in their religion, like the testimony of faith (kalimat al-shahada) among Muslims. Among their customs was the gesture of indicating the Trinity with three fingers: the thumb, the little finger, and the ring finger. The intended meaning of the verse is the prohibition of uttering the widely known meaning of this word and of believing in it. Because the basic principle of speech is truthfulness, no one speaks except from belief, so the prohibition here is a metonymy (kinaya) by intending the meaning and its implication. The addressee of His saying "do not say" is specifically the Christians.

"Three" is the predicate of an omitted subject. Its omission was so that it could apply to all the possible interpretations of their doctrines of the Trinity, since the Christians disagreed about the reality of the Trinity of God, as will come. So the omitted subject is estimated according to what the rejected sayings of theirs require about the manner of the Trinity, from among the names that can correctly be predicated with the word "three" of God, and these are several names. In another verse: ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who said, "Allah is the third of three"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 73]. And in the verse at the end of this surah: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116], that is, two gods alongside Allah, as will come. So the whole is three: each one of them is a god. But they say that the whole of the three is one God, or that the three have united and become one God. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "Three" is the predicate of an omitted subject. If it is correctly reported about them that they say, "He is one substance and three hypostases," then the estimate is "Allah is three." Otherwise, the estimate is "The gods are three." End of quote.

The Trinity is a foundation in the doctrine of all Christians, but they differ about its manner. It arose from the belief of the early theologians among the Greek Christians that Allah, exalted is He, is a "trinity" (thalut), that is, one substance, and this substance is the totality of three hypostases (aqanim), whose singular is uqnum, with the hamza vowelled with a damma and the qaf sukun. Al-Firuzabadi said in the Qamus: it is a Roman word, and the Qamus explains it as "origin." Al-Taftazani, in his book al-Maqasid, explains it as "attribute." It appears that it is an arabicized form of the word qanum with a complicated foreign qaf, meaning "the name," that is, "the word." They expressed the totality of the three hypostases with the phrase "Father, Son, Holy Spirit, Holy" (aba – ibna – ruha – qudusa). These hypostases branch out from one another. The first hypostasis is the hypostasis of essence or eternal existence, which is the Father, and it is the origin of existing things.

The second hypostasis is the hypostasis of knowledge, which is the Son. It is below the first hypostasis, and from it came the governance of all the rational faculties.

The third hypostasis is the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, which is the attribute of life. It is below the hypostasis of knowledge, and from it came the bringing into being of the world of sensible things.

They neglected to mention attributes required by divinity, such as eternity and everlastingness, and they left out the attribute of speech, power, and will. Then they wanted to interpret what occurs in the Gospel of the attributes of Allah. So they named the hypostasis of essence "the Father," the hypostasis of knowledge "the Son," and the hypostasis of life "the Holy Spirit," because the Gospel applied the name "Father" to Allah, applied the name "Son" to the Messiah His messenger, and applied the "Holy Spirit" to that by which the Messiah was formed in the womb of Mary. Moreover, they wanted to point out that the hypostasis of existence is the one who emanates the other two hypostases, so they intended to show that some attributes do not come after others, so they expressed it with "Father" and "Son," as the Greek philosophers expressed it with "begetting" (tawallud). They named the hypostasis of knowledge "the Word," because among the expressions of the Gospel is the application of the word "Word" to the Messiah. So they meant that the Messiah is a manifestation of the knowledge of Allah, that is, that he knows what Allah knows and conveys it, and this is the meaning of messengership. For at the time the Gospels were written, knowledge was adorned with the technical terms of the Roman divine wisdom. When the meanings became confused for them, they took the apparent meanings and believed that the lords were three. This is the origin of Christianity, and they came close to the doctrine of polytheism.

Then excessive zeal in sanctifying the Messiah drew them on, so they imagined that the knowledge of God became united with the Messiah. They said: the humanity (nasut) of the Messiah became divinity (lahut) through the union with the hypostasis (uqnum) of knowledge. Thus the Messiah has two substances and one hypostasis. Then the doctrine of indwelling (hulul) arose among them, that is, the indwelling of God in the Messiah, in various expressions. Then they believed in the union of God with the Messiah, and said: God is the Messiah. This is the root of the Trinity according to the Christians, and from it three doctrines branched out, to all of which the words of the Exalted refer: ﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾ and His words ﴿Certainly, they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 72] and His words ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as deities besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. They used to say: in Jesus there is divinity (lahutiyyah) from the side of the Father, and humanity (nasutiyyah), that is, human nature, from the side of the mother.

There appeared in Alexandria a monk named (Arius) (Aryus), who professed monotheism and that Jesus was a servant of God, a created being. This was in the time of Constantine (Qustantinus), sultan of the Romans, builder of Constantinople. When the aforementioned Constantine embraced Christianity in the year 327, he followed the doctrine of Arius. Then he saw that most of the monks opposed him, so he wished to unify their word. He convened a council of Christian scholars at the end of the fourth century of the Christian era, and in this council there were about two thousand Christian scholars. He found them in great disagreement, and found the largest group of them upon one view: three hundred and some ten scholars. He took their statement and made it the foundation of Christianity and supported it. This group is called (the Melkites), attributed to the king (malik).

Their statement agreed that the Word of God united with the body of Jesus, and was clothed in his humanity, that is, his human nature, and mingled with it like the mixing of wine with water. Thus the Word became a person (dhat) in the womb of Mary, and that person became a son of God, exalted is He. The God is thus a compound of three things: first, the Father, the possessor of existence; second, the Son, the possessor of the Word, that is, knowledge; and third, the Holy Spirit.

The Nestorians said: the Word united with the body of the Messiah by way of radiation, as the sun shines through a crystal window. The religious head of this sect was given the title Catholicos (jathliq). The Nestorian sect was dominant among the Arab Christians. The Jacobite and Nestorian monks competed to spread the creed of each group among the Arab tribes. The Persian kings protected the Nestorians, and the Caesars of Rome protected the Jacobites. Christianity in its two sects spread among Bakr, Taghlib, Rabi'ah, Lakhm, Judham, Tanukh, Kalb, Najran, Yemen, and Bahrain. I have elaborated on this so that the excellence of concision in His words (﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾) and its encompassing of all these doctrines may be known. So to God belongs this scientific miracle.

Divinity is incompatible with being a father or taking a son, because of the impossibility of perishing, need, separation, and resemblance to creatures with respect to God, the Exalted. Sonship entails the affirmation of these impossibilities, because procreation is a cosmic law for existing things for the wisdom of preserving the species, and people seek it for that reason and to help with the necessities of life; in it is the separation of the child from his father, and in it the son resembles his father, so the father necessarily resembles him.

(Subhan) is a noun of the verbal action (ism masdar) of sabbaha, not a verbal noun (masdar), because no sound verb form of it has been heard. Ibn Jinni affirmed that it is a proper noun for glorification, so it is among the proper nouns of genus (a'lam al-ajnas), and it is prohibited from declension (mamnu' min al-sarf) due to definiteness as a proper noun and the added letter. The discussion of it has already preceded at His words (﴿They said: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]) in Surat al-Baqarah.

His words (﴿that He should have a son﴾) are connected to (subhan) by a preposition, which is the preposition (ʿan) elided.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 4, verse 175:

﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a manifest light.﴾ [An-Nisa: 174] ﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty, and guide them to Himself on a straight path.﴾

This is a summation (fadhlaka) of the preceding discourse, comprising the taking up of guidance and the rejection of error, by means of what the Qur'an contains of the signs of truth and the restraining of falsehood. The sentence is a resumption (istiqnaf) and a turning toward the address to all of mankind, after the address had been directed specifically at the People of the Book.

Al-burhan (the proof) means the argument, and it is sometimes specified as a clear, decisive argument, which is the usual sense in which it is used in the Qur'an. For this reason, the scholars of Islam (hukama' al-Islam) called the most exalted type of evidence "burhan."

What is meant here is the signs of prophethood. As for the manifest light, it is the Qur'an, given the statement "and We sent down." The discussion of "there has come" (jaa'akum) is like the discussion of its counterpart earlier in His saying ﴿The Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord﴾ [An-Nisa: 170], and likewise the discussion of ﴿We have sent down to you﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 10].

The "amma" (as for) in His saying ﴿As for those who believed in Allah﴾ may be for detailing: a detailing of what the address "O mankind" indicates regarding the divergence of groups and inclinations, between one who accepts the proof and the light, and one who is arrogant and denying. The counterpart of this division is then omitted for emphasis (tahwil), meaning: "As for those who disbelieved, do not ask about them." It may also be that "amma" is merely conditional, without detailing, and it is a conditional for the generality of circumstances, since "amma" in the conditional carries the meaning of "whatever may be the case," and in this usage it neither conveys detailing nor requires a counterpart.

Al-i'tisam means seeking refuge, and holding fast to Allah is a metaphor for seeking refuge in His religion. It has already been mentioned in His saying ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah all together﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Admission into mercy and bounty is an expression for approval (ridha).

As for His saying ﴿and guide them to Himself on a straight path﴾: the prepositional phrase is connected to "yahdi" (guides), so it is an adverbial complement (zarf laghw), and "sirathan" (a path) is the object of "yahdi." The meaning is: He guides them on a straight path in order that they may arrive at Him, that is, to Allah, and that is their hoped-for aim, since they know that their promise is with Him.

[Page 64 of the commentary is marked here]

There is no connection between this verse and the verses before it. Its placement right after them can only be explained by its having been revealed right after the verses that precede it in this surah. It is linked to the earlier verse on the kalala (the case of an heir who has neither ascendant nor descendant, a term used in legal discussions) that appeared in the course of mentioning the shares of inheritance. This verse clarifies the reality of the kalala, which is indicated by His words, "who has no child." It was already mentioned at the beginning of the surah that the kalala includes the man who has no father, which is the view of the majority of scholars and of Malik ibn Anas.

So part of the ruling on the kalala was explained in a verse at the beginning of this surah. Then people asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about another form of the kalala. It is established in the Sahih (the most authentic collection of hadith) that the one who asked him was Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah and Abu Bakr came to visit me on foot among the Banu Salama. They found me unconscious, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed ablution and poured his ablution water over me. I regained consciousness and said: 'How should I deal with my wealth, since only a kalala inherits from me?' Then the words of Allah were revealed: 'They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalala,' to the end of the verse." It has also been said that it was revealed while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was preparing for the Farewell Pilgrimage, in the matter of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.

The plural pronoun in His words "they ask you" (*yastaftunaka*) does not refer to a plurality of askers. Rather, it refers to the category of askers in general, as in the saying: "What is the matter with people who impose conditions?" This is common in speech. It is also possible that the question was asked repeatedly and that the last of the askers was Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, so the answer was delayed for those who had asked before him, while the clarification was hastened for him because it was a time of need. He believed himself to be dying from that illness and wanted to bequeath his property, so this falls under the category of delaying clarification until the time of need.

The use of the present tense for the verb of asking is a well-known usage, as in His words: "They ask you about the crescent moons" (2:189), and "They ask you what they should spend" (2:219). This is because asking is a repeated act, so it became common to express it in the present tense. Sometimes the use of certain verb forms becomes predominant in certain contexts. An example is the predominance of the present tense in invocations used in a context of disapproval, such as the statement of 'A'isha about Ibn 'Umar: "May Allah have mercy on Abu 'Abd al-Rahman," and the common saying "May Allah forgive him." Another example is the predominance of the past tense with the negative particle *la* in invocations when *la* is not repeated, as in His words "so let him not return" (*fa-la raja'a*). Moreover, the question about the kalala was repeated both before and after the revelation of the verse. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I never questioned the Messenger of Allah about anything as often as I questioned him about the kalala, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never became as harsh with me about anything as he became about it, until he struck my chest and said: 'The verse of summer at the end of Surat al-Nisa' is sufficient for you.'"

His words "concerning the kalala" (*fi al-kalala*) can be governed by two verbs: both "they ask you" (*yastaftunaka*) and "Allah gives you a ruling" (*yuftikum*).

[Page 65]

The Prophet (ﷺ) named this verse "the verse of summer," and it became known by that name, just as the verse on the kalala at the beginning of the surah became known as "the verse of winter." This indicates that Surat al-Nisa' was revealed over a period extending from winter to summer. This was already mentioned at the opening of the surah.

It has been related that this verse on the kalala was revealed on the way to the Farewell Pilgrimage, but this is not authentic, because the Farewell Pilgrimage took place in the cold season. There is no doubt that the Battle of Tabuk took place in hot weather, when the fruits had ripened and people loved to stay among their fruit and shade. This means that the Battle of Tabuk took place around the months of August or September, which is the season of fresh dates and ripe dates. It took place in the ninth year of the Hijra, in Rajab, and in it was revealed His words: "They said, 'Do not go forth in this heat'" (9:81). Then the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr took place in Dhu al-Qa'da of that same year, the ninth year, which corresponds to December. The pilgrimage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Farewell Pilgrimage, took place in Dhu al-Hijja of the tenth year, which also corresponds approximately to the month of December.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he gave a sermon in which he said: "Three matters, if the Messenger of Allah had clarified them, would have been dearer to me than the world and all that is in it: the grandfather, the kalala, and the doors of usury." In another narration, "and the caliphate" is added. He also gave a sermon in which he said: "By Allah, I leave behind me no matter more important to me than the matter of the kalala." He said in a gathering of the Companions: "I will certainly give a judgment concerning the kalala that women will speak of in their chambers." He wrote a letter about it, but then he remained seeking Allah's guidance regarding it. When he was stabbed, he called for the letter and erased it.

'Umar's perplexity regarding the matter of the kalala was not a perplexity in understanding what Allah mentioned in His Book. Rather, it was in including what the Qur'an did not mention under what it did mention, through analogy (*qiyas*).

The Qur'an mentions the kalala in four verses: the two verses of this surah in which the word kalala appears, a verse at the beginning of this surah, namely His words, "But if he has no child and his parents inherit from him, then his mother has a third" (4:11), and a verse at the end of Surat al-Anfal, namely His words, "And blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of Allah" (8:75), according to those who hold that the kin (*dhawu al-arham*, relatives through females or distant relatives) inherit. There is no doubt that in every inheritance case where there is neither a child nor a parent, it is a kalala by consensus. As for the case where there is no child but there is a parent, the majority say it is not a kalala, while some earlier scholars said it is a kalala.

Allah commanded him to answer with the words "Allah gives you a ruling" in order to highlight the importance of this inheritance obligation. Therefore, placing the subject first (*Allah*) is for emphasis, not for exclusivity (*qasr*). The askers knew that the Messenger does not speak except by revelation. So when they asked him, they were in fact seeking the ruling of Allah. Attributing the giving of the ruling to Allah is therefore an honouring of this obligation.

By "the sister" (*al-ukht*) here is meant the full sister, or the sister of the father in the absence of a full sister. This is indicated by the context, since her share differs from the share of the uterine sister (the sister through the mother) meant in the first verse on the kalala. It is also indicated by His words "and he inherits from her," because a maternal brother does not inherit all the property if his maternal sister has no child, since he only has a sixth.

His words "if a man dies" (*in imru'un halaka*) are to be understood as "if a man dies." So *imru'un* (a man) is the subject of the verb *halaka* (died) within a conditional context. *Halaka* is not a descriptive attribute of *imru'un*. For this reason, the man in question here is a general category.

The pronoun in His words "and he inherits from her" refers to the word *imru'un* (a man), which occurs in a conditional context and conveys generality. This is because the words *imru'un* and *akh* (brother) or *ukht* (sister) all occur as indefinite nouns in a conditional context, so they are general, meaning the categories of what they denote, not a specific person who died, nor a specific sister who inherited. So when He said "and he inherits from her," the pronoun in the nominative refers to *imru'un*, not to a particular person who died. Since the concept of the word here does not have a specific individual, it should not cause difficulty to you that His words "a man who died" are reinforced by "and he inherits from her," since how can the deceased be an heir? Also, the object pronoun in *yarithuha* (he inherits her) refers to the concept of the word *ukht* (sister), not to a particular sister, since the concept of the word here has no specific individual. It is understood from His words "he inherits from her" that if a sister dies without a child, her brother inherits from her. The brother is the heir in this case, and this is the reverse of the previous case. So the meaning is: a man inherits from a sister if his sister dies and she has no child. The meaning of the plural *ikhwa* (siblings) is understood from His words "and he has a sister." This is a wonderful concision, and despite its extreme brevity, it is extremely clear. It should not be objected that the sister was an heir to her brother, so how does the pronoun refer to her such that her brother inherits from her, and she becomes the one inherited from? This is because a person knowledgeable in Arabic would not hold this view. This objection would only arise if death were a descriptive attribute of a man, as if one said: "The deceased man, his heir inherits from him, and he inherits from his heir if his heir dies before him." The difference between these two usages is elegant in Arabic.

His words "Allah makes clear to you lest you go astray" (*yubayyinu Allahu lakum an tadillu*) express a favour. *An tadillu* ("lest you go astray") is the reason for *yubayyinu* ("He makes clear"), with the preposition *li* (for) omitted. Omitting a preposition before *an* is common. The intended meaning is the reason, namely the negation of going astray, not that going astray has occurred, since clarification is contrary to misleading. So the negative particle *la* (not) is omitted, and its omission occurs in various places in their speech when the meaning is clear. This is as it occurs with the verb of oath in such phrases as:

"So we swore by it that it should be sold"

meaning "that it should not be sold." And as in the line:

"I swore that I would never taste the grain of Iraq as long as I live"

This is like the statement of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"You alighted at our place as guests, so we hastened to host you, lest you insult us"

meaning "lest you insult us with stinginess." This is the interpretation of the Kufan grammarians. The Basran grammarians interpreted the verse, the verse of poetry, and their like as having an omitted noun that the context indicates, namely the object for which the action is done, meaning "out of dislike that you go astray." This is how al-Zamakhshari interpreted it in his *al-Kashshaf*.

Some commentators made *an tadillu* the direct object of *yubayyinu*, and said: the meaning is that Allah, in what He made clear of the obligations, has made clear to you your error that you were upon in the time of ignorance (*jahiliyya*). But this is remote, since what they did in the time of ignorance was not error before the coming of the law, because dividing property is not one of the acts that involve a clear quality of good and bad, unless it involves depriving someone who truly deserves support and kindness. Also, the verbal noun with *an* must necessarily carry the meaning of the future, so how could *an tadillu* refer to an error that has already passed? More clarification on this will come at His words, "lest you say: The Book was sent down only to two groups before us" (6:156), in Surat al-An'am.

It is related from 'Umar that whenever he recited this verse he would say: "O Allah, whoever has had the kalala made clear to him, but it has not been made clear to me." This was narrated by al-Tabari, but its chain has a break (*inqita'*), and they have declared it weak.

His words "And Allah is Knower of all things" are a concluding flourish (*tadhyil*). In this verse there is an announcement of the conclusion of speech, like His words: "This is a message for mankind, that they may be warned by it" (14:52), and like His words, relating the speech of the companion of Moses: "That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience" (18:82). This announces the end of the surah.

It also announces the end of the revelation, if it is authentic that it was the last verse revealed, as some narrations say. If that is so, then I do not see the custom of the scholars of our land of ending the presentation of their lessons with the words "And Allah knows best" (*wallahu a'lam*) as anything other than seeking blessing by imitating the conclusion of the revelation.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Ma'ida

This surah is called in the books of tafsir (exegesis) and the books of Sunna (prophetic tradition) "Surat al-Ma'ida" (The Table Spread), because it contains the story of the table (*ma'ida*) that the disciples sent down from 'Isa (Jesus), upon him be peace, and it is singled out for mentioning it. In the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, the name "Surat al-Ma'ida" appears in the speech of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, 'A'isha the Mother of the Believers, Asma' bint Yazid, and others. This is the most famous of its names.

It is also called Surat al-'Uqud (The Surah of Covenants), since this word occurs at its beginning.

It is also called *al-Munqidha* (The Rescuer). In *Ahkam* by Ibn al-Faras, it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Surat al-Ma'ida is called in the kingdom of the heavens *al-Munqidha*." He said: meaning that it rescues its reciter from the hands of the angels of punishment.

In *Kinayat al-Udaba'* by Ahmad al-Jurjani, it is said: "So-and-so does not recite Surat al-Akhyar," meaning he does not fulfil the covenant. This is because the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to call Surat al-Ma'ida "Surat al-Akhyar" (The Surah of the Good Ones). Jarir said:

"Indeed al-Bu'ayth and 'Abd Al Muta'is will not recite the Surah of the Good Ones"

It is Medinan by consensus. It is related that it was revealed upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's return from al-Hudaybiyyah, after Surah al-Mumtahanah. Its revelation therefore came some time after al-Hudaybiyyah, because Surah al-Mumtahanah was revealed after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madinah from the treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, when the believing women came to him as emigrants, and the polytheists asked him to return them to them in implementation of the terms of the treaty. So Allah permitted the believers not to return them after testing them.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil that the verse ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 94] up to (a painful punishment) was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. Perhaps that is what led those who said that Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. The presence of that verse in this surah does not necessitate that the beginning of the revelation of the surah preceded the revelation of the verse, since a verse may be attached to a surah that was revealed later than it.

In al-Itqan: it was revealed before Surah al-Nisa'. But it is established that the verse ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] was revealed on the Day of Arafah in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage. For this reason they differed as to whether this surah was revealed all at once or in parts, and there should be no hesitation that it was revealed in installments (munajjamah).

It is related from Abdullah ibn 'Amr and 'A'ishah that it is the last surah revealed. It has also been said that it was revealed after al-Nisa', and nothing was revealed after it except Surah (Bara'ah), based on the view that Bara'ah is the last surah revealed, which is the statement of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib in Sahih al-Bukhari.

In Musnad Ahmad, from Abdullah ibn 'Amr and Asma' bint Yazid: that it was revealed while the Messenger of Allah was on a journey, upon his she-camel al-'Adba', and that it was revealed to him entire. al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed during the march of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to the Farewell Pilgrimage.

In Shu'ab al-Iman, from Asma' bint Yazid: that it was revealed at Mina.

From Muhammad ibn Ka'b: that it was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage between Makkah and Madinah.

From Abu Hurayrah: it was revealed on the return of the Messenger of Allah from the Farewell Pilgrimage on the eighteenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah. This hadith has been declared weak.

It has been said that the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2] were revealed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah.

Among the people, some related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed in Madinah on a Monday.

There are many reports that it was revealed in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage; so the beginning of its revelation would have been in Madinah before the departure for the Farewell Pilgrimage.

It is related from Mujahid that he said: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] up to (Forgiving, Merciful) was revealed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Similarly from al-Dahhak, so their statements imply that this surah was revealed at the Conquest of Makkah and what came after it.

From Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: the first part of this surah to be revealed was His words ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 15] up to His words ﴿a straight path﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16]. Then the rest of the surah was revealed at 'Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

It appears to me that some of this surah was revealed after some of Surah al-Nisa'. This indicates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had firmly established control over the Arabs and over the hypocrites, and that none remained in opposition to Islam except the Jews and the Christians. As for the Jews, it is because they were mixed with the Muslims in Madinah and its surroundings; and as for the Christians, it is because the conquests of Islam had reached the borders of their kingdom in the regions of al-Sham. In the hadith of 'Umar in Sahih al-Bukhari: "Those around the Messenger of Allah had been made to submit to him, and nothing remained except the kingdom of Ghassan in al-Sham, and we feared that it would come upon us."

This surah is distinguished by the broad scope of its argument with the Christians and the brevity of its argument with the Jews, compared with Surah al-Nisa'. This indicates that the matter of the Jews had begun to recede and weaken, and that mixing with the Christians had become more intense than before.

In Surah al-Nisa' there is the prohibition of intoxication only during the prayers, while in Surah al-Ma'idah it is prohibited absolutely; so this is without doubt later than some of Surah al-Nisa'. It does not follow that no surah may be revealed until the revelation of another has ended; rather, two surahs may be revealed within one period.

It is also later than Surah (Bara'ah), because (Bara'ah) includes much about the conditions of the hypocrites, whereas Surah al-Ma'idah mentions their conditions only once, and that indicates that hypocrisy had ended at the time of its revelation, or that the strength of its adherents had been broken. Since Surah (Bara'ah) was revealed in the year when Abu Bakr led the people in Hajj, I mean the ninth year after the Hijrah.

Therefore, there is no doubt that part of Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage. And sufficient as evidence is its containing the verse ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], which the people of transmitted reports agree was revealed on the Day of Arafah in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, as in the report from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. And in Surah al-Ma'idah is His words ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. In the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Satan has despaired of being worshipped in this land of yours, but he has been content with what is less than that, of your deeds which you consider insignificant."

This surah is counted as the eighty-ninth... [sic: the text states] the ninety-first surah in the count of surahs according to the order of revelation. From Jabir ibn Zayd: it was revealed after Surah al-Ahzab and before Surah al-Mumtahanah.

Its number of verses: one hundred and twenty-two according to the majority count, one hundred and twenty-three according to the count of the people of Basra, and one hundred and twenty according to the Kufans.

This surah was placed in the Mushaf before Surah al-An'am, although Surah al-An'am has more verses than it. Perhaps that is for the sake of observing that this surah includes purposes similar to those contained in Surah al-Nisa', as an aid in clarifying each of the two for the other in those purposes.

This surah contains many legislations, which indicates that it was revealed to complete the laws of Islam. For this reason it opens with the injunction to fulfil the covenants, that is, what they pledged to Allah when they entered Islam of adhering to what they are commanded. "The Prophet ﷺ used to take the pledge concerning prayer, zakat and sincere counsel to every Muslim, as in the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah in the Sahih." And he took the pledge from the people according to what is in Surah al-Mumtahanah, as related by 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit. And at its beginning occurs His words ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. So its opening was an excellent introduction.

Al-Qurtubi mentioned that it contains nineteen obligations not found elsewhere, namely: seven in His words ﴿the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and what a beast of prey has eaten﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], ﴿and what is slaughtered on the stone altars, and that you seek decision through arrows﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], ﴿and what you have taught of hunting animals, training them as trainers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4], ﴿the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], ﴿and the chaste women from those who were given the Scripture﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], and the completion of purification when you rise to prayer (that is, completing what was not mentioned in Surah al-Nisa'), ﴿the male thief and the female thief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. ﴿Do not kill game while you are in ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95] up to His words ﴿Exalted in might, Owner of retribution﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], and ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah or sa'ibah or wasilah or ham﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103], and His words ﴿The testimony between you when death approaches one of you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106], the verse, and His words (﴿And when you call to prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 58]). There is no mention of the adhan for the prayers in the Qur'an except in this surah. End quote.

It contains the distinction between the lawful and the unlawful in foods, the preservation of the rites of Allah in the Hajj and the sacred month, and the prohibition of some forbidden practices from the customs of the Jahiliyyah, such as the arrows. It contains the rulings of wudu', ghusl and tayammum; the command to justice in judgment, and the command to truthfulness in testimony; the rulings of retaliation concerning lives and limbs; the rulings of highway robbery (hirabah); consolation of the Messenger ﷺ regarding the hypocrisy of the hypocrites; the prohibition of wine and gambling; oaths and their expiation; judgment between the People of the Scripture; the principles of dealing among the Muslims, and between the People of the Scripture, and between the polytheists and the hypocrites; the warning against their guardianship lest it lead to a Muslim's apostasy from his religion; the refutation of the misguided beliefs of the People of the Two Scriptures; mention of some wrongdoings of the Jews; fairness toward the Christians regarding their good manners, and that they are closer to Islam; mention of the matter of the wandering (al-tih), and the conditions of the hypocrites; the command for Muslims to adopt conduct opposed to the morals of the misguided in prohibiting what was made lawful for them; the honouring of the Ka'bah and its virtues and blessings upon mankind; what is interwoven with that or precedes it of lessons; the reminder to Muslims of the blessings of Allah the Exalted; the allusion to what the People of the Scripture fell into of abandoning what they were commanded and neglecting it; and their invitation to believe in the Messenger promised to them.

It concludes with the reminder of the Day of Resurrection, the testimony of the messengers over their nations, the testimony of 'Isa over the Christians, and the glorification of Allah the Exalted.
